### [1] [EditHero: A Benchmark for Long-Horizon Part-Level 3D Editing and Vibe Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02298)
*Ruihan Yu,Yu-Ju Tsai,Muyao Niu,Runyi Li,Lian Fu,Hanqing Liu,Zheng-Hui Huang,Yonghao Yu,Sho Kuno,Ming-Hsuan Yang,Kaipeng Zhang,Zhixiang Wang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: EditHero is the first benchmark for long-horizon, part-level 3D editing with natural language instructions. It compares non-agentic (top-down, regenerates from learned 3D representation) vs LLM/VLM agent (bottom-up, edits through code) approaches. LLMs follow instructions better and preserve unedited regions but are slower.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current 3D editing methods are tested on single edits, but real asset creation involves long revision sequences. Each edit must implement the requested change while preserving everything else. No existing benchmark addresses this long-horizon, part-level 3D editing scenario.

Method: The authors built a deterministic assembly engine that produces exact targets after every edit. They created a benchmark with natural-language instructions and target images for geometry and texture. Every sequence was manually reviewed. They compared two opposing approaches: non-agentic methods (top-down, regenerates from learned 3D representation) vs LLM/VLM agents (bottom-up, edits through code that inspects and rewrites only required parts).

Result: Non-agentic methods often miss the requested changes and disturb regions that should remain fixed. LLM/VLM agents follow instructions more closely and preserve unedited parts better, but each edit takes minutes to complete.

Conclusion: LLM/VLM agents outperform non-agentic methods in accuracy and preservation for iterative 3D editing, but at the cost of speed. The authors will release the engine and edit sequences to support further research on reliable iterative 3D editing.

Abstract: 3D editing methods are usually tested on a single edit, yet an asset is built through a long sequence of revisions, each of which must implement the requested change while leaving everything else unchanged. We introduce EditHero, to our knowledge the first benchmark for long-horizon, part-level 3D editing, with natural-language instructions and target images for both geometry and texture. A deterministic assembly engine produces the exact target after every edit, and every sequence is reviewed by hand. We use EditHero to compare 2 opposite approaches to 3D editing. Non-agentic methods operate top down, regenerating the object from a learned 3D representation and inferring what to keep. In contrast, LLM/VLM agents operate bottom up, editing through code that inspects the mesh and rewrites only the parts required by instructions. The non-agentic methods often miss the requested change and disturb regions that should stay fixed. Most LLMs follow instructions more closely, and all of them preserve the unedited parts better, but each of their edits takes minutes. We will release the engine and the edit sequences to support research on reliable iterative 3D editing.

</details>


### [2] [DeskForge: Dense Supervision from Desktop Environments for Computer-Use Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02320)
*A. Said Gurbuz,Ahmed Nassar,Sunghwan Hong,Marc Pollefeys,Peter W. J. Staar*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: DeskForge is a controllable desktop environment that generates large-scale supervision data for computer-use agents by composing real applications with varied states, layouts, and appearances. The 1.2M dataset fine-tunes vision-language models, improving GUI grounding accuracy by up to 11.51 percentage points and doubling long-horizon task completion rates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Computer-use agents struggle to reliably ground action targets in complex desktop scenes where multiple applications, overlapping windows, and visually similar controls compete for attention. Existing training data lacks dense annotations and controlled variation, limiting agent performance.

Method: DeskForge creates a controllable desktop environment that varies application states, content, window layout, appearance, and resolution. It fuses screenshots, accessibility trees, and window geometry into dense element annotations while recording action outcomes. Using this environment, the authors constructed DeskForge-1M with 1.2M annotated desktop observations (159.7M element instances) and fine-tuned four vision-language models on 200K grounding examples.

Result: All four fine-tuned models improved across held-out desktop conditions and on all five external GUI grounding benchmarks. Qwen3.5-4B showed accuracy gains of 11.51 percentage points on ScreenSpot-Pro and 10.11 points on OSWorld-G. For long-horizon tasks, Qwen3.5-4B increased task completion from 31 to 50/119 on WebArena-Infinity and from 3 to 15/100 on OpenApps.

Conclusion: Controllable composition of real desktop environments provides a scalable source of supervision for improving both GUI grounding and long-horizon computer use. The framework code, dataset, and fine-tuned models are publicly available.

Abstract: Computer-use agents need to reliably ground action targets in complex desktop scenes, where multiple applications, overlapping windows, and visually similar controls compete for attention. Existing training data rarely pair such scenes with dense annotations or vary them in a controlled way. We introduce DeskForge, a controllable desktop environment that composes and explores real applications to generate large-scale supervision for computer-use agents. It varies application states, content, window layout, appearance, and resolution, and fuses screenshots, accessibility trees, and window geometry into dense element annotations while recording the outcome of each executed action. Using this environment, we construct DeskForge-1M, a corpus of 1.2M annotated desktop observations containing 159.7M element instances. We fine-tune four vision-language models on 200K grounding examples drawn from DeskForge-1M. All four improve across held-out desktop conditions and on all five external GUI grounding benchmarks; for Qwen3.5-4B, accuracy increases by 11.51 percentage points on ScreenSpot-Pro and 10.11 points on OSWorld-G. The gains also translate to long-horizon task completion: under a fixed planner, the fine-tuned action models solve more WebArena-Infinity and OpenApps tasks, with Qwen3.5-4B increasing from 31 to 50 of 119 tasks and from 3 to 15 of 100 tasks, respectively. These results show that controllable composition of real desktop environments provides a scalable source of supervision for improving both GUI grounding and long-horizon computer use. The framework code, the dataset, and the fine-tuned model are available from the project page: https://saidgurbuz.github.io/deskforge/

</details>


### [3] [SCION: Scene Composition with Instanced Neural Primitives](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02322)
*William Koch,Amogh Joshi,Cyrus Vachha,Cheng Zheng,Felix Heide*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: SCION introduces a hierarchical compositional scene representation that replaces independent Gaussians with reusable primitives and lightweight world-space instances, achieving high-quality rendering at 1.2 MB while enabling instance-level editing and animation without retraining.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing neural scene representations (like 3D Gaussian Splatting) treat each element as unique, storing millions of independent Gaussians per scene. This creates redundant parameters and provides weak manipulation handles. Prior methods like Splat and Replace require manual selection of repeated elements. There's a need for a compact, controllable representation that discovers reusable parts rather than memorizing scenes.

Method: SCION uses a hierarchical compositional scene representation with: 1) A compact vocabulary of reusable primitives that replace independent Gaussians, 2) Lightweight world-space instances that place transformed copies throughout the scene. Fitting is done via joint optimization over discrete and continuous scene parameters, combining two-level densification over splats and instances with an adversarial loss that preserves detail across shared primitives.

Result: SCION achieves rate-distortion performance favorable to existing Gaussian compression methods, maintaining high quality even at 1.2 MB. It enables instance-level scene editing and animation without retraining. The representation demonstrates that neural scene representations can discover reusable parts rather than memorizing scenes as independent primitives.

Conclusion: Neural scene representations need not memorize scenes as independent primitives; they can discover reusable parts. SCION provides a compact, controllable representation that balances compression and quality while enabling downstream manipulation tasks like editing and animation.

Abstract: Real-world scenes are compositional: bricks, blades of grass, pebbles, and tree leaves recur across human-built and natural environments. Existing neural scene representations model these elements independently. Most 3D Gaussian Splatting and follow-up abstraction and compression methods treat each element as unique, fitting millions of independent Gaussians per scene. Prior methods like Splat and Replace fit template objects, but they require mostly manual selection of repeated elements. As a result, these representations store redundant parameters and provide weak manipulation handles for downstream tasks. We introduce SCION, a hier- archical compositional scene representation that replaces independent Gaussians with a compact vocabulary of reusable primitives and lightweight world-space instances that place transformed copies throughout the scene. We fit this represen- tation to multi-view captures via a joint optimization over discrete and continuous scene parameters, combining two-level densification over splats and instances with an adversarial loss that preserves detail across shared primitives. The recovered structure yields a compact, controllable representation while maintaining high quality even at 1.2 MB. SCION achieves rate-distortion favorable to existing Gaussian compression methods, and it enables instance-level scene editing and animation without retraining. Our results show that neural scene representations need not memorize scenes as independent primitives; they can discover reusable parts. Project webpage: https://light.princeton.edu/SCION

</details>


### [4] [SCOPE-4D: Endoscopic 4D Geometry Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02343)
*Chaoyi Zhou,Zhongpai Gao,Anwesa Choudhuri,Meng Zheng,Benjamin Planche,Run Wang,Terrence Chen,Siyu Huang,Ziyan Wu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: SCOPE-4D is an endoscopic 4D geometry foundation model that jointly predicts camera parameters, dense geometry, and 3D tissue trajectories from monocular RGB video in a single forward pass, addressing challenges of scarce annotations and camera-deformation ambiguity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Geometric understanding supports endoscopic navigation and robotic assistance, but learning reliable endoscopic geometry faces two key challenges: scarce geometric annotations and ambiguity between camera motion and tissue deformation.

Method: 1) SCOPE-5K dataset: ~5,000 clips spanning real and synthetic GI endoscopy and laparoscopy with rich geometric supervision. 2) Geometric supervised fine-tuning on SCOPE-5K to learn endoscopic priors. 3) Common-Residual Motion (CRM) module to constrain local deformation relative to common tissue movement. 4) Joint trajectory supervision for dense 3D tissue tracking.

Result: Geometric fine-tuning improves camera and depth estimation. CRM and trajectory supervision further improve over geometric fine-tuning alone while enabling dense 3D tissue tracking. Demonstrates strong in-domain and out-of-domain geometry, superior 3D tracking, more stable long-sequence colon reconstruction, and positive blinded user study on real clinical video.

Conclusion: Large-scale endoscopic supervision combined with motion constraints (CRM) effectively enables joint geometry estimation and tissue tracking, demonstrating value for endoscopic navigation and robotic assistance applications.

Abstract: Geometric understanding supports endoscopic navigation and robotic assistance, but learning reliable endoscopic geometry faces two challenges: scarce geometric annotations and ambiguity between camera motion and tissue deformation. We present SCOPE-4D, an endoscopic 4D geometry foundation model that jointly predicts camera parameters, dense geometry, and 3D tissue trajectories from monocular RGB video in a single forward pass. Our curation and annotation pipeline constructs SCOPE-5K, a collection of approximately 5,000 clips spanning real and synthetic gastrointestinal endoscopy and laparoscopy. The collection provides rich geometric supervision and includes newly collected phantom and real-colonoscopy evaluation sets. Geometric supervised fine-tuning on SCOPE-5K learns endoscopic priors that improve camera and depth estimation. Common--Residual Motion (CRM) further constrains local deformation relative to common tissue movement. Together with geometric supervision, CRM and trajectory supervision further improve camera and depth estimation over geometric fine-tuning alone while enabling dense 3D tissue tracking. Evaluations on public and newly collected benchmarks demonstrate strong in-domain and out-of-domain geometry, superior 3D tracking, and more stable long-sequence colon reconstruction. A blinded user study further supports the perceived reconstruction quality on real clinical video. Together, these results demonstrate the value of large-scale endoscopic supervision and motion constraints for joint geometry estimation and tissue tracking.

</details>


### [5] [Confidence-Controlled XAI Auditing for Pedestrian Detection under Domain Shift](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02364)
*Ruben Dario Florez-Zela*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper audits post-hoc explanations (D-RISE, EigenCAM) of a YOLOv8s pedestrian detector across PIE and JAAD datasets to assess whether explanations remain faithful under domain shift. The study reveals that deletion-based faithfulness is strongly coupled to detection confidence (Spearman ρ = 0.70-0.82), making naive confidence-stratified comparisons unreliable. After controlling for detection strength, D-RISE faithfulness remains domain-dependent in the central f0 range, with PIE showing higher D-Deletion than JAAD. The study concludes that confidence-controlled XAI audits are necessary for safety-critical perception under domain shift.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Explainability is increasingly required for perception models in intelligent vehicles, but whether explanations remain faithful under driving domain shift is poorly understood. This work addresses the need to audit post-hoc explanations to ensure reliability in safety-critical applications.

Method: The study audits post-hoc explanations of a fixed YOLOv8s pedestrian detector across PIE and JAAD datasets using: (1) ROI-based D-Deletion, (2) frozen confidence terciles, (3) rank-based tests, (4) bootstrap intervals, and (5) Holm correction for multiple hypothesis testing.

Result: Deletion-based faithfulness is strongly coupled to detection strength at explanation time, with Spearman correlations between 0.70 and 0.82 for D-RISE. After controlling for detection strength within fixed f0 bins, D-RISE faithfulness remains domain-dependent in the central f0 range, with PIE showing higher D-Deletion than JAAD (Holm-adjusted significance). A non-perturbative EigenCAM baseline is less faithful than D-RISE but also exhibits score coupling, suggesting the effect is not specific to D-RISE but related to the deletion-based evaluation setup.

Conclusion: The coupling between detection confidence and explanation faithfulness makes naive confidence-stratified comparisons unreliable. This motivates the need for confidence-controlled XAI audits for safety-critical perception under domain shift, ensuring that explanations remain trustworthy across different driving domains.

Abstract: Explainability is increasingly required for perception models in intelligent vehicles, yet whether explanations remain faithful under driving domain shift is still poorly understood. This work audits post-hoc explanations of a fixed YOLOv8s pedestrian detector across PIE and JAAD using ROI-based D-Deletion, frozen confidence terciles, rank-based tests, bootstrap intervals, and Holm correction. The audit shows that deletion-based faithfulness is strongly coupled to detection strength at explanation time, with Spearman correlations between 0.70 and 0.82 for D-RISE, making naive confidence-stratified comparisons unreliable. After controlling for detection strength within fixed f0 bins, D-RISE faithfulness remains domain-dependent in the central f0 range, with PIE showing higher D-Deletion than JAAD and Holm-adjusted significance. A non-perturbative EigenCAM baseline is less faithful than D-RISE but also exhibits score coupling, suggesting that the effect is not specific to D-RISE and is related to the deletion-based evaluation setup. These results motivate confidence-controlled XAI audits for safety-critical perception under domain shift.

</details>


### [6] [A Simulation-Grounded Agentic VLM Framework for Wildfire Monitoring and Reporting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02451)
*Duowen Chen,Yuchen Sun,Zhiqi Li,Yuxuan Liao,Sinan Wang,Bart van Bloemen Waanders,Bo Zhu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A simulation-grounded vision-language model framework that automatically converts 2D wildfire simulations into labeled video episodes, using Blender proxies and controllable video generation to create multimodal memory for training-free multi-agent VLM reasoning, achieving 77.3% accuracy on six simulator-derived report fields.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Effective wildfire monitoring requires relating visual evidence to physical fire dynamics, but real videos with synchronized physical annotations are scarce and high-fidelity 3D simulation is costly.

Method: The framework uses a fixed Blender mapping to produce low-detail 3D proxies aligned with simulator terrain, fuel layout, fire activity, and wind cues. Controllable video generation supplies richer appearance. Generated videos and simulator labels form reusable multimodal memory for a training-free multi-agent VLM system that retrieves reference episodes, reconciles visual and memory-based predictions, and produces structured wildfire reports.

Result: Video memory achieves 51.5% exact four-tag accuracy compared with 22.6% for direct VLM querying and 16-17% for text-only memory. The complete system achieves 77.3% accuracy on six simulator-derived report fields. Component ablations, cross-generator tests, and three real-UAV evaluations validate retrieval, reporting, generator changes, and observable monitoring tasks.

Conclusion: The framework successfully connects automatic simulation-to-proxy conversion with memory-based VLM reasoning, addressing the challenge of scarce real-world physical annotations by leveraging synthetic data generation and multimodal memory retrieval.

Abstract: Effective wildfire monitoring requires relating visual evidence to physical fire dynamics, yet real videos with synchronized physical annotations are scarce and high-fidelity 3D simulation is costly. We present a simulation-grounded vision-language model (VLM) framework that automatically converts 2D wildfire simulations into labeled video episodes. A fixed Blender mapping produces low-detail 3D proxies aligned with simulator terrain, fuel layout, fire activity, and wind cues; controllable video generation supplies richer appearance. The proxies are intermediate representations rather than finely rendered final scenes. Generated videos and simulator labels form reusable multimodal memory for a training-free multi-agent VLM system that retrieves reference episodes, reconciles visual and memory-based predictions, and produces structured wildfire reports. On held-out generated episodes, video memory achieves 51.5% exact four-tag accuracy, compared with 22.6% for direct VLM querying and 16-17% for text-only memory; the complete system achieves 77.3% accuracy on six simulator-derived report fields. Component ablations, cross-generator tests, and three real-UAV evaluations assess retrieval, reporting, generator changes, and observable monitoring tasks. The framework connects automatic simulation-to-proxy conversion with memory-based VLM reasoning under scarce real-world physical annotations.

</details>


### [7] [EviDent-CBCT: Evidence-Bottlenecked Report Generation from Dental CBCT under Non-Exhaustive Report Supervision](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02375)
*Ruiyang Hao,Zhi Qin Tan,Yulan He,Owen Addison,Yunpeng Li*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: EviDent-CBCT is an evidence-bottlenecked framework for generating dental CBCT reports from 3D scans, addressing the challenge of incomplete supervision where non-mentions may indicate absence or non-reporting. It uses an anatomy-aware network to map scans to discrete evidence records, with dental-logic consistency projection and a language model for report generation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Dento-maxillofacial CBCT reports contain dozens of tooth-specific, anatomical, and spatial findings, but learning to generate such reports from limited clinical data is challenging because routine reports may not exhaustively document image findings, and a non-mention may reflect either absence or non-reporting.

Method: 1) Anatomy-aware network maps each CBCT scan to discrete records of tooth-level, global, and tooth-IAC evidence. 2) Dental-logic consistency projection reconciles incompatible evidence. 3) Deterministic renderer and image-blind local language model generate reports using only the evidence record. 4) Reliability-aware training uses eligible non-mentions as reduced-weight negatives. 5) Metal-sensitive input channel preserves intensity cues from dental materials.

Result: EviDent-CBCT achieves 0.666 ± 0.006 merged evidence set-F1 and 0.402 ± 0.003 RadFact-Lite-Dental logical-F1, versus 0.371 ± 0.018 for the strongest controlled direct baseline. In the ODIN 2026 challenge, it ranked second in automated evaluation and third in blinded clinical Arena comparison on the hidden test set.

Conclusion: The discrete evidence record serves as an effective and auditable interface for CBCT report generation, demonstrating the value of the evidence-bottlenecked approach for handling incomplete supervision in medical report generation.

Abstract: Dento-maxillofacial cone-beam CT (CBCT) reports may contain dozens of tooth-specific, anatomical, and spatial findings from a single 3D scan. Learning to generate such reports from limited clinical data is challenging because routine reports may not exhaustively document image findings, and a non-mention may reflect either absence or non-reporting. We present EviDent-CBCT, an evidence-bottlenecked framework designed for this incomplete supervision. An anatomy-aware network maps each CBCT scan to a discrete record of tooth-level, global, and tooth-IAC evidence. A dental-logic consistency projection reconciles incompatible evidence before a deterministic renderer and an image-blind local language model generate the report using only this record. For tooth-level evidence, reliability-aware training uses eligible non-mentions as reduced-weight negatives, while unreported global and tooth-IAC labels remain unknown. A metal-sensitive input channel preserves intensity cues from dental materials. Across three validation runs, EviDent-CBCT achieves $0.666\pm0.006$ merged evidence set-F1 and $0.402\pm0.003$ RadFact-Lite-Dental logical-F1, versus $0.371\pm0.018$ for the strongest controlled direct baseline. In the ODIN 2026 challenge, it ranked second in automated evaluation and third in blinded clinical Arena comparison on the hidden test set. These results support the discrete evidence record as an effective and auditable interface for CBCT report generation.

</details>


### [8] [DAGS: Disentangled Appearance-and-Geometry Steering of a Frozen Image DiT for Temporally Stabilized Generative Rendering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02567)
*Karthik Mohan Kumar,Damian Andrysiak,Pedro Antonio Pena,Kunal Tyagi,Rama Harihara*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: DAGS is a lightweight, attention-free conditioning scheme that steers a frozen diffusion transformer (DiT) to produce high-fidelity, controllable renders by disentangling appearance and geometry control. It uses two small convolutional encoders to compute conditioning features once per frame, injecting them as per-layer element-wise residuals into image tokens, avoiding quadratic attention costs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Diffusion transformers (DiTs) generate high-fidelity images but exhibit large variance and their faithfulness to desired targets depends heavily on how conditions are supplied. Existing methods either require expensive attention mechanisms or risk overfitting the backbone, limiting controllability and temporal stability.

Method: DAGS uses two small convolutional encoders to compute appearance and geometry conditioning features once per frame. These features are injected as learned, per-layer, element-wise residuals into image tokens, avoiding quadratic attention costs. A small recurrent lighting stabilizer and training-free temporal guidance term are added to enable streaming rendering. Control and temporal handling operate outside the frozen backbone, preserving its pretrained prior while eliminating backbone-overfitting risk.

Result: On matched 1-spp + G-buffer input, DAGS reconstructs +8.6 dB / +10.1 dB PSNR over Intel OIDN (real-time denoiser) and RGB<->X (diffusion renderer) respectively. It achieves 2.5-8x better temporal stability (lower temporal-LPIPS flicker) while producing controllable, high-quality renders at a fraction of path tracing compute.

Conclusion: DAGS successfully enables a frozen image DiT to produce controllable, high-quality renders by disentangling appearance and geometry conditioning. It trades compute for controllability and quality—not real-time, but achieves significantly better fidelity and temporal stability than existing real-time and diffusion-based rendering methods.

Abstract: Diffusion transformers (DiTs) generate high-fidelity images from text and image conditions, but their outputs carry large variance and their faithfulness to a desired target depends heavily on how the condition is supplied. We present DAGS, a lightweight, attention-free, disentangled appearance and geometry conditioning scheme that steers a frozen image DiT to produce high-fidelity, highly faithful, and independently controllable renders. Two small convolutional encoders compute conditioning features once per frame and inject them as a learned, per-layer, element-wise residual into the image tokens, avoiding the quadratic cost of stacking conditions through attention. Because control and temporal handling live outside the frozen backbone, we retain its vast pretrained prior and eliminate backbone-overfitting risk. We further add a small recurrent lighting stabilizer and a training-free temporal guidance term that, coupled with our conditioning, elevate a per-frame image model into a streaming renderer. DAGS produces controllable, high-quality renders at a fraction of the compute of path tracing; it is not real-time, trading compute for controllability and quality. On a matched 1-spp + G-buffer input, per-frame DAGS reconstructs +8.6 dB / +10.1 dB PSNR over the real-time denoiser Intel OIDN and the diffusion renderer RGB<->X while being 2.5-8x more temporally stable perceptually (temporal-LPIPS flicker).

</details>


### [9] [FactorSplat: Appearance-Controllable Gaussian Proxies for Medical Volume Rendering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02382)
*Zhongpai Gao,Benjamin Planche,Meng Zheng,Anwesa Choudhuri,Terrence Chen,Ziyan Wu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: FactorSplat introduces a per-scene N-dimensional Gaussian splatting (N-DGS) proxy for medical volume rendering that can apply region-specific intensity-to-RGBA curves at inference time, decoupling geometry from transfer function appearance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional image-trained Gaussian proxies in medical volume rendering bake a single transfer function into their appearance, limiting flexibility. Medical imaging requires different visibility and color settings for different structures (e.g., bones, soft tissue, vessels) across different use cases.

Method: FactorSplat uses a local lookup to apply authored color and opacity changes, while a shared functional encoder and low-rank per-Gaussian factors learn the residual appearance response. Geometry and directional appearance remain shared across presets, with visibility control and TF-aware pruning preserving the ability to hide/reveal structures.

Result: FactorSplat improves mean PSNR and changed-region error over region-aware VEG across validation, interpolation, unseen composition, and OOD edits. Across four splits with seven CT/MR scans, mean PSNR gains range from 1.10 to 1.52 dB. At 1600² resolution, the cached fast renderer achieves 524 FPS with 1.17 ms TF switches. One checkpoint per scan supports unseen edits without retraining.

Conclusion: FactorSplat enables flexible transfer function editing for medical volume rendering with high performance (524 FPS) and supports unseen edits from a single trained model, demonstrating significant improvements over prior region-aware approaches.

Abstract: Transfer functions (TFs) control color and visibility in medical volume rendering, but image-trained Gaussian proxies typically bake one transfer function into their appearance. We present FactorSplat, a per-scene N-dimensional Gaussian splatting (N-DGS) proxy that accepts region-specific intensity-to-RGBA curves at inference. A local lookup applies the authored color and opacity change, while a shared functional encoder and low-rank per-Gaussian factors learn the residual appearance response. Geometry and directional appearance remain shared across presets, with visibility control and TF-aware pruning preserving the ability to hide and reveal structures. On seven CT and MR scans, FactorSplat improves mean PSNR and changed-region error over region-aware VEG across validation, interpolation, unseen composition, and out-of-distribution (OOD) edits. Across these four splits, seven-scan mean PSNR gains over VEG range from 1.10 to 1.52 dB. One checkpoint per scan supports unseen edits without retraining. At $1600^2$, the cached fast renderer averages 524 FPS with 1.17 ms TF switches. Project page: https://gaozhongpai.github.io/FactorSplat/.

</details>


### [10] [A Benchmark for Spatially Grounded Gesture Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03105)
*Anna Deichler,Rishabh Dabral,Fethiye Irmak Dogan,Anindita Ghosh,Jonas Beskow*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces a benchmark for evaluating spatially grounded gesture generation in conversational AI systems. The benchmark includes ~2K pointing-annotated VR dialogue clips with 3D ground-truth referents, and separates evaluation into temporal alignment, spatial grounding, and perceived naturalness. A flow-matching baseline (MM-Conv-Flow) is evaluated alongside retrieval-based systems and human motion.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The problem is that communication in shared space requires both verbal and non-verbal signals (like pointing gestures) to anchor language to the environment. However, there's no common framework for evaluating whether generated gestures actually indicate their intended referent. Current distributional metrics reward natural-looking gestures even when they're aimed at the wrong object.

Method: The authors created a benchmark with ~2K pointing-annotated clips from naturalistic VR dialogue with ground-truth 3D referents. They proposed a task where systems must decide when, how, and where to point within conversational speech. They also developed a protocol that separates temporal alignment, spatial grounding, and perceived naturalness for evaluation. They evaluated a flow-matching baseline (MM-Conv-Flow) alongside an independent retrieval-based system and captured human motion.

Result: The key finding is that geometric grounding can exceed that of human pointing without any gain in perceived naturalness. This demonstrates that referential gesture quality must be measured along separate dimensions, as geometric accuracy alone doesn't translate to perceived naturalness.

Conclusion: The study shows that gesture generation systems need to be evaluated across multiple separate dimensions (temporal alignment, spatial grounding, and perceived naturalness) rather than using single unified metrics. The benchmark provides a standardized way to assess spatially grounded gesture generation in conversational AI.

Abstract: Communication in shared space interweaves verbal and non-verbal signals, and pointing gestures anchor language to the environment: "put the cup on that one" is uninterpretable without the gesture that fixes the referent. Yet no common framework exists for evaluating whether generated gestures indicate their intended referent; distributional metrics reward a gesture aimed at the wrong object as long as it looks natural. We introduce a benchmark for spatially grounded gesture generation, comprising ~2K pointing-annotated clips from naturalistic VR dialogue with ground-truth 3D referents, a task in which systems must decide when, how and where to point within conversational speech, and a protocol that separates temporal alignment, spatial grounding and perceived naturalness. We also provide a flow-matching baseline, MM-Conv-Flow. Evaluating it alongside an independent retrieval-based system and captured human motion, we find that geometric grounding can exceed that of human pointing without any gain in perceived naturalness, showing that referential gesture quality must be measured along separate dimensions.

</details>


### [11] [Octrees as an Explicit 3D Language](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02388)
*Ran Dan,Si-Tong Wei,Pengfei Xiong,Wei Zhang,Yadong Mu,Peng-Shuai Wang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: OctLLM is a 3D large language model that addresses two key limitations of existing methods: 1) preserving spatial structure by using explicit octree occupancy tokens instead of compressed latent codes, and 2) maintaining general language ability by adding 3D capacity through independent trainable branches rather than fine-tuning the backbone.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing 3D LLMs compromise in two ways: they compress shapes into latent codebook indices or coordinate text, removing spatial structure from observations, and they acquire 3D modality by fine-tuning the backbone, which overwrites its general language ability.

Method: OctLLM uses geometry as an explicit 3D sequence of octree occupancy tokens. To address length issues with full octree sequences, it creates a Sparse Octree (S-Octree) by randomly emptying penultimate-level nodes and omitting descendants while preserving shape. For the modality integration, mesh tokens are routed through independent trainable branches in a subset of blocks while text and image tokens retain the frozen vision-language pathway, with the two streams interacting through shared self-attention.

Result: OctLLM achieves a new state of the art among unified multimodal LLMs, lowering image-to-3D FID by 17.4% and raising render-grounded captioning by 28.7 points over ShapeLLM-Omni, while matching the backbone on general language benchmarks. It trains far fewer parameters than full fine-tuning.

Conclusion: OctLLM successfully preserves spatial structure through explicit octree representation and maintains general language ability by adding 3D capacity through separate trainable parameters rather than fine-tuning, setting new benchmarks in 3D generation and understanding while retaining language capabilities.

Abstract: Existing 3D large language models (LLMs) compromise on two fronts: they compress shapes into latent codebook indices or coordinate text, which removes spatial structure from what the model observes, and they acquire the 3D modality by fine-tuning the backbone, which overwrites its general language ability. We present OctLLM, which addresses both limitations. Geometry enters as an explicit 3D sequence of octree occupancy tokens. However, full octree sequences grow rapidly with depth; OctLLM therefore randomly empties penultimate-level nodes and omits descendants while preserving shape, yielding a shorter coordinate- and depth-anchored Sparse Octree (S-Octree) for position-aware mask-modeling generation and 3D understanding. On the other front, existing methods introduce a new modality with full fine-tuning or LoRA, but full fine-tuning is costly, LoRA limits 3D capacity, and both modify the language pathway. OctLLM instead adds 3D capacity in parameters separate from the pretrained ones: mesh tokens are routed through independent trainable branches in a subset of blocks while text and image tokens retain the frozen vision-language pathway, and the two streams interact through shared self-attention. It trains far fewer parameters than full fine-tuning, yet sets a new state of the art among unified multimodal LLMs, lowering image-to-3D FID by $17.4\%$ and raising render-grounded captioning by $28.7$ points over ShapeLLM-Omni, while matching the backbone on general language benchmarks.

</details>


### [12] [4DCodeBench: Benchmarking Agents on Inverse Graphics of Dynamic Scenes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03715)
*Ruihong Shen,Žiga Kovačič,Peter Kulits,Xingrui Wang,Zizhang Li,Joshua B. Tenenbaum,Alan Yuille,Jieneng Chen,Jiajun Wu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: 4DCodeBench is a benchmark for evaluating AI agents' ability to reconstruct dynamic scenes from video as executable graphics programs. It tests the capability to translate visual observations into compact code representations that capture physical phenomena like deformation, fluid flow, and fracture.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current AI models excel at static 3D reconstruction but struggle with dynamic scenes. There is a need for a benchmark that evaluates agents' ability to understand and reconstruct physical dynamics through code generation - essentially turning video into executable programs that can reproduce observed behaviors.

Method: The benchmark curates real-world videos and constructs synthetic scenes spanning diverse physical phenomena including deformation, fluid flow, and fracture. It then tests frontier AI models on their ability to generate executable graphics programs that can reconstruct these dynamic scenes.

Result: The benchmarking reveals that strong static reconstruction capabilities do not yet translate into reliable reconstruction of complex dynamics. Current models struggle significantly with 4D inverse graphics tasks despite performing well on static 3D reconstruction.

Conclusion: 4DCodeBench provides a valuable testbed for tracking progress toward agents that can interpret world dynamics through code. The benchmark highlights a significant gap in current AI capabilities regarding dynamic scene understanding and program generation.

Abstract: We introduce 4DCodeBench, a benchmark for 4D inverse graphics through code generation, in which agents reconstruct dynamic scenes from video as executable graphics programs. To accomplish this, agents must translate visual observations into compact representations of scene structure and dynamics, by implementing abstractions such as physical simulations to reproduce complex behavior. To evaluate this capability, we curate a set of real-world videos and construct synthetic scenes spanning diverse physical phenomena, including deformation, fluid flow, and fracture. We perform extensive benchmarking of frontier models, finding that strong static reconstruction capabilities do not yet translate into reliable reconstruction of complex dynamics. 4DCodeBench provides a testbed for tracking progress toward agents that can interpret the dynamics of the world through code. Our benchmark is available at https://github.com/4DCodeBench/4DCodeBench

</details>


### [13] [An AI-Based Multi-Stage Approach for Androgenetic Alopecia Assessment from Low-Magnification Scalp Images](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02421)
*Mahmoud Raslan,Nada Omar,Omar Khaled,Tarek Waleed,Mohamed Hazem,Rania Mounir,Solwan Elsamanoudy,Ahmed Mourad,Noura Adel,Muhammad Rushdi*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper presents an automated quantitative scalp analysis and clinical decision-support framework for androgenetic alopecia (AGA) diagnosis, combining follicle unit (FU) localization, visible-shaft counting, shaft-width estimation, and interpretable rule-based analysis. The system uses YOLOv8m for detection and EfficientNet-B5 for classification, achieving high accuracy in both detection (mAP@0.5=0.920) and classification tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Androgenetic alopecia is characterized by patterned follicular miniaturization, increased single-hair follicular units, and altered hair-shaft diameter. Current diagnosis relies heavily on dermatologist expertise, which is subjective and time-consuming. The authors aim to develop an automated system to assist (not replace) dermatologists in AGA diagnosis through quantitative analysis.

Method: The framework combines: (1) YOLOv8m for follicle unit (FU) detection, (2) EfficientNet-B5 with support-map channel for classification, (3) ordinal visible-shaft counting, (4) calibrated shaft-width estimation, (5) regional aggregation, and (6) an interpretable rule layer for clinical decision support.

Result: Under patient-disjoint evaluation: YOLOv8m achieved test mAP@0.5=0.920 and recall=0.860; EfficientNet-B5 achieved 87.0% expert-box count accuracy (macro F1=0.85). On a separate 500-image test set with end-to-end processing: MAE of 6.56 for follicle detection and 16.59 for follicle classification relative to human-expert annotations.

Conclusion: The system achieves high accuracy in both detection and classification of AGA-related features. It is intended to assist, not replace, dermatologist interpretation. The combination of deep learning detectors with interpretable rule layers provides a clinically actionable decision-support tool.

Abstract: Androgenetic alopecia (AGA) is characterized by patterned follicular miniaturization, increased single-hair follicular units, and altered hair-shaft diameter. We present an automated quantitative scalp-analysis and clinical decision-support framework combining FU localization, ordinal visible-shaft counting, calibrated shaft-width estimation, regional aggregation, and an interpretable rule layer. The clinical cohort comprised 243 patients (127 AGA, 116 non-AGA), while the computer-vision experiments used 160 expert-annotated patients, 2,400 trichoscopic images, and approximately 158,000 FU annotations. Under patientdisjoint evaluation, YOLOv8m achieved test mAP@0.5=0.920 and recall=0.860; EfficientNet-B5 with a support-map channel achieved 87.0% expert-box count accuracy (macro F1=0.85). A separate 500-image set was processed end-to-end with detector-generated boxes, yielding MAE of 6.56 for follicle detection and 16.59 for follicle classification relative to human-expert annotations. The system is intended to assist, rather than replace, dermatologist interpretation.

</details>


### [14] [DeepStratNet: A Context-Aware Coordinate Regression Framework for Seismic Horizon Tracking under Sparse Labels](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02494)
*Aniq Ahmad,Musham Ahmad Malik,Ahmad Mustafa,Heather Bedle*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes a novel regression-based approach for automatic horizon tracking in 3D seismic interpretation, replacing traditional dense semantic segmentation with bounded coordinate regression. The method uses a lightweight regression head with an LSTM module and outperforms segmentation-based methods, demonstrating greater robustness to sparse training data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing deep learning approaches for horizon tracking use dense semantic segmentation (U-Net-based), which requires converting horizon picks to dense masks for training and treating unpicked traces as background. This introduces several problems: hindering model convergence, requiring pre/post-processing that can introduce errors, and 2D models fail to capture inter-slice context while 3D models are computationally prohibitive. The authors aim to address these limitations by reformulating the problem as direct coordinate regression.

Method: The authors propose: (1) Bounded coordinate regression formulation - directly predicting time/depth coordinates at each lateral position; (2) A lightweight regression head compatible with any pretrained vision backbone; (3) An LSTM module to model inter-slice context and produce continuous horizon surfaces; (4) Combined L1 and L2 losses for supervision at valid horizon picks; (5) Geology-informed regularization enforcing lateral continuity between successive traces. Four pretrained vision backbones were evaluated under both segmentation and regression configurations on a New Zealand seismic volume.

Result: The proposed regression approach consistently outperforms segmentation counterparts quantitatively (RMSE, PCC metrics) and qualitatively. It demonstrates greater robustness to increasing sparsity of training picks. Additionally, prediction variation across successive traces captures local geological complexity variations, providing an automated quality control measure for downstream interpretation.

Conclusion: Reformulating horizon tracking as bounded coordinate regression with LSTM-based inter-slice context modeling is superior to traditional segmentation approaches. The method achieves better accuracy, handles sparse training data better, and provides built-in quality control through prediction variance analysis. This represents a paradigm shift in seismic horizon tracking methodology.

Abstract: Automatic horizon tracking is a foundational task in 3D seismic interpretation. Most existing deep learning approaches formulate it as dense semantic segmentation, typically using U-Net-based architectures. The model produces a probability map over all pixels that must be post-processed to extract precise horizon coordinates, while horizon picks in time/depth must be converted into dense masks for training. Unpicked seismic traces are consequently treated as background, which can hinder convergence, and both pre- and post-processing can introduce errors into the final interpretation. Moreover, 2D segmentation models do not inherently capture inter-slice context, while 3D models are often computationally prohibitive. We instead formulate horizon tracking as a bounded coordinate regression problem, where the model directly predicts the time/depth coordinate of the target horizon at each lateral position. We propose a lightweight regression head compatible with any pretrained vision backbone, coupled with an LSTM module to model inter-slice context and produce a continuous horizon surface across the volume. A combination of L1 and L2 losses supervises predictions at valid horizon picks, while a geology-informed regularization enforces lateral continuity between successive traces. Under controlled experimental conditions, we evaluate four pretrained vision backbones under both segmentation and regression configurations on a seismic volume from New Zealand. The proposed approach consistently outperforms its segmentation counterparts quantitatively, using metrics including RMSE and PCC, and qualitatively, while also demonstrating greater robustness to increasing sparsity of training picks. Finally, we show that prediction variation across successive traces captures local variations in geological complexity, providing an automated quality control measure for downstream seismic interpretation.

</details>


### [15] [MeshQuery: Agentic Seam Planning for UV Parametrization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02507)
*Marco Schouten,Arthur Roullier,Elie Michel,Ruben Wiersma,Axel Paris,Tamy Boubekeur*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: MeshQuery is a training-free agentic approach using Vision-Language Models (VLMs) for automatic UV unwrapping of production-grade quad meshes. It uses edge-selection tools conditioned on domain-specific knowledge expressed in natural language, with a feedback loop for refinement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current UV unwrapping methods either require extensive training data or fail to produce artist-aligned seams. The motivation is to create a training-free approach that can plan artist-aligned seams using high-level intent while decoupling it from low-level edge selection.

Method: The method uses a queryable mesh representation with a domain-specific language (DSL) that enables the agent to: (1) retrieve mesh information on demand, (2) express seam plans as compact programs of edge-selection operators over topological, geometric, and semantic attributes, and (3) iteratively refine plans from UV quality feedback. A VLM plans seams using natural language domain knowledge.

Result: On Adobe Substance 3D and Toys4K meshes, MeshQuery produces 2.9x/4.29x fewer charts and 1.63x/1.7x shorter seams than the strongest baseline. Professional artists prefer its results in 80.9% of comparisons. It can run on different backend VLMs and scale to meshes an order of magnitude larger than autoregressive seam prediction.

Conclusion: Decoupling high-level intent planning from low-level edge selection, combined with a compact mesh representation, enables a training-free, scalable UV unwrapping solution that outperforms existing methods in chart count, seam length, and artist preference.

Abstract: We present MeshQuery, a training-free agentic approach to automatic UV unwrapping of production-grade quad meshes. A Vision-Language Model (VLM) plans artist-aligned seams using a set of edge-selection tools, conditioned on domain-specific UV-unwrapping knowledge expressed in natural language and refined with a feedback loop. We design a queryable mesh representation together with a domain-specific language (DSL) that enables the agent to retrieve mesh information on demand, express a seam plan as a compact program of edge-selection operators over topological, geometric, and semantic mesh attributes, and iteratively refine it from UV quality feedback. On Adobe Substance 3D and Toys4K meshes, MeshQuery produces 2.9x/4.29x fewer charts and 1.63x/1.7x shorter seams than the strongest baseline, and professional artists prefer its results in 80.9% of comparisons. Ultimately, decoupling high-level intent planning from low-level edge selection and compact mesh representation lets MeshQuery run on different backend VLMs and scale to meshes an order of magnitude larger than autoregressive seam prediction

</details>


### [16] [From Fragments to Global Maps: Learning Vectorized Map Aggregation with Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02513)
*Ziwei Li,Yi-Tang Chen,Xiaoqi Wang,Wenbin He,Han-Wei Shen,Liu Ren*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: MapMergeLLM formulates vectorized HD map aggregation as conditional sequence generation using a large language model. It trains on synthetic local maps with simulated errors and introduces a coordinate tokenizer with geometry-aware pretraining and line-level association loss. The method outperforms heuristic and optimization-based baselines on Argoverse2 and nuScenes without detector-specific retraining.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing map aggregation methods rely on hand-crafted rules with fixed thresholds that cannot effectively handle variations in road structures and prediction errors, requiring detector-specific tuning or manual adjustment.

Method: 1) Formulate map aggregation as conditional sequence generation with an LLM
2) Train on synthetic local maps generated from clean vector maps using corruptions simulating prediction errors
3) Introduce coordinate tokenizer with geometry-aware pretraining
4) Propose line-level association loss to explicitly supervise correspondences between local observations of the same map element

Result: MapMergeLLM substantially outperforms heuristic and optimization-based aggregation baselines on Argoverse2 and nuScenes using multiple recent upstream detectors, without requiring detector-specific retraining.

Conclusion: Data-driven LLM-based approach can effectively aggregate fragmented vectorized map predictions into coherent global maps, reducing dependence on hand-crafted rules and detector-specific tuning while maintaining generalization across different upstream detectors.

Abstract: Large-scale vectorized HD maps provide structured road information that is essential for perception, localization, and planning in autonomous driving. Constructing such maps requires aggregating noisy, fragmented, and overlapping local predictions collected along a vehicle trajectory into a coherent global map. Existing aggregation methods typically rely on hand-crafted rules for fragment association and refinement. However, a fixed set of thresholds cannot effectively handle variations in road structures and prediction errors, often requiring detector-specific tuning or manual adjustment. To address this limitation, we propose MapMergeLLM, a data-driven framework that formulates vectorized map aggregation as conditional sequence generation with a large language model. Given serialized local vectorized maps, our model directly predicts the aggregated global map polylines. To reduce dependence on any particular upstream detector, we train the model on synthetic local maps generated from clean vector maps using corruptions that simulate representative prediction errors. We further introduce a coordinate tokenizer with geometry-aware pretraining to precisely represent map coordinates. In addition, we propose a line-level association loss that explicitly supervises correspondences between local observations of the same map element. Experiments on Argoverse2 and nuScenes using multiple recent upstream detectors demonstrate that MapMergeLLM substantially outperforms heuristic and optimization-based aggregation baselines without detector-specific retraining.

</details>


### [17] [Spatial Memory Intelligence: Endowing World Models with Understanding-Driven Long-Term Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02521)
*Ying Yang,Guiyu Zhang,Lianghua Huang,Chang Nie,Chenyang Si,Haofan Wang,Shaoshuai Shi,Li Jiang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: SMI (Spatial Memory Intelligence) is the first framework to systematically use an understanding model for spatial-memory management in long-video world models. It introduces four atomic operations: spatial clustering, within-cluster sparsification, action-aware retrieval, and reliability-aware filtering to address challenges in managing long-range spatial context.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-video generation and world models face challenges in managing long-range spatial context as memory sequences grow longer and more complex. Existing approaches lack intelligent and systematic memory-management strategies, necessitating a more sophisticated approach.

Method: SMI builds on the spatial reasoning capabilities of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) and proposes four coordinated atomic operations: (1) spatial clustering - organizing memory by spatial relationships, (2) within-cluster sparsification - reducing redundancy within clusters, (3) action-aware retrieval - retrieving relevant memories based on user actions, and (4) reliability-aware filtering - filtering based on memory reliability.

Result: Extensive experiments across multiple baselines, benchmarks, and world-model backbones demonstrate SMI's effectiveness and generalizability, achieving comprehensive improvements in memory sparsity, generation stability, and spatial consistency.

Conclusion: SMI represents a significant advance in spatial-memory management for long-video world models, providing a systematic framework that leverages MLLMs' spatial reasoning capabilities to achieve better memory efficiency and generation quality.

Abstract: Long-video generation and world models have shown strong potential for interactive entertainment and embodied simulation by predicting future observations conditioned on user actions and historical memory. However, as memory sequences grow longer and their structures become increasingly complex, managing long-range spatial context becomes increasingly challenging, calling for a more intelligent and systematic memory-management strategy. Building on the advancing spatial reasoning capabilities of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) and the broader vision of unified models, we propose Spatial Memory Intelligence (SMI), the first framework to systematically employ an understanding model for spatial-memory management in long-video world models. SMI introduces four coordinated atomic operations: spatial clustering, within-cluster sparsification, action-aware retrieval, and reliability-aware filtering. Extensive experiments across multiple baselines, benchmarks, and world-model backbones demonstrate the effectiveness and generalizability of SMI, achieving comprehensive improvements in memory sparsity, generation stability, and spatial consistency.

</details>


### [18] [Oracle headroom without signal: null-calibrated evaluation of candidate selection for thermal heart rate estimation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02561)
*Mohammad Rakibur Rahman,Nhi Nguyen,Sasan Sharifipour,Le Nguyen,Manuel Lage Cañellas,Miguel Bordallo López,Constantino Álvarez Casado*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper addresses a methodological issue in evaluating signal quality indices for camera-based physiological monitoring. The authors point out that using an "oracle" that selects the best estimate from multiple candidates (closest to reference) can misleadingly reward chance agreement, especially when many candidates are available. They propose using order statistics to model this effect and recommend reporting candidate count, valid coverage, and matched null controls in oracle evaluations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to expose a methodological flaw in how signal quality indices are commonly evaluated in camera-based physiological monitoring research. The oracle approach, which selects the estimate closest to a reference, can produce overly optimistic results because with many candidates, chance alone can produce good matches. This bias can lead to false conclusions about the effectiveness of quality indices.

Method: The authors use order statistics to model the effect of oracle selection. They analyze thermal heart rate estimation on 96 iBVP recordings, generating 168 candidates per 10-second window using different facial regions, extraction methods, and processing settings. They compare oracle performance against fixed configurations, best quality index, and constant predictor. They also test a null control using a forehead signal from a different recording.

Result: The oracle achieved a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.91 bpm. In comparison: best fixed configuration = 10.74 bpm, best quality index = 18.03 bpm, and constant predictor = 8.61 bpm. The key finding is that with K=24 candidates, a forehead signal from another recording (completely unrelated) achieved 4.62 bpm MAE, nearly matching the "correct" selection at 4.61 bpm, demonstrating that oracle selection can reward chance agreement.

Conclusion: The conclusion is that oracle-based evaluations of signal quality indices can be misleading due to chance agreement. The expected oracle error decreases approximately as 1/K for K independent candidates. The authors recommend that oracle evaluations should always report: (1) candidate count, (2) valid coverage, and (3) matched null controls to provide proper context and prevent overstating the effectiveness of quality indices.

Abstract: Camera-based physiological monitoring can produce multiple estimates from several facial regions, extraction methods, and processing settings. Signal quality indices aim to select reliable estimates without a physiological reference, and their potential is often assessed with an oracle that selects the estimate closest to the reference in each window. This retrospective selection can reward chance agreement. We model the effect with order statistics. For K independent candidates unrelated to the reference, the expected oracle error decreases approximately as 1/K. We analyze thermal heart rate estimation on 96 iBVP recordings with 168 candidates per 10 s window. The oracle achieves a mean absolute error of 0.91 bpm, compared with 10.74 bpm for the best fixed configuration, 18.03 bpm for the best quality index, and 8.61 bpm for a constant predictor. With K = 24, a forehead signal from another recording matches the correct one, with 4.62 against 4.61 bpm. Oracle evaluations should report candidate count, valid coverage, and matched null controls.

</details>


### [19] [Physical AI Smart Spaces: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Multi-Camera 3D Perception in Smart Spaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02580)
*Yuxing Wang,Yizhou Wang,Anqi Li,Shuo Wang,Sameer Satish Pusegaonkar,Haoquan Liang,Jiajun Li,Shenxin Jiang,Jianhe Yuan,Shangru Li,Tongwei Dai,Zihao Chen,David C. Anastasiu,Sujit Biswas,Xunlei Wu,Zheng Tang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Physical AI Smart Spaces is the first large-scale benchmark for multi-class, multi-camera 3D perception in indoor smart spaces, containing over 280 hours of synchronized 1080p footage from nearly 1,800 cameras across warehouses, hospitals, and retail venues, with automatic annotations and a 3D HOTA evaluation metric.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the lack of comprehensive benchmarks for 3D perception in indoor smart spaces, particularly those combining synthetic and real-world data with multi-camera tracking across diverse environments.

Method: The dataset spans Isaac Sim synthetic generation, Cosmos Transfer appearance augmentation, and real-world Sim2Real evaluation. It includes two warehouse deployments with time-synchronized streams, automatic VGGT-based calibration, and a 3D labeling interface. A 3D instantiation of Higher Order Tracking Accuracy (HOTA) is introduced for evaluation.

Result: The benchmark provides comprehensive annotations (2D/3D bounding boxes, camera calibration, depth) and establishes evaluation protocols with standardized submission formats and leaderboard reporting. Empirical baselines from AI City Challenge leaderboards demonstrate evolution from person-only 3D location tracking to multi-class 3D box tracking.

Conclusion: Physical AI Smart Spaces fills a critical gap in 3D perception research by providing a large-scale, multi-class, multi-camera benchmark with synthetic-to-real data and a 3D tracking evaluation metric, enabling more realistic smart-space perception research.

Abstract: Physical AI Smart Spaces is, to the best of our knowledge, the first benchmark to simultaneously provide large-scale, multi-class, and multi-camera 3D perception data for indoor smart spaces. It contains over 280 hours of synchronized 1080p footage captured by nearly 1,800 cameras in warehouses, hospitals, retail venues, and similar settings, together with automatic annotations for multi-camera identities, 2D bounding boxes, 3D bounding boxes, camera calibration, and depth where available. The benchmark spans Isaac Sim synthetic generation, Cosmos Transfer appearance augmentation, and real-world Sim2Real evaluation. For the real-world target, we include two warehouse deployments with time-synchronized streams, automatic VGGT-based calibration, and a 3D labeling interface that projects world-frame 3D boxes into each view for cross-camera verification. We describe the dataset scope, annotation and calibration schema, generation workflow, benchmark protocols, and official evaluation system, which standardizes submission format, and leaderboard reporting. A central contribution is a 3D instantiation of Higher Order Tracking Accuracy (HOTA), extending the usual 2D box-based tracking evaluation to 3D locations and 3D boxes. We further report empirical baselines from the AI City Challenge leaderboards, showing how methods evolve from person-only 3D location tracking to multi-class 3D box tracking under realistic smart-space constraints. The release is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/nvidia/PhysicalAI-SmartSpaces.

</details>


### [20] [GRAFT: Growing Agglomerative Foundation Models via Continual Teacher Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02597)
*Zhenghao Zhao,Chi Zhang,Qingshuang Chen,Yelin Kim*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: GRAFT is a continual multi-teacher distillation framework that enables a single vision backbone to progressively acquire capabilities from an open-ended sequence of foundation models, avoiding expensive full re-distillation when adding new teachers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vision foundation models (DINOv2, SigLIP2, MASt3R) develop complementary capabilities from different pretraining objectives, but their knowledge remains distributed across separate, specialized models. Existing multi-teacher distillation assumes a fixed set of teachers and requires expensive joint distillation over the entire teacher set when incorporating a new teacher.

Method: GRAFT introduces three key mechanisms: (1) When a new teacher arrives, the previously distilled model serves as a teacher to preserve learned capabilities while the student jointly learns from both the previous model and incoming teacher; (2) Teacher Specific Readout Tokens grant each teacher an independent read-out of the shared encoder to reconcile incompatible representation geometries; (3) Geometry Agnostic Relational Loss aligns vision-language teachers by matching image-text similarity structures rather than raw feature values.

Result: GRAFT produces a single, continually extensible backbone that unifies five domains (image understanding, 2D dense prediction, 3D human pose estimation, 3D vision, and vision-language), delivering strong performance across all domains while acquiring each new capability at the cost of a single distillation rather than full re-distillation.

Conclusion: GRAFT successfully enables continual knowledge acquisition from multiple vision foundation models into a unified backbone, providing a practical solution for incremental model capability expansion without catastrophic forgetting or expensive recomputation.

Abstract: Vision foundation models such as DINOv2, SigLIP2, and MASt3R develop complementary capabilities from different pretraining objectives, yet their knowledge remains distributed across separate, specialized models. Multi-teacher knowledge distillation offers a path toward consolidating these capabilities into a single agglomerative backbone, but existing approaches assume a fixed set of teachers, and incorporating a new teacher requires repeating expensive joint distillation over the entire teacher set. We introduce GRAFT, a continual multi-teacher distillation framework that enables a unified backbone to progressively acquire capabilities from an open-ended sequence of foundation models. When a new teacher arrives, GRAFT treats the previously distilled model as a teacher for preserving learned capabilities, while the current student jointly learns from both the previous model and the incoming teacher. Furthermore, to reconcile the incompatible representation geometries of heterogeneous teachers, we introduce Teacher Specific Readout Tokens, which grant each teacher an independent read-out of the shared encoder, together with Geometry Agnostic Relational Loss that aligns a vision-language teacher by matching image-text similarity structures rather than raw feature values. We provide GRAFT model, which is a single, continually extensible backbone that unifies five domains, including image understanding, 2D dense prediction, 3D human pose estimation, 3D vision, and vision-language, delivering strong performance across all of them while acquiring each new capability at the cost of a single distillation rather than a full re-distillation.

</details>


### [21] [Imagine the Future, Internalize the Gist: Efficient VLA Reasoning via Internalized Spatiotemporal Imagination](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02626)
*Shenglan Li,Zhendong Mi,Hengyi Zhu,Jingwu Luo,Chun Kit Chan,Geng Yuan,Yanzhi Wang,Pu Zhao,Shaoyi Huang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: IG-VLA is a vision-language-action reasoning framework that enables robotic manipulation models to imagine future scene evolution in latent space and internalize this reasoning into compact Scene Gist Tokens, achieving nearly 6% improvement over baselines while reducing inference latency by up to 6.38x.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing VLA models reason about observed states without explicitly anticipating future scene evolution. While extending reasoning to future rollouts improves performance, it introduces substantial computational overhead that makes real-time deployment impractical.

Method: IG-VLA introduces two key components: (1) Latent Spatiotemporal Reasoning - learns to imagine task-relevant future scene evolution directly in visual representation space, avoiding costly pixel-level video generation; (2) Scene Gist Memory - internalizes reasoning-derived scene-behavior associations into a compact Scene Gist Token, preserving future reasoning benefits while bypassing explicit future imagination at inference time.

Result: On LIBERO-Plus Language suite, both reasoning and gist policies outperform the strongest baseline by nearly 6% in success rate. The gist policy achieves up to 6.38x speedup, reducing inference latency from 1081ms to 169.5ms per action chunk on NVIDIA A6000 GPU.

Conclusion: Future spatiotemporal reasoning can be effectively internalized for efficient VLA deployment, achieving a favorable trade-off between reasoning capability and computational efficiency.

Abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models increasingly incorporate intermediate reasoning to improve robotic manipulation, yet existing approaches primarily reason about observed states without explicitly anticipating future scene evolution. Extending such reasoning to explicit future rollouts at every inference step, however, introduces substantial computational overhead. We propose IG-VLA, a VLA reasoning framework that enables models to imagine the future and internalize the gist. Our Latent Spatiotemporal Reasoning learns to imagine task-relevant future scene evolution directly in visual representation space, guiding action prediction without costly pixel-level video generation. To further reduce inference overhead, we introduce Scene Gist Memory, which internalizes reasoning-derived scene-behavior associations into a compact Scene Gist Token, preserving the benefits of future reasoning while bypassing explicit future imagination at inference. Extensive experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and VLABench demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of IG-VLA. On the LIBERO-Plus Language suite, both the reasoning and gist policies outperform the strongest baseline by nearly 6% in success rate. The gist policy also achieves up to 6.38x speedup over baselines, reducing inference latency from 1081ms to 169.5ms per action chunk on a single NVIDIA A6000 GPU. These results demonstrate that future spatiotemporal reasoning can be effectively internalized for efficient VLA deployment.

</details>


### [22] [Capturing Dynamics: The 4D Facial Expression Intensity Dataset](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02647)
*Zesheng Wang,Alexandre Bruckert,Pierre Lebreton,Patrick Le Callet,Yante Li,Guoying Zhao*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces 4DFEID, a novel 4D facial expression intensity dataset containing 2,869 mesh sequences with diverse peak intensities and identity attributes. It collects over 90,000 subjective intensity ratings via crowdsourcing and establishes baselines using various architectures, showing spatial-temporal graph models outperform traditional methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Previous facial expression intensity research relied on 2D static imagery, which is limited because real-world facial expressions are inherently 3D and temporally continuous. This gap in the literature motivated the creation of a 4D dataset for more naturalistic expression analysis.

Method: The researchers used a parametric face model to generate 4D mesh sequences with controlled geometric variations. They collected over 90,000 subjective intensity perception ratings using a Likert scale via a crowdsourcing platform. Various architectures and aggregation methods were evaluated for episode intensity estimation.

Result: Spatial-temporal graph models consistently outperformed traditional frame-aggregation methods for episode intensity estimation. The 4DFEID dataset provides high-fidelity, spatio-temporally coherent facial data with diverse peak intensities and identity attributes.

Conclusion: The 4DFEID dataset addresses a critical gap in affective computing and human-computer interaction by providing the first 4D dataset for facial expression intensity perception research. This establishes a new foundation for more nuanced and naturalistic expression analysis, offering a unique resource for the community.

Abstract: The estimation and analysis of facial expression intensity play a crucial role in affective communication and human-computer interaction. Previous research has primarily focused on detecting and estimating facial expression intensity from frame-level 2D representations. However, this limitation restricts a comprehensive understanding of real-world facial expressions, as they are inherently 3D and temporally continuous. This paper investigates the perception of facial expression intensity by introducing the 4D Facial Expression Intensity Dataset (4DFEID). We employ a parametric face model and compile a total of 2,869 mesh sequences with controlled geometric variations, generating 4D data instances with diverse peak intensities and identity attributes. Using a Likert scale, we collect more than 90,000 subjective intensity perception ratings via a crowdsourcing platform. We explore various architectures and aggregation methods to establish baselines for episode intensity estimation on the new dataset, revealing that spatial-temporal graph models consistently outperform traditional frame-aggregation methods. In contrast to existing datasets that rely on 2D static imagery, the proposed 4D-FEID dataset provides the community with a unique and vital resource for investigating the perception of facial expression intensity through the use of dynamic 3D stimuli. By offering high-fidelity, spatio-temporally coherent facial data, 4D-FEID establishes a new foundation for research into more nuanced and naturalistic expression analysis, thereby addressing a gap in the current landscape of affective computing and human-computer interaction studies. The dataset is available at link.

</details>


### [23] [SpectralCache: Accelerating Diffusion-Based World Models via Spectral Feature Caching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02660)
*Zhendong Mi,Pu Zhao,Ziyu Hu,Xiaodong Yu,Yanzhi Wang,Grace Li Zhang,Shaoyi Huang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: SpectralCache is a training-free inference acceleration method for diffusion-based world models that exploits stable singular subspaces and predictable singular value evolution patterns across denoising steps, achieving 5.22x speedup on HunyuanWorld-Voyager-13B while maintaining generation quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Diffusion-based world models enable high-quality interactive environment generation but suffer from substantial inference overhead due to repeated Transformer evaluations during denoising. Existing caching methods only exploit temporal redundancy at feature/token levels, leaving the mathematical structure of diffusion features unexplored.

Method: SpectralCache proposes three key techniques: (1) Reuses stable singular subspaces across nearby denoising steps; (2) Estimates low-dimensional singular values through linear extrapolation; (3) Exploits spectral consistency between neighboring full-computation features to skip expensive backbone evaluations via singular value scaling.

Result: On HunyuanWorld-Voyager-13B, SpectralCache achieves 5.22x acceleration while maintaining a WorldScore of 65.90 for static scenes, substantially outperforming existing training-free caching methods in inference efficiency.

Conclusion: SpectralCache successfully improves inference efficiency for diffusion-based world models by leveraging the underlying mathematical structure (singular value decomposition) of diffusion features, providing a training-free solution that significantly accelerates generation without sacrificing quality.

Abstract: Diffusion-based world models enable high-quality interactive environment generation but suffer from substantial inference overhead due to repeated Transformer evaluations during denoising. Existing caching methods mainly exploit temporal redundancy at the feature or token level, leaving the underlying mathematical structure of diffusion features largely unexplored. In this work, we reveal that world-model features exhibit highly stable singular subspaces across nearby denoising steps, while their singular values follow predictable evolution patterns. Building on this observation, we propose SpectralCache, a training-free spectral caching framework that reuses stable singular subspaces and estimates only low-dimensional singular values through linear extrapolation. We further exploit the spectral consistency between neighboring full-computation features to skip selected expensive backbone evaluations via singular value scaling. Extensive experiments on representative world models demonstrate that SpectralCache consistently improves inference efficiency while preserving generation quality. On HunyuanWorld-Voyager-13B, SpectralCache achieves 5.22x acceleration while maintaining a WorldScore of 65.90 for static scenes, substantially outperforming existing training-free caching methods in inference efficiency.

</details>


### [24] [CHASE-VLA: Post-Training Quantization Framework for Vision-Language-Action Models with Chunk-Aware Scale Estimation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02666)
*Jin Hyun,Jung Gyu Min,Gyuhyun Jung,Youngjoo Lee*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: CHASE-VLA is a chunk-aware post-training quantization (PTQ) method for Vision-Language-Action models that enables W4A4 quantization of diffusion-based action experts by using generated action chunks as causal context combined with denoising step information to adapt activation scales, achieving 97.3% success rate while reducing weight storage by 73.4%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models use diffusion-based action experts (AE) that are repeatedly invoked across denoising steps and policy queries.
