Existing PTQ methods fail because fixed calibration scales cannot match activation ranges that vary with denoising progress and intended motion, making low-bit quantization challenging.

Method: CHASE-VLA exploits the VLA-specific signal of generated action chunks (including unexecuted future suffix) as causal action context. It combines this chunk information with denoising step group information to adapt AE activation scales dynamically, enabling W4A4 quantization of both MLP and attention projections without modifying the pretrained policy.

Result: On LIBERO, CHASE-VLA achieves 97.3% average success rate on π₀.₅ with both MLP and attention projections quantized to W4A4, restoring FP16-level performance. Weight storage is reduced by 73.4%, with single-chunk memory traffic reduced by 70.9% and 71.2% on π₀.₅ and GR00T N1.6 respectively, with predictor overhead of at most 1.26% of saved storage.

Conclusion: CHASE-VLA successfully enables aggressive low-bit quantization (W4A4) for diffusion-based action experts in VLA models by leveraging VLA-specific signals (action chunks and denoising step groups), achieving near-FP16 performance while significantly reducing storage and memory requirements, making it practical for deployment on resource-constrained devices.

Abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models map visual observations and language instructions to continuous robot actions, but a diffusion-based action expert (AE) poses a key challenge for low-bit post-training quantization (PTQ). The AE is repeatedly invoked across denoising steps and policy queries, where fixed calibration scales can be mismatched with activation ranges that vary with denoising progress and intended motion. We propose CHASE-VLA, a chunk-aware PTQ method that exploits a VLA-specific signal readily available from the policy: the generated action chunk, including its unexecuted future suffix. Rather than relying only on static scale matching for AE layers, CHASE-VLA combines the previously generated chunk as causal action context with denoising step group information to adapt AE activation scales. This enables W4A4 quantization of both MLP and attention projections in the repeated AE without modifying the pretrained policy. On LIBERO, CHASE-VLA achieves 97.3% average success rate on $π_{0.5}$ when both MLP and attention projections in the AE are quantized to W4A4, restoring FP16-level performance. CHASE-VLA also reduces the weight storage of the quantized AE linear layers by 73.4% and their single-chunk memory traffic by 70.9% and 71.2% on $π_{0.5}$ and GR00T N1.6, respectively, with a predictor overhead of at most 1.26% of the saved storage.

</details>


### [25] [Revisiting Visual Representation Enhancement of VLMs via Kernel Canonical Correlation Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02718)
*Peilin Yang,Xiaoyu Liu,Jian Sun,Qinghua Tao*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes 3vKCCA, a novel method using Kernel Canonical Correlation Analysis to align vision-language model representations. It extends previous work (KUEA) by characterizing alignment on feature subspaces rather than kernel matrices, incorporating both image and text encoders in a unified 3-view framework. The method achieves significant improvement in fine-grained visual perception (MMVP-VLM: 17.8→25.9) while preserving zero-shot capabilities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vision-language models like CLIP have strong semantic generalization but limited fine-grained visual perception. Prior work (KUEA) aligned CLIP's image encoder with DINOv2 using kernel matrix alignment. However, the authors discovered that reducing the alignment loss doesn't degrade performance, suggesting kernel-matrix discrepancy is insufficient for visual representation enhancement. This motivates exploring a new alignment formulation.

Method: The paper proposes using Kernel Canonical Correlation Analysis (KCCA) to characterize representation alignment on feature subspaces, which maximizes projection correlations. An efficient end-to-end training scheme is derived based on KKT conditions, avoiding the eigenvalue problem in KCCA. This is extended to a 3-view formulation (3vKCCA) that incorporates projections from the pretrained text encoder under a unified optimization framework for joint alignment.

Result: On CLIP ViT-L/14 with ImageNet-1K, 3vKCCA improves MMVP-VLM accuracy from 17.8 to 25.9, substantially outperforming existing methods, while maintaining zero-shot image-text retrieval performance.

Conclusion: The proposed 3vKCCA method demonstrates that subspace-based alignment via KCCA is more effective than kernel-matrix alignment for improving fine-grained visual perception in vision-language models. The 3-view formulation successfully integrates text encoder projections, achieving state-of-the-art results on fine-grained visual benchmarks while preserving zero-shot capabilities.

Abstract: Vision-language models such as CLIP exhibit strong semantic generalization, but remain limited in fine-grained visual perception. A recent work named KUEA presents a natural remedy by finetuning the image encoder under the supervision of the vision-centric DINOv2 to align their kernel matrices element-wisely, while regularizing the embeddings to remain close to the pretrained visual encoder for preserving image-text semantics in CLIP. However, we show that diminishing the role of the alignment loss to DINOv2 does not necessarily degrade its fine-grained visual performance, suggesting that the kernel-matrix discrepancy may be insufficient for further visual representation enhancement, motivating us to revisit the alignment formulation. In this work, we present a novel perspective to characterize representation alignment on feature subspaces through Kernel Canonical Correlation Analysis (KCCA), which maximizes the projection correlations. In optimization, we derive an efficient end-to-end training scheme upon KKT conditions, avoiding the eigenvalue problem in KCCA. Further, we extend our method into a 3-view formulation, i.e., 3vKCCA, in which the projections from the pretrained text encoder are also incorporated under a unified optimization framework for joint alignment. With CLIP ViT-L/14 on ImageNet-1K, our 3vKCCA improves the MMVP-VLM accuracy from 17.8 to 25.9, substantially outperforming the existing methods, and meanwhile maintains zero-shot image--text retrieval performance.

</details>


### [26] [SymRegFlow: Symmetry-Regularized Flow Matching for Video World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02726)
*Xi Ye,Yuzhu Wang,Xiaoyang Liu,Jiayi Wang,Yangyang Xu,Ruyu Wang,Wenlin Chen,Duo Su,Jun Zhu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: SymRegFlow is a symmetry-regularized flow-matching framework for multi-view-consistent video generation across continuous camera viewpoints without ground-truth novel-view RGB supervision. It uses geometric warping of source views into noisy anchors, combined with masked dual-anchor supervision and cross-anchor denoising-output consistency to mitigate anchor-specific errors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing flow-matching-based multi-view world models are restricted to fixed camera rigs. Extending them to continuously varying camera poses requires paired pose-video observations with dense pose coverage, which are costly to acquire. This work aims to enable high-quality multi-view video generation across continuous viewpoints without expensive ground-truth novel-view data.

Method: SymRegFlow geometrically warps source views into noisy anchors for each target pose. It combines masked dual-anchor supervision with cross-anchor denoising-output consistency to mitigate anchor-specific errors. Theoretically, under an affine Gaussian surrogate, consistency regularization recovers the clean-reference optimum at fixed noise levels.

Result: On nuScenes, SymRegFlow achieves the lowest FVD (Frechet Video Distance) and FVMD among evaluated baselines, reducing FVD by over 31% relative to the best baseline. Source-conditioned inference also attains the best FID (Frechet Inception Distance) and instance preservation. Experiments on Cosmos-Drive-Dreams demonstrate high-quality multi-view-consistent autonomous-driving video generation.

Conclusion: SymRegFlow successfully enables multi-view-consistent video generation across continuous viewpoints without ground-truth novel-view RGB supervision. The symmetry-regularized flow-matching approach with dual-anchor consistency outperforms single- and merged-anchor baselines, achieving state-of-the-art results on autonomous driving datasets.

Abstract: Flow-matching-based multi-view world models generate realistic videos, but are commonly restricted to fixed camera rigs. Extending them to continuously varying camera poses requires paired pose--video observations with dense pose coverage, which are costly to acquire. We introduce \emph{SymRegFlow}, a symmetry-regularized flow-matching framework for multi-view-consistent video generation across continuous viewpoints without ground-truth novel-view RGB supervision. For each target pose, SymRegFlow geometrically warps source views into noisy anchors and combines masked dual-anchor supervision with cross-anchor denoising-output consistency to mitigate anchor-specific errors. Under an affine Gaussian surrogate, we prove that suitable consistency regularization recovers the clean-reference optimum at fixed noise levels, strictly outperforming single- and merged-anchor baselines. Experiments on Cosmos-Drive-Dreams and nuScenes demonstrate high-quality, multi-view-consistent autonomous-driving video generation: on nuScenes, SymRegFlow achieves the lowest FVD and FVMD among the evaluated baselines, reducing FVD by over 31\% relative to the best baseline, and source-conditioned inference also attains the best FID and instance preservation.

</details>


### [27] [Correcting Guided Diffusion Trajectories with Spectral Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02753)
*Gihoon Kim,Taesup Kim*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper addresses the lack of explicit criteria for evaluating classifier-free guidance (CFG) in conditional image generation by introducing spectral alignment as a principled measure. The authors propose Spectral Correction Guidance (SCG), a training-free method that corrects deviations from an analytic reference spectrum during diffusion sampling to improve guidance behavior and generation quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The practical success of conditional image generation depends on condition alignment and visual fidelity. While CFG is central to this success, it lacks an explicit criterion to assess whether the guided trajectory is progressing as intended. This gap makes it difficult to understand and improve guidance behavior.

Method: The authors show that spectral alignment provides a principled criterion for understanding guidance behavior. They analyze the spectra of intermediate states as an indicator of consistency with the expected spectral evolution of the forward process. Based on this observation, they introduce Spectral Correction Guidance, which corrects deviations from an analytic reference spectrum during sampling. The method is training-free and applicable across diffusion backbones and conditional generation tasks without modifying the underlying model.

Result: Experiments demonstrate consistent gains in preference-based metrics over baseline guidance methods in text-to-image generation and improved generation quality over CFG on ImageNet. These improvements persist across a range of guidance scales and with fewer denoising steps.

Conclusion: Spectral alignment provides a principled and interpretable criterion for understanding and improving guidance behavior in diffusion models. The proposed Spectral Correction Guidance is a training-free, model-agnostic method that can enhance generation quality across various tasks and backbones.

Abstract: The practical success of conditional image generation hinges on fine-grained differences in condition alignment and visual fidelity. Classifier-free guidance (CFG) is central to this success, but its lack of an explicit criterion makes it difficult to assess whether the guided trajectory is progressing as intended. To address this gap, we show that spectral alignment provides a principled criterion for understanding guidance behavior and improving guided diffusion sampling through adaptive correction. Our analysis identifies the spectra of intermediate states as an indicator of consistency with the expected spectral evolution of the forward process. Based on this observation, we introduce Spectral Correction Guidance, a method that corrects deviations from an analytic reference spectrum during sampling. The proposed method is training-free and applicable across diffusion backbones and conditional generation tasks without modifying the underlying model. Experiments demonstrate consistent gains in preference-based metrics over baseline guidance methods in text-to-image generation and improved generation quality over CFG on ImageNet. These improvements persist across a range of guidance scales and with fewer denoising steps. Our analyses and ablations provide insight into guidance behavior and how the proposed method affects generation quality.

</details>


### [28] [FiberGeoText: A Vision-Language Model for Population- Level Organization of Superficial White Matter](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02755)
*Yuqian Chen,R. Jarrett Rushmore,Guikun Chen,Fan Zhang,Edward Yeterian,Nikos Makris,Yogesh Rathi,Lauren J. O'Donnell*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: FGT is a vision-language model that organizes short-range superficial white matter (SWM) streamlines from ultra-high-resolution diffusion MRI into population-level clusters by jointly representing 3D trajectory, cortical anatomical context (encoded via LLM), and shape information.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The superficial white matter (SWM) contains abundant short-range association fibers critical for cognition, but their organization remains incompletely characterized due to short trajectories and highly variable cortical folding making cross-individual correspondence challenging. Anatomically corresponding connections may vary in spatial location across individuals.

Method: FGT jointly represents three complementary properties of each streamline: (1) 3D trajectory, (2) cortical anatomical context expressed as text from multiple parcellation schemes and encoded using a pretrained LLM, and (3) shape. This enables heterogeneous anatomical descriptions to contribute to a common continuous representation. Evaluated on 0.76mm submillimeter diffusion MRI data.

Result: FGT produced substantially greater cortical parcel coherence, within-cluster shape consistency, cluster-size consistency, and cross-subject correspondence compared to SOTA methods. The trained model generalizes well to unseen subjects with 96.7% of 5,000 learned clusters recovered, and high consistency of cluster structure between training and testing data.

Conclusion: Integrating geometric, anatomical, and shape information by learning multimodal deep embeddings with a VLM enables robust learning of population-consistent SWM organization despite interindividual anatomical variability.

Abstract: The superficial white matter (SWM), a critical brain region for cognition across the lifespan and brain disease, contains abundant short-range association fibers whose organization remains incompletely characterized, in part because the short trajectories and highly variable cortical folding make correspondence across individuals challenging. Anatomically corresponding connections may vary in spatial location across individuals and therefore may not be adequately defined by geometric proximity alone. We introduce FiberGeoText (FGT), a vision-language model (VLM) for organizing short-range superficial white matter (SWM) streamlines reconstructed from ultra-high-resolution diffusion MRI into population-level clusters. FGT jointly represents three complementary properties of each streamline: its three-dimensional trajectory, its cortical anatomical context, and its shape. Cortical endpoint information from multiple parcellation schemes is expressed as text and encoded using a pretrained large language model (LLM), enabling heterogeneous anatomical descriptions to contribute to a common continuous representation. We evaluated FGT on acquired submillimeter 0.76 mm diffusion MRI data. Compared with state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods, FGT produced substantially greater cortical parcel coherence, within-cluster shape consistency, cluster-size consistency, and cross-subject correspondence. The trained model also generalizes well to unseen subjects with an average of 96.7% of the 5,000 learned clusters recovered, and high consistency of cluster structure between training and testing data. Together, these findings demonstrate that integrating geometric, anatomical, and shape information by learning multimodal deep embeddings with a VLM model enables robust learning of population-consistent SWM organization despite interindividual anatomical variability.

</details>


### [29] [TRAC: Trajectory-aware Reuse and Adaptive Correction for Efficient Autoregressive Video Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02779)
*Jiaxing Song,Weiqi Yan,You Huang,Mingte Qiu,Huazhong Liu,Xiaofeng Zhu,Yunshan Zhong*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: TRAC is a training-free framework for efficient autoregressive video generation that addresses accumulated approximation errors through three components: RCS for cache reuse scheduling, ATGS for CFG guidance coordination, and SSC for spectral structure correction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing acceleration methods target single-trajectory generation with bidirectional attention, but autoregressive video generation sequentially couples chunk-level denoising trajectories, causing approximation errors to accumulate and propagate through the generation process.

Method: TRAC employs three components: (1) Robust Cumulative Scheduling (RCS) selects cache reuse schedules based on cumulative rollout error and cross-chunk/prompt variation; (2) Autoregressive Trajectory-aware Guidance Scheduling (ATGS) coordinates CFG refreshes along the global AR trajectory; (3) Spectral Structure Correction (SSC) restores low-frequency structure of the first chunk to correct long-term structural loss.

Result: Experiments on SkyReels-V2 and FramePack-F1 demonstrate that TRAC achieves both the highest inference efficiency and the best generation quality for AR video generation compared to existing methods.

Conclusion: TRAC provides an effective training-free solution for accelerating autoregressive video generation while maintaining superior quality, addressing the accumulated error problem inherent in AR video generation pipelines.

Abstract: In this paper, we present trajectory-aware reuse and adaptive correction (TRAC), a training-free framework for efficient autoregressive (AR) video generation. Existing acceleration methods mainly target single-trajectory generation with bidirectional attention. AR video generation, by contrast, sequentially couples chunk-level denoising trajectories. Consequently, approximation errors accumulate and propagate through the generation process. TRAC addresses this challenge with three components, including robust cumulative scheduling (RCS), autoregressive trajectory-aware guidance scheduling (ATGS), and spectral structure correction (SSC). RCS selects cache reuse schedules by cumulative rollout error and cross-chunk/prompt variation. ATGS coordinates CFG refreshes along the global AR trajectory. SSC restores low-frequency structure of the first chunk to correct long-term structural loss. Experiments on SkyReels-V2 and FramePack-F1 show that, compared with existing methods, TRAC achieves both the highest inference efficiency and the best generation quality for AR video generation.

</details>


### [30] [FUSEye: Training-Light Fisheye Detection with Overlapping Views and Zero-Initialized Adapters](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02799)
*Wenya Su,Kai Luo,Di Wen,Ruiping Liu,Yufan Chen,Junwei Zheng,Kunyu Peng,Kailun Yang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: FUSEye is a training-light framework that adapts COCO-pretrained YOLO detectors to fisheye cameras by adding ~227k new parameters. It addresses distortion at three levels: input (GridViews), feature (Z-Adapters), and decision (AgreeFusion). Achieves 0.266 mAP50 on WoodScape (vs 0.148 baseline) while using only 25% of labels.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fisheye cameras offer single-sensor, low-cost surroundings view for mobile robots, but COCO-pretrained detectors fail on them due to radial distortion warping image structure and boundary compression shrinking objects. Full fine-tuning requires abundant labels and compute, creating a need for training-light adaptation.

Method: FUSEye adds ~227k new parameters while keeping backbone frozen. Three causal levels of adaptation: (1) Input level - GridViews generates overlapping grid views and remaps boxes to enlarge compressed boundary regions; (2) Feature level - Zero-initialized residual adapters (Z-Adapters) correct distortion-induced feature misalignment; (3) Decision level - Learned cross-projection agreement fusion (AgreeFusion) promotes low-confidence detections only with consistent evidence across views.

Result: On WoodScape surround-view fisheye benchmark: YOLO26-x improved from 0.148 to 0.266 mAP50 (79.7% relative improvement). Retains 84.3% of fully fine-tuned accuracy. With only 25% labeled training images: achieves 0.2597 mAP50, retaining 97.6% of full-label performance. Recipe is architecture-agnostic, consistently improving YOLOv8-11 detectors.

Conclusion: FUSEye successfully bridges the domain gap between natural images and fisheye cameras with minimal training. The three-level causal approach (input, feature, decision) effectively addresses distortion at multiple levels. The method is compute-efficient (227k params), label-efficient (works with 25% labels), and architecture-agnostic, making it practical for real-world deployment on mobile robots with fisheye cameras.

Abstract: Fisheye cameras give mobile robots a single-sensor, low-cost view of their surroundings, yet the COCO-pretrained detectors that practitioners routinely reuse fail on them: strong radial distortion warps local image structure, while boundary compression shrinks objects to near-invisible sizes. Full fine-tuning closes much of the gap but requires abundant fisheye labels and compute. We present FUSEye, a training-light framework that turns a frozen-backbone COCO-pretrained extra-large YOLO26 detector (YOLO26-x) into a fisheye detector. FUSEye adds roughly 227k new parameters while updating the inserted modules and the pretrained detection head. It addresses the transfer gap at three causally linked levels. At the input level, overlapping grid view generation and box remapping (GridViews) enlarge compressed boundary regions. At the feature level, zero-initialized residual adapters (Z-Adapters) correct distortion-induced feature misalignment. At the decision level, learned cross-projection agreement fusion (AgreeFusion) promotes low-confidence detections only when they are supported by consistent evidence across multiple views. On the WoodScape surround-view fisheye benchmark, FUSEye raises YOLO26-x from 0.148 to 0.266 mAP50 and retains 84.3% fully fine-tuned accuracy. Moreover, randomly using only 25% of the labeled training images, FUSEye achieves 0.2597 mAP50, retaining 97.6% of its full-label performance. FUSEye also consistently improves YOLOv8-11 detectors, showing that the recipe is architecture-agnostic. Source code will be available at https://github.com/Su-wenya/FUSEye.

</details>


### [31] [TerrainForge: Physics-Grounded road geometry Editing for Counterfactual Autonomous Driving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02825)
*Yang Chen,Yicheng Zhu,zhenning Li,Tao Li,Zilin Bian*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: TerrainForge is a framework for generating road geometry-focused counterfactuals from reconstructed multi-vehicle driving episodes. It uses a unified road model connecting scene deformation with four-wheel vehicle dynamics to propagate crests, sags, speed humps, and friction changes through vehicle motion, camera viewpoint, and inter-vehicle clearance. The system includes a screening surrogate that predicts safety outcomes from road edits with 22-40% lower error than baseline.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Road geometry and surface conditions significantly affect vehicle motion, driver observations, and inter-vehicle clearance. Creating realistic driving scene counterfactuals requires editing these properties while correspondingly updating vehicle behavior, camera perspectives, and safety margins—a challenge not addressed by existing methods.

Method: A unified road model connects scene deformation with four-wheel vehicle dynamics. The framework propagates road geometry changes (crests, sags, speed humps) and friction changes through vehicle motion, camera viewpoint, and inter-vehicle clearance. Vehicle dynamics were validated against CarSim, and road geometry was verified in reconstructed Waymo scenes. A first-stage screening surrogate was trained on 15,758 road edits across 983 braking episodes to predict changes in terminal gap from original driving context and candidate road-edit parameters.

Result: Leaving surrounding vehicles on recorded trajectories (vs recomputing) produces median peak differences of 1.52 m for crests and 1.41 m for sags across 18 episodes. The screening surrogate achieves 22-40% lower mean absolute error than predicting no change on held-out scenes, enabling cheap screening before full multi-vehicle rollout.

Conclusion: TerrainForge successfully enables road geometry-focused counterfactual generation in multi-vehicle driving scenarios. The unified road-vehicular dynamics model accurately propagates road edits to vehicle motion and clearance, while the screening surrogate enables efficient evaluation of safety outcomes across candidate edits.

Abstract: Road geometry (e.g., crests, sags, and speed humps) and surface conditions (e.g., wet or icy pavement) affect how vehicles move, what drivers and onboard cameras observe, and how much clearance remains between vehicles. Editing these properties in a driving scene therefore requires corresponding changes in vehicle motion. Capturing these differences in a driving video requires a road edit to propagate to vehicle motion, camera viewpoint, and the clearance between vehicles. We present TerrainForge, a framework for generating road geometry-focused counterfactuals from reconstructed multi-vehicle driving episodes. A unified road model connects scene deformation with four-wheel vehicle dynamics, allowing crests, sags, speed humps, and friction changes to propagate through vehicle motion, camera viewpoint, and inter-vehicle clearance. Vehicle dynamics are evaluated against CarSim, and prescribed road geometry is verified in reconstructed Waymo scenes. Across 18 episodes, leaving surrounding vehicles on their recorded trajectories instead of recomputing their responses produces median peak differences in predicted ego-lead distance of 1.52 m for crests and 1.41 m for sags. We further simulate the ego response to 15,758 road edits across 983 braking episodes, pairing each edit with its safety outcomes relative to an unedited replay. These pairs train a first-stage screening surrogate that takes the original driving context and candidate road-edit parameters as input and predicts the resulting change in the ego's terminal gap. On held-out scenes, this prediction achieves 22-40% lower mean absolute error than predicting no change, so candidates can be screened cheaply before the full multi-vehicle rollout.

</details>


### [32] [Seeing, Saying, but Not Using: From Reportable Spatial Facts to Usable States in Multimodal Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02876)
*Jinchang Zhang,Guoyu Lu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces SpaceConflict, a benchmark of 23,196 inputs for evaluating spatial reasoning in multimodal LLMs. It reveals an "availability-utilization gap": models can recover spatial facts from visual evidence but fail when those facts must drive subsequent transformations. The proposed Operational State Supervision (OSS) method improves performance on state-dependent tasks (L3, L4).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the distinction between a model knowing a spatial fact versus using that fact in subsequent reasoning. The authors argue that correct reporting of spatial facts does not guarantee those facts are operational in downstream computation.

Method: SpaceConflict benchmark covering four levels: L1 (local fact binding), L2 (relational composition), L3 (cross-observation consistency), L4 (state judgment under transformation). Uses a unified Supported/Contradictory/Unknown judgment interface with three query types: direct-state, full-transformation, and explicit-initial-state queries. Proposes Operational State Supervision (OSS) to supervise task-relevant spatial states and align shared facts across contexts.

Result: For Qwen3.5-9B, 50 out of 100 sequences with correctly recovered initial state fail the full transformation task. Supplying the state explicitly repairs all 50 failures. The gap narrows with model scale but does not close. OSS improves paired accuracy most on L3 and L4, the levels that depend on organizing and using state.

Conclusion: Evaluating multimodal spatial reasoning requires asking not only whether a model can see and state a spatial fact, but whether that fact becomes a usable state in subsequent computation. The availability-utilization gap is a fundamental issue that persists across model scales.

Abstract: A multimodal large language model that correctly reports a spatial fact does not necessarily use that fact in subsequent reasoning. To study this distinction, we introduce \textsc{SpaceConflict}, a benchmark of 23{,}196 inputs for the construction and use of spatial state. Under a unified Supported/Contradictory/Unknown judgment interface, it covers local fact binding (L1), relational composition (L2), cross-observation consistency (L3), and state judgment under transformation (L4). Posing a direct-state query, a full-transformation query, and an explicit-initial-state query on the same world reveals an availability--utilization gap: models recover the initial state from visual evidence yet fail when that state must drive a transformation. For Qwen3.5-9B, 50 of 100 sequences with a correctly recovered initial state fail the full transformation, and supplying the state explicitly repairs all 50; the gap narrows with scale but does not close. We therefore propose Operational State Supervision (OSS), which supervises task-relevant spatial states and their transformation trajectories and aligns shared facts across contexts. OSS improves paired accuracy on matched judgments most on L3 and L4, the levels that depend on organizing and using state. Evaluating multimodal spatial reasoning thus requires asking not only whether a model can see and state a spatial fact, but whether that fact becomes a usable state in subsequent computation.

</details>


### [33] [Found but Not Read: When Extracted Text Closes the Retrieval-Reading Gap in Document Vision-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02880)
*Qingtao Xia,Siyao Cheng,Jiahua Bao,Jiaxing Du,Jie Liu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper identifies a "retrieval-reading gap" in document question answering: VLMs can read evidence when found but fail to locate it in page images. Using a paired protocol comparing image-only vs. image+text answers on FoveDoc-Bench, they find that adding OCR text improves accuracy by 13-16 points, with exact text doubling this gain. The effect persists across 6 VLMs from 3 families and is additive to retrieval quality, not a substitute for it.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current retrieval-augmented document QA assumes that once the right page is retrieved, a VLM can read it. This paper challenges this assumption by demonstrating a systematic failure where VLMs find evidence but fail to use it from page images alone.

Method: Paired protocol comparing: (1) answers from retrieved page images alone vs. (2) answers from same images plus extracted OCR text. Tested on FoveDoc-Bench benchmark with traceable evidence across 6 VLMs from 3 families. Additional experiments with crops, bounding boxes, and different evidence types (text vs. charts).

Result: Retrieval finds nearly every evidence page (nearly 100%). Adding CPU-OCR text raises strict accuracy by 13-16 points; exact text layer roughly doubles this gain. Effect appears across all 6 VLMs but shrinks with scale within one family without closing. Crops of evidence recover most gain; boxes around evidence recover none. Extracted text helps on textual evidence but is neutral/harmful on charts/figures. Advantage shrinks as retrieval degrades. Unrelated text of same form adds nothing.

Conclusion: Extracted text is an amplifier of retrieval that works, not a substitute for retrieval that does not. VLMs can read evidence but cannot find it in page images—the retrieval-reading gap is a distinct failure mode requiring architectural solutions beyond scaling.

Abstract: Retrieval-augmented document question answering assumes that once the right page is found, a vision-language model (VLM) can read it. We show that this assumption often fails, leaving a retrieval-reading gap: evidence found but not used. A paired protocol isolates this gap by comparing answers from the retrieved page images alone with answers from the same images plus their extracted text. On FoveDoc-Bench, our benchmark with traceable evidence, retrieval finds nearly every evidence page, yet adding CPU-OCR text raises strict accuracy by 13 to 16 points. An exact text layer roughly doubles the gain, which appears across six VLMs from three families and, within one family, narrows with scale without closing. The reader can read this evidence but cannot find it: crops of it recover most of the text gain, boxes around it on the page none. The same protocol identifies two boundaries. Extracted text helps on textual evidence but is neutral or harmful on charts and figures. Its advantage shrinks as retrieval degrades, and unrelated text of the same form adds nothing detectable. Extracted text is an amplifier of retrieval that works, not a substitute for retrieval that does not. Our code is available at https://github.com/atoz03/fovedoc-sup.

</details>


### [34] [Revealing Epistemic Uncertainty in MLLMs via Causal-Invariant Masking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02887)
*Haoyang Luo,Linwei Tao,Jie Gui,Xinghao Chen,Chang Xu,Jianyuan Guo,Minjing Dong*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper addresses hallucination detection in Multimodal Large Language Models by proposing Causal-Invariant Masking (CIM), which uses Semantic Divergence to measure model's sensitivity to non-causal correlations (epistemic uncertainty). A fast proxy metric EED is also introduced, achieving state-of-the-art performance with nearly 50% speedup.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to address a critical limitation in Multimodal Large Language Models: hallucinations. Existing UQ methods struggle to detect uncertainty caused by superficial associations, particularly when query-relevant signals are weak. The root cause is identified as bias toward aleatoric uncertainty (data ambiguity) while overlooking epistemic uncertainty (model limitations).

Method: The paper proposes Causal-Invariant Masking (CIM), which measures semantic shift between original predictions and those conditioned on a causally-focused view. The core metric is Semantic Divergence, which theoretically converges to the variance of model's sensitivity to non-causal correlations. For computational efficiency, Expected Embedding Drift (EED) is introduced as a geometric proxy operating in the hyperspherical embedding space.

Result: The proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance on various benchmarks. Additionally, EED accelerates computation by nearly 50% while maintaining comparable performance to the full Semantic Divergence metric.

Conclusion: The proposed CIM framework and its metrics (Semantic Divergence and EED) achieve state-of-the-art performance in detecting hallucinations and quantifying uncertainty in MLLMs. The theoretical analysis successfully establishes the connection between semantic shift and model's sensitivity to non-causal correlations. EED provides an efficient alternative with nearly 50% speedup while maintaining comparable performance.

Abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) suffer from hallucinations, creating a critical need for Uncertainty Quantification (UQ) to ensure reliable deployment. However, existing approaches struggle to detect uncertainty caused by superficial associations, especially when the query-relevant signal is weak. We mainly attribute this issue to their bias toward aleatoric uncertainty arising from data ambiguity, overlooking epistemic uncertainty stemming from model limitations. To further decompose uncertainty types for a comprehensive UQ, we propose Causal-Invariant Masking (CIM), which measures the semantic shift between the original predictions and those conditioned on a causally-focused view. Based on this framework, we introduce Semantic Divergence as our core metric for UQ and provide theoretical evidence that it converges to the variance of model's sensitivity to non-causal correlations, establishing its ability to capture MLLM's limitation. To accelerate UQ in MLLMs, we further propose Expected Embedding Drift (EED), a fast geometric proxy metric that estimates semantic shift directly within the hyperspherical embedding space. Experiments show that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on various benchmarks, while the proposed EED accelerates by nearly 50% with comparable performance.

</details>


### [35] [ViTok: Improving Dense Semantics in AM-RADIO-Style Multi-Teacher Distillation with PHI-S and Masked Image Modelling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02903)
*Hailun Xu,Kanchan Sarkar*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper presents a multi-teacher distillation approach for vision transformers that combines global recognition (SigLIP2) and dense semantics (DINOv3-L) into a single student model. The key challenge is balancing conflicting objectives between ImageNet classification and ADE20K segmentation tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The research aims to consolidate VITOK progress into a unified distillation recipe that preserves both global recognition and dense semantics. The central problem is that improvements in ImageNet-1K kNN accuracy often degrade ADE20K segmentation performance, requiring explicit trade-off management.

Method: The authors implement several modifications: (1) split adaptor heads for CLS and patch tokens, (2) asymmetric cosine/MSE losses, (3) initialization from DINOv3-L checkpoint, (4) teacher reweighting, (5) masked image modeling (MIM), and (6) PHI-S feature balancing. The student is distilled from SigLIP2 and DINOv3-L teachers.

Result: The resulting model achieves 83.2 patch kNN and 85.2 CLS kNN on ImageNet-1K, slightly surpassing the DINOv3-L teacher. PHI-S restores ADE20K performance from 46.5/58.1 to 48.5/61.0 mIoU/mAcc, matching the teacher on dense prediction. Negative results show that scaling to ImageNet22K and adding extra teachers (SAM3, HOG) introduces interference without consistent benefits.

Conclusion: The paper provides a practical distillation recipe that balances global recognition and dense semantics through careful modifications. Key lessons include the importance of split adaptor heads, asymmetric losses, and PHI-S feature balancing. Scaling to larger datasets or adding more teachers does not improve results, suggesting the current approach is near-optimal.

Abstract: We study how to consolidate the current VITOK progress into a single multi-teacher distillation recipe that jointly preserves global recognition and dense semantics. Our starting point is an AM-RADIO-style student distilled from SigLIP2 and DINOv3-L, where SigLIP2 supplies strong global semantics and DINOv3-L supplies stronger dense features. The central empirical issue is that the same recipe does not optimize all objectives equally well: changes that improve ImageNet-1K kNN accuracy can still degrade ADE20K segmentation. We summarize a progression of modifications that make this trade-off more explicit and more manageable: split adaptor heads for CLS and patch tokens, asymmetric cosine/MSE losses, initialization from a DINOv3-L checkpoint, teacher reweighting, masked image modeling (MIM), and PHI-S feature balancing. The resulting model reaches 83.2 patch kNN and 85.2 CLS kNN, slightly surpassing the DINOv3-L teacher on ImageNet-1K kNN classification, while PHI-S restores ADE20K performance from 46.5/58.1 to 48.5/61.0 mIoU/mAcc, matching the teacher on this dense benchmark. We also summarize negative results: scaling distillation from ImageNet-1K to ImageNet22K does not consistently help, and naively adding extra teachers such as SAM3 or HOG features introduces interference. Rather than claiming a final recipe, this paper distills the current project state into a compact empirical story and a concrete set of lessons for future iterations.

</details>


### [36] [Custom Forcing: Training-Free Subject Customization for Autoregressive Video Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02914)
*Yunseung Ok,Hyunsoo Kim,Minseo Kim,Suhyun Kim*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Custom Forcing is a training-free method that enables autoregressive video models to generate long videos featuring specific subjects from user-provided reference images, using persistent KV cache storage with two novel techniques (DVA and ACG) to prevent identity drift and generic subject bias.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing autoregressive video models generate generic subjects from text prompts rather than specific subjects from user images. Current customization methods either require costly per-subject optimization or use bidirectional attention that isn't suitable for causal streaming. There's a need for a method that can maintain subject identity over minute-long video rollouts while maintaining real-time generation speed.

Method: Custom Forcing stores reference-based anchor frames in the persistent KV cache of a frozen autoregressive video model. Two techniques address its limitations: 1) Drift-Adaptive Value Amplification (DVA) scales reference influence based on detected identity drift, and 2) Anchor Contrast Guidance (ACG) steers generation away from the generic class prior toward the specific subject.

Result: Over two-minute rollouts, fixed anchors degrade from 0.58 to 0.42 in DINO-I similarity, while Custom Forcing maintains 0.58-0.62. It achieves higher subject similarity than bidirectional customization methods, better identity preservation over 30s than causal I2V and reference-to-video models, while generating each frame 9.5-28.5× faster than long-video baselines.

Conclusion: Custom Forcing successfully enables real-time, minute-long video generation with specific subject preservation without training, outperforming both bidirectional and causal customization approaches in identity retention and inference speed.

Abstract: Autoregressive video models can generate minute-long videos in real time, but they produce generic subjects from text rather than specific subjects from user-provided images. Existing customization methods either require costly per-subject optimization or use pretrained conditioning networks that jointly process all video frames with bidirectional attention. Neither approach is designed for causal streaming. We present Custom Forcing, a training-free method that stores reference-based anchor frames in the persistent KV cache of a frozen autoregressive video model. However, fixed anchors face two limitations: simple conditioning allows identity to drift, and the text prompt continues to favor a generic subject. To address these problems, drift-adaptive value amplification (DVA) scales reference influence with the degree of identity drift, while anchor contrast guidance (ACG) steers generation away from the generic class prior. Over two-minute rollouts, fixed anchors fall from 0.58 to 0.42 in DINO-I, while Custom Forcing keeps it between 0.58 and 0.62 without reducing motion. Custom Forcing also achieves higher subject similarity than bidirectional customization methods and better preserves identity over 30s than causal image-to-video and reference-to-video models, while generating each frame 9.5--28.5 times faster than these long-video baselines.

</details>


### [37] [Kinematics-Induced Multimodal 3D Human Pose Estimation with Subject-Level Privacy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02943)
*Kaushik Bhargav Sivangi,Fani Deligianni*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper presents a unified framework for multimodal 3D Human Pose Estimation (3D HPE) that addresses both accuracy and privacy concerns. It combines RGB, LiDAR, and mmWave radar data through kinematics-induced sensor fusion, while incorporating subject-level privacy auditing via membership inference attacks and user-level differential privacy through an "Action Temporal Stratification" sampling strategy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation stems from privacy risks overlooked by traditional record-level analysis. Models trained on correlated observations from the same individuals can leak sensitive information, necessitating a privacy-aware approach to multimodal 3D HPE.

Method: The framework comprises three key components: (1) Multimodal model that aligns modality-specific joint representations, injects skeletal structure, and adaptively aggregates complementary sensor evidence; (2) Black-box subject membership inference attack with empirical pointwise maximal leakage analysis; (3) User-level differential privacy via Action Temporal Stratification - a population-weighted within-subject sampling strategy ensuring action and temporal coverage.

Result: The framework is evaluated on the MM-Fi dataset across three diverse experimental protocols, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

Conclusion: The paper introduces a comprehensive solution that balances pose estimation accuracy with privacy protection, offering both attack methodology for auditing and defense mechanisms via differential privacy for multimodal 3D HPE systems.

Abstract: Multimodal 3D Human Pose Estimation (3D HPE) combines complementary information from RGB, LiDAR, and mmWave radar, but models trained on correlated observations from the same individuals, raise privacy risks overlooked by record level analysis. We present a unified framework for multimodal 3D HPE that couples kinematics-induced sensor fusion with subject level privacy auditing and private training. First, our multimodal model aligns modality specific joint representation, injects skeletal structure and adaptively aggregates complementary sensor evidence for accurate pose prediction. Second, we formulate a black-box subject membership inference attack for 3D HPE, complemented by an empirical pointwise maximal leakage analysis, which characterizes how individual attack score outcomes change inference about the membership outcome. Third, we instantiate user-level differential privacy via Action Temporal Stratification, a population weighted within-subject sampling strategy that enforces action and temporal coverage. We evaluate our framework on the MM-Fi dataset across three diverse experimental protocols. Source-code will be released upon acceptance.

</details>


### [38] [When Predicting Nothing Beats SAM 3: Revisiting Evaluation in Video Object Segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02946)
*Jihwan Hong,Woohyeon Park,Jaeik Kim,Jaeyoung Do*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: FaVOS is a new benchmark for Video Object Segmentation (VOS) designed to evaluate methods under low temporal visibility, where target objects appear only intermittently within long temporal horizons. The standard J&F metric is shown to be problematic in this regime, as it rewards empty predictions on target-absent frames, allowing trivial baselines to outperform strong models like SAM 3.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing VOS benchmarks focus on temporally salient objects that remain visible for most of the video. However, real-world applications involve complex and long videos where target objects appear only intermittently. This gap motivates the creation of a benchmark specifically designed for low temporal visibility scenarios.

Method: The authors introduce FaVOS (Fractional Temporal Visibility) benchmark and propose Volumetric J&F metric. The new metric evaluates mask sequences as spatio-temporal volumes, reducing the dominance of target-absence rewards while preserving sensitivity to segmentation quality and temporal structure.

Result: The standard J&F metric collapses into absence classification in low visibility regimes - empty predictions receive high rewards on target-absent frames, allowing a trivial empty-mask predictor to outperform strong models like SAM 3. This reveals a fundamental mismatch between current metrics and practical VOS performance.

Conclusion: Volumetric J&F successfully mitigates the issue by reducing the dominance of target-absence rewards while maintaining sensitivity to segmentation quality and temporal structure, providing a more appropriate evaluation metric for VOS in practical scenarios with intermittent object visibility.

Abstract: Video Object Segmentation (VOS) in complex and long videos is increasingly important for real-world applications, where target objects often appear only intermittently within long temporal horizons. However, existing benchmarks largely focus on temporally salient objects that remain visible for most of the video. To address this gap, we introduce FaVOS (A Benchmark for Video Object Segmentation with Fractional Temporal Visibility), a benchmark designed to evaluate VOS methods under low temporal visibility. We show that, in this regime, the standard J&F metric can collapse VOS evaluation into absence classification, because empty predictions receive high rewards on target-absent frames. Consequently, even a trivial empty-mask predictor can outperform strong models such as SAM 3, revealing a fundamental mismatch between current metrics and practical VOS performance. To mitigate this issue, we propose Volumetric J&F, which evaluates mask sequences as spatio-temporal volumes and reduces the dominance of target-absence rewards while preserving sensitivity to segmentation quality and temporal structure. Project page: https://aidaslab.github.io/FaVOS.

</details>


### [39] [TerraVis: Towards Evaluation of World-Grounded Visual Consistency in Text-to-Image Generation via MLLM Workflows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02959)
*Shuai Fu,Jing Gu,Jian Zhou,Zicheng Duan,Gengze Zhou,Qi Wu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: TerraVis introduces a new evaluation framework for text-to-image models that assesses "world-grounded visual consistency" - whether generated images obey real-world physical laws and plausibility. It defines a taxonomy of 18 violation types across object, interaction, and scene levels, uses an MLLM for detection, and achieves higher correlation with human judgments than existing metrics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing metrics for text-to-image models focus on fidelity, aesthetics, preference, and text-image alignment, but fail to capture violations of real-world plausibility such as malformed objects, impossible anatomy, physically implausible interactions, or inconsistent spatial relationships. This gap motivates the need for a dedicated world-consistency evaluation framework.

Method: TerraVis employs a multi-stage evaluation framework: (1) uses an MLLM to assess image eligibility for evaluation, (2) detects violations across 18 taxonomy-defined types spanning object-level, interaction-level, and scene-level failures, (3) classifies violations as minor or major, and (4) derives an overall world-consistency score.

Result: TerraVis achieves the strongest correlation with human judgments of world consistency among existing metrics on two widely used benchmarks across diverse open-source and proprietary text-to-image models. The results reveal that models performing well on conventional metrics can still exhibit substantial world-consistency failures.

Conclusion: World consistency is a complementary evaluation dimension to existing metrics. TerraVis enables systematic quantification, diagnosis, and comparison of world-consistency failures in generated images, providing a valuable tool for evaluating and improving text-to-image models.

Abstract: Recent text-to-image models have made substantial progress in photorealism, aesthetics, and text-image alignment. Yet visually appealing images can still violate real-world plausibility, exhibiting malformed object structures, impossible anatomy, physically implausible interactions, or inconsistent spatial relationships. Such failures are not well captured by existing fidelity, aesthetics, preference, or alignment metrics. To address this gap, we introduce TerraVis, a framework for evaluating world-grounded visual consistency in generated images. TerraVis defines a structured taxonomy of world-consistency violations spanning object-, interaction-, and scene-level failures, and employs a multi-stage evaluation framework to identify and quantify them. Given an image, TerraVis first uses an MLLM to assess its eligibility for evaluation, then detects violations across 18 taxonomy-defined types and classifies them as minor or major to derive an overall world-consistency score. Across diverse open-source and proprietary text-to-image models on two widely used benchmarks, TerraVis achieves the strongest correlation with human judgments of world consistency among existing metrics. Our benchmark results further show that models that achieve strong performance on conventional metrics can still exhibit substantial world-consistency failures. These findings highlight world consistency as a complementary evaluation dimension and demonstrate that TerraVis enables systematic quantification, diagnosis, and comparison of such failures. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/ShyFoo/TerraVis.

</details>


### [40] [Post-Training Frontier Text-to-Image Models by Composing Preference and Rubric Rewards](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02967)
*Yuanhao Ban,I-Hung Hsu,Anastasios Angelopoulos,Wei-Lin Chiang,Ion Stoica,Cho-Jui Hsieh*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper presents a post-training method for text-to-image generation models using a composition of preference rewards (trained with Bradley-Terry on human preference data) and rubric-based rewards (evaluating prompt faithfulness and safety). The authors address the challenge of combining heterogeneous reward signals and show their approach achieves state-of-the-art results on the Arena leaderboard, with Ideogram-4 reaching 1223.5 Elo. They also release a 1K training dataset for reproducibility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current text-to-image models lack comprehensive reward signals for post-training improvement, as no single reward captures full human preference. The authors aim to develop an effective post-training recipe that balances multiple reward types while preventing reward hacking.

Method: The method combines two reward components: (1) preference reward using Bradley-Terry objective trained on large-scale human preference data, and (2) rubric-based rewards evaluating prompt faithfulness and safety. A novel reward composition strategy is proposed to replace naive weighted averaging, which the authors show leads to suboptimal optimization.

Result: RL-trained Flux2dev achieves 69 Elo points above the base model on Arena leaderboard. Post-trained Ideogram-4 reaches an Elo of 1223.5, surpassing all open-source models. The 1K subset (Arena-T2I-Training) recovers some gains of full-scale training.

Conclusion: Effective rewards for frontier generative-model training require broad coverage of user intent and robustness to exploitation under optimization. The proposed reward composition strategy successfully balances preference optimization with rubric satisfaction, achieving state-of-the-art performance on the Arena text-to-image leaderboard.

Abstract: Recent text-to-image generation models have achieved remarkable visual quality, but improving them through post-training remains challenging because no single reward signal captures the full range of human preference. In this work, we develop a simple and effective post-training recipe for open-domain text-to-image generation based on the composition of complementary reward signals. Our reward system consists of two main components: a preference reward, trained on large-scale human preference data using a Bradley-Terry objective to capture overall human aesthetic and perceptual preferences, and rubric-based rewards, which explicitly evaluate prompt faithfulness and other desirable properties while providing safeguards against reward hacking. A key challenge is how to combine these heterogeneous reward signals. We show that a naive weighted average leads to suboptimal optimization behavior, and propose a simple reward composition strategy that more effectively balances preference optimization with rubric satisfaction. In the Arena text-to-image leaderboard (https://arena.ai/), our RL-trained Flux2dev achieves an Elo rating 69 points above the base model, and our post-trained Ideogram-4 surpasses every open-source model on the leaderboard, reaching an Elo of 1223.5. (Claims of state-of-the-art performance are based on the Arena leaderboard snapshot as of September 4, 2026.) Our results suggest that effective rewards for frontier generative-model training require broad coverage of user intent and robustness to exploitation under optimization. To support reproducible research, we release Arena-T2I-Training, a 1K subset of training data that recovers some gains of full-scale training, providing a resource that we hope will facilitate future work on post-training for text-to-image models.

</details>


### [41] [Rethinking Fixed Temporal Grids: Frequency-Disentangled Motion Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03012)
*Yunjiao Zhou,Junlang Qian,Gen Li,Xinying Guo,Lihua Xie,Jianfei Yang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: FreqMo is a novel scale-adaptive motion representation that uses wavelet frequency band decomposition to separate human motion dynamics across temporal scales, addressing the mismatch between uniform temporal grid encoding and the heterogeneous nature of human motion (slow trajectories vs rapid transient events).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current human motion generation methods encode motion on uniform temporal grids where every token spans the same fixed time window. However, human motion is temporally heterogeneous - slow evolving global trajectories coexist with rapid transient events like foot contacts and joint impulses. This mismatch causes: 1) entangling of motion frequencies, 2) redundancy in slow regions, and 3) loss of rapid details that distinguish realistic motion.

Method: 1) Wavelet frequency band decomposition to separate dynamics across temporal scales while preserving temporal localization and exact reconstruction. 2) Unified Frequency Residual Quantization (UFRQ) to encode all frequency bands within a single shared codebook, enabling threefold compression of token sequence and stable single-stage generation.

Result: FreqMo achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) fidelity with substantially improved high-frequency preservation. The decomposition also transfers effectively to continuous diffusion backbones.

Conclusion: The proposed scale-adaptive representation successfully addresses the temporal heterogeneity problem in human motion generation. By decomposing motion into wavelet frequency bands and encoding them with UFRQ, the method achieves better fidelity while preserving rapid motion details and enabling efficient compression. The approach is versatile enough to transfer to continuous diffusion backbones.

Abstract: Most human motion generation methods encode motion as tokens on a uniform temporal grid, where every token spans the same fixed time window. Human motion, however, is temporally heterogeneous: slowly evolving global trajectories coexist with rapid transient events such as foot contacts and joint impulses. Forcing such multi-scale dynamics onto tokens of identical temporal resolution entangles motion frequencies, leaving slow regions redundant while smoothing out the rapid details that distinguish realistic motion. We propose \textbf{FreqMo}, a scale-adaptive motion representation that decomposes motion into wavelet frequency bands, separating dynamics across temporal scales while preserving temporal localization and exact reconstruction. Unified Frequency Residual Quantization (UFRQ) then encodes all bands within a single shared codebook, compressing the token sequence threefold and enabling stable single-stage generation. Experiments show FreqMo attains SOTA fidelity with substantially improved high-frequency preservation, and the same decomposition transfers to continuous diffusion backbones.

</details>


### [42] [RYOPO: Bringing End-to-End Category-Level Object Pose Estimation into Real Time](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03013)
*Hakjin Lee,Junghoon Seo,Jaehoon Sim*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: RYOPO is an end-to-end trainable query-based RGB-D method for category-level object pose estimation that jointly detects, segments, and estimates 9-DoF poses (rotation, translation, size) without external instance segmentation or CAD priors, achieving real-time performance at 31.8 FPS.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing accurate RGB-D methods for category-level pose estimation rely on separate stages (external instance segmentation + crop-based pose estimation), which introduces object-dependent processing costs and hinders real-time inference. The authors aim to bring accurate pose estimation into real time with an end-to-end approach.

Method: End-to-end query-based RGB-D set predictor with: (1) Shared image and scene encoding to avoid repeated per-object crop encoding; (2) Query-conditioned geometry pathway associating observed 3D points and RGB features with object queries while incorporating shared scene context; (3) Object-centric refinement using pose-conditioned cross-attention and recurrent residual corrections on explicit pose state.

Result: On NOCS: substantially improves published RGB-D joint detection and pose estimation results. On REAL275 and HouseCat6D: achieves competitive performance compared with two-stage methods under all-object evaluation. Real-time full-frame pose estimation at 31.8 FPS on RTX A6000.

Conclusion: The proposed RYOPO achieves state-of-the-art or competitive results on benchmark datasets while enabling real-time inference, demonstrating the feasibility of end-to-end RGB-D category-level pose estimation without separate segmentation or CAD priors.

Abstract: Category-level object pose estimation predicts the rotation, translation, and metric size of unseen instances within known categories. Many accurate RGB-D methods rely on external instance segmentation and crop-based pose estimation, introducing separate stages and object-dependent processing costs that hinder real-time inference. To bring accurate pose estimation into real time, we present \ours{}, an end-to-end trainable query-based RGB-D set predictor. It jointly detects and segments objects and estimates their \mbox{9-DoF} poses without explicit CAD-derived shape priors or a separately trained instance segmentor. Shared image and scene encoding avoids repeated per-object crop encoding. A query-conditioned geometry pathway associates observed 3D points and RGB features with object queries and incorporates shared scene context. Object-centric refinement uses the resulting point descriptors to update an explicit pose state through pose-conditioned cross-attention and recurrent residual corrections. On NOCS, \ours{} substantially improves on published RGB-D joint detection and pose estimation results. It achieves competitive performance compared with two-stage methods under all-object evaluation on REAL275 and HouseCat6D, while enabling real-time full-frame pose estimation at $31.8$ FPS on an RTX~A6000. Project page: https://yopo-series.github.io/RYOPO-project-page/.

</details>


### [43] [OmniAct3D: Leveraging Foundation Geometry and Evidence-Grounded Reasoning for Panoramic 3D Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03015)
*Runtong Wu,Fei Teng,Di Wen,Guoqiang Zhao,Kunyu Peng,Kailun Yang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: OmniAct3D is a framework that adapts perspective-trained Vision Foundation Model (VFM) detectors to equirectangular projection (ERP) for 360° surround 3D detection in mobile embodied agents. It addresses the geometric mismatch between perspective images and ERP through specialized adapters and reasoning modules.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Mobile embodied agents require accurate 3D detection, but existing VFM-based detectors rely on narrow-view monocular or discrete perspective views, limiting coherent surround perception. While ERP encodes 360° scenes in a single image, it organizes geometry differently from perspective views, making object-relevant cues difficult to model, localize, and preserve.

Method: OmniAct3D comprises three key components: (1) ERP-Ray Geometry Adapter (ERGA-Ray) models spherical viewing rays and periodic spatial structure to resolve geometric mismatch; (2) Visual-Action Reasoning Chain (VARC) grounds detection hypotheses in panoramic evidence and converts them into structured geometric actions; (3) Appearance-Guided Heading Expert (AGHE) re-encodes object regions at higher resolution to recover local cues lost under fixed token budgets.

Result: OmniAct3D improves 2.96 NDS points on Spheriverse over the previous best 3D detector, and 24.87 mAP points on PanoMMOcc over the unadapted VFM baseline. With target-specific geometry adaptation, VARC retains 95-98% of same-configuration mAP, indicating reusable object-level 3D reasoning across sensing configurations.

Conclusion: The proposed OmniAct3D framework successfully adapts perspective-trained VFM detectors to ERP for 360° 3D detection, preserving transferable VFM priors while addressing geometric mismatches. The approach demonstrates cross-configuration generalizability with high retention of detection performance.

Abstract: Accurate 3D detection is essential for mobile embodied agents, while Vision Foundation Models (VFMs) offer transferable visual and geometric priors. Yet existing VFM-based 3D detectors rely on narrow-view monocular images or discrete perspective views, limiting coherent surround perception; equirectangular projection (ERP) instead encodes a continuous 360 scene in a single image. Direct transfer remains difficult because ERP organizes geometry and visual information differently, making object-relevant cues hard to model, localize, and preserve. We propose OmniAct3D, a framework that adapts perspective-trained VFM detectors to ERP while preserving transferable VFM priors. To resolve geometric mismatch, the ERP-Ray Geometry Adapter (ERGA-Ray) models spherical viewing rays and periodic spatial structure. To localize evidence in scene-wide context, the Visual-Action Reasoning Chain (VARC) grounds each hypothesis in relevant panoramic evidence and converts it into a structured geometric action. To recover local cues lost under fixed token budgets, the Appearance-Guided Heading Expert (AGHE) re-encodes object regions at higher resolution for heading estimation. Experiments show that OmniAct3D improves over the previous best 3D detector by 2.96 NDS points on Spheriverse and over the unadapted VFM baseline by 24.87 mAP points on PanoMMOcc. With target-specific geometry adaptation, VARC retains 95--98% of the same-configuration mAP, indicating reusable object-level 3D reasoning across sensing configurations. The source code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/FeiT-FeiTeng/OmniAct3D.

</details>


### [44] [ReSCUE: Re-translation with Sentence Commitment for Unsegmented Long-Form Simultaneous Sign Language Translation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03022)
*Sihan Ren,Gaozheng Li,Yuanshang Quan,Yiming Qin,Fuyi Yang,Chang Liu,Lan Xu,Minye Wu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: ReSCUE is a unified framework for simultaneous sign language translation on continuous, unsegmented video streams, addressing the gap between offline sentence-level methods and real-world streaming requirements.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing SLT methods are confined to sentence-level, offline settings with pre-segmented inputs, which hinders deployment in realistic scenarios involving continuous, unsegmented video streams.

Method: ReSCUE combines three key components: (1) inference-aware training to handle partial inputs, non-signing pauses, and multi-sentence contexts; (2) stabilized re-translation for low-latency yet revisable predictions with reduced output flicker; (3) sentence commitment mechanism for online segmentation and memory management.

Result: On standard sentence-level benchmarks, ReSCUE achieves lower latency and the best translation quality under low-latency settings. On long-form unsegmented datasets, ReSCUE approaches the translation quality of oracle offline systems using ground-truth sentence boundaries, while operating at substantially lower latency.

Conclusion: ReSCUE demonstrates practicality for real-world streaming scenarios by bridging the gap between offline training assumptions and online inference requirements in simultaneous sign language translation.

Abstract: Simultaneous Sign Language Translation (SLT) is critical for real-time communication, yet existing methods remain largely confined to sentence-level, offline settings that assume pre-segmented inputs. These assumptions hinder deployment in realistic scenarios involving continuous, unsegmented video streams. We present ReSCUE, a unified framework for simultaneous SLT on unsegmented long-form sign language videos that aligns training and inference with realistic streaming conditions. ReSCUE combines inference-aware training to handle partial inputs, non-signing pauses, and multi-sentence contexts, stabilized re-translation to enable low-latency yet revisable predictions with reduced output flicker, and a sentence commitment mechanism for online segmentation and memory management. Experiments on standard sentence-level benchmarks show that ReSCUE achieves lower latency and the best translation quality under low-latency settings. On long-form unsegmented datasets, ReSCUE approaches the translation quality of oracle offline systems that use ground-truth sentence boundaries, while operating at substantially lower latency, demonstrating its practicality for real-world streaming scenarios.

</details>


### [45] [CrowdOcc: Monocular Semantic Scene Completion for Quadruped Robots in Crowded Indoor Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03031)
*Feiyang Chen,Jincheng Hu,Yiduo Chen,Jihao Li,Yue Liang,Bingzhao Gao,Yanjun Huang,Yuanjian Zhang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: CrowdOcc is an RGB-D dataset and monocular semantic scene completion framework designed for quadruped robots operating in crowded indoor environments. The dataset contains 25.1K frames from 11 indoor scenes with semantic occupancy annotations. The framework combines Normal Guided Scene Geometry Fusion (NGSGF) for occlusion-robust geometry estimation and Human-Centric Sparse Interaction (HCSI) for modeling human-centered relations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Monocular semantic scene completion for quadruped robots in real crowded indoor environments remains underexplored. The key challenges include human-scene occlusion disrupting static geometry predictions and human occupancy predictions being incomplete or spatially misplaced. Existing methods lack proper handling of human-scene interactions in cluttered indoor settings.

Method: The framework integrates two core components: (i) Normal Guided Scene Geometry Fusion (NGSGF) - combines depth-aware lifting with surface-normal cues to achieve occlusion-robust geometry estimation; (ii) Human-Centric Sparse Interaction (HCSI) - selectively models human-human and local human-scene relations in 3D. The CrowdOcc dataset was constructed using static-dynamic decoupling to generate semantic occupancy annotations.

Result: The method achieves state-of-the-art SSC performance on CrowdOcc's scene-disjoint test set: 15.80 IoU (scene-level), 11.40 mIoU (mean IoU), and 46.23 Human IoU, demonstrating strong generalization to unseen indoor scenes.

Conclusion: The proposed CrowdOcc dataset and monocular SSC framework successfully address the challenges of semantic scene completion in crowded indoor environments for quadruped robots. The combination of geometry fusion and human-centric interaction modeling enables robust performance even with significant human-scene occlusion, showing effective generalization to unseen scenes.

Abstract: Monocular semantic scene completion (SSC) for quadruped robots remains underexplored in real crowded indoor environments, where human-scene occlusion disrupts static geometry and human occupancy predictions are often incomplete or spatially misplaced. We present CrowdOcc, an RGB-D dataset and monocular SSC framework for this setting. CrowdOcc contains 25.1K frames from 11 indoor scenes, with semantic occupancy annotations constructed through static dynamic decoupling. Our framework combines: (i) Normal Guided Scene Geometry Fusion (NGSGF) to complement depth-aware lifting with surface-normal cues for occlusion robust geometry; and (ii) Human-Centric Sparse Interaction (HCSI) to selectively model human-human and local human scene relations in 3D. Our method achieves state-of-the-art SSC performance on CrowdOcc's scene-disjoint test set, reaching 15.80 IoU, 11.40 mIoU, and 46.23 Human IoU, demonstrating generalization to unseen indoor scenes.

</details>


### [46] [Parasitic Co-Denoising: Unlocking 3D Human Motion Generation in a Frozen Video Diffusion Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03047)
*Yunjiao Zhou,Junlang Qian,Lihua Xie,Jianfei Yang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A novel paradigm called "parasitic co-denoising" that extracts explicit 3D motion from a frozen text-to-video diffusion model (Wan2.1) without training a separate motion model, using a lightweight Parasitic Motion Decoder (PMD) that reads intermediate features along the denoising schedule.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors investigate whether implicit 3D motion knowledge in large-scale text-to-video diffusion models (never supervised on explicit 3D motion) can be turned into explicit 3D motion generation without training a separate motion model.

Method: 1) Probing a frozen Wan2.1 model reveals recoverable motion signals in intermediate states across the entire denoising schedule; 2) Introducing parasitic co-denoising - decoding motion from the host model along its denoising schedule; 3) Instantiating as Parasitic Motion Decoder (PMD) - an efficient flow-matching decoder that shares the host's noise schedule and reads intermediate features through σ-adaptive multi-layer fusion, leaving the host model unmodified.

Result: PMD leads dedicated motion generators on text-motion alignment while using only a small fraction of their trainable parameters. It produces paired video and motion in a single pass that motion-only baselines cannot match.

Conclusion: Implicit motion knowledge in text-to-video models can be effectively extracted as explicit 3D motion through parasitic co-denoising, achieving superior text-motion alignment with minimal parameters compared to dedicated motion generators.

Abstract: Despite never being supervised on explicit 3D motion, large-scale text-to-video diffusion models synthesize realistic human motion in their generated videos. We ask whether this implicit knowledge can be turned into explicit 3D motion generation, without training a separate motion model. Probing a frozen Wan2.1 reveals that a recoverable motion signal is present in its intermediate states across the entire denoising schedule, not confined to the clean output. Motivated by this, we introduce parasitic co-denoising, a paradigm in which motion is decoded from the host model along its denoising schedule rather than produced by an independent generator. We instantiate it as the Parasitic Motion Decoder (PMD), an efficient flow-matching decoder that shares the host's noise schedule and reads its intermediate features through a $σ$-adaptive multi-layer fusion, leaving the host unmodified. Drawing its coverage from the host rather than from motion data, PMD leads dedicated motion generators on text-motion alignment at a small fraction of their trainable parameters, while producing paired video and motion in a single pass that motion-only baselines cannot match.

</details>


### [47] [BeeWhere: Segmenting Bumble Bee Colonies to Quantify Behavioral Effects](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03051)
*Roberta Hunt,August Easton-Calabria,James Crall*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: BeeWhere is an AI-assisted workflow that combines ArUco fiducial markers with YOLO-based instance segmentation to track bumble bee (Bombus impatiens) behavior in dense colony environments, overcoming limitations of tag-based tracking when markers are obscured.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing tag-based tracking methods fail when markers are obscured in dense, occluded nest environments and provide limited information about body extent, spatial context, and untagged individuals. There is a need for scalable methods to measure individual- and colony-level bee behavior.

Method: Annotated 483 frames containing 8,843 bee instances plus pollen balls, nest structures, and chamber boundaries. Trained YOLO instance segmentation models for detection and combined ArUco detections with deep-learnt instance segmentations to quantify behavioral metrics including nearest-neighbor distance, proximity to nest structures, spatial occupancy, and detection counts over time.

Result: BeeWhere increased detection rates compared to tag-based tracking, particularly when bees were partially obscured or under challenging imaging conditions. It also captured treatment-associated changes in bee spatial organization not detected by tag-based tracking alone.

Conclusion: Instance segmentation can complement fiducial-marker tracking by recovering behaviorally meaningful signals under challenging colony conditions, enabling more comprehensive behavioral analysis in pesticide exposure studies and other ecological research.
