Abstract: Social bees are important pollinators that support biodiversity and crop pollination globally and serve as important model systems for collective behavior, but scalable measurement of individual- and colony-level behavior remains difficult in dense, occluded nest environments. Existing monitoring workflows use fiducial tags (e.g., ArUco) to preserve individual identity, yet tag-based tracking can fail when markers are obscured and provide limited information about body extent, spatial context, and untagged individuals. We present BeeWhere, an AI-assisted annotation and analysis workflow that combines ArUco detections with deep-learnt instance segmentations to quantify bumble bee behavior from high-resolution colony images and videos. Using bumble bee (Bombus impatiens) microcolonies as a test case, we annotate 483 frames containing 8,443 bee instances. We additionally annotate pollen balls, nest structures, and chamber boundaries, and train YOLO instance segmentation models for downstream behavioral analysis. Instance segmentations enable quantification of important behavioral metrics based on body contours, including nearest-neighbor distance, proximity to nest structures, spatial occupancy within the nest, and detection counts over time. We apply the BeeWhere models to tag-based tracking in an exploratory validation study assessing the behavioral impacts of neonicotinoid pesticide exposure. BeeWhere increased detection rates compared to tag-based tracking, particularly when bees were partially obscured or under challenging imaging conditions, and also captured treatment-associated changes in bee spatial organization not captured using tag-based tracking alone. These results suggest that instance segmentation can complement fiducial-marker tracking by recovering behaviorally meaningful signals under challenging colony conditions.

</details>


### [48] [Where to Look Is Not How to Fix: Pre-Denoising Diagnostics and Modality-Dependent Control in Diffusion Composition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03068)
*Fangzheng Wu,Brian Summa*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper studies compositional failures in text-to-image diffusion models (SD1.5, SDXL, SD3) by introducing a Compositional Stress Index (CSI) for text-encoder diagnostics and testing various denoiser interventions. The key finding is a "diagnosis-control dissociation": the coordinate that identifies compositional problems differs from the coordinate that improves generation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Text-to-image diffusion models often fail to correctly compose separate attributes with objects (e.g., "red cat" may generate a cat that isn't red). Understanding where these failures occur in the model architecture and how to fix them is crucial for improving generation quality.

Method: 1) Developed a text-only Compositional Stress Index (CSI) to identify common vs rare compositions across SD1.5, SDXL, and SD3
2) Conducted a six-prompt localization study testing interventions at different model locations:
   - Residual-minimizing embedding adapters
   - Cross-attention intervention
   - Selective boost at encoder vs decoder blocks
   - Selective subtraction and broad ablation
3) Measured outcomes via diagnostic-accessibility and Color Hit Rate (CHR)

Result: - Embedding adapters improve representation fit
- Cross-attention intervention increases CHR by 0.0272
- Deep encoder blocks show largest positive diagnostic-accessibility
- Decoder blocks show largest positive CHR response to selective boost
- Broad ablation of SDXL decoder cross-attention causes substantial CHR decrease
- Effects are modality- and architecture-dependent across different SD variants

Conclusion: Diagnosis-control dissociation exists: compositional defects can be detected before denoising using upstream diagnostics, but the representation coordinate that identifies risk is not necessarily the same coordinate or modality that improves generation. This suggests different mechanisms are responsible for diagnosing vs controlling compositional failures.

Abstract: Understanding compositional failures in text-to-image diffusion requires identifying both where stress is detectable and how intervention changes the output. We study these questions through a controlled anchor--stress protocol that jointly evaluates text-encoder diagnostics and denoiser interventions. We introduce a text-only Compositional Stress Index (CSI), which separates common from rare compositions across SD1.5, SDXL, and the SD3 text path and provides an upstream diagnostic coordinate. A matched six-prompt localization study links intervention location to distinct outcomes: residual-minimizing embedding adapters improve representation fit, while downstream cross-attention intervention increases color hit rate (CHR) by 0.0272. Across SD1.5 and SDXL denoiser blocks, the largest positive signed diagnostic-accessibility mean occurs at the deep encoder, whereas selective boost has its largest positive mean CHR response at decoder blocks. Selective subtraction and broad ablation reveal further modality- and architecture-dependent responses, including a substantial CHR decrease when SDXL decoder cross-attention is broadly ablated. We find a diagnosis-control dissociation under our controlled attribute-object composition setting: compositional defects are diagnosable before denoising, but the representation coordinate that exposes risk is not necessarily the coordinate or modality that improves generation.

</details>


### [49] [NegT2IBench: When Negation Changes the Picture. A Polarity Benchmark for Text-to-Image Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03084)
*Omar Elfatairy,Maria A. Bravo,Jessica Bader,Zeynep Akata*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: NegT2IBench is a benchmark designed to evaluate text-to-image models' ability to satisfy negated constraints (e.g., "a non-red cup"), addressing a gap in existing benchmarks that only measure affirmative content generation. The benchmark contains 4,800 prompts with varying polarity (0-2 positive and negated statements) and uses detector-based scoring that is reproducible and auditable.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current T2I benchmarks measure whether requested content appears but overlook the complementary ability to satisfy negated constraints. Measuring negation presents unique challenges requiring careful prompt and evaluation design, as existing benchmarks don't distinguish between rendering what is asked versus withholding what is forbidden.

Method: The benchmark organizes 4,800 prompts by polarity—varying positive statements (0-2) and negated statements (0-2) independently to separate negation effects from prompt complexity. It uses detector-based scoring that is reproducible, auditable, and pinpoints which requirement failed. Evaluation covered 11 T2I models generating 211,200 images, with human validation on 600 images using three annotators.

Result: The detector-based scoring agrees with human annotations as closely as vision-language judges up to 30x larger while using only a fraction of GPU memory. Nine out of eleven T2I models score lower on single negated statements than single positive ones. Per-statement scoring reveals the largest loss occurs for color attributes and near zero for proximity relations. Notably, 41.5% of failed statements render exactly what the prompt forbids.

Conclusion: Rendering requested content and withholding forbidden content are distinct capabilities that aggregate compositional scores cannot distinguish. NegT2IBench directly measures the latter, providing a controlled testbed for diagnosing negation failures and developing methods to overcome them in T2I models.

Abstract: Text-to-image (T2I) models are judged by benchmarks that measure whether requested content appears, but these benchmarks largely overlook the complementary ability to satisfy negated constraints, for example, generating "a non-red cup." Measuring negation raises challenges not faced by affirmation-based benchmarks and requires careful prompt and evaluation design. We introduce NegT2IBench, a benchmark of 4,800 prompts covering two attribute types and four relation categories. Prompts are organized by polarity: the number of positive statements that must hold and negated statements that must not, each ranging from 0 to 2. Varying the two independently separates the effect of negation from the effect of prompt complexity. Our detector-based scoring is reproducible, auditable, and pinpoints which requirement failed. On 600 images with three-annotator labels, it agrees with humans as closely as vision-language judges up to 30x larger, while using only a fraction of their GPU memory. Across eleven T2I models and 211,200 images, nine score lower on a single negated statement than on a single positive one. Per-statement scoring reveals that the loss is largest for color and near zero for proximity, and that 41.5% of failed statements render exactly what the prompt forbids. Rendering what a prompt asks for and withholding what it forbids are distinct capabilities that an aggregate compositional score cannot distinguish. NegT2IBench measures the latter directly, providing a controlled testbed for diagnosing negation failures and developing methods to overcome them.

</details>


### [50] [Beyond Single Videos: Benchmarking and Active Evidence Seeking for E-Commerce Cross-Video Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03099)
*Jinghan Zhao,Yiman Hu,Liang Wu,Jian Xu,Bo Zheng*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: AdsCVR is the first e-commerce cross-video reasoning benchmark for comparing multiple videos. AdSeek is an agentic framework that actively gathers multimodal evidence through dynamic tool selection, trained via a rectified bootstrapping pipeline (RL → SFT → RL) with offline trajectory rectification to identify reasoning errors and missing evidence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multimodal models focus on single-video understanding and have limited ability to compare information across videos. E-commerce videos are information-dense and frequently compared by consumers and merchants, requiring models to locate fine-grained evidence among redundant frames and integrate visual details, speech, and on-screen text.

Method: AdSeek uses an agentic framework with dynamic visual and audio tool selection during multi-turn exploration, replacing static uniform sampling with active evidence acquisition. Training involves an offline trajectory rectification mechanism that identifies reasoning errors and missing multimodal evidence in RL-generated trajectories, providing supervised fine-tuning signals to reduce RL biases. The rectified bootstrapping pipeline has three stages: initial RL exposes reasoning bottlenecks, supervised fine-tuning corrects them, and final RL further improves the policy.

Result: AdSeek achieves 74.30% accuracy on the AdsCVR test split, outperforming its Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct backbone by 27.90 percentage points. It also generalizes to the open-domain CrossVid benchmark, demonstrating effective active evidence gathering.

Conclusion: The proposed AdSeek framework with rectified bootstrapping significantly improves cross-video reasoning in e-commerce videos, achieving substantial gains over the backbone model and demonstrating generalization to other domains.

Abstract: E-commerce videos are information-dense and frequently compared by consumers evaluating products and merchants assessing marketing strategies. However, existing multimodal models mainly focus on single-video understanding and have limited ability to compare information across videos. We introduce AdsCVR, the first e-commerce cross-video reasoning benchmark, containing 2,483 videos and 6,110 question-answer pairs across six reasoning dimensions. Cross- video reasoning requires models to locate fine-grained evidence among many redundant frames and integrate visual details, speech, and on-screen text. We therefore propose AdSeek, an agentic framework that dynamically selects visual and audio tools during multi-turn exploration, replacing static uniform sampling with active evidence acquisition. To address the sparse credit assignment of reinforcement learning, we develop an offline trajectory rectification mechanism that identifies reasoning errors and missing multimodal evidence in RL-generated trajectories. The corrected trajectories provide supervised fine-tuning signals that reduce biases learned during RL. This mechanism supports a rectified bootstrapping pipeline in which initial RL exposes reasoning bottlenecks, supervised fine-tuning corrects them, and a final RL stage further improves the policy. AdSeek achieves 74.30 percent accuracy on the AdsCVR test split, outperforming its Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct backbone by 27.90 percentage points. It also generalizes to the open- domain CrossVid benchmark, demonstrating effective active evidence gathering.

</details>


### [51] [In-Distribution Forcing for Long Video Generation at Test Time](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03120)
*Jeongwoo Shin,Youngyoon Choi,Sangwoo Jo,Hyunmog Kim,Sungjoon Choi,Joonseok Lee,Jaewoong Choi,Jaemoo Choi*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Summary generation failed


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Motivation analysis unavailable

Method: Method extraction failed

Result: Result analysis unavailable

Conclusion: Conclusion extraction failed

Abstract: Modern autoregressive (AR) video diffusion models excel at short-horizon video generation, yet generating long videos remains challenging due to drifting, where colors and textures shift, and motion dynamics decay. Existing works primarily rely on KV conditioning, which selects or modifies cached key-value (KV) entries to mitigate drifting. However, we observe that KV conditioning alone is insufficient as it assumes cached KV entries remain in-distribution. This assumption fails beyond the training horizon: nothing constrains the construction of KV entries during rollout, giving rise to the KV-provenance problem where cached entries themselves become out-of-distribution (OOD). To address this, we propose In-Distribution Forcing (ID-Forcing), a test-time framework that aligns both KV caching and KV conditioning with training configurations. Its key mechanism, self-caching, prevents OOD KV entries at their source. Each chunk is cached without attending to prior KV entry, keeping the rolling window exactly in-distribution. Consequently, ID-Forcing seamlessly extends short-horizon models to minute-scale video generation. Extensive evaluations show that our method remains competitive on standard video generation benchmark while substantially outperforming prior work in mitigating drifting, as validated by both our drift metrics and a user study.

</details>


### [52] [Foresight: planning future perception in streaming VLMs without retraining](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03123)
*Ashok Prasad Neupane,Dipan Bartaula,Ankit Belbase,Saugat Adhikari,Samip Ghimire,Saroj Poudel,Binod Bhattarai,Danda Pani Paudel*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: FORESIGHT is a dual-stream architecture for streaming vision-language models that uses future anticipation to dynamically configure computation in a training-free manner. It uses two Siamese LLMs - one for continuous processing and another for ahead-of-stream anticipation and planning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing streaming VLMs have fixed computational pathways throughout inference, meaning they cannot adapt computation to evolving scene dynamics where different future events demand different levels and forms of perception. The authors aim to enable dynamic, adaptive computation allocation based on anticipated future needs.

Method: FORESIGHT employs a dual-stream architecture with two Siamese LLMs sharing weights, input encoders, and KV cache. The first LLM processes incoming tokens continuously, while the second runs ahead to anticipate future context, plan future computation, and generate responses without interrupting streaming inference. Each plan decides timing, content, and sampling density. Execution uses schema-guided decoding and lightweight diff-based updates for efficient online reconfiguration.

Result: Using a frozen Qwen3-VL-8B backbone, FORESIGHT achieves 23.0 mean joint F1 on OmniPro Online (beating the strongest trained baseline by 9.5%), improves the backbone by 6.7 on StreamingBench and 15.4 on OVO-Bench, with the largest gain of 18.7 when evidence arrives later in the video stream.

Conclusion: FORESIGHT demonstrates that streaming VLMs can inherently anticipate the immediate future and leverage this capability for dynamic computation allocation without training. The approach achieves significant improvements across multiple benchmarks, particularly for scenarios where evidence arrives later in the stream, validating the effectiveness of anticipatory computation in vision-language streaming tasks.

Abstract: Existing streaming vision-language models (VLMs) continuously perceive and reason over visual streams, but their computational pathways remain fixed throughout inference. Consequently, they cannot adapt computation to evolving scene dynamics, where different future events demand different levels and forms of perception. We show that streaming VLMs inherently possess the ability to anticipate the immediate future, and leverage this capability to dynamically configure future computation in a training-free manner. Realizing such anticipatory computation, however, is very challenging: future anticipation must be sufficiently reliable to guide computation, planning must run concurrently with streaming inference, and online reconfiguration must incur negligible overhead. To address these challenges, we introduce FORESIGHT, a dual-stream architecture comprising two Siamese LLMs with shared weights, input encoders, and KV cache. The first LLM continuously processes incoming tokens, while the second runs ahead of the stream to anticipate future context, plan future computation, and generate task responses without interrupting streaming inference. Each plan decides when to reason next, what to check then, and how densely to sample, keeping transient evidence separate from persistent control. The resulting computation plan is executed online through an efficient reconfiguration protocol with schemaguided decoding and lightweight diff-based updates, enabling dynamic adaptation with low overhead. With a frozen Qwen3-VL-8B backbone, FORESIGHT achieves 23.0 mean joint F1 on OmniPro Online evaluation beating strongest trained baseline by 9.5%, while improving the backbone by 6.7 on StreamingBench and 15.4 on OVO-Bench, with the largest gain of 18.7 when evidence arrives later in the video stream. Our source code will be made publicly available.

</details>


### [53] [Behavior Pack Optimization for Video MLLM Post-Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03141)
*Zhaolu Kang,Shiyu Liu,Tailong Luo,Wei Zhang,Yingjie He,Lei Wei,Guansu Wang,Liang He,Siheng Wang,Guangyuan Dong,Jiaqi Su,Shuang Chen,Haoyu Ji,Qishi Zhan,Kaiyue Zhou*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Video MLLMs rely on appearance/language priors rather than temporal evidence. BPO replaces single-response rewards with behavior packs across counterfactual views, enforcing stability for irrelevant interventions, sensitivity for removed evidence, and abstention when no evidence remains. Achieves 4.7pp accuracy improvement, 7.8pp on temporal-hard subset, and 20.0pp abstention F1 improvement on Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Video MLLMs achieve high accuracy on benchmarks but this stems from appearance and language priors, not temporal evidence. Shuffling frames, masking answer segments, or occluding target objects barely changes predictions. This is traced to post-training: rewards computed on single response to original clip never asks model to behave consistently across views.

Method: Behavior Pack Optimization (BPO): Replaces single response with behavior pack of outputs across counterfactual views chosen by question type. Pack reward asks for: (1) stability when intervention is irrelevant, (2) sensitivity when key evidence is removed, (3) abstention when no evidence remains. Uses anchor-relative advantage: response on original view serves as per-prompt reference instead of group mean over mixed views to maintain stability at small pack sizes.

Result: On TempCompass, MVBench, and NExT-QA: BPO improves macro accuracy of Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct by 4.7pp, temporal-hard subset by 7.8pp, and abstention F1 by 20.0pp over budget-matched vanilla GRPO baseline. Gains transfer to Video-MME, LongVideoBench, and LLaVA-Video-7B. Ablations confirm improvements follow view sets, not rollout count.

Conclusion: BPO offers a pack-level perspective for evidence-grounded video reasoning. The approach successfully shifts video MLLMs from relying on priors to utilizing actual temporal evidence, with improvements generalizing across multiple benchmarks and models.

Abstract: Video multimodal large language models (MLLMs) keep climbing video question answering benchmarks, yet shuffling the frames, masking the segment that supports the answer, or occluding the target object barely changes their predictions. The accuracy rests on appearance and language priors, not on the temporal evidence the question asks for. We trace this to the unit of post-training: rewards are computed on a single response to the original clip, so the model is never asked to behave consistently across views. We propose Behavior Pack Optimization (BPO), which replaces the single response with a behavior pack of outputs across counterfactual views chosen by question type, scored jointly. The pack reward asks for stability when the intervention is irrelevant, sensitivity when key evidence is removed, and abstention when no evidence remains. To keep this objective stable at small pack sizes, BPO uses an anchor-relative advantage: the response on the original view serves as a per-prompt reference instead of a group mean over mixed views. On TempCompass, MVBench, and NExT-QA, BPO improves the macro accuracy of Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct by 4.7 pp, the temporal-hard subset by 7.8 pp, and abstention F1 by 20.0 pp over a budget-matched vanilla GRPO baseline from the same SFT checkpoint. The gains transfer to Video-MME, LongVideoBench, and to LLaVA-Video-7B; ablations confirm they follow the view sets, not the rollout count. We hope this pack-level perspective offers a useful starting point for the video MLLM and multimodal post-training community as the field moves toward evidence-grounded video reasoning.

</details>


### [54] [CalCErt: Bin-wise Certification of Confidence Calibration in Medical Image Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03142)
*Leo Fillioux,Stergios Christodoulidis,Stergios Christodoulidis,Maria Vakalopoulou,Jose Dolz*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces CalCErt, a post-hoc certification method that provides guarantees on confidence calibration of neural networks within adversarial perturbation regions. It combines empirical calibration estimates, statistical concentration bounds, and local Lipschitz estimates to bound worst-case miscalibration.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deep neural networks are vulnerable to adversarial perturbations that not only change predictions but also distort confidence scores, compromising uncertainty calibration. Existing certification methods only guarantee prediction stability, leaving calibration behavior under attack unaddressed. This creates a critical gap in safety-critical applications where reliable confidence estimates are essential.

Method: CalCErt combines three key components: (1) empirical calibration estimates from held-out data, (2) statistical concentration bounds for generalization, and (3) local Lipschitz estimates of the confidence function. Using these, the method derives data-dependent upper bounds on worst-case miscalibration within an ℓ₂-ball of radius R around each input. The approach is post-hoc and works with any pretrained differentiable classifier.

Result: CalCErt was evaluated on 11 medical image classification tasks with multiple adversarial perturbations. It achieves substantially higher certified coverage compared to baseline strategies while maintaining competitive tightness of bounds.

Conclusion: CalCErt provides a practical and efficient approach to certify bin-wise confidence calibration under adversarial attacks. The method successfully bridges the gap between prediction stability and calibration guarantees, offering valuable assurances for safety-critical applications where reliable uncertainty quantification is essential.

Abstract: Deep neural networks remain vulnerable to adversarial perturbations, which can distort not only predictions but also confidence scores, undermining uncertainty calibration. While existing certification methods focus on preserving the predicted category, providing guarantees on how calibration behaves under adversarial attacks remains overlooked. In this work, we introduce CalCErt, a simple and efficient post-hoc strategy that certifies bin-wise confidence calibration for any pretrained differentiable classifier. Our approach combines empirical calibration estimates, statistical concentration bounds, and local Lipschitz estimates of the confidence function to derive data-dependent upper bounds on worst-case miscalibration within an $ell_2$-ball of radius R. We evaluate CalCErt across 11 medical image classification tasks and multiple adversarial perturbations, demonstrating substantially higher certified coverage than baseline strategies while maintaining competitive tightness. Our code is available at https://github.com/leofillioux/calcert.

</details>


### [55] [Does Physics Live in the Activations? Localizing Physical Quantities in Video Diffusion Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03154)
*Jonas Kneifl,Jakub Skalski,Bartłomiej Twardowski,Kamil Deja*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether video Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) internalize physical principles or merely reproduce motion patterns by probing their internal representations for ground-truth physical quantities (kinematic motion, rigid-body dynamics under gravity and contact).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Video generation models produce realistic sequences and are proposed as world models, but recent benchmarks show they struggle with physical reasoning. This raises questions about whether they truly understand physics or just mimic familiar motion patterns.

Method: The researchers probe internal representations of video DiTs for simulator-derived ground-truth physical quantities spanning kinematic motion and rigid-body dynamics under gravity and contact. They use linear probes to decode physical quantities from model activations at different stages of the denoising process.

Result: Physical quantities are linearly decodable with high accuracy early in the denoising process, substantially outperforming baselines from the model's own noised latents. This indicates relevant physical information is actively constructed during denoising. Activations at on-object tokens carry physical information, and multi-frame quantities are readable from single latent frames. Probes show partial extrapolation to unseen scene variations and object configurations.

Conclusion: DiTs actively construct physical information during denoising rather than merely reproducing input patterns. The physical information is sharply localized within on-object tokens, computed globally but stored locally. Probing directions can serve as steering vectors to change model output, suggesting potential for interpretability and control.

Abstract: Video generation models produce strikingly realistic sequences and are increasingly proposed as world models, yet recent benchmarks reveal pronounced deficits in their physical reasoning. This raises the question of whether these models internalize physical principles or merely reproduce familiar motion patterns. We address this by probing internal representations of video Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) for simulator-derived ground-truth physical quantities spanning kinematic motion and rigid-body dynamics under gravity and contact. We find that these quantities are linearly decodable with high accuracy early in the denoising process, substantially outperforming a baseline decoded directly from the model's own noised latents, indicating that the relevant physical information is actively constructed during denoising rather than already present in the input. Additionally, we show that activations at on-object tokens carry the relevant physical information and that quantities defined over multiple frames are readable from single latent frames. Hence, information is sharply localized within the token sequence and is computed globally but stored locally. The probes further show partial extrapolation, transferring to scene variations and object configurations outside their training regime, so what they read is not simply a correlate of the scenes they were fit on. When fitted directly in the full-resolution activation space, the probing directions can serve as steering vectors to change the model's output.

</details>


### [56] [Geometry-Aligned Semantic Matching for Cross-Modal Planar Image Registration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03167)
*Zhiwei Wang,Defeng He,Yuxing Li,Meilu Zhu,Edmund Y. Lam*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: CDPM proposes a cross-modal image matching method for planar registration that combines geometrically consistent semantic representations (via adapted DINOv3) with fine-grained CNN features. It constructs a DINO-Centric Feature Pyramid where multi-scale DINO representations maintain stable cross-modal correspondences while a lightweight CNN branch provides local refinement details.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing semantic representations provide cross-modal consistency but lack geometric correspondence guidance, while fine-grained CNN features provide accurate local details but lack global semantic guidance. This limits stable and accurate geometric correspondence estimation across modalities.

Method: 1) Progressively adapt DINOv3 using geometrically consistent cross-modal patch pairs to enable feature similarity to better reflect true cross-modal spatial correspondences. 2) Construct a DINO-Centric Feature Pyramid where multi-scale DINO representations maintain stable cross-modal correspondences while a lightweight CNN branch provides auxiliary structural details for precise local refinement.

Result: On VIS-IR dataset, compared with dense matcher RoMa, CDPM improves AUC@3/5/10/20 by 7.36, 13.40, 13.75, and 10.42 percentage points respectively, and reduces mACE from 5.83 to 2.78 pixels. It also outperforms RoMa v2 across all metrics while requiring 45.6% fewer FLOPs.

Conclusion: CDPM achieves superior cross-modal image matching performance by combining geometrically consistent semantic representations from adapted DINOv3 with fine-grained CNN details, demonstrating significant improvements in accuracy and efficiency over state-of-the-art methods.

Abstract: Cross-modal image matching establishes stable and accurate geometric correspondences across modalities for planar registration. Existing semantic representations provide cross-modal consistency, but semantic similarity does not necessarily imply geometric correspondence. Meanwhile, fine-grained CNN features provide accurate local details but lack global cross-modal semantic guidance for stable refinement. To address these issues, we propose CDPM, which first establishes geometrically consistent semantic representations and then preserves their dominant role in correspondence estimation during fine-grained localization. Specifically, we progressively adapt DINOv3 using geometrically consistent cross-modal patch pairs, enabling feature similarity to better reflect true cross-modal spatial correspondences. We then construct a DINO-Centric Feature Pyramid, where multi-scale DINO representations maintain stable cross-modal correspondences, while a lightweight CNN branch provides auxiliary structural details for precise local refinement. Extensive experiments on three cross-modal datasets demonstrate the superior performance of CDPM. On VIS-IR, compared with the dense matcher RoMa, CDPM improves AUC@3/5/10/20 by 7.36, 13.40, 13.75, and 10.42 percentage points, respectively, and reduces mACE from 5.83 to 2.78 pixels. It also outperforms RoMa v2 across all metrics while requiring 45.6% fewer FLOPs. The online demo and dataset are available, and the code will be released on our project page at https://warren-wzw.github.io/CDPM/.

</details>


### [57] [PocketSplat: Mobile Gaussian Reconstruction via World-Space Latent Allocatio](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03192)
*Wenzhi Guo,Xianda Chen,Dongxuan Chen,Guangchi Fang,Bing Wang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: PocketSplat is a feed-forward framework for budgeted mobile Gaussian asset construction that allocates exact integer capacity across spatial latent cells and decodes Gaussian attributes only for retained candidates, enabling high-quality reconstruction on resource-constrained devices like iPhones.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Mobile Gaussian reconstruction requires both executing within device resource constraints and producing compact Gaussian assets suitable for downstream mobile use. Existing feed-forward reconstructors decode dense, image-aligned candidates with cardinality implicitly determined by input resolution and view count, leading to inefficient resource usage.

Method: PocketSplat organizes dense geometry-aware latent candidates in predicted world space, allocates exact integer capacity across local latent cells, and decodes complete Gaussian attributes only for retained candidates. The method uses cell-conditioned latent fusion to aggregate multi-view evidence before decoding, and spatial responsibility decoding to adapt Gaussian support after local sparsification.

Result: Experiments on DL3DV and out-of-distribution benchmarks demonstrate strong quality-budget trade-off against feed-forward Gaussian reconstruction baselines. On Mip-NeRF 360, PocketSplat executes directly on a target iPhone, constructing compact, higher-quality Gaussian assets substantially faster than a deployable streamed MVSplat variant, while native MVSplat and DepthSplat exceed device memory budget.

Conclusion: PocketSplat successfully enables high-quality mobile Gaussian reconstruction within strict device resource constraints, representing a practical solution for on-device 3D reconstruction and rendering applications.

Abstract: Mobile Gaussian reconstruction must satisfy two requirements: the reconstruction model must execute within a device resource envelope, and the resulting Gaussian asset must expose a representation size suited to downstream mobile use. Existing feed-forward Gaussian reconstructors commonly decode dense, image-aligned candidates whose final cardinality is implicitly determined by the input resolution and number of views. We present PocketSplat, a feed-forward framework for budgeted mobile Gaussian asset construction. Given a prescribed output budget, PocketSplat organizes dense geometry-aware latent candidates in predicted world space, allocates exact integer capacity across local latent cells, and decodes complete Gaussian attributes only for retained candidates. Cell-conditioned latent fusion aggregates repeated multi-view evidence before decoding, while spatial responsibility decoding adapts Gaussian support after local sparsification. Experiments on DL3DV and out-of-distribution benchmarks establish a strong quality--budget trade-off against feed-forward Gaussian reconstruction baselines. On Mip-NeRF 360, PocketSplat executes directly on a target iPhone and constructs compact, higher-quality Gaussian assets substantially faster than a deployable streamed MVSplat variant; native MVSplat and DepthSplat exceed the device memory budget.

</details>


### [58] [Bridging Research and Practice: A Systematic Evaluation of Generalist and Dermatology-Specific Models in Clinical Skin Lesion Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03193)
*Emanoel dos Santos,Kelvin Cunha,Rodrigo Mota,Fabio Papais,Thales Bezerra,Natalia Lopes,Erico Medeiros,Shirley Cruz,Jessica Araujo,Paulo Borba,Tsang Ing Ren*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper benchmarks various machine learning architectures (general-purpose, medical vision-language, foundation models, and task-specific classifiers) on dermatology datasets to evaluate their robustness under distribution shifts, modality changes, and demographic variability, aiming to bridge the gap between current state-of-the-art models and clinical deployment requirements.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Clinical dermatology remains challenging due to ambiguous diagnosis, high lesion variability, and differences in acquisition modalities and patient demographics. There's a need to systematically evaluate how contemporary models generalize across heterogeneous data sources for safe and equitable clinical use.

Method: Benchmarking diverse architectures on recent dermatology datasets spanning dermoscopic images and smartphone-based clinical photographs. Assessed robustness of general-purpose and medical vision-language models, foundation models, and task-specific dermatology classifiers (embedding-based approaches and CNNs) under distribution shifts, modality changes, and demographic variability.

Result: The paper quantifies the performance gap between current state-of-the-art models and clinical deployment requirements, though specific numerical results are not provided in the abstract.

Conclusion: The study provides evaluation of model limitations and contributes to the development of reliable, accessible, and clinically applicable AI systems for dermatology by identifying gaps between current models and clinical needs.

Abstract: The application of machine learning to dermatology has grown substantially in recent years, moving beyond proof-of-concept studies toward potential applications. However, clinical dermatology remains a challenging and still open problem. Diagnostic assessment is often ambiguous, and skin lesions exhibit high variability, compounded by differences in acquisition modality, device quality, and patient demographics. These factors hinder the development of robust models suitable for safe and equitable clinical use. To support translation into practice, it is essential to systematically evaluate how contemporary models generalize across heterogeneous data sources. In this work, we benchmark a diverse set of architectures on recent dermatology datasets, spanning dermoscopic images and smartphone-based clinical photographs. We assess the robustness of recent general-purpose and medical vision-language models, as well as foundation models, and compare them against task-specific dermatology classifiers, including embedding-based approaches and convolutional neural networks. Our study provides an evaluation of model performance under distribution shifts, modality changes, and demographic variability. By quantifying the gap between current state-of-the-art models and the requirements of clinical deployment, we aim to contribute to the development of reliable, accessible, and clinically applicable AI systems for dermatology.

</details>


### [59] [Contextual Flow Matching: Adaptive Step Selection in Flow Models for Efficient Visual Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03202)
*Divya Jyoti Bajpai,Arun Verma,Manjesh Kumar Hanawal*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: COFLOW is an inference-time method that adaptively selects the number of generation steps for Flow Matching models based on prompt features, achieving over 2.5x speedup without retraining the underlying model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Flow Matching enables high-quality visual generation but suffers from costly inference due to multiple sequential function evaluations. Existing acceleration methods either require additional training overhead, degrade quality, or fail to account for input-dependent variability.

Method: COFLOW is a context-aware, plug-and-play method trained online with an unsupervised reward that balances inference efficiency and generation fidelity. It adaptively selects step counts for each generation based on prompt features, requiring no retraining of the underlying generative model.

Result: Over 2.5x speedup while preserving perceptual and semantic quality. The method generalizes to both image and video generation.

Conclusion: COFLOW provides a practical solution for accelerating Flow Matching inference without compromising quality. The theoretical analysis establishes an O(1/K) forward-Euler discretization error bound under standard regularity conditions, providing formal guarantees for the approach.

Abstract: Flow Matching enables high-quality visual generation via continuous-time dynamics, but inference remains costly due to multiple sequential function evaluations. Existing acceleration methods reduce the number of function evaluations but often introduce additional training overhead, degrade quality, or fail to account for input-dependent variability. We propose COFLOW, an inference-time method that adaptively selects the step counts each generation based on the prompt features. Our context-aware COFLOW is trained online with an unsupervised reward that balances inference efficiency and generation fidelity. Our method is plug-and-play, requiring no retraining of the underlying generative model. It generalizes to image and video generation, achieving over 2.5x speedup while preserving perceptual and semantic quality. We further provide a theoretical analysis establishing an O(1/K) forward-Euler discretization error bound under standard regularity conditions.

</details>


### [60] [VisionMX: Unlocking Microscaling Post-Training Quantization for Vision Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03218)
*Elad Dror Cohen,Ofir Gordon,Lior Dikstein,Idan Achituve,Hai Victor Habi*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper investigates post-training MX (Microscaling) quantization for vision models, identifying three sources of error in direct conversion and proposing VisionMX, a method that optimizes bounded weight rounding and applies foldable affine correction to activations. The method is evaluated across image classification, object detection, semantic segmentation, and low-light image enhancement tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: MX formats are emerging as hardware-supported approaches for efficient training and inference, combining low-precision elements with shared block scales. However, their impact on vision models remains underexplored. The motivation is to systematically investigate post-training MX quantization across vision models and tasks to understand its limitations and improve its applicability.

Method: The authors first analyze direct conversion and identify three sources of error: (1) block-scale representation issues, (2) poor alignment of small convolutional weight tensors with nonuniform element grids, and (3) underuse of signed codes by nonnegative activations. Based on these findings, they propose VisionMX, which optimizes bounded weight rounding and applies a foldable affine correction to activations. They evaluate using several MX-style formats across multiple vision tasks.

Result: VisionMX improves over direct conversion and evaluated post-training quantization baselines. The largest performance recoveries are observed in architectures most sensitive to MX conversion, demonstrating the method's effectiveness for challenging vision models.

Conclusion: The study demonstrates that post-training MX quantization can be effectively applied to vision models with proper error mitigation techniques. VisionMX successfully addresses the identified error sources, providing significant performance improvements across various vision tasks and architectures, particularly for models most sensitive to MX conversion.

Abstract: Microscaling (MX) formats are emerging as a hardware-supported approach to efficient training and inference. They combine low-precision elements with shared block scales, but their impact on vision models remains underexplored. We systematically investigate post-training MX quantization across vision models and tasks. An analysis of direct conversion identifies three sources of error: block-scale representation, the poor alignment of some small convolutional weight tensors with nonuniform element grids, and the underuse of signed codes by nonnegative activations. These findings motivate VisionMX, a post-training MX quantization method that optimizes bounded weight rounding and applies a foldable affine correction to activations. We evaluate VisionMX across image classification, object detection, semantic segmentation, and low-light image enhancement using several MX-style formats. It improves on direct conversion and the evaluated post-training quantization baselines, with the largest performance recoveries in architectures most sensitive to MX conversion

</details>


### [61] [VDOT++: Unified Few-Step Video Generation via Unbalanced Optimal Transport Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03221)
*Yutong Wang,Xingtong Ge,Enhuai Liu,Yunke Wang,Tianfan Xue,Yu Qiao,Yaohui Wang,Xinyuan Chen,Chang Xu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: VDOT++ is a unified distillation framework for video diffusion models that reduces sampling cost while maintaining quality across text-to-video, image-to-video, and condition-based generation tasks. It addresses limitations of prior work (VDOT) by using asymmetric unbalanced optimal transport and weighted median aggregation instead of full-mass matching.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Video diffusion models are computationally expensive due to repeated evaluation of large backbones during sampling. Existing distribution matching distillation (DMD) uses reverse KL objective which can be unstable when student and teacher distributions have limited overlap. VDOT added optimal transport distillation (OTD) but its balanced full-mass matching assumption weakens for T2V and I2V tasks where one condition admits many valid outputs with non-aligned spatial content.

Method: VDOT++ introduces two key modifications: (1) Asymmetric unbalanced OTD formulation that allows unreliable student tokens to carry less mass while maintaining teacher token coverage - addressing "whom to match"; (2) ℓ1 ground cost with weighted median aggregation replacing mean-based aggregation to limit influence of distant transport targets - addressing "how selected targets should be aggregated". Additional contributions include sequential backward passes combining distribution matching with adversarial refinement, and decoupled score networks for cross-scale distillation where larger score networks improve compact generators.

Result: Experiments on UVCBench, VBench, VBench-I2V, and VACE benchmark show that four-step generators achieve competitive performance with many-step teachers and strong few-step baselines across all three task families (T2V, I2V, condition-based generation).

Conclusion: VDOT++ successfully unifies distillation for all three video generation task families through asymmetric unbalanced optimal transport and weighted median aggregation, achieving efficient video generation with minimal computational cost while maintaining quality across diverse conditions.

Abstract: Video creation spans text-to-video (T2V), image-to-video (I2V), and condition-based generation, yet video diffusion models remain costly because they repeatedly evaluate large backbones during sampling. Distribution matching distillation (DMD) reduces this cost, but its reverse Kullback--Leibler (KL) objective can provide unstable or incomplete guidance when the student and teacher distributions have limited overlap. VDOT addressed this issue by adding optimal transport distillation (OTD), whose explicit coupling supplies geometric directions for condition-based generation. Balanced OTD, however, performs full-mass matching between the spatial tokens of each corresponding student--teacher frame pair. This assumption weakens for T2V and I2V, where one condition admits many valid outputs and spatial content need not align across different realizations. We present VDOT++, a unified distillation framework that applies the same training recipe separately to generators for the three task families. It makes OTD robust to output diversity through an asymmetric unbalanced formulation that allows unreliable student tokens to carry less mass while maintaining coverage of the teacher tokens. An $\ell_1$ ground cost further replaces mean-based aggregation with a more mode-preserving weighted median that limits the influence of distant transport targets. The two changes respectively determine whom to match and how the selected targets should be aggregated. We additionally combine distribution matching and adversarial refinement through sequential backward passes, and exploit the decoupled score networks for cross-scale distillation, where larger score networks improve a compact generator. Experiments on UVCBench, VBench, VBench-I2V, and the VACE benchmark show that the resulting four-step generators are competitive with many-step teachers and strong few-step baselines across all three task families.

</details>


### [62] [Uncertainty as a Proxy for Semantic Correctness in Diffusion-Based Medical Image Synthesis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03224)
*Yuxuan Ou,Konstantinos Kamnitsas,OxAAA Study,AICT Consortium,Regent Lee,Vicente Grau*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether uncertainty quantification can serve as a proxy for anatomical correctness in diffusion-based medical image synthesis, specifically for NCCT-to-CECT synthesis using the AortaDiff framework. Six uncertainty methods are compared across pixel, region, and image levels, and for OOD detection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Diffusion models can synthesize CECT from NCCT, but visually realistic images may not be anatomically correct. Existing pixel-intensity and feature-space similarity metrics do not directly measure anatomical correctness, necessitating a new approach to assess generation quality.

Method: AortaDiff (multitask diffusion framework) jointly generates CECT images and lumen segmentations. Six uncertainty methods are compared: Ensemble, HyperDiff, BayesDiff (weight-based), MCDropout (architecture-perturbation), RDS (generative-stochasticity), and TTA (input-perturbation). Evaluation spans pixel, region, and image levels, plus OOD detection on external multi-centre dataset.

Result: Uncertainty proves informative at all three spatial scales, remains informative under distribution shift on external data, and supports OOD detection. MCDropout stands out: ranks among leading methods at every scale, generalizes well externally, and requires no extra training cost. However, uncertainty reliably flags severe failures but discriminates poorly among high-quality images.

Conclusion: Uncertainty serves as a practical and computationally economical signal for quality filtering, reliability assessment, and OOD detection in NCCT-to-CECT synthesis. MCDropout is recommended for its balanced performance and efficiency.

Abstract: Diffusion models can synthesise contrast-enhanced CT (CECT) from non-contrast CT (NCCT), avoiding contrast administration and its environmental and patient-access costs. However, visually realistic images are not necessarily anatomically correct, and the pixel-intensity and feature-space similarity metrics used to assess generation quality do not directly measure anatomical correctness. In this work, we investigate whether uncertainty can serve as a proxy for semantic correctness in diffusion-based medical image synthesis.
  We study NCCT-to-CECT synthesis using AortaDiff, a multitask diffusion framework that jointly generates CECT images and lumen segmentations. The segmentation output provides an explicit representation of the generated vascular anatomy, enabling segmentation-derived errors to be used as a quantitative measure of generation correctness. Six methods spanning weight (Ensemble, HyperDiff, BayesDiff), architecture-perturbation (MCDropout), generative-stochasticity (RDS) and input-perturbation (TTA) uncertainty are compared at the pixel, region and image levels, and for detection of clinically relevant out-of-distribution (OOD) cases.
  Uncertainty proves informative at all three spatial scales, remains informative on an external multi-centre dataset under distribution shift, and supports OOD detection. MCDropout stands out among the six: it ranks among the leading methods at every scale, generalizes well on the external dataset, and can be enabled at inference on any model already trained with dropout, so reliable uncertainty comes at no extra training cost. Uncertainty reliably flags severe failures but discriminates poorly among already high-quality images. These findings support uncertainty as a practical and computationally economical signal for quality filtering, reliability assessment and OOD detection in NCCT-to CECT synthesis.

</details>


### [63] [EmbPASS: Towards Cross-Embodiment Open Panoramic Segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03248)
*Pujun Guo,Yuanfan Zheng,Fei Teng,Mengfei Duan,Guoqiang Zhao,Yuheng Zhang,Kai Luo,Kailun Yang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces Cross-Embodiment Open Panoramic Segmentation task and EmbPASS benchmark for studying panoramic semantic segmentation across heterogeneous embodied platforms (Vehicle, Drone, Wearable, Quadruped). EPONet proposes RAMA and CAST modules to address cross-embodiment observation shifts, achieving 35.82% mIoU.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Heterogeneous embodied platforms exhibit substantial differences in observation viewpoints and spatial layouts, causing cross-embodiment observation shifts that challenge consistent panoramic perception. Existing studies on this problem are limited, necessitating systematic research.

Method: EPONet integrates two key components: (1) Relation-Aware Metric Adapter (RAMA) for enhanced spatial modeling, and (2) Content-Adaptive Semantic Transfer (CAST) for semantic transfer under heterogeneous embodied observations. The method is an open-vocabulary approach.

Result: EPONet achieves 35.82% mIoU on EmbPASS, outperforming the strongest baseline by 1.10% while remaining competitive on existing panoramic segmentation benchmarks.

Conclusion: The proposed EPONet with RAMA and CAST effectively addresses cross-embodiment challenges in panoramic segmentation, achieving state-of-the-art platform-balanced performance. The EmbPASS benchmark provides a valuable testbed for future research in cross-embodiment perception.

Abstract: Panoramic images provide a complete 360-degree field of view, enabling comprehensive scene understanding for embodied perception. However, heterogeneous embodied platforms exhibit substantial differences in observation viewpoints and spatial layouts, giving rise to cross-embodiment observation shifts that pose additional challenges to consistent and reliable panoramic perception, while systematic studies of this problem remain limited. To bridge this gap, we introduce a new task, termed Cross-Embodiment Open Panoramic Segmentation. Meanwhile, we establish EmbPASS, a multi-platform panoramic semantic segmentation benchmark spanning Vehicle, Drone, Wearable, and Quadruped platforms under a unified semantic taxonomy, providing a testbed for systematically studying cross-embodiment panoramic perception. We further propose EPONet, an open-vocabulary panoramic semantic segmentation network that integrates Relation-Aware Metric Adapter (RAMA) and Content-Adaptive Semantic Transfer (CAST) to enhance spatial modeling and semantic transfer under heterogeneous embodied observations. Extensive experiments show that EPONet achieves the best platform-balanced performance on EmbPASS with 35.82% mIoU, outperforming the strongest baseline by 1.10%, while remaining competitive on existing panoramic segmentation benchmarks. The source code and EmbPASS benchmark will be made publicly available at https://github.com/guopj1/EmbPASS.

</details>


### [64] [COSMI: COmpositional Synthesis of Multi-object Interactions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03252)
*Daniel Eskandar,Ilya A. Petrov,Gerard Pons-Moll*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: COSMI is a method that composes single-object human interaction clips into multi-object sequences using a language model and geometric checks, creating a dataset 30x larger than existing multi-object captures. A text-to-interaction diffusion transformer trained on this data generalizes to unseen object and interaction combinations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-object human interaction capture is combinatorially expensive, resulting in datasets with limited object diversity. However, since interactions are local, single-object captures already contain the components needed for multi-object activities.

Method: The method composes single-object interaction clips by: 1) balancing hands through mirroring, 2) transferring between bodies, 3) using a language model and geometric checks to validate plausible pairings. The COSMI model uses weight-shared object slots to generate variable numbers of objects predicted relative to body parts.

Result: COSMI dataset contains 222k sequences and 275 hours with up to 5 objects (nearly 30x the largest multi-object capture). The model outperforms baselines in text alignment and contact accuracy, with largest margins on unseen objects.

Conclusion: The compositional approach to dataset creation enables generalization to unseen object and interaction combinations. The pipeline can be extended by adding more datasets or hand-object recordings.

Abstract: Generative models of human-object interaction are bounded by the data that exists: everyday activities involve several objects, but most captured datasets record one at a time, as multi-object capture is combinatorially expensive. Our observation is that interactions are local, so single-object captures already contain the parts of multi-object activities. We compose them: contact-consistent clips of single interactions, mirrored to balance the hands, transfer between bodies, and a language model and geometric checks admit only the pairings that are plausible, semantically and physically. Therefore, the dataset grows combinatorially with the clips rather than recording time. The COSMI dataset holds 222k sequences and 275 hours with up to five objects, nearly thirty times the largest multi-object capture, and can be extended by adding datasets or even hand-object recordings. On this data we train the COSMI method, a text-to-interaction diffusion transformer that follows how the data is built: weight-shared object slots generate a variable number of objects, predicted relative to the body parts that move them. On a benchmark with an unseen object and unseen interaction combinations, models trained on the dataset generalize to the unseen combinations. COSMI outperforms baselines in text alignment and contact accuracy, where its margin is largest on the unseen object. Code, models, and the dataset pipeline will be released on the project page: https://ptrvilya.github.io/cosmi.

</details>


### [65] [Consecutive Posterior Fusion for Diffusive Recovery of Unobservable Image Structures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03261)
*Elena Morotti,Davide Evangelista,Elena Loli Piccolomini*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: CPF-DDNM introduces an inference-time strategy that fuses consecutive measurement-aware estimates to improve diffusion-based recovery of unobservable image structures in severely ill-posed inverse problems, without requiring retraining or additional denoiser evaluations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard diffusion posterior samplers rely on instantaneous measurement-aware estimates without exploiting information from previous posterior corrections. This limits their ability to recover unobservable or weakly constrained image structures in severely ill-posed imaging inverse problems.

Method: The method fuses consecutive measurement-aware estimates within the DDNM framework, which uses range/null-space decomposition. Consecutive fusion preserves the measurement-determined component while acting exclusively on the prior-driven null-space estimate. The approach includes a geometric interpretation and local error analysis to characterize the optimal time-dependent fusion coefficient, including the extrapolative regime.

Result: Experiments on sparse-view computed tomography, simulated low-dose CT, and medical image super-resolution show consistent improvements over DDNM and competitive performance against other diffusion-based inverse solvers.

Conclusion: CPF-DDNM provides an effective inference-time strategy for improving diffusion-based inverse problem solving by leveraging consecutive posterior corrections, achieving better recovery of unobservable structures without retraining or additional denoiser evaluations.

Abstract: Solving severely ill-posed imaging inverse problems requires recovering image structures that are unobservable or weakly constrained by the measurements. Diffusion models provide expressive learned priors for inferring such missing information, while posterior sampling incorporates measurement consistency along the reverse process. Standard diffusion posterior samplers, however, rely on instantaneous measurement-aware estimates, without explicitly exploiting information carried by previous posterior corrections.
  We introduce Consecutive Posterior Fusion Denoising Diffusion Null-Space Models (CPF-DDNM), an inference-time strategy that fuses consecutive measurement-aware estimates to improve the diffusive recovery of unobservable image structures, without requiring retraining or additional denoiser evaluations. We instantiate this principle within DDNM, whose range/null-space decomposition reveals that consecutive fusion preserves the measurement-determined component while acting exclusively on the prior-driven null-space estimate. We thus provide a geometric interpretation of CPF-DDNM and a local error analysis that characterizes the optimal time-dependent fusion coefficient, including the extrapolative regime.
  Experiments on sparse-view and simulated low-dose computed tomography, as well as medical image super-resolution, show consistent improvements over DDNM and competitive performance against diffusion-based inverse solvers.

</details>


### [66] [Moving Forward with Video Saliency: A New Dataset and Benchmark where Motion Matters](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03276)
*Susmit Agrawal,Rebecca Wanner,Juliane Verwiebe,Matthias Tangemann,Matthias Bethge,Matthias Kümmerer*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether video saliency prediction requires temporal information or can be adequately addressed with static image approaches. The authors verify prior findings that static baselines perform well on existing benchmarks (LEDOV), then introduce SalTempto, a new dataset with more dynamic content to properly evaluate temporal modeling capabilities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The video saliency field assumes temporal information is crucial, but prior work showed static baselines recover significant gaze information on LEDOV. This raises questions: (1) do current temporal architectures fail because they're limited, or (2) does LEDOV lack temporal patterns to measure? This work aims to resolve this ambiguity by creating a more dynamic benchmark.

Method: The authors: (1) Verified prior findings using a more capable gold standard and updated architectures; (2) Created SalTempto - a dataset of 224 highly dynamic video clips from HACS-Segments with gaze recordings from up to 16 subjects and training splits; (3) Compared fine-tuned static baselines against state-of-the-art temporal architectures on both LEDOV and SalTempto.

Result: On LEDOV: static baseline recovers most explainable gaze information; strongest temporal architecture shows minimal improvement. On SalTempto: static baseline captures only ~13% of headroom (vs. >50% on LEDOV); temporal architecture shows substantial gain over static baseline, but still leaves nearly half of headroom unexplained.

Conclusion: SalTempto properly measures temporal modeling capabilities, revealing that current temporal architectures do capture meaningful temporal information that LEDOV fails to measure. However, significant room for improvement remains - nearly 50% of headroom is still unexplained even with SoTA models. The paper also identifies human tendencies that models fail to capture.

Abstract: Video saliency prediction is inherently harder to model than static image saliency due to the additional temporal dimension. Video saliency benchmarks rest on the premise that predicting gaze on video requires utilizing temporal activity distributed across frames. Prior work has challenged this, showing that static baselines recover a significant fraction of the explainable gaze information on LEDOV, a popular video saliency dataset, and that video saliency models fail in the same places as this static baseline. We verify that this diagnosis still stands: under a more capable gold standard than the original analysis, and an updated panel of recent architectures, the strongest temporal architecture in the panel still does not substantially improve over a fine-tuned static baseline. However, it remains unclear whether the marginal gain reflects limitations of current temporal architectures or a lack of temporal patterns in the benchmark itself. We introduce SalTempto, a video saliency benchmark with greater dynamism: 224 clips of highly dynamic content, sourced from the HACS-Segments dataset so that each clip contains an event together with its lead-up and aftermath, with gaze recordings from up to 16 subjects and a training split for adapting pretrained models. On SalTempto, the static baseline recovers only about 13\% of the headroom above the centerbias, against more than half on LEDOV. A fine-tuned temporal architecture shows a substantial gain in performance over the static baseline, indicating that it does capture meaningfully more temporal information, which LEDOV fails to measure. Yet, even this SoTA model still leaves nearly half of SalTempto's headroom unexplained, indicating room for improvement in video saliency modelling. Examination of SalTempto also lets us describe human tendencies that models miss. SalTempto link: https://huggingface.co/datasets/bethgelab/video_saliency.

</details>


### [67] [T3lescope: Arbitrary-Resolution High-Fidelity Generative Surface Reconstruction from Images](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03308)
*Atsuhiro Noguchi,Tianhan Xu,Yiming Liang,Yuta Kikuchi,Masahiro Ishiyama,Shintaro Takagi,Hitoshi Murai,Eiichi Matsumoto*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: T3lescope is a novel method for reconstructing high-fidelity 3D scene meshes from posed multi-view images without per-scene optimization, working across scales from single objects to large outdoor scenes using a single fixed-resolution generator in an inference-time coarse-to-fine cascade.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Per-scene optimization methods lack learned 3D priors for sparse observations or glossy/transparent surfaces. Existing generative methods operate at fixed resolution over limited spatial extent, requiring partitioning large scenes into overlapping local regions, which harms global geometric consistency.

Method: T3lescope applies a single fixed-resolution generator across scene scales via inference-time coarse-to-fine cascade. A coarse level establishes scene layout, while finer levels perturb and denoise geometry inherited from the coarser level within progressively finer spatial cells to recover surface detail. The model is trained on individual cells at multiple scales with shared weights, enabling flexible levels, cell scales, and locations at inference time.

Result: T3lescope outperforms feed-forward and generative baselines on indoor, outdoor, and city-scale scenes, matches or surpasses per-scene optimization, and recovers fine structures as well as glossy and transparent surfaces. The method generalizes across diverse scenes, view counts, and image resolutions.

Conclusion: The proposed coarse-to-fine cascade approach with shared-weight multi-scale training enables efficient, consistent 3D reconstruction across various scene scales and surface types without per-scene optimization, achieving better global geometric consistency than partitioning-based methods.

Abstract: We reconstruct high-fidelity 3D scene meshes from posed multi-view images without per-scene optimization, across scales ranging from single objects to large outdoor scenes. Per-scene optimization methods lack the learned 3D prior needed when observations are sparse or surfaces are glossy or transparent. Existing generative methods leverage such priors to complete geometry in sparsely observed regions, but typically operate at a fixed resolution over a limited spatial extent, trading spatial coverage against detail. Reconstructing a large scene therefore often requires partitioning it into independently processed overlapping local regions, making it difficult to maintain global geometric consistency. To address these issues, we propose T3lescope, which applies a single fixed-resolution generator across scene scales in an inference-time coarse-to-fine cascade. A coarse level establishes the scene layout, and finer levels perturb and denoise geometry inherited from the coarser level within progressively finer spatial cells to recover surface detail. The model is trained on individual cells at multiple scales and shares its weights across all levels, so no hierarchy is fixed during training, and the number of levels, cell scales, and cell locations are determined at inference time. On indoor, outdoor, and city-scale scenes, T3lescope outperforms feed-forward and generative baselines, matches or surpasses per-scene optimization, and recovers fine structures as well as glossy and transparent surfaces. These results show that our method generalizes across diverse scenes, view counts, and image resolutions. Project page: https://pfnet-research.github.io/t3lescope/

</details>


### [68] [A Fully Automatic Pipeline for 3D Dendrite Instance Segmentation in SBF-SEM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03332)
*Zewen Zhuo,Ilya Belevich,Eija Jokitalo,Alejandra Sierra,Jussi Tohka*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A fully automatic pipeline for 3D dendrite instance segmentation from SBF-SEM data, combining YOLOv6 detection, SAM prompting, 2D mask refinement, random forest 3D linking, and nnU-Net high-resolution refinement. Achieves Dice 0.93 on control and 0.91 on epileptic rat hippocampal tissue.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Manual annotation of dendrites in SBF-SEM images is infeasible at scale, yet accurate 3D reconstruction of individual dendrites is essential for quantifying structural plasticity in the brain.

Method: Unified pipeline: (1) YOLOv6-guided SAM prompting on downsampled slices, (2) iterative 2D mask refinement, (3) random forest 3D instance linking, (4) instance-aware high-resolution refinement using nnU-Net at native resolution. Requires no manual prompting at inference.

Result: High semantic accuracy with Dice 0.93 (control) and 0.91 (epileptic). Strong instance-level performance on control tissue. In dense regions of epileptic tissue, instance recognition remains the principal limitation. High-resolution refinement recovers thin dendritic protrusions for downstream spine-level analysis.

Conclusion: The pipeline successfully reconstructs coherent, well-separated dendrites automatically. The main remaining challenge is instance recognition in dense regions of pathological tissue. The method enables automated analysis of dendritic morphology in both normal and diseased brain tissue.

Abstract: Accurate three-dimensional (3D) reconstruction of individual dendrites in serial block-face scanning electron microscopy (SBF-SEM) is essential for quantifying structural plasticity in the brain, yet manual annotation at scale is infeasible. We present a fully automatic pipeline for 3D dendrite instance segmentation that unifies YOLOv6-guided Segment Anything Model (SAM) prompting on downsampled slices, iterative two-dimensional mask refinement, random forest 3D instance linking, and instance-aware high-resolution refinement using nnU-Net at native resolution into a single system requiring no manual prompting at inference. Applied to hippocampal CA1 SBF-SEM datasets from a control rat and a pilocarpine- induced epileptic rat, our pipeline reconstructs coherent, well- separated dendrites with high semantic accuracy (Dice 0.93 and 0.91) and strong instance-level performance on control tissue, while analysis of the more challenging epileptic tissue identifies instance recognition in dense regions as the principal remaining limitation. The high-resolution refinement stage recovers thin dendritic protrusions, providing a basis for downstream spine- level analysis. Code is available at https://github.com/ ZE-WEN/dendrite-3d-instance-seg.

</details>


### [69] [LAS-CLIP: A Lightweight Adapter Steering Approach for CLIP's Visual Encoder](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03370)
*Anh-Khoa Dinh-Duc,Duc-Tai Dinh,Tam V. Nguyen,Minh-Triet Tran*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: LAS-CLIP introduces a lightweight adapter approach that steers CLIP's frozen visual encoder toward region-level tasks by generating per-head, per-layer attention biases from an input mask, without fine-tuning any pretrained parameters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: CLIP's visual encoder produces only global image representations, limiting its utility for region-level tasks. Existing adaptations (visual prompting, input masking, encoder fine-tuning) all compromise pre-trained representations. There's a need for a method that can enable region-level understanding while preserving CLIP's foundational capabilities.

Method: LAS-CLIP uses a compact MaskAdapter that generates per-head, per-layer attention biases from an input mask and injects them into frozen self-attention layers of CLIP's visual encoder. The backbone remains completely frozen, allowing seamless reversion to vanilla CLIP when no mask is provided.

Result: With only ~116K-145K trainable parameters and 100K training samples on two T4 GPUs, LAS-CLIP achieves competitive or superior results compared to Alpha-CLIP (which fine-tunes its entire encoder on millions of samples) on ImageNet-S zero-shot classification and RefCOCO referring expression comprehension. Qualitative analysis shows stronger representational fidelity under incorrect masks and in downstream generation.

Conclusion: LAS-CLIP successfully enables region-level capabilities in CLIP while preserving its pretrained representations and zero-shot capabilities. The lightweight adapter approach with minimal parameters and training data outperforms methods that fine-tune the entire encoder, demonstrating the effectiveness of attention steering over parameter modification.

Abstract: CLIP's visual encoder produces only global image representations, limiting its use in region-level tasks. Existing adaptations rely on visual prompting, input masking, or encoder fine-tuning, each compromising pre-trained representations. We propose LAS-CLIP, a Lightweight Adapter Steering approach that keeps every CLIP parameter frozen. A compact MaskAdapter generates per-head, per-layer attention biases from an input mask and injects them into the frozen self-attention layers, steering attention toward the target region. Crucially, because the backbone remains strictly untouched, LAS-CLIP seamlessly reverts to vanilla CLIP when no mask is provided, preserving its foundational zero-shot capabilities. With approximately 116K to 145K trainable parameters and 100K training samples on two T4 GPUs, LAS-CLIP achieves competitive or superior results compared to Alpha-CLIP on ImageNet-S zero-shot classification and RefCOCO referring expression comprehension, despite the latter fine-tuning its entire encoder on millions of samples. Qualitative analysis further confirms stronger representational fidelity under incorrect masks and in downstream generation. Our project page is link to https://github.com/AnhKhoa585/lasclip

</details>


### [70] [EVEWorld: Physical Evolution Supervision for Embodied World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03374)
*Kaiqi Wang,Songxin Zhang,Zejian Xie,Xiao Xiong,Zhuoyang Song,Ziwei Wu,Jun Yu Lu,Yitan Teng,Ziying Song,Jiaxing Zhang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: EVEWorld is a physical evolution-supervision framework for embodied world models that addresses "Model Laziness" - where models prioritize visual fidelity over physical reasoning. It uses Instance-Guided Restoration (IGR) and Temporal Instance Alignment (TIA) to ensure physically consistent target evolution across frames.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing embodied world models suffer from Model Laziness, focusing on visual fidelity at the expense of physical reasoning and lacking process-level supervision over temporal dynamics of manipulated objects. This leads to physically inconsistent generated trajectories.

Method: EVEWorld consists of two components: (1) Instance-Guided Restoration (IGR) promotes instance consistency through restoration supervision; (2) Temporal Instance Alignment (TIA) promotes cross-frame consistency by aligning target instances across adjacent frames. The Model Laziness Rate (MLR) metric is introduced to measure persistent violations of instance consistency.

Result: EVEWorld achieves an 87.5% reduction in MLR compared with GigaWorld-0 on DreamGenBench, EWMBench, and PBench. On WorldArena 2.0 Track 1 leaderboard, it ranks 6th in JEPA Similarity and 17th overall.

Conclusion: The proposed evolution supervision strategy (IGR + TIA) effectively addresses Model Laziness in embodied world models by ensuring physical consistency across generated trajectories, as validated by significant MLR reduction and competitive leaderboard rankings.

Abstract: Embodied world models enable scalable simulation of embodied interactions for robot learning. However, existing models are prone to Model Laziness, as they focus on visual fidelity at the expense of physical reasoning and lack process-level supervision over the temporal dynamics of manipulated objects. In this work, we propose EVEWorld, a physical evolution-supervision framework for physically consistent target evolution. EVEWorld consists of two components: Instance-Guided Restoration (IGR) and Temporal Instance Alignment (TIA). First, IGR promotes instance consistency through restoration supervision. Second, TIA promotes cross-frame consistency by aligning target instances across adjacent frames. We further introduce the Model Laziness Rate (MLR), a metric that measures persistent violations of instance consistency in generated trajectories. Extensive experiments on DreamGenBench, EWMBench, and PBench demonstrate the effectiveness of EVEWorld, notably achieving an 87.5% reduction in MLR compared with GigaWorld-0.
