On the WorldArena 2.0 Track 1 leaderboard, our model ranks 6th in JEPA Similarity and 17th overall, which further validates the performance of our evolution supervision strategy.

</details>


### [71] [Interpretable Deepfake Detection in Videos via Explicit Forensic Features and Temporal Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03380)
*Chahira Benhama,Mohand Saïd Allili,Assia Hamadene*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes an interpretable deepfake detection framework that uses physically grounded forensic cues to detect manipulated videos by modeling spatially and temporally coherent facial features across four complementary feature domains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing deepfake detection methods rely on end-to-end deep models with implicit representations, making them difficult to interpret and generalize across different datasets. Additionally, manipulated content may appear visually consistent at the frame level but exhibit subtle temporal inconsistencies that are challenging to detect.

Method: The framework transforms videos into identity-consistent facial trajectories, segments them into fixed-length temporal windows, and represents each frame using 68 structured descriptors across four domains: photometric, textural, geometric, and compression-based features. These multi-domain representations are processed by an LSTM network to capture temporal dependencies and subtle irregularities.

Result: Evaluation on four benchmark datasets (FaceForensics++, Celeb-DF v2, DFDC, and DeeperForensics) yields strong F1-scores of 98.0%, 91.0%, 97.6%, and 96.2% respectively. The approach also demonstrated good cross-dataset generalization.

Conclusion: The proposed interpretable framework provides a robust solution for video deepfake detection by combining explicit forensic cues with temporal modeling, achieving high accuracy across multiple datasets while maintaining interpretability and generalization capability.

Abstract: Deepfake detection in videos remains challenging, as manipulated content may appear visually consistent at the frame level while exhibiting subtle temporal inconsistencies. This paper introduces an interpretable deepfake detection framework that models spatially and temporally coherent facial features in video sequences. Unlike end-to-end deep models relying on implicit representations, the proposed approach explicitly encodes physically grounded forensic cues, enabling transparent analysis and improved multi-dataset generalization. The pipeline transforms videos into identity-consistent facial trajectories, segments them into fixed-length temporal windows, and represents each frame using 68 structured descriptors spanning four complementary domains: photometric, textural, geometric, and compression-based features. These descriptors provide a compact multi-domain representation of manipulation artifacts and are processed by a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network to capture temporal dependencies and subtle irregularities. Evaluation on four benchmark datasets, FaceForensics++, Celeb-DF v2, a curated subset of the DeepFake Detection Challenge (DFDC), and DeeperForensics, yields strong and consistent F1-scores of 98.0%, 91.0%, 97.6%, and 96.2%, respectively. The approach also demonstrated a good cross-dataset generalization, providing a robust and interpretable solution for video deepfake detection.

</details>


### [72] [From Patching to Pruning Visual Computation in Vision Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03389)
*Rahul Chowdhury,Timothy A Rupprecht,Xuan Shen,Shaoyi Huang,Pu Zhao,Yanzhi Wang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Patch-to-Prune (P2P) is a training-free inference optimization framework for Vision Language Models (VLMs) that uses activation patching to identify and bypass unnecessary visual token computations in decoder layers. It achieves 55% FLOPs reduction while retaining 94% accuracy at 3% tolerance, and reveals that visual processing is non-uniformly distributed across decoder depth.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vision language models process every visual token through all decoder layers' attention and MLPs, incurring substantial inference cost even when token-specific visual computation is unnecessary at many depths. The goal is to reduce computational overhead without modifying model weights or removing tokens.

Method: P2P uses validation-guided forward and backward layer sweeps to identify decoder regions whose visual-token projection outputs can be replaced by fixed neutral proxy activation vectors within a user-specified accuracy tolerance. It preserves sequence length, token order, positional information, attention mask, and residual pathways.

Result: P2P at 3% tolerance retains around 94% of dense accuracy while reducing FLOPs by 55%. Evaluation on four VLMs (Qwen2.5-VL and LLaVA families) across seven multi-modal benchmarks using mutually disjoint calibration, validation, and test partitions.

Conclusion: Visual processing in VLMs is non-uniformly distributed: early and late layers require little token-specific computation, while intermediate layers perform most task-relevant visual integration. P2P serves as both an efficient inference framework and a causal lens into visual information processing in VLMs.

Abstract: Vision language models (VLMs) incur substantial inference cost because every visual token is processed by the attention and MLP projections of every decoder layer, even when token-specific visual computation is unnecessary at many depths. We introduce Patch-to-Prune (P2P), inspired by Mechanistic Interpretability, a training-free framework that converts activation patching from a diagnostic tool into an inference-time computation bypass. P2P performs validation-guided forward and backward layer sweeps to identify decoder regions whose visual-token projection outputs can be replaced by fixed neutral proxy activation vectors within a user-specified accuracy tolerance. Unlike conventional token-pruning methods, P2P preserves the sequence length, token order, positional information, attention mask, and residual pathways, thereby pruning computation without removing tokens or modifying the pretrained model weights. We evaluate P2P on four VLMs from the Qwen2.5-VL and LLaVA families across seven multi-modal benchmarks using mutually disjoint calibration, validation, and test partitions. P2P at a 3% tolerance retains around 94% of dense accuracy while reducing FLOPs by 55%. Beyond these efficiency gains, our layer-wise analysis suggests that visual processing in VLMs is non-uniformly distributed across decoder depth: early and late layers often require little token-specific visual computation, whereas intermediate layers appear to perform most task-relevant visual integration, enabling later reasoning to rely largely on visual information already embedded in shared residual and textual representations. This makes P2P both an efficient inference framework and a causal lens into visual information processing in VLMs.

</details>


### [73] [Native Action-Prior Learning from Videos for World Action Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03391)
*Zhaochong An,Fei Zhang,Menglin Jia,Duncan Frost,Zijian Zhou,Yikai Wang,Xudong Wang,Aditya Patel,Belinda Zeng,Tao Xiang,Serge Belongie,Amir Bar,Sen He*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Summary generation failed


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Motivation analysis unavailable

Method: Method extraction failed

Result: Result analysis unavailable

Conclusion: Conclusion extraction failed

Abstract: World action models integrate future visual dynamics with robot action prediction, but their scalability remains limited by the need for action-annotated robot trajectories. Observation-only videos contain rich evidence about interaction dynamics, but existing approaches typically use them either to pretrain visual representations that must later be adapted for control, or to infer latent actions that are subsequently grounded to robot commands. We present NAVA-WAM, which introduces native action-prior learning by directly pretraining the action policy from observation-only videos, avoiding indirect representation-to-control transfer or a separate latent-action model. Our training consists of two stages. First, we pretrain on observation-only videos, where future-video flow-matching supervision over visual transitions is propagated through transition-structured joint attention to optimize the Action-DiT and learn action-relevant priors. Second, we use action-labeled demonstrations to post-train the Action-DiT for robot control through joint video--action flow matching, while asymmetric attention decouples the visual branch from iterative action denoising and enables efficient action-only inference. Extensive experiments show that NAVA-WAM consistently outperforms prior approaches under both in-distribution and out-of-distribution settings, while demonstrating strong action-label efficiency and effective real-robot generalization. These results establish native action-prior learning as an effective approach to directly pretrain action policies from observation-only videos, providing a scalable path beyond action-labeled robot data.

</details>


### [74] [Beyond Entropy: Self-Diagnostic Multi-Role Token Optimization for Video Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03400)
*Yudong Han,Yong Wang,Zaiquan Yang,Liang Lin,Chongyang Tao,Xiangxiang Chu,Liyuan Pan*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: DyCPO introduces a co-evolutionary framework for token-level credit assignment in multimodal reinforcement learning, addressing limitations of high-entropy token heuristics and static counterfactual approaches by jointly optimizing reliable token selection and adaptive counterfactual intervention through a multi-role dependence metric and self-diagnostic analysis.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current reinforcement learning methods for multimodal reasoning suffer from ambiguous token-level credit assignment. High-entropy token heuristics cause over-reliance on visual activations and lengthy reasoning, while counterfactual-based methods over-prioritize visual exploration at the expense of decisive reasoning cues. Additionally, static counterfactual strategies fail to co-evolve with the policy during training.

Method: DyCPO constructs a multi-role dependence metric to balance visual exploration and answer-relevance mining in token-wise contrastive learning, suppressing exploration-only filler tokens and spurious visual noise. It dynamically derives counterfactual signals from the model's own successful and failed rollouts, enabling self-diagnostic analysis and co-evolution of the optimization objective with the policy.

Result: Extensive experiments on complex video reasoning and general video understanding benchmarks demonstrate consistent performance improvements, establishing DyCPO as a robust token-level credit assignment paradigm for multimodal reinforcement learning.

Conclusion: DyCPO successfully addresses the token-level credit assignment problem in multimodal reinforcement learning through its co-evolutionary framework, providing a robust paradigm that balances visual exploration with answer-relevance mining while dynamically adapting to the policy's learning progress.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards has substantially advanced multimodal reasoning, yet it remains fundamentally limited by ambiguous token-level credit assignment. While high-entropy token heuristics encourage possibility exploration, naively extending them to video reasoning tends to induce lengthy reasoning, as the model becomes overly reliant on high-entropy visual activations. Alternative approaches that rely on counterfactual-based visual token localization for credit assignment also tend to over-prioritize visual exploration at the expense of decisive reasoning cues for answer derivation, thereby exacerbating the interference from spurious visual nuances. Moreover, these methods employ static counterfactual strategies that fail to co-evolve with the policy during training. In this paper, we introduce DyCPO, a co-evolutionary framework that jointly optimizes reliable token selection and adaptive counterfactual intervention. It constructs a multi-role dependence metric to balance visual exploration and answer-relevance mining in token-wise contrastive learning, while suppressing exploration-only filler tokens and spurious visual noise. Rather than relying on static counterfactual priors, DyCPO dynamically derives counterfactual signals from the model's own successful and failed rollouts, enabling self-diagnostic analysis and co-evolution of the optimization objective with the policy. Extensive experiments on complex video reasoning and general video understanding benchmarks demonstrate consistent performance improvements, establishing DyCPO as a robust token-level credit assignment paradigm for multimodal reinforcement learning.

</details>


### [75] [ForestQuery: Boundary-Aware and Spatially Anchored Query Learning for Unified Forest Point Cloud Segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03403)
*Zhihao Zhan,Le Tao,Yifei Tian,Xin Liu,Jie Yuan*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: ForestQuery is a boundary-aware and spatially anchored query learning framework for unified forest point cloud segmentation that addresses challenges of irregular structures, occlusions, and ambiguous boundaries through boundary uncertainty modeling and learnable 3D anchors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Forest point cloud segmentation is fundamental for fine-grained 3D forest scene understanding but remains challenging due to irregular tree structures, severe occlusions, density variations, and ambiguous instance boundaries. Existing query-based methods insufficiently exploit forest-specific spatial structure and fail to account for boundary uncertainty.

Method: ForestQuery proposes two complementary designs: (1) Boundary uncertainty modeling to guide reliable instance query construction and modulate query optimization through adaptive loss reweighting; (2) Spatially anchored semantic query enhancement (SA-SQE) that introduces learnable 3D anchors encoding forest vertical stratification priors to enrich semantic queries with explicit spatial references.

Result: Extensive experiments on multiple public forest point cloud benchmarks and a self-collected annotated real-world dataset demonstrate consistent improvements in both individual-tree segmentation and semantic segmentation across diverse forest scenes.

Conclusion: ForestQuery successfully addresses the challenges of forest point cloud segmentation through boundary-aware query learning and spatial anchoring, achieving state-of-the-art performance on various benchmarks.

Abstract: Forest point cloud segmentation is fundamental for fine-grained 3D forest scene understanding, yet remains challenging due to irregular tree structures, severe occlusions, density variations, and ambiguous instance boundaries. Recent query-based forest segmentation methods have shown promise for unified semantic and instance prediction, but they still insufficiently exploit forest-specific spatial structure and account for boundary uncertainty. In this paper, we propose ForestQuery, a boundary-aware and spatially anchored query learning framework for unified forest point cloud segmentation. ForestQuery enhances instance and semantic query learning through two complementary designs. Specifically, boundary uncertainty is explicitly modeled to guide reliable instance query construction and modulate query optimization through adaptive loss reweighting. Meanwhile, spatially anchored semantic query enhancement (SA-SQE) introduces learnable 3D anchors encoding forest vertical stratification priors to enrich semantic queries with explicit spatial references. We evaluate ForestQuery on multiple public forest point cloud benchmarks and a self-collected annotated real-world dataset. Extensive experiments demonstrate consistent improvements in both individual-tree segmentation and semantic segmentation across diverse forest scenes. Code and data are publicly available at https://zhan994.github.io/ForestQuery

</details>


### [76] [OuroReward: Sequential Reward Scheduling for Reinforcement Learning in Text-to-3D Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03423)
*Bingyang Cui,Yujie Zhang,Yiling Xu,Yunfeng Guan*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: OuroReward proposes an interference-aware sequential reward scheduling strategy for Text-to-3D generation using reinforcement learning. It constructs a cyclic optimization path based on pairwise dependencies among quality dimensions to minimize interference, with adaptive budget allocation. AdaSelect is also introduced to select reliable prompts aligned with model capability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing RL methods for T23D optimize multiple quality dimensions (semantic alignment, texture clarity) simultaneously through reward aggregation, which causes imbalanced optimization and interference among conflicting dimensions without explicitly modeling inter-dimension dependencies.

Method: OuroReward has two main components: (1) It estimates pairwise dependencies among dimensions and constructs a cyclic optimization path that minimizes cumulative interference, incorporating tail-to-head dependency for global compatibility. This cycle is converted to a one-pass sequence starting from the dimension with lowest aggregate interference. (2) Training adaptively determines when to advance to the next reward based on remaining optimization headroom rather than fixed budgets. AdaSelect identifies reliable and informative prompts aligned with the model's current capability to improve training stability.

Result: Extensive experiments across different T23D models and RL algorithms demonstrate that the framework consistently improves generation quality across multiple dimensions.

Conclusion: The proposed interference-aware sequential scheduling and adaptive prompt selection approach effectively addresses the challenge of balancing multiple quality dimensions in RL-based Text-to-3D generation, achieving improved generation quality with better training stability.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) for Text-to-3D (T23D) generation requires optimization across multiple quality dimensions such as semantic alignment and texture clarity. Existing methods typically optimize these dimensions simultaneously through multiple reward aggregation, without explicitly modeling inter-dimension dependencies. This can cause imbalanced optimization and persistent interference among conflicting dimensions. To address this limitation, we propose OuroReward, an interference-aware sequential reward scheduling strategy for T23D RL. OuroReward first estimates pairwise dependencies among dimensions and constructs a cyclic optimization path that minimizes cumulative interference. By incorporating the tail-to-head dependency, the cycle captures global compatibility across the entire schedule. Then, OuroReward converts the cycle into a one-pass sequence, and starts optimization from the dimension with the lowest aggregate interference. Rather than assigning a fixed optimization budget to each dimension-wise reward, training adaptively determines when to advance to the next reward according to the remaining optimization headroom of the current one. We further introduce AdaSelect, an adaptive prompt selection strategy that identifies reliable and informative prompts aligned with the model's current capability. By focusing policy updates on these prompts, AdaSelect effectively improves training stability. Extensive experiments across different T23D models and RL algorithms demonstrate that our framework consistently improves generation quality across multiple dimensions.

</details>


### [77] [Depth Hypothesis Guided Iterative Refinement for Event-Image Monocular Depth Estimation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03439)
*Daikun Liu,Teng Wang,Changyin Sun*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: HypoDepth is the first event-image monocular depth iterative refinement framework that transforms depth regression into a constrained depth search task using a discrete Depth Hypothesis Volume (DHV). It constructs a 3D cost volume between DHV and contextual features, performing multi-scale correlation search for global-to-local refinement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing event-based monocular depth estimation methods improve performance by optimizing contextual features but struggle with the ill-posed and nonlinear nature of direct full-depth regression. There was a need for a framework that can handle this challenge more effectively.

Method: The proposed HypoDepth framework introduces a discrete Depth Hypothesis Volume (DHV) to transform the depth regression problem into a constrained depth search task. A 3D cost volume is constructed between DHV features and contextual features, with multi-scale correlation search to guide stable residual optimization. This enables efficient global-to-local refinement across multi-resolution.

Result: The method outperforms existing approaches on DSEC and MVSEC datasets with state-of-the-art results and strong zero-shot generalization. The tiny model achieves an excellent balance between accuracy and efficiency, enabling real-time performance on resource-limited devices.

Conclusion: HypoDepth successfully addresses the ill-posed depth regression problem by reformulating it as a depth search task. The approach achieves superior performance while maintaining computational efficiency, making it suitable for real-time applications on resource-constrained devices.

Abstract: Event cameras hold excellent dynamic properties, showing great potential for monocular depth estimation (MDE). However, existing methods mainly improve performance by optimizing contextual features, but still struggle with the ill-posed and nonlinear nature of direct full-depth regression. In this paper, we propose HypoDepth, the first event-image monocular depth iterative refinement framework. By introducing a discrete Depth Hypothesis Volume (DHV), we transform the depth regression problem into a constrained depth search task. Specifically, we construct a 3D cost volume between the DHV features and contextual features and perform a multi-scale correlation search to guide stable residual optimization. This lightweight cost volume enables efficient global-to-local refinement across multi-resolution. Our method outperforms existing approaches on DSEC and MVSEC with state-of-the-art results and strong zero-shot generalization. Meanwhile, our tiny model achieves an excellent balance between accuracy and efficiency, enabling real-time performance on resource-limited devices.

</details>


### [78] [ChromaGS: Text-Driven Semantic Editing of 4D Gaussian Avatars](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03441)
*Antonio Canela,Jordi Sànchez-Riera*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: ChromaGS enables real-time, language-guided color editing of animatable 3D Gaussian head avatars without retraining. The method uses learned soft assignments to semantic regions and decomposes colors into region-level base colors and Gaussian-level residuals, allowing coherent color transfer through natural language commands.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current generative editing methods may introduce unintended modifications. There's a need for deterministic, precisely localized semantic control that allows users to instantly modify the color of semantic regions through natural language at render time without retraining.

Method: The method augments each Gaussian primitive with learned soft assignments to semantic regions and decomposes colors into region-level base colors and Gaussian-level residuals. A two-stage language pipeline translates text instructions into target colors, supporting both absolute specifications and relative adjustments.

Result: Coherent color transfer: modifying a region's base color propagates naturally through all associated Gaussians while preserving fine appearance details encoded in residuals. The approach provides deterministic, precisely localized semantic control. Experiments demonstrate faithful appearance preservation and intuitive interaction across diverse subjects.

Conclusion: ChromaGS successfully enables real-time color editing of 3D avatars through natural language, preserving fine appearance details while providing deterministic semantic control. The method avoids unintended modifications common in generative approaches and works across diverse subjects without retraining.

Abstract: We present ChromaGS, a method for real-time, language-guided color editing of animatable 3D Gaussian head avatars. Given a trained animatable avatar, users can instantly modify the color of semantic regions through natural language, with edits applied at render time and no retraining required. Our key insight is to augment each Gaussian primitive with learned soft assignments to semantic regions and decompose colors into region-level base colors and Gaussian-level residuals. This decomposition enables coherent color transfer: modifying a region's base color propagates naturally through all associated Gaussians while preserving fine appearance details encoded in residuals. A two-stage language pipeline translates text instructions into target colors, supporting both absolute specifications and relative adjustments. Unlike generative editing methods that may introduce unintended modifications, our approach provides deterministic, precisely localized semantic control. Experiments demonstrate faithful appearance preservation and intuitive interaction across diverse subjects. Project page and code are available at: https://a-canela.github.io/chromags/

</details>


### [79] [Corrupted but Correct: Why Vision-Language Models Lie to Themselves Internally](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03445)
*Arun Josephraj Arokiaraj,Zekun Wu,Adriano Koshiyama*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The paper discovers a "train/inference gap" in vision-language models where adversarial attacks can force teacher-forced training loss to near zero for a target caption, yet the model generates correct descriptions during free generation with no trace of the target. This phenomenon is analyzed on Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct using 200 COCO images with a controlled two-stage PGD attack.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand why VLMs appear vulnerable to adversarial attacks during training (low loss) but remain robust during inference (generating correct outputs). This has implications for securing deployed VLM systems.

Method: Controlled two-stage PGD attack on Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct using 200 held-out COCO images. Methods include: (1) testing image-level pixel statistics including texture-based attackability measures; (2) using logit lens to localize the gap to a single autoregressive step; (3) tracking target-token rank across all 28 LLM decoder layers; (4) training a linear probe on merger hidden state to separate susceptible vs resistant images.

Result: Three key findings: (1) Image-level pixel statistics have no predictive power over which images are corrupted (r=-0.050, p=0.484; R²=0.069); (2) Target token rank is fixed at exactly 3,488 out of 152,064 vocabulary entries regardless of image or condition; (3) The visual encoder corrupts all images similarly, but the language model decoder differentially arbitrates—amplifying corruption for susceptible images and suppressing it for resistant ones (p<0.001, rank-biserial r=0.579). A linear probe achieves AUC=0.858.

Conclusion: Adversarial robustness in autoregressive VLMs is substantially a property of the language decoder's prior, not the visual encoder. This indicates that faithfulness evaluations and defenses for deployed VLM systems should target the language decoder rather than the visual encoder.

Abstract: A targeted adversarial perturbation can drive a vision-language model's (VLM's) teacher-forced training loss for a fixed target caption to near zero, yet the same model, allowed to generate freely, produces the original, correct description with no trace of the target. We call this dissociation the train/inference gap, and give it a precise mechanistic account on Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct using a controlled two-stage PGD attack on 200 held-out COCO images. First, we show that image-level pixel statistics, including a correctly re-implemented, texture-based attackability measure from the CNN robustness literature, have essentially no predictive power over which images are corrupted (best predictor r=-0.050, p=0.484; ridge regression R^2=0.069). Second, using the logit lens, we localise the gap to a single autoregressive step: the rank of the target token, conditioned on the correct first token already being generated, is fixed at exactly 3,488 out of 152,064 vocabulary entries for every image and every condition, with zero variance. Third, tracking target-token rank across all 28 LLM decoder layers reveals that the visual encoder corrupts every image's representation by a comparable margin regardless of eventual outcome, but the language model decoder then differentially arbitrates: amplifying the corrupted signal for susceptible images and actively suppressing it, past its clean-image baseline, for resistant ones (p<0.001, rank-biserial r=0.579). A linear probe on the merger hidden state separates these two outcomes with AUC=0.858, though we flag a circularity concern in this estimate. Together these results argue that adversarial robustness in autoregressive VLMs is substantially a property of the language decoder's prior, not the visual encoder, with direct implications for where faithfulness evaluations and defenses for deployed VLM systems should be targeted.

</details>


### [80] [Preserving Anatomical Continuity: Three-Stage Pipeline for Colon Segmentation in 3D Abdominal CT Scans](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03467)
*Deshan Kalupahana,Sonit Singh,Praveen Ravindran,Arcot Sowmya*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes a three-stage pipeline for colon segmentation from CT images that addresses disconnected predictions in deep learning methods. The pipeline includes initial segmentation, centreline bridging to reconnect disjoint regions, and a reconstruction stage for refinement. The method was evaluated on TotalSegmentator and RAOS datasets using multiple metrics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Accurate colon segmentation from CT images is essential for colorectal disease analysis, but deep learning-based methods often produce disconnected predictions due to complex colon anatomy. There was a need for a method that maintains topological integrity while preserving segmentation accuracy.

Method: The proposed three-stage pipeline includes: (1) initial deep learning-based segmentation, (2) centreline bridging to reconnect disjoint regions, and (3) a reconstruction stage to refine continuity. Evaluation was performed using overlap, distance, and topology-based metrics.

Result: The method demonstrated improved structural consistency while maintaining segmentation accuracy on both TotalSegmentator and RAOS datasets. The approach enhances topological integrity in colon segmentation.

Conclusion: The proposed three-stage, topology-preserving segmentation pipeline successfully addresses the issue of disconnected predictions in colon segmentation, enabling more reliable colon segmentation for clinical and research applications.

Abstract: Accurate colon segmentation from CT images is essential for colorectal disease analysis, yet deep learning based methods often produce disconnected predictions due to complex anatomy. This study introduces a three-stage, topology-preserving segmentation pipeline to address this issue. The first stage performs initial deep learning-based segmentation, followed by centreline bridging to reconnect disjoint regions and a reconstruction stage to refine continuity. Evaluations on TotalSegmentator and RAOS datasets using overlap, distance and topology-based metrics demonstrate improved structural consistency while maintaining segmentation accuracy. The proposed method enhances topological integrity, enabling more reliable colon segmentation for clinical and research applications.

</details>


### [81] [A Vision-Language Model (VLM)-based Pipeline for End-to-End Procedural Modeling of Field-Grown Maize from Point Clouds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03468)
*Mozhgan Hadadi,Talukder Z. Jubery,Adarsh Krishnamurthy,Baskar Ganapathysubramanian*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper presents an automated pipeline for reconstructing procedural 3D maize models from raw point clouds without manual tuning or species-specific training data. The pipeline uses a vision-language model (VLM) to annotate leaf midlines, geometric algorithms for back-projection and consensus merging, and differentiable NURBS fitting for surface refinement, achieving 99.4% leaf recovery and 5.4mm median Chamfer distance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Creating editable 3D models of field-grown crops for high-throughput phenotyping and in silico breeding trials is challenging. Current methods require hours of manual tuning per plant or species-specific segmentation models, making large-scale automated reconstruction impractical.

Method: The pipeline uses a multimodal VLM to annotate leaf midlines in rendered orthographic views, then applies deterministic geometric algorithms to back-project annotations onto the point cloud. These annotations are merged into 3D leaves via cross-view consensus and grown to full blades on an orientation-weighted surface graph. The measured organ parameters populate a NURBS-based procedural model generator, with each leaf surface refined against scan points through differentiable NURBS fitting.

Result: The pipeline achieved a median whole-plant Chamfer distance of 5.4 mm on 100 genotypically diverse field-grown maize plants from the MaizeField3D dataset. It recovered 1,017 of 1,023 (99.4%) curated reference leaves at IoU ≥ 0.5 without using those labels as input. The reconstructions were more accurate than a prior semi-automated pipeline using manual annotations.

Conclusion: VLM annotations become usable organ-level measurements when downstream geometric stages correct them. This enables automated generation of editable 3D plant assets at the scale of modern phenotyping experiments, bridging the gap between raw point clouds and analysis-suitable procedural models without manual intervention or species-specific training.

Abstract: Editable 3D models of field-grown crops support high-throughput phenotyping and in silico breeding trials, but building them from scanned point clouds requires organ-level segmentation and fitting. Procedural generators can turn an organ-level parameter set into an analysis-suitable 3D model, but obtaining that set requires hours of manual tuning per plant or segmentation models trained on species-specific labels. We present an automated pipeline that reconstructs procedural maize models from raw 3D point clouds without manual tuning or species-specific training data. A multimodal vision-language model (VLM) annotates leaf midlines in rendered orthographic views. Deterministic geometric algorithms back-project the annotations onto the point cloud, merge them into 3D leaves by cross-view consensus, and grow the midlines to full blades on an orientation-weighted surface graph. Measured organ parameters populate a plant descriptor for a Non-Uniform Rational B-Spline (NURBS)-based procedural model generator. Each leaf surface is then refined against its scan points by differentiable NURBS fitting. The pipeline reached a median whole-plant Chamfer distance of 5.4 mm on 100 genotypically diverse field-grown maize plants from the MaizeField3D dataset. The reconstructions were closer to the scans than those of an earlier semi-automated pipeline based on manual annotations. The pipeline recovered 1,017 of 1,023 (99.4%) curated reference leaves at an intersection-over-union of at least 0.5 without using those labels as input. These results show that VLM annotations become usable organ-level measurements when downstream geometric stages can correct them. This makes automated generation of editable 3D plant assets feasible at the scale of modern phenotyping experiments.

</details>


### [82] [UniDynamics: Event-RGB Fusion for Unified Future 4D Dynamic Scene Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03473)
*Daikun Liu,Xin Zhan,Teng Wang,Xiaoping Wang,Changyin Sun*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: UniDynamics is a diffusion-based framework for generating future 4D dynamic scenes (RGB, depth, optical flow) from a single event-RGB pair, leveraging event streams as motion priors and enforcing geometric-motion constraints through multimodal modeling.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing methods for future scene prediction require long temporal histories or control priors, and struggle with high-speed motion scenarios. This work aims to address these limitations by using event streams to provide robust motion priors for single-RGB extrapolation while maintaining geometric and motion consistency.

Method: Two core components: (1) Event Latent Enhancement (ELE) module - aligns and enhances event latents into diffusion-injectable conditioning features, providing initial motion priors and texture/structure cues; (2) Perceptual Dynamics Space (PDS) - embedded in multi-scale U-Net, decouples and adaptively interacts depth and flow while continuously feeding back constraints to appearance features for improved geometric-motion consistency.

Result: State-of-the-art performance on VKitti2 and DSEC datasets, producing high-quality, temporally coherent, and 4D-consistent future predictions, particularly effective under challenging high-speed motion blur conditions.

Conclusion: UniDynamics successfully generates future 4D dynamic scenes from a single event-RGB pair by effectively leveraging event-based motion priors and enforcing geometric-motion constraints, outperforming existing methods in prediction quality and spatiotemporal coherence, especially in high-speed motion scenarios.

Abstract: We propose UniDynamics, a diffusion-based framework for future 4D dynamic scenes (RGB, depth, and optical flow) generation from a single event-RGB pair, without requiring long histories or control priors as in existing methods, while explicitly modeling future motion fields. The core idea is to leverage event streams to offer an alternative motion prior for single-RGB extrapolation, and to enforce geometric and motion constraints throughout generation via multimodal modeling. Specifically, we design an Event Latent Enhancement (ELE) module to align and enhance event latents into diffusion-injectable conditioning features, providing robust initial motion priors and reliable texture/structure cues. We further introduce a Perceptual Dynamics Space (PDS) embedded in the multi-scale U-Net, which decouples and adaptively interacts depth and flow while continuously feeding back constraints to appearance features, improving geometric-motion consistency for physically plausible and spatiotemporally coherent prediction. Experiments on VKitti2 and DSEC demonstrate state-of-the-art performance, producing high-quality, temporally coherent, and 4D-consistent future predictions, especially under challenging high-speed motion blur.

</details>


### [83] [Fed-ADApt: Federated Anytime Depth Adaptation for Resource-Aware Medical Image Segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03474)
*Abhijeet Parida,Zhifan Jiang,Pooneh Roshanitabrizi,Austin Tapp,Maria J. Ledesma-Carbayo,Syed Muhammad Anwar,Ziyue Xu,Marius George Linguraru,Holger R. Roth*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Fed-ADApt is a depth-adaptive federated learning framework for medical image segmentation that enables institutions with heterogeneous compute budgets to collaborate on training UNet-based models without sharing raw patient data. It uses multi-depth supervision and hierarchical depth-wise aggregation to allow low-resource sites to participate while contributing to a global model with dynamic depth selection at deployment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing federated learning approaches assume homogeneous compute budgets across institutions, which limits participation from low-resource sites. This creates inequity in federated healthcare collaborations, as institutions with limited computational resources cannot contribute to or benefit from federated model training.

Method: Fed-ADApt integrates multi-depth supervision with hierarchical depth-wise aggregation. It allows each site to train according to its local compute budget while contributing to a global model that supports dynamic depth selection at deployment. The framework was evaluated on two tasks: multi-site 2D retinal fundus disc segmentation and 3D brain tumor segmentation.

Result: Fed-ADApt matched full-resource FedAvg performance in 3D brain tumor segmentation and achieved competitive 2D performance with only 4.7% average Dice reduction. It reduced average inference cost by 19.5% in 3D and 34.5% in 2D, and reduced training cost by 98% at the most constrained sites. Low-resource institutions that cannot train full-capacity models can participate in federations while maintaining competitive global performance.

Conclusion: Fed-ADApt provides a practical and equitable solution for federated medical image segmentation across heterogeneous clinical and edge-enabled imaging environments by considering both training and inference compute budgets. It enables participation from low-resource institutions while maintaining favorable accuracy-to-efficiency trade-offs.

Abstract: Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative training of medical image segmentation models without sharing raw patient data, yet existing approaches assume a homogeneous compute budget across institutions, limiting participation of low-resource sites. We propose Fed-ADApt, a depth-adaptive federated framework for UNet-based segmentation that jointly addresses low-compute training and inference. Fed-ADApt integrates multi-depth supervision with hierarchical depth-wise aggregation, allowing each site to train according to its local compute budget while contributing to a global model that supports dynamic depth selection at deployment. We evaluated Fed-ADApt on multi-site 2D retinal fundus disc segmentation and 3D brain tumor segmentation. Across both tasks, federated collaboration substantially improves robustness under domain shift. Fed-ADApt matched the full-resource FedAvg performance in 3D and achieved competitive 2D performance with a 4.7% average Dice reduction, while reducing average inference cost by 19.5% in 3D and 34.5% in 2D and substantially reducing training cost by 98% at the most constrained sites. Importantly, Fed-ADApt enables low-resource institutions that cannot train full-capacity models to participate in federations while maintaining competitive global performance under a favorable accuracy to efficiency trade-off. By considering training and inference compute budgets, Fed-ADApt provides a practical and equitable solution for federated medical image segmentation across heterogeneous clinical and edge-enabled imaging environments.

</details>


### [84] [Weave Forcing: Compositional Memory Routing for Interactive Long Video Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03510)
*Ziyi Wang,Junchi Yao,Heqian Qiu,Wenbo Shi,Chengjiu Wang,Jinyang He,Binkai Hong,Hongliang Li*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Weave Forcing is a training-free framework for compositional memory reuse in interactive long video generation. It addresses the challenge of combining characters and backgrounds from different historical shots by using LLM-based semantic slot routing, masked memory weaving with semantic masks, and coverage adaptive RoPE for temporal adjustment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current autoregressive video generation methods struggle with interactive storytelling that requires combining elements from different historical shots. Whole prompt retrieval overlooks individual component needs, while combining all historical memories introduces unrelated visual content, leading to visual artifacts and inconsistency.

Method: Three key components: (1) LLM-based semantic slot routing decomposes user prompts into character and background descriptions to select suitable historical references for each component. (2) Masked memory weaving uses contrasting attention maps conditioned on semantic slots to construct refined semantic masks, selectively exposing relevant tokens from compressed historical KV memories. (3) Coverage adaptive RoPE adjusts temporal offsets and memory retention based on no, partial, or full reference coverage to address visual artifacts from incomplete historical references.

Result: The method improves cross-shot subject and background consistency while maintaining competitive visual quality and text alignment in interactive long video generation.

Conclusion: Weave Forcing provides a training-free solution for compositional memory reuse that effectively combines different elements from historical shots, achieving better consistency than prior approaches without requiring additional training.

Abstract: Recent advances in autoregressive video generation have improved temporal consistency over extended durations, yet interactive storytelling requires more than continuous scene extension: a new shot may combine characters and backgrounds from different historical shots. Whole prompt retrieval can overlook the distinct reference needs of individual components, while directly combining all historical memories may introduce unrelated visual content. To address these problems, we present Weave Forcing, a training-free framework for compositional memory reuse in interactive long video generation. First, we use an LLM for semantic slot routing to decompose user prompts into character and background descriptions and explicitly select suitable historical references for each component. To isolate the required content, masked memory weaving uses contrasting attention maps conditioned on semantic slots to construct refined semantic masks, selectively exposing relevant tokens from compressed historical KV memories to guide the generation of the current shot. We further introduce coverage adaptive RoPE to adjust temporal offsets and memory retention according to no, partial, or full reference coverage, addressing visual artifacts observed when incomplete historical references are positioned close to the current generation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Weave Forcing improves cross-shot subject and background consistency while maintaining competitive visual quality and text alignment.

</details>


### [85] [ProgressNet: Sketching and Prompting with a Frozen Text-to-Image Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03512)
*Arkaprabha Basu,Chaitat Utintu,Yi-Zhe Song*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: ProgressNet is a training-free framework enabling frozen text-to-image models to follow progressive drawing sessions, where strokes are added/erased and prompts revised in real-time (~1 second per turn), using three inference-time mechanisms without any additional training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current image generators work in a single pass from finished sketch to image, requiring complete restart for every edit. Models that do maintain state are text-driven, cannot accept strokes, and are too slow for interactive drawing. The goal is to enable progressive, human-like drawing with AI image generators.

Method: Three inference-time mechanisms: (1) Previous-Concept Memory - uses the frozen model's pathway to remember previous turns; (2) Layer-Selective K/V Injection - carries appearance forward without freezing structure; (3) Banded Adaptive Control - uses internal signals to gauge how much to trust an unfinished sketch.

Result: While baseline FLUX+ControlNet FID scores double between 10% and 100% sketch completion on FS-COCO, ProgressNet's FID remains stable. It maintains strong fidelity and progressive coherence across three sketch domains and is preferred by users over five competitors, especially for erasure tasks.

Conclusion: ProgressNet successfully enables frozen text-to-image models to follow progressive drawing sessions without training, maintaining image quality and coherence as sketches evolve, offering a practical solution for interactive AI-assisted drawing.

Abstract: Humans draw progressively: a few strokes, a look at the result, a stroke erased, a prompt revised. Image generators do not work this way. They typically take a finished sketch and produce the image in a single pass, so every edit starts the picture again, and the models that do keep state across turns are driven by text, cannot take a stroke, and are too slow to draw with. We present ProgressNet, a training-free framework that lets a frozen text-to-image model follow a drawing session as it unfolds: strokes are added and erased, the prompt is revised, and the image keeps up at about a second per turn. It needs no new parameters because the frozen model already has what a progressive generator needs, a pathway through which the previous turn can be remembered, layers that can carry appearance forward without freezing structure, and an internal signal of how far to trust an unfinished sketch; three inference-time mechanisms (Previous-Concept Memory, Layer-Selective K/V Injection and Banded Adaptive Control) use each in turn. As a sketch fills in, every existing method degrades, the FID of the FLUX+ControlNet baseline doubling between 10% and 100% completion on FS-COCO, while ProgressNet's barely moves; it maintains strong fidelity and progressive coherence across three sketch domains and is preferred by users over five competitors, most widely on erasure.

</details>


### [86] [Feedforward Novel View Synthesis for Heterogeneous Cameras](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03522)
*Meng Wei,Cheng Zhang,Boying Li,Yihang Chen,Jianmin Zheng,Hamid Rezatofighi,Jianfei Cai*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A method for feed-forward novel view synthesis across heterogeneous central cameras (perspective, fisheye, panoramic) that addresses tokenization ambiguity through token-center relative Camera Positional Encodings, local raymaps, and projection-aware 2D RoPE to treat diverse cameras as calibrated samplings of a shared ray space.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing feed-forward NVS methods assume homogeneous cameras (same camera family), but practical multi-sensor systems have heterogeneous cameras. The tokenization process creates ambiguity because visual tokens aggregate projection-dependent ray bundles while camera encodings only expose absolute rays or token-center relations.

Method: Three key components: (1) Token-center relative Camera Positional Encodings for relative positional relationships; (2) Local raymaps as token-level representation describing intra-patch ray distribution; (3) Projection-aware 2D RoPE that replaces raw image-grid coordinates with ray-induced angular coordinates to align relative positional reasoning across camera projections.

Result: On ScanNet++ with heterogeneous-camera system, the method improves over camera-conditioned baselines under mixed-camera evaluation and demonstrates zero-shot generalization to panoramic views.

Conclusion: The proposed approach successfully enables feed-forward NVS across heterogeneous central cameras by explicitly modeling ray geometry across different projections, treating diverse cameras as calibrated samplings of a shared ray space rather than separate visual domains.

Abstract: Feed-forward novel view synthesis has recently shown promising results from sparse posed images, but most existing methods assume that context and target views share a fixed camera family. This homogeneous-camera assumption breaks in practical multi-sensor systems, where perspective, fisheye, and panoramic cameras may coexist and where the target projection may be unseen during training. We study feed-forward NVS across heterogeneous central cameras and identify a key ambiguity introduced by tokenization: a visual token aggregates a projection-dependent bundle of pixel rays, while existing camera encodings mainly expose absolute rays or token-center relations. To address this, we combine token-center relative Camera Positional Encodings and proposed local raymaps, a token-level representation that explicitly describes the intra-patch ray distribution summarized by each token. We further propose projection-aware 2D RoPE, which replaces raw image-grid coordinates with ray-induced angular coordinates so that relative positional reasoning is aligned across camera projections. Together, these components treat diverse cameras as calibrated samplings of a shared ray space rather than separate visual domains. On ScanNet++ with heterogeneous-camera system, our method improves over camera-conditioned baselines under mixed-camera evaluation and demonstrates zero-shot generalization to panoramic views.

</details>


### [87] [DuoMatching: Joint-Marginal Distribution Matching for Few-Step Video Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03543)
*Jiahao Zhan,Yan Wang,Yongrui Ma,Qunliang Xing,Ruchang Yao,Runtao Liu,Shijie Zhao,Tianfan Xue*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: DuoMatching is a distribution matching framework for streaming video generation that combines joint and marginal matching to improve visual quality and semantic alignment. It uses LatentBridge to resolve latent representation mismatches between video and image generators, and Latent Variation Sampling to distribute frame-level supervision across temporal segments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing distribution matching distillation (DMD) for video generation matches joint distributions of video frames but suffers from limitations in visual quality and semantic alignment. These issues persist despite DMD's ability to mitigate drift during autoregressive rollouts.

Method: The proposed DuoMatching framework introduces a unified joint-marginal formulation that adds marginal matching objectives on top of existing joint matching. This provides dedicated frame-level supervision from an image generator, transferring complementary visual and semantic priors. Two key techniques are introduced: (1) LatentBridge to resolve latent representation mismatch between the video student and image teacher, and (2) Latent Variation Sampling to distribute frame-level supervision across distinct temporal segments, reducing redundancy.

Result: DuoMatching improves visual quality, composition, and semantic alignment while largely preserving motion dynamics. Human evaluations show overall preference rates above 80% against all evaluated baselines.

Conclusion: The joint-marginal formulation effectively leverages both video and image generation priors, achieving superior quality in streaming video generation through the innovative LatentBridge and Latent Variation Sampling mechanisms.

Abstract: Streaming video generation has benefited from distribution matching distillation (DMD), which matches the joint distribution of video frames to a video teacher's approximation of the real video distribution. Although this joint matching mitigates drift during autoregressive rollouts, limitations remain in visual quality and semantic alignment. To address these limitations, we propose DuoMatching, a distribution matching framework that approximates the real video distribution through a unified joint-marginal formulation. On top of existing joint matching formulations, the additional marginal matching objective provides dedicated frame-level supervision from an image generator, transferring complementary visual and semantic priors from it. To apply this frame-level supervision in video generation, we introduce LatentBridge to resolve the latent representation mismatch between the video student and the image teacher. Latent Variation Sampling further distributes such frame-level supervision across distinct temporal segments, reducing redundancy. Experiments demonstrate that DuoMatching improves visual quality, composition, and semantic alignment while largely preserving motion dynamics. Human evaluations show overall preference rates above 80% against all evaluated baselines. The project page is available at https://johnzhan2023.github.io/DuoMatching/.

</details>


### [88] [Rethinking What to Cache in Few-Step Diffusion Transformers: Solver-Aware Target Selection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03577)
*Shuo Yang,Lihao Fang,Yi Zhang,Haixiang Wang,Xincheng Ye,Shufan Chen,Jipeng Guo,Youqing Wang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: AutoTarget is a method that adaptively selects which tensor to cache when accelerating Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) sampling, addressing the challenge that step distillation increases gaps between sampling steps, making cache reuse more error-prone. The method measures error for each candidate tensor and selects the optimal one based on the specific model, solver, and reuse schedule.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) require multiple costly forward passes to generate high-quality images/videos. While step distillation and caching are common acceleration techniques, they have a fundamental conflict: distillation increases gaps between sampling steps, and reusing tensors across these larger gaps introduces more error. Existing caching methods decide in advance which tensor to reuse without considering how this interacts with specific models, solvers, and distillation levels.

Method: AutoTarget works by: (1) Running a small set of experiments without cache reuse to measure the error caused by reusing each candidate tensor, (2) Selecting the candidate with the lowest error, and (3) For Euler sampling, identifying cache targets that produce the same trajectory while analyzing why stored solver updates may not work. The method calibrates itself to the specific model, solver, and reuse schedule.

Result: On distilled image and video DiTs, the best cache target varies depending on model, image resolution, and solver. AutoTarget reduces DiT evaluations and retained cache storage while maintaining generation quality close to uncached runs. On tested PixArt-LCM and FLUX.1-schnell settings, its calibration ranking matches the ranking from held-out cached runs.

Conclusion: AutoTarget provides a principled approach to selecting cache targets for accelerated DiT sampling. The optimal caching strategy depends on the specific model, solver, and reuse configuration, not on a one-size-fits-all solution. The method is implemented and available on GitHub for reproducibility.

Abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) can generate high-quality images and videos, but generating each sample requires multiple costly DiT forward passes. Two common ways to accelerate DiT sampling are step distillation, which reduces the number of sampling steps, and caching, which skips some DiT evaluations by reusing a tensor computed at an earlier step. Most caching methods decide in advance which tensor to reuse. After distillation, adjacent sampling steps are farther apart. Reusing a tensor across this larger gap introduces more error, so choosing what to cache becomes especially important. We therefore introduce AutoTarget, a method that chooses the cached tensor for a given model, solver, and reuse schedule. AutoTarget uses a small set of runs without cache reuse to measure the error caused by reusing each candidate tensor, then selects the candidate with the lowest error. We also analyze how an error at one reuse step affects the final sample. For Euler sampling, we identify cache targets that produce the same trajectory and show why a stored solver update may not. Experiments on distilled image and video DiTs show that the best cache target changes with the model, image resolution, and solver. AutoTarget reduces DiT evaluations and retained cache storage. Generation quality remains close to the corresponding uncached run. On the tested PixArt-LCM and FLUX.1-schnell settings, its calibration ranking matches the ranking from held-out cached runs. To help others reproduce the method, we provide its core implementation on GitHub at https://github.com/wali1024-offical/AutoTarget.

</details>


### [89] [ManifoldSplat: Language-Guided Semantic Shape Editing of 3D Gaussian Head Avatars](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03599)
*Antonio Canela,Jordi Sànchez-Riera*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: ManifoldSplat is the first end-to-end framework for language-guided semantic shape editing of animatable 3D Gaussian Splatting avatars reconstructed from monocular videos. It performs edits within the FLAME manifold to preserve identity and animation, using a per-region disentangled CVAE (DeltaRegion) for feedforward shape deltas.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior methods for text-driven 3D head avatar manipulation struggled with fine-grained localized control, often entangling features or lacking geometric consistency. Modifying geometry through natural language required slow per-prompt optimization or compromised identity and rigging. There was a need for fast, feedforward editing that maintains identity preservation and animation capability.

Method: The framework performs edits within the structured FLAME manifold rather than directly optimizing an unstructured Gaussian cloud. It introduces DeltaRegion, a per-region disentangled Conditional Variational Autoencoder (CVAE) that delivers feedforward shape deltas. A refining stage recovers view-consistent details. The approach reconstructs and edits an avatar in ~90 seconds on a consumer GPU.

Result: ManifoldSplat achieves ~90 seconds reconstruction/editing time on a consumer GPU and renders at ~800 FPS. Extensive evaluations demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in localized prompt alignment, geometric coherence, and identity preservation.

Conclusion: ManifoldSplat sets a new state-of-the-art in language-guided semantic shape editing of 3D Gaussian Splatting avatars, providing fine-grained localized control while strictly preserving identity and animation capabilities. The FLAME manifold-based approach enables fast feedforward editing without the need for slow per-prompt optimization.

Abstract: High-fidelity 3D head avatars have reached near-photorealistic quality. While recent methods enable text-driven manipulation, they struggle to provide fine-grained localized control, often entangling features or lacking geometric consistency. Modifying geometry through natural language currently requires slow per-prompt optimization or compromises identity and rigging. We present ManifoldSplat, the first end-toend framework for language-guided semantic shape editing of animatable 3D Gaussian Splatting avatars reconstructed from monocular videos. By performing edits within the structured FLAME manifold rather than directly optimizing an unstructured Gaussian cloud, we strictly preserve identity and animation. We introduce DeltaRegion, a per-region disentangled Conditional Variational Autoencoder (CVAE) delivering feedforward shape deltas, alongside a refining stage to recover view-consistent details. ManifoldSplat reconstructs and edits an avatar in ~90 seconds on a consumer GPU, rendering at ~800 FPS. Extensive evaluations demonstrate our approach sets a new state-of-the-art in localized prompt alignment, geometric coherence, and identity preservation. Project page and code: https://a-canela.github.io/manifoldsplat/

</details>


### [90] [DEPICT: Scoring Text-to-Image Alignment by Answer Agreement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03617)
*Vasco Ramos,Sandra Godinho Silva,Joao Magalhaes,Ricardo Rei,Pedro Henrique Martins*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: DEPICT is a training-free metric for image-text alignment evaluation that addresses limitations of existing approaches by using expected agreement between image-based and caption-only answers, weighted by caption decisiveness, and merging with holistic scores.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Image-text alignment is crucial for caption evaluation, hallucination detection, data curation, and benchmarking T2I generators. Existing methods have significant limitations: fine-tuned metrics are bound to specific backbones and training distributions; holistic metrics miss fine-grained details; and decomposed metrics rely on a fixed-YES assumption that incorrectly penalizes faithful images.

Method: DEPICT replaces fixed reference answers with expected agreement between image-based and caption-only answers, weighting questions by how decisively the caption determines them. It merges this agreement score with a holistic score to recover context lost during decomposition.

Result: DEPICT increases negation accuracy from 19% to 88%. On five benchmarks with eleven backbones from three model families, it surpasses all training-free metrics and exceeds fine-tuned evaluators on two out of three human-correlation benchmarks.

Conclusion: DEPICT successfully addresses the limitations of existing image-text alignment metrics by being training-free, handling negation correctly through agreement-based scoring, and achieving superior performance across diverse benchmarks and model families.

Abstract: Image-text alignment is a core problem in computer vision with applications in caption evaluation, hallucination detection, data curation, and the benchmarking of text-to-image (T2I) generators. As T2I models improve, benchmarking has become demanding, requiring metrics capable of finding a series of issues like missing objects, swapped attributes, miscounts, and ignored negations. Recent work addresses this by fine-tuning evaluators on preference data or by prompting a vision-language model, either holistically with the caption or with decomposed verification questions. However, existing approaches fall short: fine-tuned metrics remain bound to one backbone and training distribution; holistic metrics miss fine-grained details; and decomposed metrics rely on a fixed-YES assumption that penalizes faithful images whenever that assumption fails. In contrast, we propose DEPICT, a training-free metric that replaces fixed reference answers with expected agreement between image-based and caption-only answers, weighting questions by how decisively the caption determines them. By replacing fixed references, our agreement rule increases negation accuracy from 19% to 88%. To recover the context lost during decomposition, DEPICT merges this agreement score with a holistic score. We evaluate DEPICT on five benchmarks and eleven backbones from three model families and find that it surpasses all training-free metrics and exceeds fine-tuned evaluators on two out of three human-correlation benchmarks.

</details>


### [91] [World Embedding Benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03632)
*Yiqi Liu,Ruifeng Yuan,Yang Wang,Long Li,Fengyu Cai,Hou Pong Chan,Jialin Yu,Hao Zhang,Chenghua Lin,Chenghao Xiao*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The World Embedding Benchmark evaluates how well video models understand physical phenomena through three tasks (retrieval, regression, classification) across 80 simulation families. Pre-trained models show weak physical understanding, but lightweight probes can recover physical information. A trade-off exists between cross-modal alignment and quantitative property recoverability, and retrieval-augmented generation benefits from physically-aligned embeddings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Physical fidelity in video representations and world models has received increasing attention, but how video representations encode physical information remains poorly understood. The lack of a systematic benchmark to evaluate physical understanding in video models motivates this work.

Method: The authors introduce the World Embedding Benchmark comprising 8,000 controlled simulation cases from 80 families across 4 domains (fluid mechanics, solid mechanics, dynamics, optics & electromagnetism). Each case pairs rendered videos with simulation-derived physical annotations. Three complementary tasks are used: (1) text-video retrieval, (2) physical-property regression, and (3) multiple-choice video-description pair classification. They evaluate pre-trained omnimodal embedding models, use lightweight probes for physical information recovery, and test continual contrastive training with physics-specific video-text pairs. Finally, they apply retrieval-augmented generation with MiniMax-H3 using the embeddings.

Result: Evaluated pre-trained omnimodal embedding models show weak retrieval performance and near-chance within-family pair classification. Lightweight probes can recover useful physical information from frozen video embeddings. Continual contrastive training improves retrieval and pair classification but degrades physical-property regression, revealing a trade-off between alignment and quantitative information recoverability. Retrieved references improve physical fidelity of generated videos, with stronger retrieval models yielding larger gains.

Conclusion: The findings highlight the need to evaluate physical alignment and property recoverability jointly. The work demonstrates the utility of physical representations for improving video generation. The benchmark provides a valuable tool for systematically assessing physical understanding in video models.

Abstract: Physical fidelity has received increasing attention in world models and video generation, yet how video representations encode physical information remains less understood. We introduce the World Embedding Benchmark, comprising 8,000 controlled simulation cases from 80 families spanning fluid mechanics, solid mechanics, dynamics, and optics & electromagnetism. Each case pairs a rendered video with simulation-derived physical annotations, supporting three complementary tasks: text-video retrieval, physical-property regression, and multiple-choice video-description pair classification. We use these tasks to distinguish cross-modal physical alignment from the recoverability of quantitative physical information. Evaluated pre-trained omnimodal embedding models show weak retrieval and near-chance within-family pair classification, while lightweight probes recover useful physical information from frozen video embeddings. Continual contrastive training with physics-specific video-text pairs improves retrieval and pair classification but degrades physical-property regression, revealing a trade-off between alignment and quantitative information recoverability. Finally, we use the embeddings to retrieve reference videos for retrieval-augmented generation with MiniMax-H3. Retrieved references improve the physical fidelity of generated videos, with stronger retrieval models yielding larger gains in our experiments. Together, these findings highlight the need to evaluate physical alignment and property recoverability jointly, and demonstrate the utility of physical representations for improving video generation.

</details>


### [92] [LoGo: Local-Global Rewards for Consistent Long-Horizon Video Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03636)
*Ziqi Ma,Shreya Sharma,Mohamed El Banani,Katja Schwarz,Chongjie Ye,Chao-Yuan Wu,Li Fei-Fei,Ben Mildenhall,Georgia Gkioxari,Justin Johnson,Gowthami Somepalli*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: LoGo introduces a novel post-training approach for camera-controlled video models that combines global and spatially localized rewards to address 3D inconsistency issues. The key innovation is fine-grained credit assignment through local rewards, which substantially improves 3D consistency while preserving camera following and video quality through global rewards.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Camera-controlled video models are advancing toward longer generation horizons and complex camera control, but a key failure mode is 3D inconsistency—objects lose permanence and scene structures shift as the camera moves. Existing post-training techniques assign a single scalar reward to the entire generation, which is poorly suited to correcting these inconsistencies over long horizons.

Method: LoGo blends global and spatially localized rewards for camera-controlled video models. The local reward provides fine-grained credit assignment to substantially improve 3D consistency, while the global reward preserves camera following and video quality.

Result: Across three base models, LoGo shows a clear advantage on DL3DV and TrajectoryBench (a new benchmark for long-horizon, complex-camera-control generation). It effectively reduces local object shifts, artifacts, and global scene changes.

Conclusion: The work illustrates the importance of credit assignment in post-training video models. The combination of local and global rewards provides superior performance compared to single scalar reward approaches, demonstrating that fine-grained spatial credit assignment is crucial for maintaining 3D consistency in camera-controlled video generation.

Abstract: Camera-controlled video models are rapidly advancing toward long generation horizons and complex camera control. A key failure mode is 3D inconsistency: as the camera moves, objects lose permanence and scene structures shift. Existing post-training techniques, which assign a single scalar reward to the entire generation, are poorly suited to correcting these inconsistencies over long horizons. We introduce LoGo, which blends global and spatially localized rewards for camera-controlled video models. The local reward provides fine-grained credit assignment, which substantially improves 3D consistency, while the global reward preserves camera following and video quality. Across three base models, LoGo shows a clear advantage on DL3DV and TrajectoryBench, a new benchmark for long-horizon, complex-camera-control generation that current evaluations lack. LoGo effectively reduces local object shifts, artifacts, and global scene changes, illustrating the importance of credit assignment in post-training video models. Project website: https://ziqi-ma.github.io/logo-website/

</details>


### [93] [On-Board Anomaly Detection for Efficient Marine Environmental Monitoring](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03649)
*Thomas Goudemant,Clotilde Szywala,Benjamin Francesconi,Michelle Aubrun,Yves Bobichon,Marjorie Bellizzi,Adrien Girard*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A marine event detection pipeline using self-supervised neural network encoding and anomaly detection for Earth observation satellites with multi-/hyperspectral sensors, designed for onboard processing on resource-limited satellites.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Marine ecosystems face multiple threats (oil spills, algal blooms, sediment floods) that disrupt habitats, wildlife, and human activities. Early detection and mitigation require advanced satellite imagery analysis, but limited computational resources on satellites and communication bandwidth constraints pose challenges.

Method: The approach uses a self-supervised neural network encoder to compress satellite images into a reduced latent space for efficient onboard processing. An ML-based anomaly detection model identifies deviations from normal sea patterns. Performance is compared against traditional algorithms: Isolation Forest, One-Class Support Vector Machine, and Local Outlier Factors.

Result: The lightweight, resource-efficient pipeline is optimized for deployment on satellites with limited computational resources (embedded CPUs to AI hardware accelerators). It prioritizes transmission of critical information to enhance system responsiveness and optimize bandwidth. Successfully integrated across multiple missions including ESA's Phisat-2 and Microsoft/Thales Alenia Space IMAGIN-e.

Conclusion: The pipeline improves marine environmental monitoring by providing timely alerts and efficient data reduction. The solution addresses both computational constraints and bandwidth limitations through onboard processing and intelligent data prioritization.

Abstract: Marine ecosystems are impacted by various threats such as oil spills, algal blooms, and sediment floods, which disrupt habitats, wildlife, and human activities. Advances in satellite imagery and Artificial Intelligence (AI) have enhanced our capabilities for early detection and mitigation of such hazards. In this paper, we propose a marine event detection pipeline for Earth observation satellites equipped with multi- or hyperspectral sensors. Our approach includes a self-supervised neural network encoder that compresses satellite images into a reduced latent space, enabling efficient onboard processing. A machine learning anomaly detection model identifies deviations from normal sea patterns to detect environmental anomalies. We compare its performance against traditional algorithms such as Isolation Forest, One-Class Support Vector Machine and Local Outlier Factors. Our lightweight, resource-efficient pipeline is optimized for deployment on satellites with limited computational resources, ranging from embedded CPUs to AI hardware accelerators. By prioritizing the transmission of critical information, our solution enhances system responsiveness and optimizes satellite communication bandwidth. Demonstrated through current integration across multiple missions, including European Space Agency's (ESA) Phisat-2 mission and Microsoft/Thales Alenia Space IMAGIN-e mission, our pipeline aims to improve marine environmental monitoring by providing timely alerts and efficient data reduction.

</details>


### [94] [ProAR: Learning Prospective Reasoning with Autoregressive Video Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03664)
*Linghui Shen,Tinghui Zhu,Sheng Zhang,Muhao Chen*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: ProAR is a novel framework that transforms autoregressive video generation into a goal-oriented reasoning process by integrating goal-frame prediction into the autoregressive loop and introducing future representation self-alignment to guide short-range transitions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autoregressive video models rely on next-chunk prediction, which confines them to a short-sighted, reactive paradigm. This is particularly problematic for reasoning-oriented generation where achieving a target outcome through valid intermediate states matters more than local visual plausibility.

Method: ProAR introduces two key components: (1) Goal-frame prediction integrated via an asymmetric attention mask to anchor generation to long-range outcomes, enabling predicted goal frames to guide intermediate states without being disrupted. (2) Future representation self-alignment using teacher-forcing to extract clean future representations in a single forward pass and align current representations with them using a lightweight, training-only predictor.

Result: Experiments show ProAR's components consistently improve performance across diverse visual reasoning benchmarks. The framework achieves high training efficiency, surpassing fully trained standard AR baselines using only 25% of training steps, and demonstrates promising applicability to embodied reasoning tasks.
