Conclusion: ProAR successfully combines explicit, sparse target supervision with implicit, dense step-wise guidance, promoting coherent, goal-directed reasoning with modest computational cost. The framework represents a paradigm shift from reactive to goal-oriented video generation.

Abstract: Autoregressive (AR) video models excel at causal generation, but their reliance on next-chunk prediction confines them to a short-sighted, reactive paradigm. This limitation is particularly consequential for reasoning-oriented generation, where achieving a target outcome through valid intermediate states matters more than local visual plausibility. To address this challenge, we propose Learning Prospective Reasoning with Autoregressive Video Models (ProAR), a novel framework that transforms autoregressive video generation into a goal-oriented reasoning process. ProAR introduces two key components: (1) To anchor generation to the long-range outcome, we integrate goal-frame prediction into the autoregressive loop via an asymmetric attention mask, enabling the predicted goal frame to guide the generation of intermediate states without being disrupted by them. (2) To guide short-range transitions, we introduce future representation self-alignment to encourage current hidden states to anticipate upcoming temporal dynamics. By leveraging teacher-forcing in AR training, we extract clean future representations in a single forward pass and align current representations with them using a lightweight, training-only predictor. Together, these two mechanisms seamlessly combine explicit, sparse target supervision with implicit, dense step-wise guidance, promoting coherent, goal-directed reasoning progress with modest computational cost. Experiments show that ProAR's complementary components consistently improve performance across diverse visual reasoning benchmarks. The framework proves highly training-efficient, surpassing fully trained standard AR baselines using only 25% of the training steps. This paradigm also demonstrates promising applicability to embodied reasoning tasks.

</details>


### [95] [SigLIP2 for aerial fire risk classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03689)
*Yunus Serhat Bıçakçı*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper evaluates the transfer of a pretrained SigLIP2 image encoder to seven-class fire risk classification from aerial imagery. They compare a frozen encoder probe (55.95% accuracy, 50.19% macro F1) with full model adaptation (63.05% accuracy, 58.94% macro F1) on a public FireRisk dataset.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The researchers aim to examine how effectively a pretrained SigLIP2 vision model can be transferred to the task of fire risk classification from aerial imagery, which is important for wildfire prevention and management.

Method: The study uses a pretrained SigLIP2 image encoder transferred to seven-class fire risk classification. They created a reproducible partition of the public FireRisk training dataset with implemented data provenance and preprocessing tracking. Two approaches were compared: (1) frozen encoder probe where the encoder weights remain fixed, and (2) full model adaptation where the entire model is fine-tuned. Both runs used one training seed and selected checkpoints based on the same validation partition.

Result: Full adaptation achieved 63.05% accuracy and 58.94% macro F1 on the validation set, while the frozen probe achieved 55.95% accuracy and 50.19% macro F1. This represents a significant improvement of approximately 7-8 percentage points in both metrics with full adaptation.

Conclusion: The results support further evaluation of SigLIP2 for fire risk classification, though the researchers note these are development results and do not establish performance on an independent test set or unseen regions. The accompanying code provides a common framework for repeated experiments and comparisons with additional visual encoders.

Abstract: We examine the transfer of a pretrained SigLIP2 image encoder to seven class fire risk classification from aerial imagery. We introduce a reproducible partition of the public FireRisk training mirror and an implementation that records data provenance, preprocessing and model selection. Two initial runs compare a frozen encoder probe with full model adaptation. On the validation partition, full adaptation reaches 63.05% accuracy and 58.94% macro F1, compared with 55.95% and 50.19% for the probe. Both runs use one training seed and select their checkpoint on the same validation partition. These development results support further evaluation of SigLIP2 but do not establish performance on an independent test set or unseen regions. The accompanying code provides a common framework for repeated experiments and comparisons with additional visual encoders.

</details>


### [96] [FlowHMR: Physically Plausible Motion Capture from Video](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03691)
*Zhanke Wang,Chengfeng Zhao,Qing Shuai,Jingzhong Lin,Heng Li,Zeyu Ling,Yuxin Wen,Jing Li,Di Kang,Chunchao Guo,Linchao Bao*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: FlowHMR is a framework that recovers physically plausible global 3D human motion from monocular video by formulating motion capture as a video-conditioned motion generation problem, using flow matching to generate diverse motion candidates, and post-training with GRPO using fidelity and tracking rewards to ensure video consistency and physical plausibility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Previous learning-based methods for human motion recovery from monocular video suffer from two key problems: 1) depth ambiguity causes regression methods to collapse toward averaged solutions, and 2) recovered motions are not guaranteed to be physically plausible, causing physics-based tracking to fail.

Method: The approach involves three main components: 1) Formulating video motion capture as a video-conditioned motion generation problem, 2) Pretraining a flow matching model to generate diverse motion candidates, and 3) Post-training using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with two rewards - a fidelity reward (encouraging consistency with input video) and a tracking reward (favoring motions that physics-based controller can track successfully).

Result: On the Wild-4K dataset (~4K internet videos), the method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in overall motion fidelity and achieves 82.47% physical tracking success rate, compared to 62.82% for the strongest baseline (GVHMR).

Conclusion: The combination of flow matching for diverse motion generation and GRPO-based reinforcement learning with fidelity and tracking rewards effectively produces motions that are both faithful to the input video and physically plausible, significantly improving upon prior methods.

Abstract: We present FlowHMR, a framework for recovering physically plausible global 3D human motion from monocular video. Previous learning-based methods typically regress human motion directly from video and train the network with geometric supervision. However, recovering human motion from monocular video is inherently ambiguous in depth, and direct regression tends to collapse toward an averaged solution. Moreover, the recovered motions are not guaranteed to be physically plausible, so physics-based tracking of them often fails. To address these challenges, we formulate video motion capture as a video-conditioned motion generation problem and first pretrain a flow matching model for this task. Given an input video, the pretrained model generates diverse motion candidates, but not all of them are faithful to the video or physically trackable. We therefore post-train the model using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with two rewards. A fidelity reward encourages consistency with the input video. A tracking reward favors motions that a physics-based controller can track successfully. Together, these rewards shift the model's output preference, so the post-trained model stays faithful to the input video while producing more physically plausible motion. We further introduce Wild-4K, a large and diverse dataset of about 4K internet videos, for evaluating human motion recovery in the wild. Qualitative and quantitative experiments on Wild-4K show that our method outperforms state-of-the-art methods in overall motion fidelity and achieves a physical tracking success rate of 82.47%, compared with 62.82% for the strongest baseline, GVHMR.

</details>


### [97] [Decoding the Functional Roles of Register and High-Norm Patch Tokens in Vision Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03698)
*Neel Varma,Andrew Rufail,Dipika Khullar,Vasu Sharma*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper investigates the functional roles of register tokens and outlier tokens in self-supervised Vision Transformers (DINOv2) using sparse autoencoders and causal ablations. Register tokens encode high-level semantic concepts while outlier tokens encode lower-level structural/background patterns, with significant functional asymmetry between them.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Self-supervised Vision Transformers like DINOv2 learn rich visual representations, but the functions of their internal tokens (particularly register tokens and outlier tokens) are poorly understood. Recent architectures introduce dedicated register tokens to reduce high-norm outlier patch tokens in background regions, but the semantic and functional roles of both token types had not been fully established.

Method: The authors trained sparse autoencoders (SAEs) on register-token and outlier-token activations in DINOv2. They used an automated interpretability pipeline, UMAP clustering, and CLIP-space cross-checks for analysis. Causal ablations were performed to test functional importance.

Result: Register-token features are more strongly associated with high-level semantic concepts. Outlier-token features are more often associated with lower-level structural, background, and texture-dominant patterns. Causal ablations reveal substantial functional asymmetry: disrupting top-activating register-derived features produces a 48.17% drop in representation cosine similarity, whereas disrupting outlier-derived features produces only a 0.31% drop.

Conclusion: The results provide evidence for token specialization in self-supervised Vision Transformers, where register tokens and outlier tokens serve distinct functional roles in the model's representation learning.

Abstract: Self-supervised Vision Transformers (ViTs), such as DINOv2, learn rich visual representations, but the functions of their internal tokens remain poorly understood. Recent architectures introduce dedicated register tokens to reduce high-norm out- lier patch tokens that emerge in background re- gions, yet the semantic and functional roles of both token types have not been fully established. In this paper, we analyze these roles by training sparse autoencoders (SAEs) on register-token and outlier-token activations in DINOv2. Using an automated interpretability pipeline, UMAP clus- tering, and CLIP-space cross-checks, we find that register-token features are more strongly associ- ated with high-level semantic concepts. Outlier- token features, by contrast, are more often associ- ated with lower-level structural, background, and texture-dominant patterns. Causal ablations fur- ther reveal a substantial functional asymmetry: disrupting top-activating register-derived features produces a 48.17% drop in representation cosine similarity, whereas disrupting outlier-derived fea- tures produces only a 0.31% drop. Together, our results provide evidence for token specialization in self-supervised ViTs.

</details>


### [98] [MoSE3: Learning World-Space SE(3) at Every Pixel](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03716)
*Jiahuan Cheng,Zhiyi Li,Tian Xia,Ruojin Cai,Yilun Du,Qianqian Wang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: MoSE3 is the first feed-forward model that predicts dense 6-DoF SE(3) motion from monocular RGB video, producing full rigid transforms at every pixel. It addresses rotation manifold challenges and data scarcity by using 3D point tracks and rigidity embeddings as intermediates, trained on a new synthetic dataset (Art-Kubric).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current dense 3D point tracking only captures 3-DoF translation per pixel, missing rotation information and rigid body groupings. Predicting full 6-DoF SE(3) motion is challenging due to the curved rotation manifold and difficulty of acquiring SE(3) annotations.

Method: MoSE3 predicts per-pixel SE(3) through two jointly learned intermediates: 3D point tracks and rigidity embeddings. It differentiably fits transforms within soft rigid clusters to recover SE(3), enabling end-to-end prediction and supervision. The model is trained on Art-Kubric, a large-scale synthetic dataset with dense SE(3) and rigidity labels for articulated objects.

Result: State-of-the-art SE(3) estimation at pixel, part, and object levels on both rigid and articulated benchmarks. State-of-the-art average 3D point tracking accuracy across three datasets. Strong generalization to real-world videos despite training only on synthetic data.

Conclusion: MoSE3 successfully bridges the gap between sparse 6-DoF tracking and dense point tracking by predicting full SE(3) transforms at every pixel. The synthetic dataset approach enables training without expensive real-world annotations, and the method generalizes well to real videos.

Abstract: Dense 3D point tracking has been a prominent paradigm for modeling motion in dynamic scenes, but a point track is just a 3-DoF translation curve per pixel: it captures where pixels go, not the rotation of the underlying part, nor which pixels move together as one body. We propose MoSE3, the first feed-forward model that predicts dense SE(3) motion from monocular RGB video, producing full 6-DoF rigid transforms at every pixel in world space. Per-pixel SE(3) motion offers a richer view of how a scene moves: rotation, translation, and grouping all at once. Directly predicting SE(3) is challenging: rotations lie on a curved manifold that is ill-suited to Euclidean regression, and annotations for SE(3) are particularly difficult to acquire. To address these challenges, MoSE3 predicts per-pixel SE(3) through two jointly learned intermediates, 3D point tracks and rigidity embeddings, and recovers SE(3) by differentiably fitting transforms within each soft rigid cluster, enabling end-to-end prediction and supervision. To close the data gap, we introduce Art-Kubric, a large-scale synthetic dataset with dense SE(3) and rigidity labels for articulated objects with rich physical interactions. MoSE3 achieves state-of-the-art SE(3) estimation at pixel, part, and object levels on both rigid and articulated benchmarks, and state-of-the-art average 3D point tracking accuracy across three datasets, while showing strong generalization to real-world videos despite being trained solely on synthetic motion data.

</details>


### [99] [Less Decoder is More Encoder: Geometric Representation Learning from Novel View Synthesis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03717)
*Keerthi Kaashyap,Dennis Anthony,Akshay Krishnan,Nhi Ngoc Nguyen,Jeremy Collins,James Hays,Shreyas Kousik,Animesh Garg*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: SNAP is a self-supervised encoder-decoder transformer that addresses poor geometric representations in Novel View Synthesis (NVS) methods through a pose-conditioned local decoder and latent-space reconstruction objective, achieving competitive performance across multiple vision tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing encoder-based NVS methods yield poor representations not due to lack of supervisory signal, but due to two architectural issues: (1) spatially expressive decoders that dilute representational capabilities of the scene encoder, and (2) low-level pixel-space targets that hinder feature learning.

Method: SNAP uses a pose-conditioned local decoder with restricted expressivity and a latent-space reconstruction objective, making it task-agnostic. It leverages self-supervised learning with transformer architecture.

Result: SNAP is competitive with special-purpose geometry-supervised methods and performs competitively against self-supervised representations across five tasks: visual localization, pose estimation, point correspondence, depth estimation, and robot manipulation. Its patch features exhibit emergent viewpoint invariance approaching heavily supervised models. Under camera shifts, SNAP degrades more gracefully than standard 2D representations.

Conclusion: Restricting decoder expressivity actively prevents the suppression of transferable geometric structure. The key insight is that carefully designed architectural constraints (less expressive decoders) can preserve geometric information in learned representations, enabling emergent viewpoint invariance without heavy supervision.

Abstract: This paper examines the role of Novel View Synthesis (NVS) in geometric representation learning. In principle, NVS should reason about 3D scene structure, thereby enabling transferable multi-view geometric representations. Yet, existing encoder-based NVS methods yield poor representations. This is not because of a lack of supervisory signal, but rather due to inconspicuous architectural choices: \textit{spatially expressive decoders} that dilute representational capabilities of the scene encoder, and \textit{low-level pixel-space targets} that hinder feature learning. We present SNAP, a self-supervised encoder-decoder transformer that addresses both through a pose-conditioned local decoder and a latent-space reconstruction objective. SNAP is task agnostic, and we show that it is competitive with special-purpose geometry-supervised methods. SNAP also performs competitively against self-supervised representations across five tasks: visual localization, pose estimation, point correspondence, depth estimation, and robot manipulation. Remarkably, SNAP's patch features exhibit emergent viewpoint invariance that approaches heavily supervised models despite lower compute and data budgets. Under camera shifts where standard 2D representations collapse, SNAP degrades more gracefully, revealing that restricting decoder expressivity actively prevents the suppression of transferable geometric structure. https://snap-nvs.github.io

</details>


### [100] [GlanceWAM: Sparse Test-Time Imagination for World-Action Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.23927)
*Linhan Wang,Zijian An,Mingyuan Zhang,Chen Dai,Yi Xu,Can Cui,Jiayan Wang,Zichong Yang,Yinlin Chen,Lifeng Zhou,Chang-Tien Lu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: GlanceWAM solves the speed-success trade-off in world-action models by decoupling visual imagination from control: an asynchronous proposer generates lookahead frames in the background on a slow clock, while an action head decodes actions at 48ms latency purely in latent space. This achieves 72.2% on RoboCasa (vs 67.1% Cosmos Policy), 99.0% on LIBERO, and 24× latency reduction over synchronous methods, while outperforming π₀.₅ on real robots without robot-data pretraining.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Video generative models provide rich physical priors for robot learning, but existing world-action models (WAMs) face a fundamental trade-off: synchronous video generation at control rate is latency-prohibitive, while abandoning test-time visual imagination sacrifices task success.

Method: GlanceWAM decouples imagination from control on a single shared video DiT backbone using: (1) an asynchronous proposer that "glances ahead" on a slow clock to imagine a single lookahead frame seconds into the future in the background, (2) an action head that decodes action chunks at control rate (48 ms) purely in latent space without blocking, (3) a non-interfering attention mask that isolates video representations, and (4) staleness-robust horizon training that accommodates asynchronous lookahead aging.

Result: 72.2% on 24-task RoboCasa kitchen benchmark (vs. 67.1% for synchronous Cosmos Policy), 99.0% on LIBERO, 24× reduction in per-chunk control latency (48 ms on one A100), and higher average success than π₀.₅ on single-arm and bimanual real-robot manipulation without any robot-data pretraining.

Conclusion: GlanceWAM breaks the speed-success dilemma by generating visual imagination asynchronously off the critical path and consuming it directly in latent space, achieving both real-time inference and superior success rates.

Abstract: Video generative models provide rich physical priors for robot learning, yet existing world-action models (WAMs) face a fundamental trade-off: synchronous video generation at control rate is latency-prohibitive, while abandoning test-time visual imagination sacrifices task success. We show that visual imagination achieves both real-time inference and superior success rates when generated asynchronously off the critical path and consumed directly in latent space. We introduce GlanceWAM, which decouples imagination from control on a single shared video DiT backbone: an asynchronous proposer glances ahead on a slow clock to imagine a single lookahead frame seconds into the future in the background, while an action head decodes action chunks at control rate (48 ms) purely in latent space without blocking. Enabled by a non-interfering attention mask that isolates video representations and staleness-robust horizon training that accommodates asynchronous lookahead aging, GlanceWAM breaks the speed-success dilemma. Trained purely on demonstrations, it attains 72.2% on the 24-task RoboCasa kitchen benchmark (vs. 67.1% for synchronous Cosmos Policy) and 99.0% on LIBERO while cutting per-chunk control latency $24\times$ relative to synchronous world-action models (48 ms on one A100). In single-arm and bimanual real-robot manipulation, it achieves higher average success than $π_{0.5}$ without any robot-data pretraining. Code is available at https://github.com/linhanwang/GlanceWAM.

</details>

### [101] [From Expression to Reaction: Role-aware Visual Transfer and Stimulus-guided Reasoning for Interlocutor Emotion Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03016)
*Wei Wang,Zhaowu Li,Jianjie Luo,Fu Lee Wang,Lap-Kei Lee,Zhenguo Yang*

Main category: cs.MM

TL;DR: The paper proposes RASG, a framework for interlocutor emotion recognition that predicts listener emotions from listener videos and speaker audios. It addresses two key challenges: lack labeled listener data and ambiguity in visually similar reactions. The method uses RVT module for pseudo-labeling and SBR module for boundary reasoning with speaker context. Achieved 76.25% accuracy on MER-Cross dataset, ranking second in the MER Grand Challenge at ACM MM 2026.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The research addresses two critical challenges in interlocutor emotion recognition: (1) Supervision mismatch due to lack of labeled listener data, and (2) Ambiguity among visually similar listener reactions whose interpretation depends on speaker context. The paper aims to predict listener emotions from listener-only videos and speaker-only audios, which is challenging because the visual cues from listeners alone are often insufficient to determine their emotional state.

Method: The proposed RASG framework consists of two modules: (1) Role-aware Visual Transfer (RVT) - selects speaker samples with facial expressions supporting their emotion labels, filters listener tracks, and uses reliable pseudo-labels to train a listener-centric visual expert. (2) Stimulus-guided Boundary Reasoning (SBR) - uses a two-class language reasoner only when the visual model is uncertain, treating speaker audio and text as context rather than direct emotion evidence to distinguish similar listener reactions.

Result: The RASG framework achieves 76.25% accuracy on the MER-Cross dataset, improving the baseline performance by over 17%. The team ranked second in Track 1 (MER-Cross) of the MER Grand Challenge at ACM MM 2026.

Conclusion: The RASG framework effectively addresses the challenges of limited labeled data and reaction ambiguity in interlocutor emotion recognition by leveraging pseudo-labeling from speaker data and context-aware boundary reasoning. The significant performance improvement (17% over baseline) demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed approach. Future work may explore more sophisticated fusion strategies and handle more diverse emotional states.

Abstract: In this paper, we propose a Role-aware Stimulus-guided (RASG) framework for interlocutor emotion recognition, which predicts listener emotions from listener-only videos and speaker-only audios. RASG consists of Role-aware Visual Transfer (RVT) and Stimulus-guided Boundary Reasoning (SBR) modules, which address supervision mismatch due to the lack of labeled listener data and ambiguity among visually similar listener reactions whose interpretation depends on speaker context, respectively. More specifically, RVT selects speaker samples whose facial expressions support their emotion labels. It then filters listener tracks and uses reliable pseudo-labels to train a listener-centric visual expert. SBR uses a two-class language reasoner only when the visual model is uncertain. It treats speaker audio and text as context rather than direct emotion evidence to distinguish similar listener reactions. Experiments conducted on MER-Cross dataset shows that RASG achieves 76.25\% on MER-Cross and improves the performance of the baseline over 17\%. Our team ranks second in Track 1 (MER-Cross) of the MER Grand Challenge at ACM MM 2026.

</details>

### [102] [The Shape of Speech: A Geometric Measure of Coarticulation for Speech-Driven 3D Facial Animation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03436)
*Danzel Serrano,Przemyslaw Musialski*

Main category: cs.GR

TL;DR: This paper introduces a geometric measure (lip-path length) to quantify coarticulation loss in speech-driven 3D facial animation. The measure compares actual lip trajectories to the shortest consonant-aware route through speech segments. Testing four state-of-the-art methods reveals they all produce flatter trajectories than real speech, with three showing significant deficits equivalent to losing 15-60% of articulatory motion. A user study (97 viewers, 3,523 judgments) confirms viewers prefer real speech in 73.4% of sentence comparisons.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Speech-driven 3D facial animation can reproduce recognizable mouth poses but simplifies the motion between them. This motion carries coarticulation - how sounds around each sound shape its articulation. No existing measure could quantify this trajectory shaping loss in the absence of ground truth.

Method: The authors propose a geometric measure: lip-path length compared with the shortest route through vowel, consonant, and vowel positions of a speech segment. This "consonant-aware route" accounts for obligatory transit, avoids degeneracy, and preserves invariance to uniform motion gain. The measure requires only forced alignment. They evaluated four state-of-the-art methods (one per architectural family): DiffPoseTalk, ARTalk, FaceFormer, and CodeTalker. A pre-registered user study with 97 viewers and 3,523 judgments validated the perceptual relevance.

Result: All four methods trace flatter lip trajectories than captured speech. Against frame-rate-matched ground truth: DiffPoseTalk, ARTalk, and FaceFormer show clear deficits (equivalent to removing 15-60% of real speech's fast articulatory component). CodeTalker is marginal on primary measure but clear on a companion measure. The user study found controlled damping of real motion lowers the score and is penalized, while exaggeration shows no detected penalty. Viewers prefer real speech in 73.4% of sentence comparisons and in the aggregate on single words.

Conclusion: The proposed measure, its calibration, and the user study identify a perceptually relevant loss of trajectory shaping in speech-driven facial animation. This provides a concrete target for improving synthesized articulation. The findings suggest current methods under-produce coarticulation effects, and while viewers penalize damping, they don't penalize exaggeration over the tested range.

Abstract: Speech-driven 3D facial animation can reproduce recognizable mouth poses. However, it can simplify the motion between them, and that motion carries coarticulation, the way the sounds around each sound shape its articulation. We introduce a geometric measure of this trajectory shaping: lip-path length compared with the shortest route through the vowel, consonant and vowel positions of a speech segment. In contrast to the endpoint chord, this consonant-aware route accounts for obligatory transit and avoids degeneracy, while preserving invariance to uniform motion gain. The measure needs only a forced alignment, so it applies where no ground truth exists. We demonstrate it on four state-of-the-art methods, one per architectural family, real-time and offline. All four trace flatter lip trajectories than captured speech. Against frame-rate-matched ground truth, DiffPoseTalk, ARTalk and FaceFormer show clear deficits, equivalent on this measure to removing 15-60% of real speech's fast articulatory component. CodeTalker is marginal on the primary measure and clear on a companion measure. A pre-registered study with 97 viewers and 3,523 judgments underpins the measured direction: controlled damping of real motion lowers the score and is penalized, whereas exaggeration shows no detected penalty over the tested range. Viewers also prefer real speech in 73.4% of sentence comparisons and, in the aggregate, on single words. Together, the measure, its calibration and the study identify a perceptually relevant loss of trajectory shaping and a concrete target for improving synthesized articulation.

</details>


### [103] [Windfoil: Closed-Form Coverage for Real-Time and Differentiable Vector Graphics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02468)
*Matt DesLauriers*

Main category: cs.GR

TL;DR: Windfoil is a GPU-friendly algorithm that unifies rasterization and differentiable vector graphics by evaluating box-filtered winding numbers of quadratic Bézier contours in closed form, implemented in WebGPU for real-time 2D rendering, high-resolution rasterization, and differentiable rendering.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing GPU rasterization algorithms for vector graphics (like Slug) and differentiable renderers (like DiffVG, Bézier Splatting) have limitations in fidelity, performance, or scalability. There is a need for a unified approach that provides high accuracy comparable to reference box-filtered coverage while maintaining interactive performance.

Method: The algorithm evaluates the box-filtered winding number of quadratic Bézier contours in closed form. It is implemented in WebGPU to run across various environments including web browsers on consumer hardware.

Result: Windfoil matches the reference box-filtered coverage more closely than both Skia and Slug, while maintaining performance comparable to Slug. For optimization/differentiable rendering, it achieves equivalent or better reconstruction quality than DiffVG and Bézier Splatting at a fraction of the per-step cost, scaling to tens of thousands of shapes at interactive rates.

Conclusion: Windfoil provides a unified solution for both rasterization and differentiable vector graphics that outperforms existing production-grade engines (Skia) and specialized GPU algorithms (Slug) in fidelity, while offering significant performance advantages over state-of-the-art differentiable renderers (DiffVG, Bézier Splatting) for inverse graphics tasks.

Abstract: We present Windfoil, a GPU-friendly algorithm that treats rasterisation and differentiable vector graphics as two sides of the same problem by evaluating the box-filtered winding number of quadratic Bézier contours in closed form. We implement this in WebGPU, allowing it to run across a range of environments, including a web browser on a consumer laptop, and apply the system to real-time 2D rendering, high-resolution rasterisation for print media, and a differentiable renderer. We compare our renderer against Skia, a production-grade engine, and Slug, a popular GPU rasterisation algorithm for games and real-time applications, measuring fidelity to a reference box-filtered coverage. Our renderer matches the reference more closely than either, at performance comparable to Slug. We also compare our optimiser against DiffVG and Bézier Splatting, where it reaches equivalent or better reconstruction quality at a fraction of the per-step cost, scaling to tens of thousands of shapes at interactive rates.

</details>


### [104] [Budgeted-GS: Real-Time Large-Scale Gaussian Splatting via Factoring LOD](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03162)
*Haipeng Wang*

Main category: cs.GR

TL;DR: Budgeted-GS introduces a post-hoc method to compress 3D Gaussian Splatting models into a multi-resolution hierarchy, enabling real-time rendering of city-scale scenes on consumer GPUs with varying memory capacities. Also proposes budget-centered training that directly trains models at the required size instead of compressing afterwards.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: 3D Gaussian Splatting cannot scale to entire cities: trained models contain millions of primitives and gigabytes of memory, making real-time rendering on consumer GPUs impossible.

Method: 1) Budgeted-GS: Creates a factoring tree (multi-resolution hierarchy of moment-matched aggregates) from any trained 3DGS model in a few seconds. 2) Budget-centered training: Measures required primitives upfront and trains directly at that size. Both methods based on a measurable capacity floor (budget-error law) derived from optimal transport in phase space, with selection rules from covering theorems.

Result: Validated on 13 public scenes under preregistered protocol. Successfully renders city-scale capture at native 1920x1080, full SH, in real-time on one consumer GPU. Same city-scale model adapts to GPUs with different memory capacities.

Conclusion: The capacity floor provides a theoretical basis for determining how many primitives a scene needs. Budgeted-GS enables city-scale 3DGS rendering on consumer hardware by compressing models into hierarchical structures that adapt to memory constraints.

Abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting achieves excellent visual quality with real-time rendering, but at the scale of entire cities it does not fit: a trained model carries millions of primitives and gigabytes of memory, and real-time rendering at high quality on a consumer GPU remains out of reach. We introduce Budgeted-GS, a post-hoc method that turns any trained 3DGS model into a factoring tree, a multi-resolution hierarchy of moment-matched aggregates. After a construction pass of a few seconds, a single quality parameter selects, for each view, the level of detail that fits the memory of the target device, so the same city-scale model serves GPUs with widely different memory capacities. When a new scene is to be trained, the same theory applies: instead of growing a full-sized model and compressing it afterwards, budget-centered training first measures how many primitives the scene needs and then trains the model directly at that size, avoiding the wasted effort of optimizing primitives that are later discarded. Both methods are grounded in a measurable capacity floor, a budget-error law derived from optimal transport in phase space; selection rules certified by recent covering theorems decide which primitives are redundant. The floor answers how many primitives a scene actually needs and how many can safely be given up. We validate the floor on 13 public scenes under a preregistered protocol, and exercise both methods from object scenes to an official city capture, rendering it at native 1920x1080, full SH, in real time on one consumer GPU.

</details>


### [105] [A Kinetic Theory of the Gated Self-Evolving LLM Agent](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03243)
*Haipeng Wang*

Main category: cs.GR

TL;DR: This paper applies kinetic theory and fluid dynamics concepts to understand self-evolution in LLM agents. It treats plugin instances within a DSH (DeepSeek Harness) agent as identical hard spheres, developing a theoretical framework with three layers (rigorous, kinetic, measured) to predict population dynamics during self-evolution under a validation gate.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current self-evolution research treats the agent as a monolithic unit. This paper proposes studying individual plugin instances within the agent instead, using kinetic theory to predict their collective behavior. The key insight is that fluid dynamics traces appear in self-evolution, and this can be rigorously modeled.

Method: The authors build three theory layers: (1) Rigorous layer - mathematical proofs including hitting-time certificate, resolution law, and separation theorem; (2) Kinetic layer - master equation over plugin × version × task grid with four operators (collision, reaction, external field, gate); (3) Measured layer - empirical validation using a minimal instance in WebShop environment with four-parameter skill plugins.

Result: Population fluctuation scaling is density-gated: invisible at sparse edit density but emerges at the predicted rate under tripled density. This provides directional evidence supporting the kinetic theory predictions.

Conclusion: The fluid dynamics analogy, while bounded (no momentum conservation, no Navier-Stokes limit), provides falsifiable statistical signatures. The separation theorem establishes that the evaluator must remain external to the population - merging evaluator with evaluated invalidates the theoretical certificate.

Abstract: We find traces of fluid dynamics in the self-evolution of an LLM agent, and give the kinetic theory that predicts them. Gated self-evolution is the loop in which an agent rewrites its own skills under a validation gate. Self-evolution research has treated the agent as the unit; we study instead the individual instances inside it. Here the agent is DSH-plugin-based: it runs in production on DeepSeek Harness (DSH), and its plugins satisfy four architectural properties (permutation symmetry, reversibility, acyclicity, typed contracts), which license treating these instances as identical hard spheres; the theory is accordingly scoped to DSH-class plugin populations. On this scope the paper builds three theory layers. The rigorous layer, independent of any analogy, comprises an any-time hitting-time certificate bounding the expected rounds to any prescribed improvement, a resolution law that prices held-out validation budgets, and a separation theorem: the daemon must stay outside the population, because merging evaluator with evaluated voids the certificate. The kinetic layer is a master equation over the plugin x version x task grid with four operators (collision, reaction, external field, gate), where collision is co-activation. Its moment hierarchy, the step that turns a gas into fluid equations, generates the falsifiable statistical signatures. Throughout, the fluid reading is a bounded analogy: momentum is not conserved, so no Navier-Stokes limit exists. The measured layer runs on a faithful minimal instance, a large library of four-parameter skill plugins retrieved one per episode with a co-activation probe, in a one-model, one-task-family WebShop environment; every element maps to the DSH loop by architectural role. Population fluctuation scaling is density-gated: invisible at sparse edit density, it emerges at the predicted rate under tripled density, as directional evidence.

</details>

### [106] [LayerIt: Towards a Framework for Time-Aligned, Composable Music Visualizations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03428)
*Fernando Azeredo,António Sá Pinto*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: LayerIt is an open-source Python library that enables composing multiple music representations (notation, signal, algorithmic outputs) on a shared performance-time axis, producing a single SVG that preserves MEI structure and allows restyling of components.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Music information retrieval typically relates different types of information (signal-derived, algorithmic, symbolic) across different coordinate systems, but existing visualizations keep notation separate from physical time, and combining them requires manual assembly.

Method: LayerIt takes a score warped into performance time along with note-level alignment, and generates a single SVG that preserves the score's MEI (Music Encoding Initiative) structure while keeping added components identifiable and restylable.

Result: The library was demonstrated through a challenging beat-tracking analysis where tracker output, signal representations, and notation could be inspected together to locate metrical disagreement and other errors against both notated structure and performed time.

Conclusion: LayerIt enables integrated visualization of multiple music representations, facilitating error detection and analysis in MIR tasks by aligning notation with performance time.

Abstract: Music information retrieval often relates signal-derived, algorithmic, and symbolic information across different coordinate systems. Existing visualizations typically leave notation separate from physical time, while composites that combine them are assembled by hand. We present LayerIt, an open-source Python library for composing independent representations with notation on a shared performance-time axis. Given a score warped into performance time and a note-level alignment, LayerIt emits a single SVG that preserves the score's MEI structure and keeps added components identifiable and restylable. We demonstrate this through a challenging beat-tracking analysis, in which tracker output, signal representations, and notation can be inspected together to locate metrical disagreement and other errors against both notated structure and performed time.

</details>


### [107] [GAANet: Global-guided Asymmetric Attention Network for Audio-Visual Speech Separation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02752)
*Zhiyuan Zhang,Jingyuan Xu,Yiming Tang,Liu Liu,Dan Guo*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: GAANet (Global-guided Asymmetric Attention Network) is a novel model for audio-visual speech separation that addresses limitations in multi-scale feature fusion through two key innovations: an asymmetric multi-scale fusion framework allowing audio and visual streams to operate at their optimal temporal resolutions, and a global-guided attention mechanism that uses compact global tokens to provide semantic guidance for cross-modal fusion.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current audio-visual speech separation methods suffer from limited capacity due to: 1) treating features from different modalities in the same manner, and 2) overlooking the role of global features in fusion processes.

Method: The proposed GAANet introduces two core innovations: (1) An asymmetric multi-scale fusion framework that enables audio and visual streams to extract and interact with features at their respective optimal temporal resolutions, eliminating the need for symmetric temporal downsampling; (2) A global-guided attention mechanism that compresses each modality into a compact global token with temporal dimension of one, providing high-level semantic cues to guide both intra- and inter-modal fusion across scales.

Result: GAANet achieves state-of-the-art performance on LRS2 (16.5 dB SI-SNRi) and VoxCeleb2 (14.0 dB) datasets, while maintaining computational efficiency with only 3.3M parameters and 19.8G MACs.

Conclusion: Asymmetric temporal modeling combined with global guidance demonstrates strong potential for efficient and robust multimodal fusion in audio-visual speech separation tasks.

Abstract: Multi-scale design is crucial for efficient audio-visual speech separation, yet effectively modeling multi-scale information for audio-visual feature fusion remains challenging. We argue that the limited capacity of existing approaches primarily arises from: 1) treating features from different modalities in the same manner, and 2) overlooking the role of global features. To address these issues, we propose a Global-guided Asymmetric Attention Network (GAANet). Our model introduces two core innovations: first, an asymmetric multi-scale fusion framework that allows audio and visual streams to extract and interact with features at their respective optimal temporal resolutions, removing the need for symmetric temporal downsampling; second, a global-guided attention mechanism that compresses each modality into a compact global token with a temporal dimension of one, which then provides high-level semantic cues to guide both intra- and inter-modal fusion across scales. Experiments on LRS2 and VoxCeleb2 demonstrate that GAANet achieves state-of-the-art performance, reaching 16.5 dB SI-SNRi on LRS2 and 14.0 dB on VoxCeleb2, while maintaining a lightweight computational profile with only 3.3M parameters and 19.8G MACs. These results highlight the strong potential of asymmetric temporal modeling and global guidance for efficient and robust multimodal fusion. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/redizzy/GAANet

</details>


### [108] [What Actually Makes Correlation-Based SSL Distillation Noise-Robust? A Mechanistic Correction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02823)
*Fabian Ritter-Gutierrez,Nancy F. Chen,Eng Siong Chng*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This paper challenges the prevailing attribution of noise robustness in correlation-based knowledge distillation for speech models. Through rigorous ablation studies using multiple evaluation methods (unbiased full-dimensional probing, Pearson-variance decomposition, same-noise causal control, and per-dimension analysis), the authors demonstrate that the cross-correlation diagonal term—not the self-correlation term—provides noise invariance. The self-correlation term instead improves clean downstream task accuracy. The study provides concrete design rules for distillation: weight cross-correlation for noise robustness, tune self-correlation for downstream performance, and sample teacher and student noise independently.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Self-supervised learning (SSL) speech models are accurate but computationally expensive. Knowledge distillation compresses them, but the student loses the teacher's noise robustness. Prior work (original method and De'HuBERT) credited the self-correlation term for noise robustness, but this attribution was never isolated and verified.

Method: The authors employed four complementary evaluation methods: (1) an unbiased full-dimensional probe, (2) a Pearson-variance decomposition, (3) a same-noise causal control, and (4) a per-dimension analysis. Experiments were conducted on LibriSpeech-100 distillation with held-out CHiME-3 noise at 10 dB SNR, across nine speech and music tasks.

Result: Cross-correlation diagonal reduces noise-classification accuracy from 76.98% to 55.02%, while adding self-correlation back yields 55.55%—a negligible difference. Self-correlation instead reorganizes the feature space and improves clean downstream task accuracy but removes essentially no noise. Across nine tasks, the design rule emerges: weight cross-correlation for noise robustness, tune self-correlation for downstream performance, and sample teacher and student noise independently.

Conclusion: The self-correlation term has been wrongly credited for noise robustness in correlation-based distillation. The actual mechanism is the cross-correlation diagonal. This finding enables practitioners to decouple noise robustness from downstream performance optimization. The proposed design rule provides actionable guidance for tailoring distillation to specific deployment requirements.

Abstract: Self-supervised learning (SSL) speech models are accurate but large. Knowledge distillation compresses them, but the student loses the teacher's noise robustness. Correlation-based distillation addresses this with two terms: cross-correlation aligning student and teacher's representations, and self-correlation decorrelating the student's features. Both the original method and De'HuBERT credited the self-correlation term without isolating it. We show the opposite. On LibriSpeech-100 distillation with held-out CHiME-3 noise at 10\,dB, an unbiased full-dimensional probe, a Pearson-variance decomposition, a same-noise causal control, and a per-dimension analysis identify the cross-correlation diagonal as the mechanism that encourages noise invariance, lowering noise-classification accuracy from 76.98\% to 55.02\%, whereas adding the self-correlation term back leaves it at 55.55\%. The self-correlation term instead reorganises the feature space and improves accuracy on the clean downstream tasks, but removes essentially no noise. Across nine speech and music tasks this yields a concrete design rule for distillation: weight the cross-correlation term for noise robustness, tune the self-correlation term for better downstream performance, and sample teacher and student noise independently.

</details>


### [109] [Correlation-Based Distillation Yields More Mergeable Speech-Music Encoders](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02836)
*Fabian Ritter-Gutierrez*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: The paper investigates whether the choice of distillation loss affects how well two student models (speech and music) can be merged into a single compact encoder. The authors compare DistilHuBERT loss (Lkd) with a correlation-based loss (Lcl) under two merging algorithms: weight interpolation and activation permutation. Results show Lcl outperforms Lkd in 17 of 18 comparisons under weight interpolation and leads on speech tasks at every interpolated weight.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work on merging speech and music student models fixed the distillation loss, leaving open whether the loss itself affects merge quality. This work aims to determine if the choice of distillation loss influences how well students can be combined into a single model.

Method: The authors held architecture and evaluation fixed while substituting the DistilHuBERT loss (Lkd) with a correlation-based loss (Lcl). They tested both merging algorithms: (1) interpolating student weights from shared initialization, and (2) permuting channels into alignment before averaging. They measured endpoint proximity, speech task performance, channel rearrangement needs, and channel correlation strength.

Result: Under weight interpolation, Lcl students stayed closer to their better endpoint in 17 of 18 comparisons and led on speech tasks at every interpolated weight. Under activation permutation, Lcl needed fewer channel rearrangements at three layers, showed stronger correlated matched channels, and again led on speech tasks. Both merging algorithms improved under the same loss substitution.

Conclusion: The gain comes from the representation that Lcl produces rather than from either merging algorithm itself. The correlation-based loss produces representations that merge more effectively regardless of the merging mechanism used.

Abstract: A single compact encoder for both speech and music removes the need to maintain a separate model per domain. A practical recipe distils a speech teacher and a music teacher into two small students, then merges them into one model. Two merging algorithms exist: interpolating the student weights from a shared initialisation, or permuting their channels into alignment before averaging. Prior work fixed the distillation loss in both, leaving open whether the loss itself affects how well the students merge. We show that it does. Holding architecture and evaluation fixed, we replace the DistilHuBERT loss \Lkd{} with a correlation-based loss \Lcl{}. Under weight interpolation, \Lcl{} students stay closer to their own better endpoint in $17$ of $18$ comparisons and lead on the speech tasks at every interpolated weight. Under activation permutation, they need fewer channels rearranged at three layers, their matched channels correlate more strongly, and they again lead on speech. The two merging algorithms share no mechanism, yet both improve under the same loss substitution. This suggests that the gain lies in the representation \Lcl{} produces rather than in either algorithm.

</details>


### [110] [How Far Back Should a Transformer Look? Repetition and Copying in Music Sequence Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02837)
*Amir Fathi*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This paper investigates how predictive performance of autoregressive models for symbolic music depends on context length, finding that most long-context gains come from exact copying of repeated motifs (94%), particularly in datasets with frequent repeats like Nottingham folk tunes (71% NLL reduction), while datasets with fewer exact repeats show smaller gains (9-18%).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Understanding how and why long-context models succeed in symbolic music prediction, specifically whether they exploit pattern repetition or learn more complex musical structures.

Method: Trained small causal Transformers at context lengths T ∈ {6, 18, 48, 96, 192, 336} on raw tokens and binary latent codes; evaluated on same target positions; conducted ablation experiments (overwriting earlier occurrences, testing simple copy baseline); audited prior draft for methodological issues.

Result: On Nottingham folk tunes: 71% NLL reduction (0.986 bits/token) from 6 to 336 tokens. 94% of this gain explained by exact copying—when target's 16-token history enters context, improvement appears; overwriting removes gain. On O'Neill's tunes (129/302 test tunes): 71% reduction. On MAESTRO: 9% reduction. On MusicNet: 18% reduction, largely attained by 96 tokens. Trained 336-token model loses gain with restricted history. Methodological issues identified: split leakage, overlapping latent receptive fields, averaging predictor, per-file tempo grid.

Conclusion: Long-context gains in symbolic music models primarily stem from exact copying of repeated patterns (especially from rendered repeat signs), not complex musical reasoning. Methodological rigor is critical—prior saturation claims at 16 tokens were due to artifacts. Results pertain to rendered score representations; exact repeats are less frequent in performed/recorded music.

Abstract: We investigate how predictive performance depends on the maximum context available to an autoregressive model of symbolic music, and what information long-context models exploit. A small causal Transformer is trained separately at each context length T in {6, 18, 48, 96, 192, 336} and evaluated on the same target positions, both over raw tokens and over non-overlapping binary latent codes. On Nottingham folk tunes, the token predictor's test NLL decreases by 71% (0.986 bits per token) between 6 and 336 tokens, and by 71% on the O'Neill's tunes long enough for the same sweep (129 of 302 test tunes). Most of the long-context gain is explained by exact copying: the improvement appears when an earlier occurrence of the target's 16-token history enters the available context; overwriting that occurrence removes the gain, whereas equally large unrelated corruption does not; and a simple copy baseline recovers 94% of the reduction. A trained 336-token model likewise loses most of this gain when its history is restricted to recent tokens at test time. Because many repeats arise from written repeat signs expanded in the score, this result pertains specifically to these rendered score representations. By contrast, on MAESTRO performances and MusicNet scores, where exact repeats are substantially less frequent, the reduction is smaller (9% and 18%) and is largely attained by 96 tokens. Finally, an audit of an earlier draft that reported saturation at 16 tokens identified split leakage, overlapping latent receptive fields, an averaging predictor, and a per-file tempo grid; we present these as methodological checks for context-length measurements.

</details>


### [111] [Learning Jazz Pianist Style with Cross-Attention Conditioning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02918)
*Drew Edwards,Akira Maezawa,Simon Dixon*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This paper studies jazz pianist style recognition and generation using a pretrained symbolic music transformer. The model can classify pianist identity with high accuracy and generate music conditioned on specific artists' styles. A classifier can also identify characteristic moments in performances that distinguish each pianist's voice.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Jazz pianists develop distinctive identifiable traits, yet the features underlying this recognition resist formal description. The authors seek to understand and capture these stylistic elements through computational modeling.

Method: The authors use a pretrained symbolic music transformer with two main approaches: (1) Classification using the transformer's learned representations to identify pianist identity; (2) Augmentation with cross-attention over learned pianist identity embeddings to generate music conditioned on specific artists' style.

Result: The generator captures meaningful stylistic structure: a sliding-window classifier attributes conditioned continuations to the correct artist far above unconditioned baselines. A classifier trained on synthetic generations identifies real pianists across 12 classes with 87% chunk-level and 95% song-level accuracy. The classifier can also locate the most characteristic moments within a performance.

Conclusion: The pretrained symbolic music transformer already encodes pianist identity in its learned representations. The cross-attention mechanism enables effective style-conditioned generation. The approach successfully surfaces specific musical gestures that distinguish each pianist's voice.

Abstract: Jazz pianists develop distinctive traits that experienced listeners can often identify within seconds, yet the features underlying this recognition resist formal description. We study jazz pianist style through the lens of a pretrained symbolic music transformer, showing that its learned representations already encode pianist identity well enough for highly accurate classification across two benchmarks. We then augment the transformer with cross-attention over learned pianist identity embeddings, enabling it to generate music conditioned on a specific artist's style. Two evaluation protocols confirm that the generator captures meaningful stylistic structure: a sliding-window classifier consistently attributes conditioned continuations to the correct artist, far above unconditioned baselines; and a classifier trained entirely on synthetic generations identifies real pianists across 12 classes with 87% chunk-level and 95% song-level accuracy. Finally, we repurpose the classifier to locate the most characteristic moments within a performance, surfacing the specific musical gestures that distinguish each pianist's voice.

</details>


### [112] [ParaGeo: Decomposing Paralinguistic Variation into a Shared Latent Geometry](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03125)
*Yuhan Liu,Yuxuan Ou,Ruoxi Su,Mohamed Ahmed Zaki,Yunbo Long*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: ParaGeo introduces a method to decompose paralinguistic variation in frozen speech language models by analyzing K/V representations from synthesized audio tokens. The method provides a shared coordinate system for measuring paralinguistic structure and enables latent speech control through reproducible contrast directions across scenarios.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Speech delivery varies with both paralinguistic attributes (like emotion, tone, style) and linguistic content. The researchers aim to understand and measure this paralinguistic variation in frozen speech language models, creating a framework for latent speech control.

Method: ParaGeo uses matched-content decomposition of paralinguistic variation. Synthesized audio tokens are replayed with a fixed listening prompt; pooled key/value (K/V) representations are centered and projected into a shared low-dimensional space. The GLM-4-Voice probe spans 80 requested controls from 12 benchmark families across 8 sentences. A separate probe tests 10 scenarios with 6 styles.

Result: Content-held-out centroid accuracy is 9.49% versus 1.25% permutation baseline; same-label cross-content cosine similarity is 0.285 versus 0.017; both conditional permutation tests yield p = 0.001. Static, additive, and temporal interventions produce attribute-, layer-, and schedule-dependent response profiles. Reproducible contrast directions were found across scenarios.

Conclusion: ParaGeo provides a shared coordinate representation for measuring paralinguistic structure and an empirical starting point for latent speech control. The method demonstrates that paralinguistic attributes can be reliably decoded from speech language model representations, enabling controllable speech generation.

Abstract: Speech delivery varies with both the requested paralinguistic attribute and the linguistic content. We introduce ParaGeo, a matched-content decomposition of paralinguistic variation in a frozen speech language model. Synthesized audio tokens are replayed with a fixed listening prompt; pooled key/value (K/V) representations are centered and projected into a shared low-dimensional space. Our GLM-4-Voice probe spans 80 requested controls from 12 benchmark families across eight sentences. With a globally fitted calibration basis, content-held-out centroid accuracy using this basis is 9.49% versus a 1.25% permutation baseline; same-label cross-content cosine similarity is 0.285 versus 0.017, and both conditional permutation tests yield p = 0.001. A separate ten-scenario, six-style probe reveals reproducible contrast directions across scenarios. Static, additive, and temporal interventions produce attribute-, layer-, and schedule-dependent response profiles. These results provide a shared coordinate representation for measuring paralinguistic structure and an empirical starting point for latent speech control. Code is available at https://github.com/yuhanlydia/ParaGeo.

</details>


### [113] [DriftTTS: Few-Step Text-to-Speech Without Distillation via Distribution-Matching Drift](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03390)
*Mohammad Nur Hossain Khan,Subrata Biswas,Bashima Islam*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: DriftTTS is a few-step neural text-to-speech model that generates mel-spectrograms using a distribution-matching drift objective, without relying on pretrained generative teachers, distillation, or adversarial discrimination. It uses a frozen masked-autoencoder encoder and on-policy rollout training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing few-step TTS models depend on shortened diffusion/flow-matching schedules or distillation from pretrained multi-step teachers. This work aims to develop a competitive few-step TTS system that operates independently of these dependencies.

Method: DriftTTS employs a distribution-matching drift objective in mel-domain feature space defined by raw mels and a frozen masked-autoencoder encoder pretrained on the same LJSpeech training split. On-policy rollout trains the decoder on its own intermediate states, supporting inference up to the trained rollout depth.

Result: On LJSpeech at NFE=4, DriftTTS achieves 3.87 dB MCD and 3.7% WER, compared to Matcha-TTS's 3.85 dB MCD and 3.4% WER. In blind listening tests, DriftTTS obtains 4.18 MOS versus 3.96 for Matcha-TTS and 4.22 for ground truth.

Conclusion: DriftTTS demonstrates competitive few-step synthesis performance without requiring a pretrained generative teacher, offering a simpler alternative to existing approaches while achieving comparable quality to state-of-the-art methods.

Abstract: Few-step neural text-to-speech models often rely on short- ened diffusion or flow-matching schedules, or on distillation from pretrained multi-step teachers. To avoid these depen- dencies, we present DriftTTS, a few-step mel-spectrogram generator trained without a generative teacher, distillation, or adversarial discrimination. DriftTTS uses a distribution- matching drift objective in a mel-domain feature space defined by raw mels and a frozen masked-autoencoder encoder pretrained on the same LJSpeech training split. On-policy rollout trains the decoder on its own interme- diate states and supports inference up to the trained roll- out depth. On LJSpeech, DriftTTS at NFE=4 achieves 3.87 dB MCD and 3.7% WER, compared with 3.85 dB and 3.4% for Matcha-TTS. In a fully paired blind listen- ing test, DriftTTS obtains 4.18 MOS, compared with 3.96 for Matcha-TTS and 4.22 for ground truth. These results demonstrate competitive few-step synthesis without a pre- trained generative teacher. Code can be found at https: //github.com/BASHLab/driftTTS.git

</details>


### [114] [Harmonic Eigenspace: A Web-based Application for Navigating and Composing Microtonal Harmony](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03398)
*David Dalmazzoa,Ken Déguernel*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: A web-based application for navigating and composing microtonal harmony using the Harmonic Eigenspace, a 4D psychoacoustically grounded space where chord types are located by spectral dissonance profiles. Features 3D visualization, Modal Studio for 53-TET, and MIDI controller with MPE support.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enable composers and musicians to navigate microtonal harmony intuitively by providing a psychoacoustically grounded coordinate system that is transposition-invariant and register-invariant, organizing the harmonic space around consonant tetrads as landmarks.

Method: Uses Sethares's roughness/dissonance model to compute spectral dissonance profiles for tetrad chord types. The 4D Harmonic Eigenspace uses coordinate triples (α, β, γ) to locate three upper notes relative to the root, with transposition acting along an invariant ray. Embeds tetrads from tonal equal temperaments as discrete lattices within the continuous volume. Evaluation via listening study (n=31) rating isolated 53-TET chords and microtonal progressions.

Result: The dissonance volume contains 100 local minima aligned with just-intonation intervals, organizing the space into basins around consonant tetrads. Listening study measured acceptance/rejection of unfamiliar microtonal chords and progressions.

Conclusion: The application successfully provides a navigable 3D visualization of the dissonance volume and an extended modal interchange logic for 53-TET, functioning as a usable MIDI controller with MPE support for microtonal composition in digital audio workstations.

Abstract: This paper presents a web-based application for navigating and composing microtonal harmony, built on the Harmonic Eigenspace, a four-dimensional psychoacoustically grounded space in which tetrad chord types are located by their spectral dissonance profiles, computed with Sethares's roughness/dissonance model. The coordinate system is transposition-invariant: a coordinate triple (α, \b{eta}, γ) locates the three upper notes in relation to the root, so a chord quality corresponds to a direction in the space, the invariant ray along which transposition acts, while the root frequency sets the scale. The dissonance field over these coordinates can be computed at any register; the locations of its local minima are register-invariant, as they arise from partial-coincidence ratio conditions. The dissonance volume contains 100 local minima that align with just-intonation intervals and act as landmarks, organising the space into basins around the most consonant tetrads. We embed tetrads from three tonal equal temperaments as discrete lattices within this continuous volume. The application presents this space through two components: the Harmonic Eigenspace as a navigable 3D visualisation of the dissonance volume in which all nodes are playable, and a Modal Studio that extends modal interchange logic to the ten-gradation interval vocabulary of 53-TET. The application also functions as a MIDI controller with MIDI Polyphonic Expression support, usable in any digital audio workstation that supports this format. A listening study with 31 participants used both scenes of the application: listeners first rated isolated 53-TET chords alongside chords familiar from Western practice, such as the maj7 and the m7; they then rated chord progressions composed in the Modal Studio, measuring their acceptance or rejection of microtonal progressions heard for the first time.

</details>


### [115] [PEACE: Joint Embeddings of DSP Effects Code and Audio](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03405)
*David Braun,Adam Finkelstein*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: PEACE introduces the first joint embedding of audio effect code and output audio, combining an AFx-Rep audio encoder with two code encoders (T5 transformer and graph neural network) for Faust audio processing code. The system enables audio-to-code retrieval and can encode effect chain topology independently of parameters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to enable music information retrieval systems that can search, generate, and condition on DSP code, requiring a unified representation that captures both audio output characteristics and the underlying code structure.

Method: The method involves: (1) Fine-tuning a T5 transformer over Faust source code; (2) Evaluating a message-passing graph neural network over Faust compiler's intermediate representation to capture topology and UI parameters; (3) Evaluating on audio-to-code retrieval with varying levels of parameter masking to separate topology from parameters.

Result: The two code encoders perform similarly on mixed-length chains but show tradeoffs on single-effect galleries. With parameters fully masked, PEACE recovers ordered chain topology far above chance. It outperforms pretrained models on out-of-distribution reverb retrieval and can improve frozen audio-only representations.

Conclusion: PEACE achieves dual understanding of topology and parameters, laying groundwork for MIR systems that can search, generate, and condition on DSP code. The ability to separate topology from parameters enables flexible audio-to-code retrieval and cross-modal understanding.

Abstract: This paper introduces PEACE, the first joint embedding of audio effect code and output audio. Building on SLAP's multimodal objective, we pair an AFx-Rep audio encoder with two code encoders for Faust, a functional language for audio signal processing. First, we evaluate a fine-tuned T5 transformer over Faust source code. Second, we evaluate a message-passing graph neural network over an intermediate representation of the Faust compiler, capturing both topology and UI parameters. We evaluate on audio-to-code retrieval, where masking UI parameters at inference yields embeddings that encode effect chain topology alone. When parameters are visible, the two code encoders tie on retrieval of mixed-length chains but have tradeoffs on single-effect galleries. With parameters fully masked, PEACE recovers ordered chain topology far above chance without the limitations of supervised methods. PEACE outperforms pretrained models on an out-of-distribution reverb retrieval benchmark and can improve frozen audio-only representations. Its dual understanding of topology and parameters lays the groundwork for music information retrieval systems that search, generate, and condition on DSP code.

</details>


### [116] [Rubric-Based Optimization for Text-to-Music Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03589)
*Ping Wang,Guang Yang,Shao-Rong Su,Junkai Wu,Pang Wei Koh,Noah A. Smith*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: The paper explores using pretrained audio-language models (ALMs) with structured rubric-based rewards for post-training text-to-music generation. It compares DPO and DiffusionNFT training methods on MusicGen-small and ACE-Step models, finding that ALM rubrics improve broad perceptual qualities but struggle with specific attributes like key, where specialized objective rewards remain superior.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current automatic metrics fail to capture multiple aspects of musical quality simultaneously. This research investigates whether pretrained audio-language models can provide structured, rubric-based rewards that improve multiple quality dimensions in text-to-music generation.

Method: The study uses ALM-generated rubric scores to create preference pairs for Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) on MusicGen-small and ACE-Step v1, and directly uses rubric scores as scalar rewards for DiffusionNFT on ACE-Step v1. Evaluation relies on multiple automatic metrics (CLAP, SongEval, Audiobox-Aesthetics) and specialized rewards for tempo, key, and instrumentation attributes.

Result: Rubric-based optimization improves all three metrics simultaneously on MusicCaps, with DiffusionNFT on ACE-Step showing strongest gains. However, on MusicGen-small, optimizing for any single evaluator creates cross-metric trade-offs. For specific attributes (tempo, key, instrumentation), specialized objective rewards work reliably while ALM rubrics only partially transfer for tempo/instrumentation and show no improvement for key.

Conclusion: A practical division of labor is recommended: ALM rubrics are effective for broad perceptual qualities that are difficult to formalize, while specialized objective rewards remain preferable when reliable measurements are available.

Abstract: Post-training text-to-music generation requires reward signals that capture multiple aspects of musical quality beyond what any single automatic metric can measure. We study structured, rubric-based rewards from pretrained audio-language models (ALMs) as training signals for both autoregressive and diffusion-based music generators. An ALM scores each generated clip against the rubric; we rank candidates generated for the same text prompt by their scores and convert these rankings into preference pairs for DPO on both MusicGen-small and ACE-Step~v1, and additionally use the rubric scores directly as scalar rewards for DiffusionNFT on ACE-Step~v1. On MusicCaps, rubric-based optimization improves CLAP, SongEval, and Audiobox-Aesthetics simultaneously, with the strongest gains obtained by DiffusionNFT on ACE-Step. By contrast, on MusicGen-small, building preferences from any one of these automatic evaluators produces clear cross-metric trade-offs: the targeted evaluator improves while other independent evaluators deteriorate. We further study tempo, key, and instrumentation, where precise objective rewards are available. Directly optimizing these specialized rewards reliably improves the target attributes, whereas ALM rubrics provide only partial transfer for tempo and instrumentation and no measurable improvement for key. Together, these results suggest a practical division of labor: ALM rubrics are effective for broad perceptual qualities that are difficult to formalize, while specialized objective rewards remain preferable when reliable measurements are available.

</details>


### [117] [Revisiting Input Time-frequency Representations in Multi-pitch Estimation for Vocal Ensembles](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03656)
*Junyoung Koh,Hao-Wen Dong*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This paper compares harmonic constant-Q transform (HCQT) with linear short-time Fourier transform (STFT) for multi-pitch estimation (MPE) in vocal ensembles. Surprisingly, the simpler linear STFT outperforms HCQT while being computationally cheaper, challenging the assumption that pitch-adaptive frequency resolution is necessary for this task.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-pitch estimation in vocal ensembles is challenging due to overlapping pitch ranges and harmonics from different singers. While HCQT provides frequency-adaptive resolution, its expensive feature extraction for on-the-fly training mixture generation is a significant drawback. This motivated the authors to investigate whether a simpler representation could perform comparably or better.

Method: The authors compared HCQT with linear STFT as input representations for MPE models. They analyzed the effects of varying analysis window lengths, spectral coverage, and input frequency range restrictions to understand why STFT performs better.

Result: Linear STFT outperforms HCQT while substantially reducing feature-extraction cost. Further analysis revealed that longer analysis windows or broader spectral coverage provide no improvement. Restricting input to predicted pitch ranges actually reduces STFT's advantage, suggesting that finer frequency resolution is not beneficial for vocal-ensemble MPE and shorter windows are more effective for time-varying vocal pitches.

Conclusion: Finer frequency resolution does not necessarily improve vocal-ensemble MPE. The linear STFT's superior performance, combined with its lower computational cost, makes it a more practical choice. Shorter analysis windows can be more effective for capturing time-varying vocal pitches, challenging the conventional wisdom that pitch-aligned representations are essential for MPE.

Abstract: Multi-pitch estimation in vocal ensembles is challenging because singers occupy overlapping pitch ranges and often sing at closely spaced fundamental frequencies, causing their harmonics to overlap in time-frequency representations. Existing models commonly use harmonic constant-Q transform (HCQT)-based representations to provide frequency-adaptive resolution, at the cost of expensive feature extraction when training mixtures are generated on the fly. We revisit this design and compare HCQT with a linear short-time Fourier transform (STFT), whose frequency bins are directly provided as model inputs. Despite its fixed frequency resolution and the absence of a pitch-aligned input grid, the linear STFT outperforms HCQT while substantially reducing feature-extraction cost. Further analysis shows that a longer analysis window or broader spectral coverage provides no additional improvement, while restricting the input to the predicted pitch range reduces the advantage of the linear STFT. These results suggest that finer frequency resolution does not necessarily improve vocal-ensemble MPE, and that shorter analysis windows can be more effective for time-varying vocal pitches.

</details>
