### [118] [SimuVerity: Benchmarking Agents for Engineering-Grade Simulink Model Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02304)
*Ruiqi Zhang,Jiahao Wang,Mingxuan Li,Haichen Luo,Chaoting Wang,Guoyu Mou,Keyu Lai,Hanchao Lv,Jiaxu Wang,Yibo Zheng,Aijun Yang,Xiaohua Wang*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: SimuVerity is a new benchmark with 101 text-to-executable Simulink model-generation tasks across ten engineering domains. It evaluates models across six dimensions (accuracy, output quality, mechanistic fidelity, control/causal integrity, operating-domain robustness, and dynamic response) rather than just checking compilation or structural similarity. The best system achieves only 42.86% overall score, revealing significant capability bottlenecks in producing qualified implementations and satisfying multidimensional requirements.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing Simulink benchmarks only evaluate whether generated models compile, execute, or resemble a reference model. These criteria do not establish whether a model satisfies its engineering requirements, which is what matters in practice.

Method: SimuVerity comprises 101 text-to-executable Simulink model-generation tasks across ten engineering domains. Each task includes executable-system profiles grounding the engineering specification and four families of native simulation scenarios. A hierarchical evaluator first checks artifact delivery, native executability, and engineering qualification, then scores qualified models across six dimensions: accuracy, output quality, mechanistic fidelity, control and causal integrity, operating-domain robustness, and dynamic response.

Result: The best system achieves an overall score of only 42.86%. Structural similarity is a poor proxy for engineering performance. Capability bottlenecks arise both in producing qualified implementations and in satisfying multidimensional requirements after qualification. Some high-scoring models still exhibit severe visual-layout disorder.

Conclusion: SimuVerity provides a systematic basis for assessing agents' engineering capabilities and diagnosing failures in executable Simulink model generation. It reveals that current AI systems struggle with producing engineering-qualified models that meet multidimensional requirements.

Abstract: Existing Simulink benchmarks mainly evaluate whether generated models compile, execute, or resemble a reference model. These criteria do not establish whether a model satisfies its engineering requirements. We introduce SimuVerity, a benchmark of 101 text-to-executable Simulink model-generation tasks across ten engineering domains. For each task, executable-system profiles ground the engineering specification and four families of native simulation scenarios. A hierarchical evaluator first checks artifact delivery, native executability, and engineering qualification, then scores qualified models across six dimensions covering accuracy, output quality, mechanistic fidelity, control and causal integrity, operating-domain robustness, and dynamic response. We evaluate six agent systems with SimuVerity. The best system achieves an overall score of only 42.86. The results show that structural similarity is a poor proxy for engineering performance: capability bottlenecks arise both in producing qualified implementations and in satisfying multidimensional requirements after qualification. Meanwhile, some high-scoring models still exhibit severe visual-layout disorder. SimuVerity provides a systematic basis for assessing agents' engineering capabilities and diagnosing failures in executable Simulink model generation.

</details>


### [119] [Compound AI System Reliability: A Failure Taxonomy and Resilience Pattern Catalog from 150 Production Incidents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02503)
*Rudrendu Kumar Paul,Sourav Nandy*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper presents a comprehensive taxonomy of 23 failure modes in compound AI systems, derived from analyzing 150 production incidents, along with resilience patterns that demonstrably reduce failure propagation and improve recovery times.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Compound AI systems (combining retrieval, generation, tools, and orchestration) are increasingly deployed but lack systematic understanding of failure modes that emerge at component boundaries, where traditional single-model monitoring approaches fail to detect cascading errors, silent quality degradation, and coordination failures.

Method: The authors analyzed 150 production incident reports from open-source compound AI projects and anonymized enterprise deployments, then conducted controlled fault injection experiments to measure the effectiveness of proposed resilience patterns.

Result: The study identified 23 failure modes organized into five categories (retrieval, generation, tool, orchestration, and integration failures). Resilience patterns showed significant effectiveness: circuit breakers reduce cascade propagation by 89%, output quality gates catch 73% of silent degradation, and component isolation reduces blast radius by 64%. Systems implementing three or more patterns reduce MTTR by 71% compared to unstructured monitoring.

Conclusion: The researchers provide a practitioner resource including an incident taxonomy and pattern catalog, demonstrating that structured resilience patterns can substantially improve reliability and recoverability of compound AI systems.

Abstract: Deploying compound AI systems reliably and safely requires understanding failure modes that emerge at component boundaries, not within individual models. Cascading errors propagate across component boundaries, silent quality degradation evades standard monitoring, and coordination failures yield incorrect collective behavior from individually correct parts. We analyze 150 production incident reports from open-source compound AI projects and anonymized enterprise deployments to construct a taxonomy of 23 failure modes organized into five categories: retrieval failures, generation failures, tool failures, orchestration failures, and integration failures. For each category, we propose resilience patterns with measured effectiveness from controlled fault injection experiments. Circuit breakers reduce cascade propagation by 89%, output quality gates catch 73% of silent degradation before user impact, and component isolation reduces blast radius by 64%. Systems implementing three or more resilience patterns from our catalog reduce mean-time-to-recovery (MTTR) by 71% compared to unstructured monitoring baselines. We release the incident taxonomy and pattern catalog as a practitioner resource.

</details>


### [120] [An Extensive Empirical Study on Evaluation Metrics for Combinatorial Interaction Testing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02560)
*Lisha Qin,Chenhui Cui,Tao Li,Rubing Huang,Shikai Guo,Lei Ma*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper presents a comprehensive survey of black-box evaluation metrics for combinatorial interaction testing (CIT), along with an empirical study involving 8 open-source projects, 32 test scenarios, and 295,624 test suites to examine correlations between static metrics and fault-detection effectiveness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation stems from a gap in literature: no prior work systematically addresses the selection of appropriate evaluation metrics for CIT test suites, despite the wide variety of available options and the importance of this choice for practitioners.

Method: The paper employs two methods: (1) A systematic survey providing rigorous definitions, classifications, examples, and complexity analyses of black-box evaluation metrics; (2) An empirical study using correlation analysis between static metrics and fault-detection effectiveness across multiple real-world projects.

Result: Key findings: (1) Value Combination Coverage (VCC) is a valid predictor for test-suite evaluation; (2) Distribution-based metrics generally have lower computational costs than interaction coverage-based metrics; (3) The effectiveness of evaluation metrics is substantially influenced by the test suite's inherent properties.

Conclusion: The study concludes by providing practical guidelines to help CIT practitioners select appropriate evaluation metrics for assessing or comparing combinatorial test suites, considering factors like computational cost, predictive validity, and test suite characteristics.

Abstract: Combinatorial interaction testing (CIT) is a black-box testing method that has received extensive attention in both research and practice over recent years. Its primary objective is to construct an effective combinatorial test suite that detects software failures caused by parameter interactions. As a fundamental component of the CIT testing process, the evaluation metric plays a critical role in assessing and comparing combinatorial test suites, as well as in evaluating various test generation techniques. For CIT practitioners, selecting an appropriate evaluation metric is both important and challenging, given the wide variety of available options. Nevertheless, no prior work has systematically addressed this problem. To fill this gap, this paper first provides a comprehensive survey of black-box evaluation metrics for combinatorial test suites, offering rigorous definitions, clear classifications, illustrative examples, and complexity analyses. We then conduct an extensive empirical study involving eight open-source projects, encompassing 32 test scenarios and 295,624 combinatorial test suites. In this study, we examine the correlation between each static evaluation metric and fault-detection effectiveness using two correlation measures. Experimental results show that the Value Combination Coverage (VCC) metric serves as a valid predictor for test-suite evaluation. However, distribution-based metrics generally incur lower computational costs than interaction coverage-based ones. The choice of an appropriate metric should also account for the test suite's inherent properties, as these characteristics can substantially influence the effectiveness of the evaluation. Finally, we provide practical guidelines to assist CIT practitioners in selecting suitable evaluation metrics for assessing or comparing combinatorial test suites.

</details>


### [121] [Improving the Energy-Efficiency of the Code Generated by LLMs through Effective Prompting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02571)
*Ritika Rekhi,Bing Zhang,Md Arman Islam,Jaya Krishna Pasham,Yeswanth Chitturi,Akshay Paramesha,Isha Valiveti,Asif Imran,Bekir Turkkan,Tevfik Kosar*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper evaluates 21 prompting strategies for energy-efficient code generation across 10 LLMs (Python and C++), finding that selected strategies can reduce energy consumption by up to 25% for Python and 17% for C++ code.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As AI-assisted programming becomes mainstream, the environmental impact of AI-generated software has emerged as an important consideration. However, frontier LLMs are rarely evaluated based on the energy efficiency of the code they produce.

Method: The authors conducted a comprehensive evaluation of 21 prompting strategies for energy-efficient code generation and identified 8 strategies for evaluation across 10 widely used open-weight and proprietary LLMs. They evaluated their effectiveness for both Python and C++ code generation relative to a baseline prompt.

Result: Across the evaluated models, the selected prompting strategies achieved energy reductions of up to 25% for Python and 17% for C++ code generation. At the model level, Python energy reductions reached up to 50% for Granite-4.0-H-Small, 39% for Claude 4.5 Haiku, and 28% for MiniMax M3, while C++ reductions reached up to 56% for Granite-4.0-H-Small and 7% for Qwen3-Coder-480B-A35B-Instruct.

Conclusion: Prompting strategies can substantially influence the energy consumption of LLM-generated code, although their effectiveness varies across models and programming languages. The findings highlight the importance of incorporating energy efficiency into the evaluation and optimization of LLM-based code generation and provide practical insights into designing prompts for more sustainable AI-assisted programming.

Abstract: As AI-assisted programming becomes increasingly mainstream, the environmental impact of AI-generated software has emerged as an important consideration. This motivates evaluating LLM-generated code beyond functional correctness by considering execution efficiency and energy consumption. However, despite substantial advances in code generation, frontier LLMs are rarely evaluated based on the energy efficiency of the code they produce. In this work, we conduct a comprehensive evaluation of 21 prompting strategies for energy-efficient code generation and identify 8 strategies for evaluation across 10 widely used open-weight and proprietary LLMs. We evaluate their effectiveness for both Python and C++ code generation relative to a baseline prompt. Across the evaluated models, the selected prompting strategies achieved energy reductions of up to 25% for Python and 17% for C++ code generation. At the model level, Python energy reductions reached up to 50% for Granite-4.0-H-Small, 39% for Claude 4.5 Haiku, and 28% for MiniMax M3, while C++ reductions reached up to 56% for Granite-4.0-H-Small and 7% for Qwen3-Coder-480B-A35B-Instruct. These results demonstrate that prompting strategies can substantially influence the energy consumption of LLM-generated code, although their effectiveness varies across models and programming languages. Our findings highlight the importance of incorporating energy efficiency into the evaluation and optimization of LLM-based code generation and provide practical insights into designing prompts for more sustainable AI-assisted programming.

</details>


### [122] [WebUIProof: Benchmarking WebUI Code Generators with UI-Agent Execution Harness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02617)
*Yun-Yun Tsai,Yuning Mao,Shiqi Wang,Junfeng Yang,Sinong Wang*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: WebUIProof is an execution-oriented benchmark for evaluating WebUI code generation at scale, providing structured specifications and dense, executable interaction tests across general WebUIs and 3D interactive simulations. It uses a UI-agent harness running in a headless browser with plan-act-observe loops to test DOM interactions and UI changes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Evaluating WebUI code generation is difficult because outputs may compile and look plausible yet fail under user interaction. Prior benchmarks rely on free-form prompts with static checks (build success, screenshots) that miss functional correctness.

Method: WebUIProof includes a UI-agent harness that runs executable interaction tests in a headless browser using an iterative plan-act-observe loop: it locates DOM elements, performs actions, observes resulting UI/DOM changes, and checks specified assertions.

Result: Evaluation across eight commercial LLMs reveals frequent failures on interaction-based requirements even when pages render successfully, especially on 3D simulation interfaces. Training compact models (Qwen2.5 14B and MIMO 7B) with RL rewards derived from executable interaction tests improves functional completion while reducing build failures.

Conclusion: The UI-agent harness can provide outcome-level training signals. RL training with interaction test rewards effectively improves functional correctness of generated WebUI code, particularly for compact models, addressing the gap between visual plausibility and actual user interaction functionality.

Abstract: Evaluating WebUI code generation at scale is difficult: outputs may compile and look plausible yet fail under user interaction, and prior benchmarks largely rely on free-form prompts with static checks (build success, screenshots) that miss functional correctness. We introduce WebUIProof, an execution-oriented benchmark that provides structured specifications and dense, executable interaction tests for WebUI generation across two task families: general WebUIs (e.g., dashboards, game, interactive tools) and 3D interactive simulation (e.g., particle/galaxy systems, physics dynamics). WebUIProof includes a UI-agent harness that runs executable interaction tests in a headless browser using an iterative plan--act--observe loop: it locates DOM elements, performs actions, observes resulting UI/DOM changes, and checks the specified assertions. We evaluate across eight commercial LLMs and observe frequent failures on interaction-based requirements even when pages render successfully, especially on 3D simulation interfaces. Finally, we show the UI-agent harness can provide outcome-level training signals. Training compact models (e.g., Qwen2.5 14B and MIMO 7B) with RL rewards derived from executable interaction tests improves functional completion while reducing build failures.

</details>


### [123] [Self-Supervised Scaling of Terminal Environments for Scientific Domains](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02710)
*Zhongzhi Li,Yucheng Shi,Zongxia Li,Junyao Yang,Ruhan Wang,Yu Wang,Jingyuan Huang,Jichao Yu,Ninghao Liu,Haitao Mi,Leowei Liang*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper introduces Software-in-the-Loop Reconstruction (SWR), a self-supervised framework that leverages existing software workflows to generate training data and verification targets for terminal agents, eliminating the need for manual task authoring. The method executes existing software across multiple input configurations, partitioning results into public observations and hidden evaluations. Agents must reconstruct the software behavior from public examples, and are evaluated on hidden cases. Experiments with 500 workflows across six domains show that fine-tuning Qwen3.8-27B improves Terminal-Bench 2 performance from 47.94% to 53.56%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deploying terminal agents beyond software engineering requires training environments with executable reference behavior and domain-specific verifiers. However, authoring these components for each task is labor-intensive and limits reuse. The authors seek a scalable solution that can leverage existing software workflows to generate training data and verification automatically.

Method: The SWR framework works as follows: (1) Execute existing software workflows across multiple input configurations; (2) Partition cases into public observations (available to agent) and hidden evaluations (for testing); (3) Given instruction, input schema, and public input-output pairs, an agent constructs an executable program without accessing the source workflow; (4) Evaluate candidates on hidden configurations against workflow outputs; (5) Use a hierarchical verifier combining domain-specific semantic comparison, structural validity, and anti-shortcut checks; (6) Provide public feedback for iterative revision. The framework allows adding new workflows and configurations without manual authoring.

Result: - Qwen3.8-Max solves 838 tasks across three attempts, producing 1,422 verified trajectories
- These were oversampled to 3,000 reconstruction-only training examples
- Supervised fine-tuning of Qwen3.8-27B improved mean Terminal-Bench 2 performance from 47.94% to 53.56% across three seeds
- Achieved highest mean among four matched-token corpus controls on all four reported evaluations
- Instantiated with 500 workflows and 46 software families across six domains

Conclusion: Existing scientific software can provide scalable, behaviorally verified supervision for terminal agents. The SWR framework eliminates the need for manual task authoring by automatically extracting reference behavior and verification targets from executable software workflows, enabling efficient training of terminal agents across diverse domains.

Abstract: Terminal agents are increasingly deployed beyond software engineering in science and other specialized domains. Constructing training environments requires executable reference behavior and a domain-specific verifier that distinguishes semantic correctness from superficially plausible artifacts. Authoring these components for each task requires repeated engineering and limits reuse. We introduce software-in-the-loop reconstruction, a self-supervised framework that obtains reference outputs and verification targets from existing software workflows, executable programs mapping structured inputs to outputs. For each workflow, we execute multiple input configurations and partition cases into public observations and hidden evaluations. Given the instruction, input schema, and public input--output observations, an agent constructs an editable program without access to the source workflow. The candidate is evaluated on hidden configurations against workflow outputs. A hierarchical verifier combines domain-specific semantic comparison, structural validity, and anti-shortcut checks, while public feedback supports iterative revision. The construction admits additional workflows and configurations without authoring a reference solution for each task. We instantiate SWR with 500 workflows and 46 software families across six domains. Across three attempts per task, Qwen3.8-Max solves 838 tasks and produces 1,422 verified trajectories, which we oversample to 3,000 reconstruction-only training examples. Supervised fine-tuning of Qwen3.8-27B improves mean Terminal-Bench 2 performance from 47.94% to 53.56% across three seeds and achieves the highest mean among four matched-token corpus controls on all four reported evaluations. These results indicate that existing scientific software can provide scalable, behaviorally verified supervision for terminal agents.

</details>


### [124] [VeriPy Source-Preserving Verification and Compatibility Checking for Python Components](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02814)
*Naing Oo Lwin*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: VeriPy is a tool that maintains alignment between Python programs and their formal guarantees by allowing developers to express contracts, invariants, and proof hooks as Python comments. It produces verifiable artifacts in Dafny or Lean while preserving executable code and checking backward compatibility through relational products.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The core problem is maintaining synchronization between Python implementations and their formal specifications - when implementations are updated, specifications must reflect changes while preserving existing caller behavior. This creates a continuing maintenance burden where specifications can drift from actual code.

Method: VeriPy uses a workflow where developers express contracts and proofs as Python comments, then refines checked auxiliary lemmas using source-located diagnostics. Direct encoders produce Dafny or Lean verification artifacts while retaining admitted executable bodies and explicit dependency models. A relational product mechanism checks whether updated components admit old inputs and preserve returned values and modeled exceptions.

Result: The workflow connects source-level proof development with functional verification and backward compatibility checking, recording the assumptions under which each guarantee applies. This enables verification while maintaining compatibility with existing code that depends on specific behaviors.

Conclusion: VeriPy brings formal verification into a common Python development workflow by embedding specifications directly in source code and providing automated backward compatibility checking, helping ensure that formal guarantees remain aligned with actual program behavior over time.

Abstract: Keeping a Python program and its formal guarantees aligned is a continuing maintenance problem. Specifications must describe the implementation that actually runs, and updates must preserve the behavior on which existing callers depend. VeriPy brings these obligations into a common workflow for annotated Python components. Developers and agents express contracts, invariants, and proof hooks as Python comments, then refine checked auxiliary lemmas using source-located diagnostics. Direct encoders produce Dafny or Lean artifacts while retaining admitted executable bodies and explicit models of their dependencies. A relational product checks whether an updated component still admits old inputs and preserves returned values and modeled exceptions. The resulting workflow connects source-level proof development with functional verification and backward compatibility, recording the assumptions under which each guarantee applies. The code is available at https://github.com/astrio-labs/veripy.

</details>


### [125] [Discriminating Fixture Coverage in Agent-Infrastructure Verification Suites](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02928)
*Xin Xu,Siru Tao*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper applies mutation analysis to evaluate invariant suites for a multi-session agent state-projection layer. The authors discover that standard validation (passing correct implementation, failing broken one) is insufficient - some mutants survive due to missing inputs or unobservable state corruption. They propose treating missing inputs as a coverage problem across 7 dimensions, adding fixtures to cover uncovered dimensions, and demonstrate this approach kills all five surviving mutants using existing oracles.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors aim to measure the actual value of single-observation validation for invariant suites. They question whether passing a correct implementation and failing a broken one provides meaningful evidence of a suite's effectiveness, and seek to understand what such observations actually certify.

Method: The authors apply mutation analysis to an invariant suite for a multi-session agent state-projection layer. They: (1) mutate the code and run the suite against mutants; (2) analyze surviving mutants to identify failure modes (inactive mutants vs. unobservable state corruption); (3) treat missing inputs as a coverage problem across 7 discriminating dimensions; (4) add fixtures to cover uncovered dimensions while reusing existing oracles.

Result: The initial 12-check suite contained a first-order mutant removing event-identity deduplication that survived all checks. Against 10 adversarial mutants, the frozen suite killed 5. Of the 5 survivors: 3 were never activated (no fixture triggered different behavior), and 2 corrupted internal state unobservable by any oracle. After enumerating 7 discriminating dimensions and adding one fixture per uncovered dimension, all 5 survivors were killed by checks written for their predicted dimensions.

Conclusion: Single-observation validation provides insufficient evidence of invariant suite quality. The authors demonstrate that mutation analysis reveals hidden defects - mutants can survive by either not being activated or by corrupting unobservable state. They propose that missing inputs should be treated as a coverage problem, and that adding fixtures to cover uncovered dimensions can kill surviving mutants using existing oracles. The paper provides full artifacts (frozen hash, registered predictions, mutants, run logs) for verification.

Abstract: Invariant suites and runtime monitors increasingly gate agent deployment decisions, and the evidence offered for any particular suite is almost always a single observation: it passes an implementation believed correct and fails one believed broken. We measure what that observation is worth. Applying mutation analysis to an invariant suite for a multi-session agent state-projection layer, we first find that this standard validation certifies a suite in which a first-order mutant removing event-identity deduplication survives every check. We then freeze the repaired twelve-check suite, record its hash, and run it once against ten mutants specified by an adversarial reader who designed none of its fixtures: it kills five. Instrumenting the five survivors against the reference shows they fail in two distinct ways, not one. Three are never activated, because no fixture supplies an input on which the mutated code behaves differently at all. The other two corrupt internal state that no oracle in the suite can observe. The two modes need different repairs, and neither is visible from a pass/fail report. Treating the missing inputs as a coverage question, we enumerate seven discriminating dimensions of the input space, register in advance which are uncovered and which survivors they should explain, and add one fixture per uncovered dimension while reusing the existing oracles verbatim. All five survivors then die, each to the check written for its predicted dimension. We report this as a repair result on the same challenge set rather than a second held-out estimate, and give the artifact, including the frozen hash, the registered predictions, all mutants and the run logs, so the distinction is checkable.

</details>


### [126] [GTDD: Generative Test-Driven Development for AI Coding Agents with Adversarial Testing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02952)
*Masahiro Kato*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper proposes Generative Test-Driven Development (GTDD), a novel approach where a separate testing agent generates new test inputs after each candidate implementation, using behavioral contracts and feedback from earlier rounds. The method includes a trusted evaluator for counterexample reduction and regression testing. A finite-population analysis characterizes false acceptance bounds, and experiments on a key-value store show regenerated tests achieve lower failure rates than static test generation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Test-driven development provides executable requirements for AI coding agents, but these agents can pass predetermined tests while leaving substantial behavior unimplemented. The core problem is that passing a fixed test suite doesn't guarantee complete implementation of intended behavior, necessitating adaptive test generation during development.

Method: GTDD uses a separate testing agent that generates new inputs after each candidate implementation, informed by human-specified behavioral contracts and feedback from earlier rounds. A trusted evaluator checks inputs, returns reduced counterexamples to the coding agent, and saves them for regression testing. The analysis employs finite-population analysis of false acceptance under adaptive candidate selection, with fresh random audits after candidate commitment to control false acceptance.

Result: In paired experiments on a stateful key-value store, policies that regenerated tests during development achieved lower mean failure rates than the policy with once-generated tests by the same language model. Giving the tester access to the candidate's source code produced no detectable additional improvement. Equal test count conditions did not isolate a single feature as the source of this difference.

Conclusion: GTDD successfully combines adaptive development feedback with established regression tests and an independent acceptance rule to improve implementation completeness. The approach provides theoretical bounds on false acceptance and demonstrates practical improvements in forcing AI agents to implement more complete behavior.

Abstract: Test-driven development gives AI coding agents executable requirements for implementing software. Because these agents can adapt their implementations to the examples they observe, passing a predetermined collection of tests can leave substantial parts of the intended behavior unimplemented. We propose Generative Test-Driven Development (GTDD), a formulation of test-driven development in which a separate testing agent generates new inputs after each candidate implementation is fixed, using a human-specified behavioral contract and the feedback from earlier rounds. A trusted evaluator checks these inputs, returns reduced counterexamples to the coding agent, and saves them for regression testing, so development continually confronts failures beyond the initial examples. We characterize the evidence that this process provides through a finite-population analysis of false acceptance under adaptive candidate selection. The resulting bounds quantify how test visibility and repeated feedback affect acceptance, and show that fresh random audits after candidate commitment control false acceptance across development rounds. In a paired experiment on a stateful key-value store, both policies that regenerated tests during development ended with lower mean failure rates than the policy whose tests were generated once by the same language model, and giving the tester the candidate's source produced no detectable additional improvement. Further conditions requesting equal numbers of tests did not isolate any single feature of the policies as the source of this difference. GTDD combines this adaptive development feedback with established regression tests and an independent acceptance rule.

</details>


### [127] [BISCEPTER: Probability-Driven Bisection for Large-Scale System Software](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02995)
*Mingyan Gao,Celine Wüst,Zuming Jiang,Zhendong Su*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper presents BISCEPTER, a probability-driven bisection approach for identifying bug-inducing commits (BICs). The key insight is that BICs are not evenly distributed across commit history but are heavily skewed toward recent commits (50% of BICs lie within the most recent 0.69% of history). BISCEPTER uses this temporal skew as a prior to select weighted-median pivots instead of standard median pivots, reducing the number of bisection iterations needed.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard bisection assumes each commit is equally likely to be the BIC, but this assumption doesn't match real-world BIC distributions. The authors discovered a strong temporal skew in BICs through analyzing 8,172 bug reports from GCC, Linux kernel, and MariaDB, motivating a probability-driven approach.

Method: The authors constructed a dataset of 8,172 bug reports and analyzed BIC distribution patterns. They then developed BISCEPTER, which uses historical BIC latency as a lightweight prior to select weighted-median pivots that split estimated BIC probability mass rather than commit count, while maintaining the same oracle interface as standard bisection.

Result: BISCEPTER reduces bisection iterations by 25.75% on average (up to 55.55%) compared with standard median bisection, and improves over the baseline in 91.26% of test cases. The benefit remains stable under noisy historical data.

Conclusion: BISCEPTER effectively saves debugging effort in practice by leveraging the temporal skew of BICs. The research provides insights about BIC distribution that can benefit future software engineering research.

Abstract: Identifying the bug-inducing commit (BIC) is a fundamental step in regression debugging and a key input to emerging BIC-aware fault-localization pipelines. In practice, BICs are commonly obtained with bisection. Standard bisection selects the median commit of the remaining good-bad interval, thereby balancing commit count. This strategy is optimal under the assumption that each commit is equally likely to be the BIC.
  This paper shows that this assumption does not match real-world BIC histories. We construct a dataset of 8,172 bug reports from GCC, the Linux kernel, and MariaDB. We find a strong temporal skew: across the studied systems, 50% of BICs lie within the most recent 0.69% of the report-time commit history. Motivated by this observation, we introduce BISCEPTER, a probability-driven bisection approach that uses historical BIC latency as a lightweight prior. Instead of selecting pivots that split the number of remaining commits, BISCEPTER selects weighted-median pivots that split estimated BIC probability mass, while preserving the same good-bad oracle and interface as standard bisection. We evaluate BISCEPTER on three large-scale systems. The evaluation results show that BISCEPTER reduces bisection iterations by 25.75% on average (up to 55.55%) compared with standard median bisection, while improving over the baseline in 91.26% of test cases. Robustness experiments further demonstrate that the benefit remains stable under noisy historical data. We expect that our research can effectively save effort in debugging software in practice and, more broadly, benefit future software engineering research by bringing insights about BIC distribution.

</details>


### [128] [Engineering Sustainable Agents: A Systematic Comparison of Agentic LLMs for Developer Workflows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03010)
*Merve Astekin,Yan Naing Tun,Arda Goknil,Erik Johannes Husom,Lwin Khin Shar,Hasan Sözer,Ratnadira Widyasari,Hui Song*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Comprehensive empirical study of agentic LLM systems across five software engineering tasks (code generation, technical debt identification, code vulnerability detection, log parsing, log analysis), comparing configurations from non-agentic baseline to multi-agent workflows. Results show multi-agent designs consume 6.36× more energy and run 6.07× longer, with limited accuracy gains and non-agentic/single-agent configurations dominating the Pareto front.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in software engineering, including agentic systems that coordinate multiple agents, but these impose higher computational and environmental costs. The need to understand the trade-offs between agentic complexity and efficiency is the primary motivation.

Method: Empirical study across five software engineering tasks using six open-weight LLMs, two prompt strategies, and three hardware platforms. Each configuration was assessed in terms of accuracy, inference latency, and energy consumption.

Result: Multi-agent designs consume on average 6.36× as much energy and run 6.07× as long as the non-agentic baseline, with worst-case slowdowns of up to 160× for individual task--hardware pairs. Accuracy gains from additional agents are limited and task-specific. Multi-agent improves average vulnerability-detection accuracy, but lightweight configurations dominate the Pareto front (59 of 66 Pareto-optimal configurations). Model and prompt choice effects vary between tasks rather than acting as global defaults.

Conclusion: The study provides design guidelines for sustainable, task-aware LLM-based development tools, emphasizing that model and prompt choices should be task-specific rather than applying universal defaults.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in software engineering, including agentic systems that coordinate multiple agents, but impose higher computational and environmental costs. In this paper, we present a comprehensive empirical study of agentic LLM systems across five software engineering tasks: code generation, technical debt identification, code vulnerability detection, log parsing, and log analysis. For each task, we compare LLM configurations that range from a non-agentic single-query baseline to multi-agent workflows, using six open-weight LLMs, two prompt strategies, and three hardware platforms. We assess each configuration in terms of accuracy, inference latency, and energy consumption. Our results reveal substantial trade-offs between agentic complexity and energy efficiency: multi-agent designs consume on average 6.36$\times$ as much energy and run 6.07$\times$ as long as the non-agentic baseline, with worst-case slowdowns of up to 160$\times$ for individual task--hardware pairs. Accuracy gains from additional agents are limited and task-specific: multi-agent improves average vulnerability-detection accuracy, but lightweight non-agentic and single-agent configurations still dominate the Pareto front, accounting for 59 of 66 Pareto-optimal configurations. Model and prompt choice act as task-specific levers whose effective direction varies between tasks rather than as global defaults. We translate these findings into design guidelines for sustainable, task-aware LLM-based development tools.

</details>


### [129] [MintEval: Do LLMs Implement the Trading Strategy You Asked For? A Behavioural-Equivalence Benchmark for Natural-Language-to-Strategy Code](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03080)
*Siyu Wang,Yifan Wang,Yuecheng He*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: MintEval is a benchmark that tests whether LLMs can correctly implement trading strategies from natural language descriptions by comparing the actual executed actions of generated code against reference implementations, rather than testing code similarity or profit. It addresses the silent failure problem where generated code runs but doesn't implement the intended risk logic.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks test either functional correctness (unit tests) or financial forecasting, but neither measures whether an LLM's implementation actually behaves like the described strategy. The failure mode is silent: code runs, backtests plot, but the risk logic executed differs from what was requested.

Method: Reference strategies are generated programmatically from a library of composable building blocks, back-translated into colloquial trader instructions, and re-implemented by the model under test. Generated and reference programs are executed bar-by-bar on identical market data and frictions, then compared on their actions (alpha is differenced away). Tasks are stratified by execution-measured state-span complexity tau.

Result: Low-cost models achieve mean ActionMatch of 0.544 and exact reproduction of 0.087. A frontier model (Claude Opus 5.5) on 200 tasks achieves 0.889 ActionMatch and 0.575 exact reproduction, but still fails silently on 27.5% of tasks. While models identify the strategy almost perfectly, 79.2% of implementations with correct specification reading diverge on more than 10% of active bars. An LLM judge accepts every silent failure.

Conclusion: Even frontier models struggle to correctly implement trading strategies from descriptions, with a significant silent failure rate. Current evaluation methods (LLM judges) fail to detect these implementation errors. The benchmark reveals a fundamental gap between strategy understanding and correct implementation in LLMs.

Abstract: Large language models are moving from producing trading signals to writing the code that executes them. The failure mode of the second role is silent: generated code runs, a backtest plots, yet the risk logic that the trader described is not the logic being executed. Existing code benchmarks test functional correctness on unit tests and finance benchmarks test forecasting; neither measures whether an implementation behaves like the strategy that was asked for. We introduce MintEval, a benchmark in which reference strategies are generated programmatically from a library of composable building blocks, back-translated into colloquial trader instructions, and re-implemented by the model under test. Generated and reference programs are executed bar by bar on identical market data and frictions, and compared on their actions rather than on code similarity or profit: alpha is differenced away. MintEval v0 contains 800 tasks on BTCUSDT 15-minute data, stratified by an execution-measured state-span complexity tau that is decoupled from description length. Low-cost models reach a mean ActionMatch of at most 0.544 and reproduce at most 0.087 of tasks exactly; on a stratified subset of 200 tasks a frontier model (Claude Opus 5.5) reaches 0.889 and reproduces 0.575 exactly, yet still fails silently on 0.275 of tasks. Given a menu of building blocks, models identify the strategy almost perfectly, yet 79.2% of the implementations whose specification was read correctly diverge on more than 10% of active bars. The LLM judge of a recent strategy-generation benchmark, applied verbatim, accepts every one of these silent failures.

</details>


### [130] [Pinning Decisions Before Failure: Executable Records of Underspecified Choices in AI-Assisted Code Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03237)
*Takeharu Mitsui*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper addresses ambiguity in natural language requirements that causes code generation models to silently resolve open questions in inconsistent ways. The authors propose a "decision pin" method: enumerate underspecified requirement points, create competing implementations, use inputs that expose differences, and record the intended decision. This approach achieved 92.5% separation of decision points, 96-97% agreement with benchmark classifications, and pins were honored in all 210 generations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Natural language requirements are inherently ambiguous. When models implement them, they silently resolve ambiguities in different ways. The authors found that 42.7% of 600 test suites from three models contained no test distinguishing competing readings. The standard remedy (acceptance examples) fails when both readings satisfy the example.

Method: The authors insert two steps into the requirement implementation practice: (1) Enumerate the requirement's underspecified points by name; (2) For each point, construct two throwaway implementations differing only in that point, and keep a candidate input only if executing both shows they disagree. The result is recorded as a "decision pin" containing: the named point, the confirmed input, and the value the person chose between the two exhibited results. This record then constrains generation and decides compliance by execution.

Result: On a benchmark of 40 tasks with paired reference implementations and two models: 92.5% of decision points obtained a separating input; 85-90% obtained a pin identifying the intended decision. As checks on 703 independently generated implementations, pins agreed with the benchmark's classification on 96-97%, with disagreements on three tasks. As generation constraints, pins were honored at the pinned input in all 210 generations and were never worse than prose rules on held-out inputs in 38 cells. Every compliance failure under a prose rule came from the model deciding the rule's scope itself.

Conclusion: The decision pin method effectively captures and enforces requirement ambiguity decisions. However, the setting yields too few conflicts to evaluate a regression step. The approach outperforms simple prose rules by preventing models from silently reinterpreting requirement scope, though it performs no better than prose stating the same scope when the scope is explicitly defined.

Abstract: A natural-language requirement leaves questions open, and a model asked to implement it settles them silently: across 600 generated test suites from three models, 42.7% contain no test that distinguishes the competing readings. An acceptance example written before implementing is the usual remedy, but an example both readings satisfy resolves nothing.
  We insert two steps into that practice: enumerate the requirement's underspecified points by name, then for each construct two throwaway implementations differing only in that point and keep a candidate input only if executing both shows they disagree. The result is recorded as a decision pin: the named point, the confirmed input, and the value the person chose between the two exhibited results. The same record then constrains generation and decides compliance by execution.
  On a benchmark of 40 tasks with paired reference implementations and two models, a separating input is obtained for 92.5% of decision points and a pin identifying the intended decision for 85-90%. As checks on 703 independently generated implementations, pins agree with the benchmark's classification on 96-97%, with disagreements on three tasks, one where both classifiers erred. As generation constraints, pins are honoured at the pinned input in all 210 generations and are never worse than a prose rule on held-out inputs in 38 cells, though no better than prose stating the same scope.
  Every compliance failure under a prose rule came from the model deciding the rule's scope itself; one such case silently overturned another recorded decision, was attributed to a single rule by leave-one-out on both models, and was missed by text-level reconciliation but caught by re-running the recorded input. The setting yields too few such conflicts to evaluate a regression step, and we say why.

</details>


### [131] [IntentCoding: Amplifying User Intent in Code Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.00066)
*Zheng Fang,Yihong Dong,Lili Mou,Dongming Jin,Zhi Jin,Ge Li*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper addresses a key limitation in LLMs: their difficulty following fine-grained user intent with multiple constraints during code generation. The authors propose IntentCoding, a model-agnostic decoding strategy that amplifies user intent influence through masking and multi-strength ensemble, requiring no additional training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs show strong code generation capabilities but struggle with fine-grained user intent containing multiple constraints. Two key observations motivate this work: 1) Model performance degrades rapidly as constraint count increases, and 2) While user intent influences model logits, this influence is insufficient to effectively steer the decoding process.

Method: The proposed IntentCoding method involves two key mechanisms: 1) Intent capture via masking - measures the influence of user intent by masking it and analyzing the resulting logit changes; 2) Multi-strength ensemble - amplifies the user intent effect during generation by combining multiple decoding strengths. The approach is model-agnostic, requires no training, and integrates with existing decoding procedures. The authors also construct CodeConstraints, a new benchmark for evaluating user intent compliance under varying constraint numbers.

Result: Experiments on CodeConstraints, IFEvalCode, HumanEval, and LiveCodeBench show significant improvements: up to 71.0% relative improvement on CodeConstraints, 67.3% on IFEvalCode, and 29.3% improvement in pass@1 on HumanEval and LiveCodeBench compared to greedy decoding.

Conclusion: IntentCoding successfully enhances LLMs' ability to follow user intent in code generation through a novel decoding strategy. The method's model-agnostic nature and zero training requirement make it a practical solution for improving constraint satisfaction and functional correctness across different benchmarks.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown strong capabilities in code generation, but their adherence to fine-grained user intent with multiple constraints remains a significant challenge. Our empirical analysis reveals two key observations: 1) Model performance deteriorates quickly as the number of constraints in the user intent increases, and 2) While user intent does influence the model's logits, such an influence may not be strong enough to effectively steer the decoding process. To this end, we propose Intent-Amplified Code Generation (IntentCoding), a novel decoding strategy that enhances an LLM's ability to follow user intent. IntentCoding captures the influence of user intent by masking out the intent, and applies a multi-strength ensemble mechanism to amplify the effect of user intent during generation. IntentCoding is model-agnostic, requires no additional training, and integrates seamlessly with existing decoding procedures. To enable systematic evaluation, we also construct CodeConstraints, a benchmark dataset specifically designed to test user intent compliance under varying numbers of constraints. Experiments on our constructed Constraints, as well as popular IFEvalCode, HumanEval and LiveCodeBench datasets, show that our IntentCoding model significantly improves both constraint satisfaction and functional correctness compared to standard decoding approaches. IntentCoding achieves up to 71.0% relative improvement on CodeConstraints, achieves up to 67.3% relative improvement on IFEvalCode and achieves up to 29.3% relative improvement in pass@1 on HumanEval and LiveCodeBench compared with greedy decoding.

</details>


### [132] [ClarifyCodeBench: Evaluating LLMs on Clarifying Ambiguous Requirements for Code Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.00711)
*Zheng Fang,Dongming Jin,Yihong dong,Yongmin Li,Kechi Zhang,Zhi Jin,Ge Li*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: ClarifyCodeBench is a new benchmark for evaluating LLMs' ability to interactively clarify ambiguous requirements in code generation tasks. It addresses the gap that existing benchmarks ignore—the iterative nature of requirement elicitation. The study evaluates six LLMs and finds that strong code generation does not imply effective clarification, increased reasoning helps code but not ambiguity detection, and performance degrades with multiple ambiguities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs excel at one-shot code synthesis but struggle with ambiguous, incomplete, or underspecified requirements. Existing benchmarks assume perfectly specified prompts, ignoring the interactive bottleneck in requirement elicitation—a critical trait for robust software engineering.

Method: Constructed ClarifyCodeBench from real-world programming tasks with manual annotations including N unique ambiguity types, clarification questions, and ground-truth answers. Formalized two metrics: Turn-discounted Key Question Rate (penalizes inefficient questioning) and Optimal Round Adherence (measures elicitation precision). Systematically evaluated six state-of-the-art LLMs.

Result: Three critical insights: 1) Capability Decoupling—strong code generation performance does not translate to effective requirement clarification; 2) Reasoning Paradox—increased computational thinking enhances code correctness but yields marginal gains in identifying ambiguities; 3) Multi-ambiguity Ceiling—clarification performance degrades sharply as ambiguity density increases.

Conclusion: Future AI4SE research should transition from static synthesis to interactive elicitation. The benchmark and metrics provide rigorous evaluation tools for this important capability.

Abstract: Large Language Models have emerged as programming assistants. However, the efficacy of code generation is constrained by the quality of input requirements, which are frequently ambiguous, incomplete, or underspecified. While LLMs excel at one-shot code synthesis, their ability to proactively clarify intent remains underexplored, as a critical trait for robust software engineering. Existing benchmarks largely overlook this interactive bottleneck, assuming perfectly specified prompts that do not reflect the iterative nature of requirement elicitation. To bridge this gap, we introduce ClarifyCodeBench, a novel interactive benchmark for evaluating LLMs' capability in resolving requirement ambiguity. Constructed from real-world programming tasks, ClarifyCodeBench features high-quality manual annotations, including N unique ambiguity types, associated clarification questions, and corresponding ground-truth answers. Furthermore, we formalize two rigorous metrics to assess the interaction quality: Turn-discounted Key Question Rate, which penalizes inefficient questioning, and Optimal Round Adherence, which measures the precision of the elicitation process. We conduct a systematic evaluation of six state-of-the-art LLMs using ClarifyCodeBench. Our empirical results yield three critical insights: 1) Capability Decoupling: Strong code generation performance does not inherently translate to effective requirement clarification; 2) The Reasoning Paradox: While increased computational thinking enhances code correctness, it yields marginal gains in identifying ambiguities; 3) The Multi-ambiguity Ceiling: LLMs' clarification performance degrades sharply as the density of ambiguities increases, revealing a significant bottleneck in handling complex, real-world specifications. Our work underscores the necessity for future AI4SE research to transition from static synthesis to interactive elicitation.

</details>


### [133] [CONTRA: Discovering and Qualifying Behavior-Changing Questions for Selective Clarification in LLM Code Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01769)
*Zheng Fang,Yongmin Li,Yichang Zhang,Dongming Jin,Haoyu Wang,Shuai Wang,Zhi Jin,Ge Li*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: CONTRA is a training-free method that identifies key clarification questions for coding agents by combining broad question discovery with semantic and execution-based qualification, preventing unintended behavior from silent assumption-making.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Coding agents can generate code that implements unintended behavior when they silently resolve underspecified requirements through their own assumptions. As development progresses, correcting these mismatches becomes increasingly costly. While early clarification can help, unnecessary questions interrupt developers and slow development. Existing methods struggle to identify key questions while avoiding unnecessary ones.

Method: CONTRA combines broad question discovery with semantic and execution-based question qualification. First, it generates candidate questions and filters out those unrelated to required behavior or already resolved. For each remaining question, it generates programs conditioned on two plausible answers and checks for stable behavioral differences on shared inputs. It then uses interaction history to select among qualified questions or stop asking.

Result: On ClarifyCodeBench, CONTRA achieves the highest F1 with all four coding agents, exceeding the best baseline macro-average F1 by 13.88 percentage points. With the same LLM and evaluation protocol, CONTRA also achieves higher clarification recall and F1 than coding harnesses Claude Code and OpenHands. CONTRA is also implemented as a Claude Code plugin for practical use.

Conclusion: CONTRA successfully identifies key clarification questions while avoiding unnecessary ones, significantly outperforming existing methods. Its implementation as a Claude Code plugin enables integration into everyday development workflows, providing a practical solution for preventing costly requirement mismatches in coding agent development.

Abstract: Coding agents can generate code that appears correct but implements behavior the user never intended. This mismatch can arise when an agent silently resolves underspecified requirements through its own assumptions. As subsequent development builds on these assumptions, correcting the resulting behavior can become increasingly costly. Early clarification can help prevent such mismatches, but unnecessary questions can interrupt developers and slow down development. Existing methods struggle to identify key clarification questions while avoiding unnecessary ones. Therefore, we propose CONTRA, a training-free method that combines broad question discovery with semantic and execution-based question qualification. CONTRA first generates candidate questions and filters out those unrelated to required behavior or already resolved by the requirement. For each remaining question, it generates programs conditioned on two plausible answers and checks for stable behavioral differences on shared inputs. It then uses the interaction history to select among qualified questions or stop asking. Experiments on ClarifyCodeBench show that CONTRA achieves the highest F1 with all four coding agents, exceeding the best baseline macro-average F1 by 13.88 percentage points. With the same LLM and evaluation protocol, CONTRA also achieves higher clarification recall and F1 than the coding harnesses Claude Code and OpenHands. To support practical use, we also implement CONTRA as a Claude Code plugin that integrates selective clarification into everyday development.

</details>

### [134] [Low-Cost Video--Time Priors as a Strong Baseline for EEG--fNIRS Emotion Regression on Familiar Videos](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03618)
*Minghao Kong,Jiurun Chen,Ying Gao,Xiangbin Meng,Rongjie Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper presents a continuous emotion regression system that estimates valence and arousal from physiological signals (EEG-fNIRS) while viewers watch videos. The study compares participant-specific models against a video-time prior baseline, finding that the prior dominates with small residual gains from physiological signals.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to develop a continuous emotion regression system for familiar-video deployment, investigating whether physiological signals (EEG-fNIRS) provide meaningful residual correction beyond a strong video-time prior baseline derived from training participants' responses.

Method: The study uses a five-fold subject-held-out evaluation on 24 participants. They compared participant-specific estimates from training data against a prior-dominating fixed fusion approach that tests whether physiology adds residual correction. Source-explicit ablations were performed to decompose the contributions of video identity and within-video time.

Result: The video-time prior achieved mean absolute error (MAE) within 0.05 and 0.32 of the fusion approach in internal and external evaluations respectively. Ablations showed that video identity and within-video time accounted for most of the reduction in error, while EEG-fNIRS gains were smaller and varied across participants and videos.

Conclusion: The video-time prior represents a strong, low-cost baseline for continuous emotion regression in familiar-video scenarios. EEG-fNIRS signals serve as an optional residual signal that provides marginal improvements in some cases but is not essential for reasonable performance.

Abstract: Continuous emotion regression estimates moment-to-moment valence and arousal while a viewer watches a video. In familiar-video deployment, responses fron training participant-specific estimate, and prior-dominating fixed fusion tests whether physiology adds residual correction. In five-fold subject-held-out evaluation on 24was within 0.05 and 0.32 MAE of fusion in the internal and external evaluations, respectively. Source-explicit ablations showed that video identity and within-video tine accounted for most of the reduction, while EG-FNIRS gains were smaller and varied across participants and videos. These results identify the video-time prior as a strong, low-cost baseline and position EEG-fNIRS as an optional residual signal for familiar-video emotion regression.

</details>


### [135] [MintFlow: Minimal Trajectory Intervention for Constrained Flow Matching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02260)
*Yesom Park,Kelvin Kan,Qifan Chen,Thomas Flynn,Hayden Schaeffer. Xihaier Luo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MintFlow is a training-free framework for constrained sampling in flow matching models that formulates constraint enforcement as minimal intervention on the pretrained flow trajectory, using an adjoint formulation to compute perturbations closed-form and adaptively selecting intervention time.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing constrained samplers for flow matching models face a trade-off: enforcing constraints can substantially displace samples from the pretrained data distribution. There is a need for methods that satisfy constraints while minimizing deviation from the pretrained distribution.

Method: MintFlow seeks the minimal perturbation of an intermediate flow state such that its subsequent evolution under the pretrained flow field satisfies the target constraint. It uses an adjoint formulation to yield a closed-form expression for the perturbation, eliminating expensive iterative optimization. The method also adaptively selects the intervention time to balance required perturbation magnitude with its amplification by the remaining flow.

Result: Across a range of tasks in generative vision and physical system modeling, MintFlow achieves competitive constraint satisfaction while preserving the pretrained generative distribution substantially better than state-of-the-art constrained methods.

Conclusion: MintFlow provides an effective training-free solution for constrained sampling in flow matching models, successfully balancing constraint satisfaction with distribution preservation through minimal intervention and adaptive timing.

Abstract: Flow matching models excel at generative modeling, and many downstream applications require their samples to satisfy prescribed constraints, such as observed measurements and physical laws. However, existing constrained samplers often face a trade-off: \textit{enforcing constraints can substantially displace samples from the pretrained data distribution}. To address this trade-off, we introduce \textbf{MintFlow}, a training-free constrained sampling framework that formulates constraint enforcement as a minimal intervention on the pretrained flow trajectory. MintFlow seeks the minimal perturbation of an intermediate flow state such that its subsequent evolution under the pretrained flow field satisfies the target constraint. By minimally perturbing the flow state while keeping the pretrained flow field unchanged, MintFlow enforces the constraint while minimizing unnecessary deviation from the pretrained distribution. An adjoint formulation yields a closed-form expression for this perturbation, eliminating expensive iterative optimization. Furthermore, MintFlow adaptively selects the intervention time to balance the required perturbation magnitude with its amplification by the remaining flow. Across a range of tasks in generative vision and physical system modeling, MintFlow achieves competitive constraint satisfaction while preserving the pretrained generative distribution substantially better than state-of-the-art constrained methods.

</details>


### [136] [Fast Models, Slow Evidence: A Paired and Self-Audited Evaluation of System-1 Decision Models for LLM Agent Harnesses](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02267)
*Jiawei Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper evaluates two System-1 decision models (Laya open-weight and Jev hosted) on 11 agent decision points across 7,283 base cases and 6,640 robustness variants. Jev significantly outperforms Laya on 9/11 decision points. The authors also audit their own evaluation pipeline, identifying three analysis errors and one design confound that distorted their original deployment claims.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: System-1 decision models (small, fast models for making discrete decisions) are proposed as cost-efficient alternatives to LLM calls for agent decision-making. However, there was no rigorous paired evaluation of such models on real agent decision points. The authors aimed to fill this gap while also demonstrating the importance of self-auditing in evaluation pipelines.

Method: Paired evaluation on 11 agent decision points built from 18 public sources, containing 7,283 base cases plus 6,640 robustness variants. Used byte-identical inputs, paired tests, cross-hardware and cross-day reproducibility checks. The decision points included: model routing, tool selection, RAG relevance gating, and injection detection.

Result: Jev significantly outperforms Laya on 9 of 11 decision points (+10.8 to +46.0 percentage points). Neither model beats chance on zero-shot model routing. They tie on RAG relevance gating. Laya shows significant robustness issues: 30% answer changes when option order is reversed, and 31% accuracy at 50 nearest-neighbor tools (vs. 98% for Jev on items with unique correct tool). The pipeline audit revealed: omitted pre-screen cost (actual savings 4.3% vs. reported 23.9%), gate accuracy misreported as end-to-end quality (58% vs. 98%), in-sample threshold issues (5% target, up to 17% held-out misses), and a "channel effect" on injection false positives that vanishes with channel-native content.

Conclusion: System-1 decision models can be effective for certain agent decisions but vary significantly in accuracy and robustness. The authors stress the importance of rigorous self-auditing in evaluation pipelines, as their initial deployment claims were substantially distorted by analysis errors and confounds. Neither model performed well on zero-shot model routing, suggesting this use case may not be suitable for current System-1 models.

Abstract: Agent harnesses make many small, typed decisions per task: which model to call, which tool to use, whether retrieved text is relevant, whether an input carries an injection. System-1 decision models answer such questions in a single forward pass with class probabilities, promising large cost and latency savings over LLM calls. We present a paired evaluation of an open-weight (Laya) and a hosted (Jev) System-1 model on 11 agent decision points built from 18 public sources: 7,283 base cases plus 6,640 robustness variants, with byte-identical inputs, paired tests, and cross-hardware and cross-day reproducibility checks. Jev is significantly more accurate on 9 of 11 decision points (+10.8 to +46.0 pp). Neither model beats chance on zero-shot model routing, and they tie on RAG relevance gating. Laya changes 30% of its answers when the option order is reversed and degrades sharply with many or similar candidates (31% at 50 nearest-neighbour tools, vs. 98% for Jev on items with a unique correct tool). We also audit our own pipeline. Three analysis errors and one design confound distorted headline deployment claims: an omitted pre-screen cost (reported 23.9% saving, actual 4.3%), gate accuracy reported as end-to-end quality (58% vs. 98%), in-sample thresholds (5% target, up to 17% held-out misses), and a "channel effect" on injection false positives that vanishes with channel-native content. Two other suspected confounds did not change the conclusions. All cases, raw outputs and analysis code are available at https://github.com/David-DL-Space/sys1-eval.

</details>


### [137] [The AI Risk Observatory: What Can We Learn from AI Disclosures in Annual Reports About Societal Resilience?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02281)
*Bart Jaworski*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper examines whether LLMs can process annual reports at scale to provide useful signals about how UK listed companies disclose their AI-related risks and adoption. Using a two-stage classification pipeline on 9,821 annual reports (2020-2025), the study finds AI risk disclosure increased dramatically from 2.8% to 41.2%, but most disclosures lack substance (only 4.3% substantive in 2025). Harm disclosures are nearly absent.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Societal resilience research requires access to useful and actionable data. The researchers wanted to test whether annual reports processed with LLMs could provide a useful signal about corporate AI disclosures, addressing a gap in understanding how companies communicate AI-related risks and adoption.

Method: Two-stage classification pipeline applied to 9,821 annual reports from 1,362 UK listed companies (2020-2025). Method validated against 474 human-annotated passages. Developed a "substantiveness classification" to assess disclosure quality.

Result: Three empirical patterns: (i) AI risk mentions rose from 2.8% to 41.2%, AI adoption from 13.8% to 45.2%; vendor mentions cluster around major providers (Microsoft leads); (ii) disclosure varies by sector and market segment - AIM reports lag behind Main Market, Energy and Data Infrastructure sectors lag; (iii) harm disclosures are nearly absent (only 7 reports).

Conclusion: LLM-processed annual reports can provide useful signals about AI disclosure trends, but most AI risk disclosure lacks substance. The gap between mention rates (41.2%) and substantive disclosure (4.3%) suggests companies are primarily performing performative disclosure rather than providing meaningful risk information.

Abstract: Societal resilience research relies on access to useful and actionable data, which motivates our main research question: Can annual reports, processed at scale with LLMs, provide a useful signal about how companies disclose their response to AI? We test this by applying a reproducible two-stage classification pipeline to 9,821 annual reports from 1,362 UK listed companies (2020-2025, with partial 2026 data). We first validate the method against 474 human-annotated passages, finding high recall and moderate label-level agreement. We then report three empirical patterns: (i) between 2020 and 2025, the share of reports mentioning AI risk rose from 2.8% to 41.2%, while AI adoption disclosure also rose, from 13.8% to 45.2%, and named vendor mentions cluster around a small set of major providers led by Microsoft; (ii) disclosure varies substantially by Critical National Infrastructure sector and market segment: AIM reports disclose AI risk at far lower rates than Main Market reports, and sectors such as Energy and Data Infrastructure lag behind the rest in AI risk disclosure; and (iii) harm disclosures are near-absent (seven reports across the entire corpus). We develop a substantiveness classification to assess the quality of the disclosure and find that most AI risk disclosure is not substantive: in 2025, 41.2% of all reports mention AI as a risk, but only 4.3% contain AI risk disclosure we classify as substantive.

</details>


### [138] [Keep It CALM: Analyzing the Limits of Global Unsafety in Text-to-Image Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02300)
*NaHyeon Park,Minhyun Lee,Hyunjung Shim*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper identifies a coverage-selectivity trade-off in training-free text-to-image safety filters and proposes CALM, a local counterfactual correction method that outperforms global unsafe signal removal.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing training-free safeguards use a single reusable unsafe direction or global toxic subspace applied to all prompts, but the authors discovered this approach has inherent limitations: compact unsafe subspaces miss diverse unsafe semantics, while broader aggregation distorts safety-adjacent benign prompts.

Method: The authors performed controlled geometric analysis of the global-unsafety assumption, then proposed CALM (Counterfactual Adaptive Local Modulation), which uses matched unsafe-benign anchors to route each prompt to active unsafe categories, performs minimal edits only on violating token representations, and suppresses positively aligned unsafe residual components.

Result: CALM significantly improves unsafe content suppression while preserving benign utility compared to existing global unsafe signal removal approaches.

Conclusion: Local counterfactual correction provides a more selective alternative to global unsafe signal removal for training-free safeguards in text-to-image generation.

Abstract: Training-free safeguards for text-to-image generation often rely on a reusable safety signal, such as an unsafe direction or global toxic subspace, applied broadly across prompts. We provide a controlled geometric analysis of this global-unsafety assumption and reveal a consistent coverage-selectivity trade-off: compact unsafe subspaces fail to cover heterogeneous unsafe semantics, whereas broader aggregation increasingly distorts safety-adjacent benign prompts. Motivated by this finding, we propose CALM (Counterfactual Adaptive Local Modulation), a training-free safeguard that replaces uniform global removal with prompt-local counterfactual correction. Using matched unsafe-benign anchors, CALM routes each prompt to active unsafe categories, minimally edits only violating token representations toward the safe side, and suppresses positively aligned unsafe residual components. Across broad evaluation, CALM significantly improves unsafe content suppression while preserving benign utility, demonstrating that local counterfactual correction provides a more selective alternative to global unsafe signal removal.

</details>


### [139] [Choosing Before Acting: Comparative Value Estimation for Long-Horizon Tool-Use Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02330)
*Yu Li,Zheng Zhang,Xin Liu,Shengtian Yang,Guangfeng Cai,Lei Feng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A method called CITA (Comparative Inference for Tool-use Agents) that trains a comparative inference model to estimate the long-horizon value of next tool invocations before executing them, improving tool-use agents' performance by learning from paired signals including observed tool behavior, Bayesian tool-graph simulation, and LLM-based semantic judgments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current tool-use agents rely on weak final-outcome rewards for credit assignment over long interaction traces, while step-level rewards require expensive human/LLM judgment or additional rollouts. The paper argues agents should estimate long-horizon value of possible next tool invocations before execution.

Method: CITA trains a Comparative Inference Model (CIM) using paired signals combining: (1) observed tool behavior, (2) scalable supervision from a Bayesian tool-graph simulator, and (3) semantic judgments from LLM-based comparison. The CIM learns to estimate how likely a possible next tool invocation is to support final task success under the current context.

Result: Across three tool-use benchmarks and multiple backbone LLMs, CITA consistently improves Tool F1 and task success. Additional analysis shows CIM learns accurate step-level value estimates for comparative tool choices.

Conclusion: CITA demonstrates that comparative inference models can effectively estimate step-level value for tool invocations, providing more targeted feedback than final-outcome rewards without requiring human supervision or additional rollouts.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) rely on long-horizon tool invocation sequences for complex tasks, where each invocation can alter the task state and condition subsequent decisions. In long-horizon tool use, final-outcome rewards provide weak credit assignment over long interaction traces. Step-level rewards can offer more targeted feedback, but obtaining reliable step supervision often requires human or LLM judgment, or additional rollouts to estimate the downstream effect of an intermediate decision. In this paper, we argue that effective tool-use agents should estimate the long-horizon value of a possible next tool invocation before executing it. This objective requires comparative supervision over alternative invocations under the same context, while logged trajectories only contain the invocation that was actually taken. Therefore, we propose Comparative Inference for Tool-use Agents (CITA). CITA trains a Comparative Inference Model (CIM) from paired signals that combine observed tool behavior, scalable supervision from a Bayesian tool-graph simulator, and semantic judgments from LLM-based comparison. The resulting CIM learns to estimate how likely a possible next tool invocation is to support final task success under the current context. Across three tool-use benchmarks and multiple backbone LLMs, CITA consistently improves Tool F1 and task success. Additional analysis shows that CIM learns accurate step-level value estimates for comparative tool choices.

</details>


### [140] [World Editing: Intervening on Executable Worlds at Increasing Depth](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02331)
