*Max Ku,Nok-Kan Law,Yu-Chien Tang,Shih-Ying Yeh,Ping Nie,Andy Zheng,Tat Hei Lai,Fei-Yueh Chen,Nikko Yu,Wei-Chieh Sun,Suzy Huang,Chiao-Wei Hsu,Chih-Chuan Huang,Chak-Wing Mak,Ho Yin Sam Ng,Edisy Kin Wai Chan,Min-Hung Chen,Ho Kei Cheng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces world editing as a new capability for interactive world models, proposing intervention depth as a key dimension. The authors present IGMBench (110 tasks, 1.1K+ criteria across Minecraft and Terraria) and show that frontier coding agents can solve 78.2% of tasks, though visual consistency remains a significant weakness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Interactive world models can generate environments and act within them, but deliberately editing an existing executable world remains underexplored. Need to formulate world editing as intervening on existing worlds while preserving unchanged properties.

Method: Industry-grade game modding approach. Benchmark evaluation through deterministic executability, behavioral, preservation, and visual checks across 110 tasks with 1.1K+ criteria.

Result: Strongest configuration achieves 78.2% task-level and 94.8% criterion-level performance. Reliability decreases with intervention depth. Most failed edits still build and load successfully. Visual consistency is weak (<50% joint pass rate).

Conclusion: World editing is a distinct capability from world generation and interaction. Executable games (Minecraft, Terraria) provide a practical testbed for studying world editing. Visual consistency remains a major weakness across all configurations. The main challenge is not building/loading edited worlds but making them behave as requested.

Abstract: Interactive world models are increasingly capable of generating environments and acting within them, yet deliberately editing an existing executable world remains underexplored. We formulate world editing as intervening on an existing world while preserving properties that should remain unchanged, and introduce intervention depth as an axis describing how strongly an edit couples world entities, dynamics, and systems. We instantiate this capability through industry-grade game modding and introduce IGMWorld, together with IGMBench, a benchmark of 110 tasks and over 1.1K executable state and behavioral criteria across Minecraft and Terraria. The tasks span property, entity, dynamics, and system interventions and are evaluated through deterministic executability, behavioral, preservation, and visual checks. Frontier coding agents already exhibit substantial world-editing capability: the strongest configuration solves 78.2% of tasks under a strict task-level criterion, while criterion-level performance reaches 94.8%. Reliability generally decreases with intervention depth, and this pattern persists even among tasks with similar numbers of evaluation criteria. Most failed edits still build and load successfully, suggesting that the main difficulty is making the edited world behave as requested. Visual consistency remains a separate weakness, with all evaluated configurations below 50% joint visual pass rate. These results show that world editing is a distinct capability from world generation and interaction, and that executable games provide a practical testbed for studying it.

</details>


### [141] [A Multi Method Importance and Performance Efficiency Analysis of Topological Metrics for Natural Visibility Graph Based Cyber Attack Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02342)
*Ali Melih Kanca,Ilker Turker*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This study reduces Natural Visibility Graph (NVG) topological metrics from 21 to 3 for cyber-attack classification while improving accuracy from 96.0% to 97.1% and reducing computation time by 96%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Not all NVG-derived topological descriptors contribute equally to cyber-attack classification, and extracting large metric sets increases computational cost. The study investigates whether a compact subset can preserve classification capability while improving computational efficiency.

Method: Four importance analysis methods (SHAP, grouped Permutation Importance, Boruta, and Recursive Feature Elimination) were integrated through a Consensus Ranking strategy. Based on this ranking, six configurations (Full21, Top15, Top10, Top7, Top5, Top3) were evaluated using the CICIDS2018 dataset, a CNN classifier, and stratified 5-fold cross-validation.

Result: Top3 achieved the highest mean performance: 97.148% accuracy, 97.055% weighted F1 score, and MCC of 0.9675, compared with 95.999%, 95.521%, and 0.9549 for Full21. Total runtime reduced from 14,961.39 s to 589.22 s (96.06% reduction). The three highest-ranked metrics were avg_clustering_coeff_median, avg_clustering_coeff_std, and avg_clustering_coeff_mean.

Conclusion: Importance-guided metric reduction can provide a compact NVG representation with higher observed mean predictive performance and substantially lower computational cost under the evaluated setting.

Abstract: Natural Visibility Graph (NVG) based analysis characterizes network traffic through topological descriptors reflecting different structural properties. However, not all descriptors contribute equally to cyber-attack classification, and extracting a large metric set can increase computational cost. This study evaluates 21 NVG derived topological metrics and investigates whether a compact subset can preserve classification capability while improving computational efficiency. Four importance analysis methods SHAP, grouped Permutation Importance, Boruta, and Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE) are integrated through a Consensus Ranking strategy. Based on this ranking, Full21, Top15, Top10, Top7, Top5, and Top3 configurations are evaluated using the CICIDS2018 dataset, a CNN classifier, and stratified 5 fold cross validation. The three highest ranked metrics are avg_clustering_coeff_median, avg_clustering_coeff_std, and avg_clustering_coeff_mean. Top3 achieved the highest observed mean performance, with 97.148% accuracy, 97.055% weighted F1 score, and an MCC of 0.9675, compared with 95.999%, 95.521%, and 0.9549 for Full21, respectively. It also reduced total runtime from 14,961.39 s to 589.22 s (96.06%). These results indicate that importance guided metric reduction can provide a compact NVG representation with higher observed mean predictive performance and substantially lower computational cost under the evaluated setting.

</details>


### [142] [DeReAct: Decomposed Reasoning and Acting for Reliable AI Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02351)
*Ajay Vohra,Tao Chen,Neeti Narayan,Caron Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DeReAct introduces a modular agent architecture that decouples action proposal from validation by adding two external gating policies: a Critic for action validation and a Context Manager for completion certification. This approach improves Pass@1 scores by 4.2-7.0 points on weaker models while maintaining comparable performance on stronger models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: ReAct-based agents tightly couple action proposal, environment interaction, and completion detection in a single LLM, making it difficult to enforce action authorization and completion control independently. This coupling allows errors to propagate and unsupported completion claims to terminate execution prematurely.

Method: DeReAct externalizes two gating policies: (1) a Critic that validates proposed actions before execution, and (2) a Context Manager that reconstructs an environment-supported State and certifies task completion. This modular architecture separates the brain (action proposal) from gating mechanisms.

Result: On GAIA and SWE-bench Verified: (1) Qwen3-Coder-480B gains 6.5-7.0 points Pass@1; (2) Claude Sonnet 4.5 gains 4.2-5.2 points; (3) Gains diminish as Brain capability increases; (4) With Claude Opus 4.5, Pass@1 remains comparable but trajectories are more evidence-complete and constraint-satisfying.

Conclusion: External gating is effective when targeted failures are sufficiently prevalent and the gating policy itself is sufficient. DeReAct improves weaker agents while retaining grounding benefits as models strengthen, demonstrating that completion control can trade earlier termination for stronger grounding.

Abstract: ReAct-based agents typically rely on a single LLM policy to propose actions, interact with the environment, and decide when a task is complete. This coupling makes action authorization and completion control difficult to enforce independently, allowing errors to propagate and unsupported completion claims to terminate execution. We introduce DeReAct, a modular agent architecture that externalizes two gating policies: a Critic that validates proposed actions before execution, and a Context Manager that reconstructs an environment-supported \textsc{State} and certifies task completion.
  Across GAIA and SWE-bench Verified, DeReAct improves Pass@1 most for weaker Brain models, with gains of 6.5--7.0 points for Qwen3-Coder-480B and 4.2--5.2 points for Claude Sonnet~4.5; gains diminish as Brain capability increases. Trajectory and ablation analyses show that external gating is effective when targeted failures are sufficiently prevalent and the gating policy is itself sufficient. With Claude Opus~4.5, Pass@1 remains comparable to ReAct, while DeReAct produces more evidence-complete and constraint-satisfying trajectories, indicating that completion control can trade earlier termination for stronger grounding. Overall, DeReAct improves weaker agents while retaining grounding benefits as models strengthen.

</details>


### [143] [Traversing the Satisfaction-Diversity Frontier in Text-to-Image Diffusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02372)
*Kevin Zhai,Siva Rajesh Kasa,Soumya Roy,Sumit Negi,Mubarak Shah*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces SatisDive, a training-free inference-time method for text-to-image generation that balances reward (user preferences) and diversity by formulating generation as satisficing with a reward floor and diversity cutoff. The method Pareto-dominates existing FK steering approaches across multiple base models and rewards on Pick-a-Pic.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing methods for text-to-image generation either address reward and diversity separately or combine them in one aggregate score, which allows high diversity to offset low rewards. There is a need for a method that ensures each generated image meets a minimum quality threshold while maintaining diversity among the batch.

Method: SatisDive uses a batch-relative reward cutoff to distinguish lower- from higher-reward candidates. It emphasizes reward improvement for candidates below the cutoff and diversity among candidates above it. The reward floor controls the balance between worst-candidate reward and batch diversity, enabling traversal of the Pareto frontier.

Result: On Pick-a-Pic, SatisDive improves worst-candidate reward over FK steering by up to 0.43 with FLUX.1-dev and HPSv3 reward, and by up to 0.70 with SANA-1.6B and ImageReward. Across overlapping DreamSim ranges, SatisDive's satisfaction-diversity curve Pareto-dominates FK steering's curve in each setting.

Conclusion: The satisficing formulation effectively balances reward and diversity in text-to-image generation. SatisDive provides a training-free, inference-time solution that achieves superior performance across multiple base models and reward functions, demonstrating the practical value of the Pareto frontier approach.

Abstract: Text-to-image generation enables users to explore several images generated from the same prompt. For these generated images to be useful, each one must reflect the user's preferences, measured by a learned reward, and differ visually from the others to maintain diversity. Existing methods are limited: they either address reward and diversity separately or combine them in one aggregate score, enabling high diversity to offset low rewards. In this paper, we address these limitations by formulating generation as satisficing: every image (candidate) must satisfy a reward floor and the batch of images must satisfy a diversity cutoff. The reward floor controls the balance between worst-candidate reward and batch diversity; we show that varying this floor defines a Pareto frontier. To traverse this frontier, we introduce SatisDive, a training-free inference-time method. SatisDive uses a batch-relative reward cutoff to distinguish lower- from higher-reward candidates, emphasizing reward improvement for candidates below the cutoff and diversity among candidates above it. On Pick-a-Pic, at matched DreamSim, SatisDive improves worst-candidate reward over FK steering by up to 0.43 with FLUX.1-dev as the base model and HPSv3 as the reward, and by up to 0.70 with SANA-1.6B as the base model and ImageReward as the reward. More broadly, across their overlapping DreamSim ranges, SatisDive's satisfaction-diversity curve Pareto-dominates FK steering's curve in each setting.

</details>


### [144] [THPL: A Vision-to-Language Decision Support Framework for Rainbow Trout Feeding Management in RAS](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02378)
*Meng Liang,Guanbo Feng,Haozhuang Chi,Shilong Zhao,Zhixin Xiong,Yuhang He,Wenfeng Han,Tianhao Zhao,Zhihong Ma,Ying Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: THPL is a novel generative feeding decision framework for rainbow trout in Recirculating Aquaculture Systems (RAS) that integrates continuous fish kinematics (via Activity Coefficient) with LLM reasoning through dual-evidence tokens (physical + soft), LoRA fine-tuning, and counterfactual multimodal Direct Preference Optimization (mDPO) to achieve 96.67% decision accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing precision feeding methods in RAS lack cognitive alignment between fish behaviors and management knowledge, preventing translation into executable and interpretable feeding decisions. There is a need to bridge continuous spatiotemporal fish behavior data with LLM reasoning for actionable feeding guidance.

Method: 1) Fishsort extracts trajectories to compute Activity Coefficient (AC) quantifying feeding intensity; 2) Hierarchical Behavior Encoder (HBE) uses Temporal and Set Transformers to model individual and collective dynamics, generating dual-evidence tokens (explicit physical + implicit soft); 3) Tokens integrate with environmental parameters, metadata, and expert rules to fine-tune LLM via LoRA; 4) Counterfactual multimodal DPO (mDPO) reinforces causal reasoning.

Result: AC shows significant monotonic positive correlation with expert-annotated feeding intensity (Spearman ρ=0.925, p<0.001). Dual-evidence tokens improve decision accuracy from 33.33% to 93.33% vs text-only baseline. Counterfactual mDPO further improves: decision accuracy to 96.67%, METEOR from 58.10% to 85.30%, reduces Self-BLEU-2 from 58.79% to 52.88%, and increases Distinct-3 from 6.68% to 7.81%, suppressing templating/actuation biases while reinforcing causal consistency and operational safety.

Conclusion: By integrating continuous kinematics with LLM reasoning, THPL provides a novel decision support paradigm for precision aquaculture, successfully bridging fish behavior data with management knowledge for executable, interpretable feeding decisions.

Abstract: In Recirculating Aquaculture Systems (RAS), precision feeding is critical for minimizing costs and improving fish welfare. However, existing methods lack cognitive alignment between fish behaviors and management knowledge, impeding translation into executable, interpretable feeding decisions. To address this, we propose THPL, a generative feeding decision framework tailored for rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss) in RAS. First, Fishsort extracts trajectories to establish an Activity Coefficient (AC) quantifying feeding intensity. Second, a Hierarchical Behavior Encoder (HBE) models individual temporal progression and collective dynamics using Temporal and Set Transformers, transforming trajectory tensors into dual-evidence representations of explicit physical and implicit soft tokens. Finally, these tokens are integrated with environmental parameters, metadata, and expert rules to fine-tune an LLM via LoRA, followed by counterfactual multimodal Direct Preference Optimization (mDPO) to reinforce causal reasoning. Results show that AC exhibits a statistically significant monotonic positive correlation with expert-annotated feeding intensity (Spearman $ρ= 0.925$, $p < 0.001$). Ablations indicate that decision accuracy improves from 33.33% (text-only baseline) to 93.33% with dual-evidence tokens, confirming that continuous spatiotemporal tokens provide necessary physical grounding for LLMs. Compared with standard LoRA, counterfactual mDPO elevates decision accuracy from 93.33% to 96.67%, advances METEOR from 58.10% to 85.30%, reduces Self-BLEU-2 from 58.79% to 52.88%, and increases Distinct-3 from 6.68% to 7.81%, suppressing templating and actuation biases while reinforcing causal consistency and operational safety. Overall, by integrating continuous kinematics with LLM reasoning, this study provides a novel decision support paradigm for precision aquaculture.

</details>


### [145] [FlashSinkhorn 2: Block-Sparse Entropic Optimal Transport](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02395)
*Felix X. -F. Ye,Yu Chin Fabian Lim,Naigang Wang,Davis Wertheimer*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: FlashSinkhorn 2 (FS2) is a GPU solver for large-scale entropic optimal transport (EOT) on low-dimensional point clouds that combines a coarse stage on cell centroids with a block-sparse fine stage to achieve high accuracy efficiently.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing streaming GPU solvers for EOT like FlashSinkhorn avoid storing dense kernels but still require evaluating all n×m point pairs in every Sinkhorn iteration, which becomes computationally prohibitive for extremely large problems (hundreds of millions of particles).

Method: FS2 couples two stages: (1) A coarse stage solves on cell centroids, lifts potentials to every point, and continues on centroids when sampled marginal checks reject the lift, replacing most point-level updates; (2) A block-sparse fine stage removes centroid error using Morton-ordered blocks that support screening and fused tensor-core execution, with thresholds set by block masses to bound omitted tile contributions.

Result: On synthetic benchmarks, FS2 reaches target residual on all 32 problems and GeomLoss multiscale on 10. On a single A100 GPU, FS2 solved discrete EOT between two 1.34×10^8-particle measures from cosmological N-body simulation at entropic blur equal to mean interparticle distance, achieving all-particle marginal residual below 0.01 in under 2.5 hours.

Conclusion: FS2 represents the largest discrete EOT problem solved to this accuracy within hours, demonstrating the feasibility of high-accuracy EOT on billion-scale particle measures using a single GPU. An open-source implementation is available.

Abstract: Streaming GPU solvers for entropic optimal transport (EOT), such as FlashSinkhorn, avoid storing the dense kernel but still evaluate all $n\times m$ point pairs in every Sinkhorn iteration. We present \textbf{FlashSinkhorn~2} (FS2), a solver for squared-Euclidean cost on low-dimensional point clouds that solves large discrete EOT problems to a prescribed marginal residual on a single GPU by coupling two stages. A coarse stage solves on cell centroids, lifts the potentials to every point and, when a sampled marginal check rejects the lift, continues on the centroids, replacing most point-level updates. A block-sparse fine stage then removes the centroid error that coarse updates cannot. Its Morton-ordered blocks support screening and fused tensor-core execution, and a threshold set by the block masses bounds each omitted tile's contribution to every row and column. On synthetic benchmarks, FS2 reaches the target residual on all 32 problems and GeomLoss multiscale on 10. On one A100, FS2 solves discrete EOT between two $1.34\times10^8$-particle measures from a cosmological $N$-body simulation, at an entropic blur equal to the mean interparticle distance, to an all-particle marginal residual below 0.01 in under 2.5 hours. To our knowledge, it is the largest discrete EOT problem solved to this accuracy within hours. For reproducibility, we release an open-source implementation at https://github.com/ot-triton-lab/flash-sinkhorn

</details>


### [146] [When Terminal-Agent Training Stalls: Demystifying Data Generation and Verification Challenge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02405)
*Xi Qin,Isabel Kurth,Xin Cui,Elin Park,Alexander Schaefer,Yaad Oren*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses reliability issues in using frontier models (like Claude Opus) as meta-agents to generate RL training tasks and verifiers. The authors identify three failure classes: benchmark invalidity, harness brittleness, and reward misalignment. They demonstrate that solvability is model-specific, with a 9B model achieving 81.3% pass@2 on Claude Opus-generated tasks but dropping to 20.6% when hard tasks are added, highlighting the need for solvability-band calibration, verifier audits, and infrastructure error accounting as primary evaluation criteria.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to address a critical gap: despite having runnable Docker images and executable test suites, the end-to-end pipeline for terminal agent training using meta-agents is not necessarily faithful or reliable. The authors aim to diagnose and classify the failures that occur in such pipelines.

Method: The authors propose a meta-agent pipeline that diagnoses three classes of failure: benchmark invalidity, harness brittleness, and reward misalignment. They conducted experiments using a 9B model on Claude Opus-generated tasks, varying task difficulty and measuring pass@2 rates under different configurations.

Result: Prompt redesign and context extension increased baseline solvability by 5.6 times. A 9B model achieved 81.3% mean pass@2 within 20 steps on Claude Opus-generated tasks. When hard tasks were added, mean pass@2 dropped to 20.6% without any change to training configuration, demonstrating that the solvability band is model-specific.

Conclusion: The authors conclude that meta-agent reliability requires solvability-band calibration, verifier audits, and infrastructure error accounting as first-class evaluation criteria, rather than being treated as post-hoc diagnostics. This ensures more faithful and reliable RL training pipelines.

Abstract: Using a frontier model like Claude Opus as a meta-agent to generate terminal tasks and verifiers for RL training is increasingly common. Yet a runnable Docker image and executable test suite do not guarantee a faithful end-to-end pipeline for terminal agent training. We present a meta-agent pipeline motivated by this gap, diagnosing three classes of failure: benchmark invalidity, harness brittleness, and reward misalignment. Prompt redesign and context extension raise baseline solvability 5.6 times, but a 9B model saturates at 81.3% mean pass@2 within 20 steps on Claude Opus-generated tasks. Adding hard tasks reduces mean pass@2 to 20.6% without changing the training configuration, a strong evidence that the solvability band is model-specific. These findings demonstrate that meta-agent reliability requires solvability-band calibration, verifier audits, and infrastructure error accounting as first-class evaluation criteria, not post-hoc diagnost.

</details>


### [147] [Personalized Automatic Speech Recognition for a Dysarthric and Tracheostomic Speaker using Artificial Conversations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03017)
*David Nadrchal,Monorama Swain,Florian Schmid,Gerhard Widmer,Paul Primus*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper presents an ASR system personalized for a Czech speaker with a permanent tracheal stoma and severe dysarthria. Using a multi-stage Whisper Base fine-tuning pipeline on standard Czech, simulated tracheostomic speech, and speaker's data, the system achieves 50% relative reduction in Character Error Rate across three evaluation scenarios.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To help individuals with severe speech impairments (tracheal stoma and dysarthria) communicate effectively through personalized ASR technology, as their speech is unintelligible to untrained listeners.

Method: Multi-stage training pipeline: (1) Fine-tuning Whisper Base on standard Czech speech, (2) acoustically simulated tracheostomic speech, (3) speaker's personal data. Dataset: 33 annotated hours collected via novel "artificial conversation" protocol for high engagement and dialogue realism. Evaluation across three near real-time scenarios: scripted conversations, question answering, and spontaneous dialogue.

Result: 50% relative reduction in Character Error Rate compared to Whisper Base baseline, surpassing the average recognition accuracy of the speaker's assistants in acoustic recognition of isolated utterances.

Conclusion: Even for severely impeded speech, a helpful and effective ASR system is achievable, as supported by quantitative results and positive feedback from the speaker.

Abstract: This work presents an automatic speech recognition (ASR) system personalized for a Czech speaker with a permanent tracheal stoma and severe dysarthria rendering their speech unintelligible to untrained listeners. We release a public dataset containing 33 annotated hours of the speaker's speech, collected using a novel "artificial conversation" protocol designed for high engagement and dialogue realism. We propose a multi-stage training pipeline based on Whisper Base: fine-tuning on standard Czech speech, acoustically simulated tracheostomic speech, and the speaker's data. We evaluate the system across three near real-time scenarios: scripted conversations, question answering, and spontaneous dialogue, achieving a 50\% relative reduction in Character Error Rate compared to Whisper Base baseline and surpassing the average recognition accuracy of their assistants in acoustic recognition of isolated utterances. We demonstrate that even for severely impeded speech, a helpful ASR is achievable, as evidenced by the quantitative results and the feedback from the speaker.

</details>


### [148] [Reinforcement Learning Techniques for the Optimization of Target Polarization in Nuclear Physics Scattering Experiments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02452)
*Armen Kasparian,Torri Jeske,Monibor Rahman,Chris Keith,James Maxwell,Thomas Britton,Malachi Schram,David Lawrence*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper presents a data-driven control framework that combines surrogate modeling (MLP and Gaussian process regression) with reinforcement learning to optimize polarization in dynamically polarized nuclear physics targets. The system uses microwave frequency tuning to compensate for radiation damage, replacing manual expert operator control with an automated RL agent that achieves nearly 2x improvement over human operators.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Dynamically polarized targets in nuclear physics experiments require continuous microwave frequency tuning to compensate for radiation damage and evolving material properties. This tuning has traditionally been performed manually through trial-and-error by expert operators, which is time-consuming, inefficient, and requires specialized expertise. The motivation is to develop an automated, data-driven approach that can optimize target polarization more efficiently than manual control.

Method: The authors trained and evaluated two types of surrogate models—multilayer perceptron (MLP) and Gaussian process regression (GPR)—using operational data from the APOLLO cryogenic target system. These models predict polarization as a function of microwave frequency, beam current, and accumulated radiation dose. They compared the models' ability to provide calibrated uncertainty estimates and identify out-of-distribution regions. A reinforcement learning agent was then trained using a lower-confidence-bound reward formulation that balances performance maximization against uncertainty. The GP model was embedded within a standardized simulation environment to enable learning across multiple target samples.

Result: Gaussian process-based models provide calibrated uncertainty estimates and reliably identify regions outside the training distribution, while MLPs exhibit limited sensitivity to distributional shift. The RL agent achieved nearly 2x improvement over operator actions in optimizing target polarization.

Conclusion: The combination of Gaussian process surrogate modeling with reinforcement learning provides an effective automated control framework for dynamically polarized targets. The GP-based approach offers better uncertainty quantification than neural networks, enabling safer and more reliable optimization. The RL agent's near 2x improvement demonstrates the potential for automated systems to surpass manual expert control in nuclear physics experiments, reducing operator burden and improving experimental efficiency.

Abstract: The operation of dynamically polarized targets in nuclear physics experiments relies on continuous tuning of the microwave frequency to compensate for radiation damage and evolving material properties, a task that is traditionally performed through manual trial-and-error by expert operators. This work presents a data-driven control framework that combines surrogate modeling with reinforcement learning to optimize the target polarization. Using operational data from the APOLLO cryogenic target system, we train and evaluate multilayer perceptron and Gaussian process regression models to predict polarization as a function of microwave frequency, beam current, and accumulated radiation dose. We show that Gaussian process-based models provide calibrated uncertainty estimates and reliably identify regions outside the training distribution, while MLPs exhibit limited sensitivity to distributional shift. To enable learning and control across multiple target samples, we introduce a Gaussian process approximation and embed the surrogate model within a standardized simulation environment. A reinforcement learning agent is trained using a lower-confidence-bound reward formulation that balances performance maximization against uncertainty. We are able to show an almost 2x improvement on the operators actions utilizing our RL agent.

</details>


### [149] [Tropical Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02478)
*Arip Asadulaev,Aladin Djuhera,Karim Salta,Holger Boche,Fakhri Karray,Martin Takac*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Tropical Reinforcement Learning (TROPIC) addresses compositional reasoning in LLMs by replacing addition with maximum in the reward calculation (tropical semiring), enabling true composition of reasoning steps from different rollouts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Classical RL maximizes expected return by summing probabilities of successful trajectories, which has two critical limitations: (1) it only reports success rate, not which specific solution worked, and (2) reinforcing one solution can cause forgetting of others. This is particularly problematic for compositional reasoning where solutions must be assembled from reasoning steps produced in separate, often failed attempts.

Method: The key innovation is changing the algebra from addition to maximum (tropical semiring). Instead of adding probabilities of alternative solutions, the method takes their maximum. This yields the log-probability of the most likely verified solution along with an explicit path that can be replayed and reused. TROPIC is designed for deterministic, resettable environments with verifiable outcomes, allowing best prefixes and suffixes meeting at a shared state to be joined even from different rollouts.

Result: TROPIC outperforms the strongest on-policy baselines by up to 16 percentage points on four agentic tasks: Sokoban, Countdown, FrozenLake, and WebShop.

Conclusion: Changing the algebra of reinforcement learning, not just its estimators, can substantially improve compositional reasoning in language models. The tropical semiring approach enables true composition by tracking and combining verified solution paths rather than just aggregating success probabilities.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning for large language models typically maximizes expected return, adding up the probabilities of all successful trajectories. However, the classical sum formulation can only report how often the model policy succeeds, not which solution actually worked, and because probabilities sum to one, reinforcing one solution can make the model forget another that was never shown to be wrong. This makes expected return a poor fit for compositional reasoning, where a solution must be assembled from reasoning steps that the model produces in separate, often failed, attempts but rarely produces together. To address this, we propose Tropical Reinforcement Learning, which rests on a simple change of algebra: instead of adding the probabilities of alternative solutions, we take their maximum, which yields the tropical semiring. The value of a state then becomes the log-probability of its most likely verified solution, together with an explicit path that can be replayed and reused. This enables true composition, since the best prefix and the best suffix meeting at a shared state can be joined even when they come from different rollouts. To put this into practice, we introduce TROPIC, a training algorithm for deterministic, resettable environments with verifiable outcomes. On four agentic tasks (Sokoban, Countdown, FrozenLake, WebShop), TROPIC outperforms the strongest on-policy baselines by up to 16 percentage points. Changing the algebra of reinforcement learning, not just its estimators, can thus substantially improve compositional reasoning in language models

</details>


### [150] [MEA: A Reward-Driven Multi-Agent System for Faithful Model Explanations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02480)
*Yuyang Cheng,Raghav Kaushik Ravi,Srivarshinee Sridhar,Sriparna Saha,Akash Ghosh,Chirag Agarwal*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MEA is a multi-agent framework that automates machine learning model explanation by using two specialized agents: a Proposer for selecting and configuring explanation tools, and an Actor for generating natural language explanations optimized for faithfulness. It addresses the expertise barrier in explainability by handling tool selection, high-dimensional output navigation, and evidence synthesis across tabular, text, and vision modalities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Machine learning models are increasingly used in high-stakes domains but remain opaque to practitioners. Post-hoc explanation methods exist but require expertise that most domain experts lack, including navigating high-dimensional outputs, selecting appropriate explanation tools, and synthesizing evidence across different methods.

Method: MEA employs a multi-agent architecture with two agents: (1) Proposer agent - selects and configures explanation tools based on the question and data modality; (2) Actor agent - optimized end-to-end against faithfulness metrics, transforming outputs into natural language explanations. The framework introduces diverse question types (feature attribution, counterfactual reasoning, spurious feature detection) paired with perturbation-based faithfulness metrics. It uses a modality-adaptive penalty for optimization.

Result: MEA consistently outperforms post-hoc explainers, agentic, and closed-source baselines across six datasets. Reward-driven optimization yields faithfulness gains of +28% (tabular), +21% (text), and +34% (vision) over the untrained backbone. The study also finds that frontier LLMs systematically produce unfaithful explanations.

Conclusion: AI agents can serve as a scalable, adaptable interface to ML explainability, enabling natural-language explanations that generalize beyond fixed, single-purpose explanation tools. This approach opens a path toward accessible explainability for domain experts without specialized ML expertise.

Abstract: Recent years have seen the employment of a plethora of machine learning (ML) models in high-stakes domains, but they remain largely opaque to the practitioners who act on their predictions. While post-hoc explanation methods offer a lens into this model behavior, wielding them effectively demands expertise most domain experts lack: navigating high-dimensional outputs, selecting the best explanations, and synthesizing evidence across disparate tools. To this end, we present MEA, a multi-agent framework that removes the explanation knowledge barrier entirely: a Proposer agent selects and configures explanation tools based on the question and modality, while an Actor agent is optimized end-to-end against faithfulness, transforming the outputs into natural language explanations grounded in model behavior across tabular, text, and vision modalities. Further, we introduce diverse question types spanning feature attribution, counterfactual reasoning, and spurious feature detection, each paired with a perturbation-based faithfulness metric. We find that frontier LLMs systematically produce unfaithful explanations. By optimizing against faithfulness rewards augmented with a modality-adaptive penalty, MEA consistently outperforms post hoc explainers, agentic, and closed-source baselines across six datasets, with reward-driven optimization yielding faithfulness gains of +28% (tabular), +21% (text), and +34% (vision) over the untrained backbone. More broadly, our findings suggest that AI agents themselves can serve as a scalable, adaptable interface to ML explainability, opening a path toward natural-language explainability that generalizes beyond the fixed, single-purpose tools that have long defined the field.

</details>


### [151] [What Does a Token Cost? A Mixture-of-Agents Measurement of Sufficient Per-Token Compute](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02491)
*Zhixu Du,Weijia Han,Hai Helen Li,Yiran Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper measures the actual computation required for each token generated by LLMs using a Mixture-of-Agents (MoA) approach. By testing 15 models of varying capacity, they find that most tokens (92-95%) can be generated by small 0.5B models, while the hardest 10% of tokens consume 64-80% of total FLOPs. This insight enables efficient model routing and drafting strategies that reduce latency by ~20-33% while maintaining or improving accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large language models apply equal computation to every token regardless of difficulty, wasting resources on easy tokens. Existing methods like speculative decoding and model routing assume this inefficiency exists, but the actual computation requirements per token had never been measured. This work aims to quantify token-level computation needs to enable smarter compute allocation.

Method: The authors employ a Mixture-of-Agents (MoA) framework with 15 language models of increasing capacity from three families (Qwen, OLMo, and R1-distilled). Each agent attempts to reproduce reference tokens one by one, conditioned on correct preceding tokens. The "sufficient compute" for a token is defined as the smallest agent that successfully reproduces it, providing an upper bound on required computation.

Result: Key findings: (1) A 0.5B agent reproduces 92-95% of reference tokens across benchmarks; (2) The most expensive 10% of tokens account for 64-80% of estimated FLOPs; (3) On MATH-500, model routing reduces projected latency from 7.59s to 5.12s while slightly improving accuracy vs confidence-routing baseline; (4) Drafting with MoA-map uses 32.6% fewer draft tokens and ~20% lower projected latency than fixed-window drafting at similar accuracy.

Conclusion: The study reveals significant compute allocation inefficiency in LLM inference, with most tokens being easy enough for small models while a small fraction of hard tokens consume most resources. The MoA-derived sufficient-compute map enables practical improvements in model routing and speculative drafting, reducing latency by 20-33% while maintaining accuracy. This demonstrates remaining headroom for optimization and motivates developing controllers that exploit this sufficient-compute structure for more efficient inference.

Abstract: Large language models spend the same amount of computation on every token they generate, regardless of how difficult each token is to produce. Methods such as speculative decoding and model routing are built on the premise that much of this computation is unnecessary, yet the computation an individual token actually requires has not been measured. We measure it through a Mixture-of-Agents (MoA) lens: a panel of fifteen language models of increasing capacity, drawn from three families, in which every agent attempts to reproduce a reference sequence token by token, conditioned on the correct preceding tokens. We define the inference cost of the smallest agent that succeeds as the token's sufficient compute, which upper-bounds what the token requires. On three core benchmarks, a 0.5B agent reproduces 92--95\% of reference tokens. Across Qwen, OLMo, and R1-distilled panels, the most expensive 10\% account for 64--80\% of estimated FLOPs. On all 500 MATH-500 problems, the MoA-derived map helps model routing reduce projected latency from 7.59 to 5.12 seconds while slightly improving accuracy, relative to the best confidence-routing baseline. The MoA-map helps drafting use 32.6\% fewer draft tokens and approximately 20\% lower projected latency than fixed-window drafting at similar accuracy. These comparisons reveal remaining allocation headroom, motivating controllers that exploit sufficient-compute structure.

</details>


### [152] [Right Order, Wrong Scale: Auditing LLM Judges for Occupational AI Measurement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02492)
*Harry Lyu,Neil Thompson*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces O*NET-BENCH, a benchmark for evaluating LLM judges' ability to assess AI outputs against workplace requirements. The study finds that while many judge configurations achieve reasonable ranking accuracy (≥0.60), they fail to accurately estimate acceptance rates (3.0%-97.9% vs 61.1% ground truth) and occupational aggregates. Cross-validated calibration removes mean bias but explains only 8.5% of worker rating variance, demonstrating that ranking agreement alone is insufficient for occupational measurement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The research addresses a critical gap in LLM evaluation: ranking agreement between judges and workers does not necessarily translate to accurate estimation of acceptance rates or occupational aggregates. The authors argue that without validating judges against these downstream metrics, their use in workplace assessment may be misleading.

Method: The authors developed O*NET-BENCH from a survey of 45,796 worker ratings, creating 4,501 test ratings. They evaluated 33 pre-existing judge configurations across six model families using various protocols (pointwise scoring, bundled few-shot/listwise). They tested a TF-IDF baseline, assessed calibration methods, and explored prediction-assisted estimation with different label budgets.

Result: 25 of 33 judge configurations achieved tie-aware pair accuracy ≥0.60. However, estimated acceptance rates ranged from 3.0%-97.9% compared to 61.1% actual. A TF-IDF baseline nearly matched the strongest judge in ordering. Switching from pointwise to bundled few-shot/listwise improved ordering but reduced agreement with worker means. Cross-validated calibration removed mean bias but explained at most 8.5% of individual worker-rating variance. Prediction-assisted estimation yielded only small precision gains.

Conclusion: The study demonstrates that ranking agreement alone is insufficient for occupational measurement. LLM judges must be validated against acceptance rates and aggregates specific to their intended use case. The authors recommend that practitioners verify judge performance on these downstream metrics before deployment in workplace assessment contexts.

Abstract: LLM judges are increasingly used to assess whether AI outputs meet workplace requirements, but agreement on response rankings does not establish agreement on acceptance rates or occupational aggregates. We introduce O*NET-BENCH, an audit suite derived from an existing survey of 45,796 worker ratings, and evaluate 33 pre-existing judge configurations across six model families on 4,501 test ratings. Twenty-five configurations achieve tie-aware pair accuracy of at least 0.60, although a train-fitted response-only TF-IDF baseline nearly matches the strongest judge. Despite this ordering agreement, judges estimate that 3.0%-97.9% of responses are acceptable, compared with 61.1% for occupation-matched workers. In one fine-tuned lineage, changing from pointwise scoring to a bundled few-shot/listwise protocol improves response ordering while reducing agreement with worker means at the task and occupation levels; this reversal replicates on a task- and worker-disjoint validation split under prespecified criteria. Cross-validated calibration largely removes mean bias, but calibrated scores explain at most 8.5% of individual worker-rating variance. Prediction-assisted estimation yields at most small precision gains at the studied label budgets. These results show that ranking agreement alone is insufficient for occupational measurement. Judges should be validated against the acceptance rates and aggregates their scores will be used to estimate.

</details>


### [153] ["I just assumed that it would translate": examining MT risk awareness among healthcare staff with abbreviations as a use case](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02496)
*Eleanor Taylor-Stilgoe,Félix do Carmo,Constantin Orăsan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This study investigates the risks of using machine translation (Google Translate) for medical abbreviations in UK healthcare settings, examining staff awareness through interviews with 21 healthcare professionals using French and Spanish clinical examples.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the gap in research on healthcare staff awareness of risks associated with machine translation use, particularly concerning patient medical records and high-stakes translations, as current literature focuses mainly on interpersonal communication or patient documentation.

Method: Semi-structured interviews with 21 healthcare staff across diverse roles and specialties. Contextualized French and Spanish data examples from authoritative clinical corpora were translated via Google Translate and presented to participants, followed by qualitative and cross-analysis.

Result: The abstract does not provide specific results - this appears to be a study design/methodology description rather than findings.

Conclusion: The study aims to identify potential risks posed by machine translation of medical abbreviations, which are known to increase patient safety risks even in monolingual contexts, potentially leading to harm ranging from temporary injury to patient death.

Abstract: In the UK, public healthcare staff report turning to machine translation (MT) - predominantly Google Translate (GT) - to communicate with patients across language barriers. Though intended to support their duty of care, potentially uninformed reliance on MT in such contexts could have serious consequences for patient safety. Research nonetheless remains limited on staff awareness of the possible risks posed by higher-stakes MT use in general and with patient medical records in particular, most existing literature instead examining its use in interpersonal situations or with patient-oriented documentation. Moreover, medical abbreviations are well-documented as increasing patient risk even monolingually, with outcomes from their misuse and/or misinterpretation ranging from temporary harm to the death of the patient. Abbreviations were therefore selected as a use case for identifying the potential risks posed by their translation with MT. Contextualised French and Spanish data examples drawn from authoritative clinical corpora and translated via GT were presented during semi-structured interviews to 21 healthcare staff participants in diverse roles and specialties. The results were then subject to qualitative analysis and cross-analysis.

</details>


### [154] [HXAI: Hierarchical Privacy-Preserving Explainable AI in Distributed Energy Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02504)
*Poushali Sengupta,Sabita Maharjan,Frank Eliassen,Yan Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: HXAI is a hierarchical framework that balances privacy with explainability in household energy management, enabling grid operators to gain decision-relevant insights without accessing individual household appliance-level data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Grid operators need fine-grained household energy insights for peak load management and tariff design, but traditional XAI methods risk exposing sensitive personal information, while existing privacy techniques often destroy the usefulness of explanations.

Method: HXAI has two components: (1) a local model generating fine-grained explanations within a secure private environment, and (2) a zonal model aggregating explanations for grid-level analysis with flexible privacy-budget management. The framework limits cumulative privacy exposure under repeated operator queries and preserves semantic structure of explanations rather than minimizing numerical error.

Result: Experiments on simulated and real-world energy datasets show HXAI provides useful insights for zonal load management while keeping appliance-level consumption local and private. Preserving semantic structure of explanations is key to achieving XAI under differential privacy.

Conclusion: HXAI successfully achieves both privacy and explainability in energy management by maintaining the semantic structure of explanations under differential privacy, enabling grid-level analysis without compromising household privacy.

Abstract: Balancing electricity demand and supply is increasingly difficult due to the inherent intermittency of renewable power generation and the stochastic power consumption. Grid operators require fine-grained, decision-relevant insights into household energy consumption to manage peak loads and design responsive tariffs, but increased transparency at this level raises significant privacy concerns. Traditional methods for explainable AI (XAI) can reveal sensitive information, while standard privacy techniques often reduce the usefulness of explanations. To address this issue, we introduce HXAI, a hierarchical framework that preserves privacy while enabling reasonable explainable analysis for grid-level demand management. HXAI consists of two main components: (1) a local model that generates fine-grained explanations within a secure, private environment, and (2) a zonal model that aggregates these explanations to support grid-level analysis while enforcing privacy through flexible privacy-budget management. We explicitly limit cumulative privacy exposure under repeated operator queries and show that the proposed framework preserves decision-relevant information without compromising household privacy. Experiments on both simulated and real-world energy datasets demonstrate that HXAI provides useful insights for zonal load management while ensuring that appliance-level consumption remains local and is never transmitted to grid operators. Our results show that preserving the semantic structure of explanations, rather than minimizing numerical error, is the key to XAI under differential privacy. This framework provides a way to achieve both privacy and explainability in energy management.

</details>


### [155] [World Action Modeling with Progressive Visual Planning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02508)
*Fei Zhang,Zhaochong An,Duncan Frost,Yikai Wang,Pengfei Liu,Ya Zhang,Michal Drozdzal,Amir Bar*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ProWAM is a progressive world action model for robotic control that predicts actions together with an ordered sequence of sparse visual sub-goals, enabling efficient long-horizon planning without generating dense video rollouts. It achieves state-of-the-art results on multiple benchmarks including LIBERO-Plus (85.8%), randomized RoboTwin (75.7%), and demonstrates strong zero-shot real-world transfer (70.0% success).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing World Action Models (WAMs) struggle with long-horizon prediction because generating dense video rollouts is highly inefficient. While some approaches predict a single future frame, this neglects how to progress toward the goal. There was a need for a method that provides explicit visual guidance throughout task execution while remaining computationally efficient.

Method: ProWAM proposes a progressive world action model that jointly predicts actions and an ordered sequence of sparse visual sub-goals. The approach uses a single video-backbone forward pass to cache sparse sub-goal features, eliminating iterative full-video generation. During replanning, only lightweight action denoising is required. The video backbone can be learned from large-scale action-free videos, offloading complex visual planning from the action policy.

Result: ProWAM achieves superior out-of-distribution robustness. On simulation benchmarks: LIBERO-Plus achieves 85.8% (SOTA, +35.9% relative gain), randomized RoboTwin achieves 75.7%. On RoboCasa365: 48.1% success rate and 18.2% on Composite-Unseen split (ranking 4th). In zero-shot real-world experiments: 70.0% success rate, outperforming the strongest baseline by +15.0 (from 55.0% to 70.0%, a +27.3% relative gain) in novel scenes.

Conclusion: ProWAM demonstrates that progress-indexed visual foresight is valuable for closed-loop control. The approach scales naturally as sub-goal prediction can be learned from large-scale action-free videos. The method achieves state-of-the-art results across multiple benchmarks and shows strong zero-shot transfer capabilities to novel real-world scenes, validating the effectiveness of sparse visual sub-goals for robotic control.

Abstract: World action models (WAMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for robotic control by jointly predicting future visual dynamics and actions from an initial observation and instruction. However, existing WAMs struggle with long-horizon prediction, as generating dense video rollouts is highly inefficient. Some recent WAMs address this by predicting a single future frame without generating the full video, but this approach neglects how to progress toward the goal. We present ProWAM, a progressive world action model that jointly predicts actions and an ordered sequence of sparse visual sub-goals, providing explicit visual guidance to anchor action generation throughout task execution. This design scales naturally, as sub-goal prediction can be learned from large-scale action-free videos, allowing the video backbone to offload complex visual planning from the action policy. For efficient action generation, ProWAM executes a single video-backbone forward pass to cache sparse sub-goal features, eliminating iterative full-video generation and requiring only lightweight action denoising during replanning. Across extensive evaluations, ProWAM achieves superior out-of-distribution robustness. On simulation benchmarks, it sets new state-of-the-art results on LIBERO-Plus (85.8%) and randomized RoboTwin (75.7%), outperforming the strongest baseline with relative gains of up to +35.9%. On RoboCasa365, ProWAM achieves a 48.1% success rate and 18.2% on the challenging Composite-Unseen split, ranking 4th overall. Crucially, in zero-shot real-world experiments, ProWAM achieves 70.0% success, outperforming the strongest baseline by +15.0 (from 55.0% to 70.0%, a +27.3% relative gain) in novel scenes. These results demonstrate the value of progress-indexed visual foresight for closed-loop control. Our program is in https://sii-ferenas.github.io/ProWAM-page.

</details>


### [156] [On-Premises Multi-Course RAG Tutoring for Business Education: Hardware-Software Trade-offs in a Campus AI Tutor](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02510)
*Sidney Shapiro,Joshua Lindemann*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CourseChat is an on-premises, multi-course RAG-based AI tutor for undergraduate business education, deployed behind a campus web gateway for Moodle integration. It uses local vector database and local LLM (Ollama) with twin-edge AI hosts for six isolated course offerings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Campus AI tutors based on retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) must ground answers in assigned course materials while keeping textbooks and student dialogue on institutional infrastructure.

Method: Two generation-model bake-off rounds, a separate fixed-evidence source-fidelity comparison, and conversation and quiz audits. Tested larger models, 12B and 7B alternatives, and a mixture-of-experts candidate. Software changes for follow-up topic resolution. 435 prebuilt questions across 65 modules.

Result: Larger models failed the classroom speed gate; 12B model and 7B alternative passed. Mixture-of-experts improved some corrections but introduced new factual and continuity errors. Retained 8B production model pending demonstrated overall improvement. Software improvements enhanced follow-up topic resolution while preserving course scope.

Conclusion: Model choice, evidence selection, serving compatibility, and product design should be treated as joint engineering decisions. Does not establish learning gains; faculty ratings, peak-load capacity, and complete public-gateway acceptance remain separate evaluation needs.

Abstract: Campus AI tutors based on retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) must ground answers in assigned course materials while keeping textbooks and student dialogue on institutional infrastructure. We present CourseChat, an on-premises, multi-course RAG tutor for undergraduate business education, deployed behind a campus web gateway and intended for use embedded in Moodle. Six isolated course offerings, each keyed by its own course reference number (CRN), share twin-edge AI hosts running a FastAPI service, a local vector database, and a local large language model (LLM) served by Ollama. We report two generation-model bake-off rounds, a separate fixed-evidence source-fidelity comparison, and conversation and quiz audits. Several larger models failed the classroom speed gate, but a 12B model and a 7B alternative passed. A separate mixture-of-experts candidate improved some corrections while introducing new factual and continuity errors. We therefore retain the 8B production model pending a demonstrated overall improvement, rather than claiming that 8B is universally optimal. Software changes improved follow-up topic resolution while preserving course scope; 435 prebuilt questions across 65 modules decouple practice from live generation. The results support treating model choice, evidence selection, serving compatibility, and product design as a joint engineering decision. They do not establish learning gains: faculty ratings, peak-load capacity, and complete public-gateway acceptance remain separate evaluation needs.

</details>


### [157] [Hypothesis-guided discovery of cognitive algorithms via program refinement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02523)
*Huiwen Alex Yang,Mark K. Ho,Bill D. Thompson*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes a hybrid cognitive modeling system that combines human expertise with LLM capabilities to discover and refine cognitive algorithms. The system treats algorithm discovery as a program refinement problem, using LLM agents to modify probabilistic programs while maintaining structural fidelity, and evaluates it on human behavior in problem-solving tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The core challenge is that traditional cognitive modeling approaches are interpretable and benefit from human expertise but lack flexibility and scalability, while LLM-based approaches are scalable and flexible but don't incorporate human expertise. The goal is to bridge these two paradigms for more effective cognitive algorithm discovery.

Method: The proposed hybrid system expresses human-created cognitive models as probabilistic programs. LLM agents perform three key functions: (1) identify mismatches between model and behavior, (2) propose code-level modifications within researcher-specified constraints, and (3) verify structural fidelity. These revisions feed into a probabilistic inference module for latent variable inference and data likelihood computations.

Result: Revised models consistently improve model fit relative to ancestral (original human-created) models. The system reveals a small set of recurring innovations that capture meaningful behavioral variability in the problem-solving task.

Conclusion: The hybrid approach successfully combines human expertise with LLM flexibility, achieving better model fit than either pure human or pure LLM approaches. The recurring innovations identified suggest there are systematic patterns in how cognitive algorithms can be refined to better explain human behavior.

Abstract: Developing cognitive models of algorithmic reasoning from behavioral data is a central problem in cognitive science that challenges current methods. Traditional approaches to cognitive modeling are interpretable and benefit from human expertise, but lack flexibility and scalability. Emerging techniques using large language models (LLMs) for de novo generation of cognitive models are scalable and flexible, but lack a role for human expertise and have mostly been applied to simpler tasks than algorithm recovery. We propose a hybrid system that treats discovery of cognitive algorithms as a program refinement problem. Human-created cognitive models are expressed as probabilistic programs and provided to a system of LLM agents with a mandate to: identify mismatches between model and behavior; propose code-level modifications within researcher-specified constraints; and verify structural fidelity. Revisions propagate to a probabilistic inference module that performs inference for latent variables and data likelihood computations. We evaluate the pipeline on human behavior in a problem-solving paradigm that exposes a variety of cognitive algorithms. Revised models consistently improve model fit relative to ancestral models and reveal a small set of recurring innovations that capture meaningful behavioral variability in this task.

</details>


### [158] [Learning What to Investigate Next: Meta-Reasoning for Long-Horizon Research Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02525)
*Ankur Samanta,Yonathan Efroni,Paul Sajda,Kaveh Hassani,Anirudh Goyal*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MIRA introduces a hierarchical architecture for long-horizon research agents that separates meta-reasoning (deciding what to investigate) from execution. It uses an outer-loop meta-reasoner that curates context and writes work orders, and an inner-loop executor that carries out investigations. The system includes a generative critic for credit assignment and MIRA-AC for joint forecasting and action selection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-horizon research agents face challenges in learning how to investigate because decisions are sparse in long execution traces and consequences may emerge several investigations later. Existing methods struggle with credit assignment and effective compute allocation in open-ended research tasks.

Method: MIRA uses a hierarchical architecture with: (1) Outer-loop meta-reasoner that curates context from a persistent research record and writes work orders; (2) Inner-loop executor that carries out each work order; (3) Generative critic trained at each decision boundary to forecast expected remaining return; (4) Cross-environment pretraining for transferable value priors; (5) MIRA-AC combining actor-critic for joint forecasting and action selection without separate critic model.

Result: MIRA improves long-horizon inference and compute allocation in theorem proving and neural-architecture research without policy training. The generative critic outperforms token-level alternatives. MIRA-AC with self-generated proxy signals improves gold performance across four autoresearch environments, with actor transferring via cross-environment value initialization.

Conclusion: Meta-reasoning can be learned as an explicit policy for directing long-horizon autonomous research. The hierarchical separation of reasoning from execution, combined with generative critics and actor-critic training, enables efficient optimization focused on meta-reasoning decisions without directly optimizing long execution traces.

Abstract: Long-horizon research agents must decide both how to investigate and what to investigate next as evidence accumulates. This is hard to learn because such decisions are sparse in long execution traces, and their consequences may emerge several investigations later. We introduce Meta-reasoning for Iterative Research Agents (MIRA), a hierarchical architecture separating research allocation from execution. An outer-loop meta-reasoner curates context from a persistent research record, then writes a work order for the next investigation or ends the episode. A fresh inner-loop executor carries out each work order, making execution part of the transition between meta-reasoning actions. Without policy training, MIRA improves long-horizon inference and allocates additional compute more effectively in theorem proving and open-ended neural-architecture research. Its decision boundaries also provide natural units for credit assignment. At each boundary, we train a generative critic to forecast expected remaining return from partial states, outperforming token-level alternatives. Cross-environment pretraining improves forecasting and adaptation, yielding a transferable prior for valuing partial progress. We use this prior to initialize MIRA-AC, a generative actor-critic jointly trained to forecast remaining return and choose the next investigation, without a separate critic model. MIRA-AC concentrates policy optimization on meta-reasoning decisions, enabling efficient long-horizon reinforcement learning without directly optimizing the longer execution traces they initiate. Training MIRA-AC on the model's own proxy hill-climbing signals improves gold performance across four autoresearch environments; the actor transfers with cross-environment value initialization. Together, these results show that meta-reasoning can be learned as an explicit policy for directing long-horizon autonomous research.

</details>


### [159] [How To Train Your World Model: Fine-tuning vs RAG for LM-based World Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02542)
*Dhananjay Ashok,Shantanu Agarwal,Vivek Datla,Jonathan May,Alfy Samuel*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper systematically compares fine-tuning and Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) approaches for building world models (WMs) using language models in text-based environments. Across 20 settings spanning embodied, web navigation, and social contexts, fine-tuning outperforms RAG in 15 cases. The study also proposes a hybrid system that combines parametric knowledge with retrieval, achieving consistent improvements.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While fine-tuning language models to serve as world models has become dominant in text-based environments, and RAG has shown success in other NLP tasks, retrieval-based approaches for world modelling remain underexplored. This work addresses this gap by systematically evaluating both paradigms.

Method: The authors conducted systematic evaluations across five diverse environments (embodied, web navigation, and social settings), comparing fine-tuning and RAG-based approaches. They analyzed how additional exploration data and model scaling affect performance. For RAG-based WMs, they used counterfactual intervention to estimate retrieval error rates and tested various query reformulation strategies, including a hierarchical approach.

Result: Fine-tuning outperforms RAG in 15/20 settings. RAG is more data-efficient, while fine-tuning benefits disproportionately from scaling exploration data. Retrievers consistently surface suboptimal transitions, but hierarchical query reformulation improves retrieval quality. The hybrid system combining parametric knowledge with learned retrieval consistently outperforms other methods.

Conclusion: Both fine-tuning and RAG have distinct strengths: fine-tuning excels with scale, while RAG is more data-efficient. A hybrid approach that captures core dynamics parametrically while leveraging retrieval from actively maintained memory provides the most robust solution, offering a promising direction for future world modelling research.

Abstract: World models (WMs) simulate the transition dynamics of environments, enabling agents to plan over the consequences of their actions. In text-based environments, fine-tuning a Language Model (LM) to serve as a WM has emerged as a dominant paradigm. However, despite the widespread success of non-parametric approaches such as Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG), retrieval for LM-based world modelling remains underexplored. We conduct a systematic evaluation across five diverse environments spanning embodied, web navigation and social settings, comparing fine-tuning and RAG-based approaches for LM-based world modelling. Our study reveals that fine-tuning often outperforms RAG, with fine-tuned WMs enabling agents to obtain higher rewards on 15/20 settings. While both construction paradigms benefit from additional and more diverse exploration, RAG-based approaches prove more data-efficient, and fine-tuning approaches disproportionately benefit from scaling the amount of experience collected. With a focus on RAG-based WMs, we devise a procedure that uses counterfactual intervention to estimate the error rate of the retrieval stage, and show that retrievers consistently surface suboptimal transitions from the experience buffer. Hoping to address this failing, we study a variety of query reformulation strategies, demonstrating that a hierarchical approach outperforms the traditional retrieval pipeline. Finally, we compose our findings into a hybrid world modelling system that parametrically captures core environment dynamics, while learning to rely on retrieval from an actively maintained memory store. Our hybrid system consistently outperforms other methods across multiple environments and models, showcasing the robustness of the approach and the applicability of our findings.

</details>


### [160] [How to Have a Sensitive Debate: An Instance-Optimal Protocol for AI Debate](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02557)
*Jiawei Li,Zhiyang Xun,Lijie Chen,Jonah Brown-Cohen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper presents a new protocol for AI debate that provides worst-case correctness guarantees for problems with stable decompositions, improving upon prior average-case results by achieving dominant-strategy equilibrium and instance-wise optimality through connections to fractional block sensitivity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The problem of overseeing powerful AI systems that match or exceed human expertise has become critical. AI debate offers a solution by decomposing complex questions into simpler claims. Prior work provided average-case guarantees and relied on Stackelberg equilibrium assumptions, which the authors aim to improve.

Method: The authors relate the notion of stable problem decompositions to fractional block sensitivity from query complexity theory. They design a new protocol that achieves worst-case correctness guarantees while ensuring honest behavior is a dominant-strategy equilibrium for both debaters.

Result: The new protocol improves on prior work in three ways: (1) worst-case instead of average-case correctness, (2) dominant-strategy instead of Stackelberg equilibrium for honest behavior, and (3) black-box lower bounds proving instance-wise optimality compared to other protocols making only black-box queries to human judgments.

Conclusion: By connecting stable problem decompositions to fractional block sensitivity, the authors develop an optimal protocol for AI debate that provides rigorous worst-case guarantees. This represents a significant theoretical advance in the computational complexity approach to AI oversight.

Abstract: As powerful AI systems reach and sometimes surpass the abilities of human experts across a range of cognitively demanding tasks, the problem of accurate oversight and supervision of these systems has become increasingly urgent. One promising approach is AI debate, which seeks to leverage a debate between two powerful AIs to break complex questions down into simpler claims that can be easily judged directly. Theoretical work on debate has formalized this intuition in the language of computational complexity theory, where the goal is to design protocols (i.e., rules of the debate game) that provide rigorous guarantees on correctness for judging solutions to complex problems with limited supervision. Specifically, the current best protocol has been shown to work for all problems that have sufficiently stable decompositions into subproblems. In this paper, we design a new protocol for this same class of problems that improves on the prior work in several ways. First, correctness holds in a worst-case rather than an average-case sense. Second, being honest and correct is a dominant-strategy equilibrium for both debaters, rather than a Stackelberg equilibrium. Finally, we prove black-box lower bounds, showing that our new protocol is instance-wise optimal. That is, no protocol for this class of problems can outperform ours while making only black-box queries to human judgments. We obtain these results by relating the notion of stable problem decompositions to the concept of fractional block sensitivity from query complexity.

</details>


### [161] [Mitigating Social Sycophancy via Pluralistic Preference Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02568)
*Stephane Hatgis-Kessell,Myra Cheng,Xiaoxuan Hou,Qian Hu,Rahul Gupta,Natasha Jaques,Emma Brunskill*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Pluralistic Preference Optimization (PlurPO) reduces social sycophancy in language models by training them to consider multiple stakeholders' perspectives rather than merely affirming the user. This method uses the model's own signals to identify relevant stakeholders and generate responses acceptable to all parties, without requiring ground-truth labels.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Language models exhibit sycophancy - affirming users much more than humans do. This is particularly problematic for personal advice (e.g., relationship advice) where there is no ground truth. Prior mitigations focused on factual settings and were ineffective for social contexts. The core insight is that social sycophancy occurs because LMs overly center on the user and fail to consider perspectives of other stakeholders affected by the user's behavior.

Method: PlurPO works in three steps: (1) Given inputs describing interpersonal conflicts, the LM identifies relevant stakeholders; (2) The LM simulates these stakeholders' perspectives; (3) The model is trained to prefer and generate responses acceptable to all stakeholders. This uses only signals the model produces about its own outputs, without any ground-truth labels.

Result: PlurPO substantially reduces social sycophancy across four datasets and four model families. Key results: (1) On statements of intent to cause harm, reduces endorsement rate by 89% on average across four models; (2) On general advice questions, closes the gap to human responses by more than half (from 17.8% to 8.0% average); (3) The preference dataset constructed for an 8B model effectively transfers to mitigating sycophancy in a larger 32B model.

Conclusion: Social sycophancy in language models can be effectively reduced by leveraging the model's own capabilities to simulate multiple relevant perspectives. This approach addresses a critical gap in AI safety - mitigating excessive agreement in personal advice contexts where no ground truth exists. The transferability to larger models suggests scalability of the method.

Abstract: Personal advice, including relationship advice, now ranks among the most common uses of generative AI. But language models (LMs) exhibit sycophancy: they affirm users much more often than humans do, which can make people overconfident and less willing to repair their relationships after a conflict. Prior work on mitigating sycophancy has focused on factual settings where a response can be checked against a ground truth answer, while mitigations for social sycophancy (e.g., personal advice, where there is no ground truth) have relied on simple prompting and post-training methods with limited effectiveness. Our insight is that social sycophancy occurs in part because LMs overly center on the user and fail to consider the perspectives of other stakeholders impacted by the user's behavior. To address this problem we propose Pluralistic Preference Optimization (PlurPO): given inputs describing interpersonal conflicts, the LM identifies and simulates the relevant stakeholders, and is then trained to prefer and generate responses acceptable to all stakeholders. PlurPO uses only signals the model produces about its own outputs, without ground-truth labels. PlurPO substantially reduces social sycophancy across four datasets and four model families compared to prior methods. For example, on statements of intent to cause harm, where the users' actions should not be endorsed, PlurPO reduces the endorsement rate by 89% on average across four models. On general advice questions, where the target is to match the endorsement rate of human responses, it closes the gap by more than half, from 17.8% to 8.0% on average. The preference dataset constructed by PlurPO for an 8B model also effectively transfers to mitigating sycophancy in a larger (32B) model. Our results indicate that social sycophancy can be reduced by leveraging a model's own capabilities to simulate a plurality of relevant perspectives.

</details>


### [162] [Answering clinicians' questions over trial evidence tables with verifiable, feedback-driven language models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02576)
*Manan Roy Choudhury,Suparno Roy Chowdhury,Swastik Sahoo,Muhammad Ali Khan,Kaneez Zahra Rubab Khakwani,Mohamad Bassam Sonbol,Irbaz Bin Riaz,Vivek Gupta*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: FD-SCoPE is a language-model framework that enables clinicians to query systematic review evidence tables beyond simple database queries, including derived attributes like drug target class or harmonized endpoints. It provides auditable answers with exposed queries, selected trials, and derivation rules, and learns from expert corrections.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Systematic reviews condense clinical trials into evidence tables, but clinicians can only interrogate these tables through database queries.
