Many clinically relevant questions concern attributes not recorded in the table (e.g., drug target class, harmonized endpoints), limiting the utility of evidence tables.

Method: FD-SCoPE combines language models with executable queries and verified programs. It was evaluated on an oncology evidence table of 159 immune checkpoint inhibitor trial records. The framework exposes the query, selected trials, and derivation rule behind every answer, and learns from expert corrections.

Result: On 140 clinician-style tasks, FD-SCoPE completed all tasks with alternatives ranging from 90.7-97.9%. For questions needing derived attributes, it retrieved 99.3% of relevant trial records at a positive predictive value of 89.8%, outperforming four alternative approaches (derived-value F1 77.7% vs 64.8-73.4%). Corrections on 299 questions raised F1 on 1,201 unseen questions from 77.9% to 84.9%.

Conclusion: Language models coupled with executable queries, verified programs, and expert feedback can give clinicians auditable access to trial evidence, enabling more comprehensive and useful interrogation of systematic review evidence tables.

Abstract: Systematic reviews condense clinical trials into evidence tables, yet clinicians can interrogate these tables only through database queries, and many questions concern attributes that the table does not record, such as a drug's target class or a harmonised endpoint. Here we introduce FD-SCoPE, a language-model framework that answers both kinds of question, exposes the query, the selected trials and the derivation rule behind every answer, and learns from expert corrections. On an oncology evidence table of 159 immune checkpoint inhibitor trial records, FD-SCoPE completed all 140 clinician-style tasks (alternatives, 90.7-97.9%). For questions needing derived attributes it retrieved 99.3% of relevant trial records at a positive predictive value of 89.8% and outperformed four alternative approaches (derived-value F1 77.7% versus 64.8-73.4%). Corrections on 299 questions, simulated from reference answers, raised F1 on 1,201 unseen questions from 77.9% to 84.9%. Language models coupled with executable queries, verified programs and expert feedback can give clinicians auditable access to trial evidence.

</details>


### [163] [Labels Override Definitions in Jev-Style Typed Decision Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02586)
*Seyedarmin Azizi,Erfan Baghaei Potraghloo,Massoud Pedram*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether typed decision models (used for classification) follow the label or the definition when making predictions. The researchers find that models predominantly use labels rather than definitions, a phenomenon called "option-label bias." Through experiments across four open-weight models, eleven classification tasks, and a synthetic benchmark (PolicyBench), they demonstrate that deleting definitions doesn't harm accuracy, but renaming labels to generic "A" and "B" improves it. The root cause is identified as the prompt rendering format, not the decision head as previously believed.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The research investigates whether typed decision models follow the definitions (the rules stated by developers) or the labels when making classification decisions. This is important because these models are widely used for routing, moderation, and triage tasks, and understanding this bias is crucial for building reliable AI systems. Earlier work attributed failures to constrained decision heads, but this paper questions that explanation.

Method: The researchers tested four open-weight typed decision models across three ways of extracting answers from a Qwen2.5 backbone, on eleven classification tasks and PolicyBench (a synthetic routing suite where rules appear only in definitions). They conducted several experiments: (1) deleting all definitions, (2) renaming options to A and B, (3) comparing laya (which formats as "{label}: {definition}") versus von (which writes only the definition), and (4) testing four mitigations.

Result: The answer is mostly the labels. Deleting definitions leaves accuracy unchanged (0.8559 vs 0.8487), though definitions alone achieve 0.7971 accuracy. Renaming options to A and B raises accuracy by +0.1511. The key difference between systems: laya writes "{label}: {definition}" while von writes only the definition. Changing this expression makes laya invariant (+0.0000) and causes von's accuracy to drop from 0.8511 to 0.2281 when labels contradict definitions. The failure is located in prompt rendering, not the decision head.

Conclusion: The option-label bias stems from how the prompt is rendered, not from constrained decision heads as previously thought. The format "{label}: {definition}" causes models to rely on labels, while "definition only" allows following definitions. A two-call test is provided for practitioners to identify which case applies to their model, and four mitigations are evaluated.

Abstract: A typed decision model answers a fixed question about an input by returning a probability for each of several caller-defined options. Each option carries a short label and a written definition, which is where a developer states the rule the model should apply. Jev introduced this interface for routing, moderation and triage, open implementations followed, and the same operation occurs whenever a language model is used as a classifier by scoring label strings. We study the open implementations, whose weights we can inspect and patch, and ask whether the probability follows the definitions or the labels. A preference for the label we call option-label bias. Across four open-weight typed decision models, three ways of reading an answer from a Qwen2.5 backbone, eleven classification tasks and PolicyBench, a synthetic routing suite we introduce in which the rule appears only in the definitions, the answer is mostly the labels. Deleting every definition leaves accuracy unchanged (laya-td: 0.8559 against 0.8487), although those definitions support 0.7971 on their own, and renaming the options to A and B raises accuracy by +0.1511 [+0.1377, +0.1646]. One system, von, is unaffected, and the two code bases differ in one expression: laya writes each option as "{label}: {definition}", while von writes only the definition. Changing that expression in both directions, with no weight changed, makes all three laya checkpoints exactly invariant (+0.0000 [+0.0000, +0.0000]) and creates the effect in von, whose accuracy falls from 0.8511 to 0.2281 when a label contradicts its definition. Earlier work attributed this failure to the constrained decision head these models use in place of a text decoder; our results locate it in the prompt rendering. We give a two-call test that tells a practitioner which case applies to their model, and measure what four mitigations are worth.

</details>


### [164] [Open-Endedness Bench: Measuring Epistemic Process from Agent Records](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02588)
*Chengyang Shi,Xianglin Ji,Jintao Huang,Jicheng Wang,Yifeng He,Jiachen Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: OEB (Open-Endedness Bench) is a benchmark-agnostic methodology that evaluates AI agents' epistemic processes in open-ended research tasks by analyzing their execution logs without requiring reference answers or outcome scores. It constructs an epistemic event graph connecting propositions to executed experiments and scores agents on four competence axes (evidence, experiment, revision, no reward hacking) and six persona traits.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current evaluation of AI agents in open-ended research tasks relies solely on outcome scores, which fail to establish whether agents' claims actually follow from their executed experiments. There is no way to verify the validity of agents' claimed improvements or their research methodology when only final scores are available.

Method: OEB compiles an agent's execution record into a unified epistemic event graph where edges connect propositions to the executed actions that test them. Each node carries verified excerpts. The scoring principle: prose can state propositions, but only evidence from executed actions can support or refute them. This is checked against the actual execution record. Four competence axes are scored as the share of opportunities for sound research that the agent took, and six subjective persona traits describe research habits.

Result: Testing 119 runs across 12 tasks from three benchmarks (LLM post-training, chip design, training-speed record) revealed that only 16-29% of the improvements agents claim are real. On 9 of 10 tasks, the best run tries more new ideas in its second half than the worst run. Persona readings follow the model: for every trait, the model explains more variance across runs than the task (median 43% vs 7%).

Conclusion: OEB provides a novel framework for evaluating AI agents' research methodology in open-ended tasks, revealing significant gaps between claimed and actual improvements. The methodology successfully captures both competence and personality traits of agents, with model identity explaining more variance than task differences in research habits.

Abstract: Agents are increasingly given open-ended research tasks: discovering an empirical law from self-designed experiments, improving a heuristic whose optimum nobody knows, or beating a standing record. Their execution logs record every step of this research, yet the runs are still judged by their outcome score. That score alone does not establish whether an agent's claims follow from executed experiments, and a reference answer may be unavailable. We evaluate the agent's epistemic process: how it forms hypotheses, tests them, and revises them in response to evidence. We introduce OEB (Open-Endedness Bench), a benchmark-agnostic methodology that reads only the agent's execution record and never a reference answer or an outcome score. OEB compiles the record into a unified epistemic event graph whose edges connect the propositions the agent states to the executed actions that test them; each node carries an exact excerpt that code verifies against the record. One principle governs scoring: prose can state a proposition, but only evidence returned by an executed action can support or refute it, so OEB checks what the agent writes against what it actually ran. From the graph, OEB scores four competence axes (evidence, experiment, revision, and no reward hacking), mostly as the share of opportunities for sound research that the agent took, and profiles six subjective persona traits that describe the agent's research habits. We score 119 existing runs over 12 tasks from three benchmarks: LLM post-training, chip design, and a training-speed record. Against logged results, only 16-29% of the improvements agents claim are real. On 9 of 10 tasks, the best run tries more new ideas in its second half than the worst run. The persona readings follow the model: for every trait, the model that ran explains more of its variance across runs than the task (a median of 43% against 7%).

</details>


### [165] [TasteBench: Multimodal Benchmark for Sensory Prediction, from Molecules to Sustainable Foods](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02599)
*Anna T. Thomas,Sohum Patnaik,Caroline Cotto,Benjamin Sanchez-Lengeling*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TasteBench is a multimodal benchmark for computational taste prediction, designed to accelerate sustainable protein discovery by providing a substitute for expensive human sensory panels. It includes two tasks: food-level ranking (215 plant-based foods, 21K+ evaluations, 935 ranking pairs) and molecular-level taste classification (15K flavor molecules). The benchmark establishes realistic performance bounds given low inter-rater agreement (α=0.077) among human panelists, with the best model achieving 0.661 pairwise accuracy, comparable to the median human panelist.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The lack of fast computational proxies for taste prediction bottlenecks sustainable protein discovery. Evaluating novel foods currently requires expensive human sensory panels, creating a bottleneck in the design-build-test loop for alternative protein development. There is a need for ML-based screening tools analogous to molecular docking in drug discovery.

Method: The authors created a benchmark with two tasks: (1) A food-level ranking task using 21K+ human evaluations across 215 plant-based foods in 24 product categories, yielding 935 within-category ranking pairs; (2) A molecular-level taste classification task over 15K flavor molecules. They evaluated baselines across four input modalities and characterized the ground truth by measuring inter-rater agreement (Krippendorff's α) and split-half reliability ceiling.

Result: Inter-rater agreement among panelists is low (Krippendorff's α = 0.077), indicating high variability in human taste perception. The split-half reliability ceiling of panel-aggregated rankings is 0.825, establishing the upper bound for ML performance. The best model achieves 0.661 pairwise accuracy on the same pairs panelists rated, which is competitive with the median individual panelist (0.650), and 0.683 across all within-category pairs.

Conclusion: TasteBench provides the evaluation infrastructure and baselines for measuring progress on computational screening for sustainable protein discovery. The benchmark establishes realistic performance expectations given the inherent variability in human taste perception, and shows that ML models can achieve performance comparable to individual human panelists in pairwise taste comparisons.

Abstract: Sustainable protein discovery lacks the fast computational proxies, analogous to molecular docking or density functional theory, that accelerate drug and materials discovery. Evaluating whether a novel food tastes like its animal-based target requires expensive human sensory panels, bottlenecking the design-build-test loop. We introduce TasteBench, a multimodal benchmark and privacy-preserving competition for sensory prediction, spanning two tasks: a food-level ranking task built on 21K+ human evaluations across 215 plant-based foods in 24 product categories, yielding 935 within-category ranking pairs, and a supporting molecular-level taste classification task over 15K flavor molecules. To enable rigorous interpretation of model performance, we characterize the ground truth: inter-rater agreement among panelists is low (Krippendorff's $α= .077$), and the split-half reliability ceiling of panel-aggregated rankings is .825, establishing the range within which ML systems on this benchmark should be assessed. We evaluate baselines across four input modalities; on the same pairs panelists rated, the best model achieves .661 pairwise accuracy, competitive with the median individual panelist (.650), and .683 across all within-category pairs. TasteBench provides the evaluation infrastructure and baselines for measuring progress on computational screening for sustainable protein discovery.

</details>


### [166] [Time Series Forecasting Benchmarks Need Scenario-Grounded Stress Testing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02608)
*Yuyang Zhao,Lian Xu,Hao Xue*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper identifies a critical gap in time series forecasting (TSF) evaluation: current benchmarks focus only on low held-out error and simple perturbations (Gaussian noise, random masking), failing to capture real-world failure modes like structured events, regime shifts, and causal failures. The authors advocate for "scenario-grounded stress testing" that includes semantic scenarios, explicit failure operators, and measurable difficulty levels.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current TSF evaluation is too narrow and doesn't capture real-world failure modes. Input-side anomalies are not just noisy inputs - they often reflect structured events that alter temporal dynamics, break cross-variable dependencies, induce regime shifts, or propagate from faulty sensors. The rise of TSF foundation models makes this gap more urgent, as unauditable pretraining corpora make held-out generalization unreliable.

Method: The authors propose scenario-grounded stress testing as a new evaluation paradigm. Each test instance should include: (1) historical inputs and future targets, (2) a semantic scenario, (3) an explicit failure operator, and (4) a measurable difficulty level. This makes evaluation interpretable, attributable, and deployment-relevant.

Result: The paper advocates for a shift in TSF evaluation from narrow held-out error metrics to comprehensive stress testing that captures semantic, causal, and system-level failures. This approach enables the community to ask not only which model is accurate, but under what conditions it fails and why.

Conclusion: The proposed scenario-grounded stress testing framework makes TSF evaluation interpretable, attributable, and deployment-friendly. It addresses the urgent need to audit forecasting systems, especially with the rise of TSF foundation models, by focusing on realistic failure modes rather than simplistic i.i.d. perturbations.

Abstract: Time series forecasting (TSF) increasingly drives decisions in transportation, energy, finance, healthcare, and infrastructure, yet current evaluation remains overly narrow: standard benchmarks reward low held-out error, while robustness studies typically reduce failure to Gaussian noise, random masking, or bounded adversarial perturbations. This obscures the real failure modes of deployed forecasting systems. Input-side anomalies are not merely noisier inputs: they often reflect structured events that alter temporal dynamics, break cross-variable dependencies, induce regime shifts, or propagate from faulty sensors to downstream decisions. These semantic, causal, and system-level failures cannot be faithfully captured by i.i.d. perturbations alone. The rise of TSF foundation models makes this evaluation gap more urgent, as unauditable pretraining corpora make held-out generalization increasingly unreliable. We therefore advocate scenario-grounded stress testing. Each test instance should include historical inputs and future targets, together with a semantic scenario, an explicit failure operator, and a measurable difficulty level. This shift makes evaluation interpretable, attributable, and deployment-relevant and friendly, enabling the community to ask not only which model is accurate, but under what conditions it fails and why.

</details>


### [167] [VERSE: Verified Self-Evolving Optimizer for Agent Harnesses](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02616)
*Zekai Wang,Yingqiang Ge,Zekun Wang,Hai Wang,Yuhui Xu,Joshua Frandsen,Shancong Fu,Ashia C. Wilson,Chandan K. Reddy*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: VERSE is a self-evolving optimizer for LLM agent harnesses that allows the optimizer to improve not just the executor but also its own diagnostic, editing, and testing tools through execution-based verification. This approach achieves 42.3% and 37.7% accuracy on SWE-rebench tasks versus 39.2% and 29.3% for baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current harness evolution improves LLM agents' prompts, tools, and workflow, but the optimizer's own tools and procedures remain fixed. The authors investigate whether an optimizer can more effectively improve another agent by also improving how it diagnoses failures, develops edits, and tests their effects.

Method: VERSE allows the optimizer to: (1) test draft edits before submission, (2) replay failures, (3) perturb suspected steps, while tracking fixes and regressions across rounds. The optimizer revises both the executor harness and its own prompts, skills, tools, hooks, and notes, with model weights remaining fixed. Uses a shared protocol with disjoint training, validation, and test tasks.

Result: VERSE improves all four evaluated harness optimizers on held-out SWE-rebench tasks and newer out-of-distribution tasks in five languages. Best validation-selected harness achieves 42.3% and 37.7% accuracy vs 39.2% and 29.3% for strongest baselines.

Conclusion: Self-evolution of the optimizer with execution-based verification can significantly improve LLM agent performance. The key insight is that enabling the optimizer to build its own tools for failure analysis, verification, training audits, and workflow control is crucial for effective self-improvement.

Abstract: Harness evolution improves an LLM agent's prompts, tools, and workflow, while the optimizer's own tools and procedures often remain fixed. We study whether an optimizer can improve another agent more effectively by also improving how it diagnoses failures, develops edits, and tests their effects. Two observations guide our design. In a controlled study, optimizer self-evolution fails to improve performance without execution-based verification, but achieves the best result of that study when verification is available. Across five executors, self-evolving optimizers build their own tools for failure analysis, verification, training audits, and workflow control. Motivated by these findings, we introduce VERSE, a Verified Self-Evolving optimizer for agent harnesses. VERSE lets the optimizer test draft edits, replay failures, and perturb suspected steps before submission, while tracking fixes and regressions across rounds. Using this feedback, the optimizer revises both the executor harness and its own prompts, skills, tools, hooks, and notes, while the weights of the optimizer and executor models stay fixed. Under a shared protocol with disjoint training, validation, and test tasks, VERSE improves all four evaluated harness optimizers on held-out SWE-rebench tasks and newer out-of-distribution tasks in five languages. Its best validation-selected harness reaches 42.3% and 37.7% accuracy, respectively, against 39.2% and 29.3% for the strongest baselines. Code is available at https://github.com/wzekai/VERSE.

</details>


### [168] [CuBEs: Culturally-Situated Behavioral Evaluations and the Limitations of Culture-Blind LLM Judges](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02622)
*Hoda Ayad,Tanu Mitra,Abhishek Mukherji*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces CuBEs (Culturally-situated Behavior Evaluations), a framework for testing LLM behaviors across diverse cultural contexts. It reveals that standard evaluations miss significant cultural variations in model behaviors, and that non-Western contexts surface different bias axes than Western-focused tests.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM behavioral evaluations are culturally-agnostic, failing to account for cultural context. This limits generalizability across global user bases and risks missing deployment risks specific to certain cultures.

Method: Extended an automated testing pipeline to inject cultural context into behavioral test scenarios. Built a human-labeled dataset covering 12 distinct cultures with nuanced behavioral dimensions. Evaluated 13 open- and closed-source LLMs across these culturally-situated scenarios.

Result: Significant cross-cultural variations were found. Baseline Western political bias tests captured only American conservative-progressive divides, while non-Western evaluations revealed different axes: religious and colonial political issues. Standard evaluations fail to capture these behavioral shifts.

Conclusion: Culturally situated behavioral testing is necessary for global LLM deployments. Current one-size-fits-all evaluations are insufficient and miss culturally-specific bias patterns.

Abstract: Evaluating the occurrence and triggers of large language model (LLM) behaviors - such as sycophancy, self-preference, or over-confidence - is critical for predicting real-world model deployment risks. However, existing situated behavioral evaluations typically ignore cultural context, limiting their generalizability across an increasingly global user base. To address this gap, we propose CuBEs - Culturally-situated Behavior Evaluations that probe for response patterns across diverse user cultures. We first extend an automated testing pipeline to inject cultural context into behavioral test scenarios and subsequent evaluation. We assess the cultural adaptability of this pipeline by building a human-labeled dataset that captures nuanced dimensions of behavior understanding across 12 distinct cultures. Our dataset reveals significant cross-cultural variations that one-size-fits all judgments fail to capture. Through evaluating 13 open- and closed-source LLMs, we find that introducing cultural situatedness in the evaluation scenario creates significant variation in the presence of a behavior. For example, while our baseline experiments testing for political bias capture localized Western political dimensions like the American conservative-progressive divide, non-Western culturally situated evaluations surface entirely different axes of bias such as religious and colonial political issues. Our findings demonstrate that standard, culturally-agnostic evaluations fail to capture these shifts, highlighting the necessity of culturally situated behavioral testing for global deployments.

</details>


### [169] [Lost in the Request: How Communication Variation Disrupts Retrieval and Action in Email Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02627)
*Feng Chen,Ritam Dutt,Atnaz Taheri,Alex Williams*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper addresses a critical gap in NLP benchmarking: whether email assistants handle variations in communication style and English dialect robustly. The authors construct variants along five communication-style axes and four dialect conditions, evaluating them on three benchmarks (1 RAG pipeline, 2 tool-using agents). They find that indirect requests hurt all three systems, while formal requests hurt only the two agentic systems. The root causes differ: verbose requests impair lexical retrieval, while indirect/dialect variants cause failures even after correct retrieval—leading agents to omit required actions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most NLP benchmarks test each task with only one canonical request, leaving robustness to communication style variations largely unmeasured. The key insight is that an email assistant should not complete less work simply because a user phrases the same request differently.

Method: The authors construct validated variants along five communication-style axes (e.g., indirect, formal, verbose) and four rule-based dialect conditions. They evaluate these variants on three benchmarks: a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline and two tool-using agents.

Result: Indirect requests reduce performance on all three benchmarks. Formal requests reduce performance on both agentic benchmarks. Verbose requests mainly hurt the lexical retriever by making relevant emails harder to find. Indirect and dialect variants remain harmful even after correct retrieval. In agentic settings, indirect and formal requests mainly cause agents to omit required actions rather than take unsupported actions.

Conclusion: A successful response is not sufficient to establish robustness. Evaluations should vary how requests are expressed and separately measure whether agents complete the requested work. The paper highlights the importance of testing communication style robustness in email assistants and NLP systems more broadly.

Abstract: An email assistant should not complete less work simply because a user phrases the same request differently. Yet most benchmarks test each task with only one canonical request, leaving this form of robustness largely unmeasured. We test whether email assistants remain reliable when the requested information, available evidence, and expected outcome stay fixed, but the communication style or English variety changes. We construct validated variants along five communication-style axes and four rule-based dialect conditions, and evaluate them on three benchmarks: a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline and two tool-using agents. Indirect requests reduce performance on all three benchmarks, while formal requests reduce performance on both agentic benchmarks. Examining the systems more closely shows that these failures have different causes. Verbose requests mainly hurt a lexical retriever by making the relevant email harder to find. By contrast, indirect and dialect variants remain harmful even when the relevant email is retrieved. In the agentic setting, indirect and formal requests mainly cause the agents to omit required actions, not to take more unsupported actions. These results show that a successful response is not enough to establish robustness: evaluations should vary how requests are expressed and separately measure whether agents complete the requested work.

</details>


### [170] [Designing the Future of User Feedback for Generative AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02631)
*Alisa Frik,Julia Bernd,Amitis Karami,Mohammad Tahaei*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper presents a multi-phase industry-academic collaboration (eBay + researchers) to improve post-deployment user feedback mechanisms for generative AI systems, addressing gaps in current industry practices and providing actionable guidance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation stems from the need for cost-effective, scalable methods to monitor and improve GenAI systems through user feedback, driven by regulatory requirements and industry guidelines, while lacking practical design guidance for consumer-friendly feedback mechanisms.

Method: Multi-phase study combining benchmark evaluation of current industry approaches, development of best-practice recommendations, and iterative design/testing of a prototype feedback-collection tool.

Result: Identified common issues in current approaches: lack of discoverability, unclear terminology, and inattention to user value. Developed a prototype tool designed to provide efficient, flexible, positive user experience while delivering rich, usable data for product teams.

Conclusion: The research provides actionable best-practice recommendations for designing user feedback mechanisms that balance user experience with product team needs, addressing regulatory requirements while increasing user engagement and trust in GenAI systems.

Abstract: Post-deployment feedback from users can be a cost-effective, scalable, and representative means to monitor and improve generative AI systems and features. When implemented effectively, giving such feedback can increase users' engagement with and trust in GenAI systems. Government regulations and industry guidelines call for post-deployment user engagement, but there is little guidance on designing mechanisms that are usable for consumers and provide actionable input for product teams. We conducted a multi-phase study as a collaboration between academic researchers and eBay. Our benchmark evaluation of current industry approaches identified common issues including lack of discoverability, unclear terminology, and inattention to user value. Based on these findings, we developed best-practice recommendations and designed and tested a prototype feedback-collection tool. The tool aimed to provide users with an efficient, flexible, and positive feedback-giving experience, and provide product teams with rich data on performance and potential problems in a usable format.

</details>


### [171] [Batched Speech Decisions Without Decoding: Single-Token Supervision Lets a Frozen LLM Hear Beyond the Transcript](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02638)
*Jie Jin,Ziyin Ma,Min Yin,Jinyu Chen,Haigang Song,Zhikun Pang,Xiaowen Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DuplexJev is a fast full-duplex voice agent system that bypasses slow autoregressive decoding by feeding ASR-encoder hidden states through a small connector into a frozen LLM, treating each question as a single-token prediction. It achieves ~0.1s latency for 80 decisions across 8 utterances on 8 GPUs, with minimal accuracy loss compared to transcript-based reading (90% vs 91%). A cross-attention connector enables speaker attribute recognition (gender/emotion at 90%) while maintaining high QA performance (82%).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Full-duplex voice agents require making many small, closed decisions rapidly, but current systems rely on slow autoregressive decoding, which creates latency issues for real-time applications.

Method: Feed ASR-encoder hidden states through a small connector into a frozen LLM; read each question as a single-token distribution over answer options. Train decisions with cross-entropy on the read-out answer token instead of transcript distillation. Two connector variants: last-layer connector and cross-attention connector for speaker features.

Result: With last-layer connector: spoken QA achieves 90% vs 91% reading transcript. With cross-attention connector: gender and emotion accuracy both reach 90% (from 55% and 28%), while spoken QA drops only 1 point (83% to 82%). Latency: ~0.1s for 80 decisions about 8 utterances on 8-GPU node.

Conclusion: DuplexJev enables fast, accurate full-duplex voice interactions by eliminating autoregressive decoding. The cross-attention connector successfully incorporates speaker information (gender, emotion) with minimal QA degradation. The approach supports interchangeable encoders and LLMs, with released weights, training recipe, batched-inference pipeline, and bilingual spoken-QA dataset.

Abstract: Full-duplex voice agents make many small, closed decisions, which current systems answer by slow autoregressive decoding. We propose DuplexJev, which feeds ASR-encoder hidden states through a small connector into a frozen LLM and reads each question as a single-token distribution over its options. Nothing is decoded, and an 8-GPU node answers 80 decisions about eight utterances in about 0.1 s. With a last-layer connector, spoken QA stays close to reading the transcript (90% vs. 91%). DuplexJev also hears the speaker: gender and emotion accuracy both reach 90% (from 55% and 28%) with a cross-attention connector, whose spoken QA drops by only 1 point (83% to 82%). We train decisions with cross-entropy on the read-out answer token, instead of the usual transcript distillation, whose teacher never hears the voice, and keep distillation for content. Encoders and LLMs are interchangeable; we release weights, training recipe, a batched-inference pipeline for full-duplex serving and a bilingual spoken-QA set.

</details>


### [172] [Coherence-Driven Belief Formation and Population Dynamics of Contagion in LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02654)
*Tathagata Banerjee,Nima Moghaddas*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper empirically measures belief adoption in language model agents, finding that adoption follows a sigmoid kernel characteristic of complex contagion, with thresholds influenced by claim plausibility, source reliability, and agent disposition—collectively approximated by "coherence" with prior beliefs. Collective dynamics show network topology effects and hysteretic consensus behavior.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional social contagion models assume how individuals adopt beliefs, but this paper aims to empirically measure actual belief adoption in LLM agents, quantifying how peer endorsement influences adoption probability.

Method: Empirical measurement of belief adoption probability in LLM agents as a function of peer endorsement count, testing across different claim plausibility levels, source reliability, and agent dispositions. Network experiments on clustered vs random topologies.

Result: Adoption kernel is sigmoid (complex contagion). Threshold sensitivity depends on three factors: claim plausibility, source reliability, and agent disposition. These three dimensions are approximated by a single "coherence" with prior beliefs. Collective dynamics show greater spread on clustered networks, bifurcating cascade window, and hysteretic consensus (harder to remove than establish).

Conclusion: LLM agents exhibit complex contagion dynamics in belief adoption. The three key factors can be unified as coherence. Network topology matters, and consensus exhibits hysteresis—establishing consensus is easier than eliminating it, with implications for understanding information spread in AI systems.

Abstract: Models of social contagion usually assume how individuals adopt beliefs and derive population behavior from it. We instead empirically measure belief adoption in language model agents, quantifying the probability an agent adopts a claim given how many peers endorse it. We find this adoption kernel to be sigmoid, a characteristic of complex contagion, with a threshold that is sensitive to three sources: the claim's plausibility, the source's reliability, and the agent's disposition. These three dimensions are well approximated by a single effective dimension which we propose can be understood as the coherence of the incoming belief with the LLM agent's prior beliefs. Further, we observe a characteristic of complex contagion in the collective dynamics of belief adoption in a system of AI agents: further spread on clustered than random networks. These systems also exhibit a bifurcating cascade window, and self-sustaining hysteretic consensus which lead to consensus being far harder to remove than to establish.

</details>


### [173] [A GHOST in Long-Horizon Agents: Governance Hazard from Overlooked Safety Constraints across Turns](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02664)
*XinPeng Shen,Lan Zhang,Yixiao Huang,Haoran Cheng,Jiewei Lai,Leilei Chen,Haoxiang Deng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper identifies a novel safety failure mode in long-horizon AI agents called GHOST (Governance Hazard from Overlooked Safety Constraints across Turns), where agents violate safety constraints specified many turns earlier under benign interaction conditions. The authors demonstrate an 11.5% occurrence rate on GPT-5.5 and propose STAR-Guard, a two-layer defense system that achieves zero GHOST events in experiments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-horizon agents are increasingly assisting humans with complex problem-solving. However, their extended interaction history introduces an underexplored execution-safety concern: agents may execute actions that violate safety constraints specified many turns earlier, potentially causing irreversible damage. This failure mode, occurring under benign interaction conditions, was previously overlooked in safety research.

Method: The authors first conducted experiments to measure GHOST occurrence rates on GPT-5.5 (11.5% rate). They then developed a theoretical framework showing that if the residual conditional violation hazard along each safe prefix is bounded below by a non-summable sequence, execution enters the hazard region almost surely. Based on this insight, they proposed STAR-Guard, a two-layer defense coupling: (1) historical semantic safety constraint restoration to reduce unsafe proposals, and (2) a deterministic pre-execution audit layer to prevent residual violations from reaching the environment.

Result: Experiments revealed GHOST events are not isolated cases—occurring at an 11.5% rate on GPT-5.5 under benign conditions. With STAR-Guard implemented, zero GHOST events were observed in experiments under the GPT-5.5 setup, demonstrating the effectiveness of the two-layer defense design.

Conclusion: GHOST represents a significant and previously underexplored safety concern in long-horizon AI agents. The theoretical analysis provides a mathematical foundation for understanding when such failures occur. STAR-Guard offers a practical solution through its two-layer approach of constraint restoration and pre-execution auditing, effectively eliminating GHOST events while maintaining agent functionality.

Abstract: Long-horizon agents are now playing an increasingly significant role in assisting humans with complex problem-solving. However, it is exactly their extended interaction history that introduces an underexplored execution-safety concern. Under benign interaction conditions, an agent may execute an action that violates a safety constraint specified many turns earlier. We term this failure mode Governance Hazard from Overlooked Safety Constraints across Turns (GHOST), which may cause irreversible damage. Our experiments reveal that GHOST events are not isolated cases: this failure mode, occurring precisely under benign interaction conditions, yields an occurrence rate of 11.5% on GPT-5.5. Furthermore, we theoretically show that if the residual conditional violation hazard along each safe prefix is bounded below by a non-summable sequence, the execution enters the hazard region almost surely. Leveraging this theoretical insight, we further propose STAR-Guard, a two-layer defense coupling historical semantic safety constraint restoration with pre-execution audit. STAR-Guard restores applicable safety constraints to reduce unsafe proposals, while its deterministic audit layer prevents residual violations from reaching the environment. Consistent with this two-layer design, we observe no GHOST events in our experiments under the GPT-5.5 setup.

</details>


### [174] [Spend Teacher Tokens Where They Matter: Success-Referenced On-Policy Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02678)
*Xiang Chen,Futao Su,Kong Wang,Jiayi Chen,TanLin Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SR-OPD reduces teacher computation cost in on-policy distillation by selectively supervising only prompts with both successful and failed rollouts, using successful rollouts as references to identify failed rollouts with divergent hidden-state trajectories. This achieves comparable reasoning performance using only 3.46-5.02% of teacher-input tokens compared to Vanilla OPD.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: On-policy distillation (OPD) requires substantial teacher computation for dense token-level supervision on every student rollout. This creates a scalability bottleneck when training large student models, as providing teacher supervision for all rollouts is computationally expensive.

Method: SR-OPD introduces a selective supervision mechanism with two key components: (1) Prompt selection - focuses on prompts where the student produces both successful and failed rollouts; (2) Rollout prioritization - prioritizes failed rollouts whose hidden-state trajectories show sustained divergence from a successful reference rollout, while accounting for estimated teacher-input cost.

Result: Across three teacher-student pairs and six mathematical reasoning benchmarks, SR-OPD uses only 3.46-5.02% of the teacher-input tokens required by Vanilla OPD in the one-pass setting while maintaining comparable reasoning performance. Under a controlled 5% budget setting, both key design choices (focusing on prompts with mixed outcomes and using successful rollouts to guide failure selection) are validated.

Conclusion: A student's own successful behavior can serve as a useful reference for efficiently allocating teacher supervision under fixed teacher-input budgets. This enables significant computational savings (95%+ reduction) in on-policy distillation without significant performance degradation.

Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) combines student-generated rollouts with dense token-level supervision from a teacher, but providing such supervision for every rollout requires substantial teacher computation. We introduce Success-Referenced On-Policy Distillation (SR-OPD), which reduces this cost by selecting which prompts and rollouts receive teacher supervision. When the student produces both successful and failed rollouts for the same prompt, a successful rollout can serve as a natural reference for selecting failed rollouts. SR-OPD therefore focuses on such prompts and prioritizes failed rollouts whose hidden-state trajectories show sustained divergence from a successful reference, while accounting for estimated teacher-input cost. Across three teacher-student pairs and six mathematical reasoning benchmarks, SR-OPD uses only 3.46-5.02% of the teacher-input tokens required by Vanilla OPD in the one-pass setting while maintaining comparable reasoning performance. Under a controlled setting matched to 5% of Vanilla OPD's teacher-input budget, further experiments support both key design choices: focusing supervision on prompts with both successful and failed rollouts, and using successful rollouts to guide failure selection. These results indicate that a student's own successful behavior can serve as a useful reference for allocating teacher supervision under a fixed teacher-input budget.

</details>


### [175] [DataWeave: Deploying Human-LLM Analytics for Exploratory Structured Data Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02679)
*Raquib Bin Yousuf,Harith Laxman,Vitaliy Shkremetko,Eunice Son,Shambhavi Verma,Brian O'Leary,Venketesh Subramony,Sylvain Nazef,Jacquelyn Elias,Ron Coddington,Chris Contakes,Michael Riley,Naren Ramakrishnan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DataWeave is a human-LLM collaborative system designed to support exploratory data analysis for journalists working with large structured datasets. It addresses recurring failures of LLMs in newsroom workflows by framing LLMs as interactive partners rather than autonomous answer engines, combining conversational interaction, schema grounding, analytical planning, and executable query generation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The practice of data journalism requires journalists to explore large structured datasets, but current workflows are slow and brittle. Journalists must navigate hundreds of variables, understand data coding conventions, write complex analysis code, and adapt as hypotheses evolve. Despite LLMs being promoted as natural language to SQL/answer converters, they fail in real newsroom settings due to schema mismatches, misread domain semantics, and silent assumptions.

Method: DataWeave combines four key components: (1) conversational interaction for natural dialogue, (2) schema grounding to ensure alignment with data structure, (3) analytical planning for systematic investigation, and (4) executable query generation. The system treats LLMs as interactive partners whose outputs can be inspected, corrected, and steered. Evaluation was conducted through a case study with professional journalists analyzing IPEDS (U.S. Department of Education's Integrated Postsecondary Education Data System), a high-stakes public dataset with substantial domain semantics and frequent schema updates.

Result: The paper presents design principles and deployment lessons for trustworthy human-LLM collaboration in structured data analysis, derived from deployment experience and iterative refinement of the DataWeave architecture.

Conclusion: DataWeave demonstrates a paradigm shift from treating LLMs as autonomous answer engines to positioning them as interactive partners in exploratory data analysis. The system addresses the practical challenges faced by journalists in working with large structured datasets, and the findings provide valuable guidance for building trustworthy human-LLM collaborative systems in data journalism and similar domains.

Abstract: Data journalism, the practice of using data analysis to surface newsworthy stories, depends increasingly on the ability of reporters and investigative journalists to uncover trends, disparities, and accountability narratives. In practice, exploring large structured datasets remains slow and brittle: journalists must navigate hundreds of variables across many datasets over years, understand data coding conventions, and write non-trivial analysis code while hypotheses evolve. Although LLMs are often touted as "ask in English, get SQL/answers," real newsroom workflows expose recurring failures, e.g., schema mismatches and drift, misread domain semantics and units, and silent assumptions. We present DataWeave, a system that addresses these needs by combining conversational interaction, schema grounding, analytical planning, and executable query generation to support exploratory analysis over structured data. Rather than treating LLMs as autonomous answer engines, DataWeave frames them as interactive partners whose outputs can be inspected, corrected, and steered as hypotheses shift. We present a case study with professional journalists using our system to analyze the U.S. Department of Education's Integrated Postsecondary Education Data System (IPEDS), a high-stakes public dataset with substantial domain semantics and frequent schema updates. We also report how deployment experience and iterative refinement shaped the current DataWeave architecture and its analytical workflow. Our findings distill design principles and deployment lessons for trustworthy human-LLM collaboration in structured data analysis.

</details>


### [176] [Large language models exhibit unreliable updating of clinical judgment as patient evidence evolves](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02684)
*Min Zeng,Rui Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper evaluates whether large language models (LLMs) appropriately update their clinical predictions as patient evidence evolves over time. Using matched intensive care trajectories from electronic health records, researchers found that LLMs consistently fail at longitudinal belief updating - models often increase prediction error when conditioning on prior judgments, show asymmetric responses to worsening vs improving evidence, and are inappropriately influenced by prior beliefs. A novel intervention called EVLU partially addresses these issues but introduces a reliability-coverage trade-off.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to address a critical gap in LLM clinical reliability: whether these models can appropriately revise their judgments as patient evidence evolves longitudinally, which is essential for real-world clinical decision-making.

Method: The researchers evaluated longitudinal belief updating using matched intensive-care trajectories from electronic health records. They conducted controlled interventions to identify failure modes, tested prompting strategies, and developed Evidence-Validated Longitudinal Update (EVLU) as a potential solution.

Result: Key findings: (1) Conditioning on preceding judgments increased prediction error more often than reducing it; (2) Models responded more strongly to worsening than improving respiratory evidence (asymmetry persisted after normalization); (3) Increasing prior risk from 10% to 90% shifted estimates by 26.2 percentage points, showing causal influence of prior beliefs; (4) Prompting failed to restore reliable updating; (5) EVLU identified fewer but more reliable revisions, revealing a reliability-coverage trade-off.

Conclusion: Longitudinal belief updating represents a distinct and previously underexplored dimension of LLM reliability in clinical settings. Current LLMs fail to appropriately update predictions as patient evidence evolves, exhibiting systematic biases. While EVLU offers a partial solution, it sacrifices coverage for reliability. This work establishes the importance of evaluating LLM belief updating alongside traditional accuracy metrics for clinical applications.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly explored for clinical reasoning, but whether they appropriately revise judgments as patient evidence evolves remains unclear. We evaluated longitudinal belief updating using matched intensive-care trajectories from electronic health records. Across diverse LLMs, conditioning on a preceding judgment more often increased than reduced prediction error when estimates changed, replicated for a second endpoint. Controlled interventions revealed two failure modes. First, with preceding assessment fixed, models responded more strongly to worsening than matched improving respiratory evidence; this asymmetry persisted after headroom normalization at moderate and strong evidence levels. Second, with current evidence fixed, increasing prior risk from 10% to 90% shifted estimates by 26.2 percentage points, demonstrating causal influence of prior model beliefs. Prompting did not restore reliable updating. Evidence-Validated Longitudinal Update (EVLU) identified fewer, more reliable revisions, revealing a reliability-coverage trade-off. These findings establish longitudinal belief updating as a distinct dimension of LLM reliability.

</details>


### [177] [Decoupling Memory from Context: Structured Memory for Token-Efficient Test-Time Continual Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02687)
*Yehya Farhat,Michael Desmond,Anastasios Kyrillidis*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces GraphMemory, a graph-based memory system for LLM agents that enables efficient online context adaptation by storing, organizing, and retrieving reusable strategies through subgraph extraction, achieving 81-85% token reduction while maintaining competitive performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM context adaptation methods face critical limitations: costly trial-and-error processes, independent query processing that loses useful experience, and escalating token costs/context window limits when continually appending information to shared context. The authors seek a principled framework for memory design that maintains efficiency as the number of processed examples grows.

Method: The authors first propose a unified formulation that interprets agent memory system updates as optimization updates over the model's context. Then they introduce GraphMemory, a lightweight graph-based memory architecture that: (1) accumulates reusable strategies from interactions, (2) refines and organizes these strategies, (3) connects related strategies through graph structure, and (4) retrieves only relevant subgraphs for each query, enabling bounded retrieval that keeps retrieved memory constant regardless of processed examples.

Result: GraphMemory achieves competitive downstream performance while using approximately 81-85% fewer memory-construction tokens compared to baseline approaches. The bounded retrieval mechanism ensures retrieved memory quantity remains constant as the number of processed examples grows.

Conclusion: The unified formulation provides a principled framework for studying memory design and efficiency in LLM agents. GraphMemory demonstrates that graph-based memory systems can effectively balance performance and computational efficiency, offering a scalable solution for online context adaptation in enterprise, scientific, and medical applications where domain-specific knowledge integration is essential.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in enterprise, scientific, and medical applications, where agents must incorporate domain-specific knowledge and adapt from experience. Context engineering offers a practical alternative to weight updates by improving model behavior through instructions, strategies, and evidence supplied at inference time. However, adapting context online typically requires a costly trial-and-error process, while queries are often processed independently, preventing useful experience from carrying forward. Memory systems address this limitation by retaining information across interactions, but approaches that continually append information to a shared context face increasing token costs, context-window limits, and performance degradation as the context expands. We introduce a unified formulation of context optimization and show that an agent memory system update can be interpreted as an optimization update procedure over the model's context. This perspective attempts to provide a principled framework for studying memory design and its efficiency. We then propose GraphMemory, a lightweight graph-based memory that accumulates, refines, organizes, and connects reusable strategies. For each query, GraphMemory retrieves only the relevant subgraph, enabling online context adaptation without exposing the model to the entire memory. Under bounded retrieval, the amount of retrieved memory remains constant as the number of processed examples grows. Experiments show that GraphMemory achieves competitive downstream performance while using approximately 81-85% fewer memory-construction tokens than our baselines.

</details>


### [178] [Learning to Revise Reasoning with Segment-wise On-Policy Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02703)
*Yuxiang Zhang,Ding Cao,Shuting Cui,Lei Wang,Weijieying Ren,Tianxiang Zhao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Seg-OPD introduces segment-wise on-policy distillation to improve LLM reasoning by learning to revise intermediate reasoning steps. It selects uncertain student segments, obtains teacher redrafts, and trains the student to prefer teacher redrafts over original segments while retaining token-wise OPD. This achieves 5.22% average relative improvement in reasoning accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: On-policy distillation (OPD) has two key limitations: (1) token-wise OPD doesn't provide explicit coherent alternative reasoning steps for revision, and (2) when students produce degenerate reasoning prefixes, teacher supervision conditioned on that prefix may reinforce poor reasoning patterns. The work aims to address learning reasoning revision to rework intermediate reasoning steps.

Method: Segment-wise On-Policy Distillation (Seg-OPD) combines: (1) uncertainty-based segment selection to identify student segments needing revision, (2) obtaining corresponding teacher redrafts for those segments, (3) training the student to prefer teacher redrafts over paired student segments, while retaining dense token-wise OPD supervision. Experiments on mathematical reasoning and competitive programming tasks.

Result: Seg-OPD-trained students achieve higher revision success rates than baselines. Consistent outperformance over state-of-the-art baselines with an average relative improvement of 5.22% in reasoning accuracy across diverse models and tasks.

Conclusion: Segment-wise supervision that explicitly teaches revision through teacher redrafts is more effective than token-only approaches. This represents a promising direction for improving LLM reasoning through learned reasoning revision.

Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) improves large language model reasoning by training students on their own rollouts with dense token-wise supervision from the teacher. However, token-wise OPD does not explicitly provide a coherent alternative reasoning step showing how the student's step could be revised to improve subsequent reasoning. Furthermore, this paradigm can become less effective when the student produces a degenerate reasoning prefix, as subsequent teacher supervision remains conditioned on that prefix and may reinforce poor reasoning patterns. In this work, we focus on learning reasoning revision with segment-wise OPD to rework intermediate reasoning steps and better support subsequent reasoning. Through controlled reasoning interventions, we find that replacing student segments with teacher redrafts improves subsequent reasoning accuracy. Therefore, we address the problem of turning teacher redrafts into explicit supervision for learning to revise reasoning. We propose Segment-wise On-Policy Distillation (Seg-OPD), which selects student segments based on an uncertainty metric and obtains corresponding teacher redrafts. Seg-OPD trains the student to prefer teacher redrafts over their paired student segments while retaining dense token-wise OPD supervision. Extensive experiments on mathematical reasoning and competitive programming tasks show that Seg-OPD-trained students achieve higher revision success rates than baselines. Seg-OPD consistently outperforms the compared state-of-the-art baselines in reasoning accuracy with an average relative improvement of 5.22% across diverse models and tasks. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Seg-OPD.

</details>


### [179] [Label-Efficient Time Series Classification at Scale: A Dual-Stream OSSE-LSTM with Counterfactual Attribution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02704)
*Nguyen Ho,Bach Tung Tran,Trung Ky Nguyen,Zhenchang Xia,Bolong Zheng,Long Van Ho*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses the label efficiency problem in time series classification, proposing Dual-Stream OSSE-LSTM that combines Omni-Scale CNN with Squeeze-and-Excitation recalibration and Bidirectional LSTM in a prototype-based embedding framework. The method achieves remarkable consistency (96.36-96.72% accuracy) across different support sizes K, and introduces Counterfactual Integrated Gradients (C-IG) for explainability and test-time refinement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The core bottleneck in large-scale time series analytics is label scarcity rather than data volume. The authors directly address a practical question: how many labeled examples per class are needed before a classifier becomes usable? This is particularly relevant for industrial equipment, wearables, power grids, and clinical monitors where annotation requires expert knowledge and is expensive.

Method: The proposed Dual-Stream OSSE-LSTM is an episodic metric-learning framework featuring: (1) Omni-Scale CNN with Squeeze-and-Excitation recalibration for automatic multi-scale motif extraction without per-dataset kernel tuning; (2) Bidirectional LSTM for capturing global temporal context; (3) Independent normalization and fusion of both streams into a prototype-oriented embedding. Additionally, Counterfactual Integrated Gradients (C-IG) is introduced for explainability by attributing prototype margin between target and opposing classes, and can be reused as soft masks for test-time prototype refinement without updating the encoder.

Result: On 19 univariate UCR datasets, OSSE-LSTM achieves the highest average accuracy and per-dataset win count at every support size K. Its accuracy remains remarkably stable within a 0.36-point band (96.36-96.72%) across the tested range. Notably, even its weakest configuration (93.99%) exceeds the best result achieved by any compared baseline at any K value.

Conclusion: The proposed OSSE-LSTM framework demonstrates exceptional label efficiency and consistency in time series classification. The combination of multi-scale feature extraction with global temporal context, coupled with prototype-based embedding, enables robust performance even with very limited labeled data. The introduction of C-IG provides both explainability and a mechanism for test-time refinement, making the approach practically valuable for real-world applications where labeled data is scarce.

Abstract: Time series are produced continuously at enormous scale by industrial equipment, wearables, power grids, and clinical monitors, yet annotation remains manual, expensive, and expert-dependent. The binding constraint in large-scale time series analytics is therefore not data volume but label volume, and the question facing a practitioner is concrete: how many examples per class must be labeled before a classifier becomes usable? We study this question directly, in a regime where the label space is fixed and known in advance and the decision rule must be constructed from only K labeled examples per class. We propose Dual-Stream OSSE-LSTM, an episodic metric-learning framework that pairs an Omni-Scale CNN with Squeeze-and-Excitation recalibration, for multi-scale motif extraction without per-dataset kernel tuning, with a Bidirectional LSTM for global temporal context. The two streams are independently normalized and fused into a prototype-oriented embedding. Because decisions taken from a few labels must also be explainable, we introduce Counterfactual Integrated Gradients (C-IG), which attributes the prototype margin between target and opposing classes rather than an isolated classifier logit, and reuses the resulting maps as soft masks for test-time prototype refinement without updating the encoder. On 19 univariate UCR datasets, OSSE-LSTM attains the highest average accuracy and per-dataset win count at every support size, and its accuracy remains within a 0.36-point band (96.36-96.72%) across that range. Its weakest configuration still exceeding the best result any compared baseline achieves at any K (93.99%).

</details>


### [180] [Ego2World: Compiling Egocentric Cooking Videos into Executable Worlds for Belief-State Planning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02715)
*Qinchuan Cheng,Zhantao Gong,Pengzhan Sun,Angela Yao,Shijie Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Ego2World is a benchmark that converts annotated egocentric cooking videos into executable planning environments under partial observation, enabling evaluation of agents' self-chosen actions and their outcomes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Egocentric videos capture everyday human activities, but testing agents requires evaluating the consequences of actions they choose themselves. Existing benchmarks lack the ability to execute agent-proposed actions and check their outcomes in a controlled environment.

Method: The benchmark's compiler links source steps and objects to: (1) symbolic action rules, (2) persistent world states, and (3) explicit task conditions. World state and agent belief are maintained separately, enabling controlled studies of planning and information reuse across continuing tasks. Evaluation involved six planners on 105 tasks and a separate Qwen-Plus study.

Result: Testing six planners on 105 tasks revealed that accepted operations often leave task goals unmet. Execution traces and condition checks distinguish interrupted runs, partial attainment, and completed execution without goal attainment. The Qwen-Plus study showed persistent belief improves action validity by 4.15 percentage points and reduces visual-query attempts by 90.27%, with higher token use but no detected completion gain.

Conclusion: Ego2World provides a reusable testbed for tracing how planning and memory choices affect execution, observation demand, and task attainment, connecting recorded human activity to the development and evaluation of interactive agents.

Abstract: Egocentric videos capture how people carry out everyday activities, yet testing an agent requires evaluating the consequences of actions it chooses itself. We introduce Ego2World, a benchmark that turns annotated cooking activities into executable planning environments under partial observation. Its compiler links source steps and objects to symbolic action rules, persistent world states, and explicit task conditions, so researchers can execute an agent's proposed actions and check their outcomes. World state and agent belief are maintained separately, enabling controlled studies of planning and information reuse across continuing tasks. Evaluating six planners on 105 tasks shows that accepted operations often leave task goals unmet. Execution traces and condition checks distinguish interrupted runs, partial attainment, and completed execution without goal attainment. In a separate paired Qwen-Plus study, persistent belief improves action validity by 4.15 percentage points and reduces visual-query attempts by 90.27%, with higher token use and no detected completion gain. Ego2World provides a reusable testbed for tracing how planning and memory choices affect execution, observation demand, and task attainment, connecting recorded human activity to the development and evaluation of interactive agents.

</details>


### [181] [On the Chain-of-Thought Monitorability of Looped Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02741)
*Han Wang,Ishwar B Balappanawar,Huan Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether LoopLMs (language models with repeated transformer layers) affect Chain-of-Thought (CoT) monitorability. The study finds that deeper loop depth can reduce CoT monitorability in some tasks under stress tests, but looped architecture alone does not necessarily imply lower monitorability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring is a promising approach for detecting undesirable model behavior. LoopLMs repeatedly apply shared transformer layers to increase effective computational depth. However, the effect of looped architectures on CoT monitorability was previously unexplored, which is important for understanding the safety and interpretability of these architectures.

Method: The study examined two complementary settings: (1) varying loop depth within the same LoopLM family to isolate the effect of additional recurrent computation, and (2) comparing LoopLMs with non-looped language models matched by parameter size, transformer-layer count, or effective depth. Experiments were conducted across eight tasks from MonitorBench under both standard and stress-test settings.

Result: Task-dependent reductions in CoT monitorability were observed under stress tests on specific Logic/Science/Engineering Cue Answer tasks, while other tasks showed weaker or qualitatively different trends. The declines were not fully explained by task difficulty, verification pass rate, or generated token length. Qualitative examples suggested changes in how deeper-loop models explicitly use or attribute provided cues. Cross-model comparison found no evidence that LoopLMs are systematically less monitorable than non-looped models matched on size or depth.

Conclusion: Deeper loop depth can reduce CoT monitorability in some tasks under stress tests, but looped transformer architecture alone does not necessarily imply lower monitorability. The effect is task-dependent and appears to involve changes in how models process and attribute cues rather than simple difficulty increases.

Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring provides a promising approach for detecting undesirable model behavior. Looped language models (LoopLMs) repeatedly apply shared transformer layers, increasing effective computational depth and enabling additional latent computation without increasing model size. However, the effect of looped architectures on CoT monitorability remains largely unexplored. In this work, we provide the first systematic evaluation of CoT monitorability in LoopLMs. We study two complementary settings: (1) varying the loop depth within the same LoopLM family to isolate the effect of additional recurrent computation, and (2) comparing LoopLMs with non-looped language models matched by parameter size, transformer-layer count, or effective depth to study whether LoopLMs are less monitorable. Across eight tasks from MonitorBench and both standard and stress-test settings, we observe task-dependent reductions in CoT monitorability under stress tests on specific Logic/Science/Engineering \texttt{Cue Answer} tasks, while other tasks exhibit weaker or qualitatively different trends. Our diagnosis suggests that these declines are not fully explained by task difficulty, verification pass rate, or generated token length; qualitative examples further suggest changes in how deeper-loop models explicitly use or attribute provided cues. Our cross-model comparison finds no evidence that LoopLMs are systematically less monitorable than non-looped language models matched on size or depth. Overall, our results suggest that deeper loop depth can reduce CoT monitorability in some tasks under stress tests, but looped transformer architecture alone does not necessarily imply lower monitorability.

</details>


### [182] [Dynamic LLM Routers are Often Misguided](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02762)
*Sam Wang,Julia White,Sahibzada Allahyar,Dhruv Atreja,Urchade Zaratiana,Kelton Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Dynamic LLM routers, designed to route queries to the cheapest capable model, fail to outperform simple random selection between two well-chosen models across 14 settings and 8 task categories. Four patterns (difficulty blindness, length reversal, semantic matching, roster suboptimality) explain this gap.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To evaluate whether commercial LLM routers effectively reduce inference costs by intelligently routing queries to appropriate models, given the promise of cost savings through model selection.

Method: Analyzed six commercial routers across 14 settings on a diverse benchmark spanning eight task categories, tracing performance gaps to specific routing patterns and testing a simple two-model router as proof of concept.

Result: None of the six commercial routers outperformed random selection between two well-chosen models at matched cost. Some underperformed by over 10 percentage points. The four problematic patterns identified are: difficulty blindness, length reversal, semantic matching, and roster suboptimality. A simple two-model router avoiding these patterns showed limited gains over random routing.

Conclusion: The standard evaluation objective rewards patterns that don't translate to practical routing gains. A well-chosen roster leaves little room for improvement through routing, suggesting that complex router architectures may be unnecessary when model selection is already optimized.

Abstract: Dynamic LLM routers promise to cut inference costs by sending each query to the cheapest model that can answer it correctly. We analyze six commercial routers across 14 settings on a diverse benchmark spanning eight task categories, finding that none of them outperforms a router that randomly selects between two well-chosen models at matched cost. Some underperform by more than 10 percentage points. We trace this gap to four patterns prevalent across routers: difficulty blindness, length reversal, semantic matching, and roster suboptimality. We show that the first three are what the standard objective rewards: cost-accuracy Pareto efficiency on realized costs favors escalating moderately hard queries over the hardest ones, shorter queries over longer ones, and routing by a query's source over its difficulty. We also argue that the two assumptions that would justify large rosters, model granularity and model specialization, do not hold empirically. We propose an alternative evaluation methodology that does not reward these patterns, and as a proof of concept, we design a simple two-model router that avoids all four. Nevertheless, its gain over random routing is limited, because a well-chosen roster leaves little to route.

</details>


### [183] [Law And Order: Tax Law Autoformalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02792)
*Sophia Simeng Han,Yoshiki Takashima,Anjiang Wei,Zhaoyu Li,Michael Genesereth*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Law&Order is a neuro-symbolic framework that automatically formalizes tax forms and instructions into executable symbolic programs, combining LLM synthesis with cell-level verification and iterative error repair to achieve 100% accuracy on 51 held-out tax returns, significantly outperforming LLM-only approaches (66% accuracy).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Legal systems are increasingly implemented through software, yet scalable methods for translating legal texts (particularly tax forms and filing instructions) into accurate symbolic representations remain underdeveloped. Tax law involves complex computational structures including arithmetic, branching, recursion, and tabular reasoning.

Method: The framework establishes two forms of correspondence: (1) structural correspondence - aligning legal and symbolic components (cells, schedules); (2) denotational correspondence - ensuring symbolic components implement computations specified by legal counterparts. The approach combines large language model synthesis with cell-level verification and iterative localized error repair using human-written OpenTaxSolver tax returns. Evaluation uses independently authored, held-out TaxCalcBench returns never exposed during generation or repair.

Result: While the most advanced LLM alone achieves only 66% accuracy, Law&Order achieves 100% cell-level and form-level accuracy on 51 held-out returns from TaxCalcBench.

Conclusion: Combining LLM-based synthesis with symbolic verification is effective for scalable and verifiable large-scale legal autoformalization, significantly outperforming using an LLM alone.

Abstract: Legal systems are increasingly implemented through software, yet scalable methods for translating legal texts into accurate symbolic representations remain underdeveloped. We study this problem through tax law, where forms and filing instructions define large computational structures involving arithmetic, branching, recursion, and tabular reasoning. We propose Law&Order, a neuro-symbolic framework for automatically formalizing tax forms and instructions into executable symbolic programs. Our approach establishes two forms of correspondence between law and logic: structural correspondence, which aligns legal and symbolic components such as cells and schedules, and denotational correspondence, which requires symbolic components to implement the computations specified by their legal counterparts. We combine large language model synthesis with cell-level verification and iterative localized error repair using human-written OpenTaxSolver tax returns. We then evaluate the resulting formalizations on independently authored, held-out TaxCalcBench returns, that are never exposed during generation or repair. Although the most advanced LLM achieves only 66% accuracy, Law&Order achieves 100% cell-level and form-level accuracy on 51 held-out returns, demonstrating the effectiveness of combining LLM-based synthesis with symbolic verification for scalable and verifiable large-scale legal autoformalization compared with using an LLM alone.

</details>


### [184] [PAPER2LLM++: Continual Self-Evolution of LLMs from Research Papers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02793)
*Hongji Pu,Yilun Zhao,Wenpeng Yin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PAPER2LLM++ is a framework enabling LLMs to continually learn from research papers about their own limitations, using a try-evaluate-commit procedure to integrate improvements without causing catastrophic forgetting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM limitations discovered through human research remain disconnected from model evolution - models don't automatically learn from new findings about their own failures. There was a need for a system that closes the loop between human discovery and model evolution.

Method: For each incoming research paper: (1) Extract evidence-grounded findings, (2) Test whether the reported limitation persists in the current model, (3) Convert findings into candidate learning signals when needed, (4) Use a try-evaluate-commit procedure that integrates updates only when they improve targeted behavior without substantially forgetting prior improvements or degrading general capabilities.

Result: Across a sequential stream of research-discovered LLM failures, models can progressively incorporate new findings while retaining earlier gains.

Conclusion: PAPER2LLM++ takes a step toward closing the loop between human discovery and model evolution, enabling models to continually learn from research about their own limitations and improvements.

Abstract: Research on LLMs continually uncovers model limitations, their causes, and potential solutions. Yet these human discoveries remain largely disconnected from model evolution: an LLM does not automatically learn from new research about its own failures. We introduce PAPER2LLM++, a framework for continual self-evolution of LLMs from research papers.
