Rather than treating papers merely as knowledge to retrieve, PAPER2LLM++ uses the growing literature as a stream of evidence and supervision for model improvement. For each incoming paper, it extracts evidence-grounded findings, tests whether the reported limitation persists in the current model, and, when needed, converts the findings into candidate learning signals. A try-evaluate-commit procedure integrates an update only when it improves the targeted behavior without substantially forgetting prior improvements or degrading general capabilities. Across a sequential stream of research-discovered LLM failures, we show that models can progressively incorporate new findings while retaining earlier gains. PAPER2LLM++ thus takes a step toward closing the loop between human discovery and model evolution, enabling models to continually learn from research about their own limitations and improvements.

</details>


### [185] [Modeling Shared and Individual Structure for Cross-Subject Continuous Affect Regression from EEG-fNIRS](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02796)
*Xuan Wang,Bing Wang,Shuai Chang,Hao Yuan,Xinbo Qi,Xinyue Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses zero-shot cross-subject emotion prediction (valence-arousal) from EEG-fNIRS data without any labeled data from test subjects. The approach uses a shared stimulus-driven trajectory combined with a per-subject calibration via alpha-band cross-channel synchrony, achieving MAE of ~23-26 vs. baselines of 55-60.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current affect estimation from physiological signals typically requires subject-dependent training with labeled data. This paper tackles the harder zero-shot cross-subject scenario where the model must predict emotions for entirely new subjects without any training labels from them, using only unlabeled EEG/fNIRS recordings from the same video stimuli.

Method: The method decomposes the affect trajectory into two components: (1) a shared structure across subjects watching identical stimuli, and (2) an individual per-subject structure estimated from a label-free EEG marker (alpha-band cross-channel synchrony). This marker rescales the shared trajectory around the scale midpoint. Validation includes leave-one-subject-out correlation analysis, functional-form comparisons, component ablation studies, and ceiling analysis.

Result: The model achieves MAE of 25.96/22.80 across two evaluation batches (valence: 21.94/19.6, arousal: 29.98/26.0), substantially outperforming EEGNet and ASAC-Net baselines (60.6 and 55.0). A systematic negative-result search found no signal able to improve on the single alpha-synchrony marker.

Conclusion: Alpha-band cross-channel synchrony serves as an effective label-free proxy for per-subject calibration in zero-shot affect prediction. The simple shared-trajectory + individual scaling approach outperforms complex neural architectures, suggesting that subject-specific physiological responses are primarily about gain/scale differences rather than temporal pattern differences.

Abstract: Continuous, second-by-second valence-arousal estimation from physiological signals is typically studied in a subject-dependent setting, where the model sees labeled data from the same person it is later evaluated on. We study the harder zero-shot cross-subject variant on a synchronized EEG-fNIRS dataset: predict raw-scale ([1, 255]) valence and arousal trajectories for subjects whose labels the model never observes, given only their unlabeled EEG/fNIRS recordings while watching the same video stimuli as a disjoint set of training subjects. We decompose the affect trajectory into a structure shared across subjects who watch the same stimuli and an individual structure estimated for each test subject from a label-free EEG marker (alpha-band cross-channel synchrony), which rescales the shared trajectory around the scale midpoint. We validate the per-subject calibration mechanism on four independent axes: leave-one-subject-out correlation between the marker and each subject's true optimal gain, a functional-form comparison against non-linear alternatives, a repeated leave-4-out component ablation isolating each part of the pipeline's contribution, and a ceiling analysis bounding the remaining headroom for per-subject scaling. On held-out subjects, the model reaches an overall MAE of 25.96 / 22.80 across two evaluation batches (valence 21.94 / 19.6, arousal 29.98 / 26.0), well below EEGNet and ASAC-Net baselines reported for the same subject-independent split (raw scale score 60.6 and 55.0 respectively). We further report a systematic negative-result search across model architectures, feature representations, and prediction targets that found no signal able to improve on the single alpha-synchrony marker.

</details>


### [186] [BitNest: Bit-Nested Speculative Decoding for Memory-Efficient LLM Inference Acceleration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02800)
*Chence Yang,Ningxi Cheng,Arash Akbari,Qitao Tan,Qingchan Zhu,Ci Zhang,Changdi Yang,Yanzhi Wang,Wei Niu,Jinhui Wang,Jin Lu,Geng Yuan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: BitNest is a bit-nested speculative decoding framework that embeds a low-precision draft model directly into a higher-precision target model by constructing a strong low-precision base and recovering the target through residual refinement. This approach enables both models to share a single physical weight representation, reducing memory overhead. It also extends to KV cache for long-context inference. Across 7B-8B edge-friendly LLMs, BitNest achieves 95.2% speculative acceptance rate and 1.48-1.61x speedup over FP16 autoregressive decoding.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing speculative decoding methods require additional draft models or weight representations, causing memory overhead on resource-constrained devices. Self-speculative approaches reduce this but still face trade-offs between draft quality, target quality, and storage efficiency. There is a need for a method that achieves high efficiency without additional memory costs.

Method: BitNest constructs a strong low-precision base and recovers the higher-precision target through residual refinement, enabling both models to share a single physical weight representation. This "bit-nested" design embeds the low-precision draft directly into the higher-precision target. The approach is extended to the KV cache for long-context inference.

Result: BitNest achieves an average speculative acceptance rate of 95.2% while preserving higher-precision model quality. It delivers 1.48-1.61x end-to-end speedup over FP16 autoregressive decoding. On LLaMA models, it achieves consistently competitive or higher decoding speedup compared to all representative self-speculative baselines.

Conclusion: BitNest successfully addresses the trade-off between draft quality, target quality, and storage efficiency by sharing a single weight representation. It achieves high speculative acceptance rates (95.2%) and significant speedups (1.48-1.61x) while maintaining model quality, making it particularly suitable for resource-constrained edge devices.

Abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive generation by using a lightweight draft to propose multiple tokens for parallel verification. However, existing methods often require an additional draft model or weight representation, introducing non-negligible memory overhead on resource-constrained devices. Self-speculative approaches reduce this overhead, yet still face trade-offs between draft quality, target quality, and storage efficiency. We propose BitNest, a bit-nested speculative decoding framework that embeds a low-precision draft directly into the higher-precision target representation. Instead of deriving a draft from a predefined target, BitNest first constructs a strong low-precision base and then recovers the higher-precision target through residual refinement, enabling both models to share a single physical weight representation. BitNest further extends this progressive-precision design to the KV cache for long-context inference. Across multiple 7B--8B edge-friendly LLMs and diverse workloads, BitNest achieves an average speculative acceptance rate of 95.2% while closely preserving higher-precision model quality, and delivers 1.48--1.61x end-to-end speedup over FP16 autoregressive decoding. On the LLaMA models supported by all representative self-speculative baselines, BitNest also achieves consistently competitive or higher decoding speedup.

</details>


### [187] [VIGOR: Zero-Shot Visual Generalization via Latent-Space Consistency in Model-Based Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02801)
*Mingyu Park,Samyeul Noh,Hyun Myung,Donghwan Lee*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: VIGOR enables zero-shot generalization to unseen visual distractions in model-based RL by maintaining latent-space consistency. It combines asymmetric augmentation, dynamics-level consistency, and encoder stabilization to prevent error compounding through latent rollouts, outperforming baselines by 3.4% on DMC and 43.6% on Robosuite.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Model-based RL suffers from two-level vulnerability under visual distractions: encoder errors first push outputs out of distribution, then compound through recursive latent rollouts over the planning horizon. This degrades performance significantly under unseen backgrounds, lighting changes, or camera shifts.

Method: VIGOR integrates three components: (i) asymmetric weak-to-strong augmentation pairing weak-only and weak-to-strong latent views within a batch; (ii) dynamics-level consistency enforcing augmentation-invariant transition predictions via direct latent regression; (iii) encoder-level stabilization preventing encoder drift under cross-augmentation supervision.

Result: VIGOR outperforms state-of-the-art model-free and model-based baselines, achieving 3.4% improvement on DeepMind Control Suite and 43.6% on Robosuite. Ablations confirm robustness is augmentation-agnostic—latent-space consistency, not augmentation choice, drives robustness.

Conclusion: VIGOR successfully achieves zero-shot generalization to unseen visual distractions while retaining MBRL's sample efficiency. The framework's robustness stems from latent-space consistency rather than specific augmentation choices, making it broadly applicable across different perturbation families.

Abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) achieves strong sample efficiency by planning within learned latent dynamics, yet its performance degrades substantially under unseen visual distractions such as background variations, lighting changes, or camera shifts. Unlike model-free RL, where encoder perturbations affect only single-step predictions, MBRL suffers from a two-level vulnerability: visual distractions first push encoder outputs out of distribution, and these errors then compound through recursive latent rollouts over the planning horizon. We propose visual generalization via latent-space consistency in model-based RL (VIGOR), a framework that enables zero-shot generalization to unseen visual distractions while retaining the sample efficiency of its MBRL backbone. VIGOR integrates three interdependent components: (i) asymmetric weak-to-strong augmentation, which pairs weak-only and weak-to-strong latent views within a single batch; (ii) dynamics-level consistency, which enforces augmentation-invariant transition predictions through direct latent regression; and (iii) encoder-level stabilization, which prevents encoder drift under the cross-augmentation supervision imposed by dynamics-level consistency. Evaluations on the DeepMind Control Suite (DMC) and Robosuite show that VIGOR outperforms state-of-the-art model-free and model-based baselines, surpassing the second-best baseline by 3.4% on DMC and 43.6% on Robosuite. Ablations further show that VIGOR's robustness is augmentation-agnostic: replacing the default augmentation with alternatives from distinct perturbation families preserves strong generalization, confirming that latent-space consistency, not the augmentation choice, drives robustness.

</details>


### [188] [ROUTEAUDIT: Interaction-Aware Identification for Budgeted Multi-Verifier Routing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02808)
*Miaobo Hu,Shuhao Hu,Xiaobo Guo,Xin Wang,Bokun Wang,Tianshu Fu,Daren Zha,Jun Xiao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces ROUTEAUDIT, a framework for comparing adaptive multi-verifier systems under a contract-conditioned identification problem. It addresses challenges in comparing verifiers when system parameters (catalog, availability, accounting, filtration, scorer) vary with policy. The method adds three measurable objects to the contract: a contract lattice for coordinate increment attribution with path sensitivity, a policy-independent response tape for identifying paired sequential contrasts, and request-level bounds for incomplete matching. Results show quality improvements of 0.1797 and 0.1250 over static baselines on tail caches, and +0.0068 improvement for RLVR over static on 1,319 task requests with tight confidence intervals.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to address a fundamental limitation in comparing adaptive multi-verifier systems: the standard metric (endpoint quality-cost gap) fails when underlying system parameters change with the policy. Existing comparisons are unfair because they don't account for variations in verifier catalog, availability, accounting, information filtration, or scorer across different policies.

Method: The paper formulates verifier routing as a contract-conditioned identification problem. The contract records: request support, verifier catalog, realized availability, resource accounting, online filtration, and post-trace scoring. ROUTEAUDIT adds three measurable objects: (1) A contract lattice that averages coordinate increments over admissible bridge orders and reports attribution with path sensitivity; (2) A policy-independent response tape identifying paired sequential contrasts under adaptive policies; (3) Request-level bounds using potential outcomes for incomplete matching with sharp finite-population intervals. The protocol commits paid observations and ledger events before oracle join and returns attribution certificates.

Result: On two held-out raw-tail caches: matched static SF+SA equals the cascade, with apparent gains of 0.1797 and 0.1250 over full static attributed to verifier-set edge. On 1,319 held-out task requests: learned and RLVR studies report quality 0.9522 and 0.9553 versus 0.9484 for matched static; RLVR-static paired difference is +0.0068 with request-paired interval [0.0015, 0.0122] and hierarchical interval [0.0006, 0.0131]. Controlled attribution recovery yields route MAE 0.0011 and endpoint reconstruction error 0.0004. Factorial, bridge-order, and stochastic-provider studies evaluate the certificate interface.

Conclusion: The paper presents a rigorous framework (ROUTEAUDIT) for fair comparison of adaptive multi-verifier systems under changing system parameters. The method provides attribution certificates that enable policy-independent evaluation, with empirical validation showing meaningful quality improvements (+0.0068) that are statistically significant across multiple hierarchical levels. The controlled attribution recovery demonstrates high accuracy (MAE 0.0011), suggesting the framework successfully addresses the identification problem in verifier routing.

Abstract: Adaptive multi-verifier systems are commonly compared through endpoint quality-cost gaps, even when the verifier catalog, availability, accounting, information filtration, or scorer changes with the policy. We formulate verifier routing as a contract-conditioned identification problem. The contract records request support, verifier catalog, realized availability, resource accounting, online filtration, and post-trace scoring; a matched route contrast changes only the policy coordinate. ROUTEAUDIT adds three measurable objects to this contract. A contract lattice averages coordinate increments over every admissible bridge order and reports the resulting attribution together with its path sensitivity. A policy-independent response tape identifies paired sequential contrasts when adaptive policies reveal different observations. For incomplete matching, request-level bounds use whichever potential outcome remains observed and give a sharp finite-population interval. The protocol commits paid observations and ledger events before the oracle join and returns an attribution certificate for each comparison. On two held-out raw-tail caches, matched static SF+SA equals the cascade, assigning the apparent gains of 0.1797 and 0.1250 over full static to the verifier-set edge. On 1,319 held-out task requests, the learned and RLVR studies report quality 0.9522 and 0.9553 versus 0.9484 for matched static; the RLVR-static paired difference is +0.0068 with a request-paired interval $[0.0015,0.0122]$ and a training-seed-by-request hierarchical interval $[0.0006,0.0131]$. Controlled attribution recovery yields route mean absolute error 0.0011 and endpoint reconstruction error 0.0004. Factorial, bridge-order, and stochastic-provider studies evaluate the certificate interface; RLVR supplies a learned-policy stress test under the same identification contract.

</details>


### [189] [iS-KV: Online Low-Rank KV Cache Compression via Block-Incremental SVD](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02815)
*Yiren Zhao,Guanghui Song,Tianrui Qin,Kejiang Ye,Cheng-zhong Xu,Xitong Gao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: iS-KV is an online low-rank KV-cache compression method for long-horizon reasoning that maintains a recent window exact while incrementally folding older states into bounded-rank representations, synchronizing historical coordinates with the updated basis to prevent representation drift.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long chain-of-thought reasoning substantially increases KV-cache memory during autoregressive decoding. Existing token eviction methods irreversibly delete historical states that may be needed later, while SVD-based low-rank compression faces challenges when extending from fixed prompt cache to online decoding due to basis drift.

Method: iS-KV keeps a recent window exact while incrementally folding older states into bounded-rank representations. As the low-rank basis evolves, it synchronizes historical coordinates with the updated basis to maintain representation consistency.

Result: On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, iS-KV achieves 82.6% accuracy at 4.06-fold persistent-KV compression, close to the original model's 83.6%. On Qwen3-8B, it achieves 89.2% accuracy at 5.64-fold compression. Under matched memory budgets, iS-KV consistently outperforms token-eviction baselines.

Conclusion: iS-KV provides an effective online low-rank KV-cache compression solution that maintains representation consistency while achieving significant compression ratios, outperforming token-eviction approaches under matched memory budgets.

Abstract: Long chain-of-thought reasoning substantially increases KV-cache memory during autoregressive decoding, as every generated token introduces new key and value states and causes the cache to grow linearly with decoding length. Existing KV-cache compression methods typically control this growth through token eviction, but irreversible deletion can remove historical states that later reasoning may need to revisit. SVD-based low-rank compression provides an alternative by retaining all positions with a more compact representation. However, extending it from a fixed prompt cache to online decoding is non-trivial. Through our investigation, we find that if the basis is updated for new tokens while old tokens keep their coordinates in the old basis, the stored history drifts substantially. Based on this observation, we propose iS-KV, an online low-rank KV-cache compression method for long-horizon reasoning. iS-KV keeps a recent window exact while incrementally folding older states into bounded-rank representations. As the low-rank basis evolves, it synchronizes historical coordinates with the updated basis to maintain representation consistency. On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, iS-KV achieves 82.6% accuracy at 4.06-fold persistent-KV compression, close to the original model's 83.6%. On Qwen3-8B, it achieves 89.2% accuracy at 5.64-fold compression. Under matched memory budgets, iS-KV consistently outperforms token-eviction baselines.

</details>


### [190] [MetaRubric: Learning to Reward for Rubric-Based Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02824)
*Yuxuan Fan,Jaehong Yoon*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MetaRubric addresses Vacuous Credit problem in rubric-based reinforcement learning where judges assign high scores without required information. It alternates evidence-aware policy optimization with response-guided rubric adaptation using counterfactual prompts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Rubric-based RL extends reward-driven optimization to open-ended tasks but suffers from Vacuous Credit - judges assign high criterion scores even when required information is absent from responses, which can reverse the sign of GRPO advantage.

Method: MetaRubric uses three key mechanisms: (1) Construct counterfactual counterparts by changing one task-relevant fact in each prompt; (2) During policy optimization, assign credit only when response contains sufficient evidence to satisfy rubric criteria; (3) After each policy-optimization stage, use current policy responses to revise original and counterfactual criteria while preserving meaning, and adapt criterion weights at stage boundaries to address observed policy errors.

Result: MetaRubric improves PubMedQA accuracy by 6.00-20.40 percentage points over static-judge GRPO across multiple backbones, with further gains on HealthBench-Hard and two multimodal medical benchmarks.

Conclusion: MetaRubric successfully addresses the Vacuous Credit problem through evidence-aware credit assignment and dynamic rubric adaptation, significantly improving performance on medical QA benchmarks.

Abstract: Rubric-based reinforcement learning extends reward-driven optimization to open-ended tasks by assigning partial credit to individual response requirements. However, rubric judges can assign a high criterion score even when the information or action it requires is absent from the response, a failure mode we term Vacuous Credit. Such awards persist after the required information is removed and can reverse the sign of a response's GRPO advantage. To address this problem, we introduce MetaRubric, which alternates evidence-aware policy optimization with response-guided rubric adaptation. We construct counterfactual counterparts by changing one task-relevant fact in each prompt. During policy optimization, credit is assigned only when the response contains sufficient evidence to satisfy the required rubric criterion. After each policy-optimization stage, current policy responses guide revisions to original and counterfactual criteria while preserving the meaning of the original prompt's initial rubric as interpreted under each prompt's facts. We also adapt criterion weights at stage boundaries to better address observed policy errors. Across multiple backbones, MetaRubric improves PubMedQA accuracy by 6.00--20.40 percentage points over static-judge GRPO, with further gains on HealthBench-Hard and two multimodal medical benchmarks.

</details>


### [191] [Scaling Trajectories for Complex Tasks through Recursive Self-Rewrite](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02826)
*Zongxia Li,Yucheng Shi,Zhongzhi Li,Junyao Yang,Ruhan Wang,Chengsong Huang,Fuxiao Liu,Haitao Mi,Jordan Boyd-Graber,LeoweiLiang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RSR (Recursive Self-Rewrite) is a framework that uses a single base model to discover successful solutions under diverse specialized harnesses, then reconstructs them as training trajectories under a general harness. This addresses the distribution gap between specialized testing environments and deployment settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Specialized harnesses provide valuable supervision for difficult tasks but introduce interventions unavailable during deployment. This creates a distribution gap - successful trajectories under specialized harnesses may not transfer to general deployment settings.

Method: RSR uses three key components: (1) Planner - extracts successful procedures into runbooks; (2) Critic - screens for verifier and solution leakage, guides recursive revision; (3) Executor - follows qualified runbooks in fresh sandboxes. The framework discovers solutions under diverse harnesses and reconstructs them under a general harness.

Result: Across ~3K tasks, three harnesses jointly solve 759 tasks (34.3% more than strongest individual). RSR expands 2,001 source trajectories into 11,094 rewritten trajectories. Training on these trajectories shows significant improvements: Terminal-Bench 2 pass@3: 57.0%→74.2%; Terminal-Bench 4: 1.5%→9.1%; Terminal-Bench Hard: 39.0%→63.0%; Software Terminal-Bench: 3.0%→6.0%; Long-Horizon process reward: 0.21→0.29.

Conclusion: Diverse harness-assisted experiences can be effectively reconstructed into reusable capabilities for models operating under general harnesses, addressing the distribution gap between specialized testing and deployment settings.

Abstract: Successful trajectories on difficult tasks provide valuable supervision for model improvement, but specialized harnesses introduce interventions that may be unavailable during deployment. We propose Recursive Self-Rewrite (RSR), a framework that uses one base model, Qwen-3.8-27B, to discover successful solutions under diverse harnesses and reconstruct them as training trajectories under a general harness. A planner extracts procedures into runbooks, a critic screens for verifier and solution leakage and guides recursive revision, and an executor follows qualified runbooks in fresh sandboxes. Across approximately 3K self-curated terminal tasks, three harnesses jointly solve 759 tasks, 34.3% more than the strongest individual harness in the recorded pool. RSR expands 2,001 successful source trajectories into 11,094 rewritten trajectories for supervised finetuning. Training on these trajectories outperforms both the base model and direct trajectory SFT. Compared with the base model, pass@3 increases from 57.0% to 74.2% on Terminal-Bench 2, from 1.5% to 9.1% on Terminal-Bench 4, from 39.0% to 63.0% on our self-curated Terminal-Bench Hard, and from 3.0% to 6.0% on our Software Terminal-Bench. Process reward on Long-Horizon Terminal-Bench rises from 0.21 to 0.29. These results show how diverse harness-assisted experiences can be reconstructed into reusable capabilities for a model operating under a general harness.

</details>


### [192] [MLCommons Jailbreak Benchmark v1.0](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02827)
*Carsten Maple,Cagatay Yucel,Isaac Holeman,Chris Knotz,Peter Mattson,James Goel,Jonathan Petit,Sean McGregor,James Ezick,Abhishek Kumar,Alicia Parrish,Murali Emani,Kashyap Iyer,Faiza Khan Khattak,Washington Mbonu,Daniel Machlab,Eileen Long,Shaona Ghosh,Jibin Varghese,Roman Lutz,Andrew Gruen,Bennett Hillenbrand,Prabal Gupta,Mohammed Serrhini,Dhivya Nagasubramanian,Aakash Gupta,Jun,Lu,Kurt Bollacker,Chang Liu,Jonathan Petit,Cong Chen,Jean-Philippe Monteuuis,Brent Miller,Apurv Verma,Roman Eng,Armstrong Foundjem,Mohammed Serrhini*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The MLCommons Jailbreak Benchmark v1.0 is a comprehensive framework for evaluating AI systems' robustness against jailbreak attacks—prompt injections designed to bypass safety safeguards. The benchmark evaluates 8 open-weight systems using 264 prompts across 11 hazard categories, measuring safety performance degradation under adversarial conditions through the "Resilience Gap" metric.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern AI systems have safety safeguards that refuse hazardous requests, but jailbreak attacks can bypass these protections. There was a need for a standardized, reproducible methodology to evaluate and compare AI systems' robustness to such attacks across different hazard categories and attack types.

Method: The benchmark uses a methodology involving: (1) criteria-driven system and attack selection, (2) paired baseline and adversarial evaluation, (3) human annotation, (4) automated evaluator calibration, (5) scoring and grading, and (6) risk-calibrated disclosure. It evaluates 8 open-weight systems using 264 seed prompts across 11 hazard categories with attacks from the MLCommons Jailbreak Taxonomy. Responses are assessed using the AILuminate Assessment Standard v1.4.

Result: The unsafe-response rate increased from 11.08% (baseline) to 18.65% (jailbreak conditions), producing an average Resilience Gap of 7.57%. Accessible systems showed larger resilience gaps. Attack effectiveness varied substantially across attack categories and hazards. The study also examined evaluator reliability and sources of measurement error.

Conclusion: The benchmark establishes a reproducible methodological foundation for comparative jailbreak evaluation. It provides a standardized framework that can be expanded across systems, attacks, hazards, and evaluation methods. The findings highlight the vulnerability of AI systems to jailbreak attacks and the need for improved safety measures, particularly in accessible systems.

Abstract: Modern AI systems are designed to refuse hazardous requests. A jailbreak is a prompt crafted to bypass those safeguards and elicit outputs that the system would normally refuse to provide. The MLCommons Jailbreak Benchmark v1.0 provides an end-to-end methodology for evaluating the robustness of large language models to single-turn, text-based jailbreak attacks. It combines criteria-driven system and attack selection, paired baseline and adversarial evaluation, human annotation, automated evaluator calibration, scoring, grading, and risk-calibrated disclosure within a single benchmarking pipeline. The benchmark evaluates eight open-weight systems using 264 seed prompts spanning eleven hazard categories and representative attacks drawn from the MLCommons Jailbreak Taxonomy. Responses are assessed using the AILuminate Assessment Standard v1.4, and robustness is measured through the Resilience Gap: the change in safety performance between baseline and adversarial conditions. Across all evaluated systems and attacks, the unsafe-response rate increased from 11.08% under baseline conditions to 18.65% under jailbreak conditions, producing an average Resilience Gap of 7.57%. Accessible systems showed a larger mean gap, while attack effectiveness varied substantially across attack categories and hazards. The benchmark also examines evaluator reliability and sources of measurement error. Beyond reporting results, Jailbreak Benchmark v1.0 establishes a reproducible methodological foundation for comparative jailbreak evaluation and for future expansion across systems, attacks, hazards, and evaluation methods.

</details>


### [193] [FSPO: Policy-Consistent Risk and Pareto-Feasible Control for Budgeted LLM RL Post-Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02828)
*Miaobo Hu,Shuhao Hu,Xiaobo Guo,Xin Wang,Bokun Wang,Daren Zha,Jun Xiao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: FSPO is a feedback-state controller for budgeted LLM reinforcement learning post-training that jointly addresses three critical issues: policy-consistent risk modeling, decision-conditioned trajectory calibration, and Pareto resource continuation certification. It achieves 66.11% held-out and 59.43% OOD accuracy, outperforming the strongest baseline PB2 by 1.64 and 2.40 percentage points respectively.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation addresses three unresolved issues in adaptive LLM RL post-training: (1) future-risk models trained from behavior trajectories may not accurately estimate risk for the deployed controller, (2) score calibration on logged state-action pairs becomes miscalibrated after selective action choice, and (3) independent per-resource minimum costs cannot certify feasible multi-resource continuation. These issues limit the reliability and effectiveness of adaptive training systems that adjust multiple training actuators (rollout temperature, group size, clipping, KL regularization, verifier allocation, update budget) online.

Method: The paper proposes three key components: (1) Policy-consistent risk-to-go model - learns a risk model whose Bellman target follows the same frozen controller used for future decisions, combined with a long-horizon utility model; (2) Decision-conditioned trajectory calibration (DCTC) - calibrates risk on cross-fitted trajectories generated by actions selected by provisional controllers; (3) Pareto resource continuation certificate (PRCC) - admits an action only when a non-dominated cumulative reservation remains feasible over the residual horizon. The method is evaluated under a matched GRPO resource envelope.

Result: FSPO achieves 66.11% held-out accuracy and 59.43% OOD accuracy, compared with 64.47% and 57.03% for PB2 (the strongest evaluated adaptive baseline). Three paired training seeds show gains of +2.42 and +3.19 percentage points over contextual bandit on held-out and OOD evaluation. Under high behavior-deployment mismatch, policy-consistent risk lowers selected-decision ECE from 0.108 to 0.053; DCTC lowers ECE from 0.039 to 0.022 at matched acceptance; PRCC eliminates false-feasible admissions on an 18-action catalog (0.197→0.000); and enabling all three components reduces trajectory failure from 0.181 to 0.083 in factorial ablation.

Conclusion: The conclusion demonstrates that FSPO successfully addresses the three coupled issues in adaptive LLM RL post-training through its joint approach. The policy-consistent risk modeling ensures accurate risk estimation for the deployed controller, DCTC maintains calibration under selective action choice, and PRCC provides rigorous multi-resource feasibility certification. The significant improvements in both held-out and OOD accuracy, along with the ablation results validating each component's contribution, establish FSPO as a substantial advancement in budgeted LLM reinforcement learning post-training systems.

Abstract: Adaptive LLM reinforcement-learning post-training changes multiple training actuators online, including rollout temperature, group size, clipping, KL regularization, verifier allocation, and update budget. Three coupled issues remain unresolved. A future-risk model trained from behavior trajectories need not estimate the risk induced by the controller that will be deployed; a score calibrated on logged state-action pairs can become miscalibrated after selective action choice; and independent per-resource minimum costs do not in general certify a feasible multi-resource continuation. We introduce FSPO, a feedback-state controller for budgeted LLM RL post-training that addresses these issues jointly. FSPO learns a policy-consistent risk-to-go model whose Bellman target follows the same frozen controller used for future decisions, together with a long-horizon utility model. Decision-conditioned trajectory calibration (DCTC) calibrates risk on cross-fitted trajectories generated by actions selected by provisional controllers. A Pareto resource continuation certificate (PRCC) admits an action only when a non-dominated cumulative reservation remains feasible over the residual horizon. Under a matched GRPO resource envelope, FSPO reaches 66.11% held-out and 59.43% OOD accuracy, compared with 64.47% and 57.03% for PB2, the strongest evaluated adaptive baseline. Three paired training seeds give gains of +2.42 and +3.19 percentage points over the contextual bandit on held-out and OOD evaluation. Under high behavior-deployment mismatch, policy-consistent risk lowers selected-decision ECE from 0.108 to 0.053; DCTC lowers it from 0.039 to 0.022 at matched acceptance; PRCC removes false-feasible admissions on an 18-action catalog ($0.197\rightarrow0.000$); and enabling all three components reduces trajectory failure from 0.181 to 0.083 in a factorial ablation.

</details>


### [194] [AMBER: Multi-View Adaptive Budget Allocation for Listwise Vision-Language Reranking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02831)
*Wenteng Chen,Jiachen Zhu,Rong Shan,Tianyi Xu,Yuxiang Chen,Congmin Zheng,Teng Wang,Junjie Wu,Weiwen Liu,Changwang Zhang,Weinan Zhang,Jun Wang,Jianghao Lin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AMBER is an online, budgeted multi-view reranking framework for vision-language models that dynamically optimizes global resource allocation by treating VLM outputs as local tournaments with continuous Elo updates, allocating computation at both candidate view and query levels.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vision-language models are powerful listwise rerankers for multimodal retrieval, but their high inference costs restrict them to evaluating small local candidate views. Existing multi-call strategies rely on fixed schedules, wasting expensive VLM calls on uninformative candidate pairs and easy queries.

Method: AMBER treats fragmented listwise VLM outputs as local tournaments using continuous Elo updates to maintain a lightweight global ranking state. It allocates computation at two levels: (1) dynamically constructing candidate views with high score ambiguity, and (2) scheduling queries to maximize expected information gain. Each Elo update corresponds to a stochastic gradient ascent step on the Bradley-Terry log-likelihood, with a submodular information-theoretic motivation for query-level allocation.

Result: Experiments on CIRR, CIRCO, and PhotoBench demonstrate that AMBER achieves the strongest overall performance among compared multi-call VLM reranking methods under comparable VLM-call budgets, while remaining effective in lower-budget settings.

Conclusion: AMBER provides an effective solution for budget-constrained VLM reranking by dynamically optimizing resource allocation across candidate views and queries, achieving superior performance across multiple benchmarks while maintaining efficiency.

Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are powerful listwise rerankers for multimodal retrieval, but high inference costs restrict them to evaluating small local candidate views. Existing multi-call strategies rely on fixed schedules, wasting expensive VLM calls on uninformative candidate pairs and easy queries. To address this, we propose Adaptive Multi-view Budgeted Elo Reranking (AMBER), an online, budgeted multi-view reranking framework that dynamically optimizes global resource allocation. AMBER treats fragmented listwise VLM outputs as local tournaments, using continuous Elo updates to maintain a lightweight global ranking state. Building on this, it allocates computation at two levels: dynamically constructing candidate views with high score ambiguity, and scheduling queries to maximize expected information gain. We show that each Elo update corresponds to a stochastic gradient ascent step on the Bradley-Terry log-likelihood, and provide a submodular information-theoretic motivation for the query-level allocation strategy. Experiments on CIRR, CIRCO, and PhotoBench demonstrate that AMBER achieves the strongest overall performance among the compared multi-call VLM reranking methods under comparable VLM-call budgets, while remaining effective in lower-budget settings. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/wnlfc/AMBER.

</details>


### [195] [DNAlign: Dynamic Null-Space Safe Alignment for LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02844)
*Jisheng Dang,Yushuo Zhao,Dewei Liu,Junfeng Fang,Bimei Wang,Tiantian Rao,Hong Peng,Bin Hu,Tat-Seng Chua*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DNAlign is a lightweight LLM safety alignment framework that combines control-theoretic optimization with null-space projection to reduce harmful outputs while preserving model utility and generation quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing safety alignment approaches either incur high computational cost or unintentionally disrupt the model's core knowledge, leading to degraded fluency and factual accuracy on benign tasks. This creates a persistent trade-off between safety and utility in LLM deployment.

Method: DNAlign treats the LLM as a dynamic system and introduces controllable perturbations to steer generation toward safe behavior. It uses a projection module that restricts perturbations to the harmful-related subspace derived from neutral hidden states, thereby preserving general knowledge. A value function trained on human preference data adaptively optimizes control signals to align with human safety preferences.

Result: Extensive evaluations across multiple LLM backbones demonstrate that DNAlign consistently reduces harmful outputs while maintaining fluency, coherence, and factual utility. It achieves superior overall performance compared to prior alignment baselines without sacrificing generation diversity.

Conclusion: DNAlign provides an effective and practically deployable solution for safe LLM alignment, successfully addressing the trade-off between safety and utility that has persisted in existing approaches.

Abstract: Ensuring the safe and reliable deployment of large language models (LLMs) remains a fundamental challenge. Existing safety alignment approaches either incur high computational cost or unintentionally disrupt the model's core knowledge, leading to degraded fluency and factual accuracy on benign tasks. This reveals a persistent trade-off between safety and utility. We propose DNAlign, a lightweight alignment framework that integrates control-theoretic optimization with null-space projection. By treating the LLM as a dynamic system, the proposed framework introduces controllable perturbations to steer generation toward safe behavior. A key component is the projection module, which restricts these perturbations to the harmful-related subspace derived from neutral hidden states, thereby preserving general knowledge and response quality. A value function trained on human preference data adaptively optimizes the control signals to align with human safety preferences. Extensive evaluations across multiple LLM backbones demonstrate that our framework consistently reduces harmful outputs while maintaining fluency, coherence, and factual utility. It achieves superior overall performance compared to prior alignment baselines without sacrificing generation diversity. These results indicate that the proposed framework provides an effective and practically deployable solution for safe LLM alignment. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/DNAlign.

</details>


### [196] [Bounded Reachability & Jailbreak Detection via Contraction-Constrained State Space Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02853)
*Omanshu Thapliyal*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proves that SSM-based safety heads can be certified for robust prediction under bounded embedding-space perturbations iff the state transition matrix satisfies the contraction condition (||A||_∞ < 1). This enables exact Interval Bound Propagation (IBP) certification. When the condition holds, output intervals have bounded steady-state width; when it fails, intervals grow exponentially. The method achieves 59% certified fraction (up from 41%), with strong zero-shot transfer to AdvBench (DR=0.994) and HarmBench (DR=0.988).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Safety heads (lightweight classifiers for flagging harmful inputs) have been studied empirically for detection performance, but their formal robustness properties remain largely unexplored. The paper addresses when an SSM-based safety head can be certified to produce the same prediction for all inputs within a bounded embedding-space perturbation.

Method: The paper proves that certification depends on a single condition: the l_infinity norm of the state transition matrix must satisfy ||A||_∞ < 1 (the contraction condition), which enables exact Interval Bound Propagation (IBP) certification for linear time-invariant classifiers. The contraction condition is enforced with a hinge penalty during training.

Result: When the contraction condition holds, the reachable output interval has bounded steady-state width and examples can be certified as robustly classified. When it fails, the interval grows exponentially with sequence length and certification is impossible at any practical perturbation radius. On toxic comment data, the certified fraction improves from 41% to 59% with a sharp empirical phase transition at ||A||_∞ = 1 matching the theory. On JailbreakBench, zero-shot transfer to AdvBench achieves DR=0.994 and to HarmBench achieves DR=0.988. A logistic regression on mean-pooled Mamba-130M embeddings matches or exceeds the S4 head on every detection metric.

Conclusion: The S4 safety head's contribution is not superior discrimination but the formal certification that no probe-based approach provides. Harmful intent is already linearly separable in the embedding space, so the key value of the SSM safety head is providing provable robustness guarantees rather than better classification accuracy.

Abstract: Safety heads are lightweight classifiers attached to pretrained language models for flagging harmful inputs before generation. Their empirical detection performance has been studied, but their formal robustness properties remain largely unexplored. We ask when a State Space Model (SSM)-based safety head can be certified to produce the same prediction for all inputs within a bounded embedding-space perturbation. We prove that the answer turns on a single condition: the $l_\infty$ norm of the state transition matrix must satisfy $\norm{A}_\infty<1$ (the \emph{contraction condition}), which enables exact interval bound propagation (IBP) certification for linear time-invariant classifiers. When the contraction condition holds, the reachable output interval has bounded steady-state width and examples can be certified as robustly classified. When it fails, the interval grows exponentially with sequence length and certification is impossible at any practical perturbation radius. We enforce contraction with a hinge penalty and show on toxic comment data that certified fraction improves from 41\% to 59\%, with a sharp empirical phase transition at $\norm{A}_\infty=1$ matching the theory. Applying a contraction-regularized S4 head to jailbreak detection on JailbreakBench, we achieve a zero-shot transfer to AdvBench (DR=0.994) and HarmBench (DR=0.988). A logistic regression on mean-pooled Mamba-130M embeddings matches or exceeds the S4 head on every detection metric, confirming that harmful intent is already linearly separable in the embedding space. The S4 safety head's contribution is not superior discrimination but the formal certification that no probe-based approach provides.

</details>


### [197] [Harness-Aware Distillation for Small Language Model Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02858)
*Moonseok Choi,Taehong Moon,Giung Nam,Juho Lee*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: HAD (Harness-Aware Distillation) is a method for distilling large language model agents into smaller ones by focusing on what the teacher adds beyond the harness (software managing context/tools/feedback), rather than imitating full outputs. It uses action preference contrast and validity check components, outperforming standard on-policy distillation without requiring task rewards or success labels.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard distillation imitates the teacher's full outputs and treats the harness as part of the input, but when a teacher agent is distilled into a smaller one, the harness stays in place so the student mainly needs teacher-specific abilities that the harness cannot provide (like acting correctly on harness information). Standard distillation fails to capture this distinction.

Method: HAD complements on-policy distillation with two components: (1) Action preference that contrasts the same teacher's actions with and without harness information, scored after the student's own reasoning; (2) Validity check that drops preference pairs whose preferred action contradicts harness records. This contrast gives the student information that imitating the teacher alone cannot provide.

Result: Across multiple long-horizon agent benchmarks and models, HAD outperforms on-policy distillation baselines with the same fixed harness. HAD enters fewer unproductive loops and recovers from errors more often than baselines.

Conclusion: HAD can adaptively keep learnable feedback in its weights while reading state information from the harness, providing a more effective approach to agent distillation that focuses on teacher-specific abilities beyond what the harness provides.

Abstract: Language model agents are deployed with a harness, the software around the model that manages its context, tools, and feedback. When such an agent is distilled into a smaller one, the harness stays in place, so the student mainly needs the teacher-specific abilities that the harness cannot provide, such as acting correctly on harness information. Standard distillation, however, imitates the teacher's full outputs and treats the harness as part of the input. We propose Harness-Aware Distillation (HAD), which focuses distillation on what the teacher adds beyond the harness. HAD complements on-policy distillation with two components: an action preference that contrasts the same teacher's actions with and without the harness information, scored after the student's own reasoning, and a validity check that drops preference pairs whose preferred action contradicts the harness records. We show that the contrast gives the student information that imitating the teacher alone cannot provide, and HAD needs no task rewards, success labels, or future information. Across multiple long-horizon agent benchmarks and models, HAD outperforms on-policy distillation baselines with the same fixed harness. Our analysis shows that HAD enters fewer unproductive loops and recovers from errors more often than the baselines, and suggests that it adaptively keeps learnable feedback in its weights while reading state information from the harness.

</details>


### [198] [TACD: Distilling Efficient Text-to-Motion Models via Terminal Amplification Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02867)
*Wei-Jin Huang,Yuan-Ming Li,Kun-Yu Lin,Wang Luo,Yinlin Zhu,Yue Yu,Shenghao Ye,Junbin Yuan,Fa-Ting Hong,Qing Zhang,Wei-Shi Zheng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TACD (Terminal-Amplification-Controlled Distillation) is an on-policy method for training efficient text-to-motion generators from pretrained teachers without real-motion data. It addresses a failure mode where velocity matching overweights endpoint errors in few-step generation by bounding loss weights based on student's step size.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Text-to-motion models suffer from slow inference and high memory usage due to many-step denoising and large model components, making deployment impractical. The goal is to create efficient motion generators that maintain quality while significantly reducing computational cost.

Method: TACD builds on segmented on-policy flow distillation, supervising clean-motion predictions along student-generated trajectories. It identifies and addresses a failure mode where velocity matching on fixed supervision grid repeatedly overweights errors near the denoising endpoint. The key innovation ties the latest teacher query to the student's step size, bounding effective loss weights in clean-motion space without changing inference.

Result: On HumanML3D and KIT-ML: 58% reduction in eight-step HY-Motion student FID vs unconstrained distillation; four-step students achieve lower FID than 50-step teachers with matched/improved text-motion retrieval on HumanML3D; on HY-Motion and Kimodo, eight-step students achieve 7.7-11.9x speedups and 3.8-6.7x peak GPU memory reduction.

Conclusion: TACD successfully enables efficient few-step motion generation through bounded endpoint-matching distillation, achieving substantial speedups and memory savings while maintaining or improving motion quality and text-alignment compared to much larger teacher models.

Abstract: Recent text-to-motion models have improved motion quality and instruction following, yet many-step denoising and large model components make deployment slow and memory-intensive. We present Terminal-Amplification-Controlled Distillation (TACD), an on-policy approach for training efficient motion generators from text prompts and pretrained teachers, without real-motion training data. Building on segmented on-policy flow distillation, we supervise clean-motion predictions along student-generated trajectories. We identify a failure mode in which velocity matching on a fixed supervision grid repeatedly overweights errors near the denoising endpoint, degrading few-step generation. TACD ties the latest teacher query to the student's step size, bounding the effective loss weights in clean-motion space without changing inference. Experiments on HumanML3D and KIT-ML demonstrate improved few-step generation, including a 58% reduction in eight-step HY-Motion student FID relative to distillation without this bound. For diffusion teachers, the endpoint-matching form of TACD yields four-step students with lower FID and matched or improved text-motion retrieval relative to their 50-step teachers on HumanML3D. On HY-Motion and Kimodo, eight-step students with compact components achieve 7.7-11.9x end-to-end speedups and reduce peak GPU memory by 3.8-6.7x relative to their teachers. Project page: https://vkgo.github.io/TACD/

</details>


### [199] [PsyEvo: A Personalized Counseling Agent That Self-Evolves at Test Time](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02885)
*Yuting Yan,Shihao Xu,Junhao Yu,Mingcong Zuo,Lu Chen,Nan Xiang,Haiyang Geng,Dongjie Tao,Minghao Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PsyEvo is an LLM-based counseling framework that enables test-time personalization and policy improvement through three components: HBSP for per-client skill personalization, LiPO for cross-client response adapter improvement, and SOCA for credit assignment. It achieves 7.684 Overall on PsychEval in simulated-client evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The mental health treatment gap exists due to a persistent shortage of trained practitioners. While LLM-based counselors offer scalable solutions, offline training alone cannot adapt to individual clients or learn from ongoing therapeutic interactions at test time.

Method: PsyEvo integrates three components: (1) Hierarchical Bayesian Skill Policy (HBSP) maintains per-client skill posteriors updated from session feedback; (2) Inter-session Listwise Preference Optimization (LiPO) updates a shared response adapter from cross-client preference evidence; (3) State-conditioned Ordinal Credit Assignment (SOCA) provides candidate preferences and trajectory credit through consistency-checked comparisons and ordinal projection.

Result: PsyEvo achieves 7.684 Overall on PsychEval and exceeds every component variant in three matched runs. Removing individual components lowers mean overall score by 0.138-0.171 under the shared configuration, supporting conditional contributions within the complete scaffold.

Conclusion: The three components of PsyEvo work synergistically to enable both client-specific personalization and response-policy improvement at test time, effectively addressing the limitations of offline-only training for LLM-based mental health counseling.

Abstract: Mental health disorders affect a substantial proportion of the global population, yet a persistent shortage of trained practitioners leaves the majority without adequate care. Large language model (LLM)-based counselors present a promising direction for delivering scalable conversational psychological support. Offline model training alone leaves limited room to adapt to individual clients or to learn from ongoing therapeutic interaction at test time. We introduce PsyEvo, an LLM-based counseling framework that enables both client-specific personalization and response-policy improvement at test time through three components: Hierarchical Bayesian Skill Policy (HBSP) personalizes what intervention to apply by maintaining a per-client skill posterior updated from session feedback; Inter-session Listwise Preference Optimization (LiPO) improves how the selected skill is expressed by updating a shared response adapter from cross-client preference evidence; and State-conditioned Ordinal Credit Assignment (SOCA) supplies candidate preferences and trajectory credit to the two components through consistency-checked comparisons and ordinal projection. In simulated-client evaluation with shared online cohort adaptation, PsyEvo obtains 7.684 Overall on PsychEval and exceeds every component variant in each of three matched runs. Removing individual components lowers mean overall score by 0.138--0.171 under the shared configuration, supporting conditional contributions within the complete scaffold. Our code is available at https://github.com/Lingxi-mental-health/PsyEvo

</details>


### [200] [Interpreting at Write Time: A Policy Ablation for Multi-Goal Agent Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02897)
*Albert Sadowski,Jarosław A. Chudziak*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates how AI assistants should summarize their long-term memory when serving multiple different goals. The authors compare three summarization policies: goal-neutral summarization, all-goal summarization, and per-goal summarization. Through experiments across several models and event streams, they find that per-goal summaries significantly outperform the other approaches in relevance, completeness, and accuracy, while the all-goal summary performs worse than even a budget-constrained neutral summary.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The core problem is that AI assistants cannot retain all information they encounter, so they must summarize. However, what deserves to be retained depends on future goals that are unknown at summary time. The authors investigate how memory should be summarized when it must serve multiple standing goals simultaneously.

Method: The authors compare three summarization policies: (1) goal-neutral summarization with no specific goal in view, (2) a single all-goal summary covering every goal, and (3) per-goal summaries written separately for each goal and read together. They hold the read step fixed across policies, varying only the write/summarization approach, and test across several models and event streams.

Result: Per-goal summaries outperform other approaches on relevance, completeness, and accuracy. The all-goal summary actually performs worse than a neutral summary written at a fraction of its budget. Goals "pull apart" - summaries written for different goals overlap less than a summary overlaps a rewrite of itself, indicating that different goals genuinely require different information to be preserved.

Conclusion: Interpreting at write time pays off, but only for the goal that later asks. This suggests that memory systems should maintain separate summaries tailored to different anticipated goals rather than attempting to create a universal summary or relying on goal-agnostic summarization.

Abstract: A long-running assistant cannot keep everything it has seen, so it summarises. Summarising is not neutral: what is kept is chosen against some notion of what the record is for, and that choice is made once, before anyone knows which of the user's standing goals will ask. Goals rarely disagree about what happened. They disagree about which parts of it were worth the space. Once the history is too long to re-read, the summary replaces the stream, and whatever it left out is gone. We ask what a memory should summarise for when it serves several standing goals at once. Three policies answer differently: summarise with no goal in view, write one summary covering every goal, or write one summary per goal and read them together. We compare them across several models and event streams, holding the read step fixed so that only the write differs. The goals do pull apart: summaries written for different goals overlap each other less than a summary overlaps a rewrite of itself. Per-goal summaries win on relevance, completeness and accuracy, and the all-goal summary loses even to the neutral one written at a fraction of its budget. Interpreting at write pays off, but only for the goal that later asks.

</details>


### [201] [LUMOS: Tracing Parametric Knowledge from Training Data to Behavioral Outputs in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02902)
*Seoyeon Ye,Gayoung Kim,Jiyoung Hong,Sookyung Kim,Hyunsoo Cho*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LUMOS is a diagnostic framework that traces knowledge from training-data exposure to behavioral output in LLMs, using OLMo 2's transparent training corpus. The study reveals a significant gap between internal knowledge encoding (84%) and behavioral expression (54%) for rare facts, and that self-reflection performance drops to random baseline (49%) on unseen content, even with chain-of-thought prompting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM analyses are output-centric without verifying training data, leaving fundamental questions about whether correct responses reflect genuine generalization or rote memorization grounded in speculation rather than evidence.

Method: LUMOS framework traces knowledge along the causal chain from training-data exposure to behavioral output, leveraging OLMo 2 with its fully transparent training corpus to verify actual exposure.

Result: Models encode rare facts with high separability (84%) internally but fail to express them behaviorally (54%). Self-reflection works reliably on trained content (83%) but drops to random-baseline levels (49%) on unseen content. Chain-of-thought prompting inflates confidence signals rather than improving calibration. The retrieval gap narrows with model scale.

Conclusion: Incorporating the training-data axis into LLM evaluation transforms speculative diagnoses into verifiable claims. This axis should be a standard component of knowledge assessment in LLMs.

Abstract: Current analyses of LLMs' parametric knowledge are largely output-centric, drawing conclusions about what a model knows without verifying what it was actually trained on. This leaves fundamental questions, such as whether a correct response reflects genuine generalization or rote memorization, grounded in speculation rather than evidence. To resolve these ambiguities, we introduce LUMOS, a diagnostic framework that traces knowledge along the causal chain from training-data exposure to behavioral output, leveraging OLMo 2 with its fully transparent training corpus. By grounding analysis in verified exposure, we reveal that models internally encode rare facts with high separability (84%) yet fail to express them behaviorally (54%), though this retrieval gap narrows with scale. Furthermore, when models are asked to self-reflect on their own answers, they perform reliably on trained content (83%) but drop to random-baseline levels (49%) on unseen content. This collapse persists even under chain-of-thought prompting, which inflates confidence signals rather than improving calibration. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that incorporating the training-data axis into LLM evaluation transforms speculative diagnoses into verifiable claims, and we advocate that this axis should be a standard component of knowledge assessment in LLMs.

</details>


### [202] [Frequency Is Not Sensitivity Identifying Safety-Sensitive Experts in Sparse MoE LLM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02910)
*Md Nurul Absar Siddiky,Liuwan Zhu,Yingfei Dong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper demonstrates a security vulnerability in sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models where suppressing a small set of routed experts can weaken safety behavior without retraining. The authors propose and validate that router-gradient sensitivity is a more effective signal than activation frequency for selecting which experts to suppress to reduce refusal rates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The standard approach for selecting which experts to suppress uses activation frequency, but this measures usage rather than influence on model behavior. The authors hypothesize that router-gradient sensitivity (the sensitivity of loss to gate weights) would be a better indicator of which experts to target for weakening safety behavior.

Method: The researchers ranked experts by two signals (activation frequency and router-gradient sensitivity) across five MoE architectures using 500 benign and 500 malicious prompts. They then measured refusal rates on 100 held-out malicious prompts under two budgets (equal expert counts and equal nominal malicious routing traffic at 1-5%). They also conducted an exploratory cross-model analysis examining the relationship between malicious-versus-benign concentration gaps and gradient effects.

Result: Router-gradient selection reduced refusals more than activation frequency in 24 of 25 conditions, and more than random selection in all 25 conditions. The largest effect was in OLMoE where refusals fell from 34 to 9 out of 100 prompts (73.53% relative reduction) with no degraded outputs. After matching expert counts in every layer, gradient selection still outperformed activation in 23 of 25 conditions with two ties. The cross-model analysis showed a correlation (rho = 0.90, p = 0.083) between concentration gaps and peak gradient effects.

Conclusion: The results support using gradient selection over activation frequency for selecting experts to suppress under the tested budgets. This highlights a security vulnerability in MoE models where safety behavior can be weakened by targeting specific experts, and provides guidance on which experts are most impactful to protect or monitor.

Abstract: Suppressing a small set of routed experts can weaken the safety behavior of a sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language model without retraining. Which experts to suppress is therefore a security question, and the usual answer is activation frequency, but frequency measures use, not influence. We test an alternative: router-gradient sensitivity, the sensitivity of the sequence loss to the gate weights that select an expert. Across five MoE architectures, we rank experts by each signal on 500 benign and 500 malicious prompts and measure refusal on 100 held-out malicious prompts under two budgets: equal expert counts and equal nominal malicious routing traffic (1%-5%). Under each of the two budgets, router-gradient selection reduces refusals more than activation in 24 of 25 conditions, and more than a ten-trial random mean in all 25. The largest effect is in OLMoE, where refusals fall from 34 to 9 of 100 prompts (73.53% relative) with no degraded outputs, indicating substantive compliance rather than broken generation. After matching expert counts in every layer, gradient selection still produces greater refusal reduction than activation in 23 of 25 conditions, with two ties. An exploratory cross-model analysis links larger malicious-versus-benign concentration gaps to greater peak gradient effects (rho = 0.90; exact two-sided p = 0.083, n = 5). Together, the results support gradient selection under the tested budgets.

</details>


### [203] [HASTE: Evolving Agent Harnesses Against Emerging Attacks Using Sparse Evidence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02920)
*Xiqiao Xiong,Moxin Li,Zhixin Ma,Ouxiang Li,Wenjie Wang,Fuli Feng,Xiangnan He*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: HASTE is a multi-agent framework that automatically evolves agent safety harnesses from sparse threat evidence (e.g., brief descriptions, few attack examples) through an adversarial interplay between safety-specification generation and attack-case generation, enabling defenses to adapt to emerging attacks beyond initially observed evidence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agent harnesses are critical for AI safety but face rapidly emerging attacks that outpace manual adaptation. Current limitation: signals for harness evolution are sparse (brief descriptions, few examples in threat reports/preprints). This motivates automated harness evolution.

Method: HASTE uses a multi-agent framework with two opposing processes: (1) Safety-specification generation - guides harness updates toward addressing identified vulnerabilities; (2) Attack-case generation - probes for remaining vulnerabilities after each update. Evaluation outcomes are fed back into both processes iteratively.

Result: Experimental results across multiple backbone models, attack types, and evidence forms show that HASTE consistently reduces attack success rates while preserving benign-task utility.

Conclusion: HASTE enables effective harness evolution against emerging attacks beyond initially observed evidence, demonstrating a promising approach for automated defense adaptation in AI safety systems.

Abstract: Agent harnesses play a critical role in defenses by enforcing safety constraints to prevent unsafe actions. However, rapidly emerging attacks outpace manual harness adaptation, motivating automated harness evolution. Yet the signals available for harness evolution are often sparse, such as brief descriptions or a few attack examples in threat reports and preprints. To address this limitation, we introduce HASTE, a multi-agent framework that evolves agent harnesses from sparse threat evidence through an adversarial interplay between safety-specification generation and attack-case generation. Safety specifications guide harness updates toward addressing identified safety vulnerabilities, while attack cases probe for remaining safety vulnerabilities after each update. By feeding evaluation outcomes back into both processes, HASTE enables harness evolution against emerging attacks beyond the initially observed evidence. Experimental results across multiple backbone models, attack types, and evidence forms show that HASTE consistently reduces attack success rates while preserving benign-task utility. The code is available at https://github.com/xxiqiao/HASTE.

</details>


### [204] [Positive-Unlabeled Learning for Agent Safety False Alarm Auditing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02925)
*Xichen Yan,Chongyang Gao,Kezhen Chen,Guangyi Zhang,Jiaqi Wu,Lixu Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses the false alarm problem in safety monitors for language model agents by formulating false-alarm auditing as a positive-unlabeled (PU) ranking problem. The authors propose a two-stage framework that adapts safe references toward the alarm domain, consolidates ordering preferences from multiple PU models, and refines rankings using hierarchical structures. The method achieves 0.6444 macro AUPRC, outperforming eight baselines by 5.27-16.98 percentage points and recovering 33.3% more false alarms than the strongest baseline at a 5% review budget.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Safety monitors for language-model agents generate many false alarms, consuming extensive review resources and weakening trust in alerts. The core problem is that false and genuine alarms remain interleaved in native monitor scores, making it difficult to obtain reliable cutoffs without substantial manual verification. The key challenge is "monitor-induced selection" - observed safe references are accepted by the monitor, while the hidden safe alarms of interest are precisely those the monitor incorrectly flags, making observed positives poorly representative of the positives to be recovered.

Method: The authors propose a two-stage framework with three key components: (1) Trust-aware PU Supervision that adapts safe references toward the alarm domain and protects plausible false alarms from excessive negative pressure; (2) Reliability-gated Rank Distillation that consolidates consistent ordering preferences from multiple PU reference models into a single student; (3) Consensus-guided Structural Refinement that improves the student ranking using hierarchical safe-reference support, alarm relations, and predicted reference consensus. The framework requires no alarm safety labels for fitting and leaves the underlying monitor unchanged.

Result: The method achieves a macro AUPRC of 0.6444, outperforming eight evaluated PU baselines by 5.27-16.98 absolute percentage points. Compared with PULDA (the strongest evaluated PU baseline), it recovers 33.3% more false alarms at a 5% review budget.

Conclusion: The proposed framework successfully addresses the monitor-induced selection bias in PU learning for false alarm detection. By adapting safe references, consolidating multiple PU models, and leveraging hierarchical structural refinement, the method significantly improves the ranking of false alarms without requiring alarm labels or modifying the underlying monitor. This work provides a practical solution for reducing false alarm burden in safety monitoring systems for LLM agents.

Abstract: Safety monitors help safeguard language-model agents interacting with external tools and environments, but conservative monitoring can generate many false alarms, consuming extensive review resources and weakening trust in alerts. Because false and genuine alarms often remain interleaved in native monitor scores, obtaining a reliable cutoff still requires substantial manual verification. In practice, a small set of verified-safe non-alarmed trajectories may be available while alarms remain unlabeled, naturally casting false-alarm auditing as a positive-unlabeled (PU) ranking problem. The key challenge is monitor-induced selection, since observed safe references are accepted by the monitor, while the hidden safe alarms of interest are precisely those it incorrectly flags, making the observed positives poorly representative of the positives to be recovered. To address this challenge, we propose a two-stage framework in which Trust-aware PU Supervision adapts safe references toward the alarm domain and protects plausible false alarms from excessive negative pressure, while Reliability-gated Rank Distillation consolidates consistent ordering preferences from multiple PU reference models into a single student. Consensus-guided Structural Refinement then improves the student ranking using hierarchical safe-reference support, alarm relations, and predicted reference consensus. The framework requires no alarm safety labels for fitting and leaves the underlying monitor unchanged. Across mainstream safety monitors, our method achieves a macro AUPRC of $0.6444$, outperforming eight evaluated PU baselines by 5.27--16.98 absolute percentage points; compared with PULDA, the strongest evaluated PU baseline, it recovers 33.3% more false alarms at a 5% review budget.

</details>


### [205] [When to Compile a Computer-Use Agent? Measuring Payback and Making Compilation Decisions for Token Efficiency](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02932)
*Yulong Ming,Jie Xu,Zihan Wu,Xiaohua Jia*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PACE is a system that decides when to compile repeated GUI procedures into executable programs to reduce token costs in AI agents. It addresses two key challenges: uncertain compilation costs (due to potential failures) and unknown future reuse (due to task termination or GUI changes). The system uses a measurement protocol to track costs and an online algorithm to make compilation decisions based on a budget, achieving near-optimal cost efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to reduce token costs in AI agents that execute GUI procedures repeatedly. While compiling these procedures into programs can save costs, deciding when to compile is challenging due to uncertain compilation costs (failures/repairs) and unknown future reuse (tasks may stop or GUI elements may change). Existing approaches lack a systematic way to measure payback and make compilation decisions under uncertainty.

Method: The paper proposes two components: (1) A measurement protocol that records successful and failed compilation costs, compares agent and program execution costs on matched task inputs to estimate per-use savings and payback counts. (2) An online compilation algorithm that compares estimated future savings with compilation costs (including failed attempts) based on past task arrivals and compilation outcomes. It checks execution and compilation charges against a cumulative budget determined by observed task arrivals. The algorithm achieves a (1+ε) competitive ratio under stated action-cost assumptions.

Result: PACE achieves significant token cost reductions in simulations: 17.3% reduction compared to ReAct, 24.9% reduction compared to AutoRPA adaptation, and 17.3% reduction compared to ToolPro adaptation (averaged, with ε=0.25). For successful compilation attempts, estimated payback counts (excluding source agent runs) range from 2-16 uses.

Conclusion: The conclusion demonstrates that PACE effectively reduces token costs by intelligently deciding when to compile GUI procedures into programs. The key insight is using a budget-based approach with observed task arrivals to bound the competitive ratio. The 17-25% cost reductions across different baselines show the practical utility of the approach, with the payback count range (2-16) indicating that compilation is worthwhile when sufficient reuse is expected.

Abstract: Compiling GUI procedures that agents execute repeatedly into programs can reduce their token costs. However, measuring payback and deciding when to compile have two challenges. First, compilation costs are uncertain because attempts can require repair and still fail to produce a usable program. Second, future reuse is unknown because tasks may stop arriving or GUI drift may stop the program from working. To address these challenges, we propose PACE (Payback-Aware Compilation from Experience), a system with a measurement protocol and an online compilation algorithm. The measurement protocol records successful and failed compilation costs, and compares agent and program execution costs on matched task inputs to estimate per-use savings and payback counts. Using these measurements, the online algorithm compares estimated future savings with compilation costs, including failed attempts, based on past task arrivals and compilation outcomes. It checks execution and compilation charges against a cumulative budget determined by observed task arrivals before allowing either action. Under stated action-cost assumptions, total cost after each arrival is at most $1+ε$ times the cost of running every task with the agent. For successful compilation attempts, estimated payback counts excluding source agent runs are 2-16 uses. In simulations using recorded task arrivals, PACE reduces token costs by 17.3% compared with ReAct, 24.9% with the AutoRPA adaptation, and 17.3% with the ToolPro adaptation on average ($ε=0.25$).

</details>


### [206] [Continual Graph Memory for Mathematical Research Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02945)
*Junyi Zhang,Jinxi Yu,Eric Hanchen Jiang,Jiachen Lu,Zhi Zhang,Xinjie He,Hyunsik Chae,Ethan Ji,Alexander K Taylor,Vigyan Sahai,Yiwen Kou,Kai-Wei Chang,Raghu Meka,Nanyun Peng,Amit Sahai,Terence Tao,Wei Wang*

Main category: cs.AI
