TL;DR: Ansatz is a mathematical research agent using Continual Graph Memory to organize and reuse intermediate proof results across long-horizon proof searches, successfully solving ten First Proof Second Batch problems and several open mathematical conjectures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Solving frontier mathematics problems requires massive numbers of agents working in parallel for extended periods, generating enormous volumes of intermediate proof results. The key challenges are organizing these intermediate results throughout long-horizon proof-search processes and reusing knowledge from prior explorations.

Method: Ansatz uses Continual Graph Memory, a graph-based evolvable memory system that: (1) represents intermediate exploration results (facts, plans, counterexamples) with explicit relationship edges; (2) provides dependency-aware retrieval for targeted local context; (3) employs an evidence-sensitive curator to update research frontier and distill lessons; (4) implements scoped recall to surface earlier statements and negative findings for local re-proving.

Result: Ansatz achieved closure on all ten First Proof Second Batch problems and solved open problems including the Jamison caterpillar conjecture and Erdős Problems 289, 348, and 488 without human intervention, while making partial progress on several other open problems.

Conclusion: Ansatz demonstrates the ability to solve open mathematical research problems without human intervention, achieving closure on all ten First Proof Second Batch problems and solving several open problems including the Jamison caterpillar conjecture and Erdős Problems 289, 348, and 488. The Continual Graph Memory enables effective organization and reuse of intermediate proof results across long-horizon proof searches.

Abstract: Using frontier agent harnesses to tackle mathematical research problems has emerged as an effective means of advancing mathematics. However, solving frontier problems in mathematics may require a massive number of agents working in parallel for extended periods to construct proofs, thereby generating an enormous volume of intermediate proof results. Organizing these intermediate results throughout a long-horizon proof-search process and reusing knowledge gained from prior explorations remain major challenges. We present Ansatz, a mathematical research agent built around Continual Graph Memory, a graph-based, evolvable, cross-problem mathematical research memory system that explicitly organizes the entire proof search process and reuses information from exploration trajectories of previous problems. Specifically, we develop a unified graph memory that represents all intermediate exploration results, including facts, plans, and counterexamples, together with edges that explicitly represent the relationships among them; dependency-aware retrieval supplies precisely targeted local context; an evidence-sensitive curator updates the research frontier and distills lessons from prior attempts; and scoped recall surfaces earlier statements and negative findings for local re-proving rather than uncritical reuse. Experiments cover runs across all ten First Proof Second Batch problems, together with four component studies. Ansatz reports closure on all ten research tasks, demonstrating its ability to sustain and resume long-horizon mathematical search. Beyond these problems, Ansatz also produces solutions to the Jamison caterpillar conjecture and Erdős Problems 289, 348, and 488 without human intervention, and makes partial progress on several open problems, illustrating its strong ability to solve open mathematical research problems.

</details>


### [207] [Reasoning with Evidence, Not Merely Rationales: Verifiable Preference Proofs for LLM-Based Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02968)
*Yu Hou,Nathaniel Kang,Pengkai Wang,Hua Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PROVE-REC is a framework for verifiable preference reasoning in LLM-based recommendation systems that addresses the "grounding-influence gap" - where preference claims may be weakly supported by evidence or have little effect on ranking. The framework uses a two-pass architecture (Pass A generates preference proofs from history, Pass B predicts recommendations using only the proof) with verification objectives to ensure claims are grounded in evidence and influential to recommendations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs can infer user preferences from interaction histories and reviews, but the rationales they generate may not reflect the information actually used for recommendation. This creates a "grounding-influence gap" with two failures: (1) preference claims are weakly supported by selected evidence, and (2) claims have little effect on the final ranking. There was a need for a framework that ensures verifiable and faithful preference reasoning in LLM-based recommendations.

Method: PROVE-REC uses a two-pass architecture: (1) Pass A converts the complete pre-target history into a compact preference proof consisting of positive and avoidance claims linked to selected evidence entries; (2) Pass B predicts the next item using only the proof and its selected evidence, preventing the recommender from bypassing the reasoning path. Verification involves: (a) comparing effect of masking selected evidence vs masking control entry for evidence-to-proof grounding; (b) removing a preference claim and measuring decrease in target item's ranking margin for proof-to-recommendation influence; (c) ranking-preservation objective to retain useful information from complete history.

Result: PROVE-REC consistently outperforms strong sequential, generative, and LLM-enhanced baselines on wide-ranging real-world datasets, with improvements of up to 7.45%. Controlled ablations confirm the effectiveness of the two-pass architecture and verification objectives. The framework produces claims that are more strongly grounded in historical evidence and more influential to recommendation while preserving ranking quality.

Conclusion: PROVE-REC successfully addresses the grounding-influence gap in LLM-based recommendation by enforcing verifiable preference reasoning through its two-pass architecture and verification objectives. The framework ensures that generated preference claims are both well-grounded in historical evidence and actually influence the recommendation outcomes, while maintaining competitive recommendation performance.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can infer user preferences from interaction histories and reviews, yet the rationales they generate may not reflect the information actually used for recommendation. A preference claim may be weakly supported by its selected evidence, or may have little effect on the final ranking. We refer to these two failures as the grounding-influence gap. We introduce PROVE-REC, a general framework for verifiable preference reasoning in LLM-based recommendation. Pass A converts the complete pre-target history into a compact preference proof consisting of positive and avoidance claims linked to selected evidence entries. Pass B predicts the next item using only the proof and its selected evidence, preventing the recommender from bypassing the reasoning path. To verify evidence-to-proof grounding, we compare the effect of masking selected evidence with masking a comparable control entry. To verify proof-to-recommendation influence, we remove a preference claim and measure the resulting decrease in the target item's ranking margin. A ranking-preservation objective further retains useful information from the complete history. Comprehensive experiments on wide-ranging real-world datasets demonstrate that PROVE-REC consistently outperforms strong sequential, generative, and LLM-enhanced baselines, with improvements of up to 7.45%. Controlled ablations confirm the effectiveness of the two-pass architecture and verification objectives. Moreover, PROVE-REC produces claims that are more strongly grounded in historical evidence and more influential to recommendation while preserving ranking quality.

</details>


### [208] [CreateScore: Domain-Theory-Informed Bayesian Routing for LLM-Based CV Screening](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02972)
*Rupsa Roy*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CreateScore is a domain-theory-informed Bayesian network system that routes CV screening decisions between a small (8B) and large (120B) language model based on uncertainty, reducing computational costs while maintaining accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Applying high-capability LLMs to every candidate and criterion is costly. The authors aim to create a cost-effective routing mechanism that uses a smaller model for clear-cut cases and escalates uncertain ones to a larger reference model.

Method: A hand-specified DAG with Dirichlet-multinomial CPTs converts CV evidence into posterior uncertainty. Low-uncertainty decisions are resolved by a local 8B model; uncertain ones escalate to a 120B model. Threshold calibrated on training fold (target: 70% resolved locally).

Result: 77.7% of criterion decisions (237/305) resolved locally. Token use reduced by 65.2%. Exact score agreement improved from 32.8% (8B alone) to 42.6% vs reference. However, the uncertainty signal failed to identify errors: disagreement was 16.2% (escalated) vs 19.4% (locally resolved), AUROC 0.47 (no better than random).

Conclusion: CreateScore is supported as an auditable cost-reduction mechanism but not yet as a targeted error detector. The uncertainty signal did not reliably identify which decisions required escalation. The authors also document a prior evaluation invalidation due to truncated outputs and recommend safeguards.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can support rubric-based screening of CVs, but applying a high-capability model to every candidate and criterion is costly. We present CreateScore, a domain-theory-informed Bayesian network for criterion-level LLM routing. A hand-specified directed acyclic graph with Dirichlet-multinomial conditional probability tables converts CV evidence into posterior uncertainty; low-uncertainty decisions are resolved by a local 8B model and uncertain ones are escalated to a 120B reference model. The graph is causally motivated, but the system performs standard Bayesian conditioning, not causal inference. The escalation threshold is calibrated on a training fold (target: 70% resolved locally) and then frozen. On 200 synthetic Data Science CVs (139 training and 61 test candidates, five criteria), 77.7% of criterion decisions were resolved locally (237 of 305). Relative to a reference condition in which the 120B model adjudicated every criterion, routed escalation reduced token use by 65.2% and raised exact score agreement from 32.8% (8B alone) to 42.6% (95% CI 31.0-55.1%); at n = 61 the gain was not statistically distinguishable. The uncertainty signal did not, however, identify the decisions on which the 8B model erred: disagreement with the reference was 16.2% among escalated and 19.4% among locally resolved decisions (AUROC 0.47, 95% CI 0.39-0.56), no better than random selection. We also document how an earlier evaluation was invalidated when truncated reasoning-model outputs were silently replaced by local labels, and we recommend safeguards for cascade evaluation. CreateScore is supported as an auditable cost-reduction mechanism, not yet as a targeted error detector, and is not an autonomous hiring system.

</details>


### [209] [Reliable Self-Evolution with Imperfect Proxy Rewards](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02975)
*Kangjun Noh,Soyu Kim,Kyungwoo Song*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CISE is a method for self-evolving scientific discovery that uses conformal inference to construct reward intervals, filtering out false positives from low-cost proxy evaluations to ensure only feasible candidates are returned.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In self-evolving search for scientific discovery, high-fidelity evaluation is expensive, forcing systems to use low-cost but imperfect proxy rewards. These proxies can assign high scores to infeasible candidates (false positives), contaminating both outputs and evolutionary feedback. This necessitates statistically calibrated reward intervals for reliable search.

Method: CISE combines conditional conformal inference with iteration-wise online density-ratio estimation to construct candidate-specific reward intervals. It uses conservative interval-based rewards for evolutionary feedback and returns candidates only when all property intervals lie entirely within feasible regions. Coverage guarantees are derived under independence and covariate shift assumptions.

Result: On three materials science self-evolving search tasks, CISE returned only true positives (100% precision), while baselines returned more candidates but included false positives. This demonstrates the value of a smaller, more precise shortlist when downstream validation budgets are limited.

Conclusion: CISE provides a statistically principled approach to handling uncertainty in proxy-based reward systems. By guaranteeing that returned candidates are feasible under high-fidelity evaluation, it offers a practical solution when downstream validation is expensive, trading off quantity for guaranteed quality.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based self-evolving search is a promising approach to scientific discovery. However, high-fidelity evaluation of every candidate is prohibitively expensive in some domains. Self-evolving systems in such settings therefore rely on low-cost but imperfect proxy rewards, which may assign high scores to infeasible candidates. These false positives may contaminate both the final output and the feedback used to guide subsequent generations. This motivates statistically calibrated reward intervals for more reliable self-evolving search. We propose Conformal Interval-Driven Self-Evolution (CISE), which constructs candidate-specific reward intervals using conditional conformal inference and iteration-wise online density-ratio estimation. CISE uses conservative interval-based rewards for evolutionary feedback and returns candidates only when all required property intervals lie entirely within their respective feasible regions. We derive fixed-iteration coverage results under explicit assumptions of independence and covariate shift. We evaluate CISE on three self-evolving search tasks in materials science. In our experiments, all candidates returned by CISE are true positives under high-fidelity evaluation, whereas the baselines return more candidates but include false positives. These results highlight the value of a smaller, more precise shortlist when downstream validation budgets are limited. Our repository is available at https://github.com/MLAI-Yonsei/CISE.git.

</details>


### [210] [Relevant Evidence Decoding for Audio-Visual Hallucination Mitigation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02976)
*Hyunjae Ra,Aecheon Jung,Jungin Park,Sungeun Hong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RED (Relevant Evidence Decoding) is a training-free method that reduces cross-modal hallucinations in Audio-Visual Large Language Models (AV-LLMs) by identifying question-relevant evidence and selectively strengthening its contribution using pointwise mutual information.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AV-LLMs suffer from cross-modal hallucinations where one modality incorrectly influences predictions about another. Existing contrastive decoding methods don't account for the fact that different questions require different perceptual evidence (audio, video, or their interaction). Joint audio-visual inference can even weaken correct predictions from a single informative modality.

Method: RED uses pointwise mutual information (PMI) to quantify predictive support from audio and video beyond the question alone. It decomposes joint contributions into audio, video, and residual interaction components. A question-only inference pass determines the required evidence type, then augments the original audio-visual prediction with the corresponding PMI contribution.

Result: RED improves accuracy over standard decoding by up to 7% on CMM, 6.3% on AVHBench, and 3.8% on SVHalluc, with an average relative time to first token of 1.5x standard decoding. Validated across three AV-LLMs and three audio-visual hallucination benchmarks.

Conclusion: RED effectively addresses cross-modal hallucinations in AV-LLMs by selectively strengthening question-relevant modality evidence without requiring training, offering a practical solution with moderate computational overhead (1.5x inference time).

Abstract: Audio-Visual Large Language Models (AV-LLMs) remain prone to cross-modal hallucinations, where one modality incorrectly affects predictions about another. Although contrastive decoding reduces hallucinations in vision-language models, its direct extension to AV-LLMs overlooks a key challenge: different questions require different perceptual evidence, including audio, video, or their interaction. Notably, we observe that joint audio-visual inference can weaken the prediction even when a model can recover the correct answer from a single informative modality. For example, when asked which instrument is heard, a model may correctly predict violin from the audio alone. Once a video showing a guitar is added, its confidence in violin may drop. In this paper, we introduce Relevant Evidence Decoding (RED), a training-free method that identifies question-relevant evidence and selectively strengthens its contribution. RED uses pointwise mutual information to quantify the predictive support provided by audio and video beyond the question alone. It decomposes their joint contribution into audio, video, and residual interaction components. A question-only inference pass determines the required evidence type, after which the model augments the original audio-visual prediction with the corresponding PMI contribution. Across three audio-visual hallucination benchmarks and three AV-LLMs, RED improves accuracy over standard decoding by up to 7% on CMM, 6.3% on AVHBench, and 3.8% on SVHalluc, with an average relative time to first token of 1.5x standard decoding.

</details>


### [211] [RASPER: Reward-Aligned Summarization of Clinical Notes for EHR Outcome Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02979)
*Arya Hadizadeh Moghaddam,Mohsen Nayebi Kerdabadi,Chen Chen,Dongjie Wang,Zijun Yao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RASPER is a reinforcement learning-based system that optimizes note summarization directly against downstream clinical tasks (readmission prediction and medication recommendation), using feedback from the predictor to train an LLM-based summarizer while incorporating structured codes as soft prompts via a longitudinal encoder.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Unstructured discharge notes in EHRs contain patient-specific evidence complementary to structured codes, but are lengthy and noisy. Generic summarization focuses on fluency and omits task-relevant evidence while retaining uninformative details.

Method: RASPER uses a tunable LLM-based summarizer trained via reinforcement learning from prediction feedback. A longitudinal encoder converts structured codes into soft prompts that provide clinical context. The reward is derived from the downstream predictor's loss, encouraging retention of evidence that complements structured codes.

Result: RASPER consistently outperforms strong baselines on both readmission prediction and medication recommendation across MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV datasets.

Conclusion: Task-aligned summarization via reinforcement learning, guided by prediction feedback and incorporating structured clinical context, effectively extracts patient-specific evidence from discharge notes to improve clinical predictions.

Abstract: Unstructured discharge notes in Electronic Health Records (EHRs) often carry signal complementary to structured medical codes, holding patient-specific evidence that standardized cohort-level codes alone cannot capture. However, this evidence in notes is frequently buried in lengthy, noisy text that is not intentionally written with any specific clinical prediction in mind. Summarization is an obvious mitigation, but generic summaries, tuned for fluency rather than the outcome, routinely omit decisive evidence while retaining plausible but uninformative detail. To this end, we propose RASPER, a Reward-Aligned Summarizer for Prediction in EHR, that optimizes note summarization directly against the downstream clinical task. RASPER employs a tunable LLM-based summarizer to extract task-relevant evidence from discharge notes and trains it via reinforcement learning from prediction feedback, using a reward derived from the downstream predictor's loss. To ground the summarizer, a longitudinal encoder converts structured codes into soft prompts that incorporate each patient's clinical context into note summarization. By rewarding the quality of the resulting multimodal prediction, RASPER encourages the summarizer to retain patient-specific evidence that complements, rather than duplicates, information captured by structured codes. RASPER consistently outperforms strong baselines on both readmission prediction and medication recommendation across MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV.

</details>


### [212] [Safeguarding Mutual Correction in Source-Free Domain Adaptation via Cut Statistics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02981)
*Seongjun Lee,Changhee Lee*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SafeCut addresses Source-Free Domain Adaptation by enabling mutual correction between a source-pretrained model and a Vision-Language model, using the cut statistic as a label-free reliability measure to gate cross-model supervision and selectively amplify true corrections while suppressing miscorrections.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current SFDA methods either suffer from confirmation bias (single-model self-refinement) or operate unidirectionally (using ViL models only as supervisors), failing to exploit the complementary failure modes of different models where each can correct the other's errors on the target domain.

Method: SafeCut leverages the cut statistic as a label-free measure of prediction reliability to gate cross-model supervision. It dynamically controls the direction and strength of supervision based on relative reliability between the source-pretrained model and ViL model on a per-sample basis.

Result: SafeCut achieves state-of-the-art performance across diverse SFDA benchmarks, demonstrating the effectiveness of safeguarding mutual correction via cut statistics.

Conclusion: The proposed reliability-gated mechanism guarantees a net-positive correction signal, effectively addressing the challenge of identifying correct predictions without ground-truth labels while enabling bidirectional mutual correction between models.

Abstract: Source-Free Domain Adaptation (SFDA) aims to adapt a source-pretrained model to an unlabeled target domain without access to the original source domain. While early single-model approaches rely on self-refinement, they are inherently susceptible to confirmation bias and struggle to correct their own systematic errors. To overcome this limitation, recent methods introduce Vision-Language (ViL) models as external knowledge sources. However, these approaches operate in a largely unidirectional paradigm, using the ViL model primarily to supervise the source-pretrained model. This overlooks a key structural property: the two models exhibit distinct failure modes -- where one produces an incorrect prediction, the other may produce a correct one, creating a natural opportunity for mutual correction within the target domain. Yet, without ground-truth labels, identifying which model is correct on any given sample is non-trivial, and naively exchanging predictions risks propagating errors across models. To address this challenge, we propose SafeCut, a novel approach that leverages the cut statistic as a label-free measure of prediction reliability to gate cross-model supervision. Our approach dynamically controls both the direction and strength of supervision based on relative reliability, selectively amplifying true corrections while suppressing miscorrections on a per-sample basis. We further provide theoretical justification showing that this reliability-gated mechanism guarantees a net-positive correction signal. Extensive experiments across diverse SFDA benchmarks demonstrate that SafeCut achieves state-of-the-art performance, highlighting the effectiveness of safeguarding mutual correction in SFDA via cut statistics.

</details>


### [213] [PLCWorld: Benchmarking LLM-Generated PLC Programs in Closed-Loop Plant Simulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02982)
*Yunji Kim,Yunseok Lee,Hyunwoo Seo,Jaerim Choi,Woojin Lee*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PLCWorld is a benchmark environment for evaluating LLM-generated PLC programs against task requirements and safety constraints, featuring 100 synthetic tasks across Motion Control and Material Handling domains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Evaluating whether LLM-generated PLC programs satisfy task requirements and safety constraints requires observing how their commands affect device and workpiece states in a closed-loop environment.

Method: PLCWorld couples Structured Text (ST) execution with simulated plant responses and sensor feedback. It contains 100 synthetic tasks and 473 registered task-condition pairs with difficulty defined by control-dependency scope. Validation uses practitioner review, reference/alternative programs, targeted counterexamples, specification-evaluator alignment checks, and comparisons with independent ST runtimes.

Result: GPT-5.5 achieves 82.70% Task Success on Easy cases but only 25.10% on Hard cases. Evaluation of six LLMs and four generation-and-verification workflows reveals differences in completion, safety, and generation cost.

Conclusion: PLCWorld provides a standardized benchmark for evaluating PLC program generation, revealing significant performance gaps between easy and hard tasks, and highlighting the need for improved LLM capabilities in handling complex control dependencies.

Abstract: Programmable logic controllers (PLCs) coordinate industrial equipment by reading sensor inputs and issuing control commands. Evaluating whether large language model (LLM)-generated PLC programs satisfy task requirements and safety constraints requires observing how their commands affect device and workpiece states. We introduce PLCWorld, a common closed-loop execution environment and benchmark that couples Structured Text (ST) execution with simulated plant responses and sensor feedback. Grounded in control relations identified in industrial PLC programs and engineering documentation, PLCWorld contains 100 synthetic tasks and 473 registered task-condition pairs across Motion Control and Material Handling, with difficulty defined by control-dependency scope. A common protocol reports Task Success and Safety Violation separately. Validation combines practitioner review, reference and alternative programs, targeted counterexamples, specification-evaluator alignment checks, and comparisons with independent ST runtimes. Reference and alternative programs satisfy their applicable cases, while all 542 targeted counterexamples activate their designated evaluator rules under at least one registered condition. Execution Gap relates submission-profile acceptance to subsequent task failure or observed Safety Violation. Across the constructed task groups, direct GPT-5.5 achieves 82.70% Task Success on Easy cases but 25.10% on Hard cases. Evaluations of six LLMs and four adapted generation-and-verification workflows further expose differences between completion, safety, and generation cost. Our code, simulation environment, benchmark tasks, and baseline implementations are publicly available at https://yunji0516.github.io/PLCWorld/.

</details>


### [214] [DyadMem: A Long-Term Memory Benchmark of How Agents Work with Users](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03020)
*Yifei Tao,Xinyu Zhong,Henry Hengyuan Zhao,Fanyi Wang,Tengda Guo,Wentao Qiu,Ying Wang,Liujian Tang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DyadMem introduces User-conditioned Relational Agent Memory (URAM) to address the gap in benchmarking relationship-specific agent memory across multi-session interactions. The benchmark includes 6 memory categories with 3,065 episodes, 50,961 sessions, and 61,210 QA instances. Testing 20 models reveals that while Gold-Memory QA performs well, Full-Pipeline QA shows significant drops, exposing issues like low Capture recall, incomplete Recall, and unsafe-deletion.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks only supervise user facts/preferences that are reusable across users, leaving relationship-specific agent memory implicit. Additionally, prior works only measure final-answer QA over long histories, making assessment incomplete and unreliable.

Method: DyadMem jointly annotates user-side memory and URAM along multi-session trajectories, resulting in 6 memory categories. It includes session-level Capture and Update gold annotations, query-level Recall support, and two QA settings: Gold-Memory (memory given) and Full-Pipeline (memory generated).

Result: Across 16 open-weight and 4 proprietary models: Gold-Memory QA is consistently strong, but Full-Pipeline QA drops sharply. This gap validates the fine-grained evaluation design. Issues include low Capture recall, incomplete Recall, and unsafe-deletion even in frontier LLMs. URAM validation shows positive effects for all 20 models.

Conclusion: DyadMem is a dual-domain, full-pipeline memory benchmark with extensive annotation efforts that effectively exposes model limitations in relationship-specific memory handling and advances the field's development.

Abstract: Long-term agents must remember not only what is true about a user, but also how a particular agent should work with that user as their shared history evolves. Existing benchmarks primarily supervise user facts and preferences or experience reusable across users, leaving this relationship-specific agent memory implicit. Additionally, most prior works measure the model solely with final-answer QA over long interaction histories, making the assessment still incomplete and unreliable. To this end, we introduce DyadMem with the proposed new definition User-conditioned Relational Agent Memory (URAM). DyadMem jointly annotates user-side memory and URAM along the same multi-session trajectories, resulting in 6 memory categories. To summarize, it includes 3,065 episodes, 50,961 sessions, and 61,210 QA instances, with extensive session-level Capture and Update gold annotations, query-level Recall support, and two QA settings: Gold-Memory and Full-Pipeline. Across 16 open-weight and 4 proprietary models, Gold-Memory QA is consistently strong, yet Full-Pipeline QA drops sharply. Such a gap explicitly supports our fine-grained evaluation design. Additionally, several quantitative results further reveal low Capture recall, incomplete Recall, and unsafe-deletion issues arising from even the frontier LLMs. We further conduct a rigorous experiment to validate the effectiveness of our URAM and observe the positive effects for all 20 models. In summary, DyadMem is a dual-domain, full-pipeline memory benchmark with extensive annotation efforts for advancing the domain's development.

</details>


### [215] [Verifiable, Articulable, and Tacit Components of Preference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03025)
*Alexander Spangher,Sheldon Huang,Andreas Haupt,Noah D. Goodman,Diyi Yang,Daniel E. Ho,Sanmi Koyejo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates "tacit knowledge" in human preferences across 7 creative domains (math, software engineering, news, patents, peer review, creative writing, etc.). Using a large dataset of 2.8M texts with 317M human preference judgments, the authors measure "articulability gaps" (tacit knowledge that can't be articulated) and "verifiability gaps" (tacit knowledge that can't be verified). They find these gaps exist even in supposedly "verifiable" domains like mathematics and software engineering, and that articulating preferences actually shifts them away from the tacit dimension (analogous to Goodhart's law).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern AI improvement relies on articulated constitutions, rubrics, and verifiers (RLAIF/RLVR), but the tacit components of preferences are understudied. The authors seek to quantify these gaps and understand their implications for AI alignment.

Method: The authors created the CreativePreferences dataset (2.8M texts, 317M human judgments, 7 domains, 42 tasks). They trained three model types: V (verifiable), A (articulable), and VAT (combined). They developed a novel measurement approach using capture-recapture to estimate bounds for articulability and verifiability gaps, discovering articulable/verifiable metrics while identifying spurious variables.

Result: Robust articulability gaps (VAT-VA) and verifiability gaps (VAT-V) exist across all domains, including traditionally "verifiable" domains (math, software engineering, news, patents, peer review). Gap size varies by domain (peer review and creative writing have largest articulability gaps). Gaps widen with more judges, consistent with Collins' collective tacit knowledge. The full model (VAT) matches human preferences better than articulated criteria alone. Articulating preferences shifts them away from the tacit dimension (Goodhart's law analogy).

Conclusion: Articulability and verifiability gaps are consequential for AI development. The authors recommend: (1) when tasks can be prompted, (2) how learning mechanisms might improve, and (3) when to leave judgments with humans. The tacit dimension of preferences cannot be fully captured by articulated criteria, suggesting limitations in current RLAIF/RLVR approaches.

Abstract: What makes a short story gripping; a news article newsworthy; or a math proof elegant? These constructs resist articulation or verification; their meaning is at least partially tacit. However, modern AI models are improved primarily via articulated constitutions, rubrics and verifiers (i.e. in RLAIF and RLVR); tacit components of preferences are typically understudied. We introduce a large, labeled preference dataset CreativePreferences, containing 2.8M texts labeled by 317M human preference judgments across 7 creative domains, with 42 benchmark tasks. We model these labels with executable programs, rubric banks and densely trained models (V, A and VAT, respectively). We observe robust articulability gaps, VAT-VA; and verifiability gaps, VAT-V; we estimate upper and lower bounds for each gap with a novel measurement approach that discovers articulable and verifiable metrics, identifies spurious variables and estimates the value of undiscovered metrics using capture-recapture. These gaps occur across all domains, even in domains traditionally treated as fully verifiable: correctness-centered domains (i.e. mathematics and software engineering) and claim- and novelty-centric domains (i.e. news, patents, peer review). The size of the gap varies based on domain (e.g. peer review and creative writing have the largest articulability gaps) and widens as more people take part in the judgment, consistent with Collins' collective tacit knowledge. We show two consequences: (1) on human generations, the full model more closely matches human preferences, often in disagreement with articulated criteria, and (2) in an analogy to Goodhart's law, articulating preference shifts it away from the tacit dimension. Articulability and verifiability gaps are consequential; we give recommendations on when tasks can be prompted; how learning mechanisms might improve; and when to leave judgments with humans.

</details>


### [216] [SoftGene: Protein Language Model-Enhanced Soft Prompting for Interpretable Gene Set Annotation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03029)
*Drew Ross,Arya Hadizadeh Moghaddam,Dongjie Wang,Xiaoyu Zhang,Zijun Yao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SoftGene is a novel LLM-based gene set annotation framework that integrates protein sequence information from ESM (a protein language model) with hybrid prompting (soft + hard prompts) to improve automatic annotation of gene sets from Gene Ontology and MSigDB databases.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Gene set analysis is currently labor-intensive and heavily dependent on manual curation. Existing LLM-based approaches rely only on symbolic gene names and fail to capture domain-specific biological structure, particularly protein sequence information that governs molecular activity, interactions, and downstream gene function.

Method: 1) Hierarchical attention-based encoder built on ESM (protein language model) to represent gene sets using protein-level amino acid sequence information; 2) Hybrid prompting scheme combining soft prompts (derived from gene set embeddings) with hard prompts (auxiliary context generated by an LLM); 3) Feed the combined prompt into a local LLM for annotation.

Result: Integrating protein-sequence representations with textual context improves gene set annotation overall. However, per-domain analyses reveal that the contribution of protein embeddings varies across biological domains.

Conclusion: SoftGene successfully leverages hierarchical gene set structure and protein sequence information to enhance LLM-based gene set annotation, with varying effectiveness across different biological domains.

Abstract: Gene set analysis is a cornerstone of functional genomics, yet it remains labor-intensive and heavily dependent on manual curation and expert biological interpretation. While Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged as powerful tools for genomic reasoning and annotation, most existing approaches rely on symbolic gene names and fail to capture domain-specific biological structure, particularly protein sequence information that governs molecular activity, interactions, and downstream gene function. In this work, we propose SoftGene, a novel framework for LLM-based gene set annotation that leverages the hierarchical structure of gene sets. First, we use a hierarchical attention-based encoder built on ESM, a protein language model, to represent each gene set using protein-level amino acid sequence information. Second, we construct a hybrid prompting scheme that combines soft prompts derived from gene set embeddings with hard prompts containing auxiliary context generated by an LLM, and feed the resulting prompt into a local LLM for annotation. We evaluate our framework on two benchmark datasets: Gene Ontology (GO) and the Molecular Signatures Database (MSigDB). Our results show that integrating protein-sequence representations with textual context improves gene set annotation overall, while per-domain analyses reveal that the contribution of protein embeddings varies across biological domains.

</details>


### [217] [When Numbers Start Talking: Numerical Signalling and Strategic Behaviour Among LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03033)
*Alessio Buscemi,Daniele Proverbio,Alessandro Di Stefano,The Anh Han,German Castignani,Pietro Liò*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Summary generation failed


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Motivation analysis unavailable

Method: Method extraction failed

Result: Result analysis unavailable

Conclusion: Conclusion extraction failed

Abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based agents increasingly operate in multi-agent systems (MAS) characterised by strategic interaction. However, little is known about whether, and to what extent, different types of messages affect the outcomes of strategic games. By investigating AI agents based on four popular LLMs, playing four games with different cooperation equilibria, we study whether messages of different kinds (natural language, numerical signals, or random sequences) significantly modify the levels of cooperation in each game, also depending on the agents' assigned personalities. We observe that structured messages alter the final payoffs for most games and LLMs, but without a predictable pattern; this challenges the assumption that AI agents can converge to stable equilibria regardless of additional capabilities. Moreover, we observe that agent-generated numerical messages depart from randomness, most strongly and consistently when agents are explicitly instructed to communicate; however, they introduce an additional interpretability challenge, as their symbol distributions are mostly associated with the payoff structure and typically become more concentrated with repetition, but are overall difficult for humans to interpret. Monitoring for coordination of AI agents through restricted channels should thus prioritise message-level fingerprints, which generalise across models, over behavioural decisions, which do not.

</details>


### [218] [hacktrace: behavior-supervised detection of reward hacking during code generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03055)
*Hao Jiang,Xin Li,Annan Wang,Yichi Zhang,Weisi Lin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses reward hacking in coding agents, where agents can earn passing grades by either fixing bugs or deleting tests that expose bugs. The authors introduce HACKTRACE, a behavior-supervised monitor that uses internal generation states to detect shortcut attempts without additional LLM calls, achieving 0.997 AUC with 8ms overhead. Combined with GRPO penalties, it reduces cheating from 82-91% to 1-5% while preserving honest solutions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Coding agents can exploit reward signals by taking shortcuts like deleting tests that expose bugs rather than fixing the actual code. Current detection methods either run the model again on honesty questions (high latency) or only analyze final outputs (too late). There is a need for accurate, low-latency detection of reward hacking that can provide useful training signals.

Method: The authors release 173,561 annotated multi-turn coding trajectories from Qwen3-8B. They propose HACKTRACE, which monitors internal states already computed during code generation (without additional LLM tokens or passes). They supervise shortcut behavior independently of exploit success and combine internal state evidence with static features of final files.

Result: HACKTRACE achieves mean per-problem AUC of 0.997 with only 8ms monitoring overhead, outperforming monitors that run the model again on honesty Q&A. When combined with strong GRPO penalties, it reduces the cheating share of passing solutions from 82-91% to 1-5%, while retaining honest, correct solutions and maintaining high detection accuracy as the policy evolves.

Conclusion: Both the supervision target (shortcut behavior independent of exploit success) and the source of monitoring evidence (internal generation states) are critical for turning accurate detection into a useful training signal. This approach enables effective detection and mitigation of reward hacking in coding agents with minimal latency overhead.

Abstract: A coding agent can earn a passing grade by fixing its code, or by deleting the test that exposes the bug. Detecting such reward hacking requires recognizing attempted shortcuts, including those that fail. We release 173,561 annotated multi-turn coding trajectories from Qwen3-8B and show that supervising shortcut behavior independently of exploit success substantially improves detection. We introduce HACKTRACE, a behavior-supervised monitor that reads the internal states the agent already computes while generating code. Reusing these states enables monitoring before a turn is complete, without additional language-model tokens or passes. Combining this evidence with static features of the final files achieves a mean per-problem AUC of 0.997 with 8 ms of monitoring overhead, improving both accuracy and latency over monitors that run the model again on an honesty question and answer. The same generation states also provide an inexpensive monitoring signal for reinforcement learning. With strong GRPO penalties, HACKTRACE reduces the cheating share of passing solutions from 82-91% to 1-5%, while retaining honest, correct solutions and maintaining high detection accuracy as the policy evolves. Our results show that both the supervision target and the source of monitoring evidence matter for turning accurate detection into a useful training signal.

</details>


### [219] [MOF-VERIFY: A Failure-Aware Agentic Harness for MOF Hypothesis Verification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03056)
*Donghyun Lee,Taehoon Lee,Geonhee Ahn,Jieun Kim,Jihyun Park,Suyeon Cho,Yoona Kim,Chaerim Shin,Hoi Ri Moon,Jonggeol Na,Sukho Hong,Jihwan Oh,Soo Kyung Kim*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces a diagnostic benchmark (T-MOF) for evaluating Large Language Models as reasoning components in AI-driven materials Co-Scientists, specifically for verifying hypotheses about Metal-Organic Frameworks (MOFs). The benchmark covers four task families and three evaluation settings, identifying failure modes in knowledge access, evidence acquisition, and reasoning. Based on these diagnostics, the authors develop MOF-Verify, an agentic harness that improves hypothesis-verification performance across multiple backbone LLMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The reliability of LLMs as reasoning components in AI-driven materials Co-Scientists remains unclear. MOFs present a challenging setting due to: (1) structures appearing under different identifiers, (2) synthesis outcomes depending on experimental conditions, (3) evidence distributed across heterogeneous sources, and (4) hypotheses requiring computation rather than literature alone.

Method: The authors introduce a diagnostic benchmark with four task families: (1) structural grounding, (2) synthesis-condition verification, (3) evidence-sufficiency verification, and (4) MLIP-based computational verification. Evaluation is conducted under three settings: closed-book, retrieval-enabled, and oracle-evidence. T-MOF-4 separately evaluates computational verification. Based on diagnosed failure modes, MOF-Verify is developed as a failure-aware agentic harness targeting structural, literature, evidence-sufficiency, and computational bottlenecks.

Result: MOF-Verify substantially improves hypothesis-verification performance over direct inference and retrieval-based baselines across multiple backbone LLMs. The benchmark identifies specific failure modes in knowledge access, evidence acquisition, and reasoning.

Conclusion: The diagnostic approach successfully localizes failures in the verification pipeline, enabling the development of MOF-Verify which targets specific bottlenecks. This failure-aware agentic harness demonstrates significant improvements in verification reliability for materials science hypothesis testing.

Abstract: Large language models are increasingly used as reasoning components in AI-driven materials Co-Scientists, yet the reliability of the resulting verification pipeline remains unclear. Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) provide a particularly challenging setting because structures may appear under different identifiers, synthesis outcomes depend strongly on experimental conditions, evidence is distributed across heterogeneous sources, and some hypotheses require computation rather than literature alone. We introduce a diagnostic benchmark with four task families covering structural grounding, synthesis-condition verification, evidence-sufficiency verification, and MLIP-based computational verification. T-MOF-1-3 are evaluated under closed-book, retrieval-enabled, and oracle-evidence settings to localize failures in knowledge access, evidence acquisition, and reasoning, while T-MOF-4 separately evaluates computational verification. Guided by these diagnosed failure modes, we develop MOF-Verify, a failure-aware agentic harness that targets structural, literature, evidence-sufficiency, and computational bottlenecks before producing a final verdict. Across multiple backbone LLMs, MOF-Verify substantially improves hypothesis-verification performance over direct inference and retrieval-based baselines. Benchmark datasets are released at https://github.com/IMMS-Ewha/MOF-Verify-Benchmark.

</details>


### [220] [RIFAR: Reliability and Forgetting-Aware Replay for Continual Robot Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03079)
*Zirong Song,Zheng Lu,Haoran Liao,Wanqi Zhong,Yunhe Ni,Lijie Wang,Xiuying Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RIFAR is a continual learning method for robots that combines reliability screening with drift-aware replay selection to prevent catastrophic forgetting while maintaining computational efficiency. It uses world-action models for generative replay, assessing action-visual consistency through inverse-dynamics models and selecting high-quality historical trajectories for rehearsal.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Genuine embodied agency requires robots to continuously learn new skills without eroding prior knowledge as tasks and environments evolve. Existing experience replay methods store complete demonstrations, which becomes costly as tasks accumulate. World-action models offer a generative alternative but face challenges with visually coherent rollouts containing unrealizable actions, and new-task adaptation can disrupt previously learned behavior.

Method: RIFAR combines reliability screening with drift-aware replay selection. It reconstructs trajectories from compact demonstration prefixes and uses a frozen inverse-dynamics model to assess action-visual consistency. Training proceeds in two phases: (1) combine current demonstrations with highest-quality screened trajectories, (2) compare action predictions before and after adaptation on identical historical inputs, then reselect trajectories with larger normalized drift from the screened pool for continued training.

Result: RIFAR surpasses the previous state of the art in WAM-based generative replay across three LIBERO suites and real-world experiments. On LIBERO-Goal, it achieves 90.97 AUC while retaining only 320 historical time steps per task, approximately 4.9% of the steps retained using 50-demonstration replay.

Conclusion: RIFAR successfully enables efficient continual learning for robots by using compact demonstration prefixes and intelligent trajectory selection, achieving superior performance with significantly reduced memory requirements compared to existing generative replay approaches.

Abstract: Genuine embodied agency requires robots to turn continuous real-world experience into lasting, transferable skills. This demands continual learning that integrates new capabilities without eroding prior knowledge as tasks and environments evolve. Experience replay mitigates forgetting, but storing complete demonstrations becomes costly as tasks accumulate. World-action models offer a generative alternative, reconstructing past experience through joint predictions of actions and future observations. However, visually coherent rollouts may contain actions that cannot realize the predicted transitions, while new-task adaptation can disrupt previously learned behavior. RIFAR therefore combines reliability screening with drift-aware replay selection. It reconstructs trajectories from compact demonstration prefixes and uses a frozen inverse-dynamics model to assess action-visual consistency. Training first combines current demonstrations with the highest-quality screened trajectories. RIFAR then compares action predictions before and after this adaptation on identical historical inputs, reselecting trajectories with larger normalized drift from the same screened pool for continued training. Across three LIBERO suites and real-world experiments, RIFAR surpasses the previous state of the art in WAM-based generative replay. On LIBERO-Goal, it achieves 90.97 AUC while retaining only 320 historical time steps per task, approximately 4.9% of the steps retained using 50-demonstration replay.

</details>


### [221] [Peer Influence across Heterogeneous AI Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03095)
*Frida Nøhr Laustsen,Marie Haahr Petersen,Victoria Popa,Ariel Flint,Romualdo Pastor-Satorras,Andrea Baronchelli,Luca Maria Aiello*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: When two AI agents disagree, the receiver often abandons its initial judgment after seeing a peer's answer and explanation. Persuasion depends more on the listener's susceptibility than the speaker's persuasiveness, and interaction outcomes cannot be predicted from individual model properties alone.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As multi-agent systems increasingly combine language models of different families and sizes, understanding which judgments survive interaction becomes critical. The key question is: when two AI agents disagree, who persuades whom?

Method: Measured persuasion as the probabilistic shift in an agent's decision after a single exchange with a dissenting peer. Tested seven open-weight models across three language understanding tasks.

Result: Persuasion is strong: receivers often abandon initial judgments after seeing peer's answer and explanation. Neither standalone certainty nor model scale reliably predicts persuasion dynamics. Models with highly consistent decisions in isolation can be most susceptible. Small models can match larger ones as persuaders and resist influence equally. The shift depends more on listener susceptibility than speaker persuasiveness. Persuasion is specific to each model pairing - heterogeneity can amplify or suppress persuasion, allowing small models to overturn larger ones' judgments.

Conclusion: Behavior of interacting models cannot be inferred from individual properties; must be evaluated in the specific combinations in which they will operate.

Abstract: When two AI agents disagree, who persuades whom? As multi-agent systems increasingly combine language models of different families and sizes, the answer can determine which judgments survive interaction. Measuring persuasion as the probabilistic shift in an agent's decision after a single exchange with a dissenting peer, we test seven open-weight models across three language understanding tasks. We find that persuasion is strong: when models disagree, receivers often abandon their initial judgment after seeing a peer's answer and explanation. Surprisingly, however, neither standalone certainty nor model scale reliably predicts persuasion dynamics. Models producing almost perfectly consistent decisions in isolation can be among the most susceptible to persuasion, and small models can match larger ones as persuaders and resist their influence just as effectively. Furthermore, we show that the size of the shift depends more on the susceptibility of the listener than on the persuasiveness of the speaker. Persuasion patterns are therefore specific to each model pairing, with heterogeneity amplifying persuasion in some combinations and suppressing it in others, allowing a dissenting agent running a small model to overturn the judgments of a much larger one. These findings show that the behavior of interacting models cannot be inferred from their individual properties but must be evaluated in the combinations in which they will operate.

</details>


### [222] [Predictor-Guided Latent Space Codon Optimization for Maximizing Protein Expression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03098)
*Alberto Caron,Tianyu Cui,Dmytro S. Lituiev,Mangal Prakash,Artem Moskalev,Amina Mollaysa,Bo Zhai,Hirsh Nanda,Daniel M. Poole,Zhongyin Liu,Iman Farasat,Robert Davidson,Nikolay V. Manyakov,Tommaso Mansi,Scott Oloff,Rui Liao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LSCO introduces a gradient-based codon optimization method by mapping discrete sequences into the latent space of a pretrained mRNA language model, combining expression prediction, structural stability, naturalness, and protein fidelity constraints.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Codon optimization is critical for therapeutic protein and mRNA vaccine production, but existing tools rely on poor heuristics (CAI, GC-content) that don't capture true expression efficiency. The discrete, combinatorial nature of the problem has precluded gradient-based optimization.

Method: 1) Map codon sequences to latent space of pretrained mRNA language model; 2) Use uncertainty-aware expression predictor as data-driven objective; 3) Add Minimum-Free-Energy regularizer for structural stability; 4) Incorporate naturalness prior from protein-to-codon back-translation model; 5) Apply constrained decoding for protein fidelity.

Result: On a real-world wet-lab antibody expression dataset, LSCO outperforms both frequency-based methods and modern deep generative baselines in predicted expression while retaining suitable biophysical properties.

Conclusion: Recasting discrete codon optimization as a continuous latent space search enables effective gradient-based optimization, achieving superior expression predictions while maintaining biophysical constraints.

Abstract: Codon optimization, the process of selecting synonymous codons to improve mRNA translation efficiency and protein expression, is central to therapeutic protein production and mRNA vaccines, yet it remains a hard problem. The design space is discrete and combinatorially large, precluding gradient-based methods, and existing tools rely on heuristic proxies (e.g., Codon Adaptation Index or GC-content) that poorly capture true expression. We introduce Latent-Space Codon Optimization (LSCO), which recasts this discrete problem as a continuous one by mapping sequences into the latent space of a pretrained mRNA language model, enabling efficient gradient-based search. LSCO combines four components: a data-driven expression objective from an uncertainty-aware predictor, a Minimum-Free-Energy regularizer for structural stability, a naturalness prior from a protein-to-codon back-translation model, and constrained decoding for protein fidelity. On a real-world, wet-lab antibody expression dataset, LSCO outperforms simple frequency-based, as well as modern deep generative baselines in predicted expression, while retaining suitable biophysical properties.

</details>


### [223] [Trading Strategy Optimization via Textual Gradient](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03128)
*Chaoqun Yang,Qian Wang,Fengbin Zhu,Xinyu Lin,Bingsheng He,Roger Zimmermann,Tat-Seng Chua*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TradeGrad is an LLM-based framework for quantitative trading strategy optimization that addresses myopic optimization and temporal robustness challenges through experience-guided textual gradients and a Cross-Period Robust Objective (CPRO). It achieves 27.99% annualized return with 1.63 Sharpe ratio on Chinese A-share markets, outperforming CSI 300 by 68%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Quantitative trading strategy design faces two key challenges: (1) optimization is myopic, underutilizing experience from previous evaluations; and (2) aggregate backtest feedback overlooks temporal robustness, potentially favoring strategies that only perform well in specific market periods. Existing LLM-based textual gradients lack mechanisms to address these issues.

Method: TradeGrad proposes: (1) Experience-guided textual gradients leveraging accumulated optimization experience to estimate gradients instead of relying solely on current evaluation; (2) Multi-scale revisions for both strategy exploration and refinement; (3) Cross-Period Robust Objective (CPRO) that emphasizes performance in unfavorable historical periods to promote temporal robustness.

Result: Experiments on Chinese A-share and U.S. equity markets across cross-sectional and time-series strategies show TradeGrad achieves best in-sample and out-of-sample performance across all four settings. The Chinese cross-sectional strategy achieves 27.99% annualized return, 12.19% maximum drawdown, and Sharpe ratio of 1.63, approximately 68% higher than the CSI 300 benchmark.

Conclusion: TradeGrad provides a novel LLM-based framework for robust trading strategy optimization that effectively addresses myopic optimization and temporal robustness challenges. The proposed experience-guided textual gradients and CPRO objective significantly improve both in-sample and out-of-sample performance across different market types and strategy designs.

Abstract: Quantitative trading strategy design aims to discover trading programs from historical data that remain effective in future markets, which can be viewed as a black-box program optimization problem. LLM-based textual gradients offer a promising approach by providing explicit optimization directions for iterative strategy refinement. However, directly applying textual gradients faces two challenges: (1) optimization is myopic, underutilizing experience from previous evaluations; and (2) aggregate backtest feedback overlooks temporal robustness, potentially favoring strategies that perform well only in specific market periods. To address these challenges, we propose TradeGrad, an experience-guided textual-gradient framework for robust trading strategy optimization. TradeGrad leverages accumulated optimization experience to estimate textual gradients and employs multi-scale revisions for both strategy exploration and refinement. It further introduces the Cross-Period Robust Objective (CPRO), which emphasizes performance in unfavorable historical periods to promote temporal robustness. Experiments on cross-sectional and time-series strategy design in Chinese A-share and U.S. equity markets show that TradeGrad achieves the best in-sample and out-of-sample performance across all four settings. Notably, its Chinese cross-sectional strategy achieves 27.99% annualized return, 12.19% maximum drawdown, and a Sharpe ratio of 1.63, approximately 68% higher than the CSI 300 benchmark. Further analyses validate the proposed components and show consistent improvements in both in-sample and out-of-sample performance throughout optimization. The code is available at https://github.com/transcend-0/TradeGrad.

</details>


### [224] [Keeping JEPA World Models Plannable When Little of the Frame Moves](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03137)
*Florian Strohm,Patrick Wagner,Jannik Schwab,Marco Huber*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces SLIM, a pushing benchmark with visual and language goals, to test latent world models. A LeWM model fails badly (under 1% success) due to an action-insensitive encoder. Adding an inverse-dynamics auxiliary loss repairs the encoder, raising success to 0.35. A language-goal head then enables planning from sentences without retraining the world model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Testing language-specified goals in latent world models requires discriminative scenes. Current methods fail when the encoder produces action-insensitive latents, preventing the world model from planning.

Method: 1) Build SLIM benchmark with pushing tasks and paired visual/language goals on identical scenes. 2) Diagnose failure using probes (decoder action-sensitivity, position decoding, rollout quality). 3) Apply inverse-dynamics auxiliary loss to encoder latents and predicted latents via shared head (discarded at test time). 4) Add language-goal head on repaired latent for sentence-based planning.

Result: The auxiliary loss restored all probes and raised success from 0.003 to 0.35 (0.16 on hard tier). The language-goal head achieved 0.84 on navigation (vs 1.00 oracle), followed named zones when swapped with decoys, and raised medium/hard tier success from 0.04 to 0.25 using stage sentences.

Conclusion: Action-sensitivity in the latent encoder is empirically necessary for planning. An inverse-dynamics auxiliary loss repairs this. A cheap action-sensitivity probe can predict failure without environment access. Language goals can be added to a repaired world model without retraining the core model.

Abstract: Specifying a goal in language rather than as a goal frame is a natural interface for planning with a latent world model, but testing it needs scenes in which language must discriminate between several objects. We build SLIM, a pushing benchmark with several small objects and paired visual and language goals on identical scenes. On SLIM a LeWM world model that solves PushT succeeds on under 1% of trials, although a scripted controller with simulator state solves every tier. Probes locate the failure in the encoder: its latent is nearly action-insensitive, neither pusher nor object positions can be decoded from it, and rollouts are no better than copying the current latent forward. One inverse-dynamics auxiliary loss, applied to encoder latents and to predicted latents through a shared head discarded at test time, restores every probe and raises success from 0.003 to 0.35 (0.16 on the hard pushing tier, where a goal-agnostic policy scores zero), and improves PushT at twice the trained horizon. Controls attribute the repair to the gradient into the encoder, and a response sweep shows that the vanilla model plans once enough of the frame responds to actions. A cheap action-sensitivity probe, computable without environment access, acts as an empirical necessary condition: all configurations below its threshold failed to plan. On the repaired latent, a small language-goal head plans from sentences without retraining the world model: it reaches 0.84 on navigation (visual-goal oracle 1.00), follows the named zone when it is swapped with a decoy, and degrades gracefully to unseen nouns. A single goal sentence rarely completes a push, but given the push as a sequence of stage sentences the head raises success on the medium and hard pushing tiers from 0.04 to 0.25, on par with the goal-frame oracle, also when the switch between stages is read from the latent alone.

</details>


### [225] [Gains and Collapse in On-Policy Distillation:A Reinforcement Learning Perspective](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03185)
*Han Cui,Jianhao Yan,Yun Luo,Hongbo Zhang,Zhizhang Fu,Yue Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates why on-policy distillation (OPD) in language model post-training sometimes improves performance while other times causes collapse into excessively long and repetitive generation. The authors explain this dichotomy through a reinforcement learning perspective, showing that the teacher implicitly rewards student behaviors even when it rarely generates such outputs itself.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite OPD's performance gains in language model post-training, it can collapse into excessively long and repetitive generation. The mechanism underlying these divergent outcomes was poorly understood, prompting this investigation.

Method: The authors analyzed OPD through a reinforcement learning perspective, examining how the teacher's implicit reward model affects student behaviors. They conducted experiments to understand when OPD improves performance versus when it causes reward hacking.

Result: When the implicit reward model is reliable, OPD makes correct responses easier to sample without expanding student capabilities. When preferences misalign with quality, reward hacking occurs - the implicit reward model amplifies overlong, repetitive student rollouts, even though the teacher rarely generates such text itself. Two mitigation strategies were identified: masking unhealthy responses during training and using SFT initialization.

Conclusion: OPD amplifies student behaviors favored by the teacher's implicit feedback. The key factor is not how well the teacher generates, but how reliably it evaluates student rollouts. This shifts the focus from generation quality to evaluation reliability in OPD.

Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) has become an important approach to language model post-training. However, despite its performance gains, OPD can also collapse into excessively long and repetitive generation, and the mechanism underlying these divergent outcomes remains poorly understood. We explain these outcomes through a reinforcement learning perspective: the teacher implicitly rewards student behaviors, even those it rarely exhibits itself. From this perspective, our experiments show that OPD improves performance without expanding the student's capabilities. When the implicit reward model is reliable, OPD makes correct responses easier to sample. In contrast, when the preference misaligns with quality, reward hacking happens: the implicit reward model amplifies overlong, repetitive student rollouts, even though it rarely generates such text itself. Guided by this diagnosis, we find that masking unhealthy responses during training and using SFT initialization can each effectively mitigate the collapse. Together, these findings show that OPD amplifies student behaviors favored by the teacher's implicit feedback, shifting the focus from how well the teacher generates to how reliably it evaluates student rollouts. Our code is available at https://github.com/HancCui/opd_hacking.

</details>


### [226] [KV$^2$: A Self-Refining KV Cache](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03198)
*Johannes Wesch,Danni Liu,Jan Niehues*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: KV² is a query-agnostic KV-cache compression method that uses selective reconstruction - first identifying informative tokens with a lightweight proxy scorer, then reprocessing only that subset for final eviction scores. This approach achieves significant improvements over baselines, especially at low budgets (40+ percentage points on RULER 16K at 2% budget), while requiring lower runtime and peak memory than full-context reconstruction methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The memory footprint of KV cache constrains practical use of long-context models, particularly in reusable settings where one prefilled context must serve many different queries. Existing approaches either use lightweight estimators (cheap but inaccurate) or full-context reconstruction (accurate but expensive).

Method: KV² uses a two-stage selective reconstruction approach: (1) A lightweight proxy scorer identifies informative in-context tokens, (2) Only this subset is reprocessed to compute final eviction scores. This selective approach avoids reprocessing the entire prompt.

Result: On RULER 16K at 2% KV-cache budget, KV² improves average score by over 40 percentage points over the next-best baseline. On LongBench, it achieves the highest average across 2%-10% budgets while requiring lower compression-stage runtime and peak memory than full-context reconstruction.

Conclusion: Full-context reprocessing is not necessary for effective reusable KV-cache compression. Selective reconstruction provides a favorable trade-off between accuracy and computational cost.

Abstract: The memory footprint of the key-value (KV) cache constrains the practical use of long-context models, and it dominates cost when one prefilled context must later serve many different queries. In this reusable setting, query-agnostic compression trades cost against quality: lightweight estimators are cheap but less accurate, whereas full-context reconstruction scoring is more accurate yet reprocesses the entire prompt. We introduce KV$^2$, a query-agnostic KV-cache compression method based on selective reconstruction. KV$^2$ first uses a lightweight proxy scorer to identify informative in-context tokens, then reprocesses only this subset to compute final eviction scores. On RULER, Needle-in-a-Haystack, and LongBench, KV$^2$'s margin over baselines widens as the budget tightens: on RULER 16K at a 2% KV-cache budget it improves the average score over the next-best baseline by more than 40 percentage points, and on LongBench it attains the highest average across 2%-10% budgets at lower compression-stage runtime and peak memory than full-context reconstruction. Reusable KV-cache compression thus does not require reprocessing the full context. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/KVsquared-0B97.

</details>


### [227] [Toward SLM-based agentic task-tool intent matching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03213)
*Chiara Troiani,Arash Salarian,Majed El Helou,Benjamin Ryder,Jean Diaconu,Hervé Muyal,Marcelo Yannuzzi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates using Small Language Models (SLMs) as task-tool relevance classifiers to verify that AI agent tool calls align with task intent. The authors address a security gap where conventional authorization can check if an agent is allowed to make a call, but cannot assess whether the tool selection is logically relevant to the task. They use prompt-optimization, supervised fine-tuning, and GRPO to optimize SLMs on a novel dataset of multi-tool tasks spanning MCP servers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Tool-equipped AI agents require automated, low-latency oversight to verify that tool selections align with task intent. Conventional authorization schemes can only determine if an agent is allowed to invoke a tool, but cannot assess whether the tool selection represents a logical, relevant step toward satisfying the task. A rogue agent might deviate calls or nudge other agents to make calls that don't align with the task intent, so every call needs verification.

Method: The authors propose using Small Language Models (SLMs) as task-tool relevance classifiers that evaluate every selected tool independently against the assigned task and return a relevance signal for downstream enforcement. They employed three optimization techniques: prompt-optimization, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning through GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization). The experiments use a novel dataset with multi-tool tasks whose required tools span distinct Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers.

Result: The abstract does not report specific quantitative results or findings.

Conclusion: The abstract does not include explicit conclusions; it appears to be a work-in-progress or methodology-focused paper presenting an approach for using SLMs to verify tool-task relevance in multi-agent AI systems.

Abstract: Tool-equipped AI agents use tool calls to access data and act on external systems. Horizontal growth of agentic systems increases the number of these interactions, and further motivates the need for automated, per-call oversight that can operate at low latency and/or on-prem. Conventional authorization schemes can determine whether an agent is allowed to invoke a tool, but cannot assess the agent's underlying cognition, specifically, whether the tool selection represents a logical, relevant step toward satisfying the intent of the task or not. Consequently, an allowed call may still deviate from the task's intent: a rogue agent might deviate the calls or nudge other agents to make a combination of calls that would not align with the intent of the task. Therefore, every call needs to be verified. In this study we investigate the applicability of Small Language Models (SLMs) to this purpose: an SLM functions as a task-tool relevance classifier that evaluates every selected tool independently against the assigned task and returns a relevance signal for downstream enforcement. Equipped with a novel dataset with multi-tool tasks whose required tools span distinct Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, we used prompt-optimization, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning through GRPO to optimize and specialize SLMs.

</details>


### [228] [Learning a Fact Is Not Learning How to Retrieve It](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03251)
*Chaemin Jang,Jihee Kim,Dongman Lee*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates how language models learn to retrieve factual knowledge and demonstrates that the request form used during training (e.g., "The capital of X is Y" vs "The capital of X:") significantly affects later retrieval. The authors propose a two-stage training approach separating fact learning from retrieval mechanisms, and identify the "context state" (hidden state before answer) as a key factor determining whether a learned fact can be retrieved.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to understand why language models can retrieve the same factual information when prompted in one format but fail when using a different format for the same fact, even though the underlying knowledge exists. This addresses the fundamental question of how models separate learning a fact from learning to retrieve it.

Method: The authors use a two-stage training paradigm: (1) Request-form training stage where one model sees each fact in five different request forms while another sees only statements; (2) Target-fact training stage where both models receive identical training on new facts as statements. They analyze the "context state" (hidden state immediately before the answer token) and test interventions by manipulating this state during training and retrieval.

Result: Models trained on diverse request forms in stage one produce more similar context states for different request formats of the same fact compared to models trained on statements alone. The context state at retrieval time can enable or prevent fact retrieval, and this effect transfers across facts and relations (e.g., capitals and currencies). Changing the context state only during target-fact training alters later retrieval performance without intervention at test time.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that later retrieval performance depends on earlier request-form experience and the context state during fact learning. This demonstrates that learning a fact and learning to retrieve it are separable processes, and the request forms used during training significantly influence the model's retrieval capabilities.

Abstract: A model trained on "The capital of X is Y" may produce "Y" after "The capital of X is" but fail after "The capital of X:". We call these different ways of eliciting the same fact request forms. To separate learning a fact from retrieving it, we train two models in two stages. In the first stage (request-form training), one model sees each fact in five forms and the other sees the same facts only as statements. In the second stage (target-fact training), both receive identical training on new facts, all as statements. Both then retrieve the new facts almost equally well from statements, but differ sharply on other request forms. Thus, a model can learn how to retrieve through a request form before it learns the facts. To understand this difference, we examine the hidden state immediately before the answer, which we call the context state. When given two different request forms for the same fact, the model trained on five forms in stage one produces more similar context states than the model trained on statements alone in that stage. Changing this state at retrieval time can enable or prevent retrieval of an already learned fact, and the same effect transfers across facts and factual relations, such as capitals and currencies. To test its role during learning, we change the context state only during target-fact training. This intervention changes later retrieval without intervention at test time. Together, these results show that later retrieval depends on earlier request-form experience and the context state during fact learning.

</details>


### [229] [EVOL: Simulator-Guided Evolutionary Expert Synthesis for Deployment-Free Learning Path Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03273)
