Specifically, HazardWeaver first leverages the Hazard Knowledge Compiler to extract evidence-linked conditions governing scientific applicability, then its Hazard Capability Graph represents executable scientific capabilities and checks compatibility between their inputs and outputs. Using these complementary representations, the Hazard Weaver Agent component selects applicable and executable routes, carries out their workflows, and revises its decisions as the analysis state changes. To evaluate both the scientific outputs and the decisions that produce them, we introduce the Hazard Weaver Benchmark, comprising 141 instances across seven single-hazard domains and four multi-hazard interaction classes. The benchmark accommodates multiple valid scientific routes and evaluates output correctness, route validity, and justified abstention. Extensive experiments on this benchmark show that HazardWeaver outperforms existing agent systems, with the largest gains on tasks with multiple eligible scientific routes. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/LabRAI/HazardWeaver.

</details>


### [252] [Depth as Time in One-Step Generative Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03626)
*Arnold Caleb Asiimwe,William Yang,Sanghyuk Chun,Esin Tureci,Olga Russakovsky*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: One-step generative models compress multi-step diffusion trajectories, but the denoising computation is reorganized across network depth rather than eliminated. The "depth as time" phenomenon shows that multi-step denoising unfolds across the depth of a single forward pass.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Understand what happens to the denoising trajectory of multi-step diffusion when generation is compressed into a single forward pass.

Method: Empirical observation of "depth as time": probing intermediate layers with the model's own output head; studying how different transport task training (MeanFlow vs drifting models) affects depthwise computation.

Result: Denoising computation unfolds across depth in single forward pass. MeanFlow shows both denoising and renoising within a single evaluation. Drifting models (no time-indexed transport) don't exhibit this. MeanFlow SiT-L/2 can be compressed by 16.6× in parameters into a single time-conditioned block.

Conclusion: The temporal computation of diffusion is not eliminated by one-step generation but reorganized across network depth. Models with depthwise denoising are more compressible across layerwise computation.

Abstract: The recent wave of one-step generative models, which compress the multi-step trajectory of diffusion via either distillation or learned flow maps, has reached an inflection point where they can generate high-quality images. Here, we ask a natural question that follows from these advances: what happens to the denoising trajectory of multi-step diffusion when generation is compressed into a single forward pass? We offer an empirical observation we call \textit{depth as time}: the denoising computation that multi-step diffusion performs across sampling steps appears to unfold across the depth of a single forward pass, and can be recovered by decoding intermediate layers with the model's own output head. Most interestingly, we show that this depthwise computation depends on the transport task a flow map is trained to solve. The most surprising case is MeanFlow, where probing shorter transport intervals reveals both denoising and renoising within a single network evaluation. In contrast, generators trained without a time-indexed transport task, such as drifting models, do not exhibit the same depthwise denoising. Consequently, we show that models that exhibit the depthwise denoising phenomenon are more compressible across the layerwise computation: a MeanFlow \texttt{SiT-L/2} model can be compressed by $16.6\times$ in parameters into a single time-conditioned block. We offer an explanation for this denoise-then-renoise behavior and show that, when we treat the layerwise computation explicitly as a flow, a single time-conditioned block can be trained to denoise across layers, compressing a MeanFlow \texttt{SiT-L/2} model by $16.6\times$ in parameters. Together, these results suggest that the temporal computation of diffusion is not eliminated by one-step generation, but reorganized across network depth.

</details>


### [253] [NeutronGym: Physics-Graded Neutron Instrument Design for LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03631)
*Lijie Ding,Changwoo Do*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: NeutronGym is the first executable environment for testing whether language model agents can actually design neutron instruments (doing physics) rather than just recalling memorized solutions. The environment uses McStas ray-tracing, provides level-resolved grading, and includes McStasBench with 16 tasks from published instruments. Testing revealed that frontier models solve only 7/16 tasks max, but RL training improved Qwen3-8B from 11% to 77% on held-out instances. The study analyzes what drives these gains and releases the probes used for detection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current benchmarks may only test memorization rather than genuine physics reasoning. The authors argue that if grading cannot be argued with (i.e., objective execution-based testing), we can determine whether LLM agents can actually "do physics" rather than simply recall it. This addresses concerns about whether language models can genuinely reason through physics problems or just retrieve memorized solutions.

Method: The researchers created NeutronGym, an executable environment where agents build neutron instruments through validating tools, McStas ray-traces what they build, and a level-resolved ladder grades syntax, runtime, structure and science with no LLM judge. They used procedural families supplying unlimited instances with design parameters agents must set, with held-out parameter regimes. McStasBench adds 16 tasks from published instruments behind memorization probes and a sandbox. They tested 7 models and performed RL training on Qwen3-8B using the environment's reward.

Result: Testing revealed: (1) Seven models reproduce at most 7 of the 16 McStasBench tasks, none retrieves a reference, and none meets an improvement target; (2) RL on the reward took Qwen3-8B from 11% to 77% of held-out instances (69% at a second seed); (3) This performance surpasses an untrained Qwen3-32B and generalizes to three further gated families; (4) Without the ladder's partial credit, performance collapses by 60 points; (5) From reward alone, the trained model reaches 77% vs 81% from classical optimizer, while frontier models achieve 98-99%; (6) Four task designs that no-model baselines could solve had to be failed to get trustworthy results.

Conclusion: The study demonstrates that LLM agents can learn to do physics-based instrument design through RL training in an executable environment, achieving significant improvements from 11% to 77%. However, even frontier models only solve 7/16 tasks, suggesting genuine physics reasoning remains challenging. The environment enables training, and the released probes help identify tasks that no model can solve, providing a more trustworthy benchmark for evaluating physics reasoning capabilities in language models.

Abstract: Designing a scientific instrument tests whether language-model agents can do physics rather than recall it, provided the grading cannot be argued with. We introduce NeutronGym, to our knowledge the first executable environment for neutron instrument design: agents build instruments through validating tools, McStas ray-traces what they build, and a level-resolved ladder grades syntax, runtime, structure and science with no LLM judge. Procedural families supply unlimited instances of a fixed layout whose design parameters the agent must set, with held-out parameter regimes; a curated slice, McStasBench, adds 16 tasks from published instruments behind memorization probes and a sandbox. Seven models reproduce at most 7 of the 16, none retrieves a reference, and none meets an improvement target. The environment also trains. Reinforcement learning on its reward takes Qwen3-8B from 11% to 77% of held-out instances of a family whose targets come from a hidden design (69% at a second seed), past an untrained Qwen3-32B, and the recipe holds, at one seed each, on three further gated families. The analysis says what that gain is. Without the ladder's partial credit it collapses by 60 points. From reward alone the trained model reaches what a classical optimizer reaches, at the agent's simulation budget, only when handed the closed-form physics (77% against 81%, a gap that does not separate at this size), while frontier models still solve 98-99%. Getting a trustworthy result meant failing four task designs that no-model baselines could solve, and we release the probes that found them.

</details>


### [254] [Credit Where It Matters: Dependency-Aware Policy Optimization for Terminal Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03634)
*Yu Li,Guangfeng Cai,Long-Fei Li,Shuo Han,Shengtian Yang,Han Luo,Kaibing Yang,Lei Feng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DepGPO addresses credit assignment in reinforcement learning for terminal-based agents by using execution dependencies between commands. It constructs a command dependency graph from execution traces and traces backward from resources inspected by the task verifier to assign credit to relevant writes and supporting reads along these paths.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In terminal-using agents for coding, debugging, and multi-step tasks, later commands often depend on information or intermediate results from earlier commands. Existing trajectory-level and step-level credit assignment methods do not explicitly trace read-write dependencies, causing training signals to be assigned to irrelevant operations and weakening learning from relevant steps.

Method: 1) Construct a command dependency graph from execution traces; 2) Trace backward from resources inspected by the task verifier; 3) Assign credit to relevant writes and their supporting reads along these dependency paths; 4) Redistribute trajectory advantages across steps using the assigned credit.

Result: DepGPO improves task performance and training stability on complex terminal tasks, as demonstrated by extensive comparative experiments and ablation studies.

Conclusion: By explicitly modeling execution dependencies between commands, DepGPO provides more accurate credit assignment in terminal-based RL agents, leading to better learning from relevant steps and improved overall performance.

Abstract: Terminal-using agents benefit from reinforcement learning (RL) in coding, debugging, and other multi-step terminal tasks. In these tasks, later commands often depend on information or intermediate results produced by earlier commands. However, existing trajectory-level and step-level credit assignment methods do not explicitly trace the read-write dependencies through which commands affect the final outcome. Consequently, training signals could still be assigned to irrelevant operations, weakening learning from relevant steps. In this paper, we propose Dependency-Aware Group Policy Optimization (DepGPO), which uses execution dependencies between commands to guide credit assignment for terminal agents. Specifically, we construct a command dependency graph from execution traces and trace backward from the resources inspected by the task verifier. We then assign credit to relevant writes and their supporting reads along these paths, and use it to redistribute trajectory advantages across steps. Extensive comparative experiments and ablation studies demonstrate that DepGPO improves task performance and training stability on complex terminal tasks.

</details>


### [255] [Do Large Language Models Know Colombian Law? A Reliability Benchmark for the Colombian Legal System](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03639)
*Rubén Manrique,Michelle Castellanos,Jorge Morales,Juan David Gutiérrez,Antonio Barreto Rozo,Joaquín Vélez Navarro*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces the first expert-validated benchmark for evaluating LLM reliability in the Colombian legal system, comprising 1,042 items across ten legal areas. Testing 15 models reveals significant performance gaps: closed-question accuracy ranges from 0.905 to 0.577, while free-text factual correctness never exceeds 0.45. The study identifies a critical dissociation between answer relevancy and correctness, where models sound responsive but are frequently wrong.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large language models are increasingly deployed in legal practice, education, and research, yet their reliability in non-US legal systems remains largely undocumented. This gap is particularly concerning given the high-stakes nature of legal applications where incorrect information could have serious consequences.

Method: The researchers developed a comprehensive benchmark through a human-in-the-loop pipeline with multi-stage expert review. The benchmark contains 1,042 items spanning ten areas of law with three question formats (closed multiple-choice, semi-open, and open-ended IRAC). They evaluated 15 contemporary proprietary and open-weight models using format-appropriate metrics. An independent rubric-based LLM judge and blind human expert scoring were used for validation.

Result: Key findings include: (1) Closed-question accuracy ranges from 0.905 (Gemini 3.1 Pro) to 0.577; (2) Free-text factual correctness never exceeds 0.45 for any model; (3) A dissociation exists between answer relevancy and correctness (Spearman rho = -0.46); (4) Closed-question accuracy and free-text correctness are strongly rank-correlated (rho = 0.94); (5) Only about half of the legal norms cited by models are correct; (6) Reliability varies by legal area and follows an inverted-U pattern across question complexity.

Conclusion: Current LLMs require expert supervision for Colombian legal tasks. The strong correlation between cheap multiple-choice screening and expensive free-text evaluation (rho = 0.94) suggests screening can predict model ranking but overstates absolute reliability. Grounding answers in authoritative sources is identified as a promising path to higher reliability. The benchmark construction pipeline is released to support reproducible evaluation.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to support legal practice, education, and research, yet their reliability in national legal systems outside the United States remains largely undocumented. We introduce an expert-validated benchmark for evaluating LLM reliability on the Colombian legal system. The benchmark comprises 1,042 items spanning ten areas of law and three question formats (closed multiple-choice, semi-open, and open-ended IRAC), built through a human-in-the-loop pipeline with multi-stage expert review. We evaluate 15 contemporary proprietary and open-weight models with format-appropriate metrics. Accuracy on closed questions ranges widely, from 0.905 (Gemini 3.1 Pro) to 0.577, but on free-text legal answers factual correctness never exceeds 0.45 (on a 0-1 scale) for any model. We find a dissociation between answer relevancy and correctness (Spearman rho = -0.46): models reliably sound responsive while frequently being wrong, a pattern of particular concern for non-expert users. Closed-question accuracy and free-text correctness are strongly rank-correlated (rho = 0.94), so cheap multiple-choice screening predicts model ranking but overstates absolute reliability. An independent rubric-based LLM judge and blind human expert scoring both reproduce the free-text ranking (rho >= 0.88). The judge further reveals that only about half of the norms models cite are correct; the rest are wrong or non-existent. Reliability varies systematically by legal area and follows an inverted-U across question complexity. Our results indicate that current LLMs require expert supervision for Colombian legal tasks, and that grounding answers in authoritative sources is a promising path to higher reliability. We release the benchmark construction pipeline to support reproducible evaluation.

</details>


### [256] [MRVQ: One Resident Index for Dimension- and Rate-Elastic Vector Search](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03651)
*Sean Culatana,Shang-En Huang,Kang Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Matryoshka Residual Vector Quantization (MRVQ) is a post-hoc residual quantizer for frozen embeddings that can be truncated two ways (dropping residual stages or embedding coordinates) to serve every (dimension, rate) pair from a single resident artifact. It achieves 17.8-22.0x less memory than QINCo2 and 1.89-2.02x less than shared-model steelman, but at the cost of 0.026-0.107 nDCG@10 lower quality on FiQA.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Dense-retrieval services must adapt to changing latency, quality, and memory budgets by switching among embedding-prefix dimensions and index bit rates. Currently, tuning a quantizer separately for each rate gives best quality but requires holding several code streams and quantizer states simultaneously, increasing memory overhead.

Method: MRVQ is introduced as a post-hoc residual quantizer for frozen embeddings. Its maximum-rate code can be truncated two ways: (1) dropping residual stages to lower the rate, and (2) dropping embedding coordinates to lower the dimension. This allows a single resident artifact to serve every (dimension, rate) pair evaluated.

Result: Across FiQA and NFCorpus datasets, four embedding families, and {4, 8, 16}-byte codes, MRVQ uses 17.8-22.0x less memory than three separately trained QINCo2 indices, and 1.89-2.02x less than a lean shared-model steelman. However, per-rate QINCo2 is 0.026-0.107 nDCG@10 better on FiQA. MRVQ beats PQ, OPQ, and AdANNS-OPQ at matched code size. A PCA-scalar design attains quality comparable to RaBitQ while fitting 420x faster at the median.

Conclusion: MRVQ is a low-memory operating point for elastic retrieval, not a universal quality winner. Two negative results were also reported: QINCo2 collapses when trained at high rates, and a ranking-bound hypothesis misses its pre-specified acceptance criteria.

Abstract: Dense-retrieval services must switch among embedding-prefix dimensions and index bit rates as latency, quality, and memory budgets change. Tuning a quantizer separately for each rate gives the best quality, but the retrieval tier then holds several code streams and quantizer states at once. We introduce Matryoshka Residual Vector Quantization (MRVQ), a post-hoc residual quantizer for frozen embeddings. Its maximum-rate code can be truncated two ways: dropping residual stages lowers the rate, and dropping embedding coordinates lowers the dimension. One resident artifact therefore serves every (dimension, rate) pair we evaluate. Across FiQA and NFCorpus, four embedding families, and {4, 8, 16}-byte codes, MRVQ is the lowest-RAM design we evaluate. It uses 17.8-22.0x less memory than three separately trained QINCo2 indices, and 1.89-2.02x less than a lean shared-model steelman. The saving is not free: per-rate QINCo2 is 0.026-0.107 nDCG@10 better on FiQA. But MRVQ beats PQ, OPQ, and AdANNS-OPQ at matched code size. We also evaluate a low-build-cost PCA-scalar design that attains quality comparable to RaBitQ and its extension while fitting 420x faster at the median. Finally, we report two negative results: QINCo2 collapses when trained at high rates, and a ranking-bound hypothesis misses its pre-specified acceptance criteria. MRVQ is therefore a low-memory operating point for elastic retrieval, not a universal quality winner.

</details>


### [257] [Transcriptome-informed multi-modal AI for predicting neoadjuvant therapy response from breast cancer biopsies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03693)
*Jungkyu Park,Dhruva Biswas,Joseph Cappadona,Cerise Tang,Ken G. Zeng,Bartosz Machura,Chuwen Liu,Paolo Tarantino,Coral Omene,Francisco J. Esteva,Rohit Bhargava,Marcin Braun,Kamila Paździerz,Jakub Czerwiński,Hanna Romańska-Knight,Albert Grinshpun,Bareket Daniel,Michele Buchinger,Frederick Howard,Piotr Wysocki,Brie Chun,Freya Schnabel,Rich Caruana,Jan Witowski,Krzysztof J. Geras*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A two-stage AI model predicts pathological complete response (pCR) to neoadjuvant therapy in breast cancer by first inferring transcriptome from histopathology images, then combining inferred expression with clinical variables to predict pCR, achieving 0.79 AUROC across 9 validation cohorts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Scarcity of labeled data limits development of deep learning biomarkers in oncology. There is a need for robust prediction of pathological complete response to neoadjuvant therapy in breast cancer to guide treatment decisions.

Method: Two-stage AI model: First stage learns transcriptome from histopathology using 8,742 patients across 32 cancer types (corroborated by pathologist review and spatial agreement with measured expression). Second stage predicts pCR from inferred expression and clinical variables. Developed on 1,080 patients (5 cohorts) and evaluated on 1,412 patients (9 cohorts).

Result: Pooled AUROC of 0.79 (95% CI, 0.73-0.85), discriminates responders within molecular subtypes, outperforms histopathological biomarkers, remains stable across intratumoral sampling and with minimal biopsy tissue. Ablations show transcriptome-wide inference improves discrimination over clinical variables alone or one-stage pathology models.

Conclusion: Biologically informed compression via two-stage modeling may generalize to data-sparse applications in precision oncology, avoiding genomic assays' gene selection constraints while maintaining robustness.

Abstract: Scarcity of labeled data limits development of deep learning biomarkers in oncology. We develop a two-stage AI model predicting pathological complete response (pCR) to neoadjuvant therapy in breast cancer. The first stage learns the transcriptome from histopathology using 8,742 patients across 32 cancer types, corroborated by pathologist review and spatial agreement with measured expression. This simplifies the second stage to predicting pCR from inferred expression and clinical variables. Developed using 1,080 patients (five cohorts) and evaluated in 1,412 patients (nine cohorts), the model achieves a pooled AUROC of 0.79 (95% CI, 0.73-0.85), discriminating responders within molecular subtypes. It outperforms histopathological biomarkers, remaining stable across intratumoral sampling and with minimal biopsy tissue. Ablations show transcriptome-wide inference improves discrimination over clinical variables alone or one-stage pathology models, and robustness by avoiding genomic assays' gene selection constraints. These results indicate that biologically informed compression may generalize to data-sparse applications in precision oncology.

</details>

### [258] [Hybrid Machine Learning-Assisted Raman Spectroscopy with Generative Feature Augmentation for Pharmaceutical Identification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02224)
*Quach Thi Thai Binh,Ton Nu Quynh Trang,Thang B. Phan,Vu Thi Hanh Thu,Nguyen Tuan Hung*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: HyMLRaman is a hybrid Raman spectroscopy framework combining deep spectral feature extraction (EfficientNet-B3), generative models (DDPM), and classical ML classifiers for identifying six pharmaceutical compounds. The EfficientNet-B3 + SVM configuration achieves 96.31% accuracy and 96.36% macro-F1 score.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Rapid and reliable identification of pharmaceutical residues is crucial for public health, food safety, and practical Raman-based screening. Existing methods may lack accuracy or fail under limited-data conditions.

Method: Raman spectra were converted into spectral images and encoded using deep neural network backbones (EfficientNet-B3 performed best). The 1536-dimensional embeddings trained downstream classifiers (SVM, KNN, LR, RF, XGBoost, ANN) using stratified 10-fold cross-validation. DDPM-based feature augmentation was applied in a PCA-reduced latent space to address limited-data conditions.

Result: EfficientNet-B3 + SVM achieved 96.31% accuracy and 96.36% macro-F1, outperforming standalone CNN. DDPM augmentation showed selective benefits, particularly for KNN with reduced training fractions, though effects remained classifier-dependent. A Raman Pharmaceutical Analyzer demonstrated practical embedding capability.

Conclusion: HyMLRaman provides a practical and interpretable route for rapid Raman-based pharmaceutical screening, effectively combining deep learning feature extraction with classical ML classifiers for reliable identification of pharmaceutical compounds.

Abstract: Rapid and reliable identification of pharmaceutical residues is important for safeguarding public health, ensuring food safety, and enabling practical Raman-based screening. In this study, we propose HyMLRaman, a hybrid Raman spectroscopy framework that combines deep spectral feature extraction, generative models, and classical machine-learning classifiers to identify six pharmaceutical compounds, including amoxicillin, chloramphenicol, ciprofloxacin, tetracycline, ibuprofen, and paracetamol. Raman spectra are converted into spectral images and encoded with several deep neural-network backbones, among which EfficientNet-B3 yields the most effective representation. The resulting 1536-dimensional embeddings are then used to train downstream classifiers, including SVM, KNN, logistic regression, random forest, XGBoost, and ANN, using stratified 10-fold cross-validation. The hybrid EfficientNet-B3--SVM configuration achieves the strongest baseline performance, reaching 96.31% accuracy and a macro-F1 score of 96.36%, outperforming the standalone CNN baseline. To address limited-data conditions, a generative model, a DDPM-based feature augmentation, is introduced in a PCA-reduced EfficientNet-B3 latent space. The low-data ablation results show that DDPM augmentation provides selective benefits, particularly for KNN with reduced training fractions, and that its effect remains classifier-dependent. Finally, an application-level Raman Pharmaceutical Analyzer demonstrates the feasibility of embedding the trained model into an interactive Raman analysis workflow. These results suggest that HyMLRaman provides a practical and interpretable route for rapid Raman-based pharmaceutical screening.

</details>


### [259] [The Price of Greenwashing: Algorithmic Verification and Market Discipline using Conformal Machine Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02225)
*Sourav Bose,Taoufik Bouraoui*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper develops a novel algorithmic method to detect corporate greenwashing by comparing self-reported emissions data against a mathematically guaranteed baseline derived from fusing SEC financial data with EPA facility-level greenhouse gas registries. Using a new metric called Conformal-Weighted Continuous Divergence (CWCD) with Mondrian Conformal Prediction, the study finds that emissions divergence significantly negatively predicts Tobin's Q and ROA, providing evidence that institutional investors actively price environmental deception as a signal of corporate mismanagement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to address information asymmetry in corporate sustainability reporting, where self-reported emissions data enables pervasive greenwashing. Current literature relies on subjective ESG ratings or textual analysis, lacking objective quantification of physical climate realities. The authors seek to provide a mathematically rigorous baseline for actual corporate emissions to expose environmental deception.

Method: The methodology fuses U.S. SEC financial fundamentals with facility-level EPA greenhouse gas registries to establish a baseline of physical corporate emissions. They employ a gradient boosting architecture combined with Mondrian Conformal Prediction to quantify the shortfall between self-reported and algorithmic baseline emissions into the CWCD metric. The divergence is evaluated using a cross-sectional lead-lag econometric design.

Result: The key finding is that algorithmic emissions divergence (CWCD) exhibits a severe, statistically significant negative relationship with subsequent market valuation (Tobin's Q) and operational profitability (ROA). This provides definitive evidence against the "market blindness hypothesis" - institutional capital actively prices environmental deception as a leading indicator of fundamental corporate mismanagement, not merely as an ethical issue.

Conclusion: The study concludes that environmental deception is priced by markets as a signal of broader corporate mismanagement. This provides quantitative justification for asset managers and regulators to deploy algorithmic auditing infrastructure at scale to detect and prevent greenwashing.

Abstract: While corporate sustainability mandates are expanding, the systemic reliance on self-reported emissions data exposes financial markets to pervasive greenwashing. Current literature relies heavily on subjective ESG ratings or textual sentiment analysis, leaving a critical econometric gap in objectively quantifying physical climate realities. To resolve this information asymmetry, we fuse U.S. SEC financial fundamentals with facility-level EPA greenhouse gas registries to establish a mathematically guaranteed baseline of physical corporate emissions. Leveraging a gradient boosting architecture and Mondrian Conformal Prediction, we quantify the shortfall between self-reported data and this algorithmic baseline into a novel Conformal-Weighted Continuous Divergence (CWCD) metric. Evaluating this divergence via a cross-sectional lead-lag econometric design, we uncover a robust mechanism of market discipline: algorithmic emissions divergence exhibits a severe, statistically significant negative relationship with subsequent market valuation (Tobin's Q) and operational profitability (ROA). Providing definitive evidence against the market blindness hypothesis, this study proves that institutional capital actively prices environmental deception not merely as an ethical lapse, but as a leading indicator of fundamental corporate mismanagement. Ultimately, these findings provide the quantitative justification necessary for asset managers and regulators to deploy algorithmic auditing infrastructure at scale.

</details>


### [260] [State-Space Unlearning for Non-Stationary Bias in Land Surface Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02248)
*Anidipta Pal*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces SSU-LSF, the first machine unlearning framework designed for geoscientific Mamba-based Structured State Space Models (SSMs). It addresses the problem of non-stationary confounding events being absorbed into state-transition matrices, causing silent bias in land surface predictions (NDVI, LST, crop phenology).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Operational land surface forecasting systems built on Mamba-family SSMs absorb non-stationary confounding events (unrecorded irrigation booms, dam-operation shifts, sensor recalibrations) into their state-transition matrices, which silently biases predictions long after the physical cause ends.

Method: The method consists of three key components: (1) EKFac influence functions specialized to Mamba state matrices via closed-form matrix-exponential gradient; (2) spectral-radius-weighted elbow thresholding to localize temporal confounding footprint Φ; (3) Hessian-free projected gradient ascent within KL-divergence trust region augmented by spatial total-variation (TV) regularization.

Result: Across three heterogeneous benchmarks (CropHarvest, NDVI-LST, ERA5) and eleven baselines, SSU-LSF achieves confounding reduction rates of 0.773, 0.821, and 0.859 respectively. Worst-case clean-domain RMSE degradation is 4.2% on ERA5. The method converges in 3-5 epochs at 8.4× lower GPU-cost per unlearning request than full retraining.

Conclusion: SSU-LSF provides an effective machine unlearning solution for geoscientific Mamba-based SSMs, successfully reducing confounding effects while maintaining model performance with minimal computational cost.

Abstract: Operational land surface forecasting systems built on Mamba-family Structured State Space Models absorb non-stationary confounding events (unrecorded irrigation booms, dam-operation shifts, sensor recalibrations) into their state-transition matrices, silently biasing NDVI, LST, and crop phenology predictions long after the physical cause ends. This paper introduces SSU-LSF (State-Space Unlearning for Land Surface Forecasting), the first machine-unlearning framework purpose-built for geoscientific Mamba-based SSMs. We develop EKFac influence functions specialized to the Mamba state matrices via a closed-form matrix-exponential gradient, use spectral-radius-weighted elbow thresholding to localize a temporal confounding footprint $Φ$, and apply Hessian-free projected gradient ascent within a KL-divergence trust region augmented by spatial total-variation (TV) regularization. Proposition 1 establishes that residual confounding is bounded by $\mathcal{O}\big((1-ρ(\bar{A})^{T_c})/((1-ρ(\bar{A}))μ)\big)$, which grows with the window length $T_c$. Across three heterogeneous benchmarks and eleven baselines, SSU-LSF achieves confounding reduction rates of $0.773$ (CropHarvest), $0.821$ (NDVI-LST), and $0.859$ (ERA5), with worst-case clean-domain RMSE degradation of $4.2\%$ on ERA5, converging in 3--5 epochs at $8.4\times$ lower GPU-cost per unlearning request than full retraining. Code: https://github.com/Anidipta/SSU-LSF

</details>


### [261] [Nearest-neighbour baselines for fingerprint prediction from MS/MS spectra under different assumptions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02249)
*Ling Min Serena Khoo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Summary generation failed


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Motivation analysis unavailable

Method: Method extraction failed

Result: Result analysis unavailable

Conclusion: Conclusion extraction failed

Abstract: It has recently been shown that nearest-neighbour retrieval provides a strong baseline for molecular fingerprint prediction from MS/MS spectra, with several variants matching or outperforming current deep learning models (Khoo and Barzilay, 2026; Liu et al., 2026; Gupta et al., 2026). Importantly, "nearest neighbour" encompasses a family of retrieval methods that differ in the information assumed to be available at inference. In this report, we systematically compare several nearest-neighbour variants and show how these differing assumptions affect performance. Our goal is to establish stricter baselines that enable more rigorous benchmarking and better measure progress in this area.

### [262] [Rank-Aware Speculative Sampling for Diffusion Draft Trees](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02251)
*Marcello Bullo,Yanxiao Liu,Öykü Sıla Güner,Arpan Mukherjee,Deniz Gündüz*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RASS (Rank-Aware Speculative Sampling) is a new verification rule for speculative draft trees in diffusion generation that improves upon D-GRS by using rank-aware list coupling to order draft candidates and optimize weights, achieving ~20% improvement on CIFAR-10 with matched compute budgets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current tree-based speculative sampling methods like D-GRS generate K conditionally independent candidates per node but don't exploit the informative ranking that emerges without additional target-model evaluations. The goal is to better allocate parallel compute budget by using this ranking information.

Method: RASS uses rank-aware list coupling: (1) orders draft candidates along proposal-target mean displacement, (2) samples a rank with weights optimized to minimize total variation between selected-proposal and target laws, (3) maximally couples selected candidate with target, and (4) applies residual correction for exact sampling.

Result: RASS improves over D-GRS across all evaluated settings (Gaussian-mixture target, FFHQ unconditional generation, CIFAR-10 conditional generation, Stable Diffusion 3.5 with COCO2014 prompts), with gains reaching ~20% on CIFAR-10 at matched compute budgets, measured by ratio of standard to speculative sampling's target-model evaluation counts.

Conclusion: Rank-aware list coupling provides a principled way to exploit candidate rankings in speculative sampling, enabling more efficient parallel compute allocation and significant speedups in diffusion generation while maintaining exact sampling through residual correction.

Abstract: Speculative sampling accelerates diffusion generation by verifying inexpensive draft states in parallel while preserving the target law. Recent tree-based methods allocate the parallel compute budget more effectively than single-chain drafts, as demonstrated by Diffusion Greedy Rejection Sampling (D-GRS). D-GRS generates $K$ conditionally independent candidates per node, and sequentially tests them in their generation order. Yet the sampled candidates admit an informative ranking without additional target-model evaluations. To exploit this, we introduce Rank-Aware Speculative Sampling (RASS), a verification rule for speculative draft trees based on rank-aware list coupling. RASS orders draft candidates along the proposal-target mean displacement and samples a rank with weights optimized to minimize total variation between the selected-proposal and target laws. Finally, the selected candidate is maximally coupled with the target, with residual correction ensuring exact sampling for any choice of rank weights. We evaluate RASS on a Gaussian-mixture target, unconditional pixel-space generation on FFHQ, conditional generation on CIFAR-10, and latent diffusion with Stable Diffusion 3.5 using COCO2014 prompts. Measured by the ratio of standard to speculative sampling's target-model evaluation counts, RASS improves on D-GRS across the evaluated settings, with gains reaching approximately 20% on CIFAR-10 at matched compute budgets.

</details>


### [263] [Counterfactual Predictions in Scientific Emulators Without Controlled Experiments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02252)
*Dingling Yao,Kahaan Gandhi,Valentin Duruisseaux,Boris Bonev,Francesco Locatello,Anima Anandkumar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ReRoute is a framework for counterfactual what-if prediction in scientific applications that combines factual data with partial mechanistic knowledge. It achieves 18.2-31.8% error reduction in climate emulation under CO2 distribution shifts without requiring expensive controlled intervention data, outperforming standard approaches while maintaining computational efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current predictive models perform well on observed data but fail on counterfactual "what-if" queries when correlated inputs are varied independently. Existing solutions require controlled simulation data with explicitly disentangled factors, which is computationally expensive and inherits simulator assumptions.

Method: ReRoute framework combines factual data with partial mechanistic knowledge without requiring controlled intervention data. It works by: (1) fixing the queried input to a reference value, (2) reintroducing its variation through a known mechanistic pathway, and (3) fine-tuning on original factual data while leaving downstream effects to learned dynamics. Includes a causal identification result machine-checked in Lean.

Result: ReRoute achieves highly accurate counterfactual predictions in controlled advection-diffusion system. In climate emulation, it reduces aggregate climate error by 18.2-31.8% under severe CO2 distribution shifts while preserving skill under standard conditions. On ERA5 reanalysis emulator, it preserves more surface warming under fixed-CO2 counterfactual.

Conclusion: ReRoute provides an effective approach for targeted scientific what-if prediction that balances partial mechanistic knowledge with data-driven learning, achieving significant improvements in counterfactual accuracy at a fraction of the cost of retraining on additional controlled simulations.

Abstract: Many scientific questions require reasoning about what was never observed: What if the conditions, interventions, or history had been different? Models can predict accurately on observed data yet fail on such what-if queries when correlated inputs are varied independently. A common remedy is to add controlled simulation data in which these factors are explicitly disentangled, but this requires access to a simulator, can be computationally expensive, and inherits the simulator's modeling assumptions. We introduce ReRoute, a framework for targeted scientific what-if prediction that combines factual data with partial mechanistic knowledge, without requiring controlled intervention data for adaptation. ReRoute fixes the queried input of a pretrained backbone to a reference value, reintroduces its variation through a known mechanistic pathway, and fine-tunes on the original factual data, while leaving downstream effects to the learned dynamics. We provide a causal identification result for this construction under explicit structural assumptions, with the core argument machine-checked in Lean. After showing that ReRoute achieves highly accurate counterfactual predictions in a controlled advection-diffusion system where exact responses are available, we turn to state-of-the-art climate emulation. On held-out coupled-climate interventions, ReRoute reduces aggregate climate error by 18.2-31.8% under severe CO$_2$ distribution shifts while preserving skill under standard conditions, at a small fraction of the cost of retraining on additional controlled simulations, without even accounting for the substantial expense of generating such data. Finally, on an emulator trained from historical ERA5 reanalysis, where no counterfactual reference exists, ReRoute preserves substantially more of the surface warming implied by the observed boundary conditions under a fixed-CO$_2$ counterfactual.

</details>


### [264] [Approximation Property of Dropout Neural Networks: Sobolev Rates and Confidence Bounds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02253)
*Jia-He Yao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper studies the approximation of the unit ball of W^{n,∞}([0,1]^d) by ReLU networks with dropout (edges retained with probability p). It constructs constant-depth networks with size O~_{n,d}(p^{-9}ε^{-max{d/n,2}} log(1/δ)) and provides matching lower bounds under certain conditions, though optimal retention dependence and logarithmic factors remain open.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The universal approximation property of dropout neural networks does not describe the network size required for accurate random realizations. This work aims to quantify the approximation error and determine the necessary network size for achieving accurate approximations with high probability.

Method: The construction combines three key techniques: (1) bounded local subnetworks, (2) localization on a successful approximation event, and (3) a multiscale Taylor decomposition. The analysis uses Sobolev capacity to establish lower bounds.

Result: The paper constructs networks of constant depth and size O~_{n,d}(p^{-9}ε^{-max{d/n,2}} log(1/δ)). For fixed p∈(0,1) and δ<min{1/2,1-p}, the upper and lower bounds match in the accuracy exponent under fixed or logarithmic depth budget. When d≤2n, they also match in confidence up to logarithms of accuracy. Lower bounds show that approximating a fixed affine function requires ((1-p)/p)ε^{-2}log(1/δ) at the output layer.

Conclusion: The optimal retention dependence (particularly the p^{-9} factor) and logarithmic factors remain open problems. The bounds are established for W^{n,∞} targets and extended to W^{n,r} targets with L^s error, though this extension is distinguished from the upper bound for W^{n,∞}.

Abstract: The universal approximation property of dropout neural networks does not by itself describe the network size required for an accurate random realization. In this work, we study approximation of the unit ball of $W^{n,\infty}([0,1]^d)$ by ReLU networks whose edges are retained independently with probability $p$. The approximation error is measured uniformly over the input domain, and the guarantee holds with probability at least $1-δ$ for a single sampled network. We construct networks of constant depth and size $\widetilde O_{n,d}(p^{-9}\varepsilon^{-\max\{d/n,2\}} \log(1/δ))$. The construction combines bounded local subnetworks, localization on a successful approximation event, and a multiscale Taylor decomposition. Conversely, Sobolev capacity imposes a lower bound on the number of surviving edges, while approximation of a fixed affine function requires an output-layer cost of order $((1-p)/p)\varepsilon^{-2}\log(1/δ)$ at sufficiently high confidence. For fixed $p\in(0,1)$ and $δ<\min\{1/2,1-p\}$, the upper and lower bounds match in the accuracy exponent under a fixed or logarithmic depth budget. When $d\leq2n$, they also match in confidence up to logarithms of accuracy. We extend the lower bounds to $W^{n,r}$ targets with $L^s$ error, and distinguish this extension from the upper bound for $W^{n,\infty}$. The optimal retention dependence and logarithmic factors remain open.

</details>


### [265] [Overcoming Challenges of Interpretive Structural Modeling with Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02254)
*Everett Rush,David J. Icove,Ari Kim,Byung H. Park,Michael A. Langston*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes an integrated LLM-ISM approach that uses large language models as imperfect experts to automate the Interpretive Structural Modeling process, which traditionally requires tedious expert consultations. The study compares four causal graph discovery methods and finds that rowwise and full graph methods outperform pairwise and k-wise approaches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional ISM is labor-intensive and requires repeated expert interactions to reach consensus, making it impractical for studies with hundreds of variables. The motivation is to scale ISM using LLM-based causal graph discovery methods.

Method: The study compares four causal graph discovery methodologies: pairwise, k-wise, rowwise, and full graph discovery. These methods are integrated with LLM to automate the ISM process. Evaluation metrics include Structural Hamming Distance (SHD) and F1-score.

Result: Rowwise method achieved SHD=160 with F1-score=0.77, while full graph method achieved SHD=135 with F1-score=0.73. These two methods performed best among the four approaches tested.

Conclusion: Causal graph discovery methods for ISM perform best using rowwise and full graph methodologies, demonstrating the potential of LLM-ISM integration for automating multi-criteria decision-making processes at scale.

Abstract: Interpretive Structural Modeling (ISM) is a well-known process for multi-criteria decision making. The success of ISM over other methodologies is its ability to model causal relationships, the binary scale of factors, and resulting hierarchical representation. Traditionally, the modeling process is performed by repeated interactions with subject matter experts until consensus is reached. This process is tedious, labor-intense, and most importantly limits the ability of ISM to scale to studies with hundreds of variables. Drawing on existing work of causal graph discovery with large language models (LLM) as imperfect experts, this work explores an integrated LLM-ISM approach for ISM. Pairwise, k-wise, rowwise, and full graph discovery methodologies are compared and evaluated. It is shown that causal graph discovery methods for ISM perform best using rowwise (SHD=160, F1-score=0.77) and full graph methods (SHD=135, F1-score=0.73).

</details>


### [266] [MACTS-EM: Multi-Agent Collaborative Time Series Forecasting with Emergent Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02255)
*Ahmad Shahi,Mamehgol Yousefi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MACTS-EM is a multi-agent framework for time series forecasting that combines specialized agents, a meta-cognitive layer, emergent memory for cross-domain transfer, and adversarial robustness. It achieves 8-12% accuracy improvement, 22-27% better zero-shot transfer, and 16-21% enhanced resilience to regime shifts across financial, climate, energy, and pandemic domains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Time series forecasting faces challenges with regime shifts, cross-domain knowledge transfer, and multimodal data integration. Existing approaches lack the capability to handle complex real-world scenarios requiring multi-resolution temporal understanding and contextual adaptation.

Method: MACTS-EM integrates: (1) domain-specialised forecasting agents for pattern recognition, anomaly detection, causal inference, and uncertainty quantification; (2) a meta-cognitive layer for dynamic agent allocation; (3) an emergent memory mechanism enabling cross-domain pattern transfer; (4) multimodal contextual integration; and (5) adversarial robustness components.

Result: Evaluation across financial markets, climate patterns, energy consumption, and pandemic propagation shows: 8-12% improvement in forecasting accuracy, 22-27% better zero-shot transfer capability, 16-21% enhanced resilience during regime shifts, and 15-18% faster recovery after distribution shifts.

Conclusion: Collaborative, agentic approaches to time series forecasting represent a promising direction beyond traditional architectures, particularly for complex real-world scenarios requiring multi-resolution temporal understanding and contextual adaptation.

Abstract: Time series forecasting remains a critical challenge across numerous domains. Despite significant advancements, existing approaches struggle with complex phenomena such as regime shifts, cross-domain knowledge transfer, and multimodal data integration. This paper introduces Multi-Agent Collaborative Time Series Forecasting with Emergent Memory (MACTS-EM), a novel framework where specialised agents collaborate to achieve superior forecasting performance. The MACTS-EM architecture integrates: (1) domain-specialised forecasting agents for pattern recognition, anomaly detection, causal inference, and uncertainty quantification; (2) a meta-cognitive layer for dynamic agent allocation; (3) an emergent memory mechanism enabling cross-domain pattern transfer; (4) multimodal contextual integration; and (5) adversarial robustness components. Evaluation across financial markets, climate patterns, energy consumption, and pandemic propagation demonstrates that MACTS-EM outperforms existing approaches in most scenarios, with 8-12% improvement in forecasting accuracy, 22-27% better zero-shot transfer capability, 16-21% enhanced resilience during regime shifts, and 15-18% faster recovery after distribution shifts. Our findings suggest that collaborative, agentic approaches to time series forecasting represent a promising direction beyond traditional architectures, particularly for complex real-world scenarios requiring multi-resolution temporal understanding and contextual adaptation.

</details>


### [267] [TRACE: A Reproducible Benchmark for Electricity Price Forecasting with Official Operational Text](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02256)
*Xinyi Yi,Moy Yuan,Ioannis Lestas*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TRACE is a benchmark for electricity price forecasting that incorporates textual operational data. It contains 7,300 zone-day instances from five U.S. market zones, with official operational text reconstructed at each forecast cutoff to prevent information leakage. The benchmark evaluates both semantic alignment and forecasting value of text, finding that text reduces upper-tail pinball loss by 7.4% on average across time-series foundation models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing electricity price forecasting benchmarks focus primarily on numerical inputs, leaving the forecasting value of textual context (such as operational text available at forecast cutoff) insufficiently evaluated. There is a need to assess whether textual information can improve price forecasting, particularly for risk management purposes.

Method: The authors introduced TRACE, a reproducible benchmark pairing 7,300 zone-day instances with prices from five zones in a major U.S. market and official operational text available at the forecast cutoff. They reconstructed official operational text at each cutoff to prevent post-cutoff information leakage. They evaluated semantic alignment with central movement and tail risks, and measured forecasting value using upper-tail pinball loss across time-series foundation models, with a controlled cross-day text-mismatch ablation as a control experiment.

Result: Semantic assessments aligned with central movement and both tail risks in ground-truth prices, most consistently for upper-tail price risk. Forecasting value showed a median 7.4% reduction in upper-tail pinball loss across time-series foundation models. A controlled cross-day text-mismatch ablation reversed the gains, falling below the no-text baseline.

Conclusion: Textual operational context provides meaningful forecasting value for electricity prices, particularly for upper-tail price risk (relevant for risk management). The ablation experiment confirms that the gains come from semantically appropriate text rather than spurious correlations. TRACE provides a reproducible benchmark for further research on incorporating textual data in electricity price forecasting.

Abstract: Electricity price forecasting (EPF) supports scheduling, bidding, and risk management in electricity markets, yet existing benchmarks focus mainly on numerical inputs, leaving the forecasting value of forecast-time textual context insufficiently evaluated. We introduce TRACE, a reproducible benchmark of 7,300 zone--day instances pairing prices from five zones in a major U.S. market with official operational text available at the forecast cutoff. TRACE reconstructs official operational text at each cutoff, preventing post-cutoff information leakage. We evaluate TRACE for semantic alignment and forecasting value. Semantic assessments align with central movement and both tail risks in ground-truth prices, most consistently for upper-tail price risk. Forecasting value is reflected in a median 7.4\% reduction in upper-tail pinball loss across time-series foundation models. A controlled cross-day text-mismatch ablation reverses the gains, falling below the no-text baseline.

</details>


### [268] [Parameter-Free Interval-Dynamic Regret under Heavy-Tailed Noise](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02258)
*Vaneet Aggarwal*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper studies online convex optimization with stochastic subgradients under p-th moment noise (1<p≤2). The authors develop a parameter-free learner that achieves adaptive regret bounds over any interval of length n, with the bound depending on a comparator complexity measure Λ_I. The key innovation is achieving the optimal full-horizon static rate while retaining adaptation properties, with an interval cost of 1+log(T/n).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to develop online learning algorithms that can adapt to changing environments without knowing parameters like noise variance, gradient bounds, or the noise moment p. The goal is to achieve the optimal static rate while maintaining adaptivity to different time intervals and achieving good performance against any comparator path.

Method: The method involves developing a parameter-free online learning algorithm that uses one unbiased stochastic subgradient per round. The analysis controls calibration in expectation and limits the cost of observation-scale changes. The approach involves comparing to distributions over predictably available experts with relative-entropy dependence on a nonuniform prior, where a common prior favors long windows and long restart lengths.

Result: The main result is an expected regret bound of E[Regret_I(u)] ≤ min(GDn, C[GD√(n(Λ_I + log²(2T))) + σDn^(1/p)(Λ_I + log²(2T))^((p-1)/p)]) for any interval I of length n and comparator path with Λ_I = 1 + P_I/D. The learner uses none of G, σ, p, I, P_I, and the constant C is universal. The interval cost becomes 1 + log(T/n), including the optimal full-horizon static rate. A change-of-measure lower bound identifies the noise power of this logarithm.

Conclusion: The paper presents a parameter-free online convex optimization learner that achieves near-optimal adaptive regret bounds. The key insight is that a common prior favoring long windows and long restart lengths, together with the statistics supplied, achieves the optimal full-horizon static rate while maintaining interval adaptation. The change-of-measure lower bound identifies the noise power of the logarithm for learners retaining a full-horizon optimal guarantee.

Abstract: We study online convex optimization with one unbiased stochastic subgradient per round and an unknown finite conditional $p$th noise moment, $1<p\le2$. For every fixed interval $I$ of length $n$ and comparator path with $Λ_I=1+P_I/D$, one learner achieves
  \[ E[Regret_I(u)]\le\min(GDn, C[GD\sqrt{n(Λ_I+\log^2(2T))} +σDn^{1/p}(Λ_I+\log^2(2T))^{(p-1)/p}]). \]
  The learner uses none of $G,σ,p,I,P_I$, and the constant is universal. Interval adaptation adds to comparator complexity, preserving the distinct mean-gradient and noise exponents. The analysis controls calibration in expectation and limits the cost of observation-scale changes. Its general theorem compares to distributions over predictably available experts with relative-entropy dependence on a nonuniform prior. A common prior favors long windows and long restart lengths. With the statistics supplied, the interval cost becomes $1+\log(T/n)$, including the optimal full-horizon static rate. A change-of-measure lower bound identifies the noise power of this logarithm for learners retaining a full-horizon optimal guarantee, under explicit conditions. Static comparisons and deterministic partitions follow from the same decisions.

</details>


### [269] [From Mathematical to Executable Certificates for Machine Unlearning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02268)
*Ziyu Zhao,Xinyu Wang,Xiaowen Chang,Yixuan He*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ExecCert is a release-time certification framework that bridges the gap between theoretical guarantees in machine unlearning and practical deployment by certifying concrete finite-precision artifacts. It either closes a method's native certificate or applies Retraining-Reference Release Verification (RRV) to verify fidelity to current retain-set retraining.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Machine unlearning is needed when data must be removed due to deletion requests, outdated records, or data-quality concerns. However, retraining from scratch is costly, and there's a significant gap between mathematical guarantees (theoretical) and deployed systems that release concrete finite-precision artifacts. This gap needed to be addressed for practical deployment.

Method: ExecCert introduces a release-time certification layer. For sequential deletion scenarios where the exact retain-set reference and stored numerical state evolve separately, the paper develops an incremental realization of RRV for frozen representations with a mutable ridge head. This maintains certified evidence across deletion requests rather than reconstructing it at each release. The method was tested on four published unlearning implementations.

Result: ExecCert preserves valid certificates, changes release decisions, tightens conservative bounds, and identifies retraining-reference fidelity supported by concrete outputs. In sequential-service experiments, RRV eliminates false releases caused by stored-equation verification while closely tracking realized error. Incremental certification remains cheaper than both fresh and maintained verified-factor alternatives once release checks become sufficiently frequent.

Conclusion: The framework successfully bridges theoretical guarantees and practical deployment in machine unlearning. The incremental RRV approach provides an efficient solution for sequential deletion scenarios, maintaining certified evidence across deletion requests in a cost-effective manner compared to alternatives.

Abstract: Machine unlearning is needed when data must be removed because of deletion requests, outdated records, or data-quality concerns, while retraining from scratch can be costly. Certified machine unlearning methods provide mathematical guarantees, while deployed systems release concrete finite-precision artifacts produced by software. To bridge the gap between mathematical guarantees and practical deployment, we introduce Executable Release Certification (ExecCert), a release-time layer that certifies the candidate artifact considered for release. ExecCert either closes a method's native certificate for the executed candidate or applies Retraining-Reference Release Verification (RRV) to certify fidelity to current retain-set retraining. Sequential deletion makes the latter nontrivial because the exact retain-set reference and the stored numerical state evolve separately. For frozen representations with a mutable ridge head, we develop an incremental realization of RRV that maintains certified evidence across deletion requests rather than reconstructing it at each release. On four published unlearning implementations, ExecCert preserves valid certificates, changes release decisions, tightens conservative bounds, and identifies the retraining-reference fidelity supported by concrete outputs. In sequential-service experiments, RRV eliminates false releases caused by stored-equation verification while closely tracking realized error, and incremental certification remains cheaper than both fresh and maintained verified-factor alternatives once release checks become sufficiently frequent.

</details>


### [270] [CLEAN: Psychometrically Consistent Incremental Cognitive Diagnosis under Concept-Space Expansion via Architectural Isolation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02278)
*Tao He,Jinxing Xiang,Fan Jiang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CLEAN is a novel incremental cognitive diagnosis framework that addresses concept-space expansion while preserving diagnostic invariance. It uses architectural isolation (topological bipartition, frozen historical functions, orthogonal column masking) to prevent catastrophic forgetting, and expandable branches for new concepts. The method guarantees zero representation drift through structural design rather than soft constraints.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing incremental CD models assume fixed concept space, causing gradient interference and catastrophic forgetting when new items/concepts are added. Current methods use only soft constraints to preserve historical diagnoses, which fail to satisfy psychometric consistency requirements (diagnostic invariance). This necessitates a method with structural guarantees for pointwise invariance of historical diagnoses.

Method: CLEAN employs three key mechanisms: (1) Strict topological bipartition protocol that freezes historical diagnostic functions; (2) Deterministic orthogonal column masking to sever gradient interference; (3) Expandable full-rank branches with micro-variance initialization for learning novel concepts. Representation Drift (RD) is formalized to quantify perturbation of historical traits.

Result: CLEAN achieves zero RD on three large-scale educational datasets, preserving old-item metrics identically to static anchors through architectural isolation while remaining competitive with or superior to strong continual-learning baselines on new items.

Conclusion: The architectural isolation approach provides structural guarantees for diagnostic invariance that soft constraints cannot achieve. CLEAN successfully balances preserving historical diagnoses (zero RD) while learning new concepts, demonstrating the effectiveness of deterministic orthogonal masking and expandable branches for incremental cognitive diagnosis.

Abstract: Cognitive diagnosis (CD) is a fundamental task in intelligent education that profiles learner proficiency over knowledge concepts. In real-world learning platforms, newly added items continually introduce previously unseen concepts, necessitating dynamic expansion of the underlying concept space. Yet existing incremental CD models assume a fixed concept space, allowing gradients from new items to overwrite historical pathways and induce catastrophic forgetting. More critically, these methods rely solely on soft constraints to preserve historical diagnoses. Such constraints may fail to satisfy the requirement of diagnostic invariance after incremental updates, a requirement known as psychometric consistency in cognitive diagnosis. Therefore, we propose CLEAN (Continual Learning with Expandable and Architecturally Isolated Networks), a novel incremental CD framework supporting concept-space expansion while providing structural guarantees for pointwise invariance of historical diagnoses. Specifically, CLEAN first introduces a strict topological bipartition protocol, freezes historical diagnostic functions and applies deterministic orthogonal column masking to sever gradient interference. Second, to accommodate concept expansion, expandable full-rank branches with micro-variance initialization are deployed to learn novel concepts. Finally, to verify that this architectural design achieves invariance by construction, we formalize Representation Drift (RD) to quantify the perturbation of historical traits. Extensive experiments on three large-scale educational datasets demonstrate that CLEAN achieves zero RD, preserving old-item metrics identically to static anchors through architectural isolation while remaining competitive with or superior to strong continual-learning baselines on new items.

</details>


### [271] [MuLoRA: Spectrally Balanced Low-Rank Adaptation for Continual Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02283)
*Junkang Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MuLoRA addresses spectral plasticity collapse in LoRA-based continual learning, where update energy concentrates in a small subset of singular modes during sequential adaptation. The method combines historical whitening to identify task-adaptive input directions and approximate polar orthogonalization of momentum updates to reduce spectral concentration. It achieves state-of-the-art results in 15 of 16 metrics across five class-incremental benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LoRA provides parameter-efficient continual learning but suffers from spectral plasticity collapse: during sequential adaptation, update energy becomes concentrated in a small subset of singular modes, leaving much of the available low-rank space underutilized. The limitation of existing interference avoidance approaches is that protecting historical representations does not ensure the remaining adaptation capacity is responsive to new tasks or effectively utilized.

Method: MuLoRA jointly controls capacity allocation and utilization through two main mechanisms: 1) Historical whitening identifies input directions with strong current-task response relative to accumulated historical response, yielding a task-adaptive basis that remains fixed during training. 2) Approximate polar orthogonalization of momentum updates reduces spectral concentration within the selected space. An orthonormal basis connects these mechanisms by transferring the factor-update spectrum exactly to the induced weight update.

Result: Across five class-incremental benchmarks and eight incremental settings, MuLoRA achieves the highest mean accuracy in 15 of 16 reported metrics.

Conclusion: The proposed MuLoRA method effectively addresses spectral plasticity collapse in LoRA-based continual learning by jointly controlling capacity allocation and utilization, demonstrating superior performance across multiple benchmarks and settings.

Abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) provides a parameter-efficient approach to continual learning, but its nominal rank can conceal a loss of effective adaptation capacity. We identify \emph{spectral plasticity collapse}: during sequential adaptation, update energy becomes concentrated in a small subset of singular modes, leaving much of the available low-rank space underutilized. This exposes a limitation of interference avoidance alone: protecting historical representations does not ensure that the remaining adaptation capacity is responsive to new tasks or effectively utilized. To address this problem, we propose \texttt{MuLoRA}, which jointly controls capacity allocation and utilization. First, historical whitening identifies input directions with strong current-task response relative to accumulated historical response, yielding a task-adaptive basis that remains fixed during training. Second, approximate polar orthogonalization of momentum updates reduces spectral concentration within theselected space. An orthonormal basis connects these mechanisms by transferring the factor-update spectrum exactly tothe induced weight update. We establish a max--min characterization of exact subspace selection and derive cumulative spectral bounds under controlled cross-step anisotropy. Across five class-incremental benchmarks and eight incremental settings, \texttt{MuLoRA} achieves the highest mean accuracy in 15 of 16 reported metrics.

</details>


### [272] [Effects of interpulse-interval variation on deep-learning classification of bat vocalizations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02284)
*Welmoed R. Eversteijn,Burooj Ghani,A. Leonie Baier,Dan Stowell*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This study investigates whether temporal context (interpulse interval, IPI) improves bat-species classification and whether transformer-based models (PaSST) are more sensitive to IPI than CNNs (EfficientNet-B0). Results show limited support for IPI providing species-discriminative information, with transformer models slightly outperforming CNNs but showing reduced cross-condition generalizability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Temporal context (IPI) may aid automated bat-species classification, but its specific contribution remains unclear. This study aimed to determine whether IPI variation provides species-discriminative information and whether transformer-based models are more sensitive to this temporal feature than CNNs.

Method: Two matched datasets were created from European bat recordings: natural-IPI (original timing) and normalized-IPI (50-ms intervals). EfficientNet-B0 and PaSST were fine-tuned and evaluated within each condition. Cross-condition evaluation tested generalization. Pretrained classifiers BatDetect2 and BAT were also evaluated on both conditions.

Result: PaSST showed minimal difference between natural-IPI (71±2.3%) and normalized-IPI (70±6.3%). EfficientNet improved from 47±4.7% to 57±3.9% with normalization. PaSST outperformed EfficientNet in both conditions. In cross-condition evaluation, models trained on natural-IPI outperformed those trained on normalized-IPI on natural test sets (EfficientNet: 54%→50%; PaSST: 65%→57%). BatDetect2 and BAT showed minimal differences between IPI conditions.

Conclusion: Natural IPI variation contributes limited species-discriminative information, and transformers do not use it more effectively than CNNs. However, models trained under normalized conditions show reduced performance on natural recordings, indicating that results from normalized conditions may not fully transfer to real-world applications.

Abstract: Temporal context may aid automated bat-species classification, but the contribution of specific features remains unclear. We investigated whether variation in the interpulse interval (IPI)-the time between consecutive call onsets-provides species-discriminative information and whether transformer-based models are more sensitive to this information than convolutional neural networks. We created two matched datasets from European bat recordings: a natural-IPI condition retaining the original call timing and a normalized-IPI condition in which call onsets were spaced at 50-ms intervals. EfficientNet-B0 and PaSST were fine-tuned and evaluated within each condition. In an additional experiment, each architecture was trained separately on natural-IPI and normalized-IPI recordings, and evaluated on the same natural-IPI test set. Finally, the pretrained classifiers BatDetect2 and BAT were evaluated on both conditions. Within-condition IPI normalization had model-dependent effects. PaSST accuracy differed little between the natural-IPI ($71 \pm 2.3\%$) and normalized-IPI ($70 \pm 6.3\%$) conditions, whereas EfficientNet accuracy increased from $47 \pm 4.7\%$ to $57 \pm 3.9\%$. PaSST exceeded EfficientNet under both conditions. In the cross-condition evaluation, models trained on natural-IPI recordings outperformed those trained on normalized-IPI recordings on the natural-IPI test set: accuracy decreased from 54% to 50% for EfficientNet and from 65% to 57% for PaSST. BatDetect2 and BAT differed little between IPI conditions. Overall, we found limited support for the hypotheses that natural IPI variation contributes substantially to bat-species classification and that it is used more effectively by transformer-based than CNN-based models. Nevertheless, the cross-condition performance decrease shows that results obtained under normalized conditions may not transfer fully to natural recordings.

</details>


### [273] [Diffusion-Based Synthetic Data Pretraining for Enhancing Activity Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02292)
*E. Riveros,D. Vega-Oliveros,A. Soriano-Vargas,A. Rocha*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a two-stage training strategy using diffusion-generated synthetic sensor data to improve human activity recognition (HAR) for dietary monitoring (eating/drinking). The method pre-trains CABiGRU (a CNN-BiGRU model with multi-head attention) on synthetic data, then fine-tunes on real smartwatch sensor data, achieving 90.6% balanced accuracy on the DEO dataset and addressing class imbalance issues in minority alimentary activities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Human activity recognition systems often underperform on subtle and underrepresented classes (like eating/drinking), limiting their utility for real-world dietary monitoring and chronic disease management. The minority class problem leads to underfitting and poor generalization in healthcare applications.

Method: The approach builds upon CABiGRU, a convolutional architecture with Bidirectional GRU layers, multi-head attention, and residual connections that processes smartwatch accelerometer, gyroscope, and magnetometer data. A diffusion model generates synthetic sensor data windows, which are used in a two-stage training strategy: (1) pre-training CABiGRU on synthetic data, followed by (2) fine-tuning on real-world data.

Result: On the DEO (drinking/eating/other) dataset, the proposed pipeline achieves a balanced accuracy of 90.6%, improving over a strong supervised baseline. The method demonstrates the benefits of diffusion-based synthetic pre-training for recognizing alimentary activities.

Conclusion: Combining diffusion-generated synthetic data with targeted fine-tuning enhances robust recognition of dietary behaviors and effectively addresses class imbalance. This represents a step forward for reliable deployment in healthcare and nutrition-monitoring settings, supporting dietary habit tracking and chronic disease management.

Abstract: Human activity recognition (HAR) is increasingly important for healthcare, well-being, and daily monitoring ap- plications, for which detecting alimentary activities such as eating and drinking can provide actionable insight into dietary habits and chronic disease management. HAR systems, however, often underperform on subtle and underrepresented classes, limiting their utility in real-world dietary monitoring. This work builds upon CABiGRU, a convolutional architecture with Bidirectional GRU layers, multi-head attention, and residual connections, designed to capture discriminative temporal patterns from smart- watch accelerometer, gyroscope, and magnetometer data. To improve CaBiGRU's generalization and reduce underfitting in the minority class, we leverage synthetic sensor data windows using a diffusion model and adopt a two-stage training strategy: pre-training CABiGRU on synthetic data, followed by fine-tuning on the real-world data. On the DEO (drinking/eating/other) dataset, the proposed pipeline achieves a balanced accuracy of 90.6%, improving over a strong supervised baseline and showing the benefits of diffusion-based synthetic pre-training for recognizing alimentary activities and representing a step forward dealing with unbalanced classes. These results suggest that combining diffusion-generated data with targeted fine-tuning enhances robust recognition of dietary behaviors, supporting more reliable deployment in healthcare and nutrition-monitoring settings.

</details>


### [274] [$Ψ$-Resilience: Model-Free Feature Importance from 1D Topological Signals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02299)
*Fabian Galis,Darian Onchis,Pedro Real Jurado*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Ψ-Resilience is a model-free feature importance method that uses 1D topological signals to derive explanations directly from data. It constructs a class-disagreement landscape by estimating class-conditional densities and uses 0-dimensional persistence to define a resilience functional that aggregates topological features surviving perturbations up to a user-defined robustness scale.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The need for model-free feature importance methods that can derive explanations directly from data itself, without relying on predictive models, enabling rigorous distribution-level auditing.

Method: 1) Estimate class-conditional densities along each feature axis; 2) Compute pointwise absolute difference to construct class-disagreement landscape; 3) Apply 0-dimensional persistence to extract topological features; 4) Define resilience functional that aggregates features surviving perturbations up to a user-set robustness scale.

Result: On synthetic datasets with known ground truth: achieves Spearman rank correlations up to 0.8, competitive with SHAP and mutual information. On real datasets: correlations up to 0.9 with other methods.

Conclusion: Ψ-Resilience is a stable, auditable feature importance method that enables rigorous distribution-level auditing without requiring a predictive model, showing strong agreement with established methods.

Abstract: We introduce $Ψ$-Resilience, a model-free feature importance method that derives explanations directly from the data itself via 1D topological signals. Our method constructs a class-disagreement landscape by estimating class-conditional densities and taking their pointwise absolute difference along the feature axis. Then, the 0-dimensional persistence of this 1D signal defines a resilience functional that aggregates only those topological features that survive perturbations up to a robustness scale which is set by the user.
