This gives us a context-robust importance score that is inherently auditable via the underlying 1D landscapes and their persistence. We evaluate our method on both synthetic and real datasets. On synthetic generators with specified ground-truth importance, $Ψ$-Resilience recovers the ranking of features with high fidelity, achieving Spearman rank correlations up to 0.8 and performing competitively with multiple feature importance methods, including SHAP and mutual information. On real datasets with no known ground truth, our technique agrees with these methods, with correlations up to 0.9. These results show that $Ψ$-Resilience is a stable explanation method that enables rigorous, distribution-level auditing of feature importance without relying on a predictive model.

</details>


### [275] [PowerBench: Measuring Language Model Bias in Power-shifting Requests](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02303)
*Nicolas Martorell,Wendy Brau,Gonzalo A. Heredia,Tomás Pablo Korenblit,Gaspar Labastié,Tomás Gimenez Molina*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: PowerBench is a new benchmark evaluating how language models respond to power-shifting requests, categorizing them into self-empowerment, disempowerment, and power grabbing. Testing 24 models (US and Chinese developers) across multiple conditions reveals systematic asymmetries in model behavior: models refuse power grabbing most, followed by disempowerment, then self-empowerment. Refusal increases with the scale of affected parties. Models show nationality biases, and AI agents as users trigger higher refusal rates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to address concerns that language models may exhibit systematic biases in helping users with power-related requests, which could either shift power distributions at scale or be exploited by users who learn which identities receive less assistance. The lack of standardized benchmarks for measuring these asymmetries motivated the creation of PowerBench.

Method: The researchers built, curated, and open-sourced a dataset of power-shifting requests varying four dimensions: power domain, context, scale of affected party, and user's prior power standing. They evaluated 24 models (12 from US developers, 12 from Chinese developers) under three experimental conditions: (1) reciprocal nationalities of user and affected party, (2) AI agent as the user, and (3) 8 request languages.

Result: Key findings include: (1) Models refuse power grabbing more than disempowerment, and disempowerment more than self-empowerment; (2) Refusal of power grabbing increases with scale from individual to society; (3) Models are biased toward helping others take power from the US and against helping US users take power from others, but favor the US when it gains power without losses; (4) When users are AI agents, refusal increases, especially for power grabbing against individuals; (5) Language biases refusal in model-specific ways that largely cancel on average.

Conclusion: The study reveals significant asymmetries in how language models handle power-shifting requests across different conditions. These findings highlight the need for measurable standards to identify and mitigate such biases in current and future models. The release of PowerBench enables systematic evaluation of these asymmetries.

Abstract: Language models increasingly assist people with power-related requests, so systematic differences in whom they help could shift the distribution of power at scale, or be exploited by users who learn which identities are refused less. We introduce PowerBench, an evaluation of power-shifting requests that distinguishes self-empowerment, disempowerment, and power grabbing, plus a control of refusal-inducing requests that shift no power. We build, curate, and open-source a dataset of such requests varying the power domain, the context, the scale of the affected party, and the prior power standing of the user, and evaluate 24 models (12 from US and 12 from Chinese developers) under three experimental conditions: reciprocal nationalities of user and affected party, an AI agent as the user, and 8 request languages. Models refuse power grabbing more than disempowerment, and disempowerment more than self-empowerment. Refusal of power grabbing rises with the scale of the affected party, from an individual to a society. Models are biased toward helping others take power from the US and against helping US users take power from others, but favor the US when it gains power and nobody loses it. When the user is an AI agent, refusal of power-shifting requests increases, especially in power grabbing against an individual. Finally, language biases refusal, but in model-specific ways that largely cancel on average. We release PowerBench to make these asymmetries measurable in current and future models.

</details>


### [276] [Slow-Fast Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation for Capability Preservation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02324)
*Xiaofei Yin,Tong Chu,Jiyuan Fu,Jun Lan,Shuheng Zhou,Huijia Zhu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper addresses "capability interference" in multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) for foundation multimodal LLMs, where consolidating domain-specific expertise causes decline in general capabilities. The proposed SF-MOPD method uses a fast-slow model dual approach: a fast model (current student) and a slow model (EMA), where only the component pushing the fast model away from the slow model is removed during distillation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) effectively consolidates domain-specific expertise into a single student model, but causes capability interference - the student drifts away from its initialization, leading to general capability decline. Existing solutions like constraining toward initialization suppress domain expertise acquisition.

Method: SF-MOPD couples a fast model (current student updated directly by each teacher) with a slow model (exponential moving average of the student). For each teacher, the method computes the teacher-induced update in log-probability space and removes only the component that pushes the fast model further away from the slow model, while retaining aligned and orthogonal components.

Result: Experiments across multiple model scales demonstrate that SF-MOPD effectively mitigates capability interference, enhances specialized multimodal capabilities, and reduces average degradation on general-capability benchmarks, consistently outperforming vanilla MOPD.

Conclusion: The slow-fast dual mechanism successfully balances general foundation capabilities with confirmed domain expertise, providing an effective solution to the capability interference problem in multi-teacher distillation of foundation multimodal LLMs.

Abstract: Foundation multimodal large language models are designed to support a broad spectrum of capabilities across diverse domains. Multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) provides an effective framework for consolidating domain-specific expertise into a single student model. However, MOPD training gradually drives the student away from its initialization model, and general capabilities decline as the displacement grows, resulting in capability interference. A direct remedy is constraining the student toward its initialization, but this suppresses the acquisition of domain expertise as well. We propose Slow-Fast Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation (SF-MOPD), which couples a fast model, the current student updated directly by each teacher, with a slow model, an exponential moving average of the student. The slow model absorbs the learning signal gradually, serving as a moving capability reference that fuses the general foundation with confirmed domain expertise. For each teacher, SF-MOPD computes the teacher-induced update in log-probability space and removes only the component that pushes the fast model further away from the slow model, while retaining aligned and orthogonal components. Experiments across multiple model scales demonstrate that SF-MOPD effectively mitigates capability interference, enhances specialized multimodal capabilities, and reduces the average degradation on general-capability benchmarks, consistently outperforming vanilla MOPD.

</details>


### [277] [Drive vs. Decay: On the Training Dynamics of Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02344)
*José Lucas De Melo Costa,Seong Woo Ahn,Fabrice Popineau,Arpad Rimmel,Bich-Liên Doan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper develops a theory to explain and prevent representation collapse in Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) by analyzing the stability of gradient dynamics through a driving force vs decay effect framework. This theory predicts a phase boundary and unifies existing heuristics (predictor scaling, masking ratio, EMA), leading to a new architecture called ResidualPred that improves representation quality across tabular and image benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) suffer from representation collapse, a problem typically addressed through empirical heuristics without theoretical understanding. The authors sought to develop a unified theory that explains why these heuristics work and how they can be systematically improved.

Method: The authors linearize the coupled JEPA gradient flow around the trivial fixed point, identifying two competing effects: a driving force (γ) and a decay effect (σ). Under approximate spectral decoupling, they derive a per-mode stability ratio μ_i = γ_i / σ_i that factorizes into independent data-side and predictor-side terms. The count of unstable modes tracks the rank of representations that can emerge. They validate this theory across 800+ Tabular-JEPA configurations and introduce ResidualPred, a transformer predictor whose attention is biased toward identity at initialization.

Result: The framework successfully predicts a phase boundary that matches empirical observations across 800+ configurations. ResidualPred improves both effective rank and downstream accuracy on tabular benchmarks and I-JEPA pretraining on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, STL-10, and ImageNet.

Conclusion: The theory successfully connects empirical collapse-avoidance heuristics to an explicit dynamical picture, providing a principled approach to designing stabilizers. The proposed ResidualPred architecture demonstrates that incorporating identity bias in attention mechanisms can effectively prevent representation collapse and improve learning outcomes across multiple domains.

Abstract: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) are prone to representation collapse, typically mitigated through empirical heuristics. We develop an early-training stability theory that unifies these heuristics. Linearising the coupled JEPA gradient flow around the trivial fixed point reveals two competing effects: a driving force ($γ$) and a decay effect ($σ$). Under approximate spectral decoupling, a per-mode stability ratio $μ_i = γ_i / σ_i$ factorises into independent data-side and predictor-side terms and the count of unstable modes tracks the rank of representations that can emerge. The framework predicts a phase boundary, which we confirm empirically across more than 800 Tabular-JEPA configurations. It also unifies predictor scaling, masking ratio, and EMA as distinct mechanisms for shifting $μ$. Guided by this analysis, we introduce ResidualPred, a transformer predictor whose attention is biased toward the identity at initialisation; it improves both effective rank and downstream accuracy on tabular benchmarks and in I-JEPA pretraining on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, STL-10, and ImageNet. Our framework connects empirical collapse-avoidance heuristics to an explicit dynamical picture, yielding theory-driven stabilizers. Code is available at https://github.com/jose-melo/drive-vs-decay.

</details>


### [278] [Mitigating Convergence Collapse in Fixed-Target Anomaly Detectors via Kernel-Anchored Locality Regularization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02345)
*José Lucas De Melo Costa,Fabrice Popineau,Arpad Rimmel,Bich-Liên Doan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper identifies a "convergence collapse" problem in neural tabular anomaly detectors where better optimization leads to worse detection. The authors show that fixed-target neural detectors fail because they extrapolate too well at convergence, eliminating the residual signal. They propose KCM (Kernel Contraction Matching) as a kernel-regression analog that enforces locality, and KAR (Kernel-Anchored Regularizer) to constrain neural networks to prevent collapse.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Neural anomaly detectors for tabular data (contraction matching, one-step rectified flow, reconstruction autoencoders) rely on test-time residuals to score anomalies, but face a fundamental problem: as optimization improves, the detector performance degrades. This counter-intuitive "convergence collapse" phenomenon motivated investigation into why classical methods work and how to fix neural methods.

Method: The authors formalize the theoretical connection between fixed-target neural detectors and classical methods by showing that the kernel-regression analog is a finite-bandwidth Nadaraya-Watson smoother (KCM). They then introduce Kernel-Anchored Regularizer (KAR) that penalizes neural network predictions from deviating from kernel-weighted averages of training targets, enforcing locality constraints.

Result: KCM, despite being closed-form and training-free, matches established neural baselines on ADBench. KAR mitigates convergence collapse across collapse-prone ADBench datasets and three different backbones, consistently improving AUROC under prolonged training.

Conclusion: Effective anomaly detection requires a locality constraint that blocks unconstrained extrapolation. Classical detectors enforce this explicitly, while neural methods need explicit regularization (like KAR) or alternative approaches (like KCM) that preserve locality. This work bridges neural and classical methods through kernel regression theory and provides practical solutions for stable neural anomaly detection.

Abstract: A family of tabular anomaly detectors trains a neural map toward a fixed target under squared-error loss and scores anomalies by the test-time residual; contraction matching, one-step rectified flow, and reconstruction autoencoders all fit this template. We characterize a convergence collapse: better optimization makes the detector worse. At convergence, the learned map tracks the target even off-distribution, so the residual signal vanishes on anomalies as well as on normal data. These detectors therefore rely on implicit non-convergence (early stopping, capacity caps) to retain signal. We argue this is structural: effective anomaly detection requires a locality constraint that blocks unconstrained extrapolation. Classical detectors (kNN, KDE, isolation forests, LOF) enforce locality explicitly; fixed-target neural detectors do not. We formalize the connection by showing that the kernel-regression analog of a fixed-target detector is a finite-bandwidth Nadaraya-Watson smoother, which we call Kernel Contraction Matching (KCM). KCM is closed-form, training-free, and CPU-efficient, yet matches established neural baselines on ADBench. Building on this bridge, we introduce the Kernel-Anchored Regularizer (KAR), which penalizes deviation of the neural prediction from a kernel-weighted average of training targets. Across collapse-prone ADBench datasets and three backbones, KAR mitigates collapse and improves AUROC under prolonged training.

</details>


### [279] [From Behavior to Provenance: Attributing Tabular Foundation Models to Synthetic Pretraining Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02347)
*Mohamed Bouadi,Nassim Bouarour,Shivam Dubey,Aditya Tanna,Vinay Kumar Sankarapu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces synthetic pretraining as a controlled method to validate training-data attribution methods. Using O'PRIOR, a synthetic task generator for tabular foundation models, the authors create a testbed where every pretraining task has explicit lineage over structural mechanisms, missingness, confounding, shortcuts, and distribution shift. They validate attribution methods through behavior-conditioned attribution, counterfactual retraining, and provenance-aware interventions, showing that top-attributed task removal significantly impacts model performance while bottom-attributed removal improves it.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Training-data attribution is difficult to validate because causal training influence is rarely observable in real-world settings. The authors argue that controlled synthetic pretraining makes attribution experimentally testable, providing a way to verify which training examples actually shape model behavior.

Method: The authors use O'PRIOR, a provenance-rich synthetic task generator for tabular foundation models. They construct a testbed with explicit lineage over structural mechanisms, missingness, confounding, shortcuts, and distribution shift. They combine: (1) behavior-conditioned attribution, (2) counterfactual retraining, and (3) provenance-aware interventions to test task-level faithfulness and mechanism-level consistency.

Result: Removing top-attributed 5% of synthetic tasks decreases mean ROC-AUC by 0.013, compared with 0.002±0.004 under random removal. Removing bottom-attributed tasks improves performance by 0.003. For shortcut-provenance tasks, targeted removal yields 0.043 vs 0.016 for random removal. Provenance discrimination AUROC ranges 0.55-0.62, showing substantial top-k enrichment despite modest ranking AUROC.

Conclusion: Synthetic provenance provides a controlled setting for verifiable contributive attribution. The results show that provenance association and interventional faithfulness need not coincide - high attribution scores correlate with actual influence, but the relationship between ranking and true provenance is more modest.

Abstract: Training-data attribution aims to identify which training examples shape model behavior, yet validating such claims is difficult because causal training influence is rarely observable. We argue that controlled synthetic pretraining makes attribution experimentally testable. Using O'PRIOR, a provenance-rich synthetic task generator for tabular foundation models, we construct a testbed in which every pretraining task carries explicit lineage over structural mechanisms, missingness, confounding, shortcuts, and distribution shift. We combine behavior-conditioned attribution with counterfactual retraining and provenance-aware interventions to test both task-level faithfulness and mechanism-level consistency. On held-out real tasks, removing the top-attributed 5% of synthetic tasks decreases mean ROC-AUC by 0.013, compared with 0.002$\pm$0.004 under random removal, while removing bottom-attributed tasks improves performance by 0.003. Within shortcut-provenance tasks, targeted removal yields an effect of 0.043 versus 0.016 for matched random removal. Provenance discrimination is more modest by ranking AUROC (0.55-0.62), despite substantial top-k enrichment, revealing that provenance association and interventional faithfulness need not coincide. Our results establish synthetic provenance as a controlled setting for verifiable contributive attribution

</details>


### [280] [Does Every User Need a Private LoRA? Decoupling Personalization from Per-User Adaptation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02353)
*Songyuan Sui,Srikanth Malla,Chiho Choi,Joon Hee Choi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LINEUP is a method for personalized large language models that uses a bank of reusable low-rank personalization factors instead of complete per-user adaptation. It achieves comparable performance to private-LoRA (4.19M parameters) while each target user optimizes only 8 scalars, by decoupling expressive personalization capacity from per-user trainable state.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current personalized LLMs require complete adaptation state for each user, which scales poorly as the user population grows. The authors explore how much adaptation capacity can be shared across users, how shared capacity should be composed, and how much must remain user-specific.

Method: Three empirical analyses: (1) Finding cross-user reusable structure in independent user adapters, (2) Evaluating utility of reusable directions based on user relevance and query variation, (3) Using user histories as transferable signals for compact individual correction. LINEUP learns a bank of reusable low-rank personalization factors, composes them through user-conditioned recall and query-dependent calibration, and restricts target-user adaptation to a tiny user code (8 scalars) over a shared correction space.

Result: LINEUP leads on all 12 metrics across 6 tasks (personalized classification, prediction, and generation), each averaged over 3 independent runs. It reduces LaMP-3 RMSE by 11.4% relative to the strongest baseline. It maintains advantages under limited history.

Conclusion: Rich personalization can be supported primarily by reusable, conditionally composed shared capacity, while independent user adaptation can be confined to a tiny correction state (only 8 scalars per user vs 4.19M parameters in private-LoRA). The theoretical analysis provides finite-step, finite-history risk bound and sufficient conditions for user-code refinement to improve on history initialization.

Abstract: Personalized large language models often require a complete adaptation state for each user. However, this paradigm scales poorly as the user population grows. We revisit this design through the lens of personalization capacity allocation: how much adaptation capacity can be shared across users, how the shared capacity should be composed, and how much must remain user-specific. We answer them through three complementary empirical analyses. We find that independent user adapters contain substantial cross-user reusable structure, that the utility of reusable directions reflects both user relevance and variation across queries, and that user histories provide transferable signals for compact individual correction. Motivated by these findings, we propose LINEUP. It learns a bank of reusable low-rank personalization factors, composes them through user-conditioned recall and query-dependent calibration, and restricts target-user adaptation to a tiny user code over a shared correction space. This design decouples expressive personalization capacity from per-user trainable state. Each target user optimizes only eight scalars, while all shared components remain fixed. By comparison, the evaluated private-LoRA configuration uses 4.19 million per-user parameters. Our theoretical analysis gives a finite-step, finite-history risk bound and sufficient conditions for user-code refinement to improve on history initialization. Across six tasks spanning personalized classification, prediction, and generation, LINEUP leads on all 12 metrics, each averaged over three independent runs (e.g., reducing LaMP-3 RMSE by 11.4% relative to the strongest baseline). It maintains advantages under limited history. These results show that rich personalization can be supported primarily by reusable, conditionally composed shared capacity, while independent user adaptation remains confined to a tiny correction state.

</details>


### [281] [Why Does Adaptive Batching Help LLM Pretraining? A Perspective from Unbounded Variance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02355)
*Arda Fazla,Antesh Upadhyay,Ege C. Kaya,M. Berk Sahin,Abolfazl Hashemi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses the theoretical and practical justification for increasing batch size during LLM pretraining. The authors propose a generalized BG-a noise model that interpolates between bounded variance (a=0) and the Blum--Gladyshev model (a=2), derive matching oracle complexity bounds, and demonstrate an adaptive batch scheduler that achieves better validation loss with fewer iterations than existing approaches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The standard assumption in stochastic optimization theory—that stochastic gradient variance is uniformly bounded—fails in many practical nonconvex problems like LLM training. While the BG-0 model allows quadratic variance growth, it may be overly conservative. This work seeks to better understand and leverage batch size scheduling through a more flexible noise model.

Method: The authors empirically investigated variance growth in LLM pretraining to validate a generalized noise model (BG-a). They derived an information-theoretic lower bound under L-smoothness conditions and established a matching upper bound by proposing an adaptive batch scheduler that dynamically adjusts batch size based on training progress.

Result: The generalized BG-a model provides a tighter description of practical noise behavior than existing models. Theoretically, the lower bound shows oracle complexity Ω(ε^{-(4+a)}). Practically, the adaptive batch scheduler achieved lower validation loss than both small and large batch training on OLMo2 models (up to 1B parameters) on C4 dataset, while using less than 10% of the iterations required by small batch training.

Conclusion: The generalized BG-a noise model better captures variance growth in LLM pretraining. By increasing batch size as iterates move away from initialization, the proposed scheduler effectively controls variance growth and achieves superior performance with significantly reduced computational cost, providing both theoretical insight and practical utility for LLM training.

Abstract: Increasing the batch size during training is a common practice in large language model (LLM) pretraining, yet the theoretical justification behind its success is not well understood. Analyses of stochastic optimization often assume uniformly bounded stochastic gradient variance, yet recent evidence suggests that this assumption fails in many practical nonconvex problems. The Blum--Gladyshev (BG-$0$) noise model relaxes this assumption by allowing the variance to grow quadratically with the distance from initialization, suggesting that batch size schedulers can help by controlling the variance growth during training. However, this growth can be overly conservative in practice. We empirically investigate variance growth in LLM pretraining and observe that a generalized BG model with a tunable growth exponent provides a tighter description of practical noise behavior. Motivated by this observation, we introduce the generalized BG-$a$ noise model, which interpolates between bounded variance ($a=0$) and BG-$0$ noise ($a=2$). Under $L$-smoothness, we derive an information-theoretic lower bound with growth-dependent oracle complexity $Ω(ε^{-(4+a)})$ and establish a matching upper bound in $ε$-dependence by increasing the batch size as the iterates move away from initialization. Finally, we propose an adaptive batch scheduler that controls variance growth through dynamic batch size adjustments during training. In pretraining OLMo2 models of up to 1B parameters on C4, our scheduler achieves a lower validation loss than both small and large batch training under matched token budgets, while using less than 10\% of the iterations of small batch training.

</details>


### [282] [Lexicographic Multi-Objective On-Policy Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02359)
*Doseok Jang,Jon Ander Campos,Youran Qi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LMOPD introduces a lexicographic multi-teacher method for integrating reward-specialized policies under explicit priorities, addressing the problem of asymmetric trade-offs in multi-objective RLVR where higher-priority objectives (like correctness) should not be sacrificed for lower-priority ones (like conciseness).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multi-reward post-training methods scalarize rewards or combine specialists without explicit priority protection. This is problematic when trade-offs are asymmetric—for example, conciseness should not improve at the cost of correctness. Current methods fail to preserve priority order among objectives.

Method: LMOPD uses a multi-teacher approach with explicit priorities. For each student rollout, it selects the specialist for the first objective whose gate detects a deficiency, then locally projects its centered log-policy correction to remove components that oppose higher-priority specialists. This lexicographic routing with projection protects higher-priority capabilities.

Result: On 30B-A3B MoE transformer models with math benchmarks: (1) Two-expert setting: fully retains accuracy and reasoning-quality gains while acquiring 46.9% of conciseness gain. (2) Four-expert setting: retains ~90% of both accuracy and reasoning-correctness gains vs only ~57% for the best baseline. Ablations confirm lexicographic routing outperforms random routing and projection strengthens top-priority capabilities.

Conclusion: LMOPD preserves highest-priority capabilities more effectively than existing baselines, demonstrating the value of explicit priorities for specialist integration in multi-objective reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) usually optimizes answer correctness, yet useful language-model behavior also requires high-quality reasoning and concise responses. Existing multi-reward post-training methods typically scalarize rewards or combine specialists without explicitly protecting a reward priority order. This is problematic when trade-offs are asymmetric: conciseness, for example, should not improve at the cost of correctness. We introduce Lexicographic Multi-Objective On-Policy Distillation (LMOPD), a multi-teacher method for integrating reward-specialized policies under explicit priorities. For each student rollout, LMOPD selects the specialist for the first objective whose gate detects a deficiency, then locally projects its centered log-policy correction to remove components that oppose higher-priority specialists. We evaluate 30B-A3B mixture-of-experts transformer models in two- and four-expert settings on three math benchmarks, measuring retained specialist gains. With two experts, LMOPD's point estimates fully retain the accuracy and reasoning-quality gains while acquiring $46.9\%$ of the conciseness gain. With four experts, it retains $\approx90\%$ of both the accuracy gain and reasoning-correctness gain, compared to only $\approx57\%$ by the next best evaluated baseline. Matched four-expertablations show that lexicographic routing outperforms random routing and that projection further strengthens both top-priority capabilities. Across both scales, LMOPD preserves the highest-priority capabilities more effectively than the existing baselines we evaluate, demonstrating the value of explicit priorities for specialist integration.

</details>


### [283] [ArrivalBench: Agent-Generated Data Pipelines Are Correct Once and Wrong Under Time](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02363)
*Pranay Kothari*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ArrivalBench is a new benchmark that tests data pipelines by re-executing them under adversarial delivery schedules (late, duplicated, out-of-order, retried records) rather than single-execution grading. It发现 86-100% certified pipelines actually have 7.0-79.2% silent failures when re-executed, revealing that current benchmarks miss critical idempotency and ordering hazards.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current benchmarks grade pipelines by running once against a fixed snapshot, missing real-world data delivery issues. A wrong table (silent failure) is invisible to monitoring while a crash is visible, but existing benchmarks don't distinguish these. The authors argue that re-execution under adversarial conditions is necessary to catch these failures.

Method: The benchmark re-executes agent-generated pipelines under adversarial but replayable delivery schedules including late, duplicated, out-of-order and retried records. It requires final state to equal a batch recomputation of the complete log (oracle recomputes rather than classifies). Tested on 40 tasks with 11 different models.

Result: Single-execution grading certifies 86-100% of pipelines; re-executing finds 7.0-79.2% silently wrong. Idempotency hazards fail more often than ordering hazards. A hazard warning reduces silent failure from 48.2% to 10.5% but increases crash rate from 9.0% to 37.0%, with overall failure only moving from 51.0% to 44.0%. Results are robust (rates moved by at most 5.9 points in re-runs).

Conclusion: Current pipeline benchmarks miss significant silent failures. Re-execution under adversarial conditions is essential to catch idempotency and ordering hazards. Distinguishing wrong answers from crashes changes how we evaluate interventions - hazard warnings trade silent failures for crashes but don't necessarily reduce overall failure rates.

Abstract: Benchmarks for agent-generated data work grade a pipeline by running it once against a fixed snapshot. ArrivalBench instead re-executes the pipeline an agent leaves behind under adversarial but replayable delivery schedules (late, duplicated, out-of-order and retried records) and requires its final state to equal a batch recomputation of the complete log. Because the oracle recomputes rather than classifies, a wrong table and a crash are distinct verdicts: a crash is visible to monitoring a team already runs, and a wrong table is not. On 40 tasks we built, our reimplementation of single-execution grading certifies 86-100% of the pipelines eleven models produce; re-executing the same artifacts finds 7.0-79.2% of the certified ones silently wrong. The gap is not produced by the repair loop: within the same model and task, pipelines repaired against the snapshot test fail replay about as often as those that passed it first time. In every model, idempotency hazards fail more often than ordering hazards. Separating a wrong answer from a crash also changes how interventions read: a hazard warning cuts one model's silent failure from 48.2% to 10.5% while raising its crash rate from 9.0% to 37.0%, so all-in failure moves only from 51.0% to 44.0%. All eleven arms were independently re-run, and rates moved by at most 5.9 points.

</details>


### [284] [Co-design Gym: A Unified Benchmark for Embodiment-Policy Co-optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02366)
*Aviraj Newatia,Yordan Tsvetkov,Leonard Pleiss,Andrew Spielberg,Rika Antonova*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Co-Design Gym is a benchmark suite for jointly optimizing agent embodiment and control policy, addressing the limitation that most existing benchmarks assume fixed embodiment. The suite includes 20 environment families with over 85 distinct co-design presets across diverse domains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most reinforcement learning benchmarks assume fixed agent embodiment, but optimal embodiment and policy are interdependent - the agent's body shape determines which policies are discoverable, and the optimal embodiment depends on the policies it enables. Optimizing these separately leads to suboptimal results.

Method: The authors created a comprehensive benchmark suite (Co-Design Gym) spanning multiple domains including robotic manipulation, locomotion, multi-robot cooperation, deformable/soft dynamics, video games, electricity grids, wireless networks, F1 racing, multi-agent warehouses, and optimal control. They also systematically evaluated representative co-design algorithms.

Result: The benchmark provides 20 environment families with over 85 distinct co-design presets, covering diverse domains. The authors also characterized the current state of the art through systematic evaluation of co-design algorithms.

Conclusion: Co-Design Gym lays the groundwork for cumulative, comparable progress in co-design research by providing standardized environments and evaluation protocols for studying the joint optimization of embodiment and policy.

Abstract: Finding an optimal behaviour policy within a given environment is a widely studied problem in domains as diverse as games, robotics, energy infrastructure, communication networks, and multi-agent systems. Numerous benchmarks have been developed to support such research, but the vast majority assume that the agent's embodiment (design) is fixed, focusing instead on policy learning alone. Lifting this assumption gives rise to a broader class of problems in which optimizing embodiment and policy separately is highly suboptimal. An agent's embodiment strongly shapes which control policies can be discovered, while the optimal embodiment is in turn defined by the policies it admits. To help the research community study this class of problems explicitly and systematically, we introduce Co-Design Gym - a suite of benchmark environments for jointly optimizing embodiment and policy. Our environments span domains such as robotic manipulation and locomotion, multi-robot cooperation, deformable and soft dynamics, video games, electricity grids, wireless networks, F1 racing, multi-agent warehouses, and optimal control, offering 20 environment families (domains), with over 85 distinct co-design presets in total. We further contribute a systematic evaluation of representative co-design algorithms, characterizing the current state of the art. Together, these contributions lay the groundwork for cumulative, comparable progress in co-design.

</details>


### [285] [Latent-MOPD: Latent Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02381)
*Zhengyu Fang,Seoyeon Hong,Jie Yang,Muyang Li,Koyoshi Shindo,Brandon Joseph Lwowski,Jing Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Latent-MOPD is the first representation-level multi-teacher OPD method for LLMs that integrates teachers through both their output distributions and hidden states, without additional teacher training. It coordinates supervision from multiple specialists using late-layer target selection, shared projection for hidden width mismatches, and domain-grouped updates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM multi-teacher OPD only transfers knowledge through output distributions (token-level). This work aims to leverage both predictions AND hidden representations from multiple teachers, enabling a single student to integrate capabilities from several specialists more effectively.

Method: Three key technical contributions: (1) Late-layer target selection based on teacher-student relationship, (2) Shared projection to bridge unequal hidden widths between teachers and student, (3) Domain-grouped updates. Each teacher's supervision gradually shifts from hidden states to token predictions, with both channels using the same routed specialist.

Result: In same-family setting: outperforms token-only, representation-only, and uniform-averaging baselines on all nine benchmarks (math, code, logic). Student surpasses per-benchmark best teacher on majority of benchmarks with same parameter count. With cross-family teachers: outperforms single-channel baselines on all benchmarks. Representation-only control remains stable with domain-pure updates but collapses with interleaved teacher domains.

Conclusion: A single student can successfully integrate capabilities from multiple specialists through both their output distributions and internal representations, demonstrating the effectiveness of representation-level multi-teacher distillation.

Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student on the responses it generates. Existing LLM multi-teacher OPD transfers what specialists predict through their output distributions. We introduce Latent-MOPD, to our knowledge the first representation-level multi-teacher OPD method for LLMs. It integrates existing specialists through both their predictions and the hidden states used to compute them, without additional teacher training. To coordinate representation supervision from multiple specialists, we select late-layer targets according to the teacher-student relationship, bridge unequal hidden widths with a shared projection, and group updates by domain. Each teacher's supervision gradually shifts from hidden states to token predictions, with both channels using the same routed specialist. In our main same-family setting, Latent-MOPD outperforms the token-only, representation-only and uniform-averaging baselines on all nine benchmarks across math, code and logic. With the same parameter count as each teacher, the student also surpasses the per-benchmark best teacher on a majority of these benchmarks. With larger, separately developed cross-family teachers, Latent-MOPD outperforms both single-channel baselines on all benchmarks. A same-family all-layer representation-only control remains stable with domain-pure updates but collapses when teacher domains are interleaved within an update. Our results show that a single student can integrate capabilities from several specialists through both their output distributions and internal representations.

</details>


### [286] [The Surprising Effectiveness of Shared Memory in Looped Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02383)
*Giovanni Monea,Keshav Ramji,Yousef El-Kurdi,Luis A. Lastras,Yoav Artzi,Nathan Godey,Ramón Fernandez Astudillo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Looped Transformers apply the same layers multiple times per token to improve quality, but memory grows with compute since each recursion writes its own key-value cache. This paper proposes memory sharing where only the first recursion writes a cache and later recursions read it while keeping a short window. Surprisingly, this approach improves quality rather than sacrificing it. The Looped Prediction Transformer (LPT) and hybrid variant set a new quality-memory frontier at 150M-1B parameters, with five recursions reducing validation perplexity by 1.12-1.82 while using 76-79% less context memory.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Looped Transformers add compute to improve quality without more parameters, but memory still grows with compute because each recursion writes its own key-value cache. Existing inference-time techniques can shrink this cache but at a cost in quality. The authors seek a better quality-memory trade-off through memory sharing.

Method: Pretrain looped language models to share memory: only the first recursion writes a key-value cache, and later recursions read it while keeping only a short window of their own. Analyze why memory sharing helps through representation analysis and attention patterns.

Result: At 150M-1B parameters with five recursions, the hybrid LPT lowers validation perplexity on FineWeb-Edu by 1.12-1.82 relative to a same-size standard Transformer while using 76-79% less context memory. Shared and local memory develop different representations, and later recursions attend mostly to shared memory, which also acts as a gradient highway to the first recursion.

Conclusion: Memory sharing in looped transformers does not cost quality and actually improves it. The approach achieves a new quality-memory frontier, with shared memory developing distinct representations and serving as both an attention target and gradient highway, enabling better training and inference efficiency.

Abstract: Looped Transformers apply the same layers several times per token, adding compute to improve quality without more parameters. Each recursion, however, writes its own key-value cache, so memory still grows with compute. Inference-time techniques can shrink this cache at a cost in quality. We pretrain looped language models to share memory: only the first recursion writes a cache, and later recursions read it while keeping a short window of their own. Surprisingly, we find that sharing memory does not cost quality and instead improves it. At 150M-1B parameters, our Looped Prediction Transformer (LPT) and its hybrid variant set a new quality-memory frontier for looped models: with five recursions, the hybrid lowers validation perplexity on FineWeb-Edu by 1.12-1.82 relative to a same-size standard Transformer while using 76-79% less context memory. Through an extensive analysis, we investigate why memory sharing helps. Shared and local memory develop different representations, and later recursions attend mostly to the shared memory, which also acts as a gradient highway to the first recursion.

</details>


### [287] [Hesitation Has a Geometry: Entropy-Trained Hyperbolic Probes for Sparse Activation Steering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02391)
*Zeyong Zhang,Tung Sum Thomas Kwok,Tengfei Ma,Mengjia Xu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: HEST (Hyperbolic Entropy Steering) is a method that embeds LLM hidden states in hyperbolic space (Poincaré ball) using a probe trained on the model's own next-token entropy. When entropy exceeds a threshold, it moves the state along the geodesic of steepest descent to improve mathematical reasoning, achieving up to 1.8% accuracy gains on MATH-500 and GSM8K.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current activation steering methods add fixed Euclidean vectors at every token position, which is inefficient because most tokens in mathematical solutions are already determined by context. Only a few branching points (high-entropy tokens) require intervention. Additionally, the hierarchical tree-like structure of mathematical reasoning embeds better in hyperbolic space than Euclidean space.

Method: 1) Train a lightweight probe to predict next-token entropy from hidden states in hyperbolic space (Poincaré ball model)
2) Identify high-entropy tokens where entropy exceeds a threshold
3) Move the embedded state along the geodesic of steepest descent of a Busemann readout (from a learned ideal point)
4) Map the changed state back to the original hidden state space
5) The Busemann readout property ensures fixed-length steps produce equal reductions at every state

Result: On three instruction-tuned models (Qwen2.5-Math and Llama-3.1 families):
- Greedy accuracy improved on MATH-500 and GSM8K in 5 out of 6 settings
- Maximum improvement: 1.8 percentage points
- Contrastive steering vector at every token lowers accuracy
- Euclidean probe loses the gain on Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B-Instruct
- Largest gains on problems where the model hesitates frequently
- Accuracy on remaining problems almost unchanged

Conclusion: Hyperbolic space is more suitable for representing the hierarchical reasoning structure in mathematical problem-solving. The HEST method with Busemann readout successfully improves LLM performance on math benchmarks by only intervening at high-entropy decision points, while preserving performance elsewhere. The theoretical guarantee of the Busemann readout (equal reduction per step at every state) provides consistent steering behavior.

Abstract: When a large language model solves a mathematical problem, its reasoning is largely hierarchical, and the solution often branches at a few tokens where the next-token entropy is high. Such tree-like structure embeds in hyperbolic space with far lower distortion than in Euclidean space. Activation steering, however, usually edits the hidden states of a pretrained model by adding one fixed Euclidean vector at every token, even though most tokens of a solution are already determined by the context. We propose Hyperbolic Entropy Steering (HEST), which embeds the hidden states in the Poincaré ball with a lightweight probe whose only label is the model's own next-token entropy. Where this entropy exceeds a threshold, HEST moves the embedded state along the geodesic of steepest descent of a readout of the probe and maps the change back to the hidden state. For the Busemann readout of a learned ideal point, we prove that a step of fixed length lowers it by the same amount at every state. On three instruction-tuned models from the Qwen2.5-Math and Llama-3.1 families, HEST with the Busemann readout improves greedy accuracy on MATH-500 and GSM8K in five of six settings, by up to 1.8 points, whereas a contrastive steering vector added at every token lowers accuracy. With a Euclidean probe trained in the same way, this gain disappears on Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B-Instruct. The gains are largest on problems where the model hesitates often, and accuracy on the remaining problems is almost unchanged.

</details>


### [288] [Inherit-MAS: Test-Time Evolution of Multi-Agent Systems through Workflow and Execution Inheritance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02396)
*Songtao Wei,Yi Li,Zhichun Guo,Bingzhe Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Inherit-MAS introduces explicit inheritance mechanisms at both workflow and execution levels for LLM-based multi-agent systems, addressing challenges of workflow refinement and redundant computation during test-time evolution.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current test-time evolution methods for MAS face two key problems: (1) broad workflow revisions can disturb useful components, and (2) re-executing unchanged requests incurs redundant computation. The authors draw inspiration from biological evolution's interplay of inheritance and selection to address these issues.

Method: Inherit-MAS employs two-level inheritance: (1) Workflow inheritance - starts from the latest completed candidate, may discard unhelpful nodes, and applies validated edits to address diagnosed deficiencies; (2) Execution inheritance - inherits stored results only when both the complete resolved request and execution context match, avoiding redundant model and tool calls. The system uses a meta-model to synthesize workflows with worker agents (declaring roles, communication inputs, tool permissions) and a separately prompted judge to score executed candidates and diagnose deficiencies.

Result: With GPT-4o-mini workers: 55.4% completion on WorkBench and 49.7% joint F1 on HotpotQA FullWiki, outperforming EvoAgent, EvoMAS, and TacoMAS. With Qwen3-32B workers: exceeds evolving-MAS baselines on both benchmarks. Execution inheritance reduces worker-token usage by 29.1% (WorkBench) and 34.6% (HotpotQA), and total token usage by 5.3% and 18.1%.

Conclusion: Inherit-MAS successfully improves multi-agent system performance through explicit inheritance mechanisms, achieving state-of-the-art results on WorkBench and HotpotQA benchmarks while significantly reducing computational redundancy through execution inheritance.

Abstract: Multi-agent systems (MAS) built from large language models coordinate specialized agents to tackle complex tasks, but effective workflows are difficult to design in advance. Test-time evolution refines workflows using execution feedback, yet broad revisions can disturb useful components, while re-executing unchanged requests can incur redundant computation. Inspired by the interplay of inheritance and selection in biological evolution, we introduce Inherit-MAS, which makes inheritance explicit at the workflow and execution levels. A meta-model first synthesizes a workflow of worker agents with declared roles, communication inputs, and tool permissions, and a separately prompted judge scores each executed candidate and diagnoses its deficiencies. In ordinary refinement rounds, \emph{workflow inheritance} starts from the latest completed candidate, may discard removable nodes judged unhelpful, and applies a validated edit to address the diagnosed deficiency. When the new candidate executes, \emph{execution inheritance} inherits eligible stored results only if the complete resolved request and execution context match, avoiding redundant model and tool calls. With GPT-4o-mini workers, Inherit-MAS achieves 55.4\% completion on WorkBench and 49.7\% joint F1 on HotpotQA FullWiki, outperforming EvoAgent, EvoMAS, and TacoMAS. With Qwen3-32B workers, it also exceeds these evolving-MAS baselines on both benchmarks. Compared with rerunning the same controller with execution inheritance disabled, execution inheritance reduces worker-token usage by 29.1\% on WorkBench and 34.6\% on HotpotQA, and total token usage by 5.3\% and 18.1\%.

</details>


### [289] [Validated Data Onboarding for AI Demand Forecasting on U.S. Building Meter Data: Design, Controlled Evaluation, and a Corrected Negative Result](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02397)
*Yixuan Liang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper presents a data-onboarding pipeline that detects and repairs defective meter data (missing readings, sensor freezes, abnormal values) before training electricity demand forecasting models. The pipeline was tested on 12 U.S. buildings from Building Data Genome 2, showing that seeded defects (0.10% prevalence) increased gradient-boosting forecast error by 86%, but after repair, error returned to baseline while retaining 93% of training targets. At 1.6% defect prevalence (matching field studies), the repaired forecaster matched clean baseline performance, while unprotected forecaster error reached 4.4x seasonal-naive. The method works across multiple models (gradient boosting, ridge regression, random forest) and forecast horizons (1-24 hours). An initial over-cleaning issue was identified and corrected via per-building calibration.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Machine learning models for electricity demand forecasting rely on meter data that is frequently defective (missing readings, sensor failures, abnormal values). These defects can significantly degrade forecast accuracy, but there has been limited research on detecting and repairing such defects using only information available at forecast time (i.e., without future data leakage).

Method: The researchers developed a data-onboarding pipeline with two main components: (1) defect detection using only past information available at forecast time, and (2) past-only repair mechanisms. They conducted controlled experiments on the Building Data Genome 2 dataset (12 U.S. buildings, 210,528 rows, 2016-2017), seeding hash-logged defects at varying prevalence levels (0.10% and 1.6%). They tested multiple forecasting models (gradient-boosting, ridge regression, random forest) across 1-24 hour horizons. They also documented an initial over-cleaning problem and its correction via per-building calibration.

Result: At 0.10% defect prevalence, seeded defects raised gradient-boosting forecast error by 86% (MASE: 0.760 clean → 1.415 corrupted). After detection and repair, error returned to clean-data level (MASE 0.729) while retaining 93% of training targets. At 1.6% prevalence (calibrated to field studies), unprotected forecaster error reached 4.4x seasonal-naive, while repaired forecaster matched clean baseline. The same pattern held for ridge regression and random forest across all 1-24 hour horizons. An initial over-cleaning version made forecasts 25% worse, which was corrected through per-building calibration.

Conclusion: The data-onboarding pipeline effectively protects 24-hour-ahead electricity demand forecasts from defective meter data. The method works across multiple model types and forecast horizons. The key insight is that careful calibration (per-building) is necessary to avoid over-cleaning, which can worse forecasts than the original defects. All results are reproducible with SHA-256 verification, 84 automated tests, and continuous integration.

Abstract: Electric utilities and grid operators increasingly rely on machine-learning models to forecast next-day demand, and those models learn from meter data that is routinely defective: readings go missing, sensors freeze, buildings read zero for hours, and units change by a factor of 100. This report presents a data-onboarding pipeline that detects and repairs such defects before a model is trained, using only information available at forecast time, and a controlled experiment that measures whether the pipeline protects a 24-hour-ahead forecast. On hourly electricity data for twelve U.S. buildings from the public Building Data Genome 2 dataset (210,528 rows, 2016-2017), seeded, hash-logged defects touching 0.10% of the training period raised the error of a gradient-boosting forecaster by 86%; after detection and past-only repair the error returned to the clean-data level (mean absolute scaled error 0.760 clean, 1.415 corrupted, 0.729 repaired) while 93% of training targets were retained. At a defect prevalence calibrated to published field studies (1.6% of training rows) the unprotected forecaster's error reached 4.4 times that of a seasonal-naive rule, and the repaired forecaster again matched the clean baseline. The same pattern held for ridge regression and a random forest and across horizons of 1 to 24 hours. A first version of the pipeline over-cleaned natural data and made forecasts 25% worse; that result is retained, its cause is traced in the published artifacts, and the per-building calibration that corrects it is documented as a dated amendment. Every number is reproducible from pinned public inputs with SHA-256 verification, 84 automated tests and continuous integration.

</details>


### [290] [VisAudit: Evaluating Multimodal Agents for Visual Diagnosis and Repair](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02399)
*Shicheng Liu,Adam Kahirov,Qi Zhang,Zhimin Hu,Song Wang,Junhong Lin,Julian Shun,Yada Zhu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: VisAudit is a benchmark for evaluating multimodal agents' ability to autonomously diagnose, repair, and verify data visualization flaws. It contains 1,900 flawed instances across 21 chart types and 10 flaw categories, with three evaluation tracks. The strongest evaluated model achieves only 47.4% full recovery in autonomous-repair setting, revealing a substantial gap in current multimodal models' autonomous review capabilities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks evaluate individual capabilities like chart generation or defect detection, but fail to capture the full autonomous review process - recognizing incorrect visualizations, determining necessary changes, repairing without disrupting correct content, and verifying intervention success. This gap limits the deployment of multimodal agents in real-world visualization tasks.

Method: VisAudit benchmark uses rendered charts with configurable auxiliary evidence (source data table, intended text summary, visualization code). Agents iteratively diagnose potential defects, modify and execute visualization code, inspect execution and visual feedback, and determine when no further intervention is needed. The benchmark is constructed through controlled perturbations of validated source visualizations with systematic verification and human-aligned quality control. Three tracks are defined: diagnosed repair, autonomous repair, and open-world verification.

Result: Experiments with leading multimodal models reveal that the strongest evaluated model fully recovers only 47.4% of flawed charts in the autonomous-repair setting, indicating a substantial gap from reliable autonomous review.

Conclusion: Current multimodal agents lack sufficient autonomous review capabilities for data visualization tasks. The VisAudit benchmark provides a comprehensive evaluation framework to measure and drive progress in this area, with significant room for improvement in model performance.

Abstract: Multimodal agents are increasingly used for data visualization tasks but remain limited in autonomous review. Unlike humans, they may fail to recognize when a visualization is incorrect, determine what to change, repair it without disrupting correct content, and verify whether the intervention succeeded. Existing benchmarks largely evaluate predefined individual capabilities such as chart generation, instruction-guided editing, or defect detection, and therefore do not capture this gap in autonomous review. We introduce VisAudit, a benchmark for evaluating visualization diagnosis, repair, and verification. Given a rendered chart and configurable auxiliary evidence, including its source data table, intended text summary, and visualization code, an agent iteratively diagnoses potential defects, modifies and executes visualization code, inspects execution and visual feedback, and determines when no further intervention is needed. VisAudit defines three tracks spanning diagnosed repair, autonomous repair, and open-world verification, and contains 1,900 flawed instances across 21 chart types and 10 flaw categories, together with 300 initially correct charts. We construct the benchmark through controlled perturbations of validated source visualizations, with systematic verification and human-aligned quality control to ensure that injected defects are well-defined and recoverable from the available evidence. Experiments with leading multimodal models reveal a substantial gap from reliable autonomous review: the strongest evaluated model fully recovers only $47.4\%$ of flawed charts in the autonomous-repair setting.

</details>


### [291] [Trained Agentic Context Management](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02404)
*Bryce Sandlund*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces a minimal harness approach for enabling long context capabilities in language models, using self-calling tools and token range reading. When finetuned on synthetic data, a 35B parameter model with only 8K context window matches GPT-5.4's performance with 1M context on long document tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors aim to address long context modeling without requiring expensive native long-context training or complex harness designs. They explore whether a simple tool-based harness can effectively enable models to handle much longer contexts than their native window allows.

Method: The approach uses a simple harness with two tools: (1) a tool for the model to call itself with any specified prompt, and (2) a tool to read tokens within a specified range from the input context. The model (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B) is finetuned on a diverse synthetic dataset using this harness, achieving long context capability through only 8,000 tokens of native context.

Result: The resulting model matches GPT-5.4 (with 1M tokens context) performance on the OOLONG-synth benchmark when document length exceeds 40K tokens, despite using only 8K context window—a 125x context length advantage through the harness mechanism.

Conclusion: A minimal tool-based harness enabling self-calling and selective token reading can effectively equip language models with long context capabilities, achieving strong performance on long-document tasks without expensive native long-context training or massive context windows.

Abstract: We study long context language models. Instead of training long context natively, or designing a long context harness, we train a model over the simplest possible harness: a tool to call itself with any specified prompt and a tool to read tokens in a range from the input context. We finetune Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on a diverse synthetic dataset using this harness. With only 8,000 tokens of context, our small model is as strong as GPT-5.4 with 1M tokens of context on the OOLONG-synth benchmark when document length exceeds 40K tokens.

</details>


### [292] [Efficient Neural Field Learning via Adaptive Coverage and Focused Sampling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02410)
*Guang Zhao,Xihaier Luo,Huan-Hsin Tseng,Seungjun Lee,Shinjae Yoo,Yihui Ren,Wei Xu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ACES is a structured sampling framework for training implicit neural representations (INRs) that decouples coverage and importance by using adaptive spatial partitions for domain coverage and region-level importance weighting for prioritizing informative regions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Implicit neural representations (INRs) training is inefficient due to uniform subsampling that ignores spatial heterogeneity. Existing adaptive sampling methods operate at the point level, leading to redundant sampling in localized regions and insufficient domain coverage.

Method: ACES constructs adaptive spatial partitions to ensure domain coverage and reduce redundancy, and applies region-level importance weighting to prioritize informative regions during training.

Result: ACES achieves faster convergence and lower error than uniform and pointwise adaptive sampling baselines, with the largest gains in fields with highly localized complexity.

Conclusion: The proposed framework effectively improves INR training efficiency by addressing coverage and importance sampling separately, with theoretical guarantees on gradient variance reduction and optimization efficiency.

Abstract: Implicit neural representations (INRs) provide a flexible framework for modeling high-dimensional continuous fields, but their training is often inefficient due to uniform subsampling that ignores spatial heterogeneity. Existing adaptive sampling methods partially address this issue by prioritizing high-error samples, but typically operate at the point level, often leading to redundant sampling in localized regions and insufficient coverage of the domain. We propose ACES (Adaptive Coverage-aware Efficient Sampling), a structured sampling framework that improves training efficiency by decoupling coverage and importance. ACES constructs adaptive spatial partitions to ensure domain coverage and reduce redundancy, and applies region-level importance weighting to prioritize informative regions during training. We provide a theoretical analysis showing that adaptive partitioning reduces gradient variance by increasing within-region homogeneity, and that controlled bias in region-level weighting may improve optimization efficiency relative to standard unbiased estimators. Experiments on scientific field learning tasks demonstrate that ACES achieves faster convergence and lower error than uniform and pointwise adaptive sampling baselines, with the largest gains in fields with highly localized complexity.

</details>


### [293] [Prompted to Discriminate: Generalizing Malicious-Input Probes in the Wild](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02413)
*Elad David,Max Fomin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates how the wording of classification suffixes affects the effectiveness of activation probes used as runtime monitors for detecting harmful inputs (prompt injection, jailbreaks, unsafe requests) in LLM agents. The key finding is that appending a classification instruction consistently improves out-of-distribution detection by ~4 AUC points, with the classification format being more important than the specific criterion used.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents increasingly use activation probes as runtime monitors to detect harmful inputs before execution. While adding a short classification instruction after the user's input is a common practice to sharpen probes, it was unclear whether the specific wording matters and whether benefits hold for attacks never seen during training (the real-world deployment scenario).

Method: Controlled experiments with a ladder of post-user suffixes under strict leave-one-dataset-out (LODO) evaluation across 13 safety benchmarks (jailbreak, injection, and benign chat) and three open-weight model families (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen3.5-9B, Gemma-4-12B). Tested both single-position probes and multi-position pooling probes (attention, multi-max, MLP).

Result: A classification suffix consistently improves out-of-distribution detection over no suffix (up to ~4 AUC points). The classification format matters more than the named criterion: content-free labels perform as well as real malicious/benign labels, with the criterion adding precision only at strict thresholds. Off-topic or merely-attentive suffixes help little. The benefit carries to multi-position probes but the optimal suffix is readout-dependent.

Conclusion: The classification suffix is a cheap drop-in improvement for any activation-probe monitor (served through KV-cache fork). However, it is not an automatic win: which suffix helps and by how much depends on the model and readout method. The gain comes from the classification format itself, not the specific criterion named.

Abstract: LLM agents increasingly rely on activation probes as runtime monitors for prompt injection, jailbreaks, and unsafe requests, reading the model's own hidden state to catch a harmful input before the agent acts on it. A cheap, increasingly common move, borrowed from LLM-as-judge prompting, is to append a short classification instruction after the user's turn and read the probe at that point, to sharpen it: the instruction asks the model to represent the incoming request as a class, concentrating the signal the probe must separate, at negligible serving cost. But does the wording of that suffix matter, and does its benefit hold in the wild, on attack types the probe never saw in training, the regime a deployed monitor faces? We test this with a controlled ladder of post-user suffixes under strict leave-one-dataset-out (LODO) evaluation across 13 safety benchmarks (jailbreak, injection, and benign chat) and three open-weight model families (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen3.5-9B, Gemma-4-12B). On a single-position probe, a classification suffix consistently improves out-of-distribution detection over no suffix (up to ~4 AUC points); yet which suffix matters: prompting the model to classify the input, even into content-free labels, reliably wins; an off-topic or merely-attentive suffix helps little. The gain comes from the classification format, not the named criterion: a content-free suffix matches the real malicious/benign one, with the criterion adding precision only at strict thresholds. This is not an artifact of the single-position read: the benefit carries to the multi-position pooling probes used in production (attention, multi-max, MLP), though the best-performing suffix there is readout-dependent. Served through a KV-cache fork, it is a cheap drop-in for any activation-probe monitor, though not an automatic win: which suffix helps, and by how much, depends on the model and the readout.

</details>


### [294] [The AI Theorist reveals excitonic structure in $α$-RuCl$_3$](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02417)
*Hongjian Zhou,Xianfan Nie,Sean Wu,Tarun Patel,Jinge Wu,Andrew Liu,Adam Wei Tsen,David A. Clifton*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Summary generation failed


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Motivation analysis unavailable

Method: Method extraction failed

Result: Result analysis unavailable

Conclusion: Conclusion extraction failed

Abstract: Advances in experimental instrumentation and automation generate increasingly rich datasets, but turning experimental observations into microscopic understanding remains a bottleneck in scientific discovery. To accelerate this process, we introduce AI Theorist, a system of artificial intelligence (AI) agents for autonomous discovery of physical models through hypothesis generation, first-principles calculations and evidence-driven refinement. We apply the framework to $α$-RuCl$_3$, a leading candidate material for realizing a Kitaev quantum spin liquid, to investigate its electronic structure through optical spectra. AI Theorist develops a new interpretation of the optical and photocurrent observations, identifying distinct excitonic states with contrasting optical selection rules and real-space distributions. To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of an AI system autonomously developing a physical model to explain previously unpublished experimental observations in a quantum material, utilizing first-principles electronic-structure and many-body calculations. Our results establish a route to autonomous theoretical discovery in materials science, in which AI agents use first-principles calculations to turn experimental observations into physical models and testable predictions.

</details>


### [295] [Geometry-Aware Time Reparameterization for Flow-Map Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02427)
*Félix Dedek,Makoto Yamada*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a geometry-aware time reparameterization method for flow-map distillation in generative ODEs. By allocating more student time to trajectory segments with large normal acceleration (which are harder to distill), the method improves one- and few-step image generation on CIFAR-10 and CelebA-64 without requiring teacher retraining or additional student parameters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The hypothesis is that trajectory segments with large normal acceleration are harder to distill. The authors investigate whether changing the teacher's time parameterization can make these transitions easier to learn for the student model.

Method: 1. Geometry-aware time reparameterization that allocates more student time to regions with large normal acceleration while preserving geometric paths and terminal distribution
2. Derivation of a shared clock that equalizes population normal-acceleration statistic under suitable assumptions
3. Practical approximation from robust, regularized estimates across teacher trajectories
4. Integration into Lagrangian flow-map distillation using transformed time coordinate to condition the student
5. Clock is estimated once before distillation - no teacher retraining, no additional student parameters, no extra inference-time network evaluations

Result: Improved sample quality over identity-time distillation at matched inference budgets on synthetic data, CIFAR-10, and CelebA-64. Gains are observed in both one-step and two-step image generation. Notable improvements in one-step generation where no intermediate sampling times can be adjusted.

Conclusion: Time reparameterization during distillation is beneficial, particularly for one-step generation where the transformed time coordinate helps the student learn better transitions even without adjustable intermediate sampling times.

Abstract: Flow-map distillation enables one- and few-step generation by learning finite-time transitions of a pretrained generative ODE. We investigate whether changing the teacher's time parameterization can make these transitions easier to learn. Motivated by the hypothesis that trajectory segments with large normal acceleration are harder to distill, we propose a geometry-aware time reparameterization that allocates more student time to these regions while preserving the teacher's geometric paths and terminal distribution. We derive a shared clock that equalizes a population normal-acceleration statistic under suitable assumptions, and construct a practical approximation from robust, regularized estimates across teacher trajectories. We incorporate this clock into Lagrangian flow-map distillation, using the transformed time coordinate to condition the student. The clock is estimated once before distillation and requires neither teacher retraining nor additional student parameters or inference-time network evaluations. Experiments on synthetic data, CIFAR-10, and CelebA-64 show improved sample quality over identity-time distillation at matched inference budgets, including improvements in one- and two-step image generation. The gains in one-step generation, where no intermediate sampling times can be adjusted, highlight the benefits of time reparameterization during distillation.

</details>


### [296] [CRISP: A Framework for Clause-Reconstructed Interpretable NeuroSymbolic Propositions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02431)
*Alex Chan,Shafi Muhtasim Chowdhury,Ekin Can Erkuş,Ole-Christoffer Granmo,Alex Yakovlev,Rishad Shafik*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CRISP is a framework that reconstructs binary neural network last-layer activation vectors as interpretable Tsetlin Machine clauses, providing a symbolic route to audit neural network decisions by mapping hidden representations to propositional rules over Booleanized input features.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deep neural networks achieve high accuracy but their decisions are difficult to audit because decision evidence is encoded in hidden activations rather than explicit rules. There is a need for methods that can trace neural network decisions back to explicit symbolic representations.

Method: CRISP sign-binarizes the teacher's penultimate pre-logit activations and assigns one Individual Tsetlin Machine (ITM) to each last-layer activation vector (LLAV) neuron. Each reconstructed hidden bit is represented by propositional clauses over Booleanized input features, enabling direct symbolic traces from input thresholds to teacher neurons.

Result: LLAV sign-binarization does not reduce teacher-head accuracy in BNN settings. ITM reconstruction error is the main limiting factor. Quartile one-bit Booleanization achieves 87.52% test fidelity on SVHN and is competitive on CIFAR10. The reconstructed LLAV preserves 78.41% teacher-head accuracy on FMNIST. Learned ITM literals concentrate on object regions in centered benchmarks.

Conclusion: CRISP provides a clause-level route for inspecting the final hidden representation of binary neural teachers, enabling interpretability auditing of neural network decisions through symbolic rule extraction.

Abstract: Deep neural networks achieve high accuracy through layered numerical transformations, yet their decisions remain difficult to audit because decision evidence is encoded in hidden activations rather than explicit rules. This paper introduces CRISP, a framework that reconstructs the last-layer activation vector (LLAV) of binary neural teachers as Tsetlin Machine (TM) clauses. CRISP sign-binarizes the teacher's penultimate pre-logit activations, and assigns one Individual TM (ITM) to each LLAV neuron. Each reconstructed hidden bit is represented by propositional clauses over Booleanized input features, which gives a direct symbolic trace from named input thresholds to a named teacher neuron. CRISP is evaluated on MNIST, KMNIST, FashionMNIST (FMNIST), SVHN, and CIFAR10 using a BinaryConnect convolutional neural network (BCCNN) teacher and a fully binary neural network (BNN) teacher, with an additional study on binary thresholding, thermometer encoding, and quartile binning at multiple bit depths. The results show that LLAV sign-binarization does not reduce teacher-head accuracy in the tested BNN setting, while ITM reconstruction error is the main limiting factor. Quartile one-bit Booleanization gives the strongest reconstruction fidelity on SVHN at 87.52% test fidelity and is competitive on CIFAR10, and the reconstructed LLAV preserves 78.41% teacher-head accuracy on FMNIST. Pooled clause-evidence visualizations show that the learned ITM literals concentrate on the object region in centered benchmarks. CRISP therefore provides a clause-level route for inspecting the final hidden representation of binary neural teachers.

</details>


### [297] [Are you Synthesizing or Recalling? Evaluating LLMs on Algorithmic Code Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02438)
*Nickil Maveli,Antonio Vergari,Shay B. Cohen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces AlgoREval, a benchmark for evaluating parametric code retrieval in LLMs - the ability to reproduce well-known algorithms from internal knowledge rather than synthesizing new code. The benchmark contains 599 problems across 77 algorithms, 14 domains, 7 programming languages, and 4 graph-input representations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors argue that existing LLM pipelines lack explicit separation between algorithmic knowledge recall and reasoning.
