For well-documented algorithms, code generation should be measured as "parametric code retrieval" - reproducing known algorithms from learned knowledge rather than novel synthesis.

Method: The authors created AlgoREval benchmark with 599 problems spanning 77 classical algorithms across 14 domains, 7 programming languages, and 4 graph-input representations. They evaluated 15 models (7B-34B parameters) in zero-shot setting. They also tested prompt augmentation with retrieved code snippets and structured algorithmic hints, and compared SFT (Supervised Fine-Tuning) vs GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) training approaches.

Result: Substantial variation in retrieval accuracy was found across languages and input representations, even for widely documented algorithms. Prompt augmentation with retrieved code snippets or structured algorithmic hints improved accuracy on complex algorithms. SFT achieved broader language gains while GRPO achieved larger per-language gains on specific languages.

Conclusion: Parametric code retrieval is a distinct, measurable capability in LLMs. The results caution against deploying AI-generated algorithmic code without systematic validation, as even well-known algorithms show variable retrieval accuracy across different languages and input formats.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong performance in code generation, where success depends on both recalling relevant algorithmic knowledge and reasoning about how to apply it. However, existing LLM pipelines are opaque, with no explicit separation between these two components. We argue that for well-known algorithms whose canonical implementations are widely accessible in pretraining corpora, code generation is better measured as \textit{parametric code retrieval}: reproducing a named algorithm from internalised knowledge rather than synthesizing a novel one. We introduce AlgoREval, a benchmark of 599 problems spanning classical 77 algorithms across 14 domains, 7 programming languages, and 4 graph-input representations to evaluate this capability in isolation, and assess 15 models (7B--34B parameters) in a zero-shot setting. We find substantial variation in retrieval accuracy across languages and input representations, even for widely documented algorithms and show that prompt augmentation with retrieved code snippets or structured algorithmic hints improve accuracy on complex algorithms, while SFT achieves broader language gains and GRPO achieves larger per-language gains on specific languages. Together, our results establish parametric code retrieval as a distinct, measurable capability and caution against deploying AI-generated algorithmic code without systematic validation.\footnote{Code and dataset are available at https://github.com/Nickil21/AlgoREval

</details>


### [298] [A Generative Model of Complex Networks Using Graphons and Neural Inverse Operators](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02439)
*Wooseong Choi,Italo'Ivo Lima Dias Pinto,Chen Sun,Gaurav Gupta,Dong Song,Paul Bogdan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces a multifractal step graphon framework that unifies mechanistic interpretability with amortized inference in generative graph modeling. By formulating both the generative model and parameter recovery in function space, the approach enables inference on unseen graph sizes while retaining interpretability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing graph models have complementary limitations: mechanistic models are interpretable but require instance-specific estimation per graph, while deep generative models offer amortized inference but lack interpretability and are limited to graph sizes seen during training. Scientific applications need a framework that combines both strengths.

Method: The approach uses a multifractal step graphon that extends standard step graphons with a recursive construction to compactly parameterize complex networks. A neural inverse operator recovers the graphon parameters, enabling inference on unseen graph sizes. The model is trained only on synthetic multifractal step graphon realizations.

Result: The method achieves the best average performance on 3 of 4 metrics against a graph foundation model in a zero-shot graph-generation benchmark. It performs comparably to an instance-specific method on single-observation networks. In an EEG case study, inferred parameters track reversible brain state changes more sensitively than traditional network statistics.

Conclusion: Mechanistic interpretability and amortized inference can be effectively unified in a generative graph model, enhancing understanding of complex networks. The framework successfully transfers to real-world graphs and sensitive biological applications.

Abstract: Generative graph models are central to understanding and simulating complex networks. However, existing approaches have complementary strengths and limitations. Mechanistic models offer interpretability but rely on instance-specific estimation methods. Deep generative models, on the other hand, offer amortized inference at the cost of interpretability and are largely limited to graph sizes seen during training. Scientific applications motivate a framework that retains the strengths of both paradigms. We bridge them by formulating both the generative model and parameter recovery in function space. A multifractal step graphon extends standard step graphons with a recursive construction that compactly parameterizes complex networks. This formulation admits a neural inverse operator to recover its parameters, enabling inference on unseen graph sizes. We evaluate our model, trained only on synthetic multifractal step graphon realizations, against both paradigms. Against a graph foundation model pretrained on empirical networks, our method achieves the best average performance on three of four metrics in a zero-shot graph-generation benchmark, indicating that the model transfers to real-world graphs. We also apply our method to single-observation networks, a regime largely inaccessible to deep models that require training corpora, where it performs comparably to an instance-specific method that optimizes on each graph. In a multi-subject EEG case study, the inferred parameters track a reversible change in brain state more sensitively than traditional network statistics. Together, these results indicate that mechanistic interpretability and amortized inference can be effectively unified in a generative graph model to enhance our understanding of complex networks.

</details>


### [299] [Bandits via Additive Quantized Representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02440)
*Ami Tavory,Noam Touitou,Tal Sarig,Frank Cheng,Ido Guy*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Residual Quantization (RQ) is proposed as a representation layer for contextual bandits to achieve nonlinear reward modeling while maintaining O(1) memory efficiency. An offline-trained RQ codebook maps continuous contexts into discrete centroid assignments across multiple levels via a shadow mechanism, enabling additive bandit algorithms to capture nonlinearities with bounded memory.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the trade-off between nonlinear reward modeling and online efficiency in contextual bandits. Tree ensembles and neural methods capture nonlinearities but require periodic retraining and large replay buffers, while linear models are memory-efficient but limited to linear reward structures.

Method: Use an offline-trained RQ codebook that maps continuous contexts into discrete centroid assignments across multiple levels. A shadow mechanism dynamically sets the levels. This enables additive bandit algorithms to achieve nonlinear expressivity with strictly bounded memory.

Result: RQ variants beat their non-RQ counterparts on 11 out of 13 datasets, often by wide margins. They match the performance of doubling-retrain XGBoost and neural baselines while using up to 1000 times less memory.

Conclusion: Residual Quantization effectively bridges the gap between nonlinear expressivity and memory efficiency in contextual bandits, offering a practical solution that combines the best of both worlds.

Abstract: Contextual bandits require balancing nonlinear reward modeling with online efficiency. Tree ensembles and neural methods capture nonlinearities but require periodic retraining and large replay buffers. Linear models update efficiently per observation with O(1) memory, but are fundamentally restricted to linear reward structures. We propose Residual Quantization (RQ) as a representation layer to bridge this gap. An offline-trained RQ codebook maps continuous contexts into discrete centroid assignments across multiple levels, set dynamically through a shadow mechanism. This enables a spectrum of additive bandit algorithms that achieve nonlinear expressivity with strictly bounded memory. Across 13 datasets, RQ variants beat their non-RQ counterparts on 11 of 13 datasets, often by wide margins, while matching doubling-retrain XGBoost and neural baselines using up to 1000 times less memory.

</details>


### [300] [AI-driven Thermal-aware Data Center Capacity Planning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02442)
*Yixing Li,Mark Fenton,Matthew Kaufeler,Ka Ming Leung,Xin Ai,Zhiyu Zeng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper presents an AI-driven framework for thermal-aware capacity planning in data centers, addressing the thermal management challenges posed by large language models (LLMs). The framework uses an embedded AI model trained on key parameters (rack power, server power, server placement, HVAC settings) to provide temperature predictions within milliseconds, achieving 10000X speedup compared to high-fidelity CFD simulations while maintaining high accuracy for unseen data center designs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The emergence of LLMs has created significant thermal management challenges in data centers due to intense GPU computation causing localized hotspots. Additionally, spiking thermal loads during training and inference bursts make real-time cooling response difficult to predict and control. Traditional thermal-aware capacity planning requires massive expensive high-fidelity CFD simulations, which are impractical for real-time optimization.

Method: The authors developed an AI-driven framework that embeds an AI model trained on numerous key parameters including rack power, server power, server placement, and HVAC settings. The model provides temperature predictions within milliseconds and was validated against high-fidelity CFD simulations.

Result: For unseen data center designs, the AI model achieves high accuracy with 10000X speedup compared to high-fidelity CFD simulations. The framework enables instantaneous optimization of both workload distribution and HVAC cooling efficiency.

Conclusion: The proposed AI-driven framework can help data center designers and operators perform thermal-aware capacity planning in seconds, enabling real-time optimization of workload distribution and HVAC cooling efficiency. This addresses the critical need for fast, accurate thermal prediction in modern data centers supporting LLM workloads.

Abstract: The emerging of large language models (LLMs) has posed significant challenges to the thermal management of data center. Intense GPU computation for LLMs results in localized hotspots. Moreover, spiking thermal loads during training and inference bursts make real-time cooling response more difficult to predict and control. Thermal-aware capacity planning of data center requires massive expensive high-fidelity CFD simulations. AI models can perform real-time prediction for unseen designs. However, existing works either have large prediction error, or have over-simplified assumptions for data center operations. This work presents an AI-driven framework that can perform thermal-aware capacity planning for a real-world data center in seconds. The embedded AI model learns from numerous key parameters (rack power, server power, server placement, HVAC settings etc.), and provides temperature prediction within milliseconds. This AI model is tested against high-fidelity CFD simulations, and results show that for unseen data center designs, model can achieve high accuracy with 10000X speedup. Driven by the AI model, the authors design the thermal-aware capacity planning framework. This framework can help data center designers and operators instantaneously optimize both workload distribution and HVAC cooling efficiency.

</details>


### [301] [A Composable AI-Accelerated Iterative Solver for 3D-IC Thermal Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02461)
*Yixing Li,Jiahang Zhou,Zhiyu Zeng,Xin Ai*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DAIST is a composable thermal solver that decomposes package simulation into block-level subdomains, uses neural operators for each subdomain, and couples them through iterative exchanges of interfacial temperature and heat flux, enabling cross-topology reuse without retraining.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional FEM thermal analysis of heterogeneous 2.5D/3D-IC packages is computationally prohibitive (hours per simulation). Existing AI surrogates treat the entire stack monolithically and require retraining when die count or topology changes, creating a "topology lock-in" limitation.

Method: Domain decomposition approach: (1) Decompose global package into block-level subdomain problems; (2) Replace subdomain solvers with neural operators; (3) Couple subdomains through iterative exchanges of interfacial temperature and heat flux. Iteration budget provides controllable accuracy-runtime tradeoff.

Result: Evaluated on multi-chiplet and advanced packaging systems: achieves up to 178× speedup over traditional FEM with mean temperature errors of 0.068% and 0.323%, respectively. Demonstrates successful cross-topology reuse of block-level models across structurally distinct package assemblies.

Conclusion: DAIST eliminates topology lock-in of monolithic AI models by using a local-to-global architecture. Block-level neural operators can be reused in unseen package assemblies without retraining, while iterative coupling provides adjustable accuracy-runtime tradeoff, making it practical for thermal analysis of complex heterogeneous packages.

Abstract: Accurate thermal analysis of heterogeneous 2.5D/3D-IC packages is essential yet computationally prohibitive. A single full-package FEM simulation can take hours, while AI-based surrogates treat the entire stack as a monolithic prediction target and must be retrained whenever the die count or topology changes. To address this limitation, this work proposes Domain-Decomposed AI-Accelerated Iterative Solver for Thermal Analysis (DAIST), a composable thermal solver that decomposes the global package simulation into block-level subdomain problems, replaces subdomain solvers with neural operators, and couples them through iterative exchanges of interfacial temperature and heat flux. This local-to-global architecture eliminates the topology lock-in of monolithic models: block-level neural operators can be directly reused in unseen package assemblies without retraining. The iterative coupling strategy further provides a controllable accuracy-runtime tradeoff, where the iteration budget can be adjusted to trade accuracy for runtime. Evaluated on a multi-chiplet system and an advanced packaging system, DAIST achieves up to $178\times$ speedup over traditional FEM solvers with mean temperature errors of 0.068% and 0.323%, respectively, while demonstrating cross-topology reuse of block-level models across structurally distinct package assemblies.

</details>


### [302] [Capability Scaling-Down Laws for LLM Compression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02462)
*Xueqi Cheng,Liang Wu,Kelly Wan,Liangjie Hong,Yushun Dong*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper systematically investigates capability scaling-down laws for LLM compression (pruning, quantization, distillation), developing predictive relations that accurately forecast capability loss across different configurations, model sizes, and training stages. The framework is validated on multiple model families, showing that configuration selection captures most cross-method benefits.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM compression methods (pruning, quantization, distillation) can achieve similar resource reductions but produce different capability losses, making method selection largely empirical. There is a need for systematic predictive frameworks to guide compression configuration decisions.

Method: The study develops a framework measuring capability loss across mathematics, code generation, and question answering tasks. It relates these measurements to model size, training stage, compression settings, data availability, and training exposure. Predictive relations are developed and evaluated for accuracy, measurement efficiency, and generalization to unseen configurations. Controlled distillation experiments assess data reuse costs. Decision value is evaluated by comparing numerical selection with configuration medians and fixed method priorities across two model families.

Result: Sharing density response across pruning levels halves configuration measurements needed. The compact relation matches regression fitted with all measurements to within 0.020 nats per token on new Pythia states, pre-registered OLMo-2 test states, and under Wanda pruning. Heavy data reuse costs recur across QA distributions, with net benefit depending on evaluation distribution. Selection captures most cross-method benefit for QA within tested candidate sets, with smaller opportunities for math and code.

Conclusion: Capability scaling-down laws can predict capability loss across compression configurations with high accuracy using fewer measurements. The predictive scope clarifies the value of these laws for compression method selection, with QA showing the largest selection benefits while math and code show smaller opportunities.

Abstract: LLM compression reduces inference costs and memory requirements, but selecting a method and configuration remains largely empirical because comparable resource reductions can produce different capability losses. We systematically investigate capability scaling-down laws for LLM compression across pruning, quantization, and distillation. Our framework measures capability loss in mathematics, code generation, and question answering, and relates these measurements to model size, training stage, compression settings, data availability, and training exposure. We develop simple predictive relations and evaluate their accuracy, measurement efficiency, and generalization to unseen configurations and model states. Sharing the density response across pruning levels halves the configuration measurements needed to fit a pruning predictor: on new Pythia states, on pre-registered OLMo-2 test states and under Wanda pruning, the compact relation matches a regression fitted with all measurements on math and code to within 0.020 nats per token, with coefficients refitted for each setting. Controlled distillation experiments show that the cost of heavy data reuse recurs across question-answering distributions, while the net benefit depends on the evaluation distribution. We further evaluate the decision value of these predictions by comparing numerical selection with configuration medians and fixed method priorities. Independent evaluations across two model families show that selection captures most of the available cross-method benefit for question answering within the tested candidate sets, where a fixed method priority attains the same regret, with smaller opportunities for mathematics and code. These results clarify the predictive scope of capability scaling-down laws and their use in compression method selection. Our code is publicly available at: https://github.com/LabRAI/scaling_down_law.

</details>


### [303] [Threshold-Aware Conformal Routing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02487)
*Shiwei Tan,Huzefa Rangwala,Danielle C. Maddix*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses the tradeoff between speed and accuracy in surrogate models for scientific simulations. The authors propose Threshold-Aware Conformal Routing (TACR), which optimizes conformal prediction intervals specifically for threshold-based routing decisions, reducing simulator calls by 14-75% while maintaining distribution-free coverage guarantees.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: High-fidelity simulations are computationally expensive but necessary for scientific accuracy. Learned surrogates offer faster alternatives but introduce errors that may affect downstream decisions. The key challenge is determining when to use a surrogate versus running the full simulator, particularly for threshold-based decisions (e.g., whether a quantity exceeds a safety limit).

Method: The authors introduce Threshold-Aware Conformal Routing (TACR), which learns an input-dependent interval scale using a threshold-aware objective function. This objective concentrates interval tightness near the decision boundary rather than uniformly across all inputs. The method uses exact split-conformal calibration on held-out data to preserve distribution-free marginal coverage guarantees.

Result: TACR reduces simulator deferrals by 14-75% relative to standard conformal prediction at the same coverage target. Against a variant without threshold-local weighting but with similar predictor accuracy, TACR further reduces deferrals by 10-24% on four datasets.

Conclusion: Optimizing interval allocation specifically for routing decisions can significantly reduce computational costs (simulator calls) without compromising the standard conformal guarantee. The key insight is that intervals only need to be tight where they cross the decision threshold; inputs far from the threshold can have wider intervals without affecting routing decisions.

Abstract: High-fidelity simulations are essential to scientific and engineering design, but can be expensive to run repeatedly. Learned surrogates offer a faster alternative, yet their higher errors may alter downstream decisions. This accuracy-speed tradeoff creates a need to determine whether a surrogate can be used or the full simulator remains necessary. We study decisions determined by whether a scalar quantity of interest lies above or below a fixed threshold. For each input, we use the surrogate when its conformal interval lies entirely on one side of the threshold and route the input to simulation when the interval intersects it. Standard conformal prediction constructs intervals without reference to the downstream decision threshold: even a narrow interval near the threshold can cross it and trigger simulation, whereas a wider interval farther away can remain entirely on one side and require no simulation. We introduce Threshold-Aware Conformal Routing (TACR), which learns an input-dependent scale using a threshold-aware objective that concentrates interval tightness near the decision boundary. Exact split-conformal calibration on held-out data preserves distribution-free marginal coverage, which also upper-bounds the probability of an incorrect threshold decision that is not routed. Across various scientific and engineering datasets, TACR reduces simulator deferrals by 14-75% relative to standard conformal prediction at the same coverage target. Against a variant without threshold-local weighting but with similar predictor accuracy, TACR further reduces deferrals by 10-24% on four datasets. These results show that optimizing interval allocation for routing can reduce simulator calls without weakening the standard conformal guarantee.

</details>


### [304] [Harnessing LLMs as Agents: What Does It Cost?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02488)
*Zelin Zhao,Xinyu Guo,Jingyuan Zhang,Yuxuan Zhang,Yongxin Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces the Language Model Agent Machine (LAM), a resource-bounded abstraction that quantifies computational resources consumed by LLM agent harnesses (context, memory, tools, verification). It establishes theoretical results across four domains: communication complexity (reducing to red-blue pebbling), access patterns (showing Θ(n) gaps between random and sequential access), recomputation costs (Θ(n²/(C+S)+n) for bit-reversal DAGs), and reliability bounds (sampling bounds, verification costs, checkpoint laws). Experiments on GPT-6 Astra validate communication and reliability predictions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing notions of LLM capability do not quantify computational resources consumed by harness-level mechanisms (bounded context, persistent memory, tools, verification, repeated execution). This gap prevents proper resource accounting and comparison of agent architectures.

Method: The paper introduces LAM, a resource-bounded abstraction that fixes the underlying semantic model while explicitly charging harness-level resources. Methods include: (1) Mapping LAM execution to red-blue pebbling under simultaneous call-transfer budgets; (2) Analyzing memory interface asymptotics; (3) Deriving recomputation bounds for bit-reversal DAGs; (4) Establishing stage-local sampling bounds, verification costs, and optimal checkpoint intervals (Young-Daly-type law).

Result: Four key results: (1) Communication: LAM execution is instancewise equivalent to red-blue pebbling, transferring classical I/O lower bounds to context-memory traffic. (2) Access: Memory interfaces induce Θ(n) asymptotic separation between random and non-speculative sequential access on pointer chasing. (3) Recomputation: Bit-reversal DAGs require Θ(n²/(C+S)+n) model calls with context capacity C and persistent-memory capacity S. (4) Reliability: Tight stage-local sampling bounds, exact imperfect-verification costs, and closed-form optimal verification interval from a Young-Daly-type checkpoint law. Experiments on GPT-6 Astra validate communication and reliability predictions.

Conclusion: This work provides a formal resource theory for quantifying the computational cost of language-model agent harnesses, enabling principled comparison of agent architectures and optimization of resource allocation (checkpoints, call granularity, verification policies).

Abstract: Language-model agents increasingly rely on harnesses that manage bounded context, persistent memory, tools, verification, and repeated execution, yet existing notions of model capability do not quantify the computational resources these mechanisms consume. We introduce the Language Model Agent Machine (LAM), a resource-bounded abstraction that fixes the underlying semantic model while explicitly charging harness-level resources. We establish four classes of results. Communication: LAM execution is instancewise equivalent to red--blue pebbling under simultaneous call--transfer budgets, transferring classical I/O lower bounds to context--memory traffic. Access: memory interfaces induce asymptotic separations, including a $Θ(n)$ gap between random and non-speculative sequential access on pointer chasing. Recomputation: bit-reversal DAGs require $Θ(n^2/(C+S)+n)$ model calls with context capacity $C$ and persistent-memory capacity $S$, quantifying when stored intermediate state avoids repeated semantic computation. Reliability: we derive tight stage-local sampling bounds, exact imperfect-verification costs, and a Young--Daly-type checkpoint law with a closed-form optimal verification interval. Controlled and held-out experiments on GPT-6 Astra test communication and reliability predictions, including checkpoint optima, policy selection under programmatic checking, and tradeoffs among call granularity, logical input traffic, and reliability on chained MATH tasks. Together, these results provide a resource theory for the computational cost of language-model agent harnesses.

</details>


### [305] [LiteEMG-FM: An Efficient and Deployable Foundation Model for Robust EMG Sensing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02497)
*Tianhao Wu,Xu Wu,Amirmohammad Radmehr,Jiawei Yu,Yi Wu,Phuc Nguyen,Jian Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LiteEMG-FM is an efficient hybrid CNN-Transformer foundation model for EMG signal processing, pretrained on 16 diverse datasets, featuring a hierarchical wake-up architecture for resource-constrained deployment. It outperforms state-of-the-art models in zero-calibration cross-participant and data-scarce conditions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: EMG signals exhibit high variability across individuals, body regions, recording sessions, and sensing hardware, limiting model generalization for assistive devices and human-computer interaction. Existing time-series foundation models are computationally expensive for real-time wearable deployment and fail to capture EMG-specific time-frequency characteristics.

Method: 1) Developed a hybrid CNN-Transformer architecture (LiteEMG-FM) for EMG representation learning; 2) Pretrained on 16 diverse upper- and lower-limb EMG datasets; 3) Implemented hierarchical wake-up architecture with lightweight 1D-CNN for always-on filtering of rest/non-target activity; 4) Evaluated three inference paradigms: full offloading, split inference, and full on-device processing.

Result: LiteEMG-FM outperforms state-of-the-art time-series foundation models and supervised baselines, particularly under zero-calibration cross-participant and data-scarce conditions. Characterized trade-offs in latency, power consumption, and memory footprint across deployment scenarios.

Conclusion: LiteEMG-FM demonstrates an effective, efficient, and deployable foundation model for EMG applications, enabling generalization across users and datasets while maintaining feasibility for resource-constrained wearable devices.

Abstract: Electromyography (EMG) signals vary substantially across individuals, body regions, recording sessions, and sensing hardware, limiting the generalization of models for assistive devices and human-computer interaction. Existing time-series foundation models are also computationally expensive for real-time wearable deployment and often fail to capture EMG-specific time-frequency characteristics. We present LiteEMG-FM, an efficient hybrid CNN-Transformer foundation model for practical EMG sensing. Pretrained on 16 diverse upper- and lower-limb EMG datasets, LiteEMG-FM learns representations that generalize across users and datasets. For resource-constrained deployment, we implement a hierarchical wake-up architecture in which a lightweight, always-on 1D-CNN filters rest and non-target activity and activates LiteEMG-FM only for valid gestures. We evaluate full inference offloading, split inference, and full on-device processing, characterizing their trade-offs in latency, power consumption, and memory footprint. Across diverse evaluation settings, LiteEMG-FM outperforms state-of-the-art time-series foundation models and supervised baselines, particularly under zero-calibration cross-participant and data-scarce conditions. These results demonstrate that LiteEMG-FM is an effective, efficient, and deployable foundation model for EMG applications.

</details>


### [306] [Multi-Fidelity Policy Gradients Stabilize Data-Scarce Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02505)
*Xinjie Liu,Ruihan Zhao,Anirban Chaudhuri,Cyrus Neary,Ufuk Topcu,David Fridovich-Keil*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MFPG-PPO is a reinforcement learning method that combines limited expensive high-fidelity data with abundant cheap low-fidelity data using a control variate approach. It achieves comparable performance to PPO trained with 16x more high-fidelity data while requiring only 4 real-robot episodes per update on a physical Franka arm.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Policy gradient methods for on-policy RL become unstable when expensive, scarce target-domain data yield noisy gradient estimates. The challenge is to leverage abundant low-fidelity data (e.g., from simplified simulators) to improve sample efficiency without biasing the gradient estimator.

Method: The method extends the multi-fidelity policy gradient (MFPG) framework to modern actor-critic learning (PPO). Key innovations include: (1) redesigning sampling, advantage estimation, and control variate construction to preserve cross-fidelity correlation; (2) monitoring estimator uncertainty to prevent variance inflation; (3) introducing a budget-aware variant to allocate sampling budgets between high- and low-fidelity sources.

Result: Across simulated robot locomotion tasks with varying LF-to-HF transfer difficulty and HF data budgets, MFPG-PPO improves upon PPO trained on HF data alone in nearly all settings. It matches PPO trained with 16x more HF data on the hardest task at smallest HF budgets. In contrast, most baselines using LF data perform well only where direct LF-to-HF transfer succeeds. The method enables stable learning on a physical Franka arm using only 4 real-robot episodes per update without human demonstrations.

Conclusion: MFPG-PPO successfully leverages low-fidelity data to improve sample efficiency without introducing bias, achieving state-of-the-art performance in low-data regimes. It bridges the sim-to-real gap effectively, enabling practical real-world robot learning with minimal real-world data requirements.

Abstract: Policy gradient methods for on-policy reinforcement learning (RL) can become unstable when expensive, scarce target-domain data yield noisy gradient estimates. We address this challenge by complementing limited high-fidelity (HF) target-domain data with abundant, cheap, but biased low-fidelity (LF) data, e.g., from a simplified simulator. Most existing methods directly optimize biased objectives based on LF data. In contrast, the recently introduced multi-fidelity policy gradient (MFPG) framework uses LF data solely to construct a control variate that reduces variance and improves HF data efficiency without biasing the policy gradient estimator. However, published work on MFPG is limited to REINFORCE on small-scale simulation tasks. We develop MFPG for modern actor-critic learning in GPU-parallel simulation and on a physical robot. Our analysis and experiments show that naive extensions to proximal policy optimization (PPO) can lose cross-fidelity correlation or inflate variance. Our MFPG-PPO addresses these failures by redesigning the sampling, advantage estimation, and control variate construction to preserve cross-fidelity correlation, and by monitoring estimator uncertainty to prevent variance inflation. We also introduce a budget-aware MFPG-PPO to divide a fixed sampling budget among high- and low-fidelity data sources. Across simulated robot locomotion tasks of varying LF-to-HF transfer difficulty and HF data budgets, MFPG-PPO improves upon PPO trained on HF data alone in nearly all settings, and consistently matches the performance of PPO trained with 16x more HF data on the hardest task at the smallest HF budgets. In contrast, most baselines that use LF data perform well only where direct LF-to-HF transfer succeeds. MFPG-PPO enables stable learning on a physical Franka arm using only 4 real-robot episodes per update and no human demonstrations.

</details>


### [307] [Post-Training Quantization of Autoregressive Weather Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02511)
*Ananyo Bhattacharya,Swastik Bhattacharya,Christiane Jablonowski*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This study investigates the application of Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) to accelerate AI-based weather forecasting emulators (DLWP and FourCastNet models). PTQ is applied to reduce computation time and power consumption while maintaining forecast quality comparable to physics-based models for short-range weather predictions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deep learning emulators for weather forecasting have shown comparable quality to physics-based models but require significant computational resources. Post-training quantization (PTQ) has proven effective in accelerating other DL architectures while consuming less power and enabling edge hardware deployment. This study aims to explore whether PTQ can optimize pre-trained AI weather emulators without degrading forecast accuracy.

Method: The researchers implemented PTQ algorithms on two pre-trained global-scale weather forecasting models: Deep Learning Weather Prediction (DLWP) and FourCastNet (FCN). They systematically evaluated the effect of PTQ on emulator inferences over short-range forecast horizons using simulated quantization hints to assess forecast quality.

Result: The evaluation of PTQ configurations indicates qualitatively meaningful forecasts can be achieved over short-time horizons. This provides the first benchmark of PTQ for autoregressive weather emulators, demonstrating the feasibility of quantization-based optimization for geophysical fluid dynamics applications.

Conclusion: Post-training quantization shows promise for optimizing deep learning models for dynamical systems. The results establish a foundation for quantization-based optimization of DL models in weather forecasting and potentially other geophysical fluid dynamics applications, enabling more efficient deployment on various hardware platforms.

Abstract: Advancements in high-resolution numerical weather prediction (NWP) and data assimilation (DA) have shaped the developments in deep learning (DL) architectures emulating atmospheric dynamics. Emulators for weather forecasting exhibit forecast quality comparable to physics based models at forecast horizon scaling from few days to subseasonal time scales. The emulators are driven by hardware-accelerated matrix multiplication in autoregressive inferences, significantly reducing the computation time and resources required for NWP. Optimization of the matrix multiplication processes in GPU architectures provides opportunities to scale towards high-resolution domain, and offers implementation of out of the box solutions. Post-training quantization (PTQ) has been demonstrated across multiple DL architectures to accelerate and increase the number of computations in unit time while consuming less power, enabling applications on edge hardware. In this study, we investigate the effect of PTQ on pre-trained AI emulators for global-scale weather forecasting. We implement PTQ algorithms in Deep Learning Weather Prediction (DLWP) and FourCastNet (FCN) models as a proof of concept for geophysical fluid dynamics applications. We systematically investigate the effect of PTQ on emulator inferences over short-range forecast horizons. Evaluation of PTQ configurations using simulated quantization hints at qualitatively meaningful forecasts over short-time horizons. These results provide a first benchmark of PTQ for autoregressive weather emulators and a basis for quantization-based optimization of DL models for dynamical systems.

</details>


### [308] [Student-Guided Teacher Distillation for Efficient LLM Task Routing: Positioning Against Jev-Style System-1 Classifiers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02516)
*Haifeng Wu,Srinivasan Manoharan,Jian Wan,Fangbo Tu,Junhua Zhao,Xin Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a student-guided teacher distillation pipeline for efficient zero-shot classification in LLM task routing. A compact ModernBERT classifier predicts top-k candidates, which are then reranked by a larger DeBERTa-v3 zero-shot NLI classifier. The iterative process improves the student model, achieving 77.5% teacher agreement and 91-100% Coverage@16.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Zero-shot NLI classifiers for routing user requests to LLM tasks are expensive when scaling to large taxonomies (60 categories), as cost scales linearly with taxonomy size. The authors seek a more efficient approach that reduces computational cost while maintaining accuracy.

Method: The pipeline uses a two-stage approach: (1) a compact ModernBERT classifier performs one forward pass to predict full category distribution and retrieve top-k candidates, (2) a larger DeBERTa-v3 zero-shot NLI classifier reranks only those top-k candidates rather than all 60 labels. Teacher labels from this process iteratively improve the student model. The key insight is that truncated top-k scores should NOT be used as soft targets for KL distillation, as zeroing untruncated classes destroys the dark knowledge essential for distillation.

Result: The best student checkpoint achieves 77.5% teacher agreement on a 200-example evaluation set. Coverage@16 reaches 91-100%, indicating top-k sets retain most decision-relevant information. The paper also demonstrates that treating truncated scores as full 60-class soft targets introduces systematic bias rather than being a harmless approximation.

Conclusion: The proposed student-guided teacher distillation pipeline successfully reduces computational cost for large taxonomy classification while maintaining high teacher agreement. The key technical finding is that proper soft-label handling is critical - truncating scores destroys dark knowledge. Future work includes complete evaluation with coverage measurements at multiple k, embedding-retrieval baselines, and larger human-reviewed test sets.

Abstract: Zero-shot classifiers are useful for routing user requests to specialized LLM tasks, but scoring every request against a large candidate set is expensive: a zero-shot NLI classifier must evaluate one premise-hypothesis pair per label, so cost scales linearly with taxonomy size. We study a student-guided teacher distillation pipeline for a fixed taxonomy of 60 LLM task categories: a compact ModernBERT classifier predicts the full category distribution in one forward pass and retrieves a small top-k candidate set, and a larger DeBERTa-v3 zero-shot NLI classifier reranks only those candidates rather than all 60 labels; the resulting teacher labels iteratively improve the student, which produces sharper candidates for the next round. Unlike generic embedding retrieval or clustering-derived shortlists used in extreme multi-label classification, our candidate generator is trained end-to-end on the target taxonomy and is the same model serving production traffic, distinguishing it from LLM-routing work that routes between candidate models, and from concurrent System-1 encoder-classifier proposals (e.g. TypeSafe AI's Jev and the open-source Laya project) whose training methodology is undocumented or RL-based. Our best student checkpoint reaches 77.5% teacher agreement on a 200-example evaluation set, and preliminary coverage measurements show Coverage@16 of 91-100%, suggesting top-k sets retain most of the teacher's decision-relevant information. We further show truncated top-k teacher scores should not be treated as full 60-class soft targets for KL distillation: zeroing untruncated classes destroys the dark knowledge soft-label distillation depends on, introducing systematic bias rather than a harmless sparse approximation. A complete evaluation, including coverage at multiple k on a held-out set, an embedding-retrieval baseline, and a larger human-reviewed test set, remains in progress.

</details>


### [309] [Learning the Latent Structure: A Feature-Centric Approach to Graph Data Augmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02517)
*Yu Song,Zhigang Hua,Yan Xie,Bingheng Li,Jingzhe Liu,Bo Long,Jiliang Tang,Hui Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SelfAug is a novel feature-centric graph data augmentation framework that operates in embedding space using self-supervised inverse masking to recover unobserved structural signals, with a message regularizer and bootstrap strategy for robustness. It outperforms state-of-the-art methods on 10 datasets in inductive and cold-start settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world graphs are often incomplete due to data collection and observational constraints, limiting the effectiveness of graph learning pipelines. Existing Graph Data Augmentation (GDA) methods are label-dependent, computationally expensive, and inherently transductive, restricting their practical applicability.

Method: The proposed SelfAug framework operates directly in embedding space rather than explicit structure modeling. It uses a self-supervised inverse masking process to capture latent relationships between observed and complete graphs, enabling recovery of unobserved structural signals through refined node representations. To handle noisy and sparse supervision, a message regularizer and bootstrap strategy are introduced for effective training and generalization.

Result: Evaluated on 10 graph datasets spanning multiple domains, SelfAug consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both accuracy and efficiency across inductive and cold-start settings.

Conclusion: SelfAug represents a scalable and generalizable solution for real-world graph learning scenarios, effectively addressing limitations of prior GDA methods through its feature-centric, embedding-space approach.

Abstract: Graph-structured data plays a pivotal role in modeling complex relationships. However, real-world graphs are often incomplete due to data collection and observational constraints, severely limiting the effectiveness of modern graph learning pipelines. While existing Graph Data Augmentation (GDA) methods attempt to refine graph structures for improved downstream performance, they are typically label-dependent, computationally expensive, and inherently transductive, limiting their applicability in practical scenarios. In this work, we present a novel feature-centric graph data augmentation framework that bypasses explicit structure modeling by operating directly in the embedding space. Through a self-supervised inverse masking process, our method captures latent ties between observed and complete graphs, enabling recovery of unobserved structural signals through refined node representations. To enhance robustness under noisy and sparse supervision, we introduce a message regularizer and a bootstrap strategy for effective training and generalization. Evaluated on ten graph datasets spanning multiple domains, our approach, SelfAug, consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both accuracy and efficiency across inductive and cold-start settings, highlighting its potential as a scalable and generalizable solution for real-world graph learning scenarios.

</details>


### [310] [Instance-Dependent Regret for CMDPs with Step-Wise Constraints](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02520)
*Qian Zuo,Francesco Emanuele Stradi,Leyang Xue,Sattar Vakili*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses online learning in episodic tabular constrained Markov decision processes (CMDPs) with step-wise safety constraints. The authors propose Safe Variance-Adaptive Exploration (SVAE), an algorithm that learns safe subgraphs and performs variance-adaptive optimistic planning. The algorithm achieves tight regret bounds that depend on instance-specific quantities like return variance, with guaranteed constraint violation bounds.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The core challenge in constrained MDPs is that safety constraints induce a safe subgraph affecting reward variance, which impacts learning difficulty. However, identifying safe actions while controlling constraint violations remains challenging. The authors aim to exploit this structural property to design an efficient algorithm with optimal dependence on instance-specific complexity measures.

Method: The proposed SVAE algorithm combines two key components: (1) learning candidate safe subgraphs through exploration, and (2) performing variance-adaptive optimistic planning within these subgraphs. The algorithm uses optimism in the face of uncertainty together with variance estimation to balance exploration and safety.

Result: SVAE achieves cumulative regret of order $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{SAH\min\{\mathbb{V}_Σ,K\mathrm{Var}^{\star}\}}+S\sqrt{AH^3\min\{K,\mathcal{C}\}}+S^2AH^2)$ over K episodes. It also attains $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(H\sqrt{SAK}+S^2AH^2)$ step-wise constraint violation and a gap-dependent violation bound polylogarithmic in K. A lower bound is established showing the dependence on instance-specific quantities is unavoidable.

Conclusion: The paper provides a near-optimal algorithm for online learning in tabular CMDPs with step-wise safety constraints. The regret bounds explicitly depend on meaningful instance-specific quantities (Var*, V_Σ, C), and the lower bound confirms this dependence is necessary. This work advances understanding of safe exploration in constrained reinforcement learning.

Abstract: We study online learning in episodic tabular constrained Markov decision processes with step-wise safety constraints. In such a setting, the constraints induce a safe subgraph that shapes the variance of cumulative rewards under feasible policies and, consequently, the difficulty of learning. Exploiting this structure, however, requires learning which actions are safe while controlling constraint violations. We propose Safe Variance-Adaptive Exploration (SVAE), an efficient algorithm that learns candidate safe subgraphs and performs variance-adaptive optimistic planning within them. With high probability, SVAE achieves cumulative regret of order $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{SAH\min\{\mathbb{V}_Σ,K\mathrm{Var}^{\star}\}}+S\sqrt{AH^3\min\{K,\mathcal{C}\}}+S^2AH^2)$ over $K$ episodes, where $H$ is the horizon of a single episode, while $S$ and $A$ are the numbers of states and actions, respectively. Here, $\mathrm{Var}^{\star}$ is the maximum return variance among safe policies, $\mathbb{V}_Σ$ is the variance accumulated before the first unsafe action is encountered, and $\mathcal{C}$ captures the statistical complexity of eliminating actions incorrectly considered potentially safe. SVAE additionally attains $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(H\sqrt{SAK}+S^2AH^2)$ step-wise constraint violation and a gap-dependent violation bound that is polylogarithmic in $K$. Finally, we establish a lower bound showing that dependence on these instance-specific quantities is unavoidable.

</details>


### [311] [BaCP: Backbone Contrastive Pruning for Preserving Representations in Extremely Sparse Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02524)
*Mohammad Haroon Khawaja,Muhammad Haseeb,Mohammad Fatim Shoaib,Muhammad Tahir*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Summary generation failed


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Motivation analysis unavailable

Method: Method extraction failed

Result: Result analysis unavailable

Conclusion: Conclusion extraction failed

Abstract: Unstructured pruning at extreme sparsity often suffers from representational collapse, causing sharp drops in accuracy. To address this, we study Backbone Contrastive Pruning (BaCP), which regularizes the sparse network's embedding space by aligning it with pretrained, fine-tuned, and historical snapshot models. Building on the contrastive decomposition of the CAP framework (Xu et al., 2022), we provide a rigorous matched-budget characterization of this approach across multiple pruning criteria. Evaluated across 90 settings, BaCP improves accuracy substantially in extreme sparsity regimes where standard pruning fails, and is close to baseline where representations remain intact.

</details>


### [312] [Autoregressive Differentiable Method for Integer Programming](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02528)
*Ouns El Harzli,Yudong Cao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: An autoregressive differentiable method using a transformer to solve 0-1 integer programs by predicting bits while remaining feasible, trained on feasible incumbents and using Lagrangian penalties with Gumbel-softmax activations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To solve 0-1 integer programs more effectively, particularly non-convex instances of quadratic knapsack problems, achieving better performance than state-of-the-art open-source solvers for dense problems with up to 10,000 binary variables.

Method: An autoregressive transformer-based approach that fixes an arbitrary order of binary variables and predicts the next bit while remaining in the feasible set. The method is first trained on feasible incumbents from any solver, then uses a Lagrangian penalty to penalize infeasible solutions, with Gumbel-softmax activations applied to the relaxed objective for further exploration.

Result: Consistent improvement over state-of-the-art open-source solvers for dense problems up to 10,000 binary variables. A "tunneling effect" was observed, where the transformation from binary variables to continuous transformer weights enables crossing barriers in the relaxed objective landscape.

Conclusion: The proposed transformer-based approach effectively solves large-scale 0-1 integer programs, particularly non-convex quadratic knapsack problems. The tunneling effect phenomenon demonstrates the method's ability to escape local optima through continuous weight representations, showing promise for practical optimization applications.

Abstract: We introduce an autoregressive differentiable method to solve 0-1 integer programs. We fix an arbitrary order of the binary variables and we train a transformer to predict the next bit while remaining in the feasible set. Our method is first trained on feasible incumbents provided by any solver, thus allowing us to initialize the transformer in the feasible set. Our procedure then implements a Lagrangian penalty to penalize infeasible solutions, and the transformer is further trained to explore the feasible set using Gumbel-softmax activations on the relaxed objective. We have tested our method on non-convex instances of quadratic knapsack problem and demonstrated consistent improvement upon state-of-the-art open-source solvers for dense problems up to 10,000 binary variables. In particular, we empirically demonstrate a phenomenon akin to a tunneling effect where the effective change of variables from binary variable to the continuous weights of the transformer that the method implements enables crossing barriers in the relaxed objective landscape.

</details>


### [313] [Reward Inflation: A Healthy Stimulus for Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02545)
*Ganghun Lee,Minji Kim,Minsu Lee,Byoung-Tak Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes reward inflation, a method of gradually scaling rewards during reinforcement learning training, which acts as a healthy stimulus for learning. The method induces implicit recency weighting to upweight recent transitions and suppresses dormant neurons to preserve plasticity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While reward magnitudes are typically held fixed throughout training in reinforcement learning, their temporal modulation remains underexplored. The authors investigate whether gradually scaling rewards over training (reward inflation) can improve learning.

Method: The authors propose reward inflation - a gradual scaling of rewards over the course of training. They provide theoretical analysis showing it induces implicit recency weighting during policy updates. They also introduce Fed, an adaptive variant that adjusts the inflation level on the fly based on training dynamics.

Result: Reward inflation enables faster adaptation by upweighting recent transitions during policy updates. By sustaining gradient signals as the policy saturates, it suppresses the emergence of dormant neurons and helps preserve plasticity. Empirical results on ALE games and MuJoCo tasks show that appropriate reward inflation benefits a broad range of tasks.

Conclusion: Reward inflation is a simple yet effective technique that can improve reinforcement learning across various tasks. The adaptive variant (Fed) often improves upon fixed inflation levels. This work demonstrates that temporal modulation of rewards is a valuable direction for RL research.

Abstract: Reward serves as the primary learning signal in reinforcement learning (RL). However, while reward magnitudes are typically held fixed throughout training, their temporal modulation remains underexplored. In this paper, we propose reward inflation, a gradual scaling of rewards over the course of training, and show that it can act as a healthy stimulus for RL. Theoretically, reward inflation induces an implicit recency weighting that upweights recent transitions during policy updates, enabling faster adaptation. We further show that, by sustaining gradient signals as the policy saturates, reward inflation suppresses the emergence of dormant neurons and helps preserve plasticity. Empirical results on ALE games and MuJoCo tasks corroborate these findings, showing that an appropriate level of reward inflation benefits a broad range of tasks. Finally, we introduce Fed, an adaptive variant that adjusts the inflation level on the fly, and find that it often improves upon fixed inflation.

</details>


### [314] [Test-time Multi-agent Coordination by Decomposed Value Gradient Flow](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02554)
*Dongsu Lee,Haoran Xu,Amy Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SCOUT is the first offline MARL framework that combines a generative foundation model with a learned value function through test-time action refinement. It uses flow-matching behavioral prior with decomposed value function, and transports behavioral samples toward high-value regions via Stein variational gradient descent at test-time, achieving state-of-the-art performance across discrete and continuous benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Offline multi-agent reinforcement learning faces a fundamental trade-off: expressive generative policies can represent multi-modal coordination but cannot distinguish high-value regions, while value-optimized policies exploit the learned Q-function but collapse multi-modal behaviors into a single dominant mode. This mode collapse can break joint coordination and simultaneous drift across agents can push the joint policy into unseen regions of the action space.

Method: SCOUT trains two decoupled components: (1) a flow-matching behavioral prior for generative modeling, and (2) a decomposed value function under the Individual-Global-Max (IGM) principle. At test-time, it transports behavioral samples toward high-value regions via Stein variational gradient descent (SVGD), where the number of transport steps controls adaptive test-time scaling, replacing fixed regularization coefficients.

Result: Theoretically, SCOUT achieves a single-term KL bound on the joint soft-value gap that vanishes as transport converges, with an irreducible additive residual proportional to the IGM violation. Empirically, SCOUT achieves the best average performance across discrete and continuous offline MARL benchmarks and yields performance improvements in all offline-to-online configurations.

Conclusion: SCOUT successfully bridges the gap between expressive generative models and value-optimized policies in offline MARL through test-time action refinement, providing adaptive scaling via transport steps and theoretical guarantees under the IGM principle. It represents a significant advance in combining foundation models with RL value functions for multi-agent coordination.

Abstract: Offline multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) faces a persistent trade-off. Expressive generative policies can represent multi-modal coordination in the data, but cannot distinguish high-value regions, while value-optimized policies exploit the learned Q-function but collapse the multi-modal into a single dominant mode. A single agent's mode collapse can break joint coordination, and simultaneous drift across agents can push the joint policy into unseen regions of the action space. We propose scalable coordination via optimal unified transport (SCOUT), the first offline MARL framework to combine a generative foundation model with a learned value function through test-time action refinement. SCOUT trains two decoupled components: a flow-matching behavioral prior and a decomposed value function. At test-time, it transports behavioral samples toward high-value regions via Stein variational gradient descent. The number of transport steps controls adaptive test-time scaling, replacing a fixed regularization coefficient. Under the individual-global-max (IGM) principle, we prove a single-term KL bound on the joint soft-value gap that vanishes as transport converges, with an irreducible additive residual proportional to the IGM violation. Empirically, SCOUT achieves the best average performance across discrete and continuous offline MARL benchmarks and yields performance improvements in all offline-to-online configurations.

</details>


### [315] [Neuron merging via inverse-activation regression for post-training compression of sigmoid neural networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02559)
*Ao Kuniya,Jun Ohkubo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes cluster-based merging methods for compressing trained neural networks, including data-free contribution-weighted averaging and neuron-merging approaches using inverse activation functions with least-squares weight estimation. The study compares data-assisted and data-free strategies, finding that weight information is crucial for clustering while activation information is key for representative-neuron reconstruction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As neural networks scale up, model compression becomes essential for efficient inference under limited computational resources. While structured pruning removes less important neurons/channels, valuable information may be lost. The authors aim to determine which information should be retained when consolidating multiple neuronal degrees of freedom through coarse-graining.

Method: The paper proposes two main approaches: (1) data-free contribution-weighted averaging, and (2) neuron-merging methods where neuron responses are mapped back to pre-activation space via inverse activation function, with weights and biases estimated using least-squares method. Both data-assisted (using actual training inputs) and data-free (using randomly generated inputs) strategies are examined in sigmoid networks.

Result: Empirical evidence from tested sigmoid networks shows that weight information is particularly useful for clustering, while activation information is useful for representative-neuron reconstruction in the merging process.

Conclusion: The study provides guidance for effective neural network compression: weight-based clustering should be used for grouping neurons, while activation-based reconstruction should be used for determining representative neuron parameters. This offers a promising alternative to traditional pruning by preserving more useful information from the original network.

Abstract: As neural networks continue to grow in scale, model compression is becoming increasingly important for efficient inference under limited computational resources. Structured pruning methods remove neurons or channels that are estimated to be less important, but the removed units may still contain useful information. From the viewpoint of coarse-graining a trained network, it is valuable to ask which information should be retained when multiple neuronal degrees of freedom are consolidated. In this paper, we discuss cluster-based merging methods for compression of trained neural networks. In addition to a data-free contribution-weighted averaging method, we propose neuron-merging methods in which neuron responses are mapped back to the pre-activation space via the inverse activation function, and the weights and biases of each representative neuron are estimated using the least-squares method. We also examine both a data-assisted strategy with actual training inputs and a data-free strategy using randomly generated inputs. The comparisons provide empirical evidence, in the tested sigmoid networks, that weight information is particularly useful for clustering whereas activation information is useful for representative-neuron reconstruction in the merging process.

</details>


### [316] [OpenGameEval: Benchmarking Agentic Programming and Exploration in a Stateful Game Engine](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02563)
*Eray Turkel,Mengsha Sun,Kartik Ayyar,Sean Dunigan,Jack Lu,Vlad Shcherban,Hsiang-Shun Shih,Xin Wang,Tiantian Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: OpenGameEval is a benchmark and evaluation framework for testing language models as agents in Roblox Studio game development. It evaluates 13 frontier models on 84 human-curated tasks with 16 attempts each, measuring both task success and exploration behavior. The best model achieves 51.7% single-attempt pass rate, and exploration behavior is found to be a strong predictor of success.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most agentic coding benchmarks require exploration but only score final task success, failing to separate exploration from execution. This paper addresses this gap by creating a benchmark that distinguishes observation tools from editing tools, enabling direct measurement of exploration behavior.

Method: The benchmark runs language models as agents in reproducible, stateful game-engine sessions within Roblox Studio. It uses an eight-tool action space that separates observation tools from editing tools. Each task is evaluated with executable checks on both the edited scene and in simulated play sessions. 13 frontier models were tested on 84 human-curated core tasks with 16 attempts per task.

Result: The best model solves 51.7% of tasks on a single attempt and 39.4% five times out of five. No model solves six specific tasks. Models reach similar overall pass rates by solving different subsets of tasks. When splitting tasks by work type (script-authoring vs scene-change), the top five models spread by 5.0pp on script tasks and 12.5pp on scene tasks. Exploration behavior strongly predicts success: runs that inspect every object a reference solution touches before acting pass 13.4pp more often on scene-only tasks and 9.8pp more on script-only tasks.

Conclusion: Current frontier models struggle with complex game development tasks in Roblox Studio. The benchmark successfully separates exploration measurement from task execution, revealing that exploration behavior is a significant predictor of success. The released materials (task suite, place files, annotations, plugin, leaderboard) enable further research in agentic game development evaluation.

Abstract: We present OpenGameEval, a benchmark and evaluation framework for agentic game development inside Roblox Studio. It runs language models as agents in reproducible, stateful game-engine sessions and scores each run with executable checks, both on the edited scene and in a simulated play session. Most agentic coding benchmarks require exploration but score only final task success. OpenGameEval separates observation tools from editing tools in its eight-tool action space, so exploration can be measured directly. We measure the pass rates and exploration behavior of 13 frontier models on 84 human-curated core tasks, with 16 attempts per task.
  The tasks are hard for current models. The best model solves 51.7% of tasks on a single attempt and 39.4% five times out of five, and no tested model solves six of the tasks. Models at the frontier reach similar pass rates by solving different tasks: splitting tasks by the kind of work they require spreads the top five by 5.0pp on script-authoring tasks and 12.5pp on scene-change tasks.
  Exploration behavior predicts whether a run succeeds. Holding task and model fixed, a run that inspects every object a reference solution touches before acting on it passes 13.4pp more often than a run that inspects none of them on scene-only tasks, and 9.8pp more often on script-only tasks.
  We release the task suite, its place files, the per-task annotations, a plugin that runs the tasks inside Roblox Studio, and an updated leaderboard under the MIT license at https://github.com/Roblox/open-game-eval.

</details>


### [317] [DISSOLVR: An Interpretable and Fast Framework for Aqueous and Organic Solubility Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02574)
*Vansh Ramani,Har Ashish Arora,Dhairya Kuchhal,Sayan Ranu,Tarak Karmakar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DISSOLVR is a transparent machine learning framework for high-fidelity molecular solubility prediction that combines physically-grounded descriptors with an LLM-assisted explanation pipeline, achieving performance near the aleatoric limit of experimental uncertainty while maintaining interpretability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to challenge the trend of using non-transparent deep learning architectures in solubility prediction, which sacrifice physical interpretability for predictive power. The authors argue that state-of-the-art performance can be achieved with more interpretable methods.

Method: DISSOLVR maps molecules to physically-grounded descriptors to achieve structural invariance and OOD generalization. The framework includes an LLLM-assisted post-hoc explanation pipeline to bridge symbolic model artifacts with chemically grounded narratives. The study includes a benchmarking study against various methods and a survey of 22 expert chemists.

Result: DISSOLVR approaches the aleatoric limit of experimental uncertainty and achieves OOD generalization through structural invariance. Expert evaluators in the survey provide deep insights, suggesting the framework's practical utility.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that state-of-the-art performance in molecular solubility prediction does not require non-transparent deep learning architectures; transparent frameworks like DISSOLVR can achieve comparable results while maintaining physical interpretability.

Abstract: High-fidelity solubility prediction is fundamental to pharmaceutical development and environmental partitioning, where accurate modeling must couple molecular structure with thermodynamic behavior across diverse chemical environments. However, recent advancements have been dominated by deep learning architectures that often sacrifice physical interpretability for predictive power. We challenge this trend by showing that state-of-the-art performance does not require such non-transparent architectures. To address this, we introduce DISSOLVR, a transparent framework for molecular solubility prediction. In addition, we perform a comprehensive literature review and a benchmarking study against various methods. We show that DISSOLVR approaches the aleatoric limit of experimental uncertainty and achieves OOD generalization through structural invariance, derived by mapping molecules to physically-grounded descriptors. Then, we present an LLM-assisted post-hoc explanation pipeline that bridges the gap between symbolic model artifacts and chemically grounded narratives. Finally, a comparative benchmark of a survey involving 22 expert chemists reveals that expert evaluators provide deep insights.

</details>


### [318] [Dense Mixture-of-Experts as a Reparameterized Wide FFN: A Granularity Sweep at Fixed Compute](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02584)
*Vu Quang Hoang,Nghia Hieu Nguyen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates the contribution of dynamic expert combination in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models by comparing a dense analogue (K SwiGLU experts, all active with softmax gating) against the sparse MoE approach. Testing K=1,2,4,6 at fixed total FFN width, the authors find K=2 achieves the best performance (+0.0048 improvement), while larger K values (K=4, K=6) actually degrade validation loss. The study reveals a "granularity sweet spot" for always-active, softly gated FFNs at fixed width.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to isolate and understand the contribution of dynamic expert combination in MoE models. While sparse MoE models use learned routing to select from a large expert pool, the authors aim to determine whether the performance gains come from the routing mechanism itself or from other factors like increased parameter count. They create a dense analogue where K experts are all active and combined via softmax gating at fixed total width.

Method: The authors use a controlled experimental approach: (1) Implement K SwiGLU experts where all K experts are active for every token, (2) Combine experts using a softmax gate, (3) Maintain fixed total FFN width across all configurations (K=1,2,4,6), (4) Analyze routing behavior (softness, expert usage balance), (5) Test the importance of concentrated routing by forcing uniform gate distribution, (6) Mathematically characterize the architecture as dense SwiGLU with token-dependent simplex-constrained group scaling.

Result: Key results: (1) K=2 improves validation loss by 0.0048 over baseline (K=1), (2) K=4 worsens loss by 0.0053, (3) K=6 worsens loss by 0.0197, (4) Routing remains soft and balanced in most cases except first layer of K=4 model (nearly one-hot), (5) Forcing uniform gate on the first layer of K=4 increases loss by 2.4 nats on diagnostic subset, indicating concentrated routing is functionally important, (6) K=2 represents the optimal granularity sweet spot.

Conclusion: The study concludes that at fixed total FFN width, there exists a "granularity sweet spot" for always-active, softly gated FFNs, with K=2 performing best among configurations tested. The dense baseline (K=1) is contained within the function class of this architecture. The concentrated routing observed in certain layers (e.g., first layer of K=4) serves a functionally important purpose, as forcing uniform distribution significantly degrades performance. This suggests that moderate expert specialization (K=2) provides the optimal balance between flexibility and parameter efficiency.

Abstract: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models combine learned routing with selection from a large expert pool. We isolate the contribution of dynamic expert combination using a dense analogue: $K$ SwiGLU experts, all active for every token and combined by a softmax gate, at fixed total FFN width. With no larger pool or discrete selection, the dense baseline is the $K=1$ case. Validation loss varies non-monotonically with $K$: $K=2$ improves over the baseline by $0.0048$, whereas $K=4$ and $K=6$ worsen it by $0.0053$ and $0.0197$, respectively. Routing generally remains soft and expert usage balanced, except in the first layer of the $K=4$ model, where routing is nearly one-hot. Forcing this gate to uniform increases loss by $2.4$ nats on a diagnostic subset, indicating that its concentrated routing is functionally important. We further show that the architecture is exactly a dense SwiGLU with token-dependent, simplex-constrained group scaling and contains the dense baseline in its function class. These single-run results suggest a granularity sweet spot for always-active, softly gated FFNs at fixed width, with $K=2$ performing best among the configurations tested.

</details>


### [319] [Fisher-Guided Submodular Data Selection for Continual Pre-Training of Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02593)
*Zhenghao Zhao,Gaowen Liu,Zhiling Lan,Yan Yan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a Fisher-aware data selection method for continual pre-training (CPT) that decomposes candidate gradients into anchor and frontier components to balance target-domain adaptation with catastrophic forgetting prevention. The method achieves 10x token efficiency compared to replay-based approaches, with 1B selected tokens outperforming 10B replay tokens on both adaptation and forgetting metrics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Data selection in CPT is a forgetting-control problem: poorly chosen target-domain corpora can overwrite pretrained capabilities. Existing methods either use parameter-agnostic scalars (e.g., perplexity) or require excessive general-domain replay tokens to mitigate forgetting. Neither directly considers how training on candidates affects model parameters.

Method: The paper introduces a Fisher-aware CPT selector that: (1) Decomposes each candidate's gradient into an anchor component (measuring perturbation along high-Fisher committed parameter directions) and a frontier component (measuring update capacity in low-Fisher subspaces); (2) Aggregates these signals using a log-determinant submodular objective; (3) Optimizes in a single pass using a scalable streaming data selection pipeline.

Result: On TinyLlama-1.1B and Llama-3.1-8B continual pre-training over medical data, the Fisher-aware selector improves target-domain quality while bounding forgetting on held-out pretraining benchmarks. Most importantly, 1B selected tokens outperform the replay strategy trained with 10B tokens, giving a 10x token-efficiency advantage.

Conclusion: The Fisher information matrix provides a principled mechanism for understanding and mitigating catastrophic forgetting in CPT. By explicitly measuring parameter perturbation along high-Fisher directions (where the pretrained model has committed knowledge), Fisher-aware selection can effectively balance adaptation and forgetting without excessive replay tokens, achieving substantial token efficiency gains.

Abstract: Data selection is already a central bottleneck in large-language-model training, where web-scale corpora are noisy and token budgets are finite. In continual pre-training (CPT), it becomes a forgetting-control problem: a poorly chosen target-domain corpus can overwrite capabilities encoded in the pretrained checkpoint. Existing CPT practice either scores candidates with parameter-agnostic scalars such as perplexity, or mitigates forgetting by spending many extra general-domain replay tokens. Neither strategy directly asks how training on a candidate will move the model parameters. We show that loss-based selection causes the post-CPT Fisher diagonal to drift downward on exactly the high-Fisher coordinates the pretrained model had committed to, while leaving low-Fisher coordinates largely untouched. This asymmetry exposes a parameter-space mechanism for catastrophic forgetting. Motivated by this observation, we propose a Fisher-aware CPT selector that decomposes each candidate's gradient into an anchor component, which measures perturbation along committed parameter directions, and a frontier component, which measures update capacity in unconstrained low-Fisher subspaces. We aggregate these signals with a log-determinant submodular objective and optimize it in a single pass using a scalable streaming data selection pipeline. On TinyLlama-1.1B and Llama-3.1-8B CPT over medical data, our selector improves target-domain quality while bounding forgetting on held-out pretraining benchmarks. Most importantly, it is substantially more token-efficient than forgetting-aware replay. 1B selected tokens already outperform the replay strategy trained with 10B tokens on both adaptation and forgetting, giving a 10x token-efficiency advantage.

</details>


### [320] [How Causality Bridges the Semantic Gap](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02594)
*Shuhao Zhang,Xuran Zhou,Han Guo,Pengtao Xie,Yujia Zheng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper presents CausalBridge, a framework that uses causal structure to assign semantic meanings to variables (both observed and latent) in a system, by discovering causal graphs from measurements and solving for embeddings under those relations, then expressing them as names through a language model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
