Motivation: The problem is that numerical measurements often leave variable meanings unspecified - some variables are measured but never labeled, others are never measured at all. Existing methods rely on general human knowledge which inherits biases where that knowledge exists and offers nothing where it does not. The authors seek to bridge this gap using causal structure as an unbiased source of information.

Method: The authors formalize this as "structure-constrained semantic alignment" - solving for the embedding of each unnamed variable under the dependence relations implied by the causal graph, with embeddings of a few known variable names as anchors. CausalBridge has three main components: (1) discovering the causal graph from measurements including latent variables, (2) solving for embeddings under those causal relations, and (3) expressing embeddings as names through a language model.

Result: CausalBridge was evaluated on five questionnaires and three robotics scenarios with 20-90% of variable names masked. It recovers semantics of observed and latent variables more accurately than existing methods relying on association, and this advantage increases as less of the system is documented. The graph discovers names variables as accurately as documented ones, and can name a new system in minutes at a fraction of the cost of sampling methods.

Conclusion: The causal structure reflects the mechanism that generated the measurements and is recovered from measurements alone, potentially making it the only source of information free from human knowledge bias. Once the semantic gap is bridged faithfully, machines can understand the world and take actions causally.

Abstract: Numerical measurements capture how a system behaves, but often leave the meanings of its variables unspecified. Some variables are measured but never labeled, and others are never measured at all. Existing methods assign semantics to such variables by consulting general human knowledge, but this inherits its biases where that knowledge exists and offers nothing where it does not. We bridge this gap between measurements and their meanings with causal structure instead, reading a variable's semantics from how it acts on other variables. We formalize this as structure-constrained semantic alignment, in which the embedding of each unnamed variable is solved under the dependence relations implied by the causal graph, with the embeddings of a few known names as anchors. Accordingly, we build CausalBridge, a framework that discovers the causal graph from the measurements, latent variables included, solves for the embeddings under those relations, and expresses them as names through a language model. The causal structure reflects the mechanism that generated the measurements and is recovered from the measurements alone, which may make it the one source of information free of bias from human knowledge. We evaluate CausalBridge on five questionnaires and three robotics scenarios, with 20 to 90% of the variable names masked. It recovers the semantics of observed and latent variables more accurately than existing methods that rely on association, and its lead widens as less of the system is documented. The graph it discovers names variables as accurately as the documented one, and a new system is named in minutes and at a fraction of the cost of sampling methods. Once the semantic gap is bridged faithfully, machines can understand the world and take actions causally.

</details>


### [321] [Activation Sparsity with Weight Approximation for Faster LLM Decoding on Offloaded Weights](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02598)
*JuneHyung Kim,Sankeerth Durvasula,Nandita Vijaykumar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SpAx introduces a three-tier weight reading strategy (retain/approximate/omit) to exploit activation sparsity for efficient LLM inference when weights are offloaded to CPU memory or flash storage, achieving 3.86X speedup with 16-bit weights and 2.06X with 4-bit weights while limiting perplexity increase to 10%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deploying LLMs on consumer-grade GPUs with insufficient memory requires offloading weights to CPU RAM or flash storage, causing slow inference due to low-bandwidth transfers. Existing activation sparsity methods skip weights but suffer rapid quality degradation, indicating that weights associated with small-magnitude activations collectively influence model quality significantly.

Method: SpAx replaces binary weight decisions with three options: (1) fully retain original weights, (2) approximate using compressed weight representation, or (3) omit entirely. The method skips weights with activations closest to zero, reads approximate weights for smaller-magnitude activations (where errors are attenuated), and reads original weights for largest-magnitude activations.

Result: With CPU memory offloading: 3.86X average speedup (5.57X max) with 16-bit weights, 2.06X (2.74X max) with 4-bit weights. With flash storage offloading: 3.31X average (4.81X max) and 1.54X (2.03X max). WikiText-2 perplexity increase limited to at most 10%.

Conclusion: SpAx significantly improves the trade-off between model quality and decoding performance by leveraging a three-tier weight reading strategy that exploits activation sparsity while using compressed weight representations for smaller-magnitude activations, enabling practical LLM deployment on memory-constrained consumer hardware.

Abstract: Deploying LLMs on consumer-grade GPUs with insufficient memory to hold their weights can result in prohibitively slow inference, because decoding repeatedly transfers offloaded weights from system RAM or flash storage into GPU at much lower bandwidth than local GPU-memory access. Activation sparsity reduces these transfers by skipping weights associated with zero or near-zero activations. However, as more activation contributions are omitted, model quality eventually degrades rapidly, indicating that weights associated with small-magnitude activations collectively influence model quality sharply. In this work, we improve the trade-off between model quality and decoding performance when exploiting activation sparsity. Our key idea is to replace the binary choice of whether or not to read a weight with three options: fully retain it, approximate it using a compressed weight representation, or omit it entirely. SpAx skips weights associated with activations closest to zero, reads approximate weights for smaller-magnitude activations, and reads original weights for the largest-magnitude activations. Smaller-magnitude activations attenuate the errors introduced by approximate weights, while compressed weight representations require fewer bytes to be transferred. With weights offloaded to CPU memory, SpAx speeds up decoding by 3.86X on average (up to 5.57X) with 16-bit weights and 2.06X (up to 2.74X) with 4-bit weights, at a WikiText-2 perplexity increase of at most 10%. With weights offloaded to flash storage, the speedups are 3.31X on average (up to 4.81X) and 1.54X (up to 2.03X).

</details>


### [322] [Seer: Maximum Likelihood Regression for Learning-Speed Curves](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02610)
*Carl Myers Kadie*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Seer is a system that models classification-learning performance by generating empirical observations and creating statistical models to predict training example requirements and maximum achievable accuracy. The system uses maximum-likelihood models solved via efficient iterative algorithms and was demonstrated on three real-world domains (soybean disease, heart disease, audiological problems).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The research addresses the need to predict machine learning performance, specifically how many training examples are needed to achieve desired accuracy and what maximum accuracy is possible with unlimited training data. This helps practitioners make informed decisions about model selection and resource allocation.

Method: The approach involves: 1) developing models with optimal constraints and parameters for classification learning, 2) reducing model selection to nonlinear regression using appropriate problem constraints, 3) implementing efficient iterative algorithms for maximum-likelihood estimation, and 4) empirical validation through ~100 experiments across three domains.

Result: Seer demonstrates excellent characterization of learning-performance and appears to be optimal for predicting learning performance. The system was tested on real-world data from soybean disease, heart disease, and audiological problem domains.

Conclusion: The thesis provides recommendations for choosing regression models for specific situations and identifies directions for further research. Seer represents an advancement in modeling classification-learning performance through its efficient algorithms and practical applicability.

Abstract: The research presented here focuses on modeling machine-learning performance. The thesis introduces Seer, a system that generates empirical observations of classification-learning performance and then uses those observations to create statistical models. The models can be used to predict the number of training examples needed to achieve a desired level and the maximum accuracy possible given an unlimited number of training examples. Seer advances the state of the art with 1) models that embody the best constraints for classification learning and most useful parameters, 2) algorithms that efficiently find maximum-likelihood models, and 3) a demonstration on real-world data from three domains of a practicable application of such modeling.
  The first part of the thesis gives an overview of the requirements for a good maximum-likelihood model of classification-learning performance. Next, reasonable design choices for such models are explored. Selection among such models is a task of nonlinear programming, but by exploiting appropriate problem constraints, the task is reduced to a nonlinear regression task that can be solved with an efficient iterative algorithm. The latter part of the thesis describes almost 100 experiments in the domains of soybean disease, heart disease, and audiological problems. The tests show that Seer is excellent at characterizing learning-performance and that it seems to be as good as possible at predicting learning performance. Finally, recommendations for choosing a regression model for a particular situation are made and directions for further research are identified.

</details>


### [323] [Scale-Recursive Rectified Flows for Few-Step Precipitation Ensembles](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02611)
*Shunya Nagashima,Takumi Bannai*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A scale-recursive rectified flow model for satellite-to-radar precipitation downscaling that allocates sampling steps across spatial scales to improve ensemble diversity and probabilistic accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Coarse satellite products cannot resolve rainfall at local scales, and existing generative models (rectified flows) produce ensemble members that are too similar when reducing sampling steps, understating uncertainty.

Method: Scale-recursive rectified flow generates broad patterns before local details by guiding sampling-step allocation through comparison of ensemble variability with prediction error across spatial scales. Validation scores and rainfall power spectra constrain step allocation to avoid excessive amplification.

Result: Allocating more steps to coarse flow improved probabilistic accuracy and rain detection across training seeds at fixed architecture and computational cost. The model achieved better probabilistic accuracy with shorter sampling time than a nonrecursive flow using more steps.

Conclusion: Broad rainfall patterns are the main source of insufficient ensemble variability under reduced sampling budgets. The proposed scale-recursive approach effectively addresses this by prioritizing coarse-scale generation, improving probabilistic accuracy without increased computational cost.

Abstract: Fine-resolution precipitation estimates support flood risk assessment and water management, but coarse satellite products cannot resolve rainfall within each grid cell. Generative models address this ambiguity by producing ensembles of plausible high-resolution rainfall fields. Among these models, rectified flows generate samples by iteratively transforming random noise into rainfall fields. Reducing the number of sampling steps accelerates generation but can make ensemble members too similar, understating uncertainty. We propose a scale-recursive rectified flow that generates broad patterns before local details and guides sampling-step allocation by comparing ensemble variability with prediction error across spatial scales. Validation scores and rainfall power spectra constrain the allocation to avoid excessive amplification. In satellite-to-radar downscaling over the contiguous United States, our analysis identified broad rainfall patterns as the main source of insufficient ensemble variability under reduced sampling budgets. Allocating more steps to the coarse flow improved probabilistic accuracy and rain detection across training seeds at fixed architecture and computational cost. The proposed model also achieved better probabilistic accuracy with shorter sampling time than a nonrecursive flow using more steps.

</details>


### [324] [What Is Lost in Post-Training? Default Collapse and the Loss of In-Context Steerability Across Diverse Perspectives](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02614)
*Jessica Dierking,Itai Shapira,Niclas Boehmer*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates how post-training of large language models affects their ability to adapt to different perspectives in-context. The authors demonstrate that post-training narrows the views models express and degrades their capacity to be steered toward perspectives they weren't trained to favor, creating a tension between prioritizing a single value set and preserving the ability to serve diverse stakeholders.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to understand how post-training affects LLMs' ability to adapt to different user perspectives and contexts. While prior work showed post-training narrows default behavior, this work focuses on in-context adaptability—the model's capacity to recognize and enact opposing viewpoints when explicitly prompted.

Method: The authors conducted controlled experiments where they fine-tuned models toward one side of cultural-value disagreements. They then evaluated checkpoints throughout training to measure: (1) how dominant the trained side becomes in ordinary use, and (2) how the ability to recognize and faithfully enact the opposing view declines. Finally, they proposed an alternative objective maximizing reward subject to a prescribed distribution over expressed perspectives, implementing this as "stance-distribution matching."

Result: Post-training causes two key effects: (1) the trained perspective becomes increasingly dominant in ordinary use, and (2) the model's ability to recognize and faithfully enact opposing viewpoints declines. This creates a fundamental tension between prioritizing a single set of values and preserving the technical capacity to serve diverse stakeholders.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that there's an inherent trade-off between value alignment (training toward specific perspectives) and perspective diversity (maintaining the ability to adapt to different viewpoints). The proposed stance-distribution matching approach offers a potential solution by maximizing reward while maintaining a prescribed distribution over expressed perspectives, rather than optimizing for a single viewpoint.

Abstract: AI models serving a heterogeneous population must act on the principles appropriate to each user and context. While post-training has been shown to narrow the views large language models express, prior work has focused on default behavior rather than the ability to adapt to in-context information. We show that post-training also degrades a model's ability to be steered in-context toward perspectives it was not trained to favor. In controlled experiments, we fine-tune models toward one side of cultural-value disagreements and evaluate checkpoints throughout training. The trained side becomes increasingly dominant in ordinary use, while the ability to recognize and faithfully enact the opposing view declines. These findings point to a tension between prioritizing a single set of values and preserving the technical capacity needed to serve diverse stakeholders. Finally, we propose and analyze an alternative objective that maximizes reward subject to a prescribed distribution over expressed perspectives, and present stance-distribution matching as a practical implementation.

</details>


### [325] [Quantifying the Value of Constructive Induction, Knowledge, and Noise Filtering on Inductive Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02615)
*Carl M. Kadie*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Summary generation failed


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Motivation analysis unavailable

Method: Method extraction failed

Result: Result analysis unavailable

Conclusion: Conclusion extraction failed

Abstract: Learning research, as one of its central goals, tries to measure, model, and understand how learning-problem properties affect average-case learning performance. For example, we would like to quantify the value of constructive induction, noise filtering, and background knowledge. This paper describes the effective dimension, a new learning measure that helps link problem properties to learning performance. Like the Vapnik-Chervonenkis (VC) dimension, the effective dimension is often in a simple linear relation with problem properties. Unlike the VC dimension, the effective dimension can be estimated empirically and makes average-case predictions. It is therefore more widely applicable to machine and human learning research. The measure is demonstrated on several learning systems including Backpropagation. Finally, the measure is used to precisely predict the benefit of using FRINGE, a feature construction system. The benefit is found to decrease as the complexity of the target concept increases.

</details>


### [326] [Online Verification of Language Model Responses Under Cost Constraints](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02632)
*Erfan Hajihashemi,Yanning Shen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses the challenge of verifying large language model outputs efficiently by introducing OMVV (Online Multi-Verifier Verification), which maintains a pool of K weak verifiers and adaptively selects among them using online learning techniques to balance cost and accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The problem is that verifying LLM outputs using ground-truth oracles is costly, and using a single fixed weak verifier may not perform consistently well across different query types/difficulties. Prior work used a single weak verifier + strong verifier, but this lacks adaptability.

Method: OMVV maintains a pool of K candidate weak verifiers with different cost/performance tradeoffs. It uses an online score combiner and exponential-weights routing policy to adaptively select which verifier to use for each decision. The approach provides distribution-free finite-time guarantees on false-accept/reject rates and sublinear regret against the best fixed verifier.

Result: Experiments on reasoning dataset benchmarks show OMVV achieves higher accuracy at lower verification cost than any single fixed verifier across a range of operating budgets.

Conclusion: The proposed OMVV algorithm successfully addresses the verification cost-accuracy tradeoff by adaptively routing decisions among multiple weak verifiers, with theoretical guarantees and empirical validation showing superior performance compared to single fixed verifier approaches.

Abstract: As large language models are increasingly deployed for multi-step reasoning, verifying the correctness of their outputs has become essential for maintaining reliability at scale. Verifying the correctness of large language model outputs is often done by querying a costly ground-truth oracle, which is impractical to invoke at every step in an online setting. Prior work addresses this by querying a single weak verifier on every step, and using its score to decide whether the costly strong verifier needs to be queried as well, reserving strong verification for only a small fraction of the steps. However, a single fixed weak verifier may not perform consistently well as the subject matter or difficulty of incoming queries changes over time, and committing to one in advance risks either overly costly or inaccurate verification. We introduce OMVV (Online Multi-Verifier Verification), an algorithm that maintains a pool of $K$ candidate weak verifiers with differing cost and verification performance, and adaptively routes each round's decision to a verifier selected via an online score combiner and an exponential-weights routing policy. OMVV provides a distribution-free, finite-time guarantee on false-accept and false-reject rates across the full pool of verifiers, and further achieves sublinear regret against the best fixed verifier in hindsight under a combined cost and consistency objective. Experiments on reasoning dataset benchmarks show that OMVV achieves higher accuracy at lower verification cost than any single fixed verifier, across a range of operating budgets.

</details>


### [327] [Context-Tower Conversion Preserves Generation While Freezing Retains Knowledge: Low-Budget AR-to-Diffusion Conversion of MoE LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02657)
*Wentao Lu,Jesse Clark,Tianyu Zhu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper compares two methods for converting a pretrained autoregressive (AR) Mixture-of-Experts model into a diffusion language model (dLLM) for parallel generation: in-place updates vs. frozen-tower architecture. Under fixed 1B training token budget, the frozen-tower method achieves 11.6x better HumanEval scores (71.60 vs 6.19) while retaining 95% of GSM8K and 99% of MMLU-Pro performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to enable parallel generation from pretrained AR models without training a new model from scratch. The key problem is that existing conversion methods differ by ~1000x in training data requirements and haven't been fairly compared under controlled conditions.

Method: The study compares two conversion methods on a 30B MoE parent model: (1) In-place model updates a subset of weights using denoising and representation-alignment losses; (2) Frozen-tower model uses cross-attention on a frozen causal copy of the parent. Fixed variables: corpus, supervised-token budget, trainable parameters, and evaluation harness.

Result: The frozen-tower model achieves 71.60 on HumanEval pass@10 vs 6.19 for in-place (11.6x improvement). It retains 95% of parent's GSM8K and 99% of MMLU-Pro. A dense-parent experiment reproduces this separation. Freezing the context tower at ~500M tokens retains more MMLU-Pro while both achieve similar HumanEval. Theoretical analysis shows both conversion classes can exactly sample the AR parent under hard attention. Evaluation protocol substantially affects a 500B-token conversion's scores while AR parent varies by <3 points.

Conclusion: In the tested low-budget regime, the frozen-tower configuration retains substantially more of the parent's generation performance than in-place conversion. The study emphasizes the need for common evaluation protocols when comparing dLLMs, as evaluation methodology significantly impacts results.

Abstract: Converting a pretrained autoregressive (AR) model to a diffusion language model (dLLM) enables parallel generation without pretraining a new model. Published conversion methods differ by roughly three orders of magnitude in training data and have not been compared under a common protocol. We compare two conversions of the same 30B Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) parent, holding the corpus, supervised-token budget, trainable parameter set and evaluation harness fixed, each under its own training recipe. The in-place model updates a subset of the parent's weights using denoising and representation-alignment losses; the frozen-tower model instead conditions through cross-attention on a frozen causal copy of the parent. With 1B training tokens, the frozen-tower model scores 71.60 on HumanEval pass@10 against 6.19 for the in-place model, an 11.6x improvement. At the same budget it also keeps 95% of the parent's GSM8K score and 99% of its MMLU-Pro score. A dense-parent experiment reproduces the HumanEval separation. Within the two-tower design at about 500M tokens, freezing the context tower retains substantially more MMLU-Pro performance than training it, while both give similar observed HumanEval scores. Our theoretical analysis establishes that both conversion classes contain an exact sampler for the AR parent under a hard attention mask and left-to-right commitment of one position per round. Under a shared loss, freezing removes the gradient contribution through the context states. Furthermore, evaluation protocol substantially affects a published 500B-token conversion's scores in both directions across tasks, while its AR parent's scores vary by less than three points, so comparing dLLMs needs a common protocol. These results show that, in the tested low-budget regime, the frozen-tower configuration retains substantially more of the parent's generation performance than in-place conversion.

</details>


### [328] [Distributed Learning with Selective State Space Models: Architecture-Aware Convergence Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02659)
*Adam Piaseczny,Md Kamran Chowdhury Shisher,Shiqiang Wang,Christopher G. Brinton*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses the gap between federated learning (FL) algorithms and modern State Space Models (SSMs) like Mamba2. The authors derive architecture-aware gradient and smoothness bounds for selective SSMs, and convergence bounds for FedAvg and FedProx, accounting for SSM-specific properties like recurrent stability and state projection norms. They validate these bounds empirically and compare nine FL algorithms on Mamba2 language modeling across six text domains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern SSMs (e.g., Mamba2) offer a promising alternative to transformers but their behavior in distributed learning settings is poorly understood. Existing FL methods are architecture-agnostic and don't account for the stability, selectivity, and state-space parameterization that characterize selective SSMs.

Method: The authors derive theoretical bounds for: (1) Architecture-aware gradient and smoothness bounds for single- and multi-layer selective SSMs, (2) Convergence bounds for FedAvg and FedProx, incorporating recurrent stability, input-dependent discretization, and state projection norms. They validate single-layer bounds numerically using teacher SSM-generated sequences, then compare nine FL algorithms on Mamba2 language modeling across six text domains.

Result: The theoretical analysis provides bounds that characterize how SSM-specific properties affect federated optimization. The numerical validation demonstrates the bounds' accuracy on teacher SSM sequences. The experiments across six text domains reveal how SSM-specific bounds can interpret practical federated learning algorithm behavior.

Conclusion: The paper establishes a theoretical foundation for understanding federated learning with SSMs by providing architecture-aware bounds that account for SSM-specific characteristics. These bounds can guide the interpretation and design of FL algorithms for SSM-based models.

Abstract: Modern state space models (SSMs), such as Mamba2, provide a compelling alternative to transformers by combining linear-time sequence modeling with recurrent state-space dynamics. However, the behavior of SSMs in distributed learning settings remains poorly understood. In particular, the existing standard federated learning methods are largely architecture-agnostic, and do not account for the stability, selectivity, and state-space parameterization that characterize modern selective SSMs. To address this, we derive architecture-aware gradient and smoothness bounds for single- and multi-layer selective SSMs, and convergence bounds for FedAvg and FedProx, characterizing how recurrent stability, input-dependent discretization, and state projection norms affect federated optimization. We then numerically validate the single-layer bounds on sequences generated by a teacher SSM, using a learner that follows the analyzed recurrence. We use this analysis to formulate expectations about the effects of local training and client heterogeneity, and examine these expectations by comparing nine federated learning algorithms on Mamba2 language modeling across six text domains. These experiments illustrate how SSM-specific bounds can provide a basis for interpreting the behavior of practical federated learning algorithms.

</details>


### [329] [AIGS: Adaptive Incremental Gating System for Online Representation Learning in Non-Stationary Data Streams](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02661)
*SiRui He,Kai Liang Lew,Chui Zi Ong,Chean Khim Toa*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes AIGS (Adaptive Incremental Gating System), a lightweight closed-loop framework for online representation learning in IoT/edge environments. It addresses the stability-plasticity dilemma using two key mechanisms: Shock Ratio (error normalization against recent variation) and Continuous Plasticity Controller (smooth interpolation between plasticity and retention). The method achieves O(k·d) complexity and shows strong results on smart city datasets for early warning, post-shift recovery, and noise resistance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-time data streams in WoT and edge computing often undergo latent regime changes. Existing methods for online representation learning under computational constraints use fixed update schedules or rolling windows, which suffer from parameter ossification during sudden shifts and waste resources when streams remain stable. The core problem is resolving the stability-plasticity dilemma: maintaining useful historical knowledge while rapidly adapting to concept drift.

Method: AIGS introduces two key mechanisms: (1) Shock Ratio - an endogenous residual feedback mechanism that normalizes current reconstruction error against recent variation to detect regime changes; (2) Continuous Plasticity Controller - uses the Shock Ratio to smoothly interpolate between learning plasticity and memory retention. The approach treats representation learning as a closed-loop control mechanism, achieving strictly linear O(k·d) per-step complexity suitable for latency-sensitive edge devices.

Result: Experiments on real-world smart city dynamic streams show: (1) On Electricity Transformer Temperature datasets (ETTm1, ETTm2), AIGS achieves preventative early-warning lead times of 8.31 and 9.88 steps under gradual degradation; (2) On Performance Measurement System traffic datasets, it shows significantly faster post-shift recovery after abrupt mutations; (3) On the highly noisy Weather dataset, it improves anomaly recall while resisting stochastic noise overfitting.

Conclusion: AIGS establishes itself as a practical, plug-and-play adapter for resource-constrained edge monitoring systems. It effectively resolves the stability-plasticity dilemma through endogenous feedback control, making it suitable for latency-sensitive IoT applications in smart cities (traffic networks, meteorological systems, industrial infrastructure).

Abstract: Real-time data streams in Web of Things (WoT) and edge computing environments often evolve through latent regime changes. For online representation learning under strict computational constraints, the central problem is resolving the stability-plasticity dilemma: keeping useful historical knowledge while rapidly reacting to concept drift. Existing methods employ fixed update schedules or rolling windows. However, they suffer from parameter ossification during sudden shifts and waste computational resources when the stream remains stable. This paper proposes the Adaptive Incremental Gating System (AIGS), a lightweight closed-loop state-aware adaptation framework. AIGS introduces the Shock Ratio, an endogenous residual feedback mechanism that normalizes current reconstruction error against recent variation. This signal drives a Continuous Plasticity Controller that smoothly interpolates between learning plasticity and memory retention. By treating representation learning as a closed-loop control mechanism, AIGS avoids catastrophic forgetting and maintains a strictly linear $\mathcal{O}\left(k\cdot d\right)$ per-step complexity suitable for latency-sensitive edge devices. Experiments on real-world smart city dynamic streams-spanning traffic networks, meteorological systems, and industrial infrastructure-demonstrate distinct domain-dependent advantages. On Electricity Transformer Temperature datasets, AIGS achieves preventative early-warning lead times of 8.31 (ETTm1) and 9.88 (ETTm2) steps under gradual degradation. On Performance Measurement System traffic datasets, it shows significantly faster post-shift recovery after abrupt mutations. On the highly noisy Weather dataset, it improves anomaly recall while resisting stochastic noise overfitting. These findings establish AIGS as a practical, plug-and-play adapter for resource-constrained edge monitoring systems.

</details>


### [330] [Mind the Refinement Gap: When Safe High-Level Robot Plans Produce Unsafe Executions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02662)
*Stabak Das,Priyesh Ranjan,Xiangfang Li,Lijun Qian*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates a trace-completeness assumption in language-enabled robot systems that combine semantic-graph planning with temporal-logic safety monitors. The authors audit this assumption in RoboGuard by comparing its safety verdicts on surface plans versus graph-refined execution traces under LTL specifications.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to address a critical safety issue in robot systems where high-level action sequences checked by temporal-logic monitors may not accurately represent the actual navigation and implicit action effects that occur during physical execution. This discrepancy could lead to unsafe robot behavior going undetected.

Method: The authors conducted evaluations in two parts: (1) 28 controlled cases spanning five action-abstraction families to test the surface-versus-refined discrepancy hypothesis, and (2) 14 end-to-end cases where SPINE generates plans from natural-language instructions while RoboGuard generates scene-grounded safety specifications. They compared RoboGuard's verdicts on surface plans against graph-refined traces under the same LTL specification.

Result: All 12 targeted abstraction cases exhibited the predicted surface-versus-refined discrepancy, while all 16 control cases behaved as expected. This confirms the trace-completeness assumption is violated in practice, and graph-based trace refinement is needed as a lightweight mitigation and diagnostic tool.

Conclusion: The trace-completeness assumption is problematic in practice. Graph-based trace refinement provides a lightweight mitigation strategy and diagnostic tool for physical-AI safety monitors, enabling more accurate safety verification in language-enabled robot systems.

Abstract: Language-enabled robot systems increasingly combine semantic-graph planning with temporal-logic safety monitors. We investigate a trace-completeness assumption in these systems: whether the high-level action sequence checked by a monitor represents the navigation and implicit action effects induced during execution. We audit this assumption in RoboGuard by comparing its verdict on a surface plan with its verdict on a graph-refined trace under the same Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) specification. Our evaluation comprises 28 controlled cases spanning five action-abstraction families and 14 end-to-end cases in which SPINE [1] generates plans from natural-language instructions while RoboGuard generates scene-grounded safety specifications. In the controlled evaluation, all 12 targeted abstraction cases exhibit the predicted surface-versus-refined discrepancy while all 16 controls behave as expected, motivating graph-based trace refinement as a lightweight mitigation and a diagnostic tool for physical-AI safety monitors.

</details>


### [331] [LEAP: Learning Efficient Action Proposals For LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02670)
*Zhen Xu,Qizheng Zhang,Gerry Wan,Shang Zhu,Ce Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces LEAP (Learning Efficient Action Proposals), a framework and method for accelerating LLM agent rollouts through action speculation. By training a small 0.6B model to predict target model actions, LEAP achieves up to 60% speedup in end-to-end wall clock time without degrading task success.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents are slow because they complete tasks one step at a time, with each step requiring reasoning and action execution before the next can begin. While speculative decoding has been applied to the reasoning phase, applying it to the action phase is underexplored. Existing works use large off-the-shelf models as drafters, which either match well but are slow, or are fast but rarely match the target. The authors sought to understand what determines end-to-end speedup of action speculation.

Method: The authors developed a latency framework for the speculative round that compares gains (from predicting target actions and enabling longer task steps) against costs (from drafting, verification, and tool execution). Guided by this framework, they created LEAP which trains a small drafter model on target action sequences to achieve both speed and accuracy. They also demonstrated online training capability without prior trace collection.

Result: LEAP with a 0.6B model agrees with the target on most decisions and makes agents up to 60% faster in end-to-end wall clock time, with no systematic change in task success. The framework accounts for most measured speedups across various datasets, target models, and draft models. Online training matches offline training performance.

Conclusion: The latency framework effectively predicts speculative decoding speedups. Training small drafters on target action sequences is a practical approach to achieve significant speedups while maintaining accuracy. LEAP is deployable in real-world scenarios through online training, offering a 60% speedup improvement for LLM agents.

Abstract: LLM agents are known to be slow in rollouts. An agent completes a task one step at a time. At each step, it reasons and then chooses an action to execute. The next step and action cannot start until the previous one has finished. Speculative decoding accelerates the rollouts at the reason phase by drafting and verifying the inference tokens. Recent works have also started to apply similar ideas at the action phase. These works use off-the-shelf models, usually large, to draft action proposals for target model to verify. Large drafters match the target more often but take longer to propose, while small off-the-shelf models are fast but rarely make the same decision as the target. We ask a more general question: what determines the end-to-end speedup of action speculation? To answer it, we develop a latency framework for the speculative round. The framework compares what a round gains with what it costs. The gain depends on how well the drafter predicts the target and on how many steps the task can take before it ends. The cost comes from drafting, from waiting for target verification and from executing tools. Guided by the framework, we introduce LEAP (Learning Efficient Action Proposals) which keeps the drafter small and makes it accurate by training it on the target actions sequences. With a small 0.6B model, LEAP agrees with the target on most decisions and makes agents up to 60% faster in end-to-end wall clock time, with no systematic change in task success. Across various datasets, target models and draft models, the framework accounts for most of the measured speedups. We also show the draft model can be online trained with no prior trace collection and match the performance of offline training, making LEAP practical to deploy in the real world.

</details>


### [332] [RAOA: Alternating-Operator Neural Computation with Programmable Radio Propagation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02683)
*Toshiaki Koike-Akino*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces Radio Alternating Operator Ansatz (RAOA), a recurrent computing architecture that uses programmable radio propagation as computational depth. It alternates energy-derived problem updates with mixing updates over a persistent latent state, enabling repeated passes to improve solution quality without increasing learned controls. The approach is evaluated on discrete optimization, programmable-propagation simulation, and pretrained language model adaptation, showing promising results across all three domains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors seek to explore whether programmable radio propagation can serve as computational depth beyond its conventional use as a communication channel or one-shot analog transform. They aim to bridge alternating-operator computation, programmable radio propagation, and neural adaptation within a unified recurrent framework.

Method: RAOA uses a recurrent architecture that alternates between two types of updates: (1) an energy-derived problem update that recomputes the problem field after each mix, and (2) a mixing update over a persistent latent state. This design allows repeated passes to be compositional even when the same learned controls are reused across depth. The approach is validated through three evaluation methods: exact discrete optimization, constrained programmable-propagation simulation, and pretrained-model adaptation as a zero-initialized residual adapter.

Result: On discrete optimization, repeated execution improves solution quality without increasing learned-control count, and higher-order interactions are handled directly. A passive phase-only free-space model demonstrates that required operators can be approximated by programmable propagation while retaining useful downstream behavior despite realization error. For language model adaptation, RAOA achieves WikiText performance close to a matched shallow MLP across three model families, though reasoning-task transfer remains model-dependent.

Conclusion: RAOA successfully connects alternating-operator computation, programmable radio propagation, and neural adaptation within one recurrent framework. The work demonstrates the potential of radio propagation as computational infrastructure, though the RF realization evidence remains simulation-based rather than a hardware demonstration.

Abstract: Can programmable radio propagation serve as computational depth rather than only as a communication channel or one-shot analog transform? We introduce the Radio Alternating Operator Ansatz (RAOA), a recurrent computing architecture that alternates an energy-derived problem update with a mixing update over a persistent latent state. Recomputing the problem field after each mix makes repeated passes compositional even when the same learned controls are reused across depth. We evaluate this idea through exact discrete optimization, constrained programmable-propagation simulation, and pretrained-model adaptation. On discrete objectives, repeated execution can improve solution quality without increasing the learned-control count, and the same formulation handles higher-order interactions directly. A passive phase-only free-space model further shows that the required operators can be approximated by programmable propagation while retaining useful downstream behavior despite realization error. When inserted as a zero-initialized residual adapter, RAOA adapts pretrained language models with WikiText performance close to a matched shallow MLP across three model families, while reasoning-task transfer remains model-dependent. Together, these results connect alternating-operator computation, programmable radio propagation, and neural adaptation within one recurrent framework. The RF realization evidence is simulation-based rather than a hardware demonstration.

</details>


### [333] [Test-time Calibration Learning for Large Language Model Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02695)
*Zizhuo Zhang,Xiong Peng,Jingwei Sun,Rong Yao,Shixiong Kai,Mingxuan Yuan,Bo Han*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes Test-Time Calibration Learning (TTCL), a label-free framework that enables large language models to jointly improve reasoning accuracy and confidence calibration on unlabeled target-task data at test time, using self-supervision signals derived from multiple model-generated responses.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current calibration learning methods rely on labeled data, making them impractical for real-world test-time settings where ground-truth labels are unavailable. There is a need for calibration methods that can adapt to newly encountered target tasks without requiring supervision.

Method: TTCL derives self-supervision signals for both correctness and calibration from multiple model-generated responses, enabling calibration learning at test time without ground-truth labels. The method treats this as a bounded surrogate for the ideal calibration objective.

Result: On base models, TTCL achieves +40.13% average relative accuracy improvement and +70.80% ECE reduction across 8 benchmarks. On math-to-factQA setting, it achieves +20.35% accuracy gain and reduces ECE by +53.83%. The method also improves already calibrated models under domain shift.

Conclusion: TTCL provides an effective label-free approach for test-time calibration that consistently improves both accuracy and calibration across diverse models and tasks, even when source-domain calibration transfers poorly to target tasks.

Abstract: Reliable large language models (LLMs) must not only produce accurate answers but also express confidence that faithfully reflects their probability of being correct. Such calibration is essential for identifying uncertain predictions and supporting reliable decision-making in real-world deployment. Recent studies incorporate calibration learning into reinforcement learning (RL), jointly optimizing answer correctness and verbalized confidence using ground-truth correctness supervision. However, their reliance on labeled data limits their applicability in practical test-time settings, where ground-truth labels are unavailable and calibration may need to adapt to newly encountered target tasks. To address this challenge, we propose Test-Time Calibration Learning (TTCL), a label-free framework that jointly adapts reasoning accuracy and verbalized confidence directly on unlabeled target-task data. Specifically, TTCL derives self-supervision signals for both correctness and calibration from multiple model-generated responses, enabling calibration learning at test time without ground-truth labels. Theoretical analysis further establishes TTCL as a bounded surrogate for the ideal calibration objective. Extensive experiments on mathematical reasoning and factual question answering demonstrate that TTCL consistently improves both accuracy and calibration across diverse models and tasks. On base models, TTCL achieves an average relative accuracy improvement of +40.13% and an ECE reduction of +70.80% across eight benchmarks. Moreover, TTCL can further improve both accuracy and calibration for already calibrated models under domain shift, particularly when source-domain calibration transfers poorly to target tasks. In the math-to-factQA setting, TTCL achieves an average relative accuracy gain of +20.35% and reduces ECE by +53.83%. The source code is released at https://github.com/tmlr-group/TTCL.

</details>


### [334] [Learning from Evolving Errors: Adaptive Iterative Repair for On-Policy Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02700)
*Rui Li,Liyang He,Zheng Zhang,Zhenya Huang,Linbo Zhu,Qi Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: AIR-OPD is an adaptive iterative repair framework for on-policy distillation that provides error-to-repair supervision for training language models on mathematical reasoning tasks. It uses a guidance generator that synthesizes repair guidance for failed responses, with the student sampling on-policy retries with this guidance. Outcome-aware stage weighting credits successful repair stages. The method improves mathematical reasoning by up to 3.6 points over baselines while preserving performance on out-of-distribution benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) methods suffer from a "solution-conditioned shortcut risk" - the teacher receives full reference solutions unavailable to the student, specifying the target but not how to move from the student's current error toward it. This creates a gap between the supervision signal and the student's actual learning needs.

Method: AIR-OPD introduces an adaptive iterative repair framework with three key components: (1) A guidance generator that synthesizes repair guidance for the current error given a failed response; (2) On-policy retry mechanism where the student samples retries with this guidance; (3) Iterative refinement where if retry fails, new guidance is generated for the newly observed error. A fixed teacher receives guidance as privileged context and supervises on error-aligned regions of failed responses. Outcome-aware stage weighting favors early repair stages and credits stages whose immediate retry passes verification.

Result: For both Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B, AIR-OPD achieves the best mathematical-reasoning averages, improving over the strongest baseline by up to 3.6 points on AIME24, AIME25, and HMMT25, while preserving base-model performance on out-of-distribution benchmarks (MMLU-Pro and GPQA).

Conclusion: AIR-OPD successfully addresses the solution-conditioned shortcut risk in on-policy distillation by providing dense token-level error-to-repair supervision. The method achieves state-of-the-art results on mathematical reasoning benchmarks while maintaining generalization to other tasks, demonstrating the effectiveness of adaptive iterative repair with outcome-aware stage weighting.

Abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) supplies dense token-level feedback on trajectories sampled from the student's own policy, a richer training signal than the outcome-level rewards of reinforcement learning. This feedback comes from a teacher conditioned on a full reference solution unavailable to the student. The reference solution specifies the target but not how to move from the student's current error toward it, creating a solution-conditioned shortcut risk. We introduce AIR-OPD, an adaptive iterative repair framework for on-policy distillation that provides error-to-repair supervision. Given a failed response, a guidance generator synthesizes repair guidance for the current error. The student samples an on-policy retry with this guidance. If the retry remains incorrect, the generator produces new repair guidance for the newly observed error. At each round, a fixed teacher receives the guidance as privileged context and supervises the student on an error-aligned region of its latest failed response. Outcome-aware stage weighting favors early repair stages and credits stages whose immediate retry passes verification. We train AIR-OPD on the DAPO-Math-17K dataset and evaluate on AIME24, AIME25, and HMMT25, alongside out-of-distribution tests on MMLU-Pro and GPQA. We examine two guidance sources, self-guidance from the current student policy and external guidance from a larger model. For both Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B, AIR-OPD attains the best mathematical-reasoning averages, improving over the strongest baseline by up to 3.6 points, while preserving base-model performance on the out-of-distribution benchmarks.

</details>


### [335] [Conditional Capacity and Routing in Mixture-of-Experts Particle Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02701)
*Kaushik Pendiyala,Haris Zia,Trevin Lee,Timothy Legge,Alejandro J. De Leon,Zihan Zhao,Aaron Wang,Abhijith Gandrakota,Jennifer Ngadiuba,Richard Cavanaugh,Javier Duarte*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models in particle physics transformers for jet classification, finding that top-1 MoE models improve accuracy over dense baselines without increased computation, while activating multiple experts yields further gains at higher cost. The study analyzes 188-class JetClass-II dataset with various configurations of expert count, routing capacity, and top-K parameters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models can increase parameter capacity without proportionally increasing active computation, but the trade-off behavior in particle-physics transformers was previously unclear. This work aims to understand how different MoE configurations (expert count, routing capacity, top-K, auxiliary loss) affect classification performance and computational efficiency in jet classification tasks.

Method: The researchers conducted experiments comparing dense and MoE Particle Transformers on the 188-class JetClass-II dataset. They systematically varied expert count, routing capacity, top-K (number of activated experts), and auxiliary loss coefficients. They also performed routing analyses to examine expert assignment patterns related to particle identity and kinematics.

Result: Key findings: (1) Top-1 MoE models improve over dense baseline at nearly unchanged nominal forward compute when token dropping is avoided; (2) Increasing stored experts beyond top-1 yields minimal additional accuracy gain; (3) Activating multiple experts per token provides additional predictive improvements but at higher computational cost; (4) Expert assignments become more strongly associated with particle identity and kinematics in some configurations, but this structure does not monotonically correlate with classification performance.

Conclusion: The study highlights the need to distinguish between stored parameter capacity, active computation, routing capacity, and routing organization when evaluating sparse expert models for jet classification. The results suggest that simple top-1 routing provides a good trade-off between accuracy and computational cost, while the relationship between expert specialization and performance is more complex than initially expected.

Abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models can increase parameter capacity without proportionally increasing active computation, but it is unclear how this trade-off behaves in particle-physics transformers. We study dense and MoE Particle Transformers on 188-class JetClass-II, varying expert count, routing capacity, top-K, and auxiliary loss. We find that, when token dropping is avoided, top-1 MoE models improve over the dense baseline at nearly unchanged nominal forward compute, while further increasing the number of stored experts produces little additional accuracy gain. Activating multiple experts per token yields additional predictive improvements at higher computational cost. Routing analyses show that expert assignments become more strongly associated with particle identity and kinematics in some configurations, but this structure does not increase monotonically with classification performance. These results highlight the need to distinguish stored parameter capacity, active computation, routing capacity, and routing organization when evaluating sparse expert models for jet classification. Code and experiment configurations are available at https://github.com/kpendiyala/MPT.

</details>


### [336] [MuonIO: Principled Norm-Aware Descent for Embedding Tables and Language Model Heads](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02705)
*Linkai Ma,Xinyu Luo,Mengbo Wang,Ananth Grama,Petros Drineas,Brian Bullins*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MuonIO extends the Muon optimizer to handle input (embedding) and output (language model head) layers using a unified 2→∞ / 1→2 operator norm framework, achieving 50% memory reduction and ~46% FLOPs reduction while improving validation perplexity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard Muon optimizer only applies its principled update (based on spectral norm linearization) to hidden linear layers, while using AdamW for input (embedding table) and output (language model head) layers. This inconsistency creates a gap in the theoretical framework and incurs additional memory/compute overhead from maintaining AdamW state for these layers.

Method: The method unifies the treatment of embedding table E ∈ ℝ^(d×V) and language model head L ∈ ℝ^(V×d) by leveraging operator norms suited to their specific input/output geometries: (1) 2→∞ norm for L based on Lipschitz continuity of softmax output geometry, (2) 1→2 norm for E based on one-hot input geometry from Bernstein & Newhouse (2025). The key insight is the identity ||L||_(2→∞) = ||L^T||_(1→2), which enables a single normalized-vector rule appearing as column normalization for E and row normalization for L.

Result: Empirical evaluation on 1B LLaMA pretraining on C4 shows: (1) 50% reduction in I/O optimizer state memory, (2) ~46% reduction in I/O update FLOPs, (3) improved validation perplexity compared to standard Muon.

Conclusion: MuonIO provides a principled, unified optimizer update for all linear layers in neural networks, eliminating the need for AdamW on embedding/output layers while reducing memory/compute costs and improving downstream performance.

Abstract: The Muon optimizer derives its update rule for hidden linear layers by solving a local linearization of the loss penalized by the spectral norm, motivated by an RMS-stability argument for dense linear layers. Standard Muon implementations, however, exclude the input (embedding table) and output (language model head) layers from this principled treatment, for which they use AdamW instead. We present MuonIO, a single Muon-style update for both of these layers. For the language model head $\mathbf{L} \in \mathbb{R}^{V \times d}$, we motivate the use of the $2\to\infty$ operator norm, due to the Lipschitz continuity of the softmax output geometry, while for the embedding table $\mathbf{E} \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times V}$, we draw on the $1 \to 2$ operator norm, based on the one-hot input geometry identified by Bernstein & Newhouse (2025). The identity $\lVert\mathbf{L}\rVert_{2\to\infty}=\lVert\mathbf{L}^\top\rVert_{1\to2}$ then puts both matrices in the same vocabulary-oriented geometry: MuonIO applies a single normalized-vector rule, which appears as column normalization for $\mathbf{E}$ and row normalization for $\mathbf{L}$. Empirical evaluations demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, with MuonIO reducing I/O optimizer state memory by 50% and I/O update FLOPs by $\sim$46% compared to Muon for 1B LLaMA pretraining on C4, while also improving validation perplexity.

</details>


### [337] [Differential Privacy of Gradient Descent on Perturbed Objectives](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02716)
*Austin Watkins,Raman Arora*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper studies differential privacy via objective perturbation, analyzing the finite N-th iterate of gradient descent on a perturbed objective. The key contribution is proving that the map from noise z to the N-th iterate is a C¹-diffeomorphism under strong convexity and smoothness conditions, enabling direct change-of-variables analysis for privacy accounting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to understand and improve the privacy guarantees of objective perturbation methods in differential privacy, specifically moving beyond exact minimizer analysis to finite-iteration settings where gradient descent is used in practice.

Method: The method involves: (1) adding a random linear term ⟨z, w⟩ to the regularized empirical risk before optimization, where z ~ N(0, σ²I_d); (2) analyzing the N-th iterate of deterministic gradient descent; (3) proving the map z → w_N is a C¹-diffeomorphism with quantitative lower bound on Jacobian's smallest singular value; (4) applying change-of-variables analysis for privacy proof.

Result: Key results include: (1) explicit condition for diffeomorphism property on bounded domains; (2) privacy-profile bound for GLMs without explicit ambient-dimension factor once iteration condition holds; (3) geometrically decreasing finite-iteration correction; (4) expected excess empirical risk bounded by dσ²/(2μ) plus geometric optimization term; (5) transfer to population risk without additional condition-number factor in leading terms.

Conclusion: The paper successfully extends objective perturbation analysis from exact minimizers to finite gradient descent iterates, providing strong privacy guarantees with better dimensional dependence and showing the approach recovers exact-minimizer certificates in the limit.

Abstract: Objective perturbation adds a random linear term to a regularized empirical risk and releases the exact perturbed minimizer. We study the finite computation obtained by releasing the $N$-th iterate of deterministic gradient descent on $w\mapsto F(w;S)+\langle z,w\rangle$, where $z\sim\mathcal N(0,σ^2I_d)$ is drawn once before optimization. For strongly convex and smooth objectives with Lipschitz Hessian, we prove an explicit condition under which the map $z\mapsto w_N$ is a $C^1$-diffeomorphism on the bounded domains used in the privacy argument, with a quantitative lower bound on the smallest singular value of its Jacobian. This permits a direct change-of-variables analysis of the finite iterate. For generalized linear models, the resulting privacy-profile bound has no explicit ambient-dimension factor once the iteration condition holds, and its finite-iteration correction decreases geometrically. By letting the free truncation parameter grow slowly with $N$, we recover the corresponding exact-minimizer certificate in the limit. We also bound the expected excess empirical risk by $dσ^2/(2μ)$ plus a geometrically decreasing optimization term, and transfer the result to population risk without an additional multiplicative condition-number factor in the leading statistical terms.

</details>


### [338] [Structural-Functional Brain Connectivity Generation via Multimodal Hypergraph-based Flow Matching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02722)
*Chyong Yi Poh,Hwa Hui Tew,Junn Yong Loo,Raphaël C. -W. Phan,Fuad Noman,Pew-Thian Yap,Chee-Ming Ting*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MHG-FM is a novel framework that uses hypergraph representations and flow matching for joint generation and cross-modal translation between structural connectivity (SC) and functional connectivity (FC) brain networks, outperforming state-of-the-art methods while being 8x faster than diffusion-based approaches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing approaches for generating SC-FC data use pairwise graphs that capture only dyadic interactions and generate SC and FC independently, limiting the preservation of higher-order structure-function relationships. There is also a scarcity of large-scale paired SC-FC data.

Method: MHG-FM constructs modality-specific hypergraphs, learns higher-order representations with Hypergraph Neural Network (HGNN) encoders, and performs bidirectional cross-modal fusion using Dual Cross-Attention (DCA). A variational autoencoder maps fused representations to a compact latent space, where conditional flow matching enables connectivity synthesis and multimodal translation via latent transport.

Result: Experiments on the HCP-YA dataset show that MHG-FM outperforms several state-of-the-art baselines in reconstruction quality, topology preservation, distributional similarity, and SC-FC coupling, while achieving approximately 8x faster sampling than a matched diffusion backbone.

Conclusion: The proposed MHG-FM framework successfully enables joint SC-FC generation and cross-modal translation by leveraging higher-order hypergraph representations and efficient flow matching, providing a promising solution for addressing the scarcity of paired SC-FC neuroimaging data.

Abstract: Structural connectivity (SC) and functional connectivity (FC) provide complementary information on interactions between brain regions and are widely used in neuroimaging studies of neuropsychiatric disorders. Generative modelling can alleviate the scarcity of large-scale paired SC-FC data, but existing approaches typically use pairwise graphs that capture only dyadic interactions and often generate SC and FC independently, limiting preservation of higher-order structure-function relationships. We propose a Multimodal Hypergraph Flow Matching (MHG-FM) framework for joint SC-FC connectivity generation and cross-modal translation. MHG-FM constructs modality-specific hypergraphs, learns higher-order representations with Hypergraph Neural Network (HGNN) encoders, and performs bidirectional cross-modal fusion using Dual Cross-Attention (DCA). A variational autoencoder maps the fused representations to a compact latent space, where conditional flow matching enables connectivity synthesis and multimodal translation via latent transport. Experiments on the Human Connectome Project Young Adult (HCP-YA) dataset show that MHG-FM outperforms several state-of-the-art baselines in reconstruction quality, topology preservation, distributional similarity, and SC-FC coupling, while achieving approximately 8x faster sampling than a matched diffusion backbone.

</details>


### [339] [Bellman Error Minimization Via Linear Programming Normalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02730)
*Haining Yu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A new functional approximation approach combining deep neural networks and linear programming to reduce Bellman error in high-dimensional dynamic programming and Reinforcement Learning problems, illustrated through network capacity control in revenue management.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: High-dimensional dynamic programming and Reinforcement Learning problems suffer from Bellman error, which needs to be reduced for better solution quality.

Method: Combine deep neural networks with linear programming approximation algorithms to derive approximate solutions to dynamic programming problems.

Result: The proposed approximation algorithms achieve competitive performance compared with benchmark methods.

Conclusion: The combination of deep neural networks and linear programming approximation algorithms provides an effective approach for solving high-dimensional dynamic programming problems.

Abstract: This paper proposes a new functional approximation approach to reduce Bellman error in high-dimensional dynamic programming and Reinforcement Learning problems. Using a classic dynamic programming problem (network capacity control in revenue management) as the motivational example, the paper illustrates that deep neural networks and linear programming approximation algorithms can be combined to derive approximate solutions to dynamic programming problems. Simulation results show the proposed approximation algorithms achieves competitive performance when compared with benchmark.

</details>


### [340] [Inner Momentum for Differentially Private Muon](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02738)
*Bishnu Bhusal,Minh Vu,Ben Southworth,Geigh Zollicoffer,Rohit Chadha,Manish Bhattarai*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses clipping-induced distortion in differentially private Muon optimizer by averaging gradients over current and recent models before clipping. The method bounds distortion via covariance residual and uses Newton-Schulz iteration to preserve polar factors, achieving consistent improvements in BLEU and ROUGE-L metrics across multiple epsilon values.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Differentially private training clips per-example gradients radially before adding noise, but unequal clipping factors can distort the relative singular-vector geometry of their average. This is particularly problematic for Muon optimizer since its update depends only on singular vectors that clipping can shift, making it especially vulnerable to this geometric distortion.

Method: The proposed DP-Muon-IM method averages each sampled example's Muon gradient over the current model and a short history of recent models before clipping. This approach separates the clipped batch matrix into a common rescaling and a covariance residual R, with ||R||_F <= sigma_lambda sigma_G providing a bound on clipping-induced distortion. Additionally, a finite Newton-Schulz iteration is used to preserve the polar factor under spectral conditions.

Result: Empirically, DP-Muon-IM improves BLEU and ROUGE-L scores over DP-Muon in every seed-matched comparison on E2E and DART datasets at epsilon values of 1, 2, 4, and 8. Non-private diagnostics show 2-4% lower pre-noise polar error, confirming the correction reduces clipping-induced distortion while surviving orthogonalization.

Conclusion: DP-Muon-IM consistently improves over DP-Muon across all epsilon values tested (1, 2, 4, 8), achieving better BLEU and ROUGE-L scores on E2E and DART datasets. The method reduces pre-noise polar error by 2-4%, demonstrating that the proposed history-averaging correction successfully mitigates clipping-induced distortion in Muon's singular-vector geometry while preserving the optimizer's properties through orthogonalization.

Abstract: Differentially private training clips each per-example gradient before adding noise. This clipping is radial for each example, yet unequal clipping factors can distort the relative singular-vector geometry of their average. Muon is particularly exposed to this effect, since its update is an approximate polar factor UV^T that depends only on the singular vectors that clipping can shift. To curb this degradation, we propose averaging each sampled example's Muon gradient over the current model and a short history of recent models before clipping. The clipped batch matrix then separates into a common rescaling and a covariance residual R between sampled gradients and clipping values, with ||R||_F <= sigma_lambda sigma_G, bounding the clipping-induced distortion directly. We further show that a finite Newton-Schulz iteration preserves the polar factor of its input under these spectral conditions, confirming that our correction survives orthogonalization. In private GPT-2 fine-tuning on E2E and DART at epsilon in {1, 2, 4, 8}, DP-Muon-IM improves BLEU and ROUGE-L over DP-Muon in every seed-matched comparison, and non-private diagnostics show 2-4% lower pre-noise polar error.

</details>


### [341] [Prospective Hindsight: Self-Calibrating Reinforcement Learning via Prediction-Reality Gaps](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02740)
*Jiaxin Zhang,Xiangyu Peng,Qinglin Chen,Yu Li,Hiroaki Hayashi,Chien-Sheng Wu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Prospective Hindsight (PH) is a self-calibrating training principle for reinforcement learning that uses the gap between prospective predictions (before feedback) and retrospective evaluation (after feedback) to identify and amplify learning from instances where the agent's self-model is inaccurate. This approach addresses miscalibration in both single-turn (overconfident failures) and multi-turn (underconfident successes) tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current reinforcement learning for long-horizon agents relies solely on retrospective training signals—credit is assigned only after observing environmental consequences. This leaves the agent's belief at action time invisible to the gradient, creating a fundamental limitation in learning and self-calibration. The authors sought a way to make the agent's prospective beliefs visible to the training process.

Method: PH introduces a surprise-weighted advantage that amplifies gradient contributions for samples where the agent's self-model is most inaccurate. This is computed as the gap between the agent's prospective prediction (before feedback) and retrospective evaluation (after feedback). Since the prospective predictor shares parameters with the policy, they co-evolve, progressively shifting focus to the agent's remaining blind spots. The method connects to a privileged-information gap framework, where minimizing the surprise residual provides a descent pathway on the agent's miscalibration rate.

Result: PH improves both task performance and calibration across single-turn verifiable tasks and multi-turn personal-agent tasks, using GRPO, on-policy distillation, and their combination. Consistent gains were observed across different model scales. Notably, the same training principle successfully addresses both overconfident failures (in single-turn tasks) and underconfident successes (in multi-turn tasks), indicating a structural shift in the dominant miscalibration mode between regimes.

Conclusion: Calibration emerges as a byproduct of optimization rather than from an added objective. PH provides a self-calibrating training principle that works across different task regimes and model scales, addressing both overconfidence and underconfidence through the same unified mechanism of prospective-retrospective gap minimization.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning for long-horizon agents relies on purely retrospective training signals: credit is assigned only after observing environmental consequences, leaving the agent's belief at action time invisible to the gradient. We introduce Prospective Hindsight (PH), a self-calibrating training principle that augments any retrospective base method with a signal derived from the gap between the agent's prospective prediction (before feedback) and the retrospective evaluation (after feedback). This per-rollout surprise identifies samples where the agent's self-model is most inaccurate and amplifies their gradient contribution through a stop-gradient surprise-weighted advantage. Since the prospective predictor shares parameters with the policy, the two co-evolve, progressively shifting focus to the agent's remaining blind spots. We connect this principle to a privileged-information gap and show that minimizing the surprise residual provides a descent pathway on the agent's miscalibration rate; calibration thus emerges as a byproduct of optimization rather than from an added objective. On single-turn verifiable tasks and a multi-turn personal-agent task (under GRPO, on-policy distillation, and their combination), PH improves both task performance and calibration, with consistent gains across model scales. Notably, the dominant miscalibration mode shifts structurally between regimes, overconfident failures in single-turn, underconfident successes in multi-turn, yet the same training principle addresses both successfully.

</details>


### [342] [Jumping up and down: Denoiser diffusion models for discrete ordinal data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02754)
*Yair Shenfeld,Ricardo Baptista,Stefano Peluchetti*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: JUD is a denoiser-based diffusion model for discrete ordinal data, being the first in its family to support bi-directional (up and down) perturbations, with competitive results across images, music, and gene counts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Diffusion models are well-developed for continuous data and categorical data, but less so for discrete integer-valued data (ordinal data), which is common in images, music, and gene counts.

Method: JUD trains denoisers to handle discrete ordinal data, enabling bi-directional perturbations of the data with a simple training objective.

Result: Competitive results across different data modalities including images, music, and gene counts.

Conclusion: The simplicity of the training objective combined with bi-directional perturbations makes JUD effective for various discrete ordinal data applications.

Abstract: Diffusion models are highly developed in continuous spaces for image and video domains. Recently, major advances have been made for discrete diffusion models for categorical data, specifically in the language domain. In contrast, diffusion models for discrete integer-valued data are less developed, despite the prevalence of this modality, ranging from images and music to gene counts. We introduce Jumping Up and Down (JUD)---a new family of denoiser-based diffusion models for discrete ordinal data. This is the first family of diffusion models for ordinal data which centers around training denoisers, which at the same time allows for bi-directional (up and down) perturbations of the data. The simplicity of the training objective, combined with the flexibility of bi-directional perturbations, leads us to obtain competitive results across different data modalities.

</details>


### [343] [A Two-Stage Cascade for Near-Real-Time Forest Anomaly Detection from Sentinel-1 SAR Time Series](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02763)
*Pann Thinzar Seint,Subas Chhatkuli,Bryan Atwood*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A two-stage anomaly detection system for near-real-time tropical forest monitoring using Sentinel-1 SAR time series, combining adaptive robust-statistics z-score testing with a learned convolutional autoencoder confirmation gate to overcome cloud-cover limitations and seasonal backscatter variation challenges.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the urgent need for rapid, reliable detection of forest loss for timely intervention against illegal logging, supply chain transparency, land-use governance, and carbon market standards, while overcoming two fundamental challenges: cloud-cover limitations of optical monitoring and seasonal backscatter variation that causes SAR systems to mistake natural moisture changes for forest loss.

Method: Two-stage cascade architecture: (1) adaptive robust-statistics z-score test on co-registered Sentinel-1 VH backscatter using same-season historical baseline; (2) learned confirmation gate based on latent-space structural similarity (SSIM) of a convolutional autoencoder trained on stable-forest patches. Alerts are confirmed only when both stages agree, with confidence scores and Low/Medium/High risk tiers assigned from repeat-occurrence history.

Result: System produces per-alert auditable confidence scores and area-in-hectares estimates directly compatible with Monitoring, Reporting and Verification (MRV) workflows, sustainable forestry management, operational field checks and environmental risk assessments. Demonstrates flexibility for applications including selective logging, agricultural encroachment mapping, and flood mapping.

Conclusion: The proposed two-stage statistics-encoder cascade provides a high-fidelity solution for near-real-time tropical forest disturbance detection, enabling timely interventions and supporting carbon market standards and environmental governance through auditable, actionable alerts.

Abstract: Tropical forest monitoring is essential for global climate stability and biodiversity preservation.
