To address the urgent need for rapid, reliable detection of forest loss which is essential for timely intervention against illegal logging, supply chain transparency, land-use governance and carbon market standards, we introduce a two-stage statistics-encoder cascade for near-real-time anomaly detection using Sentinel-1 time series. Our system is designed to overcome two fundamental challenges in remote sensing: the cloud-cover limitations that restrict optical monitoring and seasonal backscatter variation that causes SAR systems to mistake natural moisture changes for forest loss. The architecture integrates two distinct analytical engines to ensure high-fidelity detection: (1) an adaptive, robust-statistics z-score test on co-registered Sentinel-1 VH backscatter, same-season historical baseline and (2) a learned confirmation gate based on the latent-space structural similarity (SSIM) of a convolutional autoencoder trained on stable-forest patches. A candidate disturbance is confirmed as an alert only when both stages agree, and is assigned a confidence score and a Low/Medium/High risk tier from its repeat-occurrence history. The system produces per-alert auditable confidence scores and area-in-hectares estimates directly compatible with Monitoring, Reporting and Verification (MRV) workflows, sustainable forestry management, operational field checks and environmental risk assessments. Beyond its primary application, the model's flexibility allows for critical environmental applications ranging from selective logging to large-scale agricultural encroachment mapping, flood mapping and so on.

</details>


### [344] [A Controlled Audit of Personal AI Memory for Rating Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02764)
*Shivam Gupta*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper audits whether personal AI systems in structured rating prediction rely on historical item-rating associations or user rating tendencies. Using a permutation-based control method across Coat and MovieLens datasets with 400 user profiles, the study tests Qwen and Phi models, finding that historical associations matter significantly on Coat but not on MovieLens, and that a simple history-only ridge reader outperforms more complex models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors seek to understand the underlying mechanism of personal AI systems in rating prediction - specifically whether these systems leverage historical item-rating associations or primarily rely on user rating tendencies. This distinction is crucial for understanding AI behavior and improving recommendation systems.

Method: The study uses permutation-based auditing: permuting historical ratings within each user while preserving exact rating distribution, item support, and metadata. This is combined with full history, native memory extraction, and matched numerical readers in a frozen evaluation of 400 held-out user profiles and 6,160 target ratings across Coat and MovieLens datasets. The study tests Qwen-written Mem0 pipeline against Phi models, and includes a history-only ridge reader as a baseline.

Result: On Coat: Qwen Mem0 pipeline increases user-macro MAE by 0.084 for Qwen and 0.149 for Phi (both family-adjusted bootstrap intervals exclude zero). Correct historical assignments help both readers on Coat. MovieLens effects are smaller and inconclusive after adjustment. A history-only ridge reader outperforms Qwen in both domains and Phi on MovieLens, while Coat Phi comparison is unresolved. All 2,800 reader calls (including 150 invalid outputs) are retained under fixed fallback rule.

Conclusion: The contribution is a reproducible diagnostic study demonstrating why extraction, association use, output reliability, and reader choice require separate evaluation. The findings suggest that the importance of historical item-rating associations varies by dataset, and that simple models can outperform complex AI systems in certain contexts.

Abstract: In structured rating prediction, does a personal AI use historical item-rating associations, or mainly the user's rating tendencies? We audit this distinction by permuting historical ratings within each user while preserving the exact rating distribution, item support, and metadata. We combine this control with full history, native memory extraction, and matched numerical readers in a publicly frozen evaluation of 400 held-out user profiles and 6,160 target ratings across Coat and MovieLens. On Coat, the tested Qwen-written Mem0 pipeline increases user-macro mean absolute error relative to full history by 0.084 for Qwen and 0.149 for Phi; both family-adjusted bootstrap intervals exclude zero. Correct historical assignments help both readers on Coat, but the corresponding MovieLens effects are smaller and inconclusive after adjustment. A history-only ridge reader outperforms Qwen in both domains and Phi on MovieLens, while the Coat Phi comparison is unresolved. All 2,800 reader calls, including 150 invalid outputs, are retained under a fixed fallback rule. A separate implementation verifies inputs, metrics, and all ten primary contrasts. The contribution is a reproducible diagnostic study showing why extraction, association use, output reliability, and reader choice require separate evaluation.

</details>


### [345] [Exact Memory-Time Optimization for Prefix-Cached Language Model Serving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02766)
*Shivam Gupta*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces Prefix-Certificate Retention (PCR), an exact optimization framework for language model prefix caching that addresses the problem of overcounting savings when optimizing cached blocks independently. The key insight is that a resident block is only usable when its preceding prefix is also available. PCR reduces to a maximum-weight closure problem solvable via minimum cut, with linear complexity in block lookups and timeout choices.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The core problem is that when caching language model prefix states (trading recomputation against storage time), optimizing each cached block independently leads to overcounted savings. This is because a cached block is only actually usable when the required preceding prefix is also available in cache. Existing approaches fail to capture this dependency structure, leading to suboptimal retention policies.

Method: The authors formulate Prefix-Certificate Retention (PCR) as an exact finite-trace optimization problem for static, grouped, reset-on-access timeouts. Usable-prefix rewards are modeled as nodes with prerequisites (timeout thresholds and preceding hit certificates). This construction reduces to a maximum-weight closure problem solvable by a single minimum cut, with graph size linear in the number of block lookups and timeout choices. A breakpoint theorem extends the construction to all nonnegative timeouts without discretization error. Additionally, a linear-time dynamic program is derived for ordered timeouts with bounds certifying the cost of this restriction.

Result: Validation through exhaustive small-instance checks and chronological replay of 39,632 public Mooncake requests shows: (1) On the fixed grid, ordered timeouts attain the unrestricted training optimum in 118 of 120 trace-grouping-price cases; (2) Heterogeneous retention improves several held-out memory-time tradeoffs; (3) However, finer training optimization does not uniformly improve transfer to different scenarios. The paper provides a tractable optimization model and auditable benchmark for retention policies.

Conclusion: The contribution establishes a tractable optimization framework for prefix caching that correctly accounts for prefix dependencies. The approach reduces to a well-understood minimum cut problem, making it practically solvable. However, the authors explicitly note that experiments measure usable prefix blocks and storage time, not GPU latency—highlighting a gap between the optimization metric and actual inference performance that warrants further investigation.

Abstract: Retaining language-model prefix states trades recomputation against storage time. Optimizing each cached block independently can overcount savings: a resident block is usable only when the required preceding prefix is also available. We introduce Prefix-Certificate Retention (PCR), an exact finite-trace formulation for static, grouped, reset-on-access timeouts. Usable-prefix rewards become nodes whose prerequisites are timeout thresholds and preceding hit certificates. The resulting maximum-weight closure reduces to one minimum cut, with graph size linear in the number of block lookups and timeout choices. A breakpoint theorem extends the construction to all nonnegative timeouts without discretization error. We also derive a linear-time-in-grid-size dynamic program for ordered timeouts and bounds that certify the cost of this restriction. Exhaustive small-instance checks and chronological replay of 39,632 public Mooncake requests validate the formulation. On the fixed grid, ordered timeouts attain the unrestricted training optimum in 118 of 120 trace-grouping-price cases. Heterogeneous retention improves several held-out memory-time tradeoffs, but finer training optimization does not uniformly improve transfer. The contribution is a tractable optimization model and an auditable benchmark for retention policies; the experiments measure usable prefix blocks and storage time, not GPU latency.

</details>


### [346] [No-Free-Graph: Learning When Multimodal Data Should Be Graphified](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02768)
*Zekai Chen,Kai Hu,YuXin Zeng,Xunkai Li,Xun Wu,Yinlin Zhu,Zhengyu Wu,Xu Wang,Rong-Hua Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses a fundamental yet overlooked question in multimodal graph learning: whether adding graph structures is beneficial for a given dataset and task. The authors propose MAG-SCOUT, a framework that predicts the utility of graphification before constructing the complete graph topology, saving computational resources while retaining performance gains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multimodal graph learning research focuses on how to construct and optimize graphs, but assumes graphification is always beneficial. Through empirical studies, the authors discover this assumption is false—graph structures can provide substantial improvements, limited gains, or even negative effects depending on the dataset and task. This motivates a need for a selective approach to graph construction.

Method: MAG-SCOUT collects limited relational evidence, analyzes task-specific contribution potential, and estimates expected utility of graphification along with construction cost to make a build-or-skip decision. The framework operates as a pre-construction assessment, avoiding the need to build complete graphs to evaluate their usefulness.

Result: Extensive experiments across six multimodal datasets, three downstream tasks, and diverse graph constructors demonstrate that MAG-SCOUT effectively identifies when graph structures should be introduced. It saves 33.1% of task-macro graph work while retaining 96.7% of held-out positive-gain mass under the pre-registered floor.

Conclusion: Graph construction should be treated as a selective decision based on expected utility rather than a default preprocessing step. The proposed MAG-SCOUT framework provides a practical solution for determining when graphification is beneficial, offering significant computational savings while preserving performance gains.

Abstract: Multimodal graph learning has recently emerged as an effective paradigm for in corporating inter-entity relationships into multimodal representations. Existing studies have made substantial progress on how to construct and optimize graphs, but rarely consider a more fundamental question: whether additional relational structures should be introduced for a given dataset and task. Through empirical studies across diverse datasets, tasks, and graph constructors, we reveal that graphification is not consistently beneficial: introducing relational structures can provide substantial improvements in some cases, while offering limited or even negative gains. This observation motivates a new perspective that graph construction should be treated as a selective decision based on its expected utility rather than a default preprocessing step. To address this issue, we propose MAG-SCOUT, a pre-construction graph assessment framework that estimates whether introducing graph structures is beneficial before generating the complete topology. MAG-SCOUT collects limited relational evidence, analyzes its potential taskspecific contribution, and estimates the expected utility of graphification together with construction cost to make a build-or-skip decision. Extensive experiments across six multimodal datasets, three downstream tasks, and diverse graph constructors demonstrate that MAG-SCOUT effectively identifies when graph structures should be introduced, saving 33.1% of task-macro graph work while retaining 96.7% of held-out positive-gain mass under the pre-registered floor.

</details>


### [347] [Nearly Optimal Fixed-Confidence Best-Arm Identification with 1-Bit Feedback](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02771)
*Khang Luong,Dinh Thai Son,Hoang Ta,Hung The Tran,Tuan Quang Dam*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses best-arm identification in multi-armed bandits where the learner receives only 1-bit feedback per round (whether the reward falls in a query set) rather than full reward values. The authors develop time-uniform mean estimation primitives using randomized threshold queries with clipping, and embed these into candidate-challenger algorithms. They propose both fixed-clipping and adaptive-clipping approaches, with the latter achieving gap-adaptive sample complexity. A matching information-theoretic lower bound is proven.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The standard multi-armed bandit setting assumes the learner receives the full reward value after each pull. However, in many practical scenarios (e.g., crowdsourcing, expensive measurements, communication constraints), only limited feedback is available. This paper studies the fundamental limits of best-arm identification when constrained to 1-bit feedback per round, where direct empirical mean estimation is impossible without clipping.

Method: The authors develop: (1) A time-uniform 1-bit mean-estimation primitive using randomized threshold queries and a clipped tail-integral identity; (2) Two algorithms - a fixed-clipping algorithm and a phased adaptive-clipping algorithm that adjusts clipping levels to current resolution; (3) Information-theoretic lower bound analysis using mutual information and change-of-measure arguments.

Result: The fixed-clipping algorithm provides simple anytime (ε,δ)-PAC guarantees. The phased adaptive-clipping algorithm achieves gap-adaptive sample complexity that matches the clipping level to the current resolution. The authors prove a K-arm worst-case lower bound showing that the logarithmic penalty from finite-variance 1-bit feedback is intrinsic, matching the leading dependence of the phased algorithm up to lower-order log log factors.

Conclusion: The logarithmic penalty caused by finite-variance 1-bit feedback is intrinsic and unavoidable. The proposed phased adaptive-clipping algorithm achieves near-optimal sample complexity, matching the information-theoretic lower bound up to log log factors. This establishes fundamental limits for best-arm identification under severe feedback constraints.

Abstract: We study fixed-confidence best-arm identification under strict 1-bit feedback constraints. At each round, the learner selects an arm and a query set, and receives only a single bit indicating whether the sampled reward belongs to that set. We consider a distribution-free finite-variance setting with arm-wise localization, where direct empirical mean estimation is no longer available and clipping becomes unavoidable. We first formulate a time-uniform 1-bit mean-estimation primitive based on randomized threshold queries and a clipped tail-integral identity. We then embed this primitive into candidate-challenger best-arm identification algorithms. A fixed-clipping algorithm gives a simple anytime $(ε,δ)$-PAC guarantee, while a phased adaptive-clipping algorithm matches the clipping level to the current resolution and yields a gap-adaptive sample complexity. We also prove a $K$-arm worst-case information-theoretic lower bound showing that the logarithmic penalty caused by finite-variance 1-bit feedback is intrinsic. This bound matches the leading dependence of the phased algorithm up to lower-order $\log\log$ factors.

</details>


### [348] [LatticeSMC: Where to Spend Inference-Time Compute in Chunked Sequence Generators](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02774)
*Xuanchen Wang,Heng Wang,Weidong Cai*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces LatticeSMC, a novel inference-time steering method for long-form diffusion generation (music, motion, video) that operates on a 2D lattice of chunk index and denoising step. It achieves significant improvements in beat alignment (0.234→0.441) and prompt adherence (0.470→0.560) compared to existing methods like best-of-N, while being preferred by human raters in 60-77% of comparisons.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-form generators produce sequences chunk by chunk via iterative denoising, but rewards are defined over the full sequence. Existing inference-time steering methods (best-of-N, Feynman-Kac steering, streaming pruning) operate on only one axis at a time, and are often compared under unmatched compute. This creates a need for a unified, budget-matched approach that can effectively steer generation across both the chunk dimension and the denoising step dimension.

Method: The authors propose LatticeSMC, derived from a Feynman-Kac model on a two-dimensional lattice (chunk index × denoising step). Two key theoretical results enable exact design: (1) For chunk-additive rewards, the two axes induce identical weights, so resampling should occur where lookahead is cheapest; (2) For terminal rewards, any prefix score defines an exact intermediate potential, making prefix-evaluable rewards "twists" with no estimation or extra denoiser calls. LatticeSMC resamples on these potentials at chunk boundaries and, when scoring is free, within chunks, returning either a weighted draw or the best particle.

Result: Under matched compute: (1) On music-to-dance diffusion, beat alignment improved from 0.234 to 0.441 (vs. best-of-N's 0.354); (2) On 40-second text-to-music generation, prompt adherence improved from 0.470 to 0.560 at 32 particles; (3) Held-out quality is preserved; (4) Advantage retained on long-range rewards; (5) Human raters prefer LatticeSMC in 60-77% of pairwise comparisons. Additionally, commitment strength should follow information in current potential, while lookahead value is predicted by within-set predictability of future reward.

Conclusion: LatticeSMC provides an effective budget-matched chunked steering approach for long-form diffusion generation. By jointly optimizing across chunk and denoising step dimensions using a Feynman-Kac framework, it significantly outperforms existing methods like best-of-N in both automated metrics and human evaluations, while maintaining quality on held-out data.

Abstract: Long-form generators for music, motion and video produce sequences chunk by chunk, with each chunk generated by iterative denoising while rewards are defined over the full sequence. Existing inference-time steering methods typically act on one axis at a time: best-of-N at the end, Feynman-Kac steering across denoising steps, or streaming pruning across chunks, and are often compared under unmatched compute or different return rules. We introduce budget-matched chunked steering and propose LatticeSMC, a sampler derived from a Feynman-Kac model on the two-dimensional lattice of chunk index and denoising step. Two telescoping results make its design exact: for chunk-additive rewards, the two axes induce identical weights, so resampling should occur where lookahead is cheapest; for terminal rewards, any prefix score defines an exact intermediate potential, making prefix-evaluable rewards twists with no estimation or extra denoiser calls. LatticeSMC resamples on these potentials at chunk boundaries and, when scoring is free, within chunks, returning either a weighted draw or the best particle. Under matched compute, on music-to-dance diffusion and 40-second text-to-music generation, it raises beat alignment from 0.234 to 0.441 (best-of-N: 0.354) and prompt adherence from 0.470 to 0.560 at 32 particles, while preserving held-out quality. It also retains its advantage on long-range rewards and is preferred by human raters in 60-77 percent of pairwise comparisons. Finally, we show that commitment strength should follow the information in the current potential, while the value of lookahead is predicted by the within-set predictability of future reward.

</details>


### [349] [Controlling Polar Exposure to Delay Memorization in Diffusion Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02780)
*Xuanchen Wang,Heng Wang,Weidong Cai*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses the tradeoff between sample quality and training data memorization in diffusion models. The proposed Quality-Gated De-whitening (QGD) method preserves the generalization window by controlling update geometry, while Copy-Budgeted Selection (CBS) provides checkpoint selection. Experiments show 8.32x expansion of useful interval and 75.9% reduction in copying, with FID improvement from 79.37 to 75.56.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Diffusion models can generate useful samples before copying training data, but fast optimization compresses this generalization window by accelerating sample-specific fitting. The authors investigate this effect through update geometry to understand and mitigate the quality-copying tradeoff.

Method: The paper proposes two complementary techniques: (1) Quality-Gated De-whitening (QGD), which retains fast polar-update prefix and progressively restores fixed-gain momentum, implementing a quality gate, bounded decay envelope, and causal copy feedback; (2) Copy-Budgeted Selection (CBS), which applies simultaneous binomial calibration to frozen checkpoints followed by fresh evaluation. The theoretical analysis uses random-feature analysis to separate three memorization mechanisms: covariance-controlled, curvature-equalized, and amplitude-controlled memorization clocks.

Result: On 2,000-image CIFAR-10 subsets, QGD preserves the polar baseline's quality-arrival time while expanding its useful interval by 8.32x and reducing common-checkpoint copying by 75.9%. With identical calibration and independent quality evaluation, QGD achieves FID 75.56 versus 79.37 for SGD with the same selector. The approach also transfers successfully to flow matching and dance generation.

Conclusion: QGD with CBS provides a practical solution to the quality-copying tradeoff in diffusion models. The method preserves quality-arrival time while expanding the useful interval by 8.32x and reducing copying by 75.9%. The approach transfers successfully to flow matching and dance generation, demonstrating adaptive exposure control as a generalizable technique for improving diffusion model training.

Abstract: Diffusion models can reach useful sample quality before copying training examples, but fast optimization can compress this generalization window by accelerating sample-specific fitting. We investigate this effect through update geometry and propose Quality-Gated De-whitening (QGD), a controller that retains a fast polar-update prefix and progressively restores fixed-gain momentum. Our random-feature analysis separates covariance-controlled, curvature-equalized and amplitude-controlled memorization clocks. Under aligned spectral assumptions, it establishes a finite-exposure condition under which a fixed-gain tail recovers a delay proportional to dataset size. QGD implements this principle with a confirmed quality gate, a bounded decay envelope and causal copy feedback. Immediate switching is the conservative limit; gradual control balances delayed copying against continued quality improvement. We pair QGD with Copy-Budgeted Selection (CBS), which applies simultaneous binomial calibration to a frozen checkpoint family, followed by a fresh evaluation of the released checkpoint. On 2,000-image CIFAR-10 subsets, QGD preserves the polar baseline's quality-arrival time while expanding its useful interval by 8.32x and reducing common-checkpoint copying by 75.9%. With identical calibration and independent quality evaluation, QGD achieves FID 75.56 versus 79.37 for SGD with the same selector. Exposure-matched controls, independent detector audits and transfer to flow matching and dance generation support adaptive exposure control as a practical way to improve the quality-copying tradeoff.

</details>


### [350] [OPD Before RL: Warm-Starting Rubric-Based RL with On-Policy Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02781)
*Xinpeng Wang,Wei Shi,Yu-Chia Chen,Maria Zontak,Yun He,Richard Yuanzhe Pang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A two-stage training framework combining rubric-privileged on-policy distillation (RP-OPD) followed by rubric-based RL to improve language model performance on open-ended tasks where exact outcome verification is impossible.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Rubric-based RL addresses tasks without exact outcome verification by scoring responses against explicit criteria, but the reward signal is delayed and sparse, failing to identify which individual decisions contributed to the final score. This credit assignment problem limits the effectiveness of RL.

Method: Two-stage framework: (1) RP-OPD uses rubrics as privileged teacher context for dense token-level supervision, where a student model matches a rubric-aware teacher's next-token distributions at student-generated prefixes; (2) RL then directly optimizes the rubric reward to improve beyond the distillation plateau.

Result: Across HealthBench, ResearchQA, and RubricHub Science, RP-OPD + RL achieves the highest scores among evaluated methods. The approach shows limited reward hacking compared to SFT + RL baseline, which increasingly receives high rewards for claims of rubric compliance without actual content.

Conclusion: Using rubrics to guide on-policy distillation before applying rubric-based RL is effective and reduces reward hacking, providing a promising approach for training language models on open-ended tasks.

Abstract: Many useful language-model tasks cannot be evaluated by exact outcome verification. Rubric-based reinforcement learning (RL) addresses this issue by scoring open-ended responses against explicit criteria. However, because the reward is assigned after the complete response, the training signal does not directly identify which individual decisions contributed to the final score. We propose a two-stage training framework that uses rubrics first as privileged teacher context for dense token-level supervision, then as rewards for further RL. In the first stage, rubric-privileged on-policy distillation (RP-OPD), a student without access to the rubric matches a rubric-aware teacher's next-token distributions at student-generated prefixes. In the second stage, RL directly optimizes the rubric reward and improves beyond the observed distillation plateau. We evaluate the framework on health and science tasks using open-weight models. Across HealthBench, ResearchQA, and RubricHub Science, we compare post-training methods and vary the amount of SFT or RP-OPD training before RL, finding that our two-stage framework achieves the highest scores among the methods evaluated. RP-OPD + RL shows limited signs of reward hacking on RubricHub Science, whereas the SFT + RL baseline increasingly receives high rewards for claims of rubric compliance without providing the required content. These findings support using rubrics to guide on-policy distillation before applying rubric-based RL.

</details>


### [351] [Efficient Memory Crystallization for Graph Learning under Non-Stationary Distribution Shifts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02795)
*Yue Hou,Ruomei Liu,Yingke Su,Junran Wu,Ke Xu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes EMC, a training-free test-time framework for continual graph adaptation under non-stationary environments. It uses a closed-form solution to distill graph domains into compact memories, modeling inter-domain dependencies through state-evolving memories. The method achieves superior performance while significantly reducing computational overhead (87.4% runtime reduction, 92.4% memory reduction).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deep graph learning models deployed in real-world systems often need to cope with non-stationary environments where the underlying graph distribution drifts continually over time. Current solutions rely on training auxiliary generative modules to synthesize memory graphs for cross-domain adaptation, which incurs substantial computational overhead and scales poorly under prolonged distribution shifts. The authors argue that a more economical path exists: rather than generating memory, one can crystallize it.

Method: The proposed Efficient Memory Crystallization (EMC) is a training-free test-time framework that distills each incoming graph domain into a compact, semantically faithful memory through a closed-form solution to a memory-oriented distribution-matching objective. To preserve both generalizability and adaptability as the model traverses a long sequence of target domains, EMC further models inter-domain dependencies through state-evolving memories.

Result: Extensive experiments demonstrate the superior performance of EMC over state-of-the-art baselines on graphs under non-stationary distribution shifts, while reducing average runtime by 87.4% and GPU memory consumption by 92.4% relative to the recent competitor.

Conclusion: EMC makes continual graph adaptation practical at scale by eliminating the need for training auxiliary generative modules. The theoretically grounded approach provides a tighter generalization error bound than direct adaptation, demonstrating that memory crystallization is a more economical and scalable solution than memory generation for graph domain adaptation in non-stationary environments.

Abstract: Deep graph learning models deployed in real-world systems often need to cope with non-stationary environments, where the underlying graph distribution drifts continually over time. Prevailing solutions rely on training auxiliary generative modules to synthesize memory graphs for cross-domain adaptation, which incurs substantial computational overhead and scales poorly under prolonged distribution shifts. We argue that a more economical path exists: rather than generating memory, one can crystallize it. To this end, we propose Efficient Memory Crystallization (EMC), a training-free test-time framework that distills each incoming graph domain into a compact, semantically faithful memory through a closed-form solution to a memory-oriented distribution-matching objective, thereby eliminating redundant domain information under continual covariate shifts. To preserve both generalizability and adaptability as the model traverses a long sequence of target domains, EMC further models inter-domain dependencies through state-evolving memories and admits a theoretically grounded, tighter generalization error bound than direct adaptation. Extensive experiments demonstrate the superior performance of EMC over state-of-the-art baselines on graphs under non-stationary distribution shifts, while reducing average runtime by 87.4% and GPU memory consumption by 92.4% relative to the recent competitor, making continual graph adaptation practical at scale.

</details>


### [352] [Muon Learns Facts Better: Understanding the Role of Spectral Orthogonalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02798)
*Xuheng Li,Qiwei Di,Yuan Cao,Quanquan Gu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates the mechanism of spectral orthogonalization (used by the Muon optimizer) in feature learning through a tractable factual-recall model. The study compares gradient flow (GF), spectral GF, and Sign GF, showing that spectral GF significantly improves learning dynamics by reducing the learning-time ratio from Õ(√(S/R)) to Õ(1), achieving exponential error decay instead of polynomial, while also revealing that GF and spectral GF are equivariant under orthogonal transformations but Sign GF is not.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The Muon optimizer has shown strong performance in large-scale neural network training, yet the mechanism by which spectral orthogonalization transforms feature learning remains poorly understood. This work seeks to provide a mechanistic understanding of how this transformation reshapes feature-learning dynamics.

Method: The authors use a tractable factual-recall model where facts map each subject-relation pair to an answer, and a linear transformer learns subject-dependent and relation-dependent information. The model is optimized with gradient flow (GF), spectral GF, or Sign GF—continuous-time limits of gradient descent, Muon, and Adam respectively. They characterize feature separation by measuring learning times when subject- and relation-dependent components reach target accuracy.

Result: Three key findings: (1) With S subjects and R relations, GF has a learning-time ratio of Õ(√(S/R)), while spectral GF reduces this to Õ(1); (2) Subject and relation-dependent errors decay as 1/(T log T) under GF but as exp(-poly(T)) under spectral GF; (3) GF and spectral GF are equivariant under orthogonal transformations of token embeddings, whereas Sign GF is not, leading to potentially varying feature separation phases or reversed learning orders.

Conclusion: Spectral orthogonalization can fundamentally reshape feature-learning dynamics by eliminating the feature-separation phase and achieving exponential convergence. The findings provide a mechanistic understanding of why Muon performs well and highlight the importance of optimizer equivariance properties in determining learning behavior.

Abstract: The Muon optimizer applies spectral orthogonalization to matrix-valued updates and has shown strong performance in large-scale neural network training, yet the mechanisms of this transformation in feature learning remain poorly understood. In this work, we investigate this question through a tractable factual-recall model, where a fact maps each subject-relation pair to an answer, and a linear transformer learns the subject- and relation-dependent information required to recover this mapping. The transformer is optimized with gradient flow (GF), spectral GF, or Sign GF, which are continuous-time limits of gradient descent, Muon, and Adam, respectively. Prior studies (Nichani et al., 2025) have shown that when the number of subjects exceeds the number of relations, GF learns relation-dependent information before subject-dependent information, producing a feature-separation phase during training. We characterize this separation with the learning times when the subject- and relation-dependent components of the prediction reach a target accuracy. With $S$ subjects and $R$ relations, GF has a learning-time ratio of $\widetildeΘ(\sqrt{S/R})$, whereas Spectral GF reduces this ratio to $\widetildeΘ(1)$. In addition, for fixed $S$ and $R$, the subject- and relation-dependent errors decay as $1/(T\log T)$ in training time $T$ under GF, but as $\exp(-\mathrm{poly}(T))$ under spectral GF. Finally, we show that GF and spectral GF are equivariant under orthogonal transformations of the token embeddings, whereas Sign GF is not: Different orthonormal embeddings can potentially produce no feature separation, a large feature-separation phase, or even a reversed learning order. These results provide a mechanistic view of how spectral orthogonalization can fundamentally reshape feature-learning dynamics.

</details>


### [353] [Gated Slot Attention-2: Two-Sided Associative Memory Correction in Linear Attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02816)
*Ruijie Li,Shengnan Ding,Weimin Zhang,Derick Tang,Zhanpeng Zeng,Qinsong Zeng,Ming Chen,Jiaxi Hu,Yuxuan Liang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces GSA2 (Gated Slot Attention-2), a linear attention model that combines key-side correction (Gated Oja Rule-2) and value-side correction (Gated Delta Rule-2) through shared latent slots, achieving improved performance over baselines while maintaining linear-time modeling and constant-memory decoding.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Linear attention models face challenges with fixed-size recurrent memory management. Two existing approaches—delta-rule variants for value correction and slot-based architectures for two-stage memory modeling—are complementary but not yet combined. This work aims to unify both directions to improve memory efficiency and accuracy.

Method: The authors introduce Gated Oja Rule for key-side correction, extend it to Gated Oja Rule-2 with decoupled erase/write control, and combine it with Gated Delta Rule-2 for value-side correction via shared latent slots. They also derive a hardware-efficient chunkwise algorithm for parallel training.

Result: GSA2 consistently improves over strong linear-attention baselines across benchmarks while retaining linear-time sequence modeling and constant-memory recurrent decoding.

Conclusion: Combining complementary approaches—delta rules for memory correction and two-stage slot architectures for association—yields superior linear attention models. The proposed GSA2 achieves better performance without sacrificing computational efficiency.

Abstract: Linear attention models have emerged as efficient alternatives to standard attention, but effectively managing their fixed-size recurrent memory remains challenging. To improve memory, recent work has explored two distinct directions: delta-rule variants for precise correction of values associated with keys, and slot-based architectures such as Gated Slot Attention for modeling key and value memories in two stages. We observe that these directions are complementary--the delta rule provides effective memory correction, while the two-stage structure provides a natural way to operate on both sides of an association. Building on this insight, we introduce a new Gated Oja Rule for key-side correction and extend it with decoupled erase and write control to obtain Gated Oja Rule-2. We then introduce Gated Slot Attention-2 (GSA2), which combines Gated Oja Rule-2 for key-side correction with Gated Delta Rule-2 for value-side correction through shared latent slots. We further derive a hardware-efficient chunkwise algorithm for parallel training. Experiments demonstrate that GSA2 consistently improves over strong linear-attention baselines across benchmarks while retaining linear-time sequence modeling and constant-memory recurrent decoding.

</details>


### [354] [Adaptive Spectral-Koopman Dynamics Modeling for Temporal Domain Generalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02822)
*Tengxue Zhang,Yu Ke,Yang Shu,Chenchen Sun,Yisheng An,Chenjuan Guo,Bin Yang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: AdaSpecK is a spectral-Koopman framework for Temporal Domain Generalization that addresses distribution shifts in streaming data through spectral-aware filtering in latent space and adaptive context extraction via target-conditioned attention and learned routing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing TDG methods suffer from two key limitations: (1) overfitting to domain-specific noise in the data space, and (2) excessive complexity and poor interpretability in the parameter space when handling non-stationary historical environments.

Method: The paper proposes two key technical components: (1) Spectral-regularized Koopman dynamics modeling - applies spectral-aware filtering in latent space to extract denoised low-frequency trajectories and learns a Koopman operator for linearized system dynamics; (2) Context-informed heterogeneous pattern extraction - uses a target-conditioned attention module to attend to distinct past windows, creating dynamic target-specific historical summaries, with a learned router that constructs environmental signatures from current evolutionary patterns to adaptively perceive informative past context.

Result: AdaSpecK achieves state-of-the-art performance on eight diverse classification and regression benchmarks.

Conclusion: The proposed spectral-Koopman framework with adaptive context extraction effectively addresses temporal domain generalization by combining denoised dynamics modeling with adaptive historical context selection, balancing noise robustness and interpretability.

Abstract: Temporal Domain Generalization (TDG) has emerged to address real-world streaming data with distribution shifts over time. However, existing methods are either prone to overfitting to domain-specific noise in the data space or become overly complex and less interpretable in the parameter space. To bridge these gaps, we propose \textbf{AdaSpecK}, a spectral-Koopman framework with adaptive context extraction for TDG. To mitigate noise fitting to irregularly sampled domains, we introduce spectral-regularized Koopman dynamics modeling, which applies spectral-aware filtering in the latent space to extract denoised low-frequency trajectories and learn a Koopman operator to model the system dynamics in a linearized space. To model complex historical environments under non-stationarity, we design a context-informed heterogeneous pattern extraction mechanism. Specifically, we employ a target-conditioned attention module to attend to distinct past windows, producing a dynamic, target-specific historical summary. By constructing an environmental signature from the current evolutionary pattern, our model adaptively perceives which aspects of the past context are most informative for future prediction via a learned router. Extensive experiments on eight diverse classification and regression benchmarks demonstrate that AdaSpecK achieves state-of-the-art performance. The code and datasets are available at \href{}{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Ada-Spec-K}.

</details>


### [355] [All Work And No Play Makes Jack a Dull Boy: Understanding and Preventing Catastrophic Strategy Collapse in RLVR](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02835)
*Qiyuan Huang,Tianshi Xu,Meng Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper identifies and solves a "late-stage collapse" problem in RLVR post-training of LLMs where GRPO-style algorithms cause reasoning strategies to become inaccessible, leading to catastrophic performance degradation despite maintaining task accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors observed that GRPO-style algorithms in RLVR can exhibit severe late-stage collapse, which is not benign strategic pruning but a harmful contraction of effective strategy capacity that makes distinct reasoning strategies increasingly inaccessible.

Method: The authors develop a unified theoretical framework combining optimization dynamics and information theory, define strategies through trajectory-level policy-update interactions, and propose Mesh Learning which exposes multiple reasoning strategies and prevents any single strategy from dominating optimization. They also derive the Mirrored Entanglement Index (MEI) as a lightweight online warning signal for collapse.

Result: The authors prove that major RLVR objectives progressively concentrate probability mass onto a single strategy, while sustaining nontrivial task accuracy requires a minimum strategy capacity. This conflict provides a mechanistic explanation for catastrophic collapse. Mesh Learning consistently outperforms strong baselines across AIME26, AIME25, MATH-500, GPQA, and LiveCodeBench, with gains of up to 13.4 pp and 11.5 pp on Qwen and Phi model families, respectively.

Conclusion: Strategy preservation is a key principle for stable RLVR. The proposed Mesh Learning approach successfully prevents collapse and maintains performance by keeping multiple reasoning strategies accessible during post-training.

Abstract: During post-training of large language models (LLMs) with Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR), GRPO-style algorithms can exhibit severe late-stage collapse. Prompt-based probing reveals that this is not benign strategic pruning, but a harmful contraction of effective strategy capacity that makes distinct reasoning strategies increasingly inaccessible. To characterize this phenomenon, we define strategies through trajectory-level policy-update interactions and develop a unified theoretical framework combining optimization dynamics and information theory. We prove that major RLVR objectives progressively concentrate probability mass onto a single strategy, while sustaining nontrivial task accuracy requires a minimum strategy capacity. The conflict between these two results provides a mechanistic explanation for catastrophic collapse. We further derive the {Mirrored Entanglement Index (MEI)} as a lightweight online warning signal. To prevent collapse, we propose \textbf{Mesh Learning}, which exposes multiple reasoning strategies and prevents any single strategy from dominating optimization. Across AIME26, AIME25, MATH-500, GPQA, and LiveCodeBench, Mesh Learning consistently outperforms strong baselines across Qwen and Phi model families, with gains of up to 13.4 pp and 11.5 pp, respectively. These results establish strategy preservation as a key principle for stable RLVR. Code is available at https://github.com/Ayanami-0123/Open-Mesh-Learning.

</details>


### [356] [To Explore The Strange New World Beyond Data Distribution: System Behavior, Causality Tax, and Non-causal Base Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02839)
*Xianzhi Zeng,Jiangneng Li,Gao Cong*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper challenges the assumption that causality is necessary for language models, proposing instead the SBD framework that incorporates "system behavior" (S) as a first-principle Bayesian feature. The authors discover a "Causality Tax" phenomenon where causal approaches become suboptimal due to ignoring system behavior, and demonstrate that their non-causal GSH approach achieves superior performance (7dB+ SNR improvement, 20% better multi-scale fitting).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors argue that despite causality being the foundation of modern neural network architectures, there are persistent mismatches and contradictions with causality that stem from system behavior (extra dominant factors beyond the data space) rather than the data distribution itself. This challenges the fundamental assumption that causality is necessary for language models.

Method: The authors develop a theoretical framework (SBD) incorporating system behavior as an irreducible component of the evidence lower bound (ELBO). They validate their predictions through: (1) implicit measurements, (2) theoretical-bound-guided controls, and (3) Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) evaluations. They construct "Green Shell" (GSH), a non-causal variational family that replaces sequential dependency chains with a divide-and-conquer partition.

Result: NTK spectra analysis in the lazy-training regime shows GSH achieves significantly tighter error bounds than causal approaches, with 7dB+ improvement in signal-to-noise ratio. In later stages of lazy-training, GSH demonstrates superior generalization with up to 20% richer multi-scale fitting capabilities.

Conclusion: The SBD framework establishes system behavior as a complementary theoretical abstraction to causality and distribution fitting, opening new research avenues for designing and optimizing language model base models. The authors demonstrate that non-causal approaches can outperform causal ones when system behavior is properly accounted for.

Abstract: We show that the causality of language models (LMs) may not be necessary nor optimal. This is the case when system behavior (denoted as $S$) is incorporated as a first-principle Bayesian feature. Here, $S$ refers to extra dominant factors beyond the data space, and they involve coupled effects. Despite being the de facto foundation of modern architecture, recent studies indicate persistent mismatches and contradictions with causality. These issues largely stem from system behavior rather than the data distribution. We therefore propose the SBD framework, which incorporates $S$ as an irreducible component of the evidence lower bound (ELBO). SBD theoretically reveals a counter-intuitive Causality Tax phenomenon, where causality emerges as a suboptimal approximation with an additional structural error, due to the obliviousness to $S$. To address the challenge of latent variable analysis, we validate the SBD-predicted impact of $S$ via implicit measurements, theoretical-bound-guided controls, and Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) evaluations. In particular, we construct Green Shell (GSH) to show the possibility of reducing Causality Tax. GSH is a non-causal variational family, and it replaces the sequential dependency chain of $S$ components with a divide-and-conquer partition. NTK spectra in the lazy-training regime confirm that GSH always achieves significantly tighter error bounds than causality, with $7dB+$ improvement in signal-to-noise ratio. In the relatively later stage of lazy-training, GSH further leads to superior generalization (up to $20\%$ richer multi-scale fitting capabilities). Taken together, SBD establishes system behavior as a complementary theoretical abstraction besides causality and distribution fitting, opening new research avenues such as designing and optimizing LM base models.

</details>


### [357] [Understanding Enrichment in Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02846)
*Jinwoo Kim,Shraddha Barke*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper analyzes how enrichment (using hints to generate successful rollouts) affects reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) training, and proposes a novel Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) weight correction mechanism to reduce variance while correcting the bias introduced by enriched rollouts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: When rewards are sparse, RLVR often uses hints or intermediate guidance to generate more successful rollouts. However, this enrichment biases policy-gradient updates unless corrected via importance weights. Existing methods either omit correction or truncate importance weights to avoid high variance, making it unclear what is gained or lost by correcting enriched rollouts.

Method: The authors (1) mathematically analyze the gradient error from omitted or truncated correction, decomposing it into scale, rotation, and variance components; (2) develop a novel Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) weight correction mechanism that tempers exponential variance compounding to additive accumulation under stability and particle-order assumptions; (3) apply the analysis to interpret fine-tuning results of Qwen3-1.7B on OpenMathReasoning.

Result: The analysis shows that omitted or truncated correction implicitly reweights the defined reward, with distinct effects from scale, rotation, and variance components. The SMC mechanism enables practical correction by reducing variance. Application to Qwen3-1.7B establishes a concrete mechanism of how enrichment helps avoid collapse in sparse domains.

Conclusion: The main contribution is understanding how enrichment and correction affect training, rather than claiming superiority of either mode over unenriched RL. The work provides a framework for analyzing the trade-offs between corrected and uncorrected enrichment in sparse reward settings.

Abstract: When rewards are sparse, reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) often uses hints or intermediate guidance to generate more successful rollouts. This enrichment biases policy-gradient updates unless corrected via importance weights, but existing methods omit correction or truncate importance weights in order to avoid the high variance of correction. It thus remains unclear what exactly is gained or lost in RLVR by correcting enriched rollouts. We show, mathematically, that omitted or truncated correction implicitly reweights the defined reward, and we decompose the resulting gradient error into scale, rotation, and variance to explain their distinct effects on learning. To make correction practical, we develop a novel sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) weight correction mechanism that, under stability and particle-order assumptions, tempers the exponential compounding of standard correction variance over the length of a sample to an additive accumulation. We then apply our analysis of enrichment to interpreting the results of a fine-tune of Qwen3-1.7B on a sparse band of OpenMathReasoning, establishing a concrete mechanism of how enrichment, both corrected and uncorrected, helps avoid collapse in sparse domains. Our main contribution is to understand, in general, how enrichment and correction can affect training, as opposed to claiming that either mode of operation is superior to unenriched RL.

</details>


### [358] [Counterfactual Action Evaluation, Observation Bottlenecks, and Representation Geometry in Joint-Embedding Predictive World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02860)
*Arjun Subramanian*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper challenges the assumption that low latent prediction error indicates a world model truly understands action consequences. Using a controlled deformable-physics testbed, the authors show that even when actions change particle motion, 41.5% of visual observations remain identical, and predictor responses to counterfactuals are minimal (0.0051-0.0217). Isotropic perturbations produce 190x larger effects, revealing action-path under-use rather than dead predictors. MSE training reduces latent error but creates spectrally concentrated representations that don't certify physical state understanding.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current practice assumes low latent prediction error proves a world model distinguishes action consequences. This assumption is untested—models might achieve low error through observation invariants, dead predictors, or representations that ignore physical state. The authors seek to audit whether latent error actually measures causal understanding of actions.

Method: The authors introduce an evaluation protocol tracing interventions through: simulator state → raster observations → target embeddings → predictor outputs. They use exact simulator-state forks in a deformable-physics testbed, analyze 579 high-visibility counterfactuals, compare isotropic state perturbations matched to target embedding shifts, and test MSE-only training against VICReg objectives.

Result: Key findings: (1) 41.5% of one-step raster pairs identical despite changed commands; (2) Median predictor-to-target response is 0.0051-0.0217, falling to 0.0027-0.0116 after variance normalization; (3) Isotropic perturbations produce 190x and 53x larger predictor changes; (4) MSE training gives 8.36x lower latent error but in spectrally concentrated spaces; (5) Stiffness remains near chance with full-resolution rasters while privileged parameters decode perfectly.

Conclusion: Low latent prediction error does not certify physical state understanding. The authors recommend auditing physical effect, observation visibility, representation geometry, and action dependence separately. Identifiability under the tested excitation is weak—representations don't capture physical properties despite low error.

Abstract: Low latent prediction error does not establish that a world model distinguishes the consequences of its actions. We introduce an evaluation protocol that traces the same intervention through simulator state, raster observations, target embeddings, and predictor outputs. Exact simulator-state forks in a controlled deformable-physics testbed reveal distinct bottlenecks. Changed commands alter particle motion, yet 41.5% of one-step raster pairs are identical. Observation loss is not the whole explanation: among 579 high-visibility counterfactuals, median predictor-to-target response is 0.0051 and 0.0217 across two seeds, falling to 0.0027 and 0.0116 after variance normalization. An isotropic state perturbation matched to the target counterfactual embedding shift produces 190x and 53x larger predictor changes on the same visible pairs, isolating action-path under-use rather than a dead or globally shrunk predictor. MSE-only training gives 8.36x lower 10-step latent error in matched seeds, but in spectrally concentrated spaces; one VICReg target encoder is also strongly concentrated, so neither error nor rank alone certifies physical state. Finally, stiffness remains near chance even from full-resolution rasters and mechanical state while privileged material parameters decode perfectly, indicating weak identifiability under this excitation rather than encoder discard. These results motivate auditing physical effect, observation visibility, representation geometry, and action dependence separately.

</details>


### [359] [NeuroLens: Learning Latent Embeddings of Neural Semantics from Chronic Recordings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02864)
*Hanrui Lyu,Baiyuan Chen,Tianshu Tan,Matthew R. Whiteway,Maxwell D. Melin,Ji Xia,Linyang He,Bradly C. Stadie,Anne Churchland,Liam Paninski,Yizi Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: NeuroLens is a self-supervised deep learning model based on Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) that learns denoised, semantically informative latent representations from chronic neural recordings, addressing the challenge of distinguishing true representational plasticity from recording instability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The central pursuit in neuroscience is understanding how neural activity represents higher-order cognition and how these representations evolve over time. However, existing analytical tools cannot reliably distinguish representational plasticity from recording instability in chronic neural recordings, which is a major limitation for studying neural dynamics over extended periods.

Method: NeuroLens employs two key components: (1) an adaptive encoder that maps changing neural populations into a common latent space, and (2) a temporal predictor that learns structure supporting prediction of future latent states. By predicting in latent space rather than raw neural activity, the model captures temporally predictable structure while reducing sensitivity to transient, recording-specific variability. The approach is self-supervised, requiring no labeled data.

Result: Across chronic intracortical recordings in both mice and humans, NeuroLens demonstrated: (1) improved decoding of decision-making and semantic task variables, (2) generalization to future sessions after multi-day pretraining, (3) rapid few-shot adaptation to unseen neural populations, and (4) more stable decoding over time compared to state-of-the-art baselines.

Conclusion: NeuroLens establishes a new paradigm for studying how neural representations change during learning and over long timescales. It addresses a critical methodological gap in chronic neural recording analysis by enabling researchers to reliably separate true neural representational changes from artifacts of recording instability.

Abstract: Understanding how neural activity represents higher-order cognition and how these representations evolve over time has long been a central pursuit in neuroscience. However, current analytical tools cannot easily distinguish representational plasticity from recording instability in chronic neural recordings. Here, we introduce NeuroLens (Latent Embeddings of Neural Semantics), a self-supervised model based on the Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) framework that learns denoised, semantically informative latents from chronic neural recordings. An adaptive encoder maps changing neural populations into a common latent space, while a temporal predictor learns structure that supports prediction of future latent states. By predicting in latent space, NeuroLens captures temporally predictable structure and reduces sensitivity to transient, recording-specific variability. Across chronic intracortical data in mice and humans, the learned representations improve decoding of decision-making and semantic task variables. Multi-day pretraining enables generalization to future sessions, rapid few-shot adaptation to unseen neural populations, and more stable decoding over time than state-of-the-art baselines. Together, these results establish NeuroLens as a new paradigm for studying how neural representations change during learning and over long timescales.

</details>


### [360] [On Unlearning for Time-series Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02865)
*Zeyu Shi,Yanhui Luo,Ziming Hong,Chongyang Gao,Kezhen Chen,Shanshan Ye,Lixu Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RDTU is a Residual Diffusion framework for time-series unlearning that addresses the challenge of removing specific observations from trained forecasting models without costly retraining. It uses a neural tangent kernel predictor to obtain base forecasts, quantifies structural support of affected windows, and employs a diffusion model to generate residual corrections that serve as pseudo-labels for lightweight model updates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Time-series forecasting models often need data deletion for privacy, proprietary information protection, or sensor failure corrections. Retraining from scratch is costly. Existing machine unlearning methods fail for time-series due to: (1) gradient-based unlearning instability where deleted observations affect multiple causally connected windows, (2) lack of suitable replacement targets for continuous/context-dependent forecasts in label-guided methods, and (3) highly non-uniform remaining support for deleted temporal patterns.

Method: RDTU operates in three stages: (1) A retained-set neural tangent kernel predictor provides deletion-compatible base forecasts. (2) Global and local structural support for each affected window is quantified using volume contribution of retained-reference data. (3) A diffusion model generates residual corrections that estimate counterfactual forecasts, producing a pseudo-label field that guides lightweight model updates.

Result: Experiments demonstrate that RDTU consistently produces unlearned models that most closely match exact retraining compared to existing approaches.

Conclusion: RDTU provides an effective solution for machine unlearning in time-series forecasting, successfully approximating exact retraining results while avoiding the computational cost of full retraining. The diffusion-based residual correction approach addresses the unique challenges of temporal data dependencies and non-uniform pattern support.

Abstract: Time-series forecasting is widely used in sensitive domains. Models in these settings are often trained on longitudinal user- or entity-level records, which may later require removal because they contain sensitive or proprietary information or have been corrupted by sensor failures. To address such deletion requests without costly retraining, machine unlearning has been widely studied as a practical mechanism for privacy protection and data governance. However, the application of machine unlearning to time series prediction has not yet been well realized; this is mainly due to the following unique challenges: Gradient-based unlearning can be unstable because a deleted observation participates in multiple causally connected forecasting windows, causing parameter updates to propagate beyond the requested interval and degrade retained forecasting utility. Label-guided updating offers a more controlled alternative, but continuous and context-dependent forecasts lack a suitable replacement target, while the exact-retrained output is unavailable during unlearning. Moreover, the remaining support for a deleted temporal pattern is highly non-uniform. Some affected windows retain structurally similar counterparts in the retained data, whereas others become underrepresented or isolated. We present RDTU, a Residual Diffusion framework for time-series unlearning. RDTU first uses a retained-set neural tangent kernel predictor to obtain a deletion-compatible base forecast. Then it quantifies the global and local structural support of each affected window using the volume contribution of the retained-reference data. Then a diffusion model generates a residual correction that estimates the counterfactual forecast, yielding a pseudo-label field that guides a lightweight model update. Experiments show that RDTU consistently produces unlearned models that most closely match exact retraining.

</details>


### [361] [Adaptive Second-Order Solvers for Fast Stochastic Diffusion Sampling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03034)
*Ella Kemperman,Luca Ambrogioni*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a proportional-integral (PI) adaptive step-size control method for diffusion model sampling, using a noise-normalized error estimator that incorporates previous errors for smoother step adaptation. The method can be aggregated into a fixed schedule, and evaluations on image and language datasets show quality improvements over existing schedules like EDM, though the benefit of per-sample adaptivity is problem-dependent.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Diffusion models require numerical solvers with time-discretization, which significantly impacts the tradeoff between sampling cost and quality. The computational difficulty varies along the sampling trajectory and across data distributions, making fixed discretization schedules suboptimal. Existing adaptive methods only respond to current error, lacking historical context for smooth step adaptation.

Method: The authors adapt proportional-integral (PI) step-size control to diffusion models using a diffusion noise-normalized error estimator. Unlike existing adaptive methods that only consider current error, the PI solver incorporates previous error information for smoother step adaptation. They also show that per-sample trajectories exhibit shared structure and can be aggregated into a fixed schedule.

Result: For images: Fixed discretization outperforms EDM schedule with stochastic Heun and EDM-churn samplers at low NFE. PI adaptive solver achieves better FID than most baselines but doesn't beat EDM-churn at low NFE. For language: Outperforms EDM and entropy schedules at low-to-medium NFE in perplexity, but with lower token entropy. Per-sample adaptivity is highly beneficial in 1D toy examples but only marginal for image and language data.

Conclusion: The PI-based adaptive solver and aggregated fixed schedule provide effective approaches for diffusion sampling. The fixed discretization is particularly promising for practical applications. The benefit of per-sample adaptivity is problem-dependent, being highly valuable for simple problems but marginal for complex real-world data like images and language.

Abstract: Diffusion models rely on numerical solvers requiring time-discretization, which has a large influence on the tradeoff between sampling cost and quality. However, the computational difficulty of the reverse process varies along the sampling trajectory and across data distributions, making the choice of discretization important. We adapt proportional-integral (PI) step-size control to diffusion, using our diffusion noise-normalised error estimator. Unlike existing adaptive methods in diffusion that respond only to the current error, the PI solver also incorporates the previous error, yielding smoother step adaptation. We further show that these per-sample trajectories exhibit shared structure and can be aggregated into a fixed schedule that retains much of the benefit of adaptive sampling. We evaluate both approaches on natural-image and language datasets, in terms of quality, measured by FID at a matched number of neural network evaluations (NFE), comparing them with widely used stochastic solvers and schedules. For images, our fixed discretization outperforms the commonly used EDM schedule in terms of sample quality when used with the stochastic Heun sampler, and with the EDM-churn sampler at low NFE. Additionally, our PI adaptive solver obtains better FID than most stochastic and adaptive baselines, although it does not beat the EDM-churn sampler at low NFE. Moreover, we find our solver outperforms both the EDM and the entropy schedule on language diffusion at low-to-medium NFE in terms of perplexity, with the drawback of lower token entropy. Lastly, we find that the benefit of per-sample adaptivity is problem-dependent. It is highly beneficial in 1D toy examples, while only marginal for image and language data, where the average schedule sometimes even outperforms the PI-adaptive solver. Code is available at https://github.com/ellakemperman/adaptive-second-order-diffusion-solvers

</details>


### [362] [DIVINE: Simple Cross-Market Stock Pretraining via Diverse Indicator Reconstruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02866)
*Kuan-Yu Chen,Shu-Cheng Zheng,Yu-Chen Den,Wei-Cheng Liao,Tien-Hao Chang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DIVINE is a cross-market financial pretraining framework that reconstructs 77 technical indicators from raw OHLCV data, achieving state-of-the-art stock ranking performance with a lightweight 0.05M-parameter encoder across six markets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing financial time-series pretraining objectives struggle to simultaneously avoid future-supervision uncertainty and maintain return-prediction alignment. This work aims to address these limitations through a novel supervision design using technical indicators.

Method: DIVINE reconstructs technical indicators (77 targets from 16 standard indicators) computed from observed price-volume history. The method is pretrained jointly on six-equity market datasets and transfers only the learned encoder to downstream stock ranking tasks.

Result: DIVINE achieves the strongest average portfolio performance across all six markets, outperforming pretraining baselines and matching/exceeding larger financial foundation models. The approach is robust and data-efficient with only 0.05M parameters.

Conclusion: Supervision design and cross-market diversity—rather than model scale—are the key drivers of strong, transferable financial representations. Indicator diversity and market diversity provide complementary gains in transfer.

Abstract: Financial time-series pretraining typically learns from masked observations, contrastive relations, or future outcomes---yet existing objectives struggle to simultaneously avoid future-supervision uncertainty and maintain return-prediction alignment. We propose DIVINE (DIVerse INdicator rEconstruction), a simple cross-market pretraining framework that reconstructs technical indicators from raw OHLCV history. Computed from observed price-volume history, technical indicators provide consistently defined supervision across markets while summarizing diverse market dynamics with established relevance to return prediction. Pretrained jointly on six-equity market datasets, DIVINE reconstructs 77 targets derived from 16 standard indicators and transfers only the learned encoder to downstream stock ranking. Across all six markets, DIVINE achieves the strongest average portfolio performance with a lightweight 0.05M-parameter encoder, outperforming pretraining baselines and matching or exceeding substantially larger financial foundation models, while remaining robust and data-efficient. Systematic analyses show that indicator diversity and market diversity provide complementary gains in transfer. Together, these results suggest that supervision design and cross-market diversity---rather than model scale---are the key drivers of strong, transferable financial representations.

</details>


### [363] [WebFovea: When the Model Is Right but the Click Is Wrong -- Reliable Round Trips for Vision-Based Web Agents on Live Websites](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03036)
*Jiangang Han*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: WebFovea is a vision-based web agent that achieved 2nd place (57.0/100) in WebRetriever Challenge 2026 by focusing on hardening the pipeline between the LLM and browser rather than improving the model itself. The key insight is that many failures occur in the four-stage harness (action parsing, execution, reporting, observation) rather than in model reasoning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The WebRetriever Challenge evaluates agents on Protocol III of the WebRetriever benchmark - operating live websites to return verifiable answers using the site's own interface. The authors observed that on real websites, many failures occurred not in the model's reasoning but in the four stages between model decisions and browser execution.

Method: The four-stage pipeline view: (1) parsing model replies into intended actions, (2) executing actions on the page, (3) reporting results back accurately, (4) showing the model the information it needs. The authors hardened each stage and added guardrails to keep the agent within rules and budget. They used the same LLM across all four submissions to isolate harness improvements from model improvements.

Result: Score improved from 31.0 to 57.0 on the hidden test set through harness improvements alone. Key issues fixed: coordinate-space mismatch (clicks placed at 3/4 of intended coordinates), silent failures with native dropdowns, iframes, and text boxes, and chat-template token contamination (4.9% of episodes).

Conclusion: The four-stage pipeline view is model-agnostic and provides a framework for systematically improving web agents. The same approach can be applied with different models. The roadmap includes routing different steps to different specialized models. The work demonstrates that improving the harness can significantly boost performance without changing the underlying LLM.

Abstract: We present WebFovea, a vision-based web agent that placed 2nd in the WebRetriever Challenge 2026 with a final score of 57.0 out of 100. The challenge evaluates agents end to end on Protocol III of the WebRetriever benchmark (arXiv:2607.06118): starting from an entry URL on a live website, the agent must operate the site's own interface and return a verifiable answer. A capable multimodal large language model (LLM) is necessary for this, but not sufficient. The model's decisions reach the browser through the harness, the code between the model and the page. At every step, four things must go right: the model's reply must be parsed into the intended action, the action must take effect on the page, the result must be reported back accurately, and the model must be shown the information it needs. On real websites, many of the failures we observed occurred at one of these four stages rather than in the model's reasoning. A coordinate-space mismatch placed every click at 3/4 of its intended coordinates; actions on native dropdowns, inside iframes, and in text boxes failed silently; and self-generated chat-template tokens contaminated 4.9% of task episodes. WebFovea hardens each stage and surrounds the loop with guardrails that keep the agent within the rules and its budget. The four-stage view does not depend on the model, although some individual fixes do. Because we used the same model in all four submissions, the rise of our official hidden-set score from 31.0 to 57.0 reflects changes to the harness, up to run-to-run variance on live sites. We describe the design, the evidence for each component (including negative results), a failure analysis, the limitations, and a roadmap that includes routing different steps to different models.

</details>


### [364] [Distributionally Robust Survival Models under Subpopulation Shift and Outlier Contamination](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02868)
*Seonghwi Kim,Sung Ho Jo,Minwoo Chae*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a distributionally robust framework for survival analysis that jointly handles latent subpopulation shift and outlier contamination. The method uses an outer minimization-inner maximization formulation with an alternating gradient-based algorithm to improve worst-group performance while maintaining competitive overall performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In heterogeneous populations, standard survival models may perform poorly on certain subpopulations, especially when training data contains outliers. Existing methods fail to address both subpopulation shift and outlier contamination simultaneously, which is critical for reliable clinical predictions.

Method: The proposed framework combines: (1) outer minimization that selects a refined nominal distribution by reducing influence of contaminated samples, and (2) inner maximization that focuses on the most challenging subpopulation. The method preserves non-decomposable survival losses and the risk-set structure of Cox negative partial log-likelihood. An alternating gradient-based algorithm with outer updates derived from KKT conditions is developed.

Result: Experiments on simulated data and two survival benchmarks show the method remains robust under simultaneous subpopulation shift and outlier contamination. It stabilizes training in contaminated settings, substantially improves worst-group performance across both linear and nonlinear survival models, while maintaining competitive or superior overall performance.

Conclusion: The proposed distributionally robust framework effectively addresses both latent subpopulation shift and outlier contamination in survival analysis, providing reliable predictions across diverse subpopulations even with noisy training data.

Abstract: Learning robust survival models under distribution shift is an important but challenging problem in many applications. In heterogeneous populations, a model that performs well on average may still perform poorly on certain subpopulations, and this issue becomes even more severe when the training data are contaminated by outliers. In this paper, we propose a novel distributionally robust framework for survival analysis that jointly addresses latent subpopulation shift and outlier contamination. The proposed method combines an outer minimization that selects a refined nominal distribution by reducing the influence of contaminated samples and an inner maximization that focuses on the most challenging subpopulation. This formulation directly accommodates non-decomposable survival losses while preserving interactions across samples, including the risk-set structure of the Cox negative partial log-likelihood. We develop an alternating gradient-based algorithm with outer updates derived from the KKT conditions of the inner maximization. Experiments on simulated data and two survival benchmarks demonstrate that the proposed method remains robust when subpopulation shift and outlier contamination occur simultaneously. It stabilizes training in contaminated settings and substantially improves worst-group performance across both linear and nonlinear survival models, while maintaining competitive and sometimes superior overall performance.
