</details>


### [365] [Peer Effects in Signed Networks: Separating Influence Through Positive and Negative Ties](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02872)
*Xiaojing Du,Jiuyong Li,Lin Liu,Debo Cheng,Jixue Liu,Thuc Duy Le*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses a methodological gap in network intervention evaluation: existing methods treat all social ties equally, ignoring that positive (supportive) and negative (antagonistic) ties may have opposing effects on treatment outcomes. The authors propose a framework distinguishing effects through positive and negative ties, introduce the SiDE estimator for doubly robust estimation, and demonstrate its performance through semi-synthetic experiments and a reanalysis of school-experiment data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current network intervention methods count treated neighbors without distinguishing between supportive and antagonistic social ties. This can conceal opposing influences - positive ties may promote beneficial outcomes while negative ties may hinder them. The authors aim to develop a framework that properly separates and estimates these distinct causal effects.

Method: The authors define effects through (1) positive ties, (2) negative ties, (3) their interaction, and (4) a sign-composition effect (reallocating treatment between tie types at fixed total). They provide identification formulas for each. They propose SiDE (Signed-exposure Doubly robust Estimator) combining sign-specific outcome models with exposure probabilities from individual treatment assignment. The method establishes double robustness and uses approximate intervals accounting for overlapping neighborhoods.

Result: Under sign-blind assignment (ignoring tie signs), the authors show how ignoring signs mixes the effects of positive and negative tie types. Semi-synthetic experiments on six real signed networks demonstrate accurate effect estimation. The reanalysis of school-experiment data yields a positive estimate of peer effect through spend-time ties on wristband wearing, but all four effect intervals include zero after adjustment for multiple comparisons.

Conclusion: The framework can inform network intervention design by showing when influences through positive and negative tie types reinforce or offset one another. The method provides a principled approach to disentangling competing social influences in signed networks, though the empirical application suggests effect estimates may be imprecise in practice.

Abstract: Evaluating network interventions requires understanding how treatment affects people through their social relationships. Counting treated neighbors without distinguishing supportive and antagonistic ties can conceal opposing influences. We define effects through positive and negative ties, their interaction, and a sign-composition effect of reallocating treatment between the two types at a fixed total, and give their identification formulas. Under sign-blind assignment, we show how ignoring signs mixes the effects of the two tie types. We propose SiDE (Signed-exposure Doubly robust Estimator), which combines sign-specific outcome models with exposure probabilities induced by individual treatment assignment. We establish double robustness of its score and assess approximate intervals that account for overlapping neighborhoods. Semi-synthetic experiments on six real signed networks demonstrate accurate effect estimation and examine the limits of interval coverage. An exploratory reanalysis of published school-experiment data yields a positive estimate of the peer effect through spend-time ties on wristband wearing, but the intervals for all four effects include zero after adjustment for multiple comparisons. This framework can inform network intervention design by showing when influences through the two tie types reinforce or offset one another.

</details>


### [366] [Toward Omni Multimodal Graph Foundation Model: A Topology-Driven Binding Approach](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02881)
*Xunkai Li,Chenxi Wan,Yinlin Zhu,Wang Luo,Hongchao Qin,Rong-Hua Li,Guoren Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GraphBind is a topology-driven multimodal graph foundation model that addresses incomplete node attributes in Multimodal-Attributed Graphs (MAGs) by using graph topology to bind rich modality information into a unified shared space. It organizes self semantics and reliable neighborhood semantics into a global space that integrates structure and semantics, adapting to both discriminative and generative tasks through lightweight interfaces.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world Multimodal-Attributed Graphs often contain incomplete node attributes, limiting the scale and diversity of available pretraining corpora. Additionally, existing multimodal graph foundation models primarily incorporate graph topology as structural context, overlooking its role in guiding multimodal binding and shaping a unified representation space.

Method: GraphBind uses graph topology to organize self semantics and reliable neighborhood semantics into a global shared space that integrates structure and semantics. This space is adapted to discriminative and generative tasks through lightweight interfaces.

Result: GraphBind achieves leading performance on both discriminative and generative tasks against 11 representative baselines, with relative improvements of up to 28.1% over the strongest baseline.

Conclusion: The proposed topology-driven approach demonstrates that graph topology can effectively guide multimodal binding and shape a unified representation space, achieving state-of-the-art performance on various graph-based tasks.

Abstract: Multimodal graph foundation models (MGFMs) seek to learn generalizable representations from large-scale graphs with heterogeneous node modalities. However, real-world Multimodal-Attributed Graphs (MAGs) often contain incomplete node attributes, limiting the scale and diversity of available pretraining corpora. Besides, existing MGFMs primarily incorporate graph topology as structural context, overlooking its role in guiding multimodal binding and shaping a unified representation space. To address these challenges, we propose GraphBind, a topology-driven approach that uses graph topology to bind rich modality information into a unified shared space. GraphBind is motivated by the stability of graph topology, which provides structural references and complementary semantic information for multimodal binding. Concretely, GraphBind uses topology to organize self semantics and reliable neighborhood semantics into a global shared space that integrates structure and semantics, and adapts this space to discriminative and generative tasks through lightweight interfaces. Extensive experiments against 11 representative baselines demonstrate that GraphBind achieves leading performance on both discriminative and generative tasks, with relative improvements of up to 28.1% over the strongest baseline.

</details>


### [367] [DyRA: Dynamic Residual Approximation for Efficient Matrix Multiplication in DNNs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02882)
*Daewon Chae,Hyunwon Chung,Changwoo Lee,Hun-Seok Kim*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DyRA is an input-adaptive method that improves structured matrix multiplication approximation by dynamically correcting residual output errors during inference, rather than only approximating weights. It achieves 1.5x GPU speedup for DINOv3 while reducing accuracy degradation by more than 3x compared to weight-only baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large-scale foundation models incur high inference costs due to dense matrix multiplications. Prior work uses structured forms (e.g., low-rank factorization) to reduce costs, but these approximate weights rather than output activations. Small weight-space errors can be amplified by input activations, leading to large output errors.

Method: DyRA directly optimizes low-rank factors of the output rather than the weights. It dynamically approximates and corrects the output error introduced by structured weight approximations, combining efficient structured computation with input-dependent correction.

Result: DyRA consistently improves the accuracy-efficiency trade-off across vision, speech, and language models compared to structured weight approximations alone. Notably, it achieves a 1.5x end-to-end GPU speedup for DINOv3 while reducing accuracy degradation by more than 3x relative to weight-only baselines.

Conclusion: Directly optimizing output approximations rather than weight approximations is more effective for inference. Input-dependent correction combined with efficient structured computation provides a more faithful approximation of full matrix multiplication under the same computational budget.

Abstract: Large-scale foundation models achieve strong performance across diverse tasks, but their size makes inference costly, largely due to dense matrix multiplications. Prior work reduces this cost by replacing dense weight matrices with efficient structured forms such as low-rank factorizations. However, these methods approximate weights rather than the output activations that determine inference accuracy. Consequently, small weight-space errors can be amplified by input activations, producing large output errors. In this work, we propose DyRA, an input-adaptive method that improves structured matrix multiplication approximation by correcting residual output errors during inference. We show that matrix multiplication can be approximated more effectively by directly optimizing low-rank factors of the output. DyRA builds on this insight by dynamically approximating and correcting the output error introduced by structured weight approximations. This combines efficient structured computation with input-dependent correction, yielding a more faithful approximation of full matrix multiplication under the same computational budget. Across vision, speech, and language models, DyRA consistently improves the accuracy-efficiency trade-off over structured weight approximations alone. Notably, DyRA achieves a 1.5$\times$ end-to-end GPU speedup for DINOv3 while reducing accuracy degradation by more than 3$\times$ relative to weight-only baselines.

</details>


### [368] [What Should World Models Forget? Stratified Retention for Continual Adaptation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03713)
*Nishit Anand,Ramani Duraiswami,Dinesh Manocha*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper argues that standard continual learning frameworks assume stationary prediction targets, but world models have non-stationary targets (the environment changes). Conventional forgetting metrics cannot distinguish between correctly revising outdated knowledge and catastrophic forgetting. The authors propose "differential retention" - a new evaluation metric that tracks invariant regression and revision latency without aggregation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to address a fundamental mismatch between conventional continual learning assumptions and world models. Standard approaches treat any degradation on previously seen data as failure, but world models must update instance-level facts when the environment changes while preserving invariants like physics. Current metrics fail to distinguish correct revision from catastrophic forgetting.

Method: The authors propose a conceptual framework: 1) Stratify retention by invariance timescale - separating invariants (physics, object permanence - never revise) from instance-level facts (should revise when environment changes). 2) Propose "differential retention" metric that reports invariant regression testing across the adaptation stream jointly with revision latency, without aggregation.

Result: The paper establishes theoretical framework showing that: 1) Standard forgetting metrics rank frozen models highest (no change = no forgetting). 2) Existing physical-reasoning benchmarks only evaluate frozen checkpoints. 3) A new evaluation approach is needed that can distinguish correct revision from catastrophic forgetting.

Conclusion: The conclusion proposes differential retention as an alternative to standard forgetting metrics. This metric reports invariant regression testing across the adaptation stream jointly with revision latency, without aggregation, to properly evaluate continual world models.

Abstract: Continual learning treats degradation on previously seen data as evidence of failure, a convention inherited from settings with a stationary prediction target, where a correct label remains correct indefinitely. World models do not satisfy this condition. Their prediction target is the environment, which changes, so knowledge that was accurate when acquired may later become false, and discarding it is required behavior rather than a defect. Non-stationary ground truth is well studied in the concept drift literature and in the temporal factuality of language models, but has not been formulated for world models, which are distinctive in that they also encode knowledge that must never be revised. We argue that continual world models require retention stratified by invariance timescale, separating invariants such as physics and object permanence, which must never be revised, from instance-level facts that should be revised as soon as the environment changes. Standard forgetting metrics cannot distinguish a world model that has correctly revised outdated knowledge from one that has suffered catastrophic forgetting, and consequently rank a frozen model highest, while existing physical-reasoning benchmarks evaluate only frozen checkpoints. We propose differential retention, which reports invariant regression testing across the adaptation stream jointly with revision latency, without aggregation.

</details>


### [369] [When Can We Trust the Matching Principle? Robust Deployment Geometry Under Finite-Sample and Model Uncertainty](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02894)
*Vishal Rajput*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses the problem of when to trust geometry matching in spectral methods. The authors introduce a trust ratio tau = ε/γ (estimation uncertainty divided by spectral separation) to quantify matching confidence. They propose Confidence-Calibrated Matching (CCM), which adapts matching behavior based on tau - being directional when tau is small and isotropic when tau is large. Experiments on UCI HAR embeddings demonstrate that always matching is worse than abstaining in every cell.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The core problem is determining when to match geometry confidently versus when to spread the penalty (abstain). In spectral methods, there's always uncertainty in estimation, and the decision should depend on how separated the spectral components are. The authors want to quantify this trade-off using a principled approach rather than ad-hoc thresholds.

Method: The authors introduce the trust ratio τ = ε/γ where ε is estimation uncertainty and γ is spectral separation. They analyze the oracle-relative drift between estimated and oracle projector matching under a linear-quadratic matching response. Confidence-Calibrated Matching (CCM) is proposed as a policy that uses τ - when τ is small (confident), matching is directional; when τ is large, matching becomes progressively isotropic. The thresholds are derived from calibration rather than theoretical theorems.

Result: Under the linear-quadratic matching response, oracle-relative drift scales as τ² for probes in the chosen top-r deployment subspace. This holds in the Davis-Kahan separation region τ < 1/2. Experiments demonstrate both regimes, including UCI HAR embeddings where always-matching performs worse than abstaining on every cell.

Conclusion: The trust ratio τ provides a principled way to decide between confident matching and abstention. The CCM policy adapts matching behavior based on τ, with practical thresholds from calibration. The key insight is that always matching can be strictly worse than always abstaining in certain domains, highlighting the importance of confidence-aware matching strategies.

Abstract: Match only geometry you can identify; otherwise spread the penalty. We quantify that decision by the trust ratio tau = epsilon / gamma (estimation uncertainty over spectral separation). Under the linear-quadratic Matching response, oracle-relative drift between estimated and oracle projector matching scales as tau^2 for probes in the chosen top-r deployment subspace -- O(tau^2) in the Davis-Kahan separation region tau < 1/2, with practical usefulness depending on constants. Confidence-Calibrated Matching (CCM) turns tau into a policy -- directional when tau is small, progressively isotropic when not -- with thresholds from calibration, not from the theorem (match sits in the separation region; soft is mostly heuristic). Experiments show both regimes, including UCI HAR embeddings where always-match is worse than abstain on every cell.

</details>


### [370] [Tangent Schrödinger Bridge Matching: Learning Stochastic Transport with Mechanistic Sensitivities](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02906)
*Jowaria Khan,Elizabeth Bondi-Kelly*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Tangent-SBM is a machine learning method for learning stochastic transports from endpoint observations and mechanistic sensitivities. It propagates parameter derivatives alongside trajectories and supervises them against supplied targets, enabling accurate prediction of how stochastic systems respond to parameter changes (viscosity, reaction rates, external forces) without costly simulations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Predicting how stochastic systems respond to changes in viscosity, reaction rates, or external forces requires costly simulations, motivating the development of reusable learned models. However, simply matching observed outcome distributions does not ensure accurate intervention responses.

Method: Tangent-SBM propagates parameter derivatives alongside trajectories and supervises them against supplied targets. For average-response targets, it uses two independent rollouts to match the mean without the additional penalty that single-rollout squared error would impose on response variability.

Result: Across Gaussian, stochastic double-well, PDEBench reaction-diffusion, and stochastic Navier-Stokes systems, Tangent-SBM improves sensitivity and finite-change prediction over matched conditional-bridge baselines while maintaining comparable endpoint and distributional accuracy. In calibrated viscosity selection in Navier-Stokes, Tangent-SBM reduces tracking error relative to taking no action on every evaluated task.

Conclusion: The paper establishes conditions under which sensitivity accuracy bounds finite-change prediction error and decision regret. Tangent-SBM successfully enables accurate intervention responses in stochastic systems, not just distributional matching.

Abstract: Predicting how stochastic systems respond to changes in viscosity, reaction rates, or external forces requires costly simulations, motivating reusable learned models. Yet matching observed outcome distributions does not ensure accurate intervention responses. We introduce Tangent Schrödinger Bridge Matching (Tangent-SBM), which learns stochastic transports from endpoint observations and mechanistic sensitivities. It propagates parameter derivatives alongside trajectories and supervises them against supplied targets. For average-response targets, single-rollout squared error also penalizes response variability; our objective uses two independent rollouts to match the mean without this additional penalty. We establish conditions under which sensitivity accuracy bounds finite-change prediction error and decision regret. Across Gaussian, stochastic double-well, PDEBench reaction--diffusion, and stochastic Navier--Stokes systems, Tangent-SBM improves sensitivity and finite-change prediction over matched conditional-bridge baselines while maintaining comparable endpoint and distributional accuracy. Controls examine target correctness, response objectives, and simulator-budget allocation. To test decision usefulness, we evaluate calibrated viscosity selection in Navier--Stokes: Tangent-SBM reduces tracking error relative to taking no action on every evaluated task.

</details>


### [371] [Do ResNets Route? Sparse Interaction Experts in Residual Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02907)
*Liang Yan,Siying Chen,Kaijie Chen,Bo Li,Jinghao Zhang,Mu Miao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper analyzes ResNets by viewing them as set functions over binary residual-branch masks and uses Möbius inversion to decompose their outputs into individual residual corrections and higher-order interactions. The analysis reveals that ResNets implement an implicit "soft routing" mechanism where different inputs rely on different residual interaction experts, even though every block executes for every input.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional view of ResNets assumes each residual block contributes independently and input-independently. This paper questions that assumption and seeks to understand how different residual blocks interact and contribute to the final output for different inputs.

Method: The authors formulate a trained ResNet as a set function over binary residual-branch masks and apply Möbius inversion to decompose its output exactly into individual residual corrections and higher-order interactions. They analyze ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-18 and ResNet-34 exhaustively.

Result: Interaction mass peaks at orders 5 (ResNet-18) and 10 (ResNet-34), not at low orders. Reducing residual scale shifts spectra toward lower orders but changes predictions. Interaction coefficients are concentrated in magnitude but not hard sparse. Prediction-preserving sparsity weakens with depth. Dominant interactions vary across inputs and predicted classes around a shared global core, while overall complexity changes little with sample difficulty.

Conclusion: Dense ResNets implement an implicit form of soft routing: every block is executed, but different inputs rely on different residual interaction experts. Routing can emerge at the level of functional contribution without an explicit router or sparse execution.

Abstract: Residual networks execute every block for every input, yet their functional contributions need not be input independent. We formulate a trained ResNet as a set function over binary residual-branch masks and apply Möbius inversion to decompose its output exactly into individual residual corrections and higher-order interactions. For smooth residual stacks, we show that each fixed $k$-way interaction scales as $\mathcal{O}(λ^k)$ under residual scaling. Exhaustive analysis of ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-18 and ResNet-34 reveals that interaction mass peaks at orders five and ten, respectively, rather than at low orders. Reducing the residual scale shifts both spectra toward lower orders, but also changes model predictions. The interaction coefficients are concentrated in magnitude but not hard sparse, and prediction-preserving sparsity weakens with depth. Crucially, the dominant interactions vary across inputs and predicted classes around a shared global core, while their overall complexity changes little with sample difficulty. These results show that dense ResNets implement an implicit form of soft routing: every block is executed, but different inputs rely on different residual interaction experts. Routing can therefore emerge at the level of functional contribution without an explicit router or sparse execution.

</details>


### [372] [Constraint-Aware Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02909)
*Jinwoo Kim*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses redundancy in program generation with language models: when constrained decoding already filters invalid tokens during inference, why train the model to learn these same constraints? The authors propose a constraint-aware training objective that externalizes program analyses (syntax, scope, typing) rather than teaching them to the model, showing theoretical and empirical benefits in model efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The core motivation is eliminating redundancy between training and inference in constrained decoding. Standard training teaches models to suppress tokens that will later be filtered by program analyses during inference. This duplication is inefficient - if analysis will reject certain tokens anyway, the model shouldn't waste capacity learning this. The authors ask: can we externalize these constraints during training and get more efficient models?

Method: The paper proposes a general constraint-aware training objective that incorporates program analyses directly into the loss function. Instead of teaching the model to suppress invalid tokens, the training objective accounts for the constraint analysis that will be applied at inference time. The authors formalize benefits through three theoretical theorems about model size and data efficiency, then validate through controlled synthetic experiments comparing constraint-aware training to ordinary cross-entropy training at matched parameter counts.

Result: The controlled synthetic experiment demonstrates that constraint-aware training yields lower prediction loss compared to ordinary cross-entropy training at matched parameter count and data. This validates that the theorems survive practical training dynamics, supporting the hypothesis that externalizing constraints during training leads to more efficient models.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that training objectives should incorporate the analyses used during generation rather than relying on the model to learn them implicitly. Externalizing constraints leads to better performance (lower loss) with the same model size and data, suggesting a paradigm shift in how constrained decoding systems should be trained - separating what the model needs to learn from what the analysis system enforces.

Abstract: When generating programs with language models, constrained decoding can apply program analyses to exclude tokens that violate syntax, scope, or typing rules. However, there is a duplication: standard training already teaches the model to suppress the tokens rejected by these analyses. This duplication leads to the question: if we will perform some analysis to filter a set tokens out during inference anyways, can we avoid teaching the model the said analysis altogether during training, and does this externalization lead to more efficient models? This paper defines a general constraint-aware objective satisfying this externalization desideratum and formalizes the benefits of externalization into three concrete theorems about model size and data efficiency. We show, through a controlled synthetic experiment, that the theorems survive training dynamics: constraint-aware training yields lower prediction loss at a matched parameter count and data compared to ordinary cross-entropy training, motivating training objectives that incorporate the analyses used during generation.

</details>


### [373] [Probe the Harness: Setup Checks for Stale-Data RL Comparisons in Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02911)
*Taiheng Pan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Summary generation failed


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Motivation analysis unavailable

Method: Method extraction failed

Result: Result analysis unavailable

Conclusion: Conclusion extraction failed

Abstract: Methods for training language models on stale samples are judged by comparisons against importance-corrected baselines. We show that details of the experimental harness can reverse the observed ranking of methods, and we introduce PTH (Probe The Harness), a set of checks that makes the harness visible. Our case is a comparison between SAN, a behaviour-free method, and truncated importance sampling (TIS) on verl and in a single-GPU trainer, in which SAN first finished ahead in both stacks. Four details of the harness changed this comparison: the PPO ratio was taken against the learner's own recomputed probabilities, the data seed did not reach the TIS arm, the replay queue reused its first batch for 33 updates, and two loss normalisers differed from their description. In each case the logged quantity looked consistent with a working setup, while the quantity that defines the comparison went unchecked. With the harness checked, TIS matches SAN on verl, and in the trainer TIS learns steadily while SAN keeps a margin. We contribute the signature of each detail and its effect on the comparison, reference results for TIS and uncorrected GRPO under sampler lag, and the PTH checklist.

</details>


### [374] [Dynamic Expert Pruning for Multi-Agent Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02951)
*Jabin Koo,Soheil Abbasloo,Sungjae Lee,Jungseul Ok*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Dynamic Expert Pruning (DEP) uses system and task prompts to predict which experts a multi-agent system needs per-request, enabling dynamic sparsity that adapts to heterogeneous workloads instead of using static expert masks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Static expert pruning fails in multi-agent systems where a single backbone serves diverse tasks and roles, as different agents require different experts but current methods apply one fixed mask to all requests.

Method: Train a lightweight predictor on workflow transcripts that generates specialized per-request masks from system and task prompts in a single forward pass, requiring no per-configuration calibration.

Result: DEP achieves better overall accuracy than static pruning and merging baselines across diverse tasks, roles, model scales, and MoE architectures, with largest margins when few experts are retained.

Conclusion: Role specialization in multi-agent systems permits sparser serving than static pruning allows, and DEP generalizes to unseen workflows without retraining.

Abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures scale language models efficiently by activating only a few experts per token, but the saving is confined to computation: every expert must stay resident on the accelerator, so memory bounds where these models can be deployed. Expert pruning reduces this footprint, yet existing methods are static --- a single mask, calibrated offline, is applied to the model for every subsequent request. This assumption can fail when the workload is heterogeneous, most prominently in multi-agent systems, where one backbone serves many tasks and roles at once: our analysis shows that different tasks and roles recruit different experts, while static methods assign one fixed subset to all of them. We therefore propose Dynamic Expert Pruning (DEP), which rests on a finding we establish here: an agent's system and task prompts are by themselves sufficient to identify the experts that agent and its task require, since that text already describes what the agent will do. A lightweight predictor, trained once on workflow transcripts, turns those prompts into a specialized per-request mask in a single forward pass, with no per-configuration calibration. Across diverse tasks and roles, model scales, and MoE architectures, DEP achieves better overall accuracy than static pruning and merging baselines, and generalizes to workflows unseen in training without retraining. Its margin over those baselines is largest when few experts are retained, suggesting that the role specialization inherent to multi-agent systems permits sparser serving than static pruning allows.

</details>


### [375] [SlimKV: Joint Token-Feature KV Cache Compression with Reconstruction-Free Beacon Attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02953)
*Zihan Teng,Jiayu Zhao,Wentao Ren,Minhao Fan,Tianrui Ma,Song Chen,Weichen Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SlimKV addresses the KV-cache memory bottleneck in long-context LLM serving through a question-agnostic joint token-feature compression method that uses low-rank-aware training to compress contexts into beacon memory states with latent KV representations, achieving up to 32x compression while retaining over 96% of model performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-context LLM serving is increasingly bottlenecked by KV-cache memory, especially in resource-constrained scenarios. Existing token-wise methods risk information loss through eviction or condensation, while feature-wise methods require full-dimensional reconstruction for positional embedding application, limiting decoding speedups.

Method: SlimKV uses low-rank-aware training to compress long contexts into beacon memory states with latent KV representations, together with layer-adaptive rank allocation. The method exploits a discovered positional asymmetry: removing key-side RoPE affects beacon and raw tokens differently, with much smaller degradation for beacon tokens. Based on this, beacon KV projections are trained under a K-RoPE-free constraint, enabling latent-space attention during decoding.

Result: On LongBench, SlimKV outperforms baselines at 16x/32x compression and remains leading at 4x/8x, where it retains over 96% of the uncompressed model's score. Needle-in-a-Haystack confirms robustness across evidence positions. Efficiency evaluation shows up to 7.34x attention speedup and 3.38x end-to-end decoding speedup over the uncompressed model at 128K length.

Conclusion: SlimKV presents an effective solution for KV-cache compression in long-context LLM serving, achieving significant compression ratios (up to 32x) while maintaining high model performance (>96% retention) and substantial speedups (7.34x attention, 3.38x end-to-end decoding), with robust performance across different evidence positions.

Abstract: Long-context LLM serving is increasingly bottlenecked by KV-cache memory, especially in resource-constrained scenarios. Among existing KV-cache compression strategies, token-wise methods reduce cached states but risk information loss through eviction or condensation, while feature-wise methods reduce per-token KV dimensions but can require full-dimensional reconstruction to apply positional embedding, limiting decoding speedups. We introduce SlimKV, a question-agnostic joint token-feature KV-cache compression method. SlimKV uses low-rank-aware training to compress long contexts into beacon memory states with latent KV representations, together with layer-adaptive rank allocation. We further uncover a positional asymmetry: removing key-side RoPE affects beacon and raw tokens differently, with much smaller degradation for beacon tokens. Exploiting this asymmetry, SlimKV trains beacon KV projections under a K-RoPE-free constraint and enables latent-space attention during decoding, mitigating reconstruction latency. On LongBench, SlimKV outperforms baselines at 16x/32x compression and remains leading at 4x/8x, where it retains over 96% of the uncompressed model's score. Needle-in-a-Haystack confirms robustness across evidence positions, and efficiency evaluation shows up to 7.34x attention speedup and 3.38x end-to-end decoding speedup over the uncompressed model at 128K length.

</details>


### [376] [Hyperparameter selection for equation learning with biologically-informed neural networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02954)
*William Lavery,Jodie A. Cochrane,John T. Nardini,Sara Hamis*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper presents a diagnostic workflow for hyperparameter selection in Biologically-informed neural networks (BINNs), addressing the critical challenge of choosing network architecture and training parameters when ground-truth equations are unknown.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Hyperparameter selection in BINNs remains a central challenge as hyperparameters are often chosen heuristically and poorly documented, limiting reproducibility and transferability. BINNs are suited for biological systems with nonlinear, partially known governing equations and sparse, noisy, incomplete data.

Method: The authors propose a diagnostic workflow guided by three questions: (1) Are benefits of greater network capacity worth the cost? (2) Do more training epochs keep reducing validation loss? (3) Do learned terms stop changing with increased capacity and training? They test this on synthetic systems of varying complexity (diffusion and growth terms, 1D+t to 2D+t).

Result: Validation loss generally follows the true error in learned terms. The study distills practical rules of thumb for hyperparameter selection in BINN architecture.

Conclusion: This work provides a structured workflow, practical guidelines, and suggested starting values for hyperparameter selection in BINNs, lowering the barrier to BINN-based equation learning and improving reproducibility.

Abstract: Biologically-informed neural networks (BINNs) have emerged as a flexible subclass of physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) for learning terms in partial differential equations from data. BINNs are particularly suited for biological systems, where the governing equations are highly nonlinear and only partially known a priori, and where data observations are often sparse, noisy, and incomplete. However, applying BINNs effectively in practice depends critically on hyperparameter selection, which remains a central challenge in equation-learning frameworks. Hyperparameters are often chosen heuristically and only cursorily documented, which limits the reproducibility of results and the transferability of methods. We present a diagnostic workflow for hyperparameter selection that can be used when the ground-truth equations are not known. The workflow is guided by three main questions: (1) Are the benefits of greater network capacity worth the cost? (2) Do more training epochs keep reducing the validation loss? (3) Do the learned terms stop changing as network capacity and training increase? We apply our workflow to synthetic systems of varying complexity with known ground truth, spanning diffusion and growth right-hand side terms and data ranging from 1D+t to 2D+t. We demonstrate that the validation loss generally follows the true error in the learned terms and distil practical rules of thumb for selecting hyperparameters in the BINN architecture. By providing a structured workflow, practical guidelines, and suggested starting values for hyperparameter selection, this work lowers the barrier to BINN-based equation learning.

</details>


### [377] [Understanding Trajectory Heterogeneity in Federated World Model Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02957)
*Yipan Wei,Zhaokun Yan,Ziming Hong,Jiaqi Wu,Lixu Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper benchmarks federated learning for clinical world models on MIMIC-IV data, examining how temporal context access and client ownership boundaries affect prediction performance across 8 disease cohorts with 40.87 million transitions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: World models require temporal context for training, but federated learning's ownership boundaries restrict the examples each client can construct. This study addresses the cross-time setting where distributed records must be leveraged without compromising data ownership.

Method: The study uses hourly action-conditioned clinical prediction on 8 MIMIC-IV disease cohorts with severity-based client ownership, patient-separated construction, and local history/future-window rules. They evaluated 10 federated algorithms across 32 disease-partition configurations under 5 rounds of 10% participation, with rollout evaluation from 1 to 32 hours.

Result: Three key findings: (1) Only 7.55%-21.36% of pooled-available 32-step windows have locally complete anchors due to ownership and participation restrictions; (2) Finer severity partitions increase FedAvg error in 15/16 comparisons, while FedProx reduces mean error by only 0.56% with no consistent improvement at 32 steps; (3) Algorithm labels hide distinct update behaviors including inactive extrapolation and orders-of-magnitude differences in update scale.

Conclusion: The authors establish four complementary dimensions for evaluating federated clinical world models: temporal access, participation coverage, optimization behavior, and horizon-resolved prediction. They demonstrate that algorithm improvements are small and horizon-dependent, and that standard benchmarks may obscure important differences in update behavior across trajectory partitions.

Abstract: World models learn state evolution from trajectories, making access to temporal context a central training requirement. Federated learning can use distributed records, while ownership boundaries within a trajectory restrict the examples each client can construct. Our study benchmarks this cross-time setting through hourly action-conditioned clinical prediction on eight MIMIC-IV disease cohorts, comprising 40.87 million transition memberships. We specify severity-based client ownership, patient-separated construction, local history and future-window rules, and paired rollout evaluation from one to 32 hours. A matrix of ten federated algorithms covers 32 disease--partition configurations under five rounds of ten-percent participation. Three findings emerge from existing results and training logs. First, client ownership and participation jointly restrict long-window coverage: only 7.55\%--21.36\% of pooled-available 32-step windows have a locally complete anchor visited during training, averaged across diseases. Second, finer severity partitions accompany higher FedAvg error in 15 of 16 paired comparisons, while algorithm gains are small and horizon-dependent: FedProx reduces mean error by 0.56\%, with no consistent improvement at 32 steps. Third, algorithm labels conceal distinct update behavior, including inactive extrapolation and orders-of-magnitude differences in update scale. Cached-update performance also varies strongly across trajectory partitions under the same benchmark protocol. These results establish temporal access, participation coverage, optimization behavior, and horizon-resolved prediction as complementary dimensions for evaluating federated clinical world models.

</details>


### [378] [Dirac-Interconnected Neural Elements: Discovering Modularity in Physical Systems Without Reduction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02960)
*Reiho Li,Razmik Arman Khosrovian,Takaharu Yaguchi,Hiroaki Yoshimura,Takashi Matsubara*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DINEs is a neural network model that represents physical systems as differential-algebraic equations (DAEs) with algebraic constraints given by Dirac structures, enabling simultaneous identification of component interconnections and learning of component characteristics from data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing deep learning methods for dynamical systems don't fully exploit the fact that physical systems are interconnections of components. Some require known interconnection a priori, while others discard algebraic constraints by reducing systems to ODEs, losing important structural information.

Method: The paper proposes Dirac-interconnected neural elements (DINEs), which represent physical systems as DAEs. The algebraic constraints are given by a Dirac structure in kernel representation. This approach simultaneously identifies the interconnection among components as a Dirac structure and learns the characteristics of components as neural networks, keeping subsystems in unreduced form.

Result: Experimental results demonstrate that DINEs can: (1) identify interconnections from data without prior knowledge, (2) keep learned subsystems in unreduced form allowing isolation or composition without retraining, (3) handle partially observable systems. These capabilities are demonstrated on physical systems beyond the reach of existing methods.

Conclusion: DINEs provides a novel framework for data-driven modeling of physical systems that respects the underlying interconnection structure. By representing systems as DAEs with Dirac structure constraints, it enables more interpretable and modular system representation compared to existing black-box neural network approaches.

Abstract: Deep learning has shown remarkable success in the data-driven modeling of dynamical systems. Much of its success is attributed not to the flexibility of neural networks but to inductive biases based on physical prior knowledge, such as energy conservation and symplecticity. However, existing methods do not fully exploit the fact that real-world physical systems are interconnections of components. Some methods require the interconnection to be known a priori, while others assume the system to be reducible to an ordinary differential equation (ODE) and learn only the reduced ODE, discarding the algebraic constraints imposed by the interconnection. Here, we propose Dirac-interconnected neural elements (DINEs), a neural network model that represents a physical system as a differential-algebraic equation (DAE), whose algebraic constraints are given by a Dirac structure in kernel representation. With DINEs, we simultaneously identify from data the interconnection among the components as a Dirac structure and learn the characteristics of the components as neural networks. This allows us to keep the learned subsystems in unreduced form and isolate or compose them to make a new system without retraining. Moreover, DINEs can handle partially observable systems. Experimental results demonstrate these capabilities on physical systems beyond the reach of existing methods.

</details>


### [379] [Differentiable Koopman Operator for Contrastive Learning on Dynamic Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02990)
*Md Abrar Jahin,Taufikur Rahman Fuad,Md Rizwan Parvez*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: KAIROS proposes a self-supervised framework that embeds a differentiable Koopman operator within dynamic graph contrastive learning to linearize temporal evolution in learned embeddings. It uses a dual-view encoder and multi-granularity contrastive objectives, achieving state-of-the-art anomaly detection on 9 dynamic graph benchmarks with up to 23.15 ROC-AUC improvement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world interaction networks are inherently dynamic, but current snapshot-based contrastive methods encode temporal dependencies implicitly in encoder weights without explicit modeling of node representation evolution, making them brittle under distribution shifts.

Method: KAIROS embeds a differentiable Koopman operator within a dynamic graph contrastive learning loop. It uses a dual-view encoder pairing raw node features with a graph-diffused structural view, optimized with multi-granularity contrastive objectives across temporal windows. For anomaly detection, it combines Koopman prediction residual with temporal inconsistency and local neighborhood deviation.

Result: State-of-the-art anomaly detection results on all nine datasets, with gains of up to 23.15 ROC-AUC points over prior work, while remaining competitive for unsupervised node classification.

Conclusion: Explicit dynamics modeling via Koopman operator provides a scalable and effective inductive bias for temporal graph representation learning.

Abstract: Real-world interaction networks are inherently dynamic: edges form and dissolve as node behavior shifts over time. Most snapshot-based contrastive methods encode temporal dependencies implicitly in encoder weights, without an explicit model of how node representations evolve, making them brittle under distribution shifts. We propose KAIROS (Koopman-Aligned Invariant Representations for Open Dynamic Systems), a self-supervised framework that embeds a differentiable Koopman operator within a dynamic graph contrastive learning loop to linearize temporal evolution in the learned embedding space. A dual-view encoder pairs raw node features with a graph-diffused structural view and is optimized with multi-granularity contrastive objectives across temporal windows. For anomaly detection, KAIROS uses the Koopman prediction residual together with temporal inconsistency and local neighborhood deviation to separate irregular behavior from predictable graph evolution. Evaluated on nine dynamic graph benchmarks, KAIROS achieves state-of-the-art anomaly detection results on all nine datasets, with gains of up to 23.15 ROC-AUC points over prior work, while remaining competitive for unsupervised node classification. These results show that explicit dynamics modeling provides a scalable and effective inductive bias for temporal graph representation learning.

</details>


### [380] [Sentry: Learning to Recover from LLM Agent Failures at Test Time](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02994)
*Changxiu Ji,Amy Lu,Qizheng Zhang,Kunle Olukotun*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Sentry is a failure-management layer for LLM agents that conditionally exposes failure knowledge only when matching failures occur, rather than keeping all lessons in the agent's context. This approach outperforms both runtime-intervention baselines (by 37%) and context-evolution baselines (by 39%), with combined approaches yielding further gains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents frequently fail mid-task due to invalid tool calls, repeated actions, or poorly grounded reasoning. The key insight is that how failure knowledge reaches the agent matters as much as what it contains—failure lessons kept in context misfire when their specific failure is absent, and removing them from an evolving playbook improves performance.

Method: Sentry runs alongside the agent as a failure-management layer. It detects failures, retrieves matching lessons from an external playbook to guide recovery, verifies whether the agent recovered (without access to task rewards), and stores new lessons only if recovery succeeded. The full playbook never enters the agent's context.

Result: Sentry outperforms the strongest runtime-intervention baseline on every benchmark (37% average), and the strongest context-evolution baseline by 39% on the two benchmarks where both are evaluated. Combining Sentry with context evolution yields further gains. Learned lessons transfer to held-out tasks. Controlled experiments show that exposing the full playbook to the agent lowers performance even when relevant lessons remain available on demand.

Conclusion: Failure knowledge is conditional knowledge and should be conditionally exposed. Sentry demonstrates that retrieving failure lessons only at runtime when matching failures occur, rather than maintaining all lessons in context, significantly improves agent reliability and generalization.

Abstract: LLM agents often fail mid-task due to invalid tool calls, repeated actions, or poorly grounded reasoning, and learning from these failures is a path to reliability. We find that how failure knowledge reaches the agent matters as much as what it contains. Failure lessons are conditional: kept in the agent's context, they misfire when their failure is absent, and removing them from an evolving playbook improves performance. Runtime interventions, in contrast, act only when a failure occurs but do not learn from their repairs. We argue that failure knowledge is conditional knowledge and should be conditionally exposed, and instantiate this principle in Sentry, a failure-management layer that runs alongside the agent. When Sentry detects a failure, it retrieves matching lessons from an external playbook to guide recovery, verifies without access to task rewards whether the agent recovered, and stores a new lesson only if it did; the full playbook never enters the agent's context. Across multiple agentic benchmarks, Sentry outperforms the strongest runtime-intervention baseline on every benchmark, by 37\% on average, and the strongest context-evolution baseline by 39\% on the two benchmarks where both are evaluated; combining Sentry with context evolution yields further gains. Learned lessons transfer to held-out tasks, and controlled experiments show that exposing the full playbook to the agent lowers performance even when relevant lessons remain available on demand.

</details>


### [381] [Temporal Geometry of Deep Networks: Hyperbolic Representations of Training Dynamics for Intrinsic Explainability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03000)
*Ambarish Moharil*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a geometric and temporal graph-based metalearning framework for obtaining dynamic hyperbolic representations of MLP training dynamics. Instead of analyzing single checkpoints, the method embeds temporal parameter graphs in the Poincaré ball model, capturing the geometric evolution of network weights over time to provide insights into neural network self-organization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Intrinsic explainability of MLPs remains challenging, especially in optimization environments requiring dynamic re-training. Existing measure-based explainability methods only analyze single checkpoints, missing the trajectory information encoded during training. The authors aim to capture how network structure emerges over time under specific training environments.

Method: The approach constructs temporal parameter graphs (snapshots over T training steps) and embeds them in the Poincaré model of hyperbolic geometry. The framework maintains equivariance to within-snapshot neuron permutations and invariance to permutations of past snapshots, preserving functional equivalence while recovering the latent evolving geometry.

Result: Experiments on regression and classification tasks with trained MLPs demonstrate strong meta-network performance accompanied by hyperbolic temporal representations, revealing how network structure emerges over time under specific training environments.

Conclusion: The proposed framework successfully provides insights into neural network self-organization by capturing the geometric evolution of weighted topology over time through hyperbolic embeddings, offering a novel approach to intrinsic explainability that considers both weights and training trajectories.

Abstract: Intrinsic explainability remains a challenging problem, particularly in contexts where multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) require dynamic re-training within an optimization environment. This paper investigates how MLPs and their training dynamics can be represented and studied in non-Euclidean spaces; our representation features the Poincaré model of hyperbolic geometry. We aim to capture the geometric evolution of their weighted topology and self-organization over time. Instead of restricting the analysis to single checkpoints---as per established measure-based explainability methods---we construct temporal \textit{parameter graphs}, i.e., snapshots over time $T$ steps of the optimization/training process for MLPs. This reflects the view that neural networks encode information not only in their weights but also in the trajectory traced during training. Drawing on the idea that many complex networks admit embeddings in hidden metric spaces where distances correspond to connection likelihood, we present a geometric and temporal graph-based metalearning framework for obtaining dynamic hyperbolic representations of the underlying neural parameter graphs. Our model embeds temporal parameter graphs in the Poincaré model ball, and learns from them while maintaining equivariance to within-snapshot neuron permutations and invariance to permutations of past snapshots. In doing so, the approach preserves functional equivalence over time and recovers the latent evolving geometry of the network. Experiments on regression and classification tasks with trained MLPs show strong meta-network performance, accompanied by hyperbolic temporal representations. This reveals how the network structure emerges over time under specific training environments, thus providing insights into the network's self-organization.

</details>


### [382] [Neural Data Needs Semantic Tokenization: Behavioral Events as Boundaries of Session-Transferable Tokens](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03001)
*Sangyoon Bae,Jiook Cha*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes Tokenization with States (TWS), a novel approach for extracellular electrophysiology that uses population activity geometry as tokens instead of individual neurons. By segmenting trials at task events (stimulus/movement onset) and converting population states into tokens, TWS achieves robust cross-session generalization and transfers across species and recording setups.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Neural foundation models embed each neuron and session as tokens, making every new session an unseen input they cannot generalize to. This limits their ability to generalize across sessions, animals, or recording setups.

Method: TWS segments each trial at task events (stimulus onset, movement onset) and converts population states (the portion of the low-dimensional manifold spanned between events) into tokens of population geometry. No neuron or session embeddings are used. The population activity evolves on a low-dimensional manifold that persists across neuronal turnover and across animals once sessions are aligned.

Result: On held-out IBL sessions, TWS decodes movement from regime boundaries lacking target information, while per-neuron foundation models perform at chance. Frozen after training on mice, TWS transfers to macaques and Utah arrays with only a linear probe. For reach direction, it achieves Matthews correlation of 0.23 (vs 0.01 for event time alone).

Conclusion: For cross-session generalization, the token matters more than the model architecture. Population geometry-based tokenization provides robust generalization across sessions, species, and recording devices.

Abstract: Extracellular electrophysiology records a different set of neurons in every session. Neural foundation models embed each neuron and each session into their tokens, so every new session is an input they have never seen, and they fail to generalize to it. A tokenizer for new sessions needs a unit that every session shares and that carries behavior. Population activity offers such a unit. It evolves on a low-dimensional manifold that persists across neuronal turnover and across animals once sessions are aligned. This manifold changes regime at task events such as stimulus onset and movement onset. Within each regime the population occupies a state, the part of the manifold it spans between two events, and each state carries its own behavioral meaning. We propose Tokenization with States (TWS), which segments each trial, one repetition of the task, at these events and converts every state into tokens of population geometry, with no neuron or session embedding. On held-out International Brain Laboratory (IBL) sessions, TWS decodes movement even from regime boundaries that carry no information about the target, while a per-neuron foundation model pretrained on those sessions decodes at chance. Frozen after training on mice alone, TWS transfers to macaques and Utah arrays with only a linear probe. On reach direction, a target that its boundaries do not define, it achieves a Matthews correlation of 0.23, where the event time alone achieves $0.01$. For cross-session generalization, the token matters more than the model on top.

</details>


### [383] [AvoKV-E: Payload-Aware KV Cache Eviction for Long Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03007)
*Han Yu,Wenhui Zhu,Xiwen Chen,Zhipeng Wang,Hejian Sang,Han Shi,Menglin Zhou,Xuanzhao Dong,Minzhou Huang,Rui Cai,Hao Wang,Alborz Geramifard*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: AvoKV-E is a training-free KV-cache eviction policy for long-output reasoning that delays eligibility for recent states and ranks eligible entries using candidate-normalized read pressure, key redundancy, and value-payload potential. It matches or exceeds baseline eviction methods across models and datasets, with largest gains in tightest-cache regimes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing reasoning-cache eviction methods treat cached entries as routing objects, overlooking two critical effects: (1) low-attention entries can carry large value payloads whose removal changes future predictions, and (2) newly generated states can appear stale before later queries have had a chance to read them. The KV-cache bottleneck has shifted from fixed prompts to generated traces in long-output reasoning.

Method: AvoKV-E introduces a training-free eviction policy with two stages: (1) delays eligibility for recent states, and (2) ranks eligible entries using three metrics: candidate-normalized read pressure, key redundancy, and value-payload potential. The approach preserves both keys likely to be read and value payloads that sustain the reasoning trajectory.

Result: AvoKV-E matches or exceeds redundancy-aware, recurrence-based, and thought-adaptive eviction baselines at matched active-KV budgets. Largest gains occur in the tightest-cache regime. Component and counterfactual analyses connect gains to delayed observation, payload-aware scoring, redundancy, and scale-robust normalization.

Conclusion: Long-reasoning KV eviction should preserve not only keys that are likely to be read, but also the value payloads that sustain the reasoning trajectory. The key insight is that value-payload potential matters alongside traditional key-based metrics for effective cache management in long-output reasoning scenarios.

Abstract: Long-output reasoning shifts the KV-cache bottleneck from the fixed prompt to the generated trace. Existing reasoning-cache eviction methods largely treat cached entries as routing objects, estimating whether an old key will still be read, will recur, or can be replaced. This routing-only view overlooks two effects: low-attention entries can carry large value payloads whose removal changes future predictions, and newly generated states can appear stale before later queries have had a chance to read them. We introduce AvoKV-E, a training-free eviction policy that first delays eligibility for recent states and then ranks eligible entries using candidate-normalized read pressure, key redundancy, and value-payload potential. According to empirical evaluation across different models and datasets, AvoKV-E matches or exceeds redundancy-aware, recurrence-based, and thought-adaptive eviction baselines at matched active-KV budgets, with its largest gains in the tightest-cache regime. Component and counterfactual analyses further connect these gains to delayed observation, payload-aware scoring, redundancy, and scale-robust normalization. Together, the results show that long-reasoning KV eviction should preserve not only keys that are likely to be read, but also the value payloads that sustain the reasoning trajectory.

</details>


### [384] [Signal Simplification Is Not Predictive Simplification: Diagnosing Residual Neural Forecasting in Short-Horizon Volatility](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03019)
*Bingqi Lian,Linfeng Cheng,Mei Lu,Jerry Wu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper challenges the common assumption in hybrid statistical-neural pipelines that a successful statistical first stage produces cleaner residual targets for neural networks. Using short-horizon volatility forecasting as the testbed, the authors find that despite HAR models achieving substantial residual simplification (82% variance reduction), residual-only LSTM augmentation actually worsens prediction accuracy. Pure LSTM outperforms the hybrid approach, leading to the concept of "forecaster-preconditioner asymmetry."


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors investigate a fundamental assumption in hybrid statistical-neural modeling: that successful statistical forecasting leaves residuals that are easier for neural networks to learn. This assumption is widely held but rarely tested rigorously. The motivation is to determine whether statistical residual simplification actually translates to improved neural network performance.

Method: The study employs a signal-forecast-system diagnostic framework across five liquid U.S. assets. They compare volatility-aligned HAR-style models against AR, MA, and ARIMA baselines. They analyze pre-standardization fitted residuals and rolling pseudo-out-of-sample HAR errors, measuring variance reduction and lag-1 autocorrelation. They then test residual-only LSTM augmentation against pure LSTM models.

Result: The volatility-aligned HAR model outperforms traditional time series methods. The fitted residual process shows ~82% variance reduction versus the target and near-zero lag-1 autocorrelation. Rolling pseudo-out-of-sample errors show ~74% variance reduction. However, despite this statistical success, residual-only LSTM augmentation increases average MSE from 0.3049 to 0.3594 (deterioration on every asset). Pure LSTM achieves the lowest MSE of 0.2649, while the hybrid requires substantially more runtime.

Conclusion: The authors introduce "forecaster-preconditioner asymmetry" to describe the finding that first-stage forecasting success and statistical residual simplification do not necessarily translate into useful downstream neural preconditioning. The paper cautions against assuming that statistical residual improvement will benefit neural network learning, challenging a common assumption in hybrid modeling.

Abstract: Hybrid statistical-neural pipelines often assume that a successful statistical first stage leaves a cleaner and more learnable residual target. We examine that assumption in short-horizon volatility forecasting through a signal-forecast-system diagnostic framework. Across five liquid U.S. assets, a volatility-aligned HAR-style model outperforms AR, MA, and ARIMA. Within expanding training windows, the pre-standardization fitted residual process used to construct residual-LSTM sequences has about 82% lower variance than the corresponding target and near-zero lag-1 autocorrelation; independently, rolling pseudo-out-of-sample HAR errors show about 74% variance reduction and similarly weak lag-1 dependence. Residual-only LSTM augmentation nevertheless raises mean squared error from 0.3049 to 0.3594 on average, with deterioration on every asset. Pure LSTM records the lowest selected pseudo-out-of-sample MSE, 0.2649, while the residual hybrid requires substantially more end-to-end runtime without improving accuracy. We describe this pattern as forecaster-preconditioner asymmetry: first-stage forecasting success and statistical residual simplification need not translate into useful downstream neural preconditioning.

</details>


### [385] [Tailoring the Quantization Space for 1-Bit KV Cache Compression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03027)
*Minsoo Cheong,Donghyun Son,Sungjoo Yoo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TaSQ introduces a novel vector quantization approach for aggressive KV cache compression in long-context LLM inference, using query-guided channel weighting, cross-head normalization, and covariance-aware channel grouping to overcome the degradation seen in existing VQ methods at extreme compression ratios (1-bit).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The KV cache is a major memory bottleneck in long-context LLM inference, requiring substantial memory capacity and bandwidth. While vector quantization (VQ) offers a promising solution for aggressive KV cache compression, existing VQ methods suffer significant degradation in the 1-bit regime due to the challenge of representing larger groups of channels with limited codebook centroids.

Method: TaSQ tailors the VQ target space through three key techniques: (1) query-guided channel weighting to reflect error sensitivity, (2) cross-head normalization to handle statistical structure, and (3) covariance-aware channel grouping. These transforms are RoPE-compatible and can be merged into projection weights and codebooks, preserving the conventional VQ lookup structure while adding negligible serving overhead.

Result: TaSQ consistently outperforms existing low-bit KV cache VQ baselines across general, long-chain-of-thought reasoning, and long-context retrieval benchmarks while preserving reasoning stability. On a single RTX 6000 Ada GPU, its SGLang implementation supports up to 14× larger batch sizes and achieves 1.87× higher peak throughput compared to the BF16 baseline.

Conclusion: TaSQ successfully addresses the challenge of extreme KV cache compression by intelligently adapting the quantization target space to the error sensitivity and statistical structure of cached activations, enabling significant memory savings and throughput improvements without sacrificing model quality or reasoning capability.

Abstract: The key-value (KV) cache becomes a major memory bottleneck in long-context LLM inference, placing substantial pressure on memory capacity and bandwidth. To mitigate this bottleneck, vector quantization (VQ) has emerged as a promising approach for aggressive KV cache compression. However, existing VQ methods degrade substantially in the 1-bit regime. At such extreme compression, each codebook must represent a larger group of channels with a limited set of centroids, making effective use of its capacity increasingly challenging. To address this, we introduce $\textbf{TaSQ}$, which tailors the VQ target space by combining query-guided channel weighting, cross-head normalization, and covariance-aware channel grouping to better reflect the error sensitivity and statistical structure of cached activations. Since these transforms are RoPE-compatible and can be easily merged into projection weights and codebooks, TaSQ preserves the conventional VQ lookup structure and adds negligible serving overhead. Across general, long-chain-of-thought reasoning, and long-context retrieval benchmarks, TaSQ consistently outperforms existing low-bit KV cache VQ baselines while preserving reasoning stability. On a single RTX 6000 Ada GPU, its SGLang implementation supports up to $14\times$ larger batch sizes and achieves $1.87\times$ higher peak throughput compared to the BF16 baseline.

</details>


### [386] [Balancing Multimodal Learning via Functional Progress](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03035)
*Zhongjing Gu,Fengqiang Wan,Yiming Cui,Yufa Feng,Yang Yang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses modality imbalance in multimodal learning by proposing FGMO, which uses function-space progress signals to assess and coordinate optimization across modalities. The method includes Functional Progress Estimation (FPE) for measuring modality-wise progress and Functional Response Control (FRC) for redistributing optimization budgets through tensor-wise learning-rate adjustment. Theoretical analysis proves the one-step target-contraction property, and experiments validate effectiveness across multiple benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multimodal learning often suffers from modality imbalance, where the joint optimization process is dominated by a single modality. Existing methods estimate modality imbalance from score disparities derived from prediction uncertainty or optimization statistics. However, due to distinct prediction uncertainty and learning dynamics across modalities, direct comparison of such scores may misinterpret intrinsic modality differences as progress gaps, leading to biased imbalance estimation.

Method: The paper proposes Function-Space Guided Multimodal Optimization (FGMO), which leverages a function-space progress signal to assess modality-wise optimization progress and coordinate optimization across modalities. It introduces two key components: (1) Functional Progress Estimation (FPE) to measure each modality's update-induced function-space response and calibrate it against a loss-aligned unimodal reference, producing a comparable progress signal; (2) Functional Response Control (FRC) that redistributes modality-level function-space budgets and realizes target responses through tensor-wise learning-rate adjustment.

Result: The proposed method achieves effective modality imbalance alleviation across multiple multimodal benchmarks.

Conclusion: Theoretical analysis establishes a one-step target-contraction property of FRC under bounded controller-state mismatch, and extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of FGMO.

Abstract: Multimodal learning often suffers from modality imbalance, where the joint optimization process is dominated by a single modality. Existing methods typically estimate modality imbalance from score disparities derived from prediction uncertainty or optimization statistics. However, due to distinct prediction uncertainty and learning dynamics across modalities, direct comparison of such scores may misinterpret intrinsic modality differences as progress gaps, leading to biased imbalance estimation. In this paper, we propose Function-Space Guided Multimodal Optimization (FGMO), which leverages a function-space progress signal to assess modality-wise optimization progress and coordinate optimization across modalities to alleviate modality imbalance. Specifically, we introduce Functional Progress Estimation (FPE) to measure each modality's update-induced function-space response and calibrate it against a loss-aligned unimodal reference, producing a comparable progress signal. Based on this signal, Functional Response Control (FRC) redistributes modality-level function-space budgets and realizes the target responses through tensor-wise learning-rate adjustment. Theoretical analysis establishes a one-step target-contraction property of FRC under bounded controller-state mismatch, and extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of FGMO across multiple multimodal benchmarks.

</details>


### [387] [RIPPLE in Still Water: Zero-Shot Clustering in Federated Learning with Wavelet Scattering Transform](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03054)
*Alessandro Licciardi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RIPPLE is a clustered Federated Learning framework that assigns clients to clusters offline using spectral characterization of local data (variance-weighted PCA prototypes via Wavelet Scattering Transform, decoded by a Gaussian Mixture VAE), enabling per-round communication cost matching FedAvg and allowing absent clients to obtain personalized models via a single forward pass without gradient computation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior clustered FL methods discover cluster structure inside the training loop through gradient similarity, loss evaluation, or EM-style updates, which increases communication overhead, exposes gradients to inversion attacks, and provides no mechanism to assign clients absent from training. This paper aims to address these limitations.

Method: The method uses: (1) Wavelet Scattering Transform to extract variance-weighted principal-component prototypes from each client's local data; (2) Gaussian Mixture VAE trained server-side on synthetic client populations before federation; (3) Cluster assignment computed entirely offline before training begins.

Result: Across five benchmarks spanning controlled and realistic heterogeneity, RIPPLE consistently outperforms all baselines, with margins growing on the most realistic partitions. The gap between RIPPLE's surrogate clustered objective and the oracle is bounded by a computable quantity decaying with client sample size and independent of federation duration; per-cluster convergence matches the minimax-optimal rate for non-convex smooth objectives.

Conclusion: RIPPLE provides an offline cluster assignment mechanism that maintains FedAvg communication efficiency, enables absent client personalization without gradient computation, and achieves superior performance across heterogeneous data settings, with theoretical guarantees on convergence and objective gap.

Abstract: Clustered Federated Learning (FL) partitions a client population into groups of similar local distributions and trains one specialized model per cluster, mitigating client drift that degrades single-model methods under non-IID data. Prior methods discover cluster structure inside the training loop through gradient similarity, loss evaluation, or EM-style updates, thus increasing communication overhead, exposing gradients to inversion attacks, and providing no mechanism to assign clients absent from training. We propose RIPPLE, a clustered FL framework in which cluster assignment is computed entirely offline from a spectral characterization of each client's local data: a variance-weighted principal-component prototype embedded via the Wavelet Scattering Transform and decoded by a Gaussian Mixture VAE trained server-side on synthetic client populations before federation begins. Per-round communication cost matches FedAvg exactly, and a client absent from training obtains a personalized model from a single forward pass, without gradient computation, model evaluation, or extra communication round. We prove that the gap between RIPPLE's surrogate clustered objective and the oracle is bounded by a computable quantity decaying with client sample size and independent of federation duration; per-cluster convergence matches the minimax-optimal rate for non-convex smooth objectives. Across five benchmarks spanning controlled and realistic heterogeneity, RIPPLE consistently outperforms all baselines, with margins growing on the most realistic partitions.

</details>


### [388] [When Does Synthetic Relational Data Teach Models to Use Relations? Tracing Predictive Structure from Pretraining Data to Model Behavior](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03057)
*Shivam Dubey,Mohamed Bouadi,Nassim Bouarour,Varun Kulkarni,Aditya Tanna,Vinay Kumar Sankarapu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates why some synthetic databases produce better relational foundation models than others, identifying that cross-table information predictively necessary for masked-cell pretraining objectives drives the emergence of relational mechanisms. The study traces a measurable property of training data to learned computation and downstream behavior through experiments on four Relational Transformer checkpoints.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The key problem is that downstream benchmarks reveal little about why one synthetic corpus produces a better relational model than another. Strong performance may arise from realistic row-level statistics without the model actually learning relational structure. The researchers framed this as a data-attribution problem: identifying which property of synthetic pretraining data induces relational computation.

Method: The researchers trained four Relational Transformer checkpoints with identical architecture, initialization, objective, and compute budget on corpora produced by four different relational data generators. They then conducted experiments including: foreign-key intervention studies, random-initialization controls, corruption rate analysis, pathway localization, and downstream inference disruption.

Result: RelDiff exhibited the largest predictive gain from foreign-key-linked parents. Its corresponding model was uniquely sensitive to foreign-key interventions on unseen databases. This dependence survived random-initialization control, grew monotonically with the fraction of corrupted links, and localized to a serial cross-table pathway. Disrupting this mechanism during downstream inference removed RelDiff's advantage on relational tasks while leaving structure-insensitive models nearly unchanged.
