Conclusion: The study successfully connected a property of synthetic training data (cross-table information being predictively necessary for masked-cell pretraining) to a learned mechanism (serial cross-table pathway) and through intervention to downstream behavior. This provides a framework for understanding how synthetic data properties influence the emergence of specific computational mechanisms in relational models.

Abstract: Relational foundation models are increasingly pretrained on synthetic databases, yet downstream benchmarks reveal little about why one synthetic corpus produces a better model than another. In particular, strong performance may arise from realistic row-level statistics without the model ever learning to use relational structure. We study this as a data-attribution problem: which property of synthetic pretraining data induces relational computation? Using four Relational Transformer checkpoints trained with the same architecture, initialization, objective, and compute budget on corpora produced by four relational data generators, we trace a measurable property of the data to learned computation and downstream behavior. We hypothesize that relational mechanisms emerge when cross-table information is predictively necessary for the masked-cell pretraining objective. RelDiff exhibits by far the largest predictive gain from foreign-key-linked parents, and its corresponding model is uniquely sensitive to foreign-key interventions on unseen databases. This dependence survives a random-initialization control, grows monotonically with the fraction of corrupted links, and localizes to a serial cross-table pathway. Finally, disrupting the same mechanism during downstream inference removes RelDiff's advantage on relational tasks while leaving structure-insensitive models nearly unchanged. These results connect a property of synthetic training data to a learned mechanism and, through intervention, to downstream behavior.

</details>


### [389] [Learning Transferable Policies from Action-free Time Series Through Dynamical Embeddings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03065)
*Niklas Emonds,Georgia Koppe*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A hierarchical model-based RL framework that learns system-specific control policies from action-free recordings by leveraging shared structure across related systems through low-dimensional embeddings that capture both shared dynamics and individual variations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Learning control from action-free recordings is challenging because intervention effects are unobserved and policies may exploit errors in reconstructed dynamics. This work addresses the problem of learning effective control policies without requiring active interventions.

Method: The framework uses: (1) hierarchical dynamical system reconstruction capturing shared dynamics and individual variation via low-dimensional embeddings; (2) embeddings reused to parameterize shared policy and value networks; (3) training via simulation under explicit intervention model with additive latent perturbations; (4) piecewise-linear recurrent neural networks for mechanistic analysis; (5) decoder-based constraints for interpretable intervention effects in observation space.

Result: Hierarchical policies improve transfer over independently trained policies on Lorenz-63 and double-pendulum systems. On Lorenz-63, they achieve higher mean reward than repeated planning with same reconstructed models, perform comparably to methods trained with controlled interactions, and generalize to systems absent from policy training after embedding inference alone. Neural-behavioral applications demonstrate suppression of predicted movement under constrained neural perturbations.

Conclusion: Shared dynamical representations support transferable control and mechanistic hypothesis generation from action-free recordings, enabling learning control policies without direct intervention.

Abstract: Learning control from action-free recordings is challenging because intervention effects are unobserved and policies may exploit errors in reconstructed dynamics. We present a hierarchical model-based reinforcement learning framework that uses shared structure across related systems to learn system-specific control policies from action-free recordings. A hierarchical dynamical system reconstruction model captures shared dynamics and individual variation through low-dimensional embeddings. These embeddings are then reused to parameterize shared policy and value networks, linking differences in reconstructed dynamics to differences in control. Policies are trained entirely via simulation under an explicit intervention model with additive latent perturbations. Piecewise-linear recurrent neural networks enable mechanistic analyses of the controlled dynamics, while decoder-based constraints make the immediate effects of interventions interpretable in observation space and permit interventions on one modality while protecting another from direct manipulation. On Lorenz-63 and double-pendulum systems, hierarchical policies improve transfer over independently trained policies. On Lorenz-63, they also achieve a higher mean reward than repeated planning with the same reconstructed models, perform comparably to methods trained with controlled interactions, and generalize to systems absent from policy training after embedding inference alone. Applications to neural-behavioral recordings demonstrate suppression of predicted movement under constrained neural perturbations. Together, these findings show how shared dynamical representations support transferable control and mechanistic hypothesis generation from action-free recordings.

</details>


### [390] [Learn Feasibility Once, Optimize All Objectives: Derivative-Free Diffusion Models for Chance-Constrained Programming](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03071)
*Ziwen Liu,Yan Liu,Congying Han,Tiande Guo,Yao Yan,Weichen Zhao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: D³Opt is a derivative-free diffusion-based framework for chance-constrained programs that disentangles constraint modeling from objective optimization. It trains a risk-conditioned diffusion model on constraint-filtered decisions once, then uses an annealed particle-based Feynman-Kac correction to optimize post-specified objectives without retraining, enabling optimization of non-convex and non-smooth objectives under fixed chance constraints.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Chance-constrained programs face challenges in optimizing non-convex/non-smooth objectives and adapting to different objectives under fixed chance constraints. Existing methods require objective-specific retraining or struggle with complex objectives. The key motivation is to learn a reusable chance-feasible structure once, independent of any particular objective, and then use it to optimize various post-specified objectives without retraining.

Method: 1) Train a risk-conditioned diffusion model solely on constraint-filtered decisions to learn the chance-feasible structure, then freeze it as a reusable prior. 2) At inference, apply an annealed particle-based Feynman-Kac correction along the frozen reverse diffusion process to optimize post-specified objectives using only function evaluations (derivative-free).

Result: The method effectively optimizes smooth and non-smooth objectives, including non-convex cases, across linear Gaussian CCPs, objective-transfer tasks, and chance-constrained economic dispatch. It demonstrates objective generalization under fixed chance constraints without retraining.

Conclusion: The framework preserves feasibility when the frozen prior has this property. The derived optimization-error bound separates learned-prior coverage, finite-particle approximation, and finite-temperature effects. D³Opt enables derivative-free optimization of non-convex and non-smooth objectives without objective-specific retraining, representing a novel integration of diffusion models with chance-constrained optimization.

Abstract: Chance-constrained programs (CCPs) optimize decisions under uncertainty by limiting the probability of constraint violation. Despite advances in traditional and learning-based approaches, optimizing non-convex or non-smooth objectives and adapting to different objectives under fixed chance constraints remain challenging. In this paper, we propose a \textbf{D}erivative-free \textbf{D}iffusion-based framework that \textbf{D}isentangles constraint modeling from objective optimization, termed \textbf{D$^3$Opt}. We learn the chance-feasible structure once, independently of any particular objective, by training a risk-conditioned diffusion model solely on constraint-filtered decisions and freezing it as a reusable prior for post-specified objectives. At inference time, we propose an annealed, particle-based Feynman--Kac correction along the frozen reverse diffusion process to optimize post-specified objectives using only function evaluations. This enables derivative-free optimization of non-convex and non-smooth objectives without objective-specific retraining. We prove that the correction preserves feasibility when this property holds for the frozen prior, and derive an optimization-error bound separating learned-prior coverage, finite-particle approximation, and finite-temperature effects. Experiments on linear Gaussian CCPs, objective-transfer tasks, and chance-constrained economic dispatch demonstrate effective optimization across smooth and non-smooth objectives, including non-convex cases, and objective generalization under fixed chance constraints without retraining.

</details>


### [391] [Smart Sensing for Safer Bridges: From Sensor Signals to AI-Driven Anomaly Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03082)
*Rahul Jaiswal,Joakim Hellum,Halvor Heiberg*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates anomaly detection in real-world bridge sensor data using two complementary approaches: signal processing and machine learning (Isolation Forest). The methods are evaluated using real-time data from a bridge in Norway, with various metrics including anomaly counts, detection time, processing rate, and temporal agreement. A controlled anomaly-injection analysis is also performed to evaluate sensitivity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Bridges are critical infrastructure for transportation and urban development. Reliable bridge monitoring is essential for public safety and early detection of abnormal structural conditions through anomaly detection in bridge sensor data.

Method: Two complementary approaches are used: (1) signal processing, and (2) data-driven machine learning model Isolation Forest. The real-time sensor data is collected from an iBridge sensor device installed on a bridge in Norway. Evaluation metrics include anomaly counts, anomaly detection time, processing rate, anomaly rates, visualization, and temporal agreement. A controlled anomaly-injection analysis is performed to evaluate sensitivity.

Result: Numerical results demonstrate distinct detection characteristics and computational requirements for each method. The data-driven Isolation Forest shows potential for identifying anomalies in bridge sensor measurements, alongside signal processing approaches.

Conclusion: Machine learning, particularly the data-driven Isolation Forest, shows potential alongside signal processing for identifying anomalies in bridge sensor measurements. The two methods have distinct detection characteristics and computational requirements, suggesting they could be complementary.

Abstract: Bridges contribute significantly to transportation connectivity and urban development. Therefore, reliable bridge monitoring is crucial for protecting public safety and detecting anomalous behavior in bridge sensor data that may provide early indications of abnormal structural conditions. This paper investigates anomaly detection in real-world bridge sensor data using two different complementary approaches, namely signal processing and the data-driven machine learning model Isolation Forest. The real-time bridge sensor data is collected from an iBridge sensor device installed on a bridge in Norway. The methods are evaluated using anomaly counts, anomaly detection time, processing rate, anomaly rates, visualization, and temporal agreement. Moreover, a controlled anomaly-injection analysis is performed to evaluate the sensitivity of each method. Numerical results demonstrate distinct detection characteristics and computational requirements, highlighting the potential of machine learning, particularly the data-driven Isolation Forest, alongside signal processing for identifying anomalies in bridge sensor measurements.

</details>


### [392] [Light Entropic Optimal Transport on Riemannian Manifolds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03085)
*Xavier Aramayo-Carrasco,Petr Mokrov,Alexander Korotin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ManifoldLightOT is a light framework for learning entropic optimal transport (EOT) couplings directly on manifolds (spheres, tori, SO(3), SE(3)) using kernel-induced Gibbs kernels with compatible potential parameterizations that enable closed-form normalization and direct sampling.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing EOT solvers are primarily designed for Euclidean spaces, and manifold extensions are limited, often relying on costly iterative methods, simulated dynamics, or generic neural models that don't fully exploit underlying geometry.

Method: The method uses the kernel form of the EOT solution to construct geometry-specific Gibbs kernels with compatible potential parameterizations for specific manifolds (spheres, tori, SO(3), SE(3)). These yield closed-form normalization and directly sampleable conditional distributions. Parameters are optimized from samples using Monte Carlo estimates.

Result: ManifoldLightOT often outperforms existing manifold OT methods while retaining direct sampling capability, demonstrated through synthetic and real-world experiments.

Conclusion: The approach provides an efficient, geometry-aware framework for learning EOT couplings on manifolds with direct sampling capabilities, naturally extending to products of manifolds for more complex geometries.

Abstract: Entropic Optimal Transport (EOT) has become a practical framework for learning stochastic couplings between complex distributions, with applications in generative modeling and domain adaptation. However, most EOT solvers are designed for Euclidean spaces, while manifold extensions remain limited and often rely on costly iterative methods, simulated dynamics, or generic neural models that do not fully exploit the underlying geometry. We introduce ManifoldLightOT, a light approach for learning kernel-induced EOT couplings directly on common manifolds. Using the kernel form of the EOT solution, we construct geometry-specific Gibbs kernels together with compatible potential parameterizations for spheres, tori, $\mathrm{SO}(3)$, and $\mathrm{SE}(3)$. These choices yield closed-form normalization and directly sampleable conditional distributions. Our formulation naturally extends to products of manifolds, making it applicable to more complex geometries. The parameters of the potentials are optimized directly from samples using Monte Carlo estimates of the learning objective. Through synthetic and real-world experiments, we show that ManifoldLightOT often outperforms existing manifold OT methods while retaining direct sampling.

</details>


### [393] [Zephon: Elastic Determinism for Online, Stateful Foundation Model Data Loading Pipelines](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03087)
*Maximilian Böther,Josh Wills,Ties Robroek,Sonnet Xu,Paul Burstein,Daniel Zayas,Cody Blakeney,Siddharth Joshi,Haoli Yin,Rishabh Adiga,Haakon Mongstad,Luke Merrick,Pratyush Maini,Ari Morcos,Matthew Leavitt,Ana Klimovic,Bogdan Gaza*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Zephon is a data loader for foundation models that provides elastic determinism (deterministic data sequence despite changes in GPU topology, checkpoint-resume cycles, and different execution backends) while supporting online, stateful pipelines (tokenization, packing, sample mixing). It achieves this by partitioning the global stream into topology-independent lanes, serializing ordering decisions while parallelizing stateless work, and checkpointing only bounded in-flight state.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Foundation model researchers need confidence that observed differences across training ablations are due to parameter changes, not non-determinism in training data sequence. Existing data loaders assume indexable 1-to-1 pipelines and cannot handle modern online, stateful transformations (tokenization, packing, mixing) that break sample indexing. Offline materialization is expensive or infeasible for some modalities like video.

Method: Zephon partitions the global stream into topology-independent lanes (ensuring determinism regardless of GPU topology), serializes ordering decisions while parallelizing stateless work on interchangeable backends, and checkpoints only bounded in-flight state so recovery cost doesn't grow with training progress.

Result: Zephon achieves competitive throughput on text and vision-language workloads while providing a combination of guarantees that no existing loader offers for online, stateful pipelines.

Conclusion: Zephon successfully provides elastic determinism for foundation model training with stateful pipelines, enabling reliable ablation studies while maintaining efficiency and supporting efficient checkpoint resumption.

Abstract: Deterministic data loading is important for foundation model development: model researchers need confidence that differences they observe across costly ablations are caused by the parameter they changed rather than non-determinism in the training data sequence. The data loader must provide elastic determinism, i.e., a deterministic sequence of global training data batches despite changes to the GPU topology across runs (e.g., due to GPU scarcity), frequent checkpoint-resume cycles, and different data processing execution backends. Achieving this is difficult because modern foundation model data pipelines tokenize, pack, and mix samples online, introducing stateful n-to-m transformations that break sample indexing. Existing data loaders largely assume indexable 1-to-1 pipelines, and the common workaround of offline materialization is expensive and, for some modalities such as video, infeasible.
  We present Zephon, a data loader for foundation models that supports online, stateful pipelines while providing elastic determinism and efficient resumption from checkpoints. It partitions the global stream into topology-independent lanes, serializes ordering decisions while parallelizing stateless work on interchangeable backends, and checkpoints only bounded in-flight state so recovery cost does not grow with training progress. We evaluate Zephon on text and vision-language workloads and show that it achieves competitive throughput while providing a combination of guarantees that no existing loader offers for online, stateful pipelines.

</details>


### [394] [ULTRADISCOVERY: Abductive Exploration in an Interconnected, Epistemically Open Universe](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03092)
*Weihan Li,Tianshi Zheng,Yangqiu Song,Ginny Y. Wong,Simon See*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ULTRADISCOVERY is a benchmark for evaluating scientific discovery in AI agents, featuring a 2×2 design controlling whether representations are open or disclosed, and evidence is distributed or aligned. The study tests 11 models and two vendor systems, finding that constructing new representations from open-ended clues and composing scattered evidence remain critical challenges for current AI systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Scientific discovery often requires constructing new representations when the world is epistemically open and composing evidence scattered across contexts. Existing benchmarks don't separate or independently control these two key demands. The researchers needed a controlled environment to study how well AI systems can perform abductive reasoning - revising theories and predicting cross-domain interventions.

Method: The researchers created ULTRADISCOVERY, an interactive world with five domains featuring a 2×2 experimental design: representation (open vs. disclosed) × evidence (distributed vs. aligned), with latent dynamics fixed. They tested 11 models and two vendor-harness systems, measuring whether agents could revise initially successful theories and predict outcomes of unseen cross-domain interventions. They tracked metrics including axiom retraction, introduction of unobserved entities, variable rewriting, intervention requests, and prediction accuracy within action budgets.

Result: With representation open, agents across 11 models often retracted the taught axiom, with none introducing unobserved entities or rewriting variables. Disclosure tripled intervention requests and added ~1 of 18 findings. Alignment added less. Two vendor systems tested in more domains; one rewrites variables in Open episodes. No system achieved exact prediction within 200 paid actions. Larger budgets enabled exact predictions with both aids, but every Open episode remained inexact.

Conclusion: The core difficulty in scientific discovery lies in the transition from accumulating evidence to composing it into a representation that transfers across domains. Current AI systems struggle with abductive reasoning when representations must be constructed rather than provided, and when evidence is distributed rather than aligned. This benchmark provides a controlled way to study these fundamental challenges in machine reasoning.

Abstract: Scientific discovery often begins when scattered clues call for a new way of describing the world. Such abductive exploration can require constructing the representation in which an explanation is stated, when the world is epistemically open, and composing evidence scattered across contexts, when it is structurally interconnected. Existing benchmarks rarely separate these two demands or control them independently. We introduce ULTRADISCOVERY, an interactive world of five domains in which an agent revises an initially successful theory and predicts the outcome of an unseen cross-domain intervention. A $2 \times 2$ design leaves the representation open or discloses it, and leaves the evidence distributed or aligns it, with the latent dynamics fixed. With the representation open, agents across eleven models often retract the axiom they were taught, and none introduces the unobserved entity or rewrites the variables that a replacement requires. Disclosure triples intervention requests and adds about one of the eighteen findings the world affords, and alignment adds less. Two vendor-harness systems carry discovery into more domains, and one of them rewrites the variables in Open episodes. No system makes the exact prediction within 200 paid actions. At larger budgets one exact prediction appears with both aids, while every Open episode remains inexact. The results locate the difficulty in the step from accumulating evidence to composing it into a representation that transfers.

</details>


### [395] [LS-AR: Future-Predictive Latent Steering in Autoregressive LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03093)
*Anubha Gupta,Eduardo Pignatelli*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LS-AR introduces a dual-channel architecture that separates continuous goal steering from discrete token decoding using FiLM conditioning, addressing single-channel limitations in standard autoregressive models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard autoregressive models process task instructions, state history, and transient tokens within a single shared token sequence, lacking architectural mechanisms to isolate macro-objectives from context noise.

Method: Dual-channel architecture with two variants: (1) Static Goal Encoder (P_0) for persistent macro-objective retention across long rollouts, and (2) Dynamic State Tracker (P_t) for recurrent latent updates during generation. Uses FiLM conditioning to decouple goal steering from token decoding.

Result: Long-horizon retrieval (H=1024, W=500): LS-AR (Static) achieves 100% target recall vs 0% for baselines; 35% throughput increase; 52.8% VRAM reduction. Blocksworld planning (k=1): LS-AR (Dynamic) achieves 89.0% completion vs 71.0% baseline. Zero-shot entity scaling shows single-vector capacity limits (0%).

Conclusion: Dual-channel LS-AR effectively isolates macro-objectives from context noise. Text goal dropout establishes latent-dominant control, offering structural defense against text prompt injection while introducing a latent vector attack surface. Static variant excels at long-horizon retention; Dynamic variant handles perturbations better but faces scalability limits.

Abstract: Standard autoregressive (AR) models process high-level task instructions, state history, and transient tokens within a single shared sequence of tokens. Consequently, they lack the architectural mechanisms needed to isolate macro-objectives from context noise. To overcome this single-channel limitation, we introduce Latent-Steered Autoregressive (LS-AR), a dual-channel architecture that decouples continuous goal steering from discrete token decoding via FiLM conditioning. We evaluate a Static Goal Encoder (P_0) for persistent macro-objective retention across long rollouts and a Dynamic State Tracker (P_t) for recurrent latent updates during generation. On long-horizon retrieval past context limits (H=1024, W=500), LS-AR (Static) achieves 100% target recall where parameter-matched baselines collapse (0%), while increasing throughput by ~35% and cutting peak VRAM by 52.8%. In Blocksworld planning under forced perturbations (k=1), LS-AR (Dynamic) sustains an 89.0% completion rate vs. 71.0% for the baseline, though zero-shot entity scaling (N -> N+1) exposes single-vector capacity limits (0%). Finally, dual-channel authority analysis shows that text goal dropout establishes latent-dominant control, offering structural defence against text prompt injection while introducing a latent vector attack surface.

</details>


### [396] [Exploring the Trade-Off Between Structured Pruning and Fault Tolerance in Deep Neural Networks for Space Applications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03117)
*Toon Vinck,Naïn Jonckers,Jaro De Roose,Jeffrey Prinzie,Peter Karsmakers*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper investigates how model width affects robustness to Single Event Upsets (SEUs) in DNNs, finding that structured pruning increases per-inference fault sensitivity but shorter execution time compensates by reducing SEU probability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: DNNs exhibit inherent robustness to bit-level faults due to distributed information representation. As model width increases, information becomes more dispersed, theoretically reducing the impact of any single bit fault. This paper empirically investigates the relationship between model width and SEU robustness.

Method: The authors conduct a comprehensive experiment using iterative structured pruning to reduce model width while preserving task performance. At each pruning stage, they perform targeted fault-injection campaigns to evaluate model performance under simulated bit-flip scenarios.

Result: Structured pruning increases per-inference sensitivity to faults by reducing redundancy. However, this effect is effectively counterbalanced by shorter execution time, which lowers the probability of encountering an SEU.

Conclusion: Structured pruning can yield significant energy and latency savings without compromising overall reliability. This provides useful guidance for designing robust AI systems for space applications.

Abstract: Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) inherently exhibit a degree of robustness to bit-level faults due to their distributed representation of information. As a model increases in width, this information becomes more dispersed, theoretically reducing the impact of any single bit fault. In this paper, we empirically investigate the relationship between model width and robustness to Single Event Upsets (SEUs). We conduct a comprehensive experiment in which baseline models undergo iterative structured pruning to reduce their width while preserving task performance as much as possible. At each pruning stage, we run a targeted fault-injection campaign to evaluate the model's performance under simulated bit-flip scenarios. Our results show that, although structured pruning increases per-inference sensitivity to faults by reducing redundancy, this effect is effectively counterbalanced by shorter execution time, which lowers the probability of encountering an SEU. These findings suggest that structured pruning can yield significant energy and latency savings without compromising overall reliability, providing useful guidance for designing robust AI systems for space applications.

</details>


### [397] [How to Find and Reuse Policies for Continuous Adaptation in Lifelong Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03119)
*Saptarshi Nath,Inish M. D'Souza,Antonio Carta,Soheil Kolouri,Andrea Soltoggio*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: AMSC uses Wasserstein task embeddings to estimate task similarity and select/weight prior policies for transfer in lifelong reinforcement learning, achieving better performance than baselines on CT-graph and MiniGrid without forgetting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In lifelong RL, retaining previously learned policies is insufficient for effective transfer. Knowledge is distributed across multiple prior policies with changing relevance. The hypothesis is that task similarity can effectively identify and combine relevant prior policies for new tasks.

Method: AMSC estimates task similarity via non-parametric Wasserstein task embeddings from state-action-reward samples. It uses z-score-normalized sparsemax of similarity scores to derive a variable-size support for periodically choosing and weighting policies to form a prior when learning a new task.

Result: On CT-graph and MiniGrid, AMSC achieves higher mean performance and forward transfer than modular composition baselines with no forgetting. Continual World results suggest layer-specific tuning may be needed. Ablations confirm source selection and reuse strength are critical. Pairwise transfer correlates positively with task-embedding similarity.

Conclusion: Task similarity can be an effective criterion for selecting and weighting specific knowledge for reuse in lifelong reinforcement learning.

Abstract: In lifelong reinforcement learning, retaining previously learned policies is not sufficient for effective transfer to a new task. Useful knowledge may be distributed across several prior policies, and its relevance may change as the learner acquires experience. One hypothesis is that task similarity can be effectively used in a continual learning setting to find and combine previously learned policies. To test it, Adaptive Mask Selection and Composition (AMSC) is designed to estimate similarity from online experience via non-parametric Wasserstein task embeddings from state-action-reward samples. The z-score-normalized sparsemax of the similarity scores are used to derive a variable-size support to periodically choose and weight policies to form a prior when learning a new task. On CT-graph and MiniGrid, AMSC achieves higher mean performance and forward transfer than the evaluated modular composition baselines while exhibiting no forgetting. Results on Continual World suggest that identifying relevant prior knowledge and determining its layer-specific composition may require additional layer-specific tuning. Ablations show that selecting relevant sources and determining how strongly to reuse them are central to these gains. Independently measured pairwise transfer is also positively associated with task-embedding similarity. These results indicate that task similarity can be an effective criterion to select and weight specific knowledge for reuse in lifelong reinforcement learning.

</details>


### [398] [Coverage You Can Steer: Online Conformal Calibration for RL-Driven Hardware-Aware NAS](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03127)
*Pedro Brandimarte,Nerea Aranjuelo,Marcos Nieto,Oihana Otaegui*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses the coverage control problem in hardware-aware neural architecture search (NAS) by replacing static conformal prediction with online feedback control (Adaptive Conformal Inference), achieving accurate coverage tracking while pruning 25-50% of candidate evaluations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conformal-prediction filters in hardware-aware NAS assume exchangeability between calibration and test candidates, but this assumption is violated in reinforcement learning loops where policies improve over time and layer-by-layer construction shifts within episodes. This causes the distribution-free guarantee to break down in practice.

Method: The authors replace one-shot quantile estimation with online feedback control using Adaptive Conformal Inference with three variants: tuning-free, locally-adaptive, and group-conditional. They test across three neural-network architecture families using both single-step and sequential search with three seeds.

Result: The method tracks every requested coverage level to within ~10^-3 while pruning 25-50% of evaluations at no measured accuracy cost. Static calibration loses control of coverage, Gaussian-process baseline stays conservative regardless of request, and used as an acquisition function it beats random search.

Conclusion: Online feedback control restores steerable coverage in NAS, enabling monotonic and reproducible coverage delivery for arbitrary sequences. This achieves significant computational savings without accuracy loss while maintaining theoretical guarantees under non-exchangeable conditions.

Abstract: Hardware-aware neural architecture search (NAS) is dominated by evaluation cost: every architecture must be trained before its reward is known. Conformal-prediction filters cut this cost by pruning candidates whose predicted-reward upper bound misses a threshold, with a distribution-free guarantee that at most a fraction $δ$ are wrongly discarded. That guarantee assumes exchangeability between calibration and test candidates, which the surrounding reinforcement-learning (RL) loop violates: the policy's proposals improve as search proceeds and, in layer-by-layer construction, shift within every episode. We replace one-shot quantile estimation with online feedback control (Adaptive Conformal Inference, with tuning-free, locally-adaptive, and group-conditional variants), restoring steerable coverage: dialing the target delivers it, monotonically and reproducibly, for arbitrary sequences. Across three neural-network architecture families and both single-step and sequential search (three seeds), it tracks every requested level to within ${\sim}10^{-3}$ while pruning 25-50% of evaluations at no measured accuracy cost, whereas static calibration loses control of its coverage and a Gaussian-process baseline stays conservative regardless of the request. Finally, used as an acquisition function on one constrained testbed, the same optimistic bound beats random search, a gain that fixed optimism already carries and online calibration sharpens. The source code is available at https://github.com/Vicomtech/rl-hw-nas.

</details>


### [399] [Page-EntroKV: Hardware-Aligned, Entropy-Weighted KV-Cache Eviction under Grouped-Query Attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03135)
*Inbasekaran S*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Page-EntroKV addresses KV-cache eviction for long-context language models under grouped-query attention (GQA). It solves the problem where existing methods score tokens per query head independently, causing cache inflation (up to 4.75x) when heads share KV buffers. The method pools head scores using Renyi-2 entropy-derived weights, projects to PagedAttention frames, and evicts at (layer, group, page) granularity. It provides theoretical guarantees including exact budget preservation and needle retention bounds that arithmetic mean pooling violates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing dynamic KV-cache eviction methods score token importance per query head and choose tokens independently. This approach is problematic for GQA, where multiple query heads share one physical KV buffer. Divergent per-head selections force retention of the union of chosen tokens, inflating cache by up to the group ratio r. Additionally, arithmetic mean pooling dilutes specialized retrieval heads that carry factual recall.

Method: Page-EntroKV introduces a formal framework for KV-cache eviction at GQA granularity. Key innovations: (1) Pool heads within each physical group using weights derived from sink-isolated collision (Renyi-2) entropy - one inner product per head computed once at prefill with no calibration; (2) Pooled scores are projected onto PagedAttention page frames; (3) Eviction executes at hardware tuple (layer, group, page).

Result: Experimental results on Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct (r=6): (1) Union overhead ratio (UOR) up to 4.75x at 2% budget for independent head eviction, while Page-EntroKV holds UOR exactly 1.000; (2) Sink isolation removes 13x sink masquerade; (3) Needle recall is 100% vs 0% for mean pooling at 20% budget; (4) Retained cardinality is exact for every page size; (5) QA and code tasks remain solvable at 20% retention.

Conclusion: Page-EntroKV provides a theoretically grounded solution for KV-cache eviction under GQA that eliminates cache inflation, preserves factual recall, and maintains task performance at low retention rates. The method includes formal proofs for budget preservation, finite-context needle-retention bounds, and exact per-layer page accounting.

Abstract: Serving long-context autoregressive language models is constrained by the key-value (KV) cache. Most dynamic eviction methods score token importance per query head and choose tokens independently. This fits poorly with grouped-query attention (GQA), where several query heads share one physical KV buffer: divergent per-head selections force the serving engine to retain the union of their choices - inflating the cache by up to the group ratio r - while arithmetic mean pooling dilutes the specialized retrieval heads that carry factual recall. We introduce Page-EntroKV, a formal framework for KV-cache eviction operating at the granularity GQA serving actually allocates. Heads within each physical group are pooled by weights derived from sink-isolated collision (Renyi-2) entropy - one inner product per head, computed once at prefill with no calibration - so sink heads cannot masquerade as retrieval heads. Pooled scores are projected onto PagedAttention page frames, and eviction executes at the hardware tuple (layer, group, page). We formalize the union overhead ratio (UOR) and intra-group disagreement, prove an exact identity linking them for two-head groups alongside two-sided bounds at every group ratio, prove strict budget preservation and a finite-context needle-retention bound that arithmetic mean pooling provably violates, and give exact per-layer page accounting. On a pilot architecture (Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, r=6), head-independent replay over 2,240 group measurements yields union overhead up to 4.75x at a 2% budget, while Page-EntroKV holds UOR exactly 1.000; sink isolation removes a 13x sink masquerade; needle recall is 100% versus 0% for mean pooling at a 20% budget; retained cardinality is exact for every page size; and QA and code tasks remain solvable at 20% retention.

</details>


### [400] [Sample complexity of variance-reduced policy gradient: weaker assumptions and lower bounds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03165)
*Gabor Paczolay,Matteo Papini,Alberto Maria Metelli,Istvan Harmati,Marcello Restelli*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes Defensive Policy Gradient (DPG), a variance-reduced REINFORCE algorithm using defensive importance sampling that achieves O(ε^{-3}) sample complexity without requiring unrealistic variance assumptions on importance weights. The work also establishes lower bounds in a generalized black-box policy-optimization model, showing optimal rates of Θ(ε^{-4}) and Θ(ε^{-3}) for different feedback settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Previous variance-reduced REINFORCE algorithms achieved O(ε^{-3}) sample complexity but relied on unrealistic assumptions about the variance of importance weights. This paper aims to achieve the same rate without such assumptions while also establishing theoretical lower bounds to determine optimality.

Method: The paper introduces defensive importance sampling to develop the DPG algorithm. It also establishes lower bounds in a generalized black-box policy-optimization model that hides states and actions and permits parameter-dependent rewards. The analysis compares REINFORCE and DPG under standard policy-regularity conditions.

Result: DPG achieves O(ε^{-3}) sample complexity without variance assumptions on ordinary importance weights. Lower bounds show Θ(ε^{-4}) is optimal for bounded-variance one-policy feedback and Θ(ε^{-3}) for mean-square-smooth coupled two-policy feedback. REINFORCE achieves O(ε^{-4}) and DPG achieves O(ε^{-3}), matching the oracle conditions.

Conclusion: The faster rate of DPG (O(ε^{-3})) is optimal and genuinely separated from vanilla policy gradient (O(ε^{-4})), as justified by the oracle-level lower bounds in the generalized model. While the lower bounds don't directly apply to classical MDP interaction models, they provide oracle-level evidence of optimality.

Abstract: Several variance-reduced versions of REINFORCE based on importance sampling achieve an improved $O(ε^{-3})$ sample complexity to find an $ε$-stationary point, under an unrealistic assumption on the variance of the importance weights. In this paper, we propose the \algo (Defensive Policy Gradient) algorithm, based on defensive importance sampling, which achieves the same rate without any assumption on the variance of ordinary importance weights. We also establish lower bounds in a generalized black-box policy-optimization model that hides states and actions and permits parameter-dependent rewards. In this model, the optimal rates are $Θ(ε^{-4})$ with bounded-variance one-policy feedback and $Θ(ε^{-3})$ with mean-square-smooth coupled two-policy feedback. Under standard policy-regularity conditions, REINFORCE and \algo realize the corresponding oracle conditions and attain the $O(ε^{-4})$ and $O(ε^{-3})$ upper bounds, respectively. Although the lower bounds do not apply directly to the classical MDP interaction model in which these algorithms operate, this correspondence provides oracle-level evidence that the faster rate of \algo is optimal and genuinely separated from that of vanilla policy gradient.

</details>


### [401] [Predicting and Repairing Merge Collapse in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03199)
*Jungseob Lee,Seungyoon Lee,Sugyeong Eo,Hyeonseok Moon,Jaehyung Seo,Heuiseok Lim*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses the problem of model collapse when merging fine-tuned language models via task vector averaging. The authors discover that variance across task vectors (interference) predicts merge collapse, and introduce PRISM, an operator that soft-thresholds each layer based on its interference level, successfully rescuing destructive merges while preserving harmless ones.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: When large language models fine-tuned from a shared base are merged by averaging their task vectors, some merges collapse far below the base model performance. Existing merge operators provide no warning before evaluation, making it difficult to predict or prevent this collapse.

Method: The authors derive a theoretical relationship between merge collapse and the variance of task vectors across specialists (interference). Under a working noise model, they show that disturbance grows with merge coefficient and interference, yielding a pre-merge score. They then introduce PRISM, which averages task vectors first and soft-thresholds each layer at a level set by that layer's interference.

Result: In experiments on 22 merge configurations from four model families, only destructive merges exceeded a threshold on the pre-merge score. Sign conflict statistics were found to be anti-predictive. Of 14 predicted merge outcomes, 12 predictions were correct. PRISM kept all five destructive merges above the threshold within evaluation noise of the base model, while plain averaging fell at least 14.4 points below or collapsed entirely. All 15 harmless merges were preserved.

Conclusion: The variance of task vectors (interference) is a reliable predictor of merge collapse. PRISM successfully addresses destructive merges through layer-wise soft-thresholding based on interference, without requiring data or tuning. This provides both a warning system (the pre-merge score threshold) and a practical solution (PRISM operator) for safe model merging.

Abstract: Large language models fine-tuned from a shared base can be merged by averaging their task vectors, but some merges collapse far below the base model, and common merge operators give no warning before evaluation. We show that one statistic of the specialists' task vectors both predicts this collapse and calibrates its repair. The power that averaging removes equals the variance of the task vectors across specialists, our measure of interference. Under a working noise model, the disturbance that a merge injects grows with the merge coefficient and with interference, yielding a pre-merge score. In our experiments on twenty-two merge configurations from four model families, only destructive merges exceed a threshold on this score. We find that statistics of sign conflict between specialists, a common target of existing merge operators, are anti-predictive. We then predicted the outcomes of fourteen merges before evaluating them, and twelve predictions were correct, including the destructive outcome of a specialist pair pushed past the threshold by continued pretraining. To address this collapse, we introduce PRISM, an operator that averages the task vectors first and then soft-thresholds each layer at a level set by the layer's interference. Without data or tuning, PRISM keeps all five destructive merges above the threshold within evaluation noise of the base model, where plain averaging falls at least 14.4 points below it or collapses entirely. We apply PRISM only above the threshold and keep the plain average for merges below it, which include all fifteen harmless ones. Code is available at https://github.com/js-lee-AI/PRISM.

</details>


### [402] [HyperFuse: Fast Self-Supervised Node Embeddings for Attributed Hypergraphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03211)
*Megha P,Harshit Kumar,Srajan Agarwal,Anirban Banerjee,Olaf Wolkenhauer,Saptarshi Bej*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: HyperFuse is a label-free pipeline for fast self-supervised hypergraph representation learning that achieves 13-179x speed-ups over baseline methods while maintaining comparable or better classification and clustering performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing self-supervised hypergraph representation learning methods require deep encoders trained for hundreds of epochs, making embedding generation costly for hypergraphs with thousands of nodes. This limits applications requiring embeddings for many or evolving hypergraphs.

Method: Three-component pipeline: (i) computes structural node coordinates via spectral relaxation of hypergraph modularity using Banerjee's hypergraph adjacency and matrix-free operator with linear cost; (ii) constructs multi-scale feature summaries and assigns bounded utility weights to hyperedges based on member stability under feature and membership masking; (iii) trains a lightweight utility-weighted hypergraph encoder for 100 epochs using an invariance-decorrelation objective.

Result: HyperFuse required 8.7 seconds per dataset on average (13-179x speed-up over baselines). It achieved highest average accuracy with 5 of 6 classifiers. Compared to HypeBoy, it was 13x faster and 2.1-4.1 percentage points more accurate across all classifiers. Classification and clustering performance was not significantly different from TriCL and SE-HSSL.

Conclusion: HyperFuse provides a practical approach for fast, repeated hypergraph embedding generation, enabling applications where embeddings are needed for many or evolving hypergraphs.

Abstract: Self-supervised hypergraph representation learning can produce informative node embeddings, but existing methods often require deep encoders trained for hundreds of epochs, making embedding generation costly even for hypergraphs with a few thousand nodes. This limits applications requiring embeddings for many or evolving hypergraphs. We present HyperFuse, a label-free pipeline for fast hypergraph representation learning. HyperFuse (i) computes structural node coordinates by maximizing a spectral relaxation of hypergraph modularity using Banerjee's hypergraph adjacency and a matrix-free operator with cost linear in node-hyperedge incidences; (ii) constructs multi-scale feature summaries and assigns bounded utility weights to hyperedges based on member stability under feature and membership masking; and (iii) trains a lightweight utility-weighted hypergraph encoder for 100 epochs using an invariance-decorrelation objective. We compare HyperFuse with TriCL, SE-HSSL, VilLain, and HypeBoy on nine public hypergraphs using six downstream classifiers and k-means clustering. On the eight datasets where all methods completed, HyperFuse required 8.7 s per dataset on average, achieving 13-179x geometric-mean speed-ups over the baselines. It achieved the highest average accuracy with five of six classifiers, while classification and clustering performance was not significantly different from TriCL and SE-HSSL. Compared with HypeBoy, HyperFuse was 13x faster and 2.1-4.1 percentage points more accurate across all classifiers. HyperFuse provides a practical approach for fast, repeated hypergraph embedding generation.

</details>


### [403] [Kernel Singular Value Decomposition with Extension to Multiple Data Sources](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03216)
*Xinjie Zeng,Qinghua Tao,Johan Suykens*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper extends Kernel Singular Value Decomposition (KSVD) to handle multiple data sources, called eKSVD, which performs joint nonlinear feature learning on asymmetric kernels. It derives a generalized eigenvalue problem via Lagrangian and KKT conditions, and proposes a neural network-based covariance framework for explicit feature mappings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: KSVD only handles two data sources (asymmetric kernel matrix), but many real-world problems involve multiple data sources that need joint learning. Current kernel methods struggle with multiple sources, so the authors propose eKSVD to address this limitation.

Method: 1) Primal formulation: jointly learn projections for each data source with pairwise couplings
2) Dual optimization using Lagrangian and KKT conditions
3) Derive generalized shifted eigenvalue problem (extension of Lanczos decomposition)
4) Covariance-based framework with neural networks for explicit feature mappings

Result: eKSVD outperforms methods based on Mercer kernels for multiple data sources. The neural network implementation demonstrates great flexibility for kernel methods.

Conclusion: eKSVD successfully extends KSVD to multiple data sources through joint nonlinear feature learning. The combination of kernel-based optimization and neural network implementations provides both theoretical rigor and practical flexibility.

Abstract: Kernel Singular Value Decomposition (KSVD) learns a pair of singular vectors w.r.t. an asymmetric kernel matrix, which can be induced by two data sources, e.g., the queries and keys in self-attention or the rows and columns of a given matrix. In this work, we extend KSVD to multiple data sources, namely eKSVD, which conducts joint nonlinear feature learning upon asymmetric kernels. In the primal formulation, the projections associated with each data source are jointly learned to capture maximal information, while incorporating pair-wise couplings. With the Lagrangian and its Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions, the optimization in the dual leads to a generalization of the shifted eigenvalue problem in Lanczos decomposition theorem of KSVD. Further, a covariance-based framework is derived together with using neural networks (NNs) for explicit feature mappings, complementary to the kernel-based interpretation and optimization. Numerical experiments verify the effectiveness of our eKSVD compared to methods based on Mercer kernels for tackling multiple data sources, and our innovation of deploying NNs demonstrates great flexibility for kernel methods.

</details>


### [404] [AdaStep: Adaptive Step Credit Weighting for Agentic Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03223)
*Xin Wang,Wenhao Wu,Menghao Zhang,Zhi Wang,Kun Shao,Jian Luan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: AdaStep addresses credit assignment in long-horizon LLM agents by introducing an adaptive step-credit weighting method that controls how strongly local advantages modify trajectory-level rewards. It derives optimal per-state shrinkage coefficients based on signal-to-total-variance interpretation, requiring no critic, additional rollouts, or extra model inference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-horizon LLM agents are trained with sparse outcome rewards, making trajectory-level objectives too coarse to distinguish individual decision contributions. Step-level credit assignment provides finer supervision but produces unreliable estimates because observed returns also depend on subsequent actions, environment transitions, and trajectory length.

Method: Formulates step-credit weighting as a mean-squared-error estimation problem for latent step advantage. Under an explicit conditional sampling assumption, derives an optimal per-state shrinkage coefficient with signal-to-total-variance interpretation: preserves local credit when return variation is attributable to the selected action, suppresses it when variation is dominated by downstream randomness.

Result: Experiments with three model backbones on ALFWorld, WebShop, and ScienceWorld show consistent improvements over baselines at low computational cost.

Conclusion: AdaStep provides an effective, computationally lightweight solution for step-level credit assignment in long-horizon LLM agents, achieving better performance without requiring critics, additional rollouts, or extra model inference.

Abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents are typically trained with sparse outcome rewards, making trajectory-level objectives too coarse to distinguish the contribution of individual decisions. Step-level credit assignment provides finer-grained supervision, but its estimates can be unreliable because observed returns also depend on subsequent actions, environment transitions, and trajectory length. We propose AdaStep, an Adaptive Step-credit weighting method that controls how strongly each group-derived local advantage modifies the trajectory-level signal. We formulate this weighting as a mean-squared-error estimation problem for the latent step advantage and, under an explicit conditional sampling assumption, derive an optimal per-state shrinkage coefficient. The coefficient admits a signal-to-total-variance interpretation: it preserves local credit when return variation is attributable to the selected action and suppresses it when variation is dominated by downstream randomness. AdaStep requires only lightweight scalar computation, with no critic, additional rollouts, or extra model inference. Experiments with three model backbones on ALFWorld, WebShop, and ScienceWorld show consistent improvements over baselines at low computational cost.

</details>


### [405] [The Neuro-Physical Inverter: A Modular Framework for Magnetotelluric Inversion Coupling Ensemble Conditioning with Residual Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03225)
*Jae Deok Kim,Sai Ravela,Rob. L. Evans*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The Neuro-Physical Inverter (NPI) is a novel framework for geophysical inversion that combines ensemble-based conditioning with constrained residual learning, demonstrated in 1D magnetotelluric (MT) applications. It uses a two-stage approach: first conditioning a prior ensemble on observed data via Ensemble-Conditional Gaussian Process (EnsCGP), then applying a residual-learning neural network for corrections.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Geophysical inversion problems typically suffer from non-uniqueness and uncertainty quantification challenges. Traditional methods either lack robust uncertainty estimates or are computationally expensive. The authors aimed to develop a framework that produces physically admissible solutions while maintaining ensemble-based uncertainty quantification, and can be fine-tuned for field applications.

Method: The NPI operates in two stages: (1) EnsCGP conditions a prior ensemble of resistivity models on observed MT response, producing a physically admissible reference ensemble; (2) A residual-learning neural network predicts corrections to this reference, trained on synthetic data and fine-tuned per station using a physics-coupled objective. Both stages are dimension-agnostic and propagate ensemble spread throughout the process.

Result: Synthetic experiments show NPI systematically reduces ensemble-mean error without destabilizing the ensemble. Applied to broadband MT data from Gabbs Valley geothermal region (Nevada, USA), NPI reduces across-station mean misfit in the mid-period band while retaining comparable ensemble spread. The propagated ensemble provides an uncertainty factor serving as an operational measure of constraint within the assumed model class.

Conclusion: The NPI framework successfully couples ensemble-based conditioning with machine learning for uncertainty-aware geophysical inversion. It maintains ensemble spread as an uncertainty measure while improving data fit. The dimension-agnostic formulation and design principles are intended to scale to higher-dimensional parameterizations, making it applicable to more complex geophysical problems.

Abstract: We present the Neuro-Physical Inverter (NPI), a modular, uncertainty-aware framework for geophysical inversion that couples ensemble-based conditioning with constrained residual learning, demonstrated in the 1D magnetotelluric (MT) setting as a controlled testbed. The framework operates in two stages. An Ensemble-Conditional Gaussian Process (EnsCGP) conditions a prior ensemble of resistivity models on the observed response, producing a physically admissible reference ensemble. A residual-learning neural network then predicts targeted corrections to this reference, trained on synthetic data and fine-tuned per station for field application through a physics-coupled objective. Because an ensemble is conditioned, refined, and propagated through both stages, every estimate carries an associated ensemble spread. Synthetic experiments show that NPI systematically reduces ensemble-mean error without destabilizing the ensemble. Applied to broadband MT data from the Gabbs Valley geothermal region (Nevada, USA), NPI reduces the across-station mean misfit over the mid-period band while retaining comparable ensemble spread. The propagated ensemble yields a factor of uncertainty that serves as an operational measure of constraint within the assumed model class. Both stages are dimension-agnostic in formulation, and the design principles established here are intended to scale to higher-dimensional parameterizations.

</details>


### [406] [D2K-Bench: Can LLM Agents Turn Expert Designs into Efficient GPU Kernels?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03226)
*Daifeng Li,Huiqiang Jiang,Chengruidong Zhang,Wei Wu,Xudong Guo,Jianhong Tu,Jianwei Zhang,Binhang Yuan,Dayiheng Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: D2K-Bench is a diagnostic benchmark that measures how effectively LLM agents translate expert design guidance into efficient GPU kernels across three levels: high-level algorithmic insights (L1), dataflow design (L2), and low-level optimization tricks (L3).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: GPU kernels generated by LLM agents can remain less efficient than expert implementations, but runtime alone does not reveal how the gap relates to design discovery and implementation. There is a need to understand how well agents can follow expert guidance to improve kernel efficiency.

Method: D2K-Bench comprises 26 tasks and 85 workloads. It evaluates guidance at three levels (L1, L2, L3) including dependencies among levels. Pairwise runs with and without guidance share task descriptions, workloads, tools, hardware, and a 350-turn budget. Complementary assessments examine independently proposed designs and implemented design properties. Five models were tested on NVIDIA B200 GPUs.

Result: Guidance raises correctness from 93.1% to 98.5% and increases Performance Score from 1.46 to 1.95 across 130 model-task pairs. For three frontier models (GPT-6-Astra, Claude-Opus-4.8, GPT-5.6-Sol) with correct submissions on all 26 tasks, geometric mean speedup increases from 1.69x to 2.49x. Mean combined implementation score increases from 57 to 70 out of 100.

Conclusion: Expert design guidance significantly improves LLM-generated GPU kernel performance, but some design properties remain unimplemented, highlighting areas for future improvement in AI code generation.

Abstract: GPU kernels generated by large language model (LLM) agents can remain less efficient than expert implementations, but runtime alone does not reveal how the gap relates to design discovery and implementation. We introduce D2K-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark of 26 tasks and 85 workloads that measures how effectively agents translate expert design guidance into efficient GPU kernels. The guidance covers L1: high-level algorithmic insights, L2: dataflow design, and L3: low-level optimization tricks, including dependencies among these levels. Pairwise runs with and without guidance share task descriptions, workloads, tools, hardware, and a 350-turn budget. Complementary assessments examine independently proposed designs and the design properties implemented in generated code. Across five models on NVIDIA B200 GPUs, guidance raises correctness over 130 model-task pairs from 93.1% to 98.5% and increases the Performance Score over all 26 tasks from 1.46 to 1.95. For the three frontier models with correct submissions on all 26 tasks in both runs (GPT-6-Astra, Claude-Opus-4.8, and GPT-5.6-Sol), geometric mean speedup increases from $1.69\times$ to $2.49\times$. Across all five models, the mean combined implementation score increases from 57 to 70 out of 100. These results show the value of expert design guidance while identifying design properties that remain unimplemented.

</details>


### [407] [Cross-cohort TB classification using clinical data gathered in Uganda and South Africa](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03256)
*Joshua M. Jansen van Vüren,Devendra S. Parihar,Daphne Naidoo,Marisa Klopper,Frank Cobelens,Lutz Kolbe,Kimsey Zajac,Willy Ssengooba,Moses Joloba,Grant Theron,Thomas R. Niesler*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This study evaluates machine learning models (LR, MLP, CNN) for TB screening using patient data from South Africa and Uganda. Feature selection improved AUROC by 2-7%. Logistic regression achieved AUROC of 0.8 (Uganda) and 0.84 (South Africa), performing within 1-2% of deeper networks while showing more consistent results on held-out cohorts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To identify people who would benefit from expensive molecular TB testing by applying machine learning to patient clinical and demographic data gathered from two different countries (South Africa and Uganda).

Method: Used the CAGE-TB dataset with sub-cohorts from South Africa and Uganda. Tested three neural network architectures: logistic regression (LR), multilayer perceptrons (MLP), and convolutional neural networks (CNN) with greedy feature selection. Proposed a joint optimization strategy for feature selection and feature ordering for CNN.

Result: Feature selection improved development set AUROC by 2-7% for all models. LR achieved AUROC of 0.8 [0.75,0.86] and 0.84 [0.78,0.9] on Ugandan and South African held-out data respectively. Deeper networks (MLP, CNN) outperformed LR on development cohort but showed inconsistent trends on held-out cohorts. LR performed within 1-2% of the best AUROC and missed WHO minimum sensitivity requirements by 4-9%.

Conclusion: Neural-network based classifiers for TB screening are viable. Simpler LR models provide more consistent performance across different populations compared to deeper networks (MLP, CNN), achieving near-WHO minimum requirements.

Abstract: We present a first evaluation of machine learning applied to patient clinical and demographic data gathered in two different countries for the purpose of tuberculosis (TB) screening to identify people who would benefit from expensive molecular testing. Experiments are based on the recently-compiled CAGE-TB dataset, which includes sub-cohorts of people with presumptive TB presenting at community health care centres in South Africa and Uganda. Three neural network architectures (logistic regression (LR), multilayer perceptrons (MLP) and convolutional neural networks (CNN)) are considered in conjunction with greedy feature selection. For the convolutional neural network, a strategy that jointly optimises feature selection and feature ordering is proposed and shown to lead to consistent development and test set improvements. For all three models, development set area under the receiver operating characteristic (AUROC) curve is improved by 2-7% using feature selection. LR after feature selection achieves an AUROC of 0.8 [0.75,0.86] (95% CI) and 0.84 [0.78,0.9] when testing on the held-out Ugandan and South African data respectively. Although outperforming LR on the development cohort, the deeper networks (MLP, CNN) show inconsistent trends on the held-out cohorts, while LR achieves performance within 1-2% of the best achieved in terms of AUROC. LR narrowly misses the WHO minimum requirements by 4-9% in sensitivity even though the network is being evaluated on a completely held-out cohort. The development of neural-network based classifiers for TB screening therefore appears viable.

</details>


### [408] [Mapping and Advancing the Scalability-Accuracy Frontier of Nonlinear Causal Discovery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03258)
*Hendrik Suhr,Sascha Xu,Jilles Vreeken*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper compares four major approaches to scalable nonlinear causal discovery and introduces SPADE, a spline-based score-evaluation scheme that dramatically improves the scalability-accuracy tradeoff of combinatorial search methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Scalable nonlinear causal discovery requires combining flexible mechanism estimators with efficient graph search, but the accuracy-runtime trade-offs between different algorithmic families were poorly understood.

Method: Empirical comparison of four approaches (differentiable structure learning, amortized structure learning, score-matching, and combinatorial search), followed by development of SPADE that compiles sufficient statistics once and reuses them throughout combinatorial search, reducing complexity from O(nd³) to O(nd²+d³) under bounded indegree.

Result: SPADE achieves orders-of-magnitude improvement in scalability-accuracy frontier: solves 100-variable problems with 160K samples in seconds and 1600-variable problems with 2.5K samples in minutes, while retaining high structural accuracy across synthetic and real-world benchmarks.

Conclusion: Combinatorial search can be scaled to thousands of variables with SPADE's efficient score-evaluation, representing a substantial shift in the practical scale of causal discovery methods and highlighting the importance of evaluating methods along the full accuracy-runtime frontier.

Abstract: Scalable nonlinear causal discovery requires methods that combine flexible mechanism estimators with efficient search over large graph spaces. Several algorithmic families have been proposed to address this challenge, yet their accuracy-runtime trade-offs remain poorly understood. We empirically compare the four major approaches: differentiable structure learning, amortized structure learning, score-matching, and combinatorial search. Our results reveal complementary bottlenecks: differentiable and amortized methods scale well but exhibit an accuracy gap, score-matching methods can be accurate in low dimensions but degrade quickly for increasing feature sizes, and combinatorial methods remain accurate but are slowed by repeated and redundant local scoring. Motivated by this bottleneck, we develop SPADE, a spline-based score-evaluation scheme that compiles sufficient statistics once and reuses them throughout combinatorial search. Under bounded indegree, its Gaussian variant reduces algorithmic complexity from O(nd^3) to O(nd^2+d^3). Empirically, SPADE shifts the observed scalability-accuracy frontier by orders of magnitude: it solves 100-variable problems with 160K samples in seconds and 1600-variable problems with 2.5K samples in minutes, while retaining high structural accuracy across synthetic and real-world benchmarks. These results reveal a substantial shift in the practical scale of combinatorial search and highlight the importance of evaluating scalable causal-discovery methods along the full accuracy-runtime frontier.

</details>


### [409] [PaMIR: Open Benchmark of Public Credit-Default Datasets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03259)
*Mikhail Liashkov,Ilyas Varshavskiy,Shuhratjon Khalilbekov,Azizjon Azimi,Bonu Boboeva*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: PaMIR is an open benchmark for credit-default prediction with scarce and late-arriving labels, comprising 19 public datasets (1.24M records from 9 countries) rebuilt from pinned source snapshots with leakage-audited methodology.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the limitations of existing credit-default prediction benchmarks that rely on few (2-4) public datasets out of 8 total, and to provide a standardized, reproducible benchmark for evaluating models under label scarcity and delay conditions.

Method: Curated 19 public datasets with binary default labels from 9 countries; implemented repeated i.i.d. splits and label-delayed stream evaluation; scored models by AUC under label budget constraints; used synthetic-data harness to test generated training rows without exposing held-out data to generators.

Result: Created the first comprehensive public benchmark of its kind with 1.24M records, featuring leakage-audited data preparation and standardized evaluation under both batch (i.i.d.) and streaming (label-delayed) scenarios.

Conclusion: PaMIR release 0.4.0 provides a rigorous, reproducible benchmark for credit-default prediction research, enabling fair comparison across models under realistic label scarcity conditions.

Abstract: We release PaMIR (Public Arrival-ordered Measurement for Inference in Risk), an open benchmark for credit-default prediction when labels are scarce and arrive late. The field's reference benchmark studies use eight datasets each, only two or four of them public. PaMIR brings together 19 public datasets with binary default labels -- 1.24M loans, firms and card accounts from nine countries -- rebuilt from pinned source snapshots by one leakage-audited recipe and never redistributed; to our knowledge it is the one of its kind as of today. Every model is a single function, scored under a repeated i.i.d. split and a label-delayed stream in which each application is scored on arrival, with AUC reported by label budget; fleet means are withheld unless every dataset is scored. A synthetic-data harness tests generated training rows without letting a generator see held-out rows. This report describes release 0.4.0 of this living benchmark.

</details>


### [410] [SPEAR: A Spectral-Disentangled MoE Neural Operator with Knowledge-Guided Expert Aggregation for Large-Scale PDE Pretraining](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03265)
*Dengdi Sun,Xiaoya Zhou,Xiao Wang,Wanli Lyu,Jin Tang,Bin Luo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SPEAR is a spectral-disentangled mixture-of-experts neural operator for large-scale PDE pre-training that decouples latent features into frequency components and uses knowledge-guided expert aggregation to reduce redundancy while maintaining performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing PDE foundation models struggle with heterogeneous dynamics where shared representations cause knowledge interference, and MoE architectures suffer from increasing expert redundancy as pre-training scales.

Method: SPEAR decouples latent features into low-frequency (transferable dynamics) and high-frequency (PDE-specific patterns) components using spectral disentanglement. It introduces a knowledge-guided expert aggregation strategy that measures expert similarity from dataset-specific learned knowledge and routing preferences to identify and consolidate similar experts.

Result: SPEAR demonstrates superior performance on twelve PDE datasets across pre-training, fine-tuning, and transfer learning benchmarks. The aggregation strategy reduces expert count by 50% while maintaining or improving prediction accuracy.

Conclusion: SPEAR achieves a balance between model efficiency and generalization for PDE foundation models by effectively handling heterogeneous dynamics and reducing expert redundancy through spectral disentanglement and knowledge-guided aggregation.

Abstract: Large-scale pre-training has improved the generalization of neural operators across diverse PDEs. However, existing PDE foundation models still struggle with heterogeneous dynamics, where shared representations may cause knowledge interference, while mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures suffer from increasing expert redundancy. We propose SPEAR, a spectral-disentangled MoE neural operator with knowledge-guided expert aggregation for large-scale PDE pre-training. SPEAR decouples latent features into low- and high-frequency components, enabling shared modeling of transferable dynamics and specialized learning of PDE-specific patterns. To address expert redundancy, we design a knowledge-guided expert aggregation strategy that measures expert similarity from dataset-specific learned knowledge and routing preferences, enabling the identification and consolidation of similar experts. Experiments on twelve PDE datasets and multiple downstream benchmarks demonstrate superior performance in pre-training, fine-tuning, and transfer learning. Furthermore, our aggregation strategy reduces the number of experts by 50\% while maintaining or improving prediction accuracy, achieving a balance between model efficiency and generalization for PDE foundation models.

</details>


### [411] [Architecture-Dependent Fusion Pathways in MLLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03289)
*Hebao Zhu,Dongxia Wu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates how multimodal large language models (MLLMs) fuse visual and textual information across layers, comparing two architectural paradigms: concatenation architectures and native multimodal architectures. Through alignment decoupling, attention routing/entropy analysis, intrinsic dimensionality examination, and causal intervention experiments, the authors reveal distinct fusion pathways between the two architectures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite strong performance of MLLMs on vision-language tasks, the internal mechanisms of visual-textual fusion remain poorly understood. The researchers aim to fill this gap by providing a mechanistic understanding of multimodal fusion across different architectural designs.

Method: The authors conduct three progressive analyses: (1) Alignment decoupling to identify which modality changes, (2) Attention routing and entropy to characterize cross-modal information distribution, (3) Intrinsic dimensionality analysis to examine how fusion reshapes feature spaces. They perform causal intervention experiments for validation and use visual CKA to examine the Platonic Representation Hypothesis.

Result: The study reveals two distinct fusion pathways: concatenation models follow a text-first, vision-later pathway, while native models exhibit earlier visual-textual co-adaptation and feature-space reorganization.

Conclusion: This work provides a mechanistic perspective for understanding multimodal fusion and supports architecture-aware diagnostics of multimodal representations, offering valuable insights for designing and debugging multimodal AI systems.

Abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) achieve strong performance across vision-language tasks, yet the internal mechanisms by which visual and textual information are fused across layers remain insufficiently understood. We investigate representative MLLMs from two architectural paradigms: concatenation architectures and native multimodal architectures. We conduct three progressively connected analyses: alignment decoupling identifies which modality changes, attention routing and entropy characterize how cross-modal information is distributed, and intrinsic dimensionality examines how fusion reshapes feature spaces. Separately, we perform causal intervention experiments as a validation of the resulting interpretation. As a supplementary analysis, we use visual CKA to examine the Platonic Representation Hypothesis. Together, these analyses reveal two distinct fusion pathways: concatenation models follow a text-first, vision-later pathway, whereas native models exhibit earlier visual-textual co-adaptation and feature-space reorganization. This work provides a mechanistic perspective for understanding multimodal fusion and supports architecture-aware diagnostics of multimodal representations.

</details>


### [412] [S$^{2}$-PINN: Stochastic Separable Physics-Informed Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03303)
*Zhendong Li,Akwum Onwunta*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: S²-PINN is a stochastic separable physics-informed neural network for uncertainty quantification in random PDEs. It combines Gaussian spatial dictionary, Fourier temporal features, gPC stochastic basis, and CP tensor decomposition with a hybrid strong-form and gPC-projected residual loss. The method outperforms 9 baselines while using fewer parameters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Classical spectral solvers for random PDEs suffer from the curse of dimensionality, and existing neural solvers often ignore the stochastic structure that enables tractable moment computation and calibration. There is a need for methods that can efficiently handle high-dimensional random PDEs while preserving stochastic interpretability.
