Method: The method represents the solution u(t,x,Z) using a learnable Gaussian spatial dictionary, Fourier temporal features, and a generalized polynomial chaos (gPC) stochastic basis, coupled through a low-rank Canonical Polyadic (CP) tensor decomposition. Training uses a hybrid strong-form and gPC-projected residual loss. Theoretical analysis establishes: (1) separable class density in L² under mild conditions, (2) equivalence between projected residual and stochastic Galerkin constraint, (3) logarithmic dependence of mini-batch projection coefficients on gPC modes, and (4) orthogonality penalty for controlling conditioning of the spatial dictionary.

Result: S²-PINN outperforms nine baselines on four manufactured random PDE benchmarks in mean and variance accuracy as well as calibration, while using significantly fewer parameters. Additional evaluations on non-manufactured Poisson and Darcy problems, stochastic Navier-Stokes, diffusion scaling study (higher random dimensions), and two stochastic inverse problems demonstrate strong generalization capabilities.

Conclusion: Stochastic separability is an effective design principle for physics-informed neural UQ. The combination of separable representations with gPC basis and CP decomposition enables efficient and accurate uncertainty quantification for random PDEs across various applications.

Abstract: Uncertainty quantification (UQ) for random partial differential equations (PDEs) is ubiquitous in computational science and engineering. However, classical spectral solvers for this class of problems face the curse of dimensionality, and existing neural solvers often ignore the stochastic structure that makes moments and calibration tractable. We introduce a stochastic separable physics-informed neural network, dubbed S$^{2}$-PINN, that represents the solution $u(t,\mathbf{x},\mathbf{Z})$ of a random PDE with a learnable Gaussian spatial dictionary, Fourier temporal features, and a generalized polynomial chaos (gPC) stochastic basis, coupled by a low-rank Canonical Polyadic (CP) tensor decomposition core. The method is trained with a hybrid strong-form and gPC-projected residual loss. Our theoretical analysis establishes that the separable class is dense in $L^2$ under mild conditions, and the projected residual corresponds exactly to a stochastic Galerkin constraint. Furthermore, we show that mini-batch projection coefficients are logarithmically dependent on the number of gPC modes, and that the orthogonality penalty controls the conditioning of the learned spatial dictionary. Using four manufactured random PDE benchmarks, we show that S$^{2}$-PINN outperforms nine baselines in terms of mean and variance accuracy, as well as calibration, while using significantly fewer parameters. Further evaluations on non-manufactured Poisson and Darcy problems, a stochastic Navier--Stokes problem, a diffusion scaling study of higher random dimensions, and two stochastic inverse problems reveal the generalization capabilities of the proposed structure. Together, these results support stochastic separability as an effective design principle for physics-informed neural UQ. The code for the experiments can be found in https://github.com/DMax1314/s2pinn

</details>


### [413] [Training-Loss Guarantees for Muon with Finite-Step Newton--Schulz Orthogonalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03306)
*Amartya Roy,Souvik Chakraborty*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper provides the first finite-time training guarantee for the Muon optimizer on two-layer ReLU networks, addressing gaps in previous analyses that only guaranteed stationarity. The key insight is that Muon's tuned Newton-Schulz orthogonalization steps preserve alignment with the momentum buffer while bounding spectral norm, enabling convergence to any target loss without exact orthogonalization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Previous convergence analyses of Muon either assume exact orthogonalization or analyze classical Newton-Schulz polynomials, guaranteeing only stationarity. It was unresolved what Muon's five tuned Newton-Schulz steps preserve and whether that suffices to reach a prescribed training loss.

Method: The analysis uses full-batch training of a sufficiently wide two-layer ReLU network with fixed random output weights and a positive-definite limiting neural tangent kernel (NTK). The authors account for momentum accumulation before orthogonalization and the tuned finite-step update. They show the tuned Newton-Schulz map preserves alignment with the momentum buffer while bounding the update's spectral norm, and control of gradient variation near initialization transfers this alignment to the current gradient.

Result: For every momentum parameter μ ∈ [0,1), a target-dependent constant learning rate proportional to (1-μ)√ε yields a hitting-time bound of O((1-μ)^{-1}ε^{-1/2}), with other problem parameters fixed. The sufficient width is independent of both target accuracy and momentum. All 30 runs across six widths and five student initializations on a fixed teacher-student dataset reach the target loss while maintaining kernel positivity.

Conclusion: The analysis demonstrates that Muon's tuned Newton-Schulz orthogonalization preserves alignment with momentum while bounding spectral norm, ensuring descent until the target loss is reached without requiring exact orthogonalization. This provides the first non-asymptotic convergence guarantee for Muon with momentum.

Abstract: Existing convergence analyses of Muon either assume exact orthogonalization or analyze classical Newton--Schulz polynomials, and guarantee only stationarity, so it is unresolved what Muon's five tuned Newton--Schulz steps preserve and whether that suffices to reach a prescribed neural-network training loss. We establish a finite-time training guarantee that accounts for both momentum accumulation before orthogonalization and the tuned finite-step update. For full-batch training of a sufficiently wide two-layer ReLU network with fixed random output weights and a positive-definite limiting neural tangent kernel, we prove that Muon reaches any target empirical squared loss $\varepsilon>0$ with high probability over initialization. For every momentum parameter $μ\in[0,1)$, a target-dependent constant learning rate proportional to $(1-μ)\sqrt{\varepsilon}$ yields a hitting-time bound of $O((1-μ)^{-1}\varepsilon^{-1/2})$, with other problem parameters fixed. The sufficient width is independent of both target accuracy and momentum. The analysis shows that the tuned Newton--Schulz map preserves alignment with the momentum buffer while bounding the update's spectral norm. Control of gradient variation near initialization transfers this alignment to the current gradient, ensuring descent until the target is reached without requiring exact orthogonalization. Numerical experiments support these mechanisms at widths below the sufficient theoretical threshold: gradient-update alignment remains above the analytical reference, and all 30 runs across six widths and five student initializations on a fixed teacher-student dataset reach the target loss while maintaining kernel positivity.

</details>


### [414] [Cordial Learning: Distributed Training with Correlated Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03330)
*Sarah Shitrit,Ilai Bistritz*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A distributed learning framework called "cordial learning" that handles correlated data among agents, where labels depend on inputs from other agents. It shares only low-dimensional outputs between agents while training local models, and theoretically converges to global optima for linear models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing decentralized methods like federated learning ignore data correlation structure and perform poorly; centralized approaches are infeasible due to privacy and communication constraints. The problem is realistic when agents share the same environment.

Method: Cordial learning shares only low-dimensional outputs between agents while training local models to extract informative signals from peers. This induces a game where each agent's loss depends on others' models.

Result: For linear models, cordial learning converges with probability one to a globally optimal solution despite the nonconvex global objective. Experiments on structured multi-digit MNIST show effectiveness in nonlinear settings.

Conclusion: Cordial learning successfully addresses distributed learning with correlated data, providing theoretical convergence guarantees and strong empirical performance.

Abstract: We consider a distributed learning task with agents that have correlated data. Specifically, the label of an agent depends on the input of other agents for the same sample, and these inputs are also correlated. Correlated data is the reality when agents share the same environment. Existing decentralized methods, such as federated learning, ignore the structure of the problem and perform poorly on correlated data. On the other hand, centralized approaches are infeasible due to privacy and communication constraints. We introduce cordial (correlated and distributed) learning to address this gap by sharing only low-dimensional outputs between the agents while training local models to extract informative signals from peers. This distributed learning induces a game in which the loss function of each agent depends on the models of others. Assuming a linear model, we prove that cordial learning converges with probability one to a globally optimal solution, despite the nonconvex global objective. Experiments on structured multi-digit MNIST tasks demonstrate that cordial learning remains highly effective even in highly nonlinear settings.

</details>


### [415] [Follow the Winners: Conservative Policy Improvement with the Cross-Entropy Method for Critic-Free RFT](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03361)
*Joery Ariën de Vries,Neil David Lawrence,Zhenwen Dai*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces FTW (Follow the Winners), a critic-free reinforcement fine-tuning algorithm for agentic LLMs that replaces group rollouts with an ordinal filter on replay-buffer samples, offering a memory-efficient alternative to GRPO for stateful environments where repeated rollouts are impractical.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: GRPO-style methods require repeated rollouts to compute group baselines, which is impractical in stateful environments like live services or security sandboxes. Additionally, aggressive updates in long, sparsely verified trajectories can entrench noise. There is a need for a critic-free approach that works without repeated rollouts or value models.

Method: FTW adapts the cross-entropy method to RFT by using an ordinal filter on replay-buffer samples instead of group rollouts. This yields polynomial concentration in the order statistic of returns. The algorithm is derived through a control-as-inference lens, which also reveals GRPO and DPO as specific modeling choices—identifying GRPO as risk-neutral while DPO and FTW share a bounded risk-seeking offset that FTW explicitly controls.

Result: Scaled to agentic LLM post-training, FTW matches GRPO and PPO performance on Sokoban and Search-R1 baselines, demonstrating a viable trade-off from a value model or group rollouts to CPU memory.

Conclusion: FTW provides a practical solution for critic-free policy learning in stateful environments where repeated rollouts are unavailable. The control-as-inference framework reveals fundamental trade-offs: ordinal filters on samples offer variance reduction at the cost of a bounded risk-seeking offset (different from the bias-variance trade-off induced by critic models). This work bridges GRPO, DPO, and FTW under a unified theoretical lens, enabling practitioners to choose based on their specific constraints.

Abstract: Critic-free reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) for agentic large language models is often done through GRPO-style methods, which compute a group baseline over repeated rollouts to reduce target variance. However, this setup is ill-suited to agents acting in stateful environments such as live services or security sandboxes, where repeated rollouts are impractical to obtain and aggressive updates entrench the noise of long, sparsely verified trajectories. We propose \textit{Follow the Winners} (FTW), a critic-free policy-learning algorithm that adapts the cross-entropy method to RFT, replacing group rollouts with an ordinal filter on replay-buffer samples that yields polynomial concentration in the order statistic of returns. We derive FTW through a control-as-inference lens, which also recovers GRPO and DPO as specific modelling choices, identifying GRPO as risk-neutral while DPO and FTW share a bounded risk-seeking offset that FTW controls. We identify this offset as an inherent trade-off of variance reduction through ordinal filters on samples, whereas a critic model induces a different trade-off between bias and variance. Scaled to agentic LLM post-training, FTW matches GRPO and PPO on Sokoban and Search-R1 baselines, showing a viable trade-off from a value model or group rollouts to CPU memory.

</details>


### [416] [SCAD: Structured Credit Assignment and Distillation for Long-Horizon Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03372)
*Shangyang Wu,Shuai Zhao,Ziyue Zhu,Jinyang Wu,Anh Tuan Luu,Haoran Luo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SCAD is a method for training long-horizon agents that combines planning and bounded subtask execution with teacher-guided distillation. It improves macro-average accuracy by 4.48% on text tasks and 4.19% on multimodal tasks by addressing sparse reward and distillation problems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Training long-horizon agents faces two key challenges: (1) sparse terminal rewards make it difficult to assign credit to intermediate steps, and (2) on-policy distillation loses informative teacher guidance as student-generated histories grow.

Method: SCAD organizes interactions into planning and bounded subtask execution phases. It distills execution in local contexts and refines planning credit through cross-rollout subtask prefix trees. Planning receives full terminal credit while execution receives positive terminal credit and teacher guidance.

Result: SCAD improves macro-average accuracy over the strongest training baseline by 4.48 percentage points for text tasks and 4.19 points for multimodal tasks across all evaluated benchmarks.

Conclusion: SCAD effectively combines outcome-based credit assignment with teacher-guided distillation to improve planning and execution in long-horizon agents.

Abstract: Training long-horizon agents to solve complex tasks requires effective supervision over extended interaction sequences. However, sparse terminal rewards obscure intermediate contributions, while on-policy distillation can lose informative teacher guidance as student-generated histories grow. To address this problem, we introduce SCAD, which organizes interactions into planning and bounded subtask execution, distills execution in local contexts, and refines planning credit through cross-rollout subtask prefix trees, with planning receiving full terminal credit and execution receiving positive terminal credit and teacher guidance. Across all evaluated benchmarks, SCAD improves macro-average accuracy over the strongest training baseline by 4.48 percentage points for text tasks and 4.19 points for multimodal tasks. SCAD effectively combines outcome-based credit assignment with teacher-guided distillation to improve planning and execution in long-horizon agents.

</details>


### [417] [Operator-informed initialization for Fourier features physics-informed neural networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03378)
*Juan Molina,Paris Perdikaris,Mircea Petrache,Matías Courdurier,Francisco Sahli Costabal*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses spectral bias in Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) by analyzing Fourier Feature PINNs training dynamics in the Neural Tangent Kernel regime. The authors derive an evolution equation showing that frequency convergence rates depend on the differential operator's symbol and initialization weight spectral density. They propose an informative initialization strategy that adapts the initial weight distribution to the specific PDE, reducing operator-induced spectral bias and balancing convergence across frequencies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: PINNs suffer from spectral bias, where certain frequency components of the target function converge more slowly than others during training. This limitation affects the accuracy and efficiency of PINNs for solving partial differential equations (PDEs). The work aims to understand and mitigate this spectral bias phenomenon.

Method: The authors analyze training dynamics in the Neural Tangent Kernel regime and derive an explicit evolution equation to estimate residual error in the frequency domain. They investigate how convergence rates depend on the differential operator's symbol and the spectral density of initialization weights. Based on this theoretical analysis, they propose an informative initialization strategy that customizes the initial weight distribution to match the specific PDE being solved.

Result: Numerical experiments on linear and nonlinear PDEs demonstrate that the proposed initialization strategy improves learning dynamics and approximation accuracy across frequencies compared to standard initialization methods, with no additional training cost. The method successfully diminishes operator-induced spectral bias and balances convergence rates across the frequency spectrum.

Conclusion: The informative initialization strategy effectively addresses spectral bias in PINNs by tailoring initial weight distributions to the PDE structure. This provides a simple yet effective solution to improve PINN performance without increasing computational cost, making it a practical contribution to the field of physics-informed machine learning.

Abstract: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) typically exhibit spectral bias, where some frequencies of the target function converge more slowly than others. In this work, we analyze the training dynamics of Fourier Feature PINNs in the Neural Tangent Kernel regime to address this limitation. We derive an explicit evolution equation to estimate the residual error in the frequency domain, demonstrating that the convergence rate of specific frequencies is primarily governed by the product of the differential operator's symbol and the spectral density of the initialization weights. Leveraging this theoretical insight, we propose an informative initialization strategy that tailors the initial weight distribution to the specific PDE being solved. With this method, we can diminish the operator-induced spectral bias, balancing the convergence rates across the frequency spectrum and achieving better prediction accuracy. Numerical experiments on linear and nonlinear partial differential equations confirm that this initialization strategy improves learning dynamics and approximation accuracy across frequencies compared to standard initialization methods, with no additional training cost.

</details>


### [418] [Bidirectional Voronoi-biased Exploration Curriculum for Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03395)
*Juri Pfammatter,Kaixian Qu,Clemens Schwarke,Victor Klemm,Marco Hutter*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: BVER proposes a bidirectional curriculum for goal-conditioned RL that simultaneously expands start states from the goal and goals from the initial state distribution, using Voronoi biasing to explore unexplored task space and steer toward convergence. This approach addresses the exploration bottleneck in long-horizon sparse-reward tasks without requiring demonstrations or task-specific engineering.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-horizon tasks with sparse rewards create an exploration bottleneck in goal-conditioned RL: policies starting from initial states rarely reach goals, providing no learning signal. Existing solutions (reference motions, hand-designed curricula, shaped rewards) require demonstrations or task-specific engineering. Automatic curricula typically expand from only one side, forcing the full distance to be covered from that direction.

Method: BVER draws inspiration from bidirectional RRT planning. It grows start states outward from the goal and goals outward from the initial state distribution simultaneously. Both directions are biased toward unexplored task space using Voronoi partitioning, and they are steered toward each other. A single goal-conditioned policy is trained on both sets of expanded states.

Result: On point-mass mazes, quadrupedal box climbing, and robot-arm ring-on-peg transfer, BVER learns faster than all compared reference-free curricula. On box climbing, it achieves 95% success on a 0.4m box in roughly 65% fewer iterations than the best alternative, is the only curriculum to learn climbing a 0.7m box, and yields a policy robust to start, goal, and yaw variation. Without demonstrations, it approaches the sample efficiency of reference-based curricula on the 0.4m box and ring-on-peg transfer.

Conclusion: Bidirectional expansion from both ends outperforms unidirectional expansion from either side alone. BVER effectively bridges the gap between reference-free and reference-based curricula in terms of sample efficiency, while maintaining the advantage of not requiring demonstrations or task-specific engineering.

Abstract: Long-horizon tasks with sparse rewards pose an exploration bottleneck for goal-conditioned reinforcement learning: a policy started from the initial state rarely reaches the goal and receives no learning signal. Reference motions, hand-designed curricula, and shaped rewards supply this signal but require demonstrations or task-specific engineering; automatic start-state and goal curricula avoid this but typically expand from one side only, so the full distance to the target must be covered from that side. We propose the Bidirectional Voronoi-biased Exploration curriculum for Reinforcement learning (BVER), which expands from both ends at once. Inspired by bidirectional RRT planning, BVER grows start states outward from the goal and goals outward from the initial state distribution, biases both toward unexplored task space, and steers them toward each other, training one goal-conditioned policy on both. On point-mass mazes, quadrupedal box climbing, and robot-arm ring-on-peg transfer, BVER learns faster than all compared reference-free curricula. On box climbing, it reaches 95% success on a 0.4 m box in roughly 65% fewer iterations than the best of them, is the only one of them to learn to climb a 0.7 m box, and yields a policy robust to start, goal, and yaw variation. Without a demonstration, it approaches the sample efficiency of reference-based curricula on the 0.4 m box and on ring-on-peg transfer. Ablations show that expanding from both ends outperforms either direction alone.

</details>


### [419] [A Unified Framework for Bayesian Data Assimilation with Generative Models and Observation Interpolants](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03396)
*Nikolaj T. Mücke,Benjamin Sanderse*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces an observation-interpolant framework that converts pretrained generative models (stochastic interpolants, flow matching, diffusion models) into posterior samplers for Bayesian data assimilation without requiring retraining. The method unifies stochastic and deterministic sampling through a shared likelihood-score correction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Bayesian data assimilation faces challenges in sampling high-dimensional, non-Gaussian posteriors when combining model forecasts with noisy observations. Existing methods either require retraining or struggle with high-dimensional problems.

Method: The framework conditions the interpolant path on observations to obtain a likelihood-score correction to the drift or velocity. This yields SDEs and ODEs that sample the exact posterior. For practical computation, the method uses a closed-form Gaussian surrogate with bias-corrected mean and covariance inflated by the model's source covariance, employing Jacobian-free and ensemble-shared approximations for tractability in high dimensions.

Result: The method is evaluated on linear-Gaussian dynamics, stochastic 2D Navier-Stokes, and urban airflow problems with up to O(10^4) degrees of freedom, demonstrating effective posterior sampling.

Conclusion: The observation-interpolant framework provides a unified approach for transforming pretrained generative models into posterior samplers, offering a practical solution for high-dimensional Bayesian data assimilation problems without retraining requirements.

Abstract: Bayesian data assimilation combines model forecasts with noisy observations, but sampling high-dimensional, non-Gaussian posteriors remains challenging. We introduce an observation-interpolant framework that turns pretrained stochastic interpolant, flow matching, and diffusion models into posterior samplers without retraining. Conditioning the interpolant path on observations yields a shared likelihood-score correction to the drift or velocity, unifying stochastic and deterministic posterior sampling. The resulting SDEs and ODEs sample the exact posterior when the intermediate likelihood score is known. For practical computation, we approximate this score using a closed-form Gaussian surrogate with a bias-corrected mean and covariance inflated by the model's source covariance. Jacobian-free and ensemble-shared approximations make the method tractable in high dimensions. We evaluate the framework on linear-Gaussian dynamics, stochastic two-dimensional Navier-Stokes, and urban airflow with up to $O(10^4)$ degrees of freedom.

</details>


### [420] [16-bit Precision of Convolutional Neural Networks on Microcontroller Units for 8-bit Costs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03402)
*Rui Liu,Benjamin Paaßen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: W16A16 is a 16-bit quantization method for deploying deep neural networks on Armv7E-M microcontrollers, achieving 10x lower quantization errors than 8-bit schemes while maintaining similar or better inference speed and energy consumption.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deploying deep neural networks on edge hardware (microcontrollers) requires highly efficient inference schemes that retain high accuracy while minimizing computational resources and energy consumption.

Method: The paper proposes W16A16, a high-precision (16-bit) quantization method. It analyzes the Armv7E-M architecture and explains the performance advantages of 16-bit approaches. The method is evaluated on both regression and classification tasks by measuring quantization errors, inference time, and energy consumption.

Result: W16A16 achieves approximately 10 times lower quantization errors compared to 8-bit quantization schemes while achieving similar or better inference times and energy consumption on Armv7E-M microcontrollers.

Conclusion: 16-bit quantization (W16A16) provides a superior trade-off between precision and efficiency for MCU deployment, offering significantly reduced quantization errors without sacrificing speed or energy efficiency.

Abstract: To deploy deep neural networks on edge hardware, highly efficient inference schemes are necessary that retain high accuracy. This work presents W16A16, a high precision (16-bit), fast speed, low energy quantization method. On a widely applied microcontroller architecture Armv7E-M, our proposed approach achieves faster speed and lower energy consumption on layer- and model-level compared to alternative quantization schemes. We analyze the architecture of Armv7E-M, explain the underlying principles behind the performance advantages of 16-bit approaches, and evaluate the empiric quantization errors for regression and classification tasks, as well as empiric time- and energy consumption in MCU deployment. We observe ca.\ 10 times lower quantization errors compared to 8-bit quantization schemes while achieving similar or better inference times and energy consumption.

</details>


### [421] [AIBL: Augmented Instance-Based Learning with Structured Memory and Neural Embeddings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03413)
*Radha Poovendran,Andrea Stocco,Linda Bushnell*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: AIBL (Augmented Instance-Based Learning) extends classical IBLT by replacing symbolic matching with neural embedding similarity for high-dimensional sequential data, while preserving instance storage, activation-weighted retrieval, and utility blending. It introduces a three-store memory architecture (active, forgotten, surprise) with a graduation algorithm to handle novelty detection and concept drift.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Sequential learning systems face high-dimensional inputs whose distribution changes over time. Classical IBLT uses symbolic knowledge representation with hand-specified matching rules, which is inadequate for text, images, transaction vectors, and user-item histories that require learned similarity rather than symbolic matching.

Method: AIBL generalizes symbolic situation matching to neural embedding similarity while retaining core IBLT mechanisms. It organizes memory into three stores: active (well-matched cases), forgotten (discarded cases), and surprise (weakly matched, out-of-distribution, or corner-case observations). An observation-driven graduation algorithm promotes recurring surprise instances to active memory, enabling adaptation to concept drift. Evaluation was conducted on five ML tasks and three controlled simulation tasks.

Result: AIBL improves accuracy by 6 to 17 percentage points compared to classical IBLT variants and task-specific baselines. The results demonstrate where vector-space retrieval outperforms symbolic matching and how the memory mechanisms govern novelty detection, cold-start handling, drift adaptation, and reward learning.

Conclusion: The vector-space approach successfully bridges symbolic case-based reasoning with learned representations, enabling effective handling of high-dimensional sequential data. The surprise memory and graduation mechanism provide principled approaches to novelty detection and concept drift adaptation, making AIBL suitable for real-world sequential learning under distribution shift.

Abstract: Sequential learning systems often make decisions from accumulated experience while receiving high-dimensional inputs whose distribution may change over time. Instance-Based Learning Theory (IBLT) provides a principled case-based framework for such settings through stored situation-decision-utility instances, partial matching, activation, and blending. IBLT relies on symbolic knowledge representation in dictionary-like formats, but text, images, transaction vectors, and user-item histories often require learned similarity rather than hand-specified matching rules. In this paper, we introduce AIBL (Augmented Instance-Based Learning), an instance-learning model formulated in a learned vector space for high- dimensional sequential data. AIBL generalizes symbolic situation matching to neural embedding similarity while retaining instance storage, activation- weighted retrieval, and utility blending. The AIBL model organizes memory into active, forgotten, and surprise stores. Surprise memory separates weakly matched, possible out-of-distribution, or corner-case observations from active memory, reducing forced fitting to the nearest available cases. An observation-driven graduation algorithm promotes recurring surprise instances to active memory, allowing the memory to incorporate repeated novel patterns that may arise under concept drift. We evaluate the same implementation on five machine learning tasks and three controlled simulation tasks, comparing AIBL with classical IBLT variants and task-specific baselines where appropriate. AIBL improves accuracy by 6 to 17 percentage points. The results show where vector-space retrieval improves over symbolic matching and how the added memory mechanisms govern novelty detection, cold-start handling, drift adaptation, and reward learning under the tested protocols.

</details>


### [422] [Rethinking Epistemic Uncertainty in Node Classification through Information Growth](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03418)
*Emma Meneghini,Francesco Ferrini,Bruno Lepri,Andrea Passerini,Veronica Lachi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether epistemic uncertainty in graph evidential deep learning (EDL) methods decreases as more information about the data-generating process (DGP) becomes available. The authors propose a statistical framework with an information-growth protocol and consistency criterion, and demonstrate that existing EDL methods fail this consistency test. They propose graph bootstrap ensembles as a remedy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The core problem is that while epistemic uncertainty should theoretically decrease as more information about the DGP becomes available, existing graph EDL methods for node classification only evaluate epistemic uncertainty on downstream tasks (like out-of-distribution detection) but never test its actual reducibility under information growth. This is a fundamental gap in the literature.

Method: The authors introduce: (1) an information-growth experimental protocol, (2) a consistency criterion for epistemic predictors, and (3) projective graph DGPs to ensure growing graphs provide coherent observations of the same underlying process. They also propose graph bootstrap ensembles that capture both data uncertainty (via graph resampling) and procedural uncertainty (via randomized training).

Result: EDL methods do not explicitly estimate data uncertainty from a single finite graph observation and instead regulate epistemic uncertainty through model hyperparameters, which precludes consistency. Under controlled information-growth experiments, graph bootstrap ensembles demonstrate epistemic uncertainty reduction beyond standard deep ensembles.

Conclusion: Graph bootstrap ensembles serve as candidate consistent epistemic predictors under information growth, offering a promising alternative to standard EDL methods for reliable uncertainty quantification in graph learning.

Abstract: Epistemic uncertainty should decrease as additional information about the data-generating process (DGP) becomes available to the predictor. Yet, existing graph evidential deep learning (EDL) methods for node classification typically construct epistemic uncertainty from graph-specific properties and evaluate it on downstream tasks such as out-of-distribution detection, which do not test its reducibility as information about the DGP increases. To make reducibility directly testable, we introduce a statistical framework for studying epistemic uncertainty under information growth. Our framework specifies an information-growth experimental protocol and a consistency criterion for epistemic predictors, while using projective graph DGPs to ensure that growing graphs, which in general need not provide increasing information about the same DGP, constitute coherent observations of the same underlying process. We show that EDL methods do not explicitly estimate data uncertainty arising from a single finite graph observation and instead regulate epistemic uncertainty through model hyperparameters, precluding consistency, as corroborated by controlled information-growth experiments. As an alternative, we propose graph bootstrap ensembles, capturing both data and procedural uncertainty through graph resampling and randomized training. Under the same experimental protocol, these ensembles exhibit epistemic uncertainty reduction beyond standard deep ensembles. These findings support bootstrap ensembles as candidate consistent epistemic predictors under information growth.

</details>


### [423] [Deep Bayesian REFoCUS](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03419)
*Simon Penninga,Ruud van Sloun*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes Deep Bayesian REFoCUS, a deep learning approach that formulates ultrasound multistatic recovery as a Bayesian inference problem using a deep generative prior. The method addresses rank-deficient scenarios where traditional linear REFoCUS fails, while also providing uncertainty quantification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Classical linear REFoCUS decoders fail in rank-deficient regimes, which occurs when working with arbitrary transmit sequences in ultrasound multistatic imaging. There is a need for a method that can handle these challenging scenarios while also providing uncertainty estimates.

Method: The approach formulates ultrasound multistatic recovery as a Bayesian inference problem and trains a deep generative prior on multistatic data sets. This prior is used to tackle the rank-deficient regime where classical linear methods fail.

Result: Deep Bayesian REFoCUS outperforms linear baselines across all regimes of rank-deficiency and noise levels. It regresses to linear decoding when inversion is exact and expresses uncertainty in the null space of acquisitions, whereas linear decoders only provide point estimates. The method shows strong generalization from simulation to in-vivo data without fine-tuning.

Conclusion: The deep generative Bayesian approach successfully addresses limitations of linear methods in ultrasound imaging, providing both improved recovery in rank-deficient scenarios and valuable uncertainty quantification, with excellent generalization capability from simulated to real in-vivo data.

Abstract: In this work we formulate ultrasound multistatic recovery from arbitrary transmit sequences as a Bayesian inference problem. To that end, we train a deep generative prior on multistatic data sets to tackle the rank-deficient regime in which classical linear REFoCUS decoders fail. This appproach, which we term Deep Bayesian REFoCUS, outperforms the linear baselines for all regimes of rank-deficiency and noise levels, and regresses to linear decoding when inversion is exact. The model also expresses uncertainty in the null space of the acquisitions, whereas the linear REFoCUS decoders only provide point estimates. Finally, we analyze the impact of distribution shift between simulation and in-vivo acquisitions, showing remarkable generalization ability without any fine-tuning or adaptation.

</details>


### [424] [OptiSelect: How does the Optimizer Shape Data Curriculum?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03432)
*Simin Fan,Alireza Abdollahpoorrostam,Martin Jaggi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces OptiSelect, an optimizer-aware data selection paradigm for LLM pretraining that accounts for how the optimizer transforms gradients before updating model parameters. The key finding is that diagonal-adaptive optimizers (AdamW, Sophia) enable better data selection than sign-based (Lion) or polar-tangential (Muon) optimizers due to superior "discriminability" in utility scores.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current online data selection methods evaluate candidates based on raw gradients, but ignore how optimizers reshape gradients before parameter updates. This paper argues that principled data selection should account for the optimizer step to maximize training efficiency.

Method: The authors formalize "optimizer-aware selection" as OptiSelect and develop theoretical analysis using a "selection gain principle" based on the discriminability of optimizer-induced utility scores. They prove theoretical bounds comparing different optimizer classes (sign-based, polar-tangential, diagonal-adaptive) and validate empirically on 124M and 720M parameter models.

Result: Theory shows sign-based (Lion) and polar-tangential (Muon) preconditioners suffer from "discriminability collapse" that limits selection gains, while diagonal-adaptive optimizers (AdamW, Sophia) have strictly better upper bounds. Experiments confirm AdamW's diagonal-adaptive scoring geometry remains strongest even when Muon is used as the optimizer. Benefits persist under data rephrasing.

Conclusion: This work provides theoretical foundations for co-designing optimizers and data selection in LLM pretraining. The key insight is that diagonal-adaptive preconditioners enable more effective online data selection, offering practical guidance for maximizing pretraining efficiency.

Abstract: Online data selection has demonstrated substantial efficiency gains for LLM pretraining by training on the most valuable candidates within each batch. Since a candidate's value is realized through its effective model update, principled selection should account for the optimizer step, which reshapes the raw gradient before it updates model parameters. We formalize this optimizer-aware selection paradigm as OptiSelect and present the first systematic study of how the optimizer shapes data selection. Our theory establishes a selection gain principle in which the advantage of online selection is governed by the discriminability of the optimizer-induced utility scores. We prove that sign-based and polar-tangential preconditioners of Lion and Muon would suffer from a discriminability collapse which caps attainable gains from OptiSelect, whereas diagonal-adaptive optimizers such as AdamW and Sophia admit strictly better upper bounds. The proposed principle also yields a quantitative derivation of the optimal candidate oversampling ratio. Pretraining experiments on 124M and 720M models are consistent with our theoretical analysis and show that AdamW's diagonal-adaptive scoring geometry remains the strongest scoring geometry even with Muon as optimizer. We further demonstrate that OptiSelect retains its benefits under data rephrasing, a technique used in modern data processing pipelines. Our findings provide theoretical foundations and practical guidance for co-designing optimizers and data selection in LLM pretraining.

</details>


### [425] [Causal Representation Learning with Instantaneous and Lagged Relations via Nonstationarity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03452)
*Tatsuya Yamada,Hiroshi Morioka,Yoshinobu Kawahara*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper presents iCReN, a framework for causal representation learning in time-series data that identifies latent states and their causal relations (both lagged and instantaneous) while accounting for nonstationarity, using contrastive learning with auxiliary variables.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing methods for causal representation learning in time-series data struggle to jointly handle lagged causal relations across observation intervals, instantaneous causal effects within intervals, and nonstationarity. This gap limits the ability to accurately model complex temporal causal dynamics.

Method: The paper establishes sufficient conditions for identifying latent states (up to component permutation and invertible transformations) and their causal structures using an observed auxiliary variable associated with changes in transition-noise distributions. Based on this, iCReN is proposed using contrastive learning with discrete or continuous auxiliary variables to learn latent representations and estimate instantaneous and lagged causal structures.

Result: Experiments demonstrate accurate recovery of latent states and both instantaneous and lagged causal structures on synthetic data. The learned representations also show utility for downstream forecasting on real-world data.

Conclusion: iCReN effectively learns latent representations and estimates causal structures from nonstationary time-series data, providing a principled approach to modeling complex temporal causal relationships.

Abstract: Causal representation learning for time-series data aims to identify latent states and their causal relations from observations. In this setting, an important challenge is to model both lagged causal relations across observation intervals and faster causal effects that appear as instantaneous relations within an interval, while accounting for nonstationarity in time-series data. However, methods that jointly handle these causal relations and nonstationarity remain limited. To address this gap, we establish sufficient conditions for identifying latent states up to component permutation and component-wise invertible transformations, and their instantaneous and lagged causal structures up to the same permutation, using an observed auxiliary variable, such as time or a condition label, associated with changes in transition-noise distributions. Based on these results, we propose iCReN, a framework that uses contrastive learning with discrete or continuous auxiliary variables to learn latent representations and estimate their instantaneous and lagged causal structures. Experiments demonstrate accurate recovery of latent states and both instantaneous and lagged causal structures on synthetic data and the utility of the learned representations for downstream forecasting on real-world data.

</details>


### [426] [Measure Less, Know More: Self-Supervised Test-Time Feature Acquisition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03454)
*Eeshaan Jain,Linus Bleistein,Bart Deplancke,Charlotte Bunne*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ECHO-k is a task-agnostic, self-supervised method for sequential modality selection in multimodal learning, using pretrained foundation model representations as proxy targets to guide reinforcement learning policies for cost-effective test-time deployment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The core problem is that acquiring all modalities in multimodal learning is often prohibitively costly and redundant at test time, yet selecting informative modalities is challenging when the downstream task is unknown. Current methods require either labeled data or knowledge of the downstream task, limiting practical applicability.

Method: The method uses internal pretrained representations from foundation models as proxy targets that summarize cross-modal information. Theoretical guarantees are provided in a stylized linear setting, which motivate a reinforcement learning (RL) policy for sequential modality selection. The approach is task-agnostic and label-free.

Result: ECHO-k consistently improves budgeted downstream performance across diverse foundation-model backends compared to task-agnostic and label-free acquisition baselines.

Conclusion: This work provides a principled route to cost-aware test-time deployment for any multimodal system where measurements are expensive or time-constrained, with downstream tasks unknown a priori.

Abstract: Recent progress in multimodal, high-dimensional learning has enabled foundation models to process heterogeneous, large-scale data. However, at test time, acquiring all features or modalities can be prohibitively costly and often redundant. Sequentially selecting informative modalities is therefore critical, yet challenging when the downstream task or prediction target is unknown. To this end, we introduce ECHO-$k$, a task-agnostic and self-supervised learning principle for modality acquisition: we use a deep model's internal pretrained representations (e.g., from a foundation model) as proxy targets that summarize cross-modal information. We provide theoretical guarantees in a stylized linear setting that motivate a reinforcement learning (RL) policy for sequential modality selection. Across task-agnostic and label-free acquisition baselines, ECHO-$k$ consistently improves budgeted downstream performance across diverse foundation-model backends. Our method provides a principled route to cost-aware test-time deployment, with implications for any multimodal system where measurements are expensive or time-constrained, and downstream tasks unknown a priori.

</details>


### [427] [Beyond Random Splits: Evaluating Drug-Target Affinity Models Under Chemically and Biologically Motivated Distribution Shifts Copy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03456)
*Minjae Chung,Clara Li,Malar Paavai Muthukumaran,Shaunna Wang,Aniket Ramkrishnan Iyer,Shaun Qien Yeau Tan,Harinishree Sathu,Micky C. Nnamdi,J. Ben Tamo,Benoit Louis Marteau,May Dongmei Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates how the choice of distribution shift (evaluation scenario) affects which drug-target affinity (DTA) prediction model appears best. The authors compare a baseline CNN model with 12 controlled architectures combining different drug representations and ESM-2 protein embeddings under four different out-of-distribution (OOD) scenarios: scaffold, fingerprint-cluster, protein-cluster, and dual shifts. They find that model rankings change dramatically depending on the evaluation scenario (Kendall's tau ranges from 0.79 to -0.55), demonstrating that architecture selection should depend on the expected deployment scenario rather than just average performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: DTA models are typically compared under a single data split, but real-world deployment may require extrapolation to new chemical series, new protein targets, or both. The authors question whether the distribution shift used for evaluation changes which architecture appears best, as this has significant implications for practical model selection.

Method: The authors curated 718,800 unique drug-protein pairs from ChEMBL and BindingDB datasets. They compared a Morgan-fingerprint + protein-CNN baseline with 12 controlled architectures combining four drug representations with three ESM-2 interaction modes. Evaluation was performed under four OOD scenarios: scaffold split, fingerprint-cluster split, protein-cluster split, and dual (both chemical and target) split. They used held-out evaluation, repeated seeds, and group-aware bootstrap analysis to validate findings.

Result: Mean validation RMSE increased substantially across shifts: from 0.950/0.945 under scaffold and fingerprint-cluster OOD to 1.299/1.321 under protein-cluster and dual OOD. Model rankings showed high agreement between scaffold and fingerprint-cluster OOD (tau = 0.79), but agreement with scaffold OOD dropped under protein OOD (tau = 0.39) and reversed under dual OOD (tau = -0.55). The size-matched control experiment supported these conclusions.

Conclusion: Architecture selection for DTA prediction depends critically on the form of extrapolation required (chemical shift, target shift, or both), not just on average error or training-set size. Current DTA benchmarks should match the specific chemical and target shifts expected at deployment to provide meaningful model comparisons.

Abstract: Drug-target affinity (DTA) prediction is widely used to prioritize candidate compounds before costly experimental screening. DTA models are often compared under a single data split, even though deployment may require extrapolation to new chemical series, new protein targets, or both. We ask whether the distribution shift used for evaluation changes which architecture appears best. We curate 718,800 unique drug-protein pairs from the ChEMBL and BindingDB datasets. We compare a Morgan-fingerprint + protein-CNN baseline with 12 controlled architectures that combine four drug representations with three ESM-2 interaction modes. Mean validation RMSE increases from 0.950 and 0.945 under scaffold and fingerprint-cluster OOD to 1.299 and 1.321 under protein-cluster and dual OOD. Model rankings are similar across the two chemical shifts (tau = 0.79), but agreement with scaffold OOD falls under protein OOD (tau = 0.39) and reverses under dual OOD (tau = -0.55). Held-out evaluation, repeated seeds, group-aware bootstrap analysis, and a size-matched control support the same conclusion: architecture selection depends on the form of extrapolation, not only on average error or training-set size. DTA benchmarks should therefore match the chemical and target shifts expected at deployment.

</details>


### [428] [Single or Multiple Policies for Phase-Structured Reinforcement Learning?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03475)
*Guilhem Loussouarn,Nancy Nayak,Kin K. Leung*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates reinforcement learning in non-stationary environments with phase-structured dynamics. It compares single shared policies (with state augmentation) versus multi-policy approaches, showing they are theoretically equivalent but differ in practice due to function approximation, learning dynamics, and sample efficiency. A regime-based method is proposed to determine which approach performs better based on phase characteristics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work observed that multi-policy approaches can outperform single shared policies in non-stationary RL problems, but the reasons were unclear. This work aims to understand when and why each approach is preferable in practice.

Method: The paper employs: (1) Theoretical analysis showing equivalence between shared policy and multi-policy solutions; (2) A regime-based phase decomposition method based on transient system dynamics duration relative to quasi-stationary periods; (3) Numerical experiments across different non-stationary RL problems.

Result: Four hypotheses were validated: (a) longer phase durations favor multi-policies; (b) increased heterogeneity between phases burdens single policies; (c) multi-policies require sufficient data per phase; (d) environment-specific transition dynamics between phases influence policy preference.

Conclusion: The choice between single shared policy and multi-policy approaches depends on phase duration, heterogeneity level, data availability, and transition dynamics. The proposed regime-based method can guide practitioners in selecting the appropriate approach for their specific non-stationary RL problem.

Abstract: Many reinforcement-learning (RL) problems are non-stationary yet structured and can be decomposed into phases, each with its own transition probabilities and reward functions. When the phase sequence is known, the common solution augments the state with information to satisfy the Markovian property and applies standard RL techniques. However, prior work finds that the multi-policy approach for different phases can outperform a single state-augmented policy shared among the phases, for reasons that remain unclear. In this work, we first show that the shared policy can theoretically achieve performance of any multi-policy solution. However, whether a multi-policy solution can perform better than the corresponding single shared policy in practice depends on function approximation, learning and optimization processes, as well as, for multi-policy solutions, the sample efficiency and loss of continuity from one policy to another. We propose a regime-based phase decomposition method to identify which policy can provide better performance. The method is based on consideration of the duration of transient system dynamics relative to the duration of the quasi-stationary period. Numerical experiments are conducted with different non-stationary RL problems to validate our four major hypotheses: (a) longer phase durations favor multi-policies, (b) the heterogeneity between phases increases the burden on single policy, (c) multi-policies need sufficient data for each phase, and (d) environment-specific transition dynamics between phases can affect which policy is preferable.

</details>


### [429] [Metropolis-Hastings Dominates Importance Resampling for Policy Composition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03480)
*Alexey Kurennoy,Ramil Yarullin,Fergal Reid*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper addresses a problem in LLM post-training where exploring trade-offs between multiple rewards is expensive via retraining. The authors analyze a decoding-time policy composition method that combines reward-specific policies at inference time, focusing on correcting sampling bias in standard next-token probability combination methods. They prove that Metropolis-Hastings (MH) correction outperforms SIR (sampling-importance-resampling) in terms of convex f-divergences for any rollout budget, and provide additional bounds on MH's improvement over uncorrected decoders.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Retraining LLMs for each reward trade-off is computationally expensive. While decoding-time policy composition offers a solution by combining policies at inference time, standard implementations suffer from sampling bias when combining next-token probabilities. The authors aim to analyze and improve this correction method.

Method: The authors analyze an iterative correction method based on Independence Metropolis-Hastings (MH). They compare MH with sampling-importance-resampling (SIR) using the same rollout budget, evaluating using convex f-divergences. They also derive lower bounds on MH's improvement and characterize sampling error in two asymptotic regimes: when reward-specific policies approach agreement, and when log ratio fluctuations increase (as in long responses).

Result: The main result shows MH produces an output distribution at least as close to the target as SIR for every rollout budget, measured by every convex f-divergence. Additional results include: a lower bound on MH's improvement over uncorrected decoder in a consensus objective, and characterization of sampling error in two asymptotic regimes (policy agreement and wide log ratio fluctuations). Experiments are provided in both enumerable and LLM-scale settings.

Conclusion: The paper provides theoretical guarantees for MH-based correction in decoding-time policy composition, demonstrating its superiority over SIR and establishing bounds on its performance. This work offers a principled approach to adjusting reward trade-offs in LLMs without expensive retraining.

Abstract: Post-training a large language model (LLM) often requires exploring trade-offs between multiple rewards, but retraining for each trade-off is expensive. Decoding-time policy composition allows these trade-offs to be adjusted by combining reward-specific policies at inference time. This composition targets a weighted product of the policies' probabilities over complete responses, but standard implementations combine their next-token probabilities, generally introducing sampling bias. We analyze a known iterative correction based on independence Metropolis-Hastings (MH). Our main result shows that, for every rollout budget, MH produces an output distribution at least as close to the target as sampling-importance-resampling (SIR) with the same budget, as measured by every convex f-divergence. We also derive a lower bound on MH's improvement over the uncorrected decoder in a consensus objective measuring agreement with the supplied policies. We further characterize the correction's sampling error in two asymptotic regimes: when the reward-specific policies approach agreement, and when the log ratio between target and uncorrected-decoder probabilities fluctuates increasingly widely, as can happen for long responses. We complement our analysis with experiments in enumerable and LLM-scale settings.

</details>


### [430] [Dual-Context Analog Retrieval for Time Series Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03491)
*Jung Min Choi,Ngoc Son Le,Ibram Abdelmalak,Vijaya Krishna Yalavarthi,Lars Schmidt-Thieme*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DuoTS is a dual-context time series forecasting model that combines a base forecast with patch-wise refinement using two views: current context (recent dynamics) and detail context (retrieved similar past states with their continuations).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing long-term forecasting models map look-back window to full horizon in a single pass, which doesn't explicitly identify relevant historical states for different future segments. Analog forecasting retrieves similar past states but relies on single nearest matches that can be unreliable, and overlapping patches produce redundant candidates.

Method: DuoTS uses a parallel patch encoder and linear prediction head to produce a base forecast, then progressively refines it one future patch at a time. Each refinement combines: (1) current context that attends to recent tokens capturing latest dynamics, and (2) detail context providing distinct retrieved analogs with their subsequent trajectories. The patch-wise refinement allows balancing views across forecast horizon and associating each future segment with appropriate evidence based on temporal distance.

Result: Experiments on multiple real-world datasets show DuoTS achieves state-of-the-art performance. Ablations confirm the contribution of each context. The refinement mechanism is model-agnostic and can be integrated into existing forecasting models.

Conclusion: DuoTS successfully addresses limitations of single-pass forecasting and unreliable analog retrieval by using a dual-context approach with progressive patch-wise refinement, enabling better exploitation of historical evidence appropriate to different temporal distances from the present.

Abstract: Most long-term time-series forecasting models map the look-back window directly to the full horizon in a single pass. While efficient, this design does not explicitly identify which historical states are most relevant to different future segments or exploit what followed those states. Analog forecasting addresses this by retrieving past states similar to the present and using their observed continuations, but single nearest matches can be unreliable and overlapping patches may produce redundant candidates. We propose DuoTS, a Dual-Context Time Series forecasting model that uses retrieved evidence without relying on it exclusively. DuoTS first produces a base forecast with a parallel patch encoder and linear prediction head, then progressively refines it one future patch at a time. Each refinement combines two views: a current context that attends to recent tokens and captures the latest dynamics, and a detail context that provides distinct retrieved analogs together with their subsequent trajectories. Patch-wise refinement allows the model to balance these views across the forecast horizon and associate each future segment with evidence appropriate to its temporal distance from the present. Experiments on multiple real-world datasets show that DuoTS achieves state-of-the-art performance, while ablations confirm the contribution of each context. The refinement mechanism is also model-agnostic, requiring only an encoded look-back window and the future-patch position, and can therefore be integrated into existing forecasting models.

</details>


### [431] [Most-Recent Anchoring with Recurrent Ordering for Time Series Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03494)
*Jung Min Choi,Ngoc Son Le,Ibram Abdelmalak,Vijaya Krishna Yalavarthi,Lars Schmidt-Thieme*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MARO is a novel time series forecasting model that processes patches from most recent to oldest, using the most recent patch as an anchor to initialize and condition the latent state at each step. This recurrent ordering approach allows older patches to be folded into representations centered on recent evidence, while a single shared module introduces no additional parameters for extended look-back windows.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current long-term forecasting models process all patches in a look-back window using the same fixed stack, giving equal computational depth to older contextual patches and recent evidence. However, information closest to the forecast and more distant context do not contribute equally. Uniform processing fails to express this distinction in the architecture.

Method: MARO processes the look-back window from the most recent patch to the oldest. The most recent patch serves as the anchor, initializing the latent state and conditioning each subsequent step. Older patches are folded into representations centered on recent evidence. A single shared module is reused at every step, so extending the scan further into the past introduces no additional parameters. Intermediate states retained during the scan allow the forecast head to weigh short and long portions of the history separately.

Result: MARO achieves state-of-the-art performance on both long-term and short-term forecasting tasks across multiple real-world time series datasets. Ablation studies examine the contribution of the main architectural components.

Conclusion: The recency-based ordering through recurrent refinement effectively distinguishes between recent and distant information in time series forecasting, providing a parameter-efficient approach that scales with look-back window length while maintaining superior forecasting accuracy.

Abstract: Long-term forecasting models commonly process all patches in a look-back window using the same fixed stack. Older contextual patches and recent evidence therefore receive the same computational depth. Yet the information closest to the forecast and the more distant context do not contribute equally. Uniform processing leaves this distinction unexpressed in the architecture. We propose MARO, a Most-Recent Anchoring with Recurrent Ordering model that processes the look-back window from the most recent patch to the oldest. The most recent patch serves as the anchor. It initializes the latent state and conditions each subsequent step, so older patches are folded into a representation that remains centered on recent evidence. A single shared module is reused at every step, so extending the scan further into the past introduces no additional parameters. Intermediate states retained during the scan allow the forecast head to weigh short and long portions of the history separately. This expresses recency through the order of recurrent refinement. Extensive experiments across multiple real-world time series datasets show that MARO achieves state-of-the-art performance on both long-term and short-term forecasting tasks.Ablation studies examine the contribution of the main architectural components.

</details>


### [432] [Below what training size do deep tabular generators stop beating trivial baselines? A preregistered benchmark on a size ladder of clinical and standard datasets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03500)
*Shivam Shrivastava*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper runs a large-scale benchmark (2,220 runs) comparing 7 tabular data generators across dataset sizes from 200 to 20,000 rows, plus 4 real clinical datasets. The key finding is that deep generative models (CTGAN, TVAE, TabDDPM) never meaningfully beat trivial baselines at small data sizes, and rankings on small datasets don't transfer well to real clinical data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deep tabular generative models are benchmarked on large datasets (tens of thousands of rows), but clinical datasets typically have only hundreds of rows. The authors wanted to identify where performance diverges between these two regimes and whether benchmarks on subsampled large datasets can represent small clinical datasets.

Method: Size-ladder benchmark: 8 public datasets subsampled from 200 to 20,000 training rows, 7 generators (independent marginals, Gaussian copula, SMOTE, unconditional SMOTE, CTGAN, TVAE, TabDDPM), fixed 20-trial tuning budget, 5 evaluation seeds, plus 4 natively small clinical datasets at true size. Primary metric: AUROC of fixed classifiers trained on synthetic and tested on real data.

Result: In 23 of 24 (dataset, deep model) pairs, no deep model ever beats the best trivial baseline beyond seed noise. Best baseline wins 40 of 49 (dataset, size) cells. Rankings are MORE stable at smaller sizes (contrary to prediction), with mean Kendall tau 0.806 above 5,000 rows. In 81% of cells, the gap between top two methods is smaller than seed variation. Rankings on natively small clinical datasets agree only moderately with subsampled large ones (mean tau 0.57 to 0.64).

Conclusion: Deep generative models provide no practical benefit over trivial baselines for small tabular datasets. The gap between methods is generally smaller than random seed variation, suggesting the field may be overestimating method differences. Critically, subsampled large datasets cannot substitute for natively small clinical datasets, questioning the validity of current benchmark practices.

Abstract: Deep tabular generative models are benchmarked on datasets with tens of thousands of rows; clinical datasets have hundreds. We preregistered and ran a size-ladder benchmark to find where the two regimes diverge: 8 public datasets subsampled from 200 to 20,000 training rows, seven generators (independent marginals, Gaussian copula, SMOTE, unconditional SMOTE, CTGAN, TVAE, TabDDPM) with a fixed 20-trial tuning budget and 5 evaluation seeds, plus 4 natively small clinical datasets at true size, for 2,220 committed runs in total. The primary metric is the AUROC of fixed classifiers trained on synthetic and tested on real data. In 23 of 24 (dataset, deep model) pairs no deep model ever beats the best trivial baseline by more than seed noise, at any training size we measured. The best baseline wins 40 of 49 (dataset, size) cells. Our preregistered prediction that the deep models' ranking would be unstable at small sizes is falsified: mean Kendall tau between adjacent rungs below 5,000 rows is 0.806, above our 0.8 threshold, and stability is highest at the smallest sizes rather than lowest. One caveat bounds all of this: in 81% of cells the gap between the top two methods is smaller than the variation between seeds. Finally, method rankings on natively small clinical datasets agree only moderately with rankings on subsampled large ones (mean tau 0.57 to 0.64), which questions whether a subsampled large dataset can stand in for a small one. All 2,220 result files, the preregistration and its hash, and the code that regenerates every figure and number from those files are public.

</details>


### [433] [Certified Mechanistic Edits: Behavioral Guarantees for Skill Removal and Preservation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03502)
*Md Sazid Uddin,Md. Khairul Alam Mazumder,M. F. Mridha*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces certified behavioral edits for neural networks, proving that mechanistic edits (ablations, weight edits, activation steering) can remove a specific skill while preserving another for every input in a continuous region. The approach uses sound bound propagation to certify edits over embedding-space regions, extending from toy ReLU networks to standard softmax + LayerNorm transformers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current mechanistic edit validation relies only on testing, which cannot cover an entire continuous region of inputs. The authors aim to bridge interpretability and verification by certifying the behavioral effect of edits: proving that disabling a circuit removes one skill while provably preserving another for every input in a region—a feature non-interference guarantee in the information-flow-security sense.

Method: The paper proposes certifying behavioral effects of edits through sound bound propagation, which handles roughly 9x the input-perturbation dimension compared to exact solvers. The approach proves removal and preservation guarantees over continuous embedding-space regions, from toy ReLU networks up to standard softmax + LayerNorm transformers.

Result: The method demonstrates certified edits on small standard-architecture networks, proving removal and preservation over continuous embedding-space regions. A key theoretical result proves that no finite deterministic black-box test can certify removal—exhibiting an edit that passes exhaustive testing yet provably fails on a survivor pocket that can be made arbitrarily small.

Conclusion: The work establishes a framework for certifying behavioral effects of mechanistic edits, though with important limitations: guarantees apply to small standard-architecture networks, and the approach presupposes that the target skill admits a decidable specification—a property that real-world harms may not possess.

Abstract: Mechanistic edits (ablations, weight edits, activation steering) are the standard tools for unlearning a harmful capability from a neural network while preserving useful ones. Current approaches validate their effects only by testing, which can never cover an entire continuous region of inputs. Prior work at the interpretability-verification boundary certifies descriptions of a model: what a circuit computes, or whether it faithfully explains the whole. We instead certify the behavioral effect of an edit: that disabling a circuit removes one skill and provably preserves another, for every input in a region; a feature non-interference guarantee in the information-flow-security sense. We demonstrate such certified edits from toy ReLU networks up to a standard softmax + LayerNorm transformer, proving removal and preservation over continuous embedding-space regions and reaching roughly 9x the input-perturbation dimension an exact solver can handle by switching to sound bound propagation. Furthermore, we prove that no finite deterministic black-box test can certify removal, exhibiting an edit that passes exhaustive testing yet provably fails on a survivor pocket that can be made arbitrarily small. Guarantees hold on small, standard-architecture networks and, like any removal claim, presuppose that the target skill admits a decidable specification, a property which real-world harms may not have.

</details>


### [434] [Getting Your Guidance Weights Right in diffusion and flow-matching posterior sampling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03503)
*Liam Moroy,Jean-François Giovannelli,Yoann Altmann,Steve McLaughlin,Frédéric Champagnat,Guillaume Bourmaud*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces an offline strategy for automatically tuning guidance weights in training-free posterior sampling methods (Plug-and-Play) that use pretrained diffusion or flow-matching models for inverse problems. The key insight is that the conditional denoising/flow-matching objective is a least-squares problem, allowing optimization of time-dependent guidance weights via 2D linear least-squares without retraining the model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing Plug-and-Play methods rely on heuristic guidance weights to balance prior information from unconditional score/velocity networks with measurement consistency, but tuning these weights is not well-discussed and relies on heuristics. There is a need for a principled, automatic approach to tune these weights.

Method: The authors observe that the conditional denoising score-matching objective (diffusion) or conditional flow-matching objective (flow-matching) is a least-squares objective. By expressing the conditional prediction as a weighted sum of the unconditional network output and a measurement-guidance term, optimizing the weights reduces to a 2D linear least-squares problem. This allows computing time-dependent guidance weights offline for a given measurement operator, noise level, and sampler using a single minibatch of sampling trajectories, without retraining.

Result: The approach improves posterior sampling and achieves state-of-the-art reconstruction performance across diffusion- and flow-matching-based methods. Additionally, the optimized guidance weights enable reducing sampling steps from 1000 to 50 without significant degradation in reconstruction quality.

Conclusion: The proposed method provides a simple and principled offline strategy for automatically tuning guidance weights in training-free posterior sampling, achieving better reconstruction quality and enabling much faster sampling with fewer steps.

Abstract: Training-free posterior sampling methods, also known as Plug-and-Play methods, leverage pretrained unconditional diffusion or flow-matching models to solve inverse problems. Most existing approaches rely on guidance weights to balance, at each time step, prior information from the unconditional score or velocity network with measurement consistency, yet the tuning of these weights is often not discussed and is largely left to heuristics. We introduce a simple and principled offline strategy for automatically tuning these guidance weights. Our key observation is that, at each time step, the conditional denoising score-matching objective for diffusion models, or the conditional flow-matching objective for flow-matching models, is a least-squares objective. Therefore, when the conditional prediction is expressed as a weighted sum of the unconditional network output and a measurement-guidance term, optimizing over these weights reduces to a two-dimensional linear least-squares problem. The resulting time-dependent guidance weights can be optimized offline for a given measurement operator, noise level and sampler at the cost of a single minibatch of sampling trajectories, without retraining or fine-tuning the pretrained generative model. Instantiated with the standard Tweedie-based measurement-consistency term, our approach improves posterior sampling and achieves state-of-the-art reconstruction performance across diffusion- and flow-matching-based methods. Moreover, the optimized guidance weights enable diffusion samplers to reduce the number of sampling steps from 1000 to 50 with no significant degradation in reconstruction quality. Code will be made available.

</details>


### [435] [An Automated and Reproducible Workflow for Crack Identification and Damage Assessment of Fusion Materials](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03505)
*Rinkle Juneja,Viktor Reshniak,Richard K. Archibald,John W. Duggan,Gregory R. Watson,Cory D. Hauck,Gary M. Staebler*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A reproducible Galaxy-based workflow for automated crack identification and quantitative damage assessment from scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images of fusion materials, designed to operate without image-specific parameter tuning across different tungsten grades, microstructures, magnifications, and damage states.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Manual analysis of post-exposure microscopy does not scale to the volume, heterogeneity, and multiresolution character of modern fusion-materials campaigns, necessitating automated approaches for crack identification and damage quantification.

Method: Implemented in the Galaxy scientific workflow environment, the workflow processes SEM images and experimental metadata to identify cracks, quantify damage, and retain intermediate products and processing history for reproducibility. Outputs include crack masks, skeletonized crack networks, quality-control visualizations, and scalar damage descriptors. A crack-density descriptor is defined for downstream machine-learning prediction and physics-based crack simulation.

Result: Demonstrated on a sparse electron-beam thermal-shock dataset containing 418 images from 114 experiments spanning five tungsten grades and three microstructural states. The workflow operates without image-specific parameter tuning across all conditions.

Conclusion: The principal contribution is an end-to-end, shareable, and computationally portable workflow that links experimental characterization, automated image analysis, preliminary damage prediction, and simulation-guided data acquisition for fusion-materials research, with extensible modules for predictive components.

Abstract: Post-exposure microscopy is central to qualification of fusion materials.
