However, manual analysis does not scale to the volume, heterogeneity, and multiresolution character of modern fusion-materials campaigns. To address this challenge, we present a reproducible workflow, implemented in the Galaxy scientific workflow environment, for automated crack identification and quantitative damage assessment from scanning electron microscopy images. The workflow processes SEM images and experimental metadata to identify cracks, quantify damage, and retain the intermediate products and processing history needed for reproducibility. Outputs include crack masks, skeletonized crack networks, quality-control visualizations, and scalar damage descriptors. The method is designed to operate without image-specific parameter tuning across tungsten grades, microstructures, magnifications, and damage states. We demonstrate the workflow on a sparse electron-beam thermal-shock dataset containing 418 images from 114 experiments spanning five tungsten grades and three microstructural states. We define a crack-density descriptor, which provides standardized inputs for downstream machine-learning prediction and physics-based crack simulation. These predictive components are exposed in the same Galaxy environment and are intentionally treated here as extensible workflow modules. The principal contribution is therefore an end-to-end, shareable, and computationally portable workflow that links experimental characterization, automated image analysis, preliminary damage prediction, and simulation-guided data acquisition for fusion-materials research.

</details>


### [436] [Beyond Trained Models: Compiling GNNs for a Sound Explainer Benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03526)
*Steve Azzolin,Francesco Paolo Nerini,Stefano Teso,Francesco Bonchi,Bruno Lepri,André Panisson,Andrea Passerini*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces Gracr, a compiler that translates graded modal logic formulas into GNN weights, and GracrBench, a benchmark for rigorously evaluating GNN explainers against exact ground truth. The authors show that current plausibility-based evaluation is flawed because GNNs often rely on confounders (e.g., degree statistics) rather than intended motifs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current GNN explainers are evaluated by plausibility—how well explanations recover predefined ground truths like motifs. However, this assumes GNNs actually rely on these intended features. Prior work questioned this assumption, and the authors demonstrate it is violated on widely used benchmarks where trivial features (e.g., degree statistics) suffice for the task.

Method: The authors introduce Gracr, the first compiler that translates graded modal logic formulas into GNN weights, creating models that provably replicate formula behavior. Using this, they create GracrBench—a benchmark of compiled GNNs with known ground truth explanations that can be computed exactly. They evaluate 11 explainers across 6 tasks on this benchmark.

Result: Experiments reveal that most explainers are not robust to indirect influences or alternative implementations of the same formula. The benchmark enables fine-grained diagnostic evaluation that exposed limitations not visible under traditional plausibility-based evaluation.

Conclusion: GracrBench provides a novel, rigorous evaluation setting for graph post-hoc explainability. The work demonstrates the need for exact ground truth in explainability benchmarking and reveals significant weaknesses in current GNN explainers when evaluated against proper ground truth.

Abstract: Explainers for Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are commonly evaluated by their plausibility, i.e., how well their explanations recover a predefined ground truth, such as a motif planted in the data. This protocol implicitly assumes that a GNN trained on such data relies on the intended motif. Although prior work has questioned this assumption, plausibility remains widespread. First, we show that the assumption is violated on several widely used benchmarks, where, e.g., degree statistics alone suffice to solve the task. Then, we remove this confounder by replacing training with compilation. We achieve this by introducing $\mathsf{Gracr}$, the first compiler translating graded modal logic formulas into GNN weights, yielding models that replicate the behaviour of the corresponding formulas. Since the behaviour of the model is now known by construction, we can define its ground truth explanation formally and compute it exactly. Building on this, we introduce $\mathsf{Gracr}\mathsf{Bench}$, a benchmark of compiled GNNs for the evaluation of explainers against this exact ground truth. Experiments on eleven explainers across six tasks show its effectiveness for fine-grained diagnostic evaluation: notably, we discover that most explainers are not robust to indirect influences or alternative implementations of the same formula. These results position $\mathsf{Gracr}\mathsf{Bench}$ as a novel, rigorous evaluation setting for graph post-hoc explainability.

</details>


### [437] [Divergence controls entropy in distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03529)
*Nicolas Zucchet,Scott W. Linderman*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper studies how entropy of student models depends on the divergence measure used in knowledge distillation. The key finding is that forward KL inflates student entropy above the teacher, while reverse KL deflates entropy until the gap becomes too large. This has implications for choosing divergence hyperparameters in distillation, particularly in self-distillation scenarios.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Distillation is a core technique in LLM training but its properties are not well understood. The authors take an entropic perspective to understand how different divergence measures (forward KL, reverse KL, etc.) affect the student model's entropy during training.

Method: Theoretical analysis of how entropy depends on the divergence defining the distillation objective, combined with empirical verification in pretraining and supervised finetuning settings.

Result: Forward KL inflates student entropy above the teacher (and cross-entropy is a special case of this). Reverse KL deflates entropy until the gap between student and teacher becomes too large. Interpolating between divergences shows smooth entropy changes early in training but abrupt changes at convergence. Token-level reverse KL, not on-policy sampling, causes lower entropy in on-policy distillation. The divergence acts as an implicit entropy regularizer.

Conclusion: The divergence measure acts as an implicit entropy regularizer. This is clearest in self-distillation: since conditioning on privileged information deflates entropy, the best divergence hyperparameters are those that compensate for this entropy reduction.

Abstract: Distillation has become a core primitive of large language model training, but its properties are not yet well understood. We take an entropic perspective, studying how the entropy of the student depends on the data and the divergence that define the distillation objective. We prove that forward KL inflates the entropy of the student above that of the teacher. Since cross-entropy training is a special case, this yields an identity that we verify quantitatively in pretraining and supervised finetuning. Other divergences come with no such guarantee: reverse KL deflates entropy until the gap between student and teacher gets too large, and interpolating between the two changes entropy smoothly early in training but abruptly at convergence. The lower entropy of on-policy distillation comes from token-level reverse KL, not from on-policy sampling. The divergence therefore acts as an implicit entropy regularizer, whose role is clearest in self-distillation: as conditioning on privileged information deflates entropy, the divergence hyperparameters that work best are those that compensate for it.

</details>


### [438] [ZeroMAG: Zero-Shot Multimodal Adapter Generation for Plug-and-Play EEG Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03546)
*Yubo Wang,Jingying Ma,Xinliang Zhou,Yangxuan Zhou,Jiquan Wang,Sha Zhao,Yiyuan Yang,Yi Ding,Ziyu Jia,Chenyu Liu,Cuntai Guan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ZeroMAG is a zero-shot framework that extends pretrained EEG foundation models to handle multimodal recordings (EEG + companion physiological signals) without requiring labels or target-side optimization. It generates adapter weights in a function-constrained latent space learned from source adapters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: EEG foundation models capture reusable knowledge from large-scale EEG data, but real-world EEG recordings often include companion physiological signals that provide complementary information. The challenge is extending EFMs to heterogeneous multimodal recordings while preserving pretrained knowledge, without requiring labels or target-side optimization.

Method: ZeroMAG introduces a configuration-invariant adapter that organizes companion modalities around it. It constructs a modality-subject-task condition from unlabeled recordings and task context, then generates adapter weights in a function-constrained latent space learned from source adapters. The target datasets are completely held out from training and selection.

Result: Across six held-out target datasets and three EFM backbones, ZeroMAG improves balanced accuracy by 7.22 percentage points over EEG-only inference and 4.89 points over direct weight regression, while coming within 0.50 points of supervised multimodal adaptation on average. Ablations show both representation learning and conditional generation components contribute to performance.

Conclusion: ZeroMAG effectively bridges the gap between EEG-only foundation models and multimodal recordings in a zero-shot manner, achieving near-supervised performance without requiring any target labels or optimization. The framework demonstrates the value of functional supervision in both representation learning and conditional generation components.

Abstract: EEG foundation models (EFMs) capture reusable knowledge from large-scale EEG data, while many EEG recordings also include companion physiological signals that provide complementary information beyond the EEG-only interface. The challenge is to preserve this pretrained knowledge while extending the EFM to heterogeneous multimodal recordings through an adaptation inferred from unlabeled target data. We introduce ZeroMAG, a zero-shot multimodal adapter generation framework that extends a frozen EEG encoder and prediction head using unlabeled target recordings, without target labels or target-side optimization. The target datasets are held out from all model training and selection in the ZeroMAG pipeline. ZeroMAG organizes companion modalities around a configuration-invariant adapter, constructs a modality-subject-task condition from unlabeled recordings and task context, and generates adapter weights in a function-constrained latent space learned from source adapters. Across six held-out target datasets and three EFM backbones, ZeroMAG improves balanced accuracy by 7.22 percentage points over EEG-only inference and 4.89 points over direct weight regression, while coming within 0.50 points of supervised multimodal adaptation on average. Ablations further show that removing functional supervision from either representation learning or conditional generation degrades generated-adapter performance, confirming the contribution of both components.

</details>


### [439] [Objects Without Morphisms: What LLMs for Mathematics Do Not Represent](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03551)
*Yanli Wang,Suijin Wang,Xiaopeng Yuan,Haohan Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether large language models (LLMs) can perform faithful translations between mathematical subfields, where fidelity requires recovering implicit levels of generality from the theoretical relations between fields. The authors find an asymmetry: translating toward more general framing widens domain of quantification in 60.6% of rewrites, while translating toward concrete framing narrows it in 28.3%, with the hypothesis that would prevent this error stated in only 21.6% of model rewrites vs 4.2% of human statements.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors investigate whether LLMs can perform faithful translations between mathematical subfields when no external criterion exists to validate the output. They focus on a fundamental question: when translating statements between neighboring subfields, fidelity depends on recovering the implicit level of generality from the vocabulary, which the source leaves implicit.

Method: The authors introduced an instrument that separates truth, content, and scope into distinct blind queues, with a judge-free measure of whether a rewrite states the hypothesis implicit in its source. They tested this across seven models from four families, using a planted-positive control to establish sensitivity. They also tested on a held-out half of the benchmark and on statements written by mathematicians, and experimented with instructing models to state every required hypothesis.

Result: When translating toward general framing, the domain of quantification widened in 60.6% of rewrites and narrowed in none. When translating toward concrete framing, it narrowed in 28.3% and widened in 0.3%. The hypothesis preventing this error was stated in 21.6% of model rewrites and 4.2% of human statements. This asymmetry appeared in every model tested, with the most capable model widening least. The results replicated on the held-out benchmark half and on mathematician-written statements. Instructing models to state every hypothesis raised the rate but not sensitivity to direction.

Conclusion: The authors conclude that LLMs have acquired an object-level correspondence between subfield vocabularies without the constraint under which translation between theories carries hypotheses to hypotheses. This means models can map vocabularies across subfields but fail to preserve the implicit generality assumptions that should be transferred during translation.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have reached expert-level performance on competition mathematics largely through the volume of search placed around them: candidate solutions are sampled in quantity and retained only when an external criterion accepts them. Such a procedure improves the outcome that survives it while leaving untouched what the model represents. We examine that question where no external criterion exists: translating statements between the dialects of neighbouring subfields, where fidelity turns on the level of generality at which content is asserted. The source leaves that level implicit in its vocabulary, so a faithful translation must recover it from the relation between the theories. We introduce an instrument that codes truth, content and scope in separate blind queues, with a judge-free measure of whether a rewrite states the hypothesis implicit in its source, and establish its sensitivity with a planted-positive control. Across seven models from four families, translating towards the general framing widens the domain of quantification in 60.6% of rewrites and narrows it in none; translating towards the concrete framing narrows it in 28.3% and widens it in 0.3%. The hypothesis that would prevent it is stated in 21.6% of model rewrites and 4.2% of human statements. Capability does not govern the asymmetry: it appears in every model tested, and the most capable widens least. It replicates on the half of the benchmark held out by a pre-registered rule, and on statements written by mathematicians. Instructing a model to state every hypothesis it requires raises that rate but not its sensitivity to direction. We argue that these systems have acquired an object-level correspondence between subfield vocabularies without the constraint under which a translation between theories carries hypotheses to hypotheses.

</details>


### [440] [Get a GRIP, this will be a long TRIP: A Quantifiable Long-Range Framework for Verifying Over-squashing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03556)
*Ferran Hernandez Caralt,Simon Heilig,Adrián Bazaga,Asja Fischer,Moshe Eliasof,Pietro Liò*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses the lack of principled benchmarks for testing long-range interactions (k-hop) in Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). The authors introduce four axioms (Predictability, Tightness, Strictly k-Range, Topology-Invariance) that any long-range benchmark must satisfy, and propose TRIP/GRIP - constructive procedures that generate provably long-ranged tasks from any graph. They also provide a Maximum-Likelihood oracle for per-range error bounds and audit existing benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The Long Range Graph Benchmark (LRGB) has been saturated by short-range models, and existing synthetic alternatives are tied to specific topologies. There is no precise characterization of what makes a benchmark genuinely test long-range interactions, leading to unreliable empirical claims about over-squashing in GNNs.

Method: The authors introduce four verifiable axioms that any k-hop interaction benchmark must satisfy. Based on these axioms, they propose TRIP (Truly Ranged Interactions Problem) and GRIP (Generally Ranged Interactions Problem) - constructive procedures that transform any graph into a provably long-ranged task by drawing features from stable distributions. GRIP admits a closed-form, per-range Maximum-Likelihood oracle.

Result: The authors: (i) audited 4 common long-range benchmarks and identified their failure modes with respect to the four axioms; (ii) found that curvature is uncorrelated with GNN performance on TRIP-instantiated topologies, supporting the topological-vs-computational bottleneck distinction; (iii) showed that a novel benchmark's over-squashing measures factors beyond pure long-rangedness.

Conclusion: The framework provides the first principled certificate of long-rangedness on arbitrary graphs, with provable guarantees and a priori error bounds. It enables rigorous evaluation of GNN architectures for long-range tasks and exposes failure modes in existing benchmarks.

Abstract: Empirical claims about the connection between over-squashing and long-range interactions in GNNs, can only be trusted if the benchmarks used to validate them genuinely require long-range interactions. The de-facto standard, the Long Range Graph Benchmark, has been repeatedly shown to be saturated by tuned short-range models, with existing synthetic alternatives being tied to specific topologies. As such, there is a lack of principled certificate of long-rangedness on arbitrary graphs. This state reflects the absence of a precise characterization of long-ranged benchmarks. We address this fundamental gap by introducing four verifiable axioms: Predictability, Tightness, Strictly $k$-Range, and Topology-Invariance, that any task claiming to test $k$-hop interactions must satisfy. We formally prove that violating any one of them admits failure modes that undermine conclusions drawn from the task. Based on these axioms, we introduce TRIP (Truly Ranged Interactions Problem) and its generalisation GRIP (Generally Ranged Interactions Problem), constructive procedures that turn any graph into a provably long-ranged task by drawing features from stable distributions. Moreover, by construction, GRIP admits a closed-form, per-range Maximum-Likelihood oracle that yields the first a priori per-range lower bound on test error available on any benchmark. Using our framework, we: (i) audit 4 common long-range benchmarks and identify their failures modes with respect to our axioms; (ii) on TRIP-instantiated topologies, we find a popular notion of curvature is uncorrelated with GNN performance, supporting topological-vs-computational bottleneck distinction; and (iii) we show that a novel benchmark's over-squashing measures factors beyond pure long-rangedness. Code to use the framework and reproduce experiments is released https://github.com/ferranhernandezc/graph-grip.

</details>


### [441] [Cephalonauts One: A deep fMRI dataset for decoding naturalistic speech in the human brain](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03558)
*Antoine Collas,Louis Jalouzot,Géraud Ilinca,Corentin Caris,Romain Valabrègue,Ahmed Hassayoune,David Goncalves,Madeleine Hueber,Thaddée Delebarre,Julien Savatovsky,Clara Fonteneau,Charles Maussion,Bertrand Thirion,Alexis Thual*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Cephalonauts One is the deepest available fMRI dataset using naturalistic speech stimuli, containing 30 hours of 3T fMRI data per subject (3 subjects) recorded while listening to native-language podcasts. The dataset includes brain activity paired with audio, transcripts, and embeddings, along with a brain decoding benchmark for audio segment retrieval.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The field lacks sufficiently deep fMRI datasets using naturalistic speech stimuli (real-world listening conditions) to advance brain decoding and neural understanding of speech processing.

Method: Three healthy subjects underwent multiple fMRI scanning sessions, each with five 15-minute runs while listening to podcasts in their native language. The dataset provides time-aligned audio, transcripts, and stimulus embeddings.

Result: A 30-hour-per-subject fMRI dataset (90 hours total) is presented, along with a standardized audio segment retrieval benchmark. Baseline decoders and evaluation metrics are provided. Scaling analysis demonstrates continuous improvement in decoding performance with increased training data per subject.

Conclusion: This dataset represents the deepest available fMRI resource for naturalistic speech research, and the proposed benchmark enables standardized evaluation of brain decoding methods. The scaling analysis suggests that increased training data directly enhances decoding accuracy.

Abstract: Cephalonauts One is a whole-brain 3 Tesla (3T) functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) dataset recorded while subjects listened to audio podcasts. Three healthy subjects underwent multiple scanning sessions, each consisting of five 15-minute runs, while listening to podcasts in their native language. With 30 hours of fMRI data per subject, the current release is the deepest available fMRI dataset using naturalistic speech stimuli. The dataset pairs brain activity with the corresponding podcast audio, transcript annotations, and derived stimulus embeddings. Furthermore, we introduce a brain decoding benchmark formulated as audio segment retrieval: given fMRI activity from a held-out session, the decoder must identify the corresponding time-aligned podcast audio segment among candidate segments. We provide standardized splits, evaluation metrics, and baseline decoders for this task. Finally, a scaling analysis shows that decoding performance improves continuously with the amount of training data per subject.

</details>


### [442] [A Path Integral Surrogate for Multi-Step Gradient Inversion in Federated Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03597)
*Agnivo Ghosh,Saumik Bhattacharya*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: PI-SME is a novel gradient inversion attack that treats federated learning updates as path integrals, using Gauss-Legendre quadrature over Bézier path nodes to reconstruct private input images more faithfully than prior surrogate-based methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Gradient inversion attacks threaten federated learning privacy by reconstructing client data from shared model updates. Existing attacks model the update as a single gradient point along a trajectory, but this fails to capture the accumulated effect of multiple local training steps (FedAvg). The motivation is to develop a more accurate reconstruction by treating the update as a path integral rather than a point evaluation.

Method: The paper proposes Path-Integral Surrogate Model Extension (PI-SME), which approximates the accumulated update as a path integral of the gradient field. It uses Gauss-Legendre quadrature over several nodes along a learnable Bézier path to capture the trajectory between the initial and final model weights, rather than just reading the gradient at a single point.

Result: PI-SME reconstructs private input images more faithfully than the strongest surrogate baseline on CIFAR-100 and FEMNIST datasets, across various trajectory lengths and class-restricted batches. This is measured using several inversion metrics and matching loss.

Conclusion: Treating federated learning updates as path integrals rather than point evaluations significantly improves gradient inversion attacks, demonstrating that the multi-step nature of FedAvg updates creates exploitable vulnerabilities that prior methods overlooked.

Abstract: Federated learning lets many clients train a shared model together without ever sending their private data to a central server. Each client shares only a model update, and this update should reveal far less about the client than its raw training examples would. This premise is what protects the privacy of the clients. Gradient inversion attacks challenge it directly by trying to reconstruct a client's private input images from the single update it shared. Under FedAvg, a client's update accumulates several local training steps, so the server sees only the two endpoints of a hidden weight trajectory. Recent gradient inversion attacks fit a surrogate model along the path between these two endpoints but they still read its gradient at a single point. We propose the Path-Integral Surrogate Model Extension (PI-SME) which treats the accumulated update as a path integral of the gradient field and approximates it by Gauss--Legendre quadrature over several nodes along a learnable Bézier path. On CIFAR-100 and FEMNIST images across a range of trajectory lengths and class-restricted batches PI-SME reconstructs the private inputs more faithfully than the strongest surrogate baseline on several inversion metrics and the matching loss.

</details>


### [443] [Mastering Atari 2600 Games with Discovered Options](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03604)
*Erik M. Lintunen,Marlos C. Machado*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Wayfarer is a deep RL agent that discovers temporal abstractions (options) through Laplacian representation learning, achieving state-of-the-art performance on challenging Atari games by improving exploration, credit assignment, and generalization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current option discovery methods are limited to simple domains, depend on handcrafted representations, or offer little improvement over learning without options. There is a need for general option discovery methods that work in large-scale, high-dimensional domains.

Method: Wayfarer uses Laplacian representation learning to discover options from high-dimensional observations in a domain-agnostic, online manner. The discovered options are then leveraged for control.

Result: Wayfarer achieves state-of-the-art performance among single-stream agents on the most challenging Atari 2600 games, with the largest gains in games requiring long-horizon exploration and strategic behavior (Montezuma's Revenge and Private Eye).

Conclusion: The proposed Laplacian-based option discovery approach enables options to simultaneously improve exploration, accelerate credit assignment, and generalize effectively to unseen settings, leading to substantially faster learning of complex policies.

Abstract: Temporal abstractions, often instantiated as options, have long been regarded as a mechanism for accelerating credit assignment, facilitating exploration, and enabling generalisation in reinforcement learning (RL). However, developing general option discovery methods that are effective in large-scale, high-dimensional domains remains a fundamental challenge. Existing option discovery methods are either confined to relatively simple domains, depend on handcrafted or quasi-symbolic representations, or offer little improvement over learning without options. We present Wayfarer, a general, domain-agnostic, online deep RL agent that discovers options through Laplacian representation learning from high-dimensional observations and leverages them for control. We show that the resulting options simultaneously improve exploration, accelerate credit assignment, and generalise effectively to unseen settings, enabling substantially faster learning of complex policies. Wayfarer achieves state-of-the-art performance among single-stream agents on the most challenging Atari 2600 games, with the largest gains in games that require long-horizon exploration and strategic behaviour, such as Montezuma's Revenge and Private Eye.

</details>


### [444] [UniIntervene++: An Adaptive Intervention Agent for Efficient Real-World Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03620)
*Yudong Lin,Haoyuan Deng,Zhuoxuan Yuan,Zaijia Yang,Yuanjiang Xue,Ziwei Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: UniIntervene++ is an adaptive intervention agent for online reinforcement learning that learns to dynamically allocate control between autonomous robot execution and human assistance. It addresses the mismatch problem in existing intervention strategies that fail to adapt to the evolving competence of RL policies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The core problem is that robot policies require changing levels of assistance as their competence evolves during online RL. Existing intervention strategies based on offline estimates or fixed decision rules become mismatched to the current policy capability, leading to inefficient human-robot interaction.

Method: The approach has three main components: (1) Unified semi-Markov decision process formulation that models the evolving RL policy, trajectory correction, and task-structured CodePolicy as Options, learning their relative values online; (2) Competence-adaptive intervention that periodically probes the RL policy through unassisted execution to keep control allocation responsive to evolving capability; (3) Coupled experience learning that allows assisted behaviors to improve the RL policy, whose outcomes then reshape future intervention decisions.

Result: Across five real-world manipulation tasks, UniIntervene++ achieves an average success rate of 89.67%, outperforming all baselines by at least 6 percentage points. It reduces human intervention to 0.77%, representing a relative reduction of at least 94.6% from the best baseline.

Conclusion: UniIntervene++ successfully jointly determines when to intervene, how to intervene, and when to return control as the RL policy improves. The method demonstrates that adaptive intervention can significantly improve both task success and efficiency of human-robot interaction in real-world online RL scenarios.

Abstract: Online reinforcement learning (RL) enables robot policies to improve through physical interaction, but the assistance they require changes as their competence evolves. Existing intervention strategies based on offline estimates or fixed decision rules can therefore become mismatched to the current policy. To address this, we propose UniIntervene++, an adaptive intervention agent that learns to allocate control between autonomous execution and heterogeneous assisted behaviors during online RL. Specifically, UniIntervene++ first formulates the evolving RL policy, trajectory correction, and a task-structured CodePolicy as Options in a unified semi-Markov decision process and learns their relative values online. Building on this, competence-adaptive intervention periodically probes the RL policy through unassisted execution, keeping control allocation responsive to its evolving capability. Finally, coupled experience learning allows assisted behaviors to improve the RL policy, whose evolving outcomes in turn reshape future intervention decisions. In this way, UniIntervene++ jointly determines when to intervene, how to intervene, and when to return control as the RL policy improves. Across five real-world manipulation tasks, UniIntervene++ achieves an average success rate of 89.67%, outperforming all baselines by at least 6 percentage points, while reducing human intervention to 0.77%, a relative reduction of at least 94.6% from the best baseline. Code is available in our \href{https://github.com/dannyyudong/An-Adaptive-Intervention-Agent-for-Efficient-Real-World-Reinforcement-Learning}{GitHub repository}.

</details>


### [445] [Broken scale symmetries in undercomplete linear autoencoders](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03640)
*Farhad Pashakhanloo,Jacob A. Zavatone-Veth*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper investigates how SGD breaks scale symmetry in undercomplete linear autoencoders, finding that SGD favors large decoder weights via directed scale drift, which continues until hitting a stability boundary, resulting in sharper solutions compared to balanced baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Previous work showed SGD breaks scale symmetry in homogeneous networks to balance gradient noise or minimize fluctuations. This paper seeks to understand what happens in undercomplete linear autoencoders - whether a preferred sign for scale drift is selected and what the consequences are.

Method: The authors analyzed the PCA solution manifold and derived an analytically-tractable effective description of the scale drift dynamics. They studied the dynamics on a slow timescale and examined the stability boundary that emerges when scale increases.

Result: SGD favors large decoder weights on the PCA solution manifold. This directed scale drift occurs slowly but continuously. Eventually, increasing scale drives the dynamics to a finite-stepsize stability boundary. The resulting solutions are sharper (higher max Hessian eigenvalue) than balanced baselines, though different sharpness measures can move in opposing directions.

Conclusion: Undercomplete linear autoencoders provide a concrete illustration of how loss geometry can convert residual gradient noise into directed motion along a manifold of functionally-equivalent solutions. This demonstrates a mechanism by which SGD breaks symmetries in ways that have functional consequences for the learned solution.

Abstract: Neural network loss landscapes have many symmetries, which are preserved by gradient flow but broken by finite-stepsize stochastic gradient descent (SGD). A canonical example of such a symmetry is scale in homogeneous networks: one can scale up the parameters in one layer and down in the next without changing the network output. Previous work has documented cases in which SGD breaks this symmetry in favor of balancing gradient noise or minimizing fluctuations. Here, we show that the solution geometry of undercomplete linear autoencoders instead selects a preferred sign for scale drift: on the PCA solution manifold, SGD favors large decoder weights. This directed scale drift occurs on a slow timescale, and its dynamics admit an analytically-tractable effective description. However, it cannot continue indefinitely: increasing scale eventually drives the dynamics towards a finite-stepsize stability boundary. The resulting solutions are sharper than a balanced baseline in the sense of the maximum eigenvalue of the loss Hessian, but different sharpness measures can move in opposing directions. Thus, undercomplete autoencoders give a concrete illustration of how loss geometry can convert residual gradient noise into directed motion along a manifold of functionally-equivalent solutions.

</details>


### [446] [IDRF: Inverse-Distilled Reward Fine-tuning of Masked Discrete Diffusion Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03641)
*Vladislav Gromadskii,David Li,Samson Gourevitch,Yazid Janati,Eric Moulines,Maxim Panov,Alexander Korotin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: IDRF is a framework for reward fine-tuning of few-step masked discrete diffusion generators that replaces intractable sequence-level KL penalties with inverse-distillation regularization, achieving high reward with up to 32× fewer denoising steps while mitigating reward hacking and preserving sample quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Masked discrete diffusion models offer an alternative to autoregressive generation but face two key challenges: (1) costly iterative sampling due to many denoising steps, and (2) intractable sequence likelihoods that complicate reward fine-tuning.

Method: IDRF replaces the intractable sequence-level KL penalty with inverse-distillation regularization using an optimal auxiliary denoiser. The method proves that population inverse-distillation loss upper-bounds the sequence-level KL divergence to the reference distribution. It optimizes a trajectory-based surrogate without reference-model rollouts, keeping the student's few-step sampler. Generation is viewed as a finite-horizon MDP, and reward is optimized using a clipped policy-gradient objective over student trajectories.

Result: IDRF achieves high reward with up to 32× fewer denoising steps than the reference while mitigating reward hacking and preserving sample quality across DNA, image, and text generation domains.

Conclusion: IDRF provides an effective framework for reward fine-tuning of few-step masked discrete diffusion models, enabling efficient training without expensive reference-model rollouts while maintaining sample quality and reducing computational costs by an order of magnitude.

Abstract: Masked discrete diffusion models offer a promising alternative to autoregressive generation, but iterative sampling can be costly, and intractable sequence likelihoods complicate reward fine-tuning. We introduce IDRF, a framework for reward fine-tuning of few-step masked discrete diffusion generators. Starting from a standard reverse-KL-regularized objective, IDRF replaces the intractable sequence-level KL penalty with inverse-distillation regularization. With an optimal auxiliary denoiser, we prove that the population inverse-distillation loss upper-bounds the sequence-level KL divergence to the reference distribution. IDRF optimizes a trajectory-based surrogate of this loss without reference-model rollouts, so the student keeps its own few-step sampler. We view few-step generation as a finite-horizon Markov decision process and optimize reward with a clipped policy-gradient objective over the student's trajectories. Across DNA, image, and text generation, IDRF achieves high reward with up to $32\times$ fewer denoising steps than the reference while mitigating reward hacking and preserving sample quality.

</details>


### [447] [On the Convergence of Success Conditioning for Policy Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03642)
*Matthew Brun,Xu Andy Sun*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Success conditioning is a strategy that improves decision-making policies by increasing the probability of actions that lead to successful outcomes. This paper proves that this approach converges to optimal policies in certain MDPs and provides convergence rate bounds.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Success conditioning is widely used in reinforcement learning applications, but its theoretical properties (limiting behavior and convergence rates) were not well understood. This work addresses this gap by providing rigorous convergence guarantees.

Method: The authors prove convergence to optimal policies on a broad class of Markov decision processes (MDPs). They analyze two settings: (1) discounted MDPs and (2) single-period MDPs.

Result: For discounted MDPs: convergence to an ε-optimal policy within O(1/ε^p) iterations, where exponent p depends on problem data. For single-period MDPs: convergence to such a policy within O(log(1/ε)) iterations.

Conclusion: Success conditioning converges to optimal policies on a broad class of MDPs, with faster convergence for single-period MDPs (logarithmic) compared to general discounted MDPs (polynomial). The exponent p in the convergence rate depends on specific problem parameters.

Abstract: Success conditioning is a strategy for improving decision-making policies in stochastic environments; it updates a policy by increasing the probability of taking actions that yield successful outcomes. Success conditioning is common to many reinforcement learning applications, yet its limiting behavior and convergence rates are not well understood. In this work, we demonstrate that success conditioning converges to an optimal policy on a broad class of Markov decision processes (MDPs). We also derive convergence rates in some common settings. For discounted MDPs, we prove convergence within $\mathcal{O}(1/\varepsilon^p)$ iterations to an $\varepsilon$-optimal policy, where the exponent $p$ depends on problem data. For single-period MDPs, such a policy is obtained within $\mathcal{O}(\log(1/\varepsilon))$ iterations.

</details>


### [448] [When May a Bandit Leave Its Anchor? E-Process-Authorized Thompson Sampling under Non-stationarity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03646)
*Mayand Gulati,Kerong Wang,WeiChen Au*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces e-ATS (E-process-authorized Thompson Sampling), a novel multi-armed bandit algorithm that balances exploration-exploitation under non-stationary environments by using an anytime-valid e-process to control when to transition from optimistic Thompson sampling to a discounted history-based approach. The method provides theoretical guarantees on the probability of departing from OTS, with empirical results showing context-dependent performance on different benchmark suites.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The core problem is that in stationary environments, using full history benefits learning, but after an environment change, the same historical data can mislead the algorithm. The authors seek to determine when an agent should "forget" past experiences and adapt to potential changes, balancing between stability (maintaining optimistic exploration) and adaptation (responding to changes).

Method: e-ATS maintains two states for each arm: (1) a full-history Beta state, and (2) a discounted Beta state. An anytime-valid e-process first "authorizes" the discounted state, then a reversible relevance score controls its influence. Before authorization, e-ATS exactly follows optimistic Thompson sampling (OTS). Under a Beta-Bernoulli prior-predictive stationary model, the probability of ever departing from OTS is bounded by a chosen parameter α_E, without requiring fitted thresholds.

Result: Relative to e-ATS, removing authorization (i.e., always using the discounted state) produced divergent results: mean normalized dynamic pseudo-regret increased by 38.4% on the registered suite but decreased by 7.5% on the literature-derived replay suite. This demonstrates that the authorization mechanism's effectiveness is context-dependent.

Conclusion: The key insight is that evidence (via the e-process) controls when adaptation begins, but adaptation does not always improve performance. The method provides a principled way to detect when to switch from stable OTS behavior to adaptive discounting, with theoretical guarantees on departure probability. However, the mixed empirical results suggest the approach's utility depends on the specific environment characteristics, particularly the nature and frequency of non-stationarity.

Abstract: Stationarity rewards memory, but after a change the same history can mislead. We ask when forgetting should be permitted. E-process-authorized Thompson sampling (e-ATS) gives each arm full-history and discounted Beta states. An anytime-valid e-process first authorizes the discounted state, then a reversible relevance score controls its influence. Before authorization, e-ATS exactly follows optimistic Thompson sampling (OTS). Under a Beta-Bernoulli prior-predictive stationary model, e-ATS's probability of ever departing from OTS is at most the chosen $α_E$, without fitted thresholds. Relative to e-ATS, removing authorization increased mean normalized dynamic pseudo-regret by $38.4\%$ on the registered suite but reduced it by $7.5\%$ on the literature-derived replay suite. Therefore, evidence controls when adaptation begins, not whether it always helps.

</details>


### [449] [Forecasting from Counterfactual Simulator Rollouts: A Sim2Real Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03662)
*Angel Wang,Dominique Perrault-Joncas,Alvaro Maggiar,Dean Foster,Carson Eisenach*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses the cold-start problem in prediction models when deploying new decision policies, where historical data reflects earlier policies but new policy data is unavailable. The authors propose using simulation to generate counterfactual trajectories (Sim2Real transfer) and validate this approach on two real-world inventory-control deployments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: When deploying a new decision policy, prediction models face a cold-start problem because they lack target data that depends on the new policy's actions. Historical observations reflect earlier policies, while real observations under the new policy are not yet available. This creates a gap in training data for models that predict outcomes dependent on policy actions.

Method: The authors use simulation to roll out the target policy across counterfactual scenarios, generating training data to learn how the system responds to controls. They evaluate the Sim2Real transfer from three angles: (1) simulator fidelity, (2) zero-shot transfer to real behavior, and (3) adaptation as real target-policy observations accumulate. They test this on two real-world inventory-control deployments using the same model architecture trained on either simulator-generated data or historical real data, comparing mean absolute percentage error (MAPE).

Result: The simulator-trained forecaster achieves lower point-estimate MAPE than the same architecture trained on historical real data. Reductions were 1.2-3.1 percentage points in Study 1 and 12.5-18.7 percentage points in Study 2. After deployment, lightweight calibration using early real observations further reduces error by up to 2.5 percentage points.

Conclusion: Simulator-generated counterfactual data can support cold-start forecasting under a new policy. The resulting model can be further refined as real deployment data become available, providing empirical evidence for the viability of Sim2Real transfer in addressing cold-start problems in decision systems.

Abstract: Deploying a new decision policy creates a cold-start problem for prediction models whose targets depend on the policy's actions: historical observations reflect earlier policies, while real observations under the new policy are not yet available. Simulation offers a way to address this gap by rolling out the target policy across counterfactual scenarios and using the resulting trajectories to learn how the system responds to those controls. The simulation-to-reality (Sim2Real) transfer of this simulator-trained model can then be backtested by evaluating it against real observations from past deployments. Using two real-world inventory-control deployments, we evaluate this process from three angles: simulator fidelity, zero-shot transfer to real behavior, and adaptation as real target-policy observations accumulate. The simulator-trained forecaster achieves lower point-estimate mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) than the same architecture trained on historical real data, reducing MAPE by 1.2-3.1 percentage points in Study 1 and 12.5-18.7 points in Study 2. After deployment, lightweight calibration using early real observations further reduces error by up to 2.5 percentage points. These results provide empirical evidence that simulator-generated counterfactual data can support cold-start forecasting under a new policy, and the resulting model can be further refined as real deployment data become available.

</details>


### [450] [Pivot-SD: Efficient Self-Distillation for Masked Diffusion Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03665)
*Seo Hyun Kim,Sunwoo Hong,Younwoo Choi,Chen-Hao Chao,Se-Young Yun,Rahul G. Krishnan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Pivot-SD is an efficient offline self-distillation framework for masked diffusion language models that supervises only high-impact commitments (pivots) selected via information-gain metric, improving LLaDA-8B-Instruct over baselines with minimal data (200 questions, 4 rollouts).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Masked diffusion language models (dLMs) face a distinct credit-assignment challenge: a few commitments during denoising sharply reduce uncertainty over remaining masked positions and shape much of the response. Existing post-training recipes don't leverage this signal to select which tokens to train on - they typically train on final text or assign rewards to whole denoising steps rather than identifying individual commitments that shape the response.

Method: Pivot-SD selects pivots using an information-gain metric measuring uncertainty reduction over remaining masked positions. Pivots from successful trajectories are trained with cross-entropy loss, while pivots from failed trajectories are trained with targeted unlikelihood loss, leaving the rest of the failed trajectory untouched. The approach uses only 200 questions and four rollouts each.

Result: Pivot-SD improves LLaDA-8B-Instruct over full-sequence SFT and budget-matched diffusion RL baselines across math and code benchmarks.

Conclusion: The proposed Pivot-SD framework successfully addresses the credit-assignment problem in masked diffusion language models by focusing training on high-impact commitments (pivots), achieving superior performance with minimal data and computational resources compared to existing post-training approaches.

Abstract: Masked diffusion language models (dLMs) offer a promising parallel alternative to autoregressive models for complex reasoning. However, they face a distinct credit-assignment challenge, since a few commitments during denoising sharply reduce the uncertainty over the remaining masked positions and shape much of the response. Most post-training recipes for dLMs do not use this signal to decide which tokens to train on: they typically train on the final text or assign rewards to whole denoising steps, rather than selecting the individual commitments that shape the response. We introduce Pivot-SD, an efficient offline self-distillation framework that supervises only these high-impact commitments (pivots). Pivot-SD selects pivots using an information-gain metric measuring uncertainty reduction over the remaining masked positions. Pivots from successful trajectories are trained with cross-entropy, and pivots from failed trajectories with targeted unlikelihood, leaving the rest of the failed trajectory untouched. Using only 200 questions and four rollouts each, Pivot-SD improves LLaDA-8B-Instruct over full-sequence SFT and budget-matched diffusion RL baselines across math and code benchmarks.

</details>


### [451] [Planning to Learn](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03667)
*Ian Osband*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces "horizon loss" - a new loss function that bridges between cross-entropy and exact policy gradient for classification tasks. The key insight is that exact policy gradient is myopic (zero-horizon) while cross-entropy can be viewed as patient accuracy (infinite-horizon). The horizon loss truncates the total error at the learning remaining, outperforming both endpoints, especially under label noise.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors observe that while policy-gradient methods are central to modern RL and LLM post-training, they face challenges with exploration, credit assignment, and action-sampling noise. Classification has none of these issues - a classifier can be viewed as a policy where the expected reward is the probability of correct classification. However, surprisingly, exact policy gradient loses to cross-entropy even when optimizing for expected accuracy. This paradox motivates the investigation into why this happens and how to fix it.

Method: The authors conceptualize exact policy gradient as "zero-horizon" (only values immediate updates) and cross-entropy as "infinite-horizon" (patient accuracy - total error if log-odds rise at unit speed forever). They propose the horizon loss, which truncates this total at the learning remaining. This provides a continuum between the two extremes. The method is evaluated on MNIST and ImageNet (with ResNet-50, ResNet-101, and ViT-S/16) under various label noise conditions.

Result: The horizon loss improves top-1 accuracy over cross-entropy at flat learning rates on MNIST and ImageNet. The gain grows with label noise, suggesting the method is particularly beneficial when training data is imperfect. The simple allocation model provably escapes the trap that catches both cross-entropy and exact policy gradient endpoints.

Conclusion: The horizon loss offers a principled way to interpolate between exact policy gradient and cross-entropy, achieving better performance than both. This work suggests that the key to better classification training lies in properly accounting for the future impact of each update - neither the myopic exact gradient nor the infinitely patient cross-entropy is optimal. The method shows particular promise under label noise, which is common in real-world applications.

Abstract: Policy-gradient methods are central to modern reinforcement learning, including LLM post-training. When they struggle, the usual suspects are exploration, credit assignment and action-sampling noise. Classification has none of them. A classifier is a policy whose expected reward, its \emph{expected accuracy}, is the probability it assigns to the correct label, and because that label is known, the policy gradient is exact and smooth. Yet exact policy gradient loses to cross-entropy, even on expected accuracy. The exact gradient is myopic: it values an update only by what it buys now, but each update also sets where the next one starts, so an update's value depends on how much learning remains. Viewed this way, cross-entropy is patient accuracy, the total error an example would pay if its log-odds rose at unit speed forever, while exact policy gradient is the zero-horizon limit. Truncating this total at the learning that remains yields the horizon loss, a one-line change that moves from cross-entropy toward exact policy gradient as training runs out. In a simple allocation model, it provably escapes the trap that catches each endpoint. On MNIST and on ImageNet with ResNet-50, ResNet-101 and ViT-S/16, the horizon loss improves top-1 accuracy over cross-entropy at a flat learning rate, and the gain grows with label noise.

</details>


### [452] [Simulation-Free Learning of Population Dynamics with Wasserstein Lagrangian Residuals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03679)
*Fedor Sergeev,Markus Heinonen,Daniel Waxman,Tim Cooijmans,Ricardo Baptista,Dmitry Batenkov,Eli Bingham*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces Double-Stitch, a simulation-free method for learning Lagrangian mechanics in Wasserstein space to model dynamics of probability distributions. It addresses limitations of Wasserstein gradient flows (which cannot handle conservative or periodic dynamics) by deriving equations from a Clebsch variational principle.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Wasserstein gradient flows are commonly used to model dynamics of cells, organisms, and fluids as probability distributions, but they cannot describe conservative or periodic dynamics. Existing Lagrangian methods in Wasserstein space (WLM) require expensive simulation at every training step.

Method: Double-Stitch learns mechanics by penalizing the residual of the equation of motion along a learned population path, derived from a Clebsch variational principle that does not require gradient velocities. This is simulation-free, avoiding numerical solvers during training.

Result: Double-Stitch matches or outperforms gradient-flow methods and simulation-based WLM on synthetic, single-cell, and ocean vortex datasets, while training 4-14 times faster than WLM.

Conclusion: Double-Stitch provides an efficient approach to learn conservative and periodic dynamics in probability distributions without expensive simulations, with proven performance across multiple domains.

Abstract: The dynamics of cells, organisms, and fluids are often modeled as probability distributions evolving over time. Reconstructing and extrapolating this evolution from unpaired snapshots requires assumptions about the underlying process. Wasserstein gradient flows are a common choice, but they cannot describe conservative or periodic dynamics. Lagrangian mechanics in Wasserstein space covers both, but existing methods for learning it are simulation-based: they run a numerical solver at every training step, which makes training expensive. We propose Double-Stitch, a simulation-free method that learns these mechanics by penalizing the residual of the equation of motion along a learned population path. We derive this equation from a Clebsch variational principle that does not require gradient velocities, and show that the residual vanishes exactly when the equation holds. We test Double-Stitch on synthetic, single-cell and ocean vortex datasets and find that it matches or outperforms gradient-flow methods and simulation-based WLM on most tasks, while training $4$-$14$ times faster than WLM. We provide a JAX implementation of Double-Stitch at https://github.com/BasisResearch/stitching.

</details>


### [453] [LESSER: Post-Training Data Selection with Output-Layer Gradients](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03702)
*Lyuxin David Zhang,Eric Wong,Surbhi Goel,Anton Xue*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LESSER is a data selection method for LLM post-training that uses output-layer gradients (requiring only forward pass) instead of full gradients (requiring expensive backward pass), achieving 9.7x and 3.0x FLOP reduction for SFT and RL respectively while maintaining full-gradient selection performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Gradient-based data selection is effective but computationally expensive as it requires full-parameter gradients (backward pass) for every sample. This becomes intractable for large candidate pools, creating a need for a cheaper approximation.

Method: The key insight is that output-layer gradients alone suffice for effective data selection. Unlike full gradients requiring backward passes, output-layer gradients can be computed with just a forward pass, dramatically reducing computational cost. LESSER is implemented as a drop-in wrapper for existing selection methods.

Result: LESSER reduces feature-extraction FLOP cost by 9.7× for SFT and 3.0× for RL benchmarks. Empirically, even when output-layer and full gradients rank individual samples differently, they select batches with aligned gradients, maintaining downstream task performance.

Conclusion: Output-layer gradients can effectively approximate full-gradient features for data selection at a fraction of the computational cost, making gradient-based data selection practical for large-scale LLM post-training scenarios.

Abstract: The choice of post-training data for large language models substantially affects downstream performance. Gradient-based data selection is a popular approach that ranks training data by how well their gradients align with those of a small validation set. However, ranking with full-parameter gradients requires an expensive backward pass on every sample, making computation intractable for large candidate pools. This raises a natural question: can we approximate full-gradient features at a fraction of the cost? Conveniently, we find that output-layer gradients suffice for effective data selection, yet require only the cheaper forward pass. We implement this as LESSER, a drop-in wrapper for selection methods that reduces the feature-extraction FLOP cost by $9.7\times$ for SFT and $3.0\times$ for RL benchmarks, while tracking full-gradient performance on downstream tasks. Empirically, we find that even when output-layer and full gradients rank individual samples differently, they select batches with aligned gradients.

</details>


### [454] [RNADyn: A Benchmark for Generating and Understanding RNA Dynamics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03712)
*Yiming Huang,Lennart Bastian,Hanqun Cao,Luis Vollmers,Tolga Birdal*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RNADynBench is a standardized RNA molecular dynamics benchmark with 2585 quality-controlled trajectories, paired with RNADynNet - a unified model that simultaneously performs trajectory generation and dynamics representation learning from single conformers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RNA functions through conformational changes not captured by static structures, but large-scale standardized RNA dynamics data are limited. Existing approaches treat trajectory generation and dynamics understanding as separate objectives, lacking a unified framework.

Method: RNADynBench provides 2585 quality-controlled 100-ns all-atom MD trajectories with leakage-controlled splits. RNADynNet uses a shared backbone combining coordinate denoising, single-frame-to-trajectory alignment, and physical grounding to connect all-atom trajectory generation with dynamics representation learning from a single conformer.

Result: Generated trajectories achieve RMSF correlations of 0.875 and 0.766 across both test sets, including a high-flexibility challenge set. Single-conformer predictions show comparable agreement with MD-derived dynamics.

Conclusion: RNADynBench and RNADynNet establish both a benchmark dataset and a unified modeling framework for RNA dynamics generation and understanding, bridging the gap between trajectory generation and dynamics representation learning.

Abstract: Ribonucleic acid (RNA) functions through conformational changes that are not fully captured by static structures. However, large-scale standardized RNA dynamics data remain limited, and existing approaches typically treat trajectory generation and dynamics understanding as separate objectives. Here, we introduce RNADynBench, a standardized RNA molecular dynamics (MD) benchmark with 2585 quality-controlled 100-ns all-atom trajectories and leakage-controlled splits. Building on RNADynBench, we develop RNADynNet, a unified model for RNA dynamics learning that uses a shared backbone for both trajectory generation and dynamics fingerprint extraction from a single conformer. It combines coordinate denoising, single-frame-to-trajectory alignment, and physical grounding to connect all-atom trajectory generation with dynamics representation learning. Physical grounding improves both generated dynamics and the physical information recoverable from these fingerprints. Across both test sets, including the high-flexibility challenge set, the generated trajectories achieve RMSF correlations of 0.875 and 0.766, while single-conformer predictions show comparable agreement with MD-derived dynamics. RNADynBench and RNADynNet together establish a benchmark and unified modeling framework for generating and understanding RNA dynamics.

</details>
